1934-03-26.text: LONDON — (U.P.) — The foreign office tonight decided not to grant a visa to Mrs. Samuel Insull which would enable her to enter Britain. The foreign office had Mrs. Insull's application for a visa, transmitted through the consulate at Athens, under advisement for several days. Authoritative quarters declined to state the reasons for the refusal, except to say, “every government has the right to refuse entrance to any alien.”

| CHICAGO, March 26—(AP)—An insurance policy which would pay (for any loss on investments in the event Franklin D. Roosevelt “ceased to be President” during the year of the contract has been offered in the United States by the underwriters at Lloyd's, London. The Chicago agency of the Lloyd’s quoted the Roosevelt insurance today at $50 a $1,000. They said the rate was nearly as low as that of ordinary life insurance, indicating the London insurance men felt the hazard was small. Insurance men said this form of insurance was rarely offered on an American event, although not rare abroad. It was offered to members of the Chicago Board of Trade and to operators in the Chicago grain markets.

Associated Press Foreign Staff ROME, March 26.—More than 10,000,000 voters registered their approval of Premier Mussolini and his Fascist regime in Sunday’s elections. With all returns in, only 15,265 contrary votes were recorded in the balloting on the 400 government-selected candidates — headed by Il Duce—for the 29th Chamber of Deputies. Of 10,433,536 electors registered, 10,041,997 voted, a percentage of 96.25. Favorable votes totaled 10,025,513 and 1,219 were disqualified. The percentage of favorable votes of the total number cast was 99.8. There was no opposition list of candidates, but electors had the right to accept or reject the official selections. Many provinces showed no contrary votes—such as Avellino which cast 112,656 votes; Brindisi, 59,692, and Salerno with 127,304. The province of Forli, Mussolini's old bailiwick, cast only three contrary votes in 105,585. Official spo

SHANGHAI, March 26 — (®) — The death of C. C. Julian, who died in poverty, was coldly and officially recorded in a Shanghai public mortuary today. C. E. Vandeveer, an American who knew Julian in California a quarter of a century ago, identified the body. It was said there would be no official opinion as to the cause of death until a formal inquest Thursday. Physicians who worked over Julian after he had been found in an Astor House hotel room yesterday by the young woman who was his dinner companion, said that without doubt Julian took his own life. However, some of Julian’s close associates here insisted they believed he killed himself unintentionally. Girl Is Recovering Vandeveer, who lived in California when Julian was getting his start in the oil business in which he became a powerful figure in Oklahoma, now is the local representative for an American paint company. PARIS, Mar. 26.—(4)—War veterans, three million strong, stepped into France's troubled politics today with a program to modernize the government. The veterans’ national federation abandoned its traditional policy of neutrality yesterday and by the unanimous vote of its council decided to take an active part in the nation’s political life. As this powerful group rallied to the support of Premier Doumergue in his drive to restore calm, extremists battled in several cities, notably Tours and Toulon. Today, fearing new outbreaks, authorities took special precaution at Tours to maintain order. Gendarmes said shots were fired there yesterday in violent street fighting between rightist and leftist factions. The anti-fascist front at Tours called a demonstration for tonight as a counter-manifestation against one by the right organization, Solidarité Française. Three naval officers were among the

SHANGHAI, China, March 26.—Penniless and a fugitive from justice from the United States, C. C. Julian, one-time oil millionaire, who operated in California and Oklahoma, took poison in a fashionable hotel in Shanghai early yesterday and will be buried at the expense of his friends. Secretary Attempts Suicide His confidential secretary, Leonora Levy, attempted suicide taking the same portion of deadly drug as killed Julian, but she is still alive in a hospital. During a moment of consciousness, she told hospital attendants Julian had confided to her that he would kill himself. Opinion OF Doctors Doctors assert the former millionaire committed suicide. Despite their opinions and the statement of Miss Levy, however, some of his friends hold to the possibility that he accidentally took an overdose of sleeping pills following a sumptuous dinner late Saturday night.

Paris, March 25. — (#) — Sharp fighting flared in provincial France today as political extremists, ignoring the plea of Premier Gaston Doumergue to guard against “civil war,” battled each other. Fifty persons were injured in a clash at Toulon between Royalists and Socialists outside a meeting hall before police reinforcements could dispel the crowd. A score of others nursed bruises suffered in violent street battles between Rightist and Leftist followers at Tours, where gendarmes reported shots were fired. Row Due Precautions were taken at Tours to prevent further violence tomorrow night at a demonstration called by the anti-Fascist front in protest against a manifestation of the Rightist organization Solidarité Française, organized by the perfume manufacturer, François Coty. 1934-11-06.text: LOS ANGELES, Nov. 5 (P)—A trans-Pacific flight of more than 7,000 miles went into the flying records of the Australian airman, Sir Charles Kingsford-Smith today upon completion of an epoch-making flight from Brisbane, Australia, to California. Back-tracking the route he flew in 1928, the British knight of the air landed at the Oakland, Calif, municipal airport early yesterday, completing a 2,408 mile flight from Honolulu in 14 hours and 59 minutes. The airman set his blue and white monoplane, Lady Southern Cross, down on the field at 7:44 (Pacific standard time) and apologized to a small group of spectators for his “early arrival.” Sir Charles, the first to make an airplane flight from the Hawaiian islands to the United States, credited his navigator, Capt. P. G. Taylor, with making it possible for them to arrive nearly two hours ahead of schedule. After resting a few hours, the two flew

LONDON, Nov. 5.—(#)—Japan, it was learned authoritatively tonight, has prepared plans for construction of a large number of warships of an entirely new type, in case her demands for naval equality go unheeded in the current conversations and a naval race be started. Whether any official hint of such plans would be given to the powers during the conversations, as a trial balloon, could not be immediately determined. The plans, secretly prepared, embrace a new ship of economical build, but so powerful that some of the present categories provided for the fleets of the world by the Washington and London treaties might be made useless in comparison, it was said. The ship in question apparently was similar to an advance model pocket battleship. It was understood it would be built only in the event no new treaty (Continued on Page ?. Col. 8)

Tokyo, Nov. 5—Japan disclaimed all responsibility for the Manchukuo oil controversy today and advised protesting American and British oil interests to enter into direct negotiations with the Manchukuo government. This Japanese attitude was disclosed in notes handed to the American and British embassies today by the foreign ministry. It was understood the notes state the Japanese government is in no wise concerned over Manchukuo’s oil measures. The Japanese government was informed by the Manchukuo government, however, that neither Manchukuo oil laws nor articles of incorporation for the Manchuria Oil Company provided for discrimination against any nationality. The notes assert Manchukuo’s contemplated oil measure does not violate the principle of the open door since it does not discriminate in favor of the Japanese or any other nationality. This would automatically bring the question into naval discussions. Officials displayed great interest in the mandate situation in Geneva, where the Japanese diplomat was questioned concerning the reports of the construction of naval bases on former

LONDON, Nov. 6.—(P)—Sir Oswald Mosley, leader of the British Fascists, today won his libel suit against the Evening Star, which he claimed has presented his political program in a false and violent light. A jury in the king's bench division awarded Sir Oswald a verdict of £5000 (£26,000) damages and ordered the defendant to pay the costs of the trial.

PARIS, (AP).—The radical members of the French cabinet withdrew from office today, wrecking the government of Premier Gaston Doumergue. Former Premier Edouard Herriot, minister without portfolio under Doumergue, and head of the radical socialists, had been in opposition to many of the premier’s ideas. The premier was understood to be prepared to give President Lebrun the collective resignation of the whole ministry which has been in power since the bloody riots of last February. Herriot is one of the strongest political veterans in France and his opposition to the premier, which has caused a series of rumors of impending breakdowns in the government in the last few weeks, was regarded as the crux of the situation.

GENEVA, NOV. 5. (AP) - The entire question of Japan's right to hold islands under mandate in the Pacific Ocean now that she has resigned from the League of Nations was thrown into discussion today as the League mandate commission heard a report that United States warships have been refused the right to visit former German islands now under Japanese mandate. According to League officials, reports exist that Japan, in violation of mandate regulations, is secretly constructing naval bases on these islands.

PARIS, (A.P)-- Edouard Daladier and five other radical men in the cabinet handed their resignations to Premier Gaston Doumergue today, precipitating a crisis which may lead to the resignation of the salvation government. The resignations, effective on Thursday, come as Doumergue persists in asking for a vote of confidence on the government's plea for three months credit, as parliament assembled for a new session which may be momentous for France and all of Europe. A tumultuous political situation has threatened to end the Doumergue government and lead to a request for dissolution of parliament, new elections, and constitutional reform.

The foreign secretary's statement was made before a house packed with those anxious to hear the government's attitude on the Japanese “hands off China” doctrine, unofficially stated April 17. Sir John said that Sir Francis Lindley, British ambassador in Tokyo, had pointed out to Koki Hirota, the Japanese foreign minister, that the principle of equal rights in China was very explicitly guaranteed by the nine-power treaty signed at Washington in 1922, to which Japan was signatory. He told his hearers that Japan has informed the British government it has no intention of interfering with “the common rights” of other powers in China and has reaffirmed its policy of the maintenance of the open door. LEIGH, England, April 30 (#)— Five miners were known to have been killed and an even heavier loss of life was feared in an explosion which wrecked a mine while a full shift was working today. The same colliery was the scene of an accident in 1932 in which 19 men were killed by a falling cage.

TOKYO (#) — The Japanese public will be kept in the dark, officially at least, concerning the note in which the United States and Great Britain were reassured concerning Japan's intentions in China. A foreign office attache told the Associated Press the government at present had no intention of publishing the note, explaining it is unnecessary since Sir John Simon is making it public in London today.

Tokyo—(#)—Resentment at America’s firm stand toward Japan’s “hands off China” policy, as expressed by Secretary of State Cordell Hull, was voiced in the Japanese press today. The reaction was in sharp contrast to the manner in which word of Great Britain's willingness to drop the whole matter raised by the Japanese foreign office declaration of April 17 was received. Morning newspapers headlined Sir John Simon's speech, delivered yesterday before the British House of Commons. “Britain Satisfied” and “England Lets Matter Rest.” Afternoon newspapers, however, splashed Secretary Hull's statement with his portrait and such headlines as. “America calls on Japan to consider the rights of other powers” and “America calls Japan's attention to the nine-power treaty.” U. 1934-11-09.text: ARUBA, D. W. I., Nov. 9—(AP)—Ten escaped prisoners from the French penal colony of Devil's Island put to sea at daybreak today from San Nicolas Bay, through the generosity of the American and English colonies. They had been provided with a 25-foot sailboat equipped with an auxiliary gasoline motor and a supply of gasoline sufficient for 400 miles travel by the use of motor alone. Furthermore they were given a month's provision, clothes, tobacco and sufficient money to help them toward a new start in life. The escaped convicts were headed by Jean Duvernay. They fled the penal colony more than two months ago in a canoe in which they spent 32 days at sea before they were picked up by a British freighter.

LOS ANGELES, Nov. 8. (AP) — Plans of Sir Charles Kingsford-Smith, Australian flier, to hop 17,000 miles from Los Angeles to Australia, via England, were disclosed here today by the trans-Pacific pilot who landed in Oakland last Sunday after a flight from Australia. Sir Charles said he planned to leave within three or four days for New York on the first leg of his flight, which would be one of the longest in aviation history. “I would much prefer to make my way home by boat in a leisurely fashion,” the Australian ace said in addressing a group of motion picture officials at the Paramount studio, “However, I think plans have just about materialized for me to fly from Los Angeles to New York, from there to London, and from London eastward to Australia.”

New Haven, Conn., Nov. 9—()— Prof. Irving Fisher of Yale said today that the NRA “on the whole, has been not a national recovery administration, but rather a national retardation one.” The professor addressed the annual convention of the (First District) New England Advertising clubs, which opened today. His topic was “The Depression and the New Deal.” In classifying himself as a person who is “partly for and partly against” the New Deal, Prof. Fisher said: “One thing of which I most wish the public would be convinced is that the New Deal’s monetary policy is mostly sound, while its other policies have largely been unsound.” He assailed the AAA and the PWA, at the same time praising the accomplishments of the CCC, “with which I can find no fault.” Prof. Fisher said “the Civilian Conservation Corps in one and a half years has enrolled nearly one million young men. Los Angeles. - (AP) — A 17,000-mile flight from Los Angeles to Australia via London is the next goal of Sir Charles Kingsford-Smith, who recently completed the first Australia-to-United States flight. The noted aviator made the announcement of his projected flight shortly after an attachment against his plane had been lifted.

London, Nov. 9.—(U. P.)—"The most powerful man in the world," The News Chronicle, organ of the Liberal party, called President Roosevelt today in an election editorial. This comment was accorded emphasis by an editorial in The Times which reflects the view of authoritative Conservatives. "It was a great personal triumph for President Roosevelt," said The Times. "If they are wise, leaders in business and finance will co-operate with the President."

LONDON, Nov. 8, (AP).—American delegates are strongly opposed to a British compromise naval program with Japan and appear determined never to grant equality to the Japanese. England’s tentative proposal, giving Tokyo equality in principle, but an inferior position to Britain and the United States actually in tonnage, goes a long way toward meeting Japanese demands, Naval circles here believed. The Japanese are studying the proposition and may not reply for several days. The suggested compromise provides for recognition of equality in principle, which is the chief demand contained in the Japanese program for a new Naval limitation treaty. Equality would be written in a far less blunt manner than Tokyo demands and would be coupled with a Japanese declaration that she would not build up to equality in tonnage in a certain number of years. .. LONDON, Nov. 9—Great Britain's proposal to Japan envisages a five-year program which would fix an approximate 5-5-4 ratio for the United States, Great Britain and Japan, it was reported today. The present attitude of the Japanese delegation, however, would not warrant the assumption that Tokyo would accept such a proposal. If, however, Japan refrains from slamming the door on the entire plan, Great Britain is ready to present a schedule for tonnage and caliber of weapons for each type of warship, as the basis for the five-year plan for scrapping old vessels and building new ones. Each nation, under this proposal, would proclaim the extent of its own program, The Japanese naval leaders are known to be solidly for complete rejection of the British plan, but some observers believed they might be forced to use it as the basis for further negotiations. LONDON (UP)—Officers and crew of the freighter Medjerda asked for light today on this mystery: The ship was rounding North Foreland of the east coast when the lookout shouted: “Airplane overhead.” As those on deck looked up, there fluttered down, to land on the deck, a woman's white silk slip and “something else,” which the hardy seamen would not describe.

1934-05-29.text: Geneva, May 28—()—Representatives of the United States and Great Britain, emerging from a long conference, indicated today that the disarmament conference was in a grave situation and that its collapse is foreshadowed unless some nation can take heroic action to save it. The Anglo-American conferees were Norman Davis, ambassador at large and Hugh Wilson, minister to Switzerland, for the United States and Sir John Simon, foreign secretary and Captain Anthony Eden for Great Britain. It was understood Sir John gave inkling that Great Britain would propose concrete steps to save the conference. Never had an international conclave been accompanied by such tenseness and such confusion. Premier Mussolini's speech in Rome, referring to the possibility of war, served to increase the pessimism. It was rumored that Italy might bolt from the conference. The economic rivalry which Mussolini mentioned

LONDON, May 21--A strong hint that Great Britain is willing to make a payment of some sort June 15 on its war debt if it could be assured of participation by the United States in a conference to thresh out a final settlement of the whole problem was given in official circles today. Should President Roosevelt hold that a token payment would not keep Britain from default then, it was believed here, Parliament would put its foot down so strongly the government would not dare make a payment of any sort. Negotiations are still continuing between Sir Ronald Lindsay, ambassador to Washington, and American officials there, it was learned officially.

DOUGLAS, Isle of Man, May 29 UPi—Kaye Don, whose flashing feats in automobile and speed boat racing have brought him face to face with death many times, has had another close shave—one which cost the life of his mechanic. His racing car overturned when he decided suddenly to make a practice midnight run for the “round the houses” race Friday. The mechanic, F. Taylor, died early today in a hospital, where Don was also taken, severely shaken up but not badly injured. Friends discovered Don's absence from his hotel and made a search for him. They found the overturned car a short way out of town, with an ambulance at hand. A policeman had found the two beside the roadside semi-conscious and telephoned for aid. Paris, May 29.—()-—Junking the entire British naval air fleet of 290 planes for a brand new force of 360 planes was recommended today in a draft of a report by the chamber of deputies finance committee. The report called the present fleet of naval planes obsolete and further hearings will be given to its allegations. The government plan estimates the cost of modernization of naval aviation would be approximately $20,000,000 as part of the $300,000,000 army program. Socialists attacked the proposed expenditures which, however, are expected to be passed by parliament.

TOKYO, May 29.--(P) Japan accepted today Great Britain's invitation to begin discussions preparatory to the vital 1935 naval conference. After the cabinet had approved the proposal, Koki Hirota, foreign minister, telegraphed Tsuneo Matsudaira, ambassador to London, to accept formally. A copy of Matsudaira’s instructions was sent to Hiroshi Saito, ambassador to Washington, for his guidance. Throughout the London talks Saito is expected to maintain close communication with the United States. Furthermore, Matsudaira is empowered to confer with Robert W. Bingham, American ambassador to Great Britain, whenever desirable. Japan understands that the London discussions are to be confined to revision of the London naval treaty and preparation for the 1935 naval conference. NORTH BAY, Ont., May 28.—Mrs. Olvia Dionne gave birth to five girls at her home, a few miles from Callender, nine miles south of here Monday. All are healthy and the mag Dr. A. R. Dafoe of Callender, the attending physician, said. Mrs. Dionne is 26 years old and has six other children.

Geneva, May 29—(AP)— The United States offered the world assistance in the reduction and control of armaments today and Soviet Russia advocated the complete abolition of armaments in proposals made before the international disarmament conference. Maxim Litvinov, Russian foreign commissar, told the conference that Soviet Russia is convinced the real renunciation of war can only be based on complete disarmament. Would Cut Naval Tonnage Norman H. Davis, American ambassador-at-large, declared that the United States is willing to join them "in a substantial and proportionate reduction of naval tonnage" and is likewise willing to join an international agreement regulating sales of war materials. The conference opened at 3:45 p. m. with Arthur Henderson of Great Britain presiding as its president. GENEVA, May 29 (UP) — The United States went squarely on record for peace at the world arms conference today by offering to reduce its navy, and to join an international agreement for control of the traffic in arms. America also declared its willingness to consult with other nations in event of trouble. The action marked a climax in the long and losing struggle for disarmament at Geneva, Norman H. Davis, special representative of President Roosevelt, in opening debate at the long postponed full meeting of the conference, made a strong bid to prevent its threatened collapse. He said: “The people of the United States are aroused by the evils which are being revealed in the production of and traffic in munitions. 1934-04-24.text: TOKYO, April 24 (#)—Confronted by Great Britain's demands for a clarification of Japan's statement of March 17 concerning the empire's China policy, official Tokyo today awaited indication as to whether the United States would follow suit in a sign of Anglo-American solidarity. Thus far, no evidence has developed in Tokyo that the United States would follow Great Britain's lead. The Associated Press learned that the state department has not acted in that direction. Great Britain's demand—which did not reach the foreign office although foreign office officials were informed of it by newspapers—gave Koko Hirota, the foreign minister, the task of explaining his policy in such a way as to appease Britain's suspicions and, simultaneously, avoid the retraction of any essential feature of the statement in which the world was warned not to meddle with internal Chinese affairs. The despair felt by some statesmen last week over the admittedly dark European outlook lightened Monday with the beginning of negotiations in three capitals. Fulvio Suvich, Italian Foreign Office undersecretary, talked with British leaders in London. Informed circles expected the outcome to be an Anglo-Italian agreement on policies for reorganizing the League of Nations, re-instituting arms negotiations, and bringing Germany and Russia into the League. Foreign Minister Louis Barthou of France conferred with Polish statesmen about Polish-French Little Entente relations and arms prospects and declared: “The Franco-Polish alliance cannot be dissolved. Our friendship remains intact and is necessary for the stabilization of peace in Europe.” Thus he spiked a feeling held in some quarters that a new German-Polish ten-year non-aggression pact would hurt Franco-Polish relations. China's impatience over the apparent passiveness of the great powers in the face of Japan's bid for Asiatic predominance was reflected in Quo Tai Chi’s visit late today to Ambassador Robert W. Bingham, accompanied by Ray Atherton, councillor of the embassy. Seeks Explanation Quo, it was understood, vainly sought an explanation of Washington’s inactivity, while Bingham replied he had not received instructions. Quo fully informed Bingham of the conversations he had with Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, in which Quo proposed a consultation of the nine power treaty signatories. 1934-12-26.text: (Copyright 1934 by United Press) President Roosevelt presided at the family’s tree in the White House, romped with his grandchildren, carved the turkey at the family dinner. King George of Great Britain delivered a family talk by radio to his farflung empire. Priests and ministers throughout the world appealed for peace on the anniversary of the birth of the Man of Peace. Bomb explosions marked Christmas in Havana. Soldiers in the South American Chaco, scene of bitter warfare, had a light day of fighting, enjoying Christmas tobaccos and liquor. Only a comparative few were killed. On the high seas, Santa Claus came down stacks of great ocean liners, delighting children among passengers. Cities throughout the world provided their poor with excellent Christmas dinners. In New York, little Gloria Vanderbilt, 10-year-old heiress, was rushed from home to church, to home again by her bodyguards

London, Dec. 25.—(A)— England counted herself today as nearing the completion of a proud year, economically and politically, but heard a warning from the king that “we have still our own anxieties to meet.” From a little room in Sandringham, King George in his annual Christmas message to the empire struck the keynote of the closing year. “The world is still restless,” he said, “and troubled. But the clouds are lifting.” Many nations, including the United States, were watching Britain even as the king spoke, learning the lessons to be gained from her progress toward recovery. Feat A budget with a surplus was probably the outstanding economic and financial feat of the year, and there are indications that there will be a similar budget next year.

CHESTER, S.C., Dec. 26 (UP)— Three bandits today stole a payroll estimated at $15,000 from messengers of the Springs Cotton mills. The robbery occurred as the money was being transferred from the main office at Lancaster to the Chester plant. The bandits escaped in an unlicensed automobile.

BETHLEHEM, Palestine, Dec. —(AP)— Historic bells pealed out from the belfry of the Franciscan monastery of the nativity this afternoon, sending their tones across 3,000 miles of ether to London, thence to be relayed throughout the British Empire. A temporary broadcasting studio was fitted out inside a whitewashed cell of the Latin Monks’ retreat, and the Paean Chimes were transmitted into microphones placed in the courtyard beneath. Outside the window could be seen a grand view of the barren mountains of Moab and the huge cleft made by the Dead Sea.

London, Dec. 26 (4)—If the record amount of money in circulation in England has anything to do with individual prosperity, today ought to be a big “boxing day,” auguring the prosperity Britain hopes to consolidate during 1935. “Boxing day” is when the housemaid, the policeman, the newsboy, the butcher boy and hosts of their ilk call at homes and get annual contributions for services they have rendered during the year. There is the equivalent of more than $2,000,000,000 in notes circulating in this country, which is a new all-time record and $50,000,000 more than last year, causing this country to greet 1935 with calm confidence. Hope was expressed for another year of slow but steady recovery, marking progress toward the old days of national prosperity which England has not seen since the sudden crisis of 1931. In 1935 three outstanding events or series of events are expected. One is a ge

ISTRES, France, Dec. 25 (Pi) America’s hold on the world speed record for land planes over a closed course was smashed today by the veteran French pilot Raymond DelMotte with an average of 214 miles an hour. The 40-year-old flier, who had held several world records during his career, shot his trim French Caudron Penault monoplane over the circuit for one lap at 321 miles an hour. It was only after a year and more of dogged attempts that he managed to crack the mark of 306 miles an hour set by the late James Wedell in 1933. Wedell died in a plane crash in Louisiana late June. Had Come Close Several times in the last few months DelMotte had come close to breaking the record, but couldn't do it until today. Failure stared him in the face again in his first trial at noon, when he attained only 209 miles an hour. An all-night rain had threatened to force postponement altogether. Late in the a

HAMILTON, Ont., (UP).—Officials of the Canadian National Railway today sought to ascertain whether the open switch which sent the crack Maple Leaf flier ploughing into the rear of a Christmas day excursion train, killing 15 and injuring 32, was faulty or did not have time to close. They pointed out that the flier may have approached so fast that the switch, which is electrically operated, may have not had time to close. The excursion train, carrying 1397 passengers, pulled onto the siding just before the limited, traveling 55 miles an hour, approached. Opinions Differ. It also was pointed out that the switch may have been faulty and remained partially open after the excursion train passed. There were differences of opinion among the passengers as to how long it was before the Maple Leaf roared onto the siding. Some said it was 10 minutes, ample time to allow the switch to close. Others s

Tokyo, Dec. 26.—While military and naval leaders talked of the empire's security being in jeopardy, the Japanese parliament met in annual session today to consider the largest defense budget in history. The figure represented about 47 per cent of the entire appropriations proposed for next year. It was an increase of about 9 per cent over expenditures for the current year.

1934-01-06.text: Exeter, Eng.—UM—When the morning mist and the remains of a champagne supper had been cleared away today, W. J. A. Grant, 82, was alive and feeling fine. Mr. Grant had just staged one of the most remarkable all-night parties ever held in the west country. It was what he called his “swan dance,” for physicians had warned him he did not have long to live. He invited 500 friends from all parts of England, including Elinor Glyn, the novelist, and Lord Vivian—and they all came. So did a bevy of beautiful dancing girls who surrounded the man for whom Cape Grant in Franz-Josef land is reputed to be named. “I am having my final kick-up,” the wealthy globe-trotter told his guests. “My doctors told me that I am dying of a complication of ailments and that my heart is hanging by a thread. “I am pleased: I don't want to live longer. I had my innings.” But the party apparently had no ill effects for,

INVERNESS, Scotland, Jan. (U.P)—Watchers on the shores of Loch Ness stretched stiffly in the morning cold today, and turned over to relief parties the job of looking out for the lake serpent. Naturalists waited for sight of the creature which would enable them to write monographs; photographers waited for a motion picture film to be rushed around the world by train, ocean liner and airplane; circus employees (with nets) waited to capture it alive. Over all these watched stolid Inverness-shire constables, ordered by county authorities to see that no harm came to the monster, because they hoped it might become an attraction ranking with Scotch whiskey and jokes. What started out some weeks ago as a threadbare jest had become the real thing. Perhaps 150 persons testified to seeing the lake serpent. Witnesses were shown tracks at the waterside, the bones of a goat it ate and the newly filled

| CHICAGO, Jan. 6 (#)—Theodore Thaddeus Ellis, vice president and part owner of the Chicago Daily News, died today of a heart attack in London, England. He was 66 years old. Mr. Ellis was a native of St. Louis, but spent most of his life in New England as a manufacturer, banker and publisher. He formerly owned the Worcester, Mass., Telegram Gazette. After the death of Walter A. Strong, late publisher of the Chicago Daily News, he joined with Col. Frank Knox in acquiring the newspaper from the Strong estate.

Worcester, Mass., Jan. 6 (AP)—Theodore T. Ellis, 67, vice-president of the Chicago Daily News, former owner of the Worcester Telegram and Evening Gazette and head of the New England Fibre Blanket Co., died suddenly today in London, England. His wife received notice of his death at her Worcester home. Mr. Ellis was a native of St. Louis, but spent most of his life in New England as a manufacturer, banker and publisher. After the death of Walter A. Strong, late publisher of the Chicago Daily News, he joined with Col. Frank Knox in acquiring the newspaper from the Strong estate. He was a noted philanthropist and art collector.

ROME, Jan. 5 (UP)—Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, today frankly said that he favored granting arms parity to Nazi Germany. Sir John, in an interview prior to departing for Paris on his way back to London, declared that he believed the demands of Chancellor Adolf Hitler for armament equality with the rest of the major powers should be recognized. The British statesman added that he believed the former allies likewise should grant the Reich "moral equality" before the world, a move sponsored by Premier Benito Mussolini during conversations with Sir John here in the last two days. He added that agreement had been reached between Italy and Britain that Europe must be "cleaned up" in an urgent effort to avoid the swiftly increasing menace of war. He insisted that the problems growing out of disarmament must be solved before all others.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 6.—Negotiations with Great Britain for an exchange of American farm products in return for Scotch whiskey imports continued deadlocked today and—with a ban on the potent beverage a possibility—the situation was reported to President Roosevelt by Secretary Wallace.

Amsterdam, dau, 3 &P)--One man drowned today when the German steamer Ceres, a 660-ton vessel, sank off the Hook of Holland after a collision in the fog with the British Chagres. The British ship, apparently unaware of the seriousness of the collision, proceeded toward England. "With the exception of the one man, all of the Ceres crew were rescued in lifeboats.

NEVERS, France, Jan. 5 (P.-- Evelyn Frost, American aviatrix, was burned to death today in the crash of an airplane. Miss Frost, who was piloting the plane en route to Egypt, collided with high tension wires in a fog. The plane burst into flames immediately and the flier was trapped in the flaming mass of wreckage. The British flier, Ruttled, who accompanied her, was slightly injured.

1934-04-02.text: ISTANBUL, Turkey, April 2—Samuel Insull Sr., a fugitive for a year and a half from Cook County, Illinois, charged in indictments with embezzlement and grand larceny, was arrested by Turkish police today. They took him from the Hotel London, despite his protestations, to the house of detention, Kenan Pey. The Attorney General stated that if an examination showed the 74-year-old former utilities czar to be ill, he would eventually be transferred to the prison infirmary to await disposition of his case. A battery of Greek legal talent was reported en route from Athens to fight in his behalf—an apparent last-ditch effort to save Insull from trial in Chicago on the charges which arose from the overthrow of one-time empire of public utilities.

Santa Monica, Calif., April 1.— Not much news the last couple of days from Astor's fishing smack. Pretty nice of England to let our President fish in their ocean. Speaking of oceans, our grand fleet of 110 ships has to leave this coast this week. Japan says they have been in their ocean long enough. We are about the only nation that has a fleet but no ocean to put it on. The thing we ought to do is dig a canal right smack dab across the United States from East to West, then when there are objections from the proprietors of the Atlantic and Pacific, we could cruise in our own waters, something we can't do now. Copyright McNaught Syndicate,
LONDON, April 2 (UP).—A severe cough forced Queen Mary to remain within Buckingham Palace today. It was said there was no anxiety over her condition.

ISTANBUL, Turkey, March 30. — The announcement that the Turkish government believes it can legally turn Samuel Insull over to American authorities brought to a climax tonight the 74-year-old fugitive’s long battle against extradition to the United States. Insull himself, weary and sick from court fights in Greece and a subsequent dash toward the Black Sea, was reported to have attempted suicide by trying to jump into the Bosporus. He was placed under a heavy guard. Arrest Is Possible The government, acting on an American request for the arrest of the former Chicago utilities operator, decided his case comes under a provision of the penal code making possible his arrest for American authorities. The final scenes in the Insull drama were scheduled for tomorrow: First, his removal from the Greek tramp steamer Maiotis, which brought him here two days ago after his flight from Greece, to a ho

Ambassador Robert P. Skinner advised the state department that Turkey had officially agreed to permit extradition of Samuel Insull. Skinner cabled from Angora that Turkey was holding Insull for whatever disposition the ambassador wished to make of him. ISTANBUL, Turkey. (UP). Samuel Insull was placed under formal arrest by Turkish authorities. They will turn him over to the United States for extradition. Insull was arrested at the little London hotel where he has been under close police guard since he was taken off his chartered Greek steamer, the Maiotis, Sunday and held by the courts to be subject to extradition. Fighting for freedom, Insull consulted his local lawyers, but it was not believed the purely executive process of surrendering him to the United States could be delayed much longer. From his hotel, he was taken to the house of detention to be kept in custody until American aut

ISTANBUL, Turkey, March 31,— Police asked Samuel Insull to go ashore for questioning today. Insull refused bluntly, and police left his chartered steamship Maiotis to get new instructions from the government at Angora. Insull remained under guard. He has been here since Thursday when his little ship cast anchor off the Leander Tower at the entrance to the Bosporus which joins the Sea of Marmara and the Black Sea to which Insull was going. Police planned, if possible, to hand Insull over to American Ambassador Robert P. Skinner, at his request. They were nonplussed when the aged utilities man, his back to the wall, refused their request to go ashore. Though he and the Maiotis’ master were under technical arrest, the Turkish position was a delicate one. The ship flies the Greek flag and police seemed somewhat afraid that there might be a violation of international law if they forced Insull

Carcassonne, France, April 2.—(—FPistols barked again today in the second political duel since the Bayonne banking scandal shook France, but—as in the previous encounter—nobody was hurt. The combatants were Deputy Jean Mistler, minister of commerce in the cabinet of former Premier Edouard Daladier, and Roger De Tour, Royalist leader. The harmless exchange of shots on a rifle range near Carcassonne was arranged to settle a political quarrel, which reached a climax when De Tour slapped Mistler Saturday night. The two left the field unreconciled, The duel was an outgrowth of the bloody Paris riots, which resulted from public indignation at the charges of government implication in the Bayonne affair. De Tour, leader of the Carcassonne Royalists, seeing Mistler playing cards in a cafe, called him an “ignoble person” because Mistler was a member of the Daladier cabinet blamed by the Royalists

MOSCOW, April 2—Experts feared today that three Russian aviators met disaster in heroic attempts to rescue 89 men marooned on an ice-floe off the northern capes of Siberia. They were fliers Kamanin, Molokoff and Pivenstein. No word has been received from them since March 29 when they hopped in three ships from Anadyir for the Cape Van Karen rescue base. Normally, only a few hours is required for the flight. They took off, however, in the face of a bitter snowstorm. A wireless report from the stranded party, survivors of the Wrangel Island expedition of Prof. Otto Schmidt, brought good news. Prof. Schmidt said a supply of fresh meat had been obtained through the killing of a polar bear. He said the men were in good spirits.

1934-04-12.text: DUBLIN, April 10— (AP) —The capital of the Irish Free State went into mourning today for William Wallace McDowell, 67-year-old American minister to Dublin, who died at the very climax of his brilliant career. Blinds were tightly drawn at all legations and flags were flown at half-staff as the city mourned the sudden death of the minister at a dinner in his honor last night. A memorial service will be held tomorrow. Afterward, the body will be sent to the United States on the first available steamer calling at Cobh. Burial will be in Montana. HE FALLS DEAD Rising at the banquet, given for him by Irish executives, Mr. McDowell started to make acknowledgment of the enthusiastic greeting that had been given him. The words, "Butte, Montana," came to his lips, then trailed off as the minister slumped forward, dead of a heart attack. Montana was the minister’s adopted state. He was born in Tenn

Lenane, Irish Free State, April 12 (UP)—John Joyce, 117, believed to be the oldest man in the British Isles, died today. He attributed his longevity to the Great Irish famine of the 1840s which instilled in him a love of good food.

LONDON, April 12.—(U.P)—The following won for George Graves, actor, last night the story-telling championship of England at the annual and highly social “banquet of humor;” “An insane asylum attendant told a rich patron that the asylum’s new swimming pool was becoming so popular with patients, particularly those who could dive, that the superintendent intended having it filled with water.—

MOSCOW, April 12—(4)—The Government Rescue Commission announced that 22 more Russians, stranded since Feb. 13 on a drifting ice pack in the Bering Sea, were rescued by airplane today. Only six persons remain on the pack, The brilliant rescue flights, executed under hazardous conditions in the Far North, brought the total of those flown to the mainland at Cape Van Karem, Siberia, within two days, to 84. An original party of more than 100 was cast away on the ice when the steamer Cheliuskin sank on the return trip from a scientific expedition to Wrangell Island. Flights to save the six remaining men were planned today or tonight if the weather remained favorable. Graphic Version Given A graphic first-hand account of the perilous situation facing the castaways when huge icebergs crushed into their pack was given by the Government Rescue Commission.

Istanbul, April 12 (UP)—Samuel Insull lost today what was believed his last chance to escape extradition to the United States tomorrow. The supreme court of appeals at Eskisehir ruled that his appeal against extradition could not be considered. Turkish police were ready to take him to Smyrna and turn him over formally to Burton Y. Berry, third secretary of the American embassy, aboard the Export Line steamship Exilona when it steams from the harbor tomorrow afternoon. 5,000 Mile Voyage Major John A. Crane, embassy military attaché, was ready to accompany Insull on the 5,000 mile voyage to Boston. It was planned to take the aged utilities man to the docks at the Golden Horn, put him aboard the little passenger boat Adnan, and convey him to Bandirma on the Marmara Sea, whence he would go to Smyrna by rail and be taken aboard the Exilona. 24 Hours More Extradition formalities were arranged

MOSCOW, April 12.—The frozen Arctic seas were cheated today of twenty-two more of the refugees of the sunken icebreaker Cheliuskin, who had been trapped for two months on the floes off northwestern Siberia. Valiant Soviet airmen who have been taking off the refugees in small groups in repeated hazardous flights from Cape Vankarem brought back the twenty-two, leaving only six still on the ice. They were expected to be rescued soon. Thus the entire band of 107 will have been saved, writing a new page in the glamorous history of the far north. The Soviet flier, Slepnov, who has played a heroic part in the rescue, flew towards Nome and Fairbanks, Alaska, with Otto Schmidt, leader of the Cheliuskin expedition. It was planned to put Schmidt in the hospital at Fairbanks. He was ill with a fever and it was feared pneumonia might develop.

ISTANBUL, April 11—Samuel Insull, pronounced fit by government doctors who examined him today, will be started back to the United States on Friday, the 13th, to face the fraud charges he has eluded for 18 months. The finding of the Turkish physicians was diametric to the aged fugitive’s long contention that his heart was in bad shape and controverted statements made by Greek doctors after repeated examinations permitted Insull to thwart American extradition attempts. The former millionaire and head of the Insull utilities empire, now fallen, was photographed and finger-printed preliminary to his departure tomorrow for Smyrna and his formal relinquishment to Burton Y. Berry, of the American embassy, aboard the S.S. Exilona Friday. Ali Riza Bey, vice governor of Istanbul, who announced these plans, said the 74-year-old man will be informed officially at noon tomorrow and removed from the I

BERLIN, April 12 (#)—The Diplomatische Korrespondenz said today that if Germany is spending more money for instruments of war—and she is—that’s Germany's own business. The newspaper is the mouthpiece of the German foreign office. “What right,” the organ demanded, “is there for astonishment in France or anywhere else” that large increases in military appropriations feature the 1934 budget? Sixty-one naval craft are being built by Britain and 54 by the United States, the Diplomatische Korrespondenz said, so it again asked, “why all this fuss about the German budget?” The newspaper reassured the world that “Germany has neither the intention nor any possibility of engaging in an armaments race. It sees its duty in providing a minimum for its own defense.”

1934-04-15.text: EXILONA, BOUND FOR THE UNITED STATES FROM SMYRNA, Turkey, April 14 (AP).—Samuel Insull, homeward bound in the custody of a United States official, was cheered today by the possibility he may be joined for most of the long journey by his wife. The Exilona is holding cabin accommodations open so that Mrs. Insull may embark at Catania, Sicily, if she can make arrangements. She is now in Athens. It was understood Mrs. Insull’s party would number six. The booking, however, was indefinite. The Exilona is expected to reach Catania late on April 16. Insull, back under the stars and stripes despite all his efforts to prevent it, was shown every courtesy, despite the fact he is a prisoner. The captive, who sought to put aside his worries by exchanging anecdotes with the American diplomat in whose custody he is being returned, was assigned to the captain’s table today. Turkey, true to its word, tur

Barkizon, France, April 16.—A police raid on a mysterious and secluded villa here Sunday revealed Leon Trotzky, exiled Soviet leader, had been living there three months in secrecy, fearing attacks on his life. Officers had surrounded the villa for 26 hours, thinking they had discovered a secret arms cache or a rendezvous of Stavisky gangsters. Threats against Trotzky’s life have kept him in flight from enemies the past year, secret police revealed. The “man without a country,” who has wandered over Europe and Turkey since his fall from power in 1927, came to France from Corsica last July, stopping at Royat. Renewed threats against him brought authorization of the French government for him to hide, with Mrs. Trotzky, at Barbizon. “From an old conspirator,” Trotzky told police. “I am now preparing for the Fourth Internationale.” A plumber who recently repaired pipes said he was mysteriousl

Rome, April 14. (AP)—The council of ministers today decreed sweeping reductions in salaries and the cost of living in order to place Italy in a position to compete with other nations in the foreign market. The council, over which Premier Mussolini presided in person, ordered all rents in Italy reduced 12 per cent. Government employees' salaries were cut from six to 12 per cent. All other costs, such as food, gasoline, and utilities are to fall in proportion so that Italy can manufacture goods that will have even price chances with those of other nations. This is the second such nationwide deflation in three years, another having been ordered in October, 1930, along almost the same lines. Government employees whose salaries range up to 6500 lire ($42.50) a month are not touched. Those with salaries between 500 and 1,000 lire (from $42.50 to $85) are reduced 6 per cent. Salaries between 1,

GKAZ, Austria, April 15 (*)— Rotten eggs were thrown at Chancellor Dollfuss and a harmless bomb exploded within 300 feet of him when he appeared here today to address a mass meeting. The bomb was a smoke and noise variety. Spoiled eggs splashed the clothes and uniforms of Dollfuss paraders, but missed the little chancellor. Socialists had painted the entire highway red from the airport where Dollfuss landed to the city limits of Graz. Pavements were splashed with slogans as “down with fascism!” and “down with Dollfuss!” Meeting Is Quiet, The mass meeting itself was quiet, but attempts to broadcast the chancellor’s speech were mysteriously sabotaged and only portions of it reached radio listeners. Dollfuss said the accusation his government was developing into a clerical autocracy was unfounded. “What we want is not clerical domination,” he said, “but a state ruled by the Christian spirit

Rome, April 14.—(4)—Every salary in Italy and every article of food, clothing, rent, heat, light and transportation went on the block today to the tune of a 6 to 20 per cent cut in order to make the kingdom able to compete in world markets with nations having lower manufacturing costs. The council of ministers, over whom Premier Mussolini himself presided, decreed the sweeping, all-inclusive action as a battle of a "deflationary" country against "inflationary" nations.

| S. S. Exilona, Bound from Smyrna, Turkey, April 14.—(AP)—Samuel Insull, bound for the United States and trial on fraud charges, regarded cheerfully today both the past and the future. On his first day out of Smyrna in the custody of an American official, the 74-year-old former utilities executive chatted happily in the ship’s saloon about his memoirs on which, he said, he had not yet started.

PARIS. (LP). Plans to strengthen the French political alliances and prevent Nazi Germany from wooing away Poland and the little entente were completed by Louis Barthou, the French minister of foreign affairs. He will present them to the cabinet Tuesday prior to his departure for Poland, where he hopes to remove signs of discontent within the once happy family. From Warsaw the minister will go to Czechoslovakia and perhaps on to Belgrade. Franco-Polish relations entered a new phase when the Poles took the unexpected step of signing a ten-year friendship treaty with the Nazis. They appealed to the French to follow their example and accept Hitler's proposal of a non-aggression pact.

Geneva, April 14. (P)—An official demand for a real reduction of armaments as against stabilization at existing levels was filed with the League of Nations today by Sweden, Spain, Switzerland, Denmark and Norway. The nations insisted at the same time on definite guarantees of security against war. The joint memorandum suggested there was danger in the rearmament of Germany on a large scale unless the powers make a real reduction in armaments.

1934-07-18.text: BRIGHTON, Eng., (AP).—Tony Mancini, a “stuttering waiter,” pleaded not guilty today when formally charged with the hammer murder of Mrs. Violette Kaye, 42 year old professional dancer. Mancini, who was charged under the name “Jack Notyre,” was remanded to jail for a hearing July

LONDON, July 18. (®)—The finishing touches today were put on Great Britain’s plans to double her air force at a cabinet meeting in 10 Downing Street. It was understood that the cabinet agreed on an increase of at least 50 squadrons during a period of years. When such extension should be completed, Great Britain would have an air force equal to any nation 'within striking distance.'

LONDON, July 18.—(AP)—Japanese-American naval discussions supplementary to the 1935 conference may be held in Washington in early August, it was indicated today. Captain Iwashita, advance junior technical officer of the Japanese delegation to bilateral talks with Great Britain, is now en route to London, via the United States. He will arrive in Washington in about two weeks. International quarters here anticipate he will take advantage of the trip at least to make acquaintance of American naval leaders and perhaps discuss the situation generally with them. A full Japanese delegation will follow Iwashita and also may come to London by way of Washington. Anglo-Japanese conversations are to be opened in October. Talks between Great Britain and the United States were suspended yesterday until September. Norman H. Davis, head of the American delegation, and Rear Admiral Richard H. Leigh, his

Associated Press Staff Writer. James V. Allred, Texas attorney general for four years, appealed to a vast central Texas audience at Austin last night to elevate him to the governorship. The young candidate spoke within hearing distance of the governor's mansion, and some things he had to say might have burned the ears of Governor Miriam A. Ferguson and her husband, former Governor James E. Ferguson. “I could have had a mansion, probably, too out in the restricted (Enfield) residential district,” Allred said. “But, as you residents of the capital know, I have lived in a little modest home in a section where dwellers are humble persons. There are any tricycles, kiddie cars and other baby things out on the sidewalk. The dust flies in there every time the ice wagon passes where I live with my wife and two babies, but one who offers his money for favors dares not show his face there.” Allred

Paris, July 18—France and Germany have reached an agreement covering payment of interest on Dawes and Young plan loans to French bondholders, it was announced today. The agreement was regarded as less favorable from the French viewpoint than the one negotiated by Germany with Great Britain. With negotiation of a Franco-German agreement following the British agreement, the United States, which holds approximately $1,000,000,000 worth of German bonds, remains the outstanding creditor whose claims have not been adjusted. Strong protests have been lodged by the United States government with Germany, but to date, as far as is known here, no basis for settlement has been arrived at.

BERLIN, July 17—(4)—Experts of the reich’s finance ministry assembled hastily today to consider what to do about a decision by the three Dawes loan trustees to withhold for foreign bondholders about 200,000,000 marks which normally would have been used to pay some of the government’s domestic bills. A government statement said the Dawes loan trustees—three foreign bankers—are jeopardizing the reich, and assurance was given that the necessary action would be taken. What that action is to be was not fully disclosed, but the government announced that the revenues of certain internal duties would no longer be credited to the trustees’ account.

LENINGRAD, U. S. S. R., July 18, (P).—Soviet aviation officials announced today that Nikolai Evdokimoff, a Red Army aviator, had established a world’s record by making a successful parachute jump from a height of 8,100 meters—26,575 feet. “They announced that the jump through space occupied 142 seconds and that Evdokimoff opened his parachute only 650 feet above the ground. It was the jumper's 100th leap in three years.
VIENNA, July 18. (P)—Former King Alfonso of Spain, driving his own Ford car, killed a young Viennese Nazi writer, Dr. Karl Smein, last night. Police said Alfonso was not responsible for the accident.

1934-07-22.text: Warsaw, Poland, July 21.—UP—More than 200 persons dead and damage estimated at about $200,000,000 were reported today as the flood waters of the Vistula river reached the very gates of the presidential palace in Warsaw. The deaths and damages have occurred during a full week of high waters. Now a flood wave from the Karpathian mountains menaces the Polish capital. The Vistula has risen to a level of 16 feet as compared with its normal 4 foot level and authorities said that if it rose above 19 feet the heart of the capital was in danger for the levees of the left bank are not expected to hold much longer. Police, soldiers, municipal workers and civilian volunteers worked madly today in efforts to strengthen the embankments. Hundreds of boats and automobiles have been drafted for the work. The streets of the suburb of Prager and the amusement center, Luna Park, are under water. Seven nearb

BERLIN, July 21—(AP)—A terse announcement that two of Germany's most powerful conservatives, President Paul von Hindenburg and Konstantin von Neurath, foreign minister, were in conference today let loose a flood of conjecture. The government veterans have their heads together at Von Hindenburg's Neudeck estate in East Prussia. It was there Adolf Hitler flew for a conference after the revolt suppression of June 30. A subject believed before them was the future of Franz von Papen, vice-chancellor and fellow-conservative, who brought opposition to extreme Nazi policies into the open by a speech June 17, a forerunner of the revolt. Von Papen, reports said, has sought five times recently to go to Neudeck for a conference. Another belief was Von Hindenburg and Von Neurath talked over the proposed East Locarno pact, sponsored by France.

BERLIN, July 21 - The general "clean up" campaign in Germany today turned sharply toward high Nazi officials, as the courts of justice were warned that a person in exalted position merits "corresponding punishment" if he is guilty of misconduct. The warning came in a decree from Minister of Justice Franz Guertner, indicating the extent of the general cleansing of the Nazi party which is following Chancellor Hitler's "purge" of three weeks ago. At the same time it was revealed that the whole set-up of student leadership is to be revamped within a short time, the first step being the removal from office today of Andreas Feickert, named national leader two days ago, and all present sub leaders. These developments came while Hitler was out of town and while two of the nation’s most powerful conservatives, President Paul Von Hindenburg and Foreign Minister Konstantin Von Neurath, were in conf

WARSAW, July 21—(#)—Flood waters of the Vistula river, which took more than 200 lives in Southern Poland, swept into Warsaw today forcing many citizens from their homes as the streets of suburbs were turned into canals. The Vistula, whose rampages have already caused damage estimated at $200,000,000 rose to a level of 16 feet, compared with the normal 4-foot reading here, and the water reached the gates of the presidential palace. Seven nearby villages were inundated, and Luna Park, huge amusement center was under water. Boats were used in suburban streets in the place of wheeled vehicles. Hundreds of persons, including police, soldiers and volunteers worked desperately today to strengthen the levees of the left bank of the river which showed signs of weakness that endangered the heart of the capital.

PRINCE GEORGE, B. C. (UR) Ten United States army bombing planes landed here at 10:53 Monday en route from Washington, D. C., to Alaska. The squadron was to leave for Whitehorse, Yukon territory, after lunch with no stops planned. It flew here Monday from Edmonton, Alberta.
REGINA, Sask., July 21.—(A)— A squadron of United States army bombing planes, proceeding to Alaska on a survey trip, landed here today after a flight from Winnipeg.

EDMONTON, Alta., July 21—Ten United States army bombing planes, en route to Alaska, arrived here from Regina at 4:40 p.m. today. They will remain here until Monday morning, when they expect to start the 490-mile hop to Prince George, B.C.

VIENNA, July 21 (INS)—New York police cabled Vienna police headquarters a request that Capt. Arvan Proderjay, and wife Mme Suzzanne Ferrand, be held in jail here pending the arrival of most important evidence in connection with the disappearance of Miss Agnes Tufverson, New York lawyer, who married Proderjay in New York. The nature of the evidence was not disclosed. Proderjay, a former Jugo-Slavian army officer, is being held on charges of bigamy, and as a suspect of murder, while Mme is being held on the suspicion of having profited by a murder.

1934-12-04.text: London.— (4?) —The home secretary's office informed George Lansbury, labor leader, late today that Mrs. May Browning, the 62-year-old mother condemned to die for the ‘mercy slaying” of her imbecile son will be reprieved. Lansbury had been one of the prime movers in the fight for clemency for the mother. The home office moved swiftly today and the reported action was taken only a few hours after an application for reprieve had been filed with it.

LONDON, Dec. 4. (UP)—Princess Juliana, heir to the crown of the Netherlands, lost a $35,000 diamond bracelet when she was here as a bridesmaid for Princess Margaret at her wedding to the Duchess of Kent, The Daily Telegraph said today.

- LONDON, Dec. 3 (AP)—A reprieve for the gray-haired mother condemned to death for the “mercy slaying” of her imbecile son was assured Monday in a communication from the office of the home secretary, where hundreds of appeals for clemency have been received. The frail, 62-year-old mother, Mrs. May Brownhill, was removed from the shadow of the gallows in an official action which set a record for speed in recent appeal cases in England.
DUBLIN, Dec. 4—00}—Films of the wedding of the Duke of Kent and Princess Marina were withdrawn today from Dublin theaters following disturbances and protests against their showing.

CAMBRIDGE, England, Dec. 4 — (UP) — Sir Horace Lamb, 85, eminent mathematician, died today. Lamb was a recognized authority on hydrodynamics. On questions involving the motion of air, he gave valuable assistance to the aeronautical research committee.

Babin, Irish I Free State, ec, 2.-- (R—Crowds rioted at movie houses Sunday night when films of the wedding of the Duke of Kent to Princess Marina were shown. Rioters sang the Irish soldiers’ song and shouted: “Long live the republic!” Police were rushed to many theaters to quell fighting patrons, trying to destroy the films.

Dublin, Dec. 3—(UP)—Violent demonstrations against the British Royal family were resumed late tonight. Hundreds of Republican youths rushed the doors of the Savoy Motion picture theater—largest in Dublin—and demanded the management immediately stop showing a film of the wedding of the Duke of Kent, youngest son of the British rulers, to Princess Marina of Greece. The theatre was partly wrecked. The demonstrators howled Republican slogans and "Down with British Imperialism" and "English Propaganda." Some of the rioters carried pots of a black, paint-like liquid, which they hurled over the silver screen of the theater. Others fought their way to the stage and finally slashed the ruined screen to ribbons. Many persons were trampled as the spectators fought to escape from the building as the management announced the performance was closed.

ROME, Dec. 3.—(4)—France and Germany today signed “an agreement of peace” over the Saar basin territory. By the terms of this agreement, which is expected to end the grave controversy over the future sovereignty of the district, Germany will pay France 900,000,000 francs (approximately $59,400,000) and 11,000,000 tons of coal for France’s mines and private credits in the Saar basin and, furthermore, Germany guarantees equal rights to voters and non-voters among all the inhabitants of the Saar regardless of race, religion, or language. Receiving the foreign press this afternoon, the Spanish delegate to the committee of three, Lopez Olivan, told the correspondents that the agreement was divided into two parts: political and economic. The political accord, he said, is divided into three parts, as follows: (1) Germany guarantees to extend to non-voters the same standing as that of voters; (2

1934-03-17.text: - Moscow, March 17.--()—More than 2,090 persons, including members of the British consulate’s staff, were reported today to have been massacred at Kashgar, in Sin-Kiang, Chinese Turkestan, by fierce Tungan natives. - The massacre, dispatches said, came in a bloody battle between the rebels and the military of the recently proclaimed “independent government.” The fighting ensued when Tungan forces swooped down upon the town and freed a garrison of Tungans which had been besieged in a fortress by troops of the independent government. A number were slain and wounded at the British consulate when government troops drew Tungan fire by taking refuge nearby after falling back from an unsuccessful counterattack upon the Tungans.

DUBLIN, March 17, (Proold) Dublin led the world's Irish today in the "wearin' of the green" to honor the memory of the good Saint Patrick. The city carried on a tradition many others have all but forgotten in observing St. Patrick's Day with a big parade in the grand old style. In the line of march were thousands of strong soldiers, including the Oriel and Dublin regiments of the new volunteers—dressed for the first time in their new gray green uniforms. Eamon De Valera, president of the executive council of the free state, attended high mass accompanied by his ministers at noon. Tonight, he was to broadcast a message to the people of Irish descent in the United States. The traditional toast to the Patron Saint had to be lofted differently, since the free state legislature ordered all public houses closed from Friday through Sunday. Hence, Irishmen here faced being forced to do their toa

LONDON, March 17.—(P)—Elsie Ferguson, American actress, and Victor Augustus Seymour Egan, wealthy Irishman, were married at noon today in the Caxton Hall Registry office. It was the bride's fourth marriage, and Egan’s second. Only the bridegroom's son, Lieutenant Rupert Egan, and a few close friends witnessed the ceremony. Miss Ferguson said she had “left the stage for good,” when they disclosed their plans to marry. She gave her age as 49. Egan gave his age as 59.

Dublin, March 16 (?)—There will be fewer shamrocks and no whiskey for St. Patrick's Day tomorrow, and Irishmen will be forced to “drown” the famous “green” in a cup of tea. Shamrocks are scarce because the weather has been abnormally dry, but supplies of the leaf were being gathered today and there may be about enough to go around. The traditional toast to the patron saint will have to be made differently. The Free State legislature ordered all public houses closed from today to Sunday and decreed that no liquor be available. Nevertheless, Dublin will celebrate tomorrow. A military parade will be the main feature. It will mark the first appearance of the gray-green uniformed volunteer troops.

(Copyright 1934 by United Press) - By Eamon De Valera, President of the Irish Free State, Dublin, Mar. 17 — Thar ceann muintir na hÉireann, fearaim míle fáilte ar ár gcairde, go léir na Stáit Aontaithe i gcomhluadar na hAthair Pádraig, agus guidhim gach beannacht agus sonas ortha. These blessings and good wishes sound on behalf of the Irish people to our kindred and to all our friends in the United States. We watch with interest and sympathy their efforts to re-adjust their economic life and we wish them complete success. Every advance made by them is a source of joy and encouragement to us. We in Ireland are doing in miniature what the people of the United States are doing on a gigantic scale. Our problem is not so complex as theirs because our country was not so developed industrially, and the extension of existing industries and the creation of new ones to meet internal needs opened u

LONDON, March 17.—Cambridge today swept to a four and a half length victory over Oxford in the 86th renewal of their annual eight-oared crew race and set a new record for the four and a quarter mile course of 18 minutes 3 seconds. The light blue boatload was never extended as it swept up the muddy Thames from Mortlake to Putney to score its 11th straight victory over Oxford and its 45th of the series begun in 1829. The new mark for the race displaced the record of 18:29 set in 1911 by one of the great Oxford crews which ruled the English rowing world for nine straight years before the war. The time first was announced as 13:38 but a check of the watches disclosed the new record.

ALGECIRAS, Spain, March 17. A British squadron of 137 ships engaged in Atlantic maneuvers were in refuge in the harbor here today after battling storms in which several members of the crews, including two officers, were reported washed overboard.

BMF. Ce | =O Tres Oo: Italy, Austria, and Hungary signed two agreements today, one designed to bring their three countries closer together politically, and the other to assure the economic independence of Austria. The pacts were signed by Il Duce, Chancellor Dollfuss of Austria, and Premier Goemboes of Hungary. The agreements provide that each of the countries concerned consult the other two before taking any steps which would react upon another. The prime effect of the pact will be to bind Austria to confer with Italy before making any move that might betray her independence—particularly through a union with Nazi Germany. The commercial accord lists preferential duties which it is hoped will serve as a basis for a more extensive Danubian agreement bringing in France, Germany and the Little Entente nations of Rumania, Czechoslovakia and Jugoslavia. 1934-03-21.text: PARIS, March 20 —(CP)— Spying against the United States, France and Great Britain was charged by police today in a widespread plot they said finally had been revealed through the testimony of two American prisoners. Investigators said Germany and Soviet Russia had been the beneficiaries of what authorities described as a vast international espionage syndicate. Police of the United States and England have been co-operating in the investigation of the spy ring, it was explained, and it is largely through their efforts that the tangled skein of the mystery of the so-called plot finally is commencing to be unraveled. Five More Arrests Police voiced their charge as developments came thick and fast following a seven-hour questioning of Mr. and Mrs. Robert Gordon Switz, the Americans, in a secret session before Judge Andre Benon, investigating magistrate, which did not end until shortly before

Hollywood, Calif., Mar. 21.—Just like to show you what our cousins are doing in the way of toting the mail, “London, March 16, the British post office showed a profit at the end of this fiscal year, ending February, of seventy million dollars. Last year 57,000,000 post office profits were applied to the reduction of taxes.” We lost 159 million a year, Who's to say now? They also run the telephone and telegraph, so when you say “a government can’t run a business,” you mean our government can’t run it, so don’t forget to always put that word “our” in there. Jim, this is no reflection on your VP, O. gang, it's on our lawmakers, who won't charge for a letter, paper, or crate of eggs what it costs to carry it, be it by plane, boat, train or mule, and charge accordingly. Yours,

(Copyright 1934 by United Press) LONDON, Mar. 21.—Japan is seeking revision of American immigration laws, abandonment of Philippine naval and air bases and recognition of Manchoukuo in return for an offer to maintain present naval ratios, it was said in a most reliable source today. It was said that basis for negotiations would be established in correspondence between Secretary of State Cordell Hull and Koki Hirota, Japanese foreign minister. Negotiations proper, it was added, would be conducted with Hull by Hirosi Saito, new Japanese ambassador to the United States. As regards the reported proposal for abandonment of the naval and air bases, it was said, Japan was believed to be willing to join in a pledge to guarantee the “neutrality of the Philippines. In specific return for the proposed American concessions; it was said, Japan was believed to be prepared to renounce its recent resist

Paris, France, March 21.—(U.P.)— Robert and Marjorie Switz, young Americans held as principals in the greatest espionage plot ever uncovered, may escape prosecution because of their revelations of the ring’s activities in France, England and the United States, it was learned today. A law, passed in 1886, makes it possible to grant pardons to suspected spies who confess and implicate others before they are brought to trial. Andre Moise, chief counsel for the young married couple, told the United Press he had advised them to talk frankly. Their talk, as announced officially, implicated many others in the ring. It led to five arrests immediately, and counter espionage aces of the secret service hoped to make additional arrests today. The Switzes, held in their solitary cells at separate prisons, were considerably relieved today at the possibility they might be released after the trial of th

LONDON, March 21. —(A4’)—Mr. and Mrs. Robert Switz, the two Americans held in Paris in the investigation of an international spy plot, were pictured today as catspaws of the vast organization. The real director of operations in Britain, the Daily Mail said, was a woman who has now left the country. Mr. and Mrs. Switz, natives of East Orange, N. J., and New York, left London hurriedly 18 months ago, leaving behind them a book containing puzzling entries, indicating a code to which different styles of handwriting were the keys, the Mail said.

(Copyright, 1934, Associated Press) LONDON, March 20 -— New moves by the United States toward the negotiation of reciprocal treaties with a number of the smaller countries of Europe are expected when President Roosevelt puts his tariff program into operation, it was said here today. Among the countries anticipating such action are Poland, Turkey, Switzerland and the Scandinavian group. Encouraged by an increase in exports to the United States in 1933, Sweden is looking hopefully in the direction of Washington for an offer by the Americans to arrange a trade pact which will bring about greater mutual business. In Poland, American goods are in great demand but import restrictions are temporarily holding sales to a reduced volume. Cotton is perhaps the chief American product wanted and needed in Poland, while Poland has a large supply of spirits it would like to sell, or to exchange for cot

| THE HAGUE, March 20 (AP).- Dowager Queen Emma, beloved for her charities and honored alike by Holland's rich and poor, died this morning of bronchitis. She was 75 years old. The Queen Mother, widow of King William III and mother of Queen Wilhelmina, had suffered from bronchitis for some time, but became gravely ill only a few days ago.

ATHENS, March 20—(/)— Samuel Insull plans to return to the United States after the excitement of his case dies down and live in America peacefully the rest of his life, one of the aged fugitive’s Greek attorneys told The Associated Press today. The lawyer, Mr. Xeros, declared he was in communication both with Insull’s ship on the Mediterranean and his London solicitors who are handling the former Chicagoan’s affairs. “Insull seems happy now in calm weather,” the lawyer said. “Wherever he is going, he will make his permanent home if the United States continues to persecute him. “Mr. Insull will go to Paris Saturday and will leave for London within a few days.” Insull may visit as many as 20 countries before he finds a haven, said Xeros. “They would go to the United States now but are afraid for their lives and afraid he will not get justice,” he continued. “Insull is afraid he may be made

1934-06-26.text: WASHINGTON, June 26.—(#)—- President Roosevelt returned to the capital today from his week’s visit to New York and New England and prepared to grapple with a mass of government business before leaving on his territorial cruise next Saturday. The president shuffled his trump card in the troublous capital-labor situation to the “top of the new deal deck today as he returned for a week of high pressure work before leaving for Hawaii. New Labor Board. A new emergency labor board, with wide power to settle such questions as collective bargaining was expected to emerge from conferences with an announcement of the board’s personnel and an order defining its authority. Many bills passed by congress also must be cleared from the presidential desk, and the chief executive faced the task of picking men for several key posts, including one to direct the vast housing drive.
