Chicago, Ill., June 20.—UP—Judge Evan A. Evans of the United States circuit court of appeals today ordered the release of John Factor, wealthy speculator, from the Sycamore, Ill., jail, where he has been held pending the issuance of a final order for his extradition to England on charges of defrauding investors of $7,000,000. The judge delayed signing the order until tomorrow, to permit counsel for the British crown to get in touch with the state department at Washington. Judge Evans acted on the writ of habeas corpus after receiving a petition presented by Factor’s wife asking the release of her husband under a section of the extradition act which provides that a prisoner shall be released if the secretary of state has failed to issue the final order within 60 days after the court order. The 60-day time limit expired Saturday night.

LONDON, June 26. P—Two of the world’s most talked about women—Queen Mary and Mrs. Sara Delano Roosevelt—sipped tea together this afternoon in Her Majesty’s private apartments at Buckingham Palace. King George was present, but most of the animated conversation was carried on by the mother of the American president and the Queen of Great Britain. Just two mothers—grandmothers, in fact—they found many common interests as they chatted merrily. Their Majesties were impressed, as the prime minister and other empire leaders had been, by the gaiety, friendliness and frankness of Mrs. Roosevelt. She radiated pride in her famous son, but Mrs. Roosevelt gave expression to a commonsense view of the world and its affairs gained in her 80 years of experience. She expects to remain here the rest of the week.

- CHICAGO, June 26. (U.P.)—John (Jake the Barber) Factor, wanted in England on charges of swindling British investors out of several million dollars, today won his release from the DeKalb County jail at Sycamore, Ill., on a writ of habeas corpus. The writ was issued by Federal Judge Evan Evans under a recent Federal Court ruling that a warrant for extradition must be served within 60 days after a defendant's arrest at the request of foreign authorities.

London, June 25 (4.—Great Britain sharpened her weapons for a trade war with Germany today while at the same time extending the hand of diplomacy to a delegation from the Reich, coming here to discuss the moratorium on foreign debts. The Anglo-German conferences, which will begin Wednesday, mark the first effort to settle peaceably the international economic controversy based on Germany's announcement of suspension of payments on the Dawes and Young loans. While expressing hope of a satisfactory agreement, the British government prepared for economic warfare by pushing through its second reading in the House of Commons a bill designed to collect interest on the loans forcibly from German commercial accounts.

Chicago, June 26.—James J. Walker, former mayor of New York City, was cabled in London a $100,000 offer for a five-weeks personal appearance with his wife, Betty Compton, at the World's fair. The offer was made last night by Lew Dufour, manager of the Hawaiian gardens concession.

- Moscow, June 26 —(AP)— Chas. Courtney, New York master locksmith who risked his life in an undersea investigation of the wreck of the British cruiser Hampshire, said today he was satisfied it did not carry £2,000,000 in gold (approximately $10,000,000) when a German mine sent it to the bottom of the North Sea. It was on the Hampshire that Lord Kitchener went to his death. Courtney said the salvage company with which he is associated would make no further effort to regain the alleged treasure. He flew here from Bergen, Norway, to interview a British subject who supervised the loading of the Hampshire before her fatal voyage. After talking with this man, Courtney said he was convinced there was nothing of such value in the Hampshire’s hold that would justify further exploration of the wreck, lying 12 miles off the Orkneys. Dublin, Irish Free State, June 6 —(AP)— The Irish Free State balloted in local elections today on the outcome of which a general election and the future of the government of President Eamon de Valera may hang. For the first time in the history of the Free State national politics were figuring in local fights. The elections followed a bitter campaign in which De Valera and his foe, General Eoin O'Duffy, stumped the country. O'Duffy, leader of opposition "blue shirt" forces, predicted his party, Fine Gael, would win 20 out of 23 county councils. Such a reversal for the government might well lead to a national election. But Sean T. O'Kelly, vice president of the Free State, said "government nominees will win everywhere."

1934-03-03.text: LONDON, March 2—(AP)—A British member of parliament calmly disclosed in a musty London courtroom today that he had tried to save the Russian royal family from death at the hands of blood-mad revolutionaries and that he had been invited to join a plot to kill the mad monk Rasputin. Commander Oliver Locker-Lampson, the witness, brought to a startling finish the four days of testimony in the $2,000,000 libel suit instituted by Princess Irena Yous- scupoff against the Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures, Ltd., producers of “Rasputin and the Empress” in which the plaintiff claims she was defamed. If thrill-seeking society members and others believed their shudders were over with the finish of accounts of how the sinister monk was poisoned, beaten, and shot in the cellar of the St. Petersburg imperial palace they were mistaken, for Locker-Lampson's story sent electric waves through the packed courtro

LONDON, March 2.—The opinion that Europe is face to face with the most serious disarmament crisis since Germany pulled up her stakes and left Geneva last October was expressed tonight in an authoritative British quarter. The indication of the American state department that the United States was in complete accord with the British government's views of disarmament gave only a glimmer of hope in the situation, for London has known for some time that Washington supports the British proposal. No Encouragement. No such encouragement, however, was evident on the European continent as a result of Captain Anthony Eden's recent tour of the capitals. The lord privy seal and arms experts returned home without tangible results and his critics labeled the trip a “talkie tour.” Commenting on reports, published abroad, that the United States had taken a new initiative in disarmament negotiations, Ameri

| With European nations frankly in an impasse on disarmament, President Roosevelt has thrown the weight of his approval behind a move by Great Britain to secure action on a four-power armaments agreement. The pact, which would include England, France, Italy and Germany, recognizes Germany's demands, proposes consultation among the signatory powers if one of them violates the projected treaty by manufacturing forbidden armaments and suggests a compromise of between 200,000 and 300,000 as the size of the German army. In Washington, the British ambassador was informed by the state department, according to an announcement yesterday that “while the American government is not in any way a participant in the European political problems, and therefore does not take part in diplomatic discussions relating thereto, it is nevertheless vitally interested in the maintenance of European peace, and the

LONDON, Mar, 3. (U.P)—Europe today viewed the close of President Roosevelt's first year in office with mixed emotions but a predominant feeling of admiration for his courage and his twelve-month accomplishments. The fears and some bitterness aroused over his international financial policies had been dissipated in nearly all quarters, and in some of the hitherto conservative capitals statesmen were swinging towards a popular demand for adoption of a “New Deal” for Europe. The popular press of London is solidly behind the President, and has been jabbing for some time at British political leaders, in attempt to prod them into adopting some of his principles. Furthermore, such outstanding economists as John Maynard Keynes and Sir George Paish are now loud in their praise of many of his policies. “He has raised prices to a considerable extent,” Paish said today, “and if he hadn't devalued the

Dublin, Irish Free State, March 3 (AP)—President Eamon De Valera, saying he feared civil war, sought to reach an agreement with the opposition Friday. He offered to establish a joint national force to preserve order—provided present forces proved inadequate—if the opposition would drop “this provocative tomfoolery of the blue shirts.” President De Valera asserted that the same political strife which led to the war of 1922 existed Friday. He said war was inevitable unless steps were taken to stem the present trend of developments.

LONDON, March 2. — (#)— Provisions for adding four new squadrons to her air force were announced today by Great Britain. Two are to be placed in home defense, one flying boat squadron will be added to the overseas strength and two flights—equivalent to one squadron—will be given to the fleet. This was announced in the air estimate for 1934, calling for a net total of 17,561,000 pounds (approximately $89,034,270) an increase of 135,000 pounds (about $684,450).

ATHENS, Mar. 3. — Foreign Minister James Maximos today notified the Ministry of Interior that Samuel Insull, Chicago utilities magnate, must be made to leave Greece at once. Insull’s 15-day period of grace, granted him as an extension of a previous expulsion order because of ill health, expires today. The Chicago utilities man had taken refuge here to avoid extradition by the United States to face charges of irregularity in operation of his vast interests which collapsed and caused losses to thousands.

PARIS, MAR, 2 (AP)—Mme. Arlette Stavisky, beautiful wife of the man who caused the notorious “Stavisky scandal” which brought in its wake the overthrow of two governments, was arrested today by the secret service. The arrest followed the recovery by the secret service of check stubs giving the names of many recipients of “bearer” checks from the master swindler. The police long have sought these stubs in their effort to identify those who had received millions of dollars from Stavisky and who likewise had cashed millions of dollars worth of checks which he had made out to himself. The police said they had recovered the stubs from “a personality.” The “personality” was not named. They revealed for the first time that Mrs. Stavisky, on the day after her husband either committed suicide or was killed in a lonely villa near Chamonix, gave the stubs to a friend. 1934-09-30.text: WARRINGTON, England, Sept. 29 —(AP) — A final check tonight showed that five men and five women were killed in the crash late last night of two trains. Many persons, 21 of which were sent to hospitals, were injured. All the casualties were English and Welsh. The accident occurred when a fast London express smashed into the rear of a slow local train at a junction.

(Copyright, 1934, by the United Press.) ROME, Sept. 29. — Up — France and Italy, after years of bickering and distrust, are about to conclude a political, military and economic alliance of vast scope, the United Press learned today. The entente will be sealed by an agreement under which the Bank of France will underwrite 2,000,000,000 lire ($172,950,000) in Italian securities. The political balance of Europe will be profoundly affected by the entente, and observers believe it would prove a powerful deterrent to German expansion or absorption of Austria. The entente moved a step nearer to final consummation when the current negotiations extended the political and military agreement to the economic and financial field. It was regarded as a sincere expression of both countries to maintain a peaceful understanding in which the economic structure would act as the cementing force. Final agreem

VIENNA, Sept. 29.—(AP)—The possibility that Turkey’s 57-year-old dictator, Mustapha Kemal Pasha, may choose a bride from among the four marriageable sisters of King Zog of Albania was under discussion here today. Belgrade dispatches to Austrian newspapers said announcement of an engagement might be made during the expected visit of King Zog to Ankara shortly. The militant, 38-year-old king of Albania once declared — publicly that Balkan tradition would not allow him to marry until he, as the eldest son of the ruling house, had successfully married off all his sisters. Two of six are now married. Kemal Pasha, the man who emancipated Turkish women, is said to have expressed a desire to remarry. He was divorced in 1925 by his own decree from the young and beautiful Latife Hanoum, daughter of a wealthy merchant of Smyrna. Would Reunite Link The four marriageable sisters of King Zog (formerly

| LEIPZIG, Germany, Sept. 29.—A key, presumably for a safe deposit box in New York used by Isidor Fisch, the man who Bruno Richard Hauptmann said gave him the Lindbergh ransom money, was obtained tonight by Detective Arthur Johnson of New York. The key was surrendered to the detective by Hanna Fisch, sister of the late Isidor. The officer also discovered a contract note belonging to Isidor and involving a transaction in Long Island real estate. Johnson also was given Isidor's bank book, which showed that at the time of his death here Hauptmann’s friend had less than £100 on deposit. Johnson, pushing his researches in Germany energetically, was at the Leipzig police headquarters until 10 p.m. He questioned Mrs. Pinkus Fisch and Hanna Fisch separately. “I am resuming my conferences with police at 11 a.m.,” Johnson told the Associated Press. “I shall question Pinkus Fisch again, I cannot te

Calgary, Sept. 29.—(4P)—A new mystery angle had been added today to the disappearance of Dr. K.F.H. Lumley, Ohio State University professor, from the Goathaunt Chalet in Glacier Park, Mont. He has been missing since August 16. It has been disclosed, according to a report from Waterton Lake National Park, a registration book at Ilmorey Lodge, where the professor's mother was a visitor earlier in the summer, had been tampered with. Beside Mrs. Lumley's name in the registration book had been added the words 'and son.' The missing man's mother declared it was not the writing of her son, or herself, and no one could be found who had any knowledge of the added entry in the lodge book. Since the disappearance of Dr. Lumley both United States and Canadian police have conducted a widespread search for him, using forestry men and bloodhounds in the hunt. Not a trace of him was found. WASHINGTON, D. C., Sept. 27—Flew in here this afternoon and what greets my eye? Washington's monument had a scaffold built up around it. I said to Jesse Jones: “Jesse, don't tell me the ‘new deal’ is rebuilding ‘George’s’ monument?” Lobby of hotel full of badges and found out it’s the police chiefs from everywhere, getting their code. They were afraid to sign. The president by tomorrow is picking five men to replace Johnson and run the NRA. I think that's what these police chiefs are all doing here. They are going to help him arrest the men that he appoints. For nobody would take a job like that voluntarily. Yours. WILL

(Copyright, 1934, by Associated Press.) NEW YORK, Sept. 29.—A mystery woman witness entered the Lindbergh kidnaping investigation tonight with the disclosure by District Attorney Samuel J. Foley that she had given him “very important” information in the case of Bruno Richard Hauptmann, accused of extorting the $50,000 ransom. Foley said he had questioned the woman privately and she had not appeared before the grand jury. Name Kept Secret “She came and went as quickly as Lindbergh and nobody knew anything about her,” he said at a press conference. The prosecutor declined to reveal the woman’s name, where she came from, or when he had conducted the examination. To a suggestion that he might be withholding this information to make her testimony at Hauptmann’s trial a surprise, Foley replied: “That is true, but it is not the principal reason. 1934-09-14.text: GENEVA, Sept. 13 (#)—Poland's curt announcement today that she will have nothing further to do with the League of Nations’ system for protecting minorities involves the very basis of the Versailles treaty, French and British spokesmen said tonight. The Warsaw government's action threatens the sanctity of treaties and opens the road to open flouting of international agreements by other nations, these sources said. A German spokesman told the Associated Press that Poland’s sensational move means that the status quo set up at Versailles is being modified and treaties no longer are valid.

An ominous quiet hung over the New England textile strike zone yesterday as violence subsided. The regular army stood by awaiting possible orders to march to reinforce 2,000 national guardsmen in Rhode Island, but the state legislature delayed action on authorizing a request for the soldiers. Keep Indoors. Woonsocket, where two youths were slain and several others wounded when the militia fired into a crowd of 5,000 rioters, was under military control. Salons and theaters were ordered closed, and citizens warned to remain indoors last night. The Woonsocket Rayon company plant, where the riot started, will be closed in the “public interest,” company officials announced. Majority leaders in the Rhode Island legislature, called into special session by Governor Green, tabled until today the governor's request for authority to ask federal troops. It was voted to support bills allowing the gov

KAIFENG, Honan Province, China, Sept. 13. (AP) — The Yellow River—'Scourge of the Sons of Han'—was roaring its turbulent way down to the sea tonight, spreading death, destruction and suffering over its great flat bed. At flood stage for the second time this month, the big river, measuring 30 miles from bank to bank at some places, made mockery of the flimsy man-made dykes barring its sweep and once again proved its right to its bitter name 'China’s scourge.'
Augusta, Me, Sept. 14 (4)-A provisional battalion of the Maine national guard was ordered into the textile mills area in Biddeford today as a defensive measure against unrest.

CALLANDER, Ont., Sept. 14-14) — Blood transfusion equipment was rushed here today from Toronto to be in readiness should the condition of the Dionne quintuplets, suffering from intestinal toxemia, become worse. Dr. W. A. Dafoe, of Toronto, brother of Dr. A. R. Dafoe, of Callander, who has attended the five baby girls since birth, brought the apparatus here. The famed children of Mr. and Mrs. Oliva Dionne passed the night so well, however, that it was found unnecessary to use the blood transfusion equipment this morning. After visiting his tiny patients today Dr. A. R. Dafoe said their condition still caused him concern but he was more hopeful of their recovery. The disease will take at least a week to run its course.

WASHINGTON, Sept. 14. (?)—Labor and capital mobilized forces today as the strife-torn textile belt became the battleground for what some expected to be a fight to the finish between industry and the American Federation of Labor. The opinion was expressed by both mill owners and labor that the strike has transcended the bounds of a single industry and become a decisive test of union strength under the national recovery act. Some cotton mill owners, who have rejected the arbitration services of the president’s mediation board, said privately that pressure has been brought upon them from other industries to resist all demands of the United Textile Workers. “You know, we know and the union knows,” one spokesman said, “that there is far more at stake than the welfare of the textile industry. If we give in, there will be a wave of strikes in all industries; it is a case of determ- (Continued o

NEW YORK, Sept. 24—(4)—Charges that officers of the Morro Castle did not give necessary orders to the crew when flames swept the ship and that highly inflammable cleaning materials were used on the vessel were made today by William O'Sullivan, a deck storekeeper on the liner. At a department of commerce inquiry into the disaster of last Saturday, O'Sullivan testified, in reply to a question concerning the discipline of the crew during the crisis, that “there were not the orders.” “Had there been the orders there should have been, the crew would have responded?” his interrogator continued. “Yes, sir,” O'Sullivan responded. NEW YORK, Sept. 14.--(#)—A charge that the inquiry into the Morro Castle disaster is being hindered by operators of the ship and that attorneys marked the grand jury investigation of the ship fire today. From United States Attorney Martin Conboy came the charge yesterda

* “New York, Sept. 14: — (Pp) — A rescue ship's four ranking officers who had sharply criticized their master for delay in sending lifeboats to the aid of Morro Castle victims, were called last night before a federal grand jury investigating the disaster. They testified earlier, before a Department of Commerce inquiry, that the Dollar liner President Cleveland might have saved additional lives if Captain Robert E. Carey had not waited 48 minutes after arriving at the scene before ordering out rescue boats. “They tried to make a goat out of me,” the master declared, “but their own testimony shows what they did.” Captain Carey, acknowledging the 48-minute delay, told the ship inquiry that two lifeboats were lowered as speedily as possible. The Cleveland did not pick up any survivors. The President Cleveland's departure for San Francisco was delayed several hours to permit the captain and t

1934-09-20.text: Aboard U.S. C.G. cutter Argo off Newport, Sept. 19—(AP)—The third race for the America’s Cup between the British challenger Endeavour, victor in the first two, and the defending American sloop Rainbow today was postponed until tomorrow for lack of a breeze. The postponement came only a few minutes before 11:30 A.M. (CST), the deadline beyond which a race cannot be started under cup rules. The sea was as flat as a mill-pond with only an occasional puff of wind out of the southwest to ruffle the waters and not enough to give any hope of sailing the race under the time limit of five and one-half hours.

Aboard U.S. C. G. Cutter off Newport, Sept. 20.—(#)— Ably handled by Harold S. Vanderbilt, the American defender Rainbow came charging through the windward leg of the thirty mile leeward-windward course today to overcome a six minute, forty second advantage Endeavor held at the halfway mark and score her first victory in three races with the British challenger.

LONDON, Sept. 17.——Will you please tell me what happened at the so-called yacht race Saturday? I never saw as many conflicting statements as in the local papers today. Some say the race was in doubt to the last minute, some say that cruisers or Roosevelt or somebody got in the way of the English boat. They say our crew is professional and that theirs just works for the love of the sea air and that ours is not built right below decks. Send all particulars to the League of Nations and let's get this thing straightened out. Yours, @ 1934. McNaught Syndicate, fae

Edinburgh, Sept. 20. — You got these Scotchmen wrong. Why they are the most liberal and hospitable people you ever saw. Course I have to carry an interpreter to tell me what they say, but they are awfully friendly. Grouse is Scotland's principal export. You got to rent a castle, then rent some drivers to drive the grouse by the castle. The grouse have been shot at so much they know just about who can hit ‘em and who can't. It's a racket and the grouse and the Scotchmen work together and the Americans and the Englishmen pay the bill. Yours,

Edinburgh, Sept. 18.—I have been coming over since 1906 when I first worked on the stage in London and do you know I had never been to Scotland before and I want to apologize for being so dumb. It sure is pretty. Saw all Glasgow, Loch Lomond and the big boat that Queen Mary launches next week. Yes, they are up here in this country with us too. Edinburgh, which we are doing now, kind of high hats Glasgow. There is a mess of class to Edinburgh. Hoot, mon WILL

To the News-Republican: London, Sept. 18 — London is awaiting the news of the second day’s yacht race. They take yacht racing seriously over here. It seems by today’s papers that any bad sportsmanship was shown by the writers and not by the owners. They are talking about holding an ammunition selling investigation over here now. Ammunition is about the only export now. Wars ought to be awful equal for they all use the same guns and ammunition. Best show in London is a colored show from Harlem. Yours,

BOARD U.S. C. G. CUTTER ARGO, OFF NEWPORT, R. I., Sept. 20.—(UP)—Eating up the wind in a spectacular homeward spurt, Harold Vanderbilt's American defender, Rainbow, today won the third heat of the America’s cup series against T. O. M. Sopwith’s British challenger, Endeavour. The victory left the series two wins to one in favor of Sopwith’s blue-hulled challenger. Vanderbilt drove his craft home in a stunning beat for the finish that turned what seemed to be certain victory for the challenger into a magnificent triumph for the American yacht. Trailing by more than six minutes at the turn, Rainbow fearfully ate up distance on the way home, biting into a fresh northeasterly breeze. The big white American cutter rode up on Sopwith's lee 10 miles from the finish, cutting down a half-mile lead in five miles of racing. Taking advantage of an inept effort at tacking, which proved the turning poi

Boston; Sept. 20.—(AP)—Interest was at its highest pitch here today in the Democratic primaries, with James M. Curley, the original "Roosevelt for President" man of New England opposing Gen. Charles R. Cole for the gubernatorial nomination. Cole has the backing of Governor Joseph B. Ely who, at the Chicago national convention, nominated Alfred E. Smith for the presidency. Curley was rejected by the pre-primary convention that endorsed Cole. David I. Walsh, incumbent, has two opponents for the senatorial nomination, former Lieutenant Governor Edward Barry and William Donahue, both of Boston. Walsh is a resident of Clinton. Gaspar G. Bacon, Republican Lieutenant Governor, is opposed for his party’s gubernatorial nomination by Frank A. Goodwin, former register of motor vehicles. The Republican candidate for U. S. senator, Robert Mo. Washburn, is unopposed.

1934-03-24.text: Associated Press Foreign Staff PARIS, March 23.—(AP)—A revival of the old Entente Cordiale which brought Great Britain into the World War is sought by France in a secret communication to London elaborating on an arms note. The latter document, made public tonight, itself referred guardedly to this French desire in discussing the necessity of safeguarding against violations of any arms convention. "If established violations endanger the security of a state, common action by the powers should be used for the benefit of the threatened nation," the note said. "This common action should come into play particularly if the violation degenerated into aggression." If British guarantees of aid against an aggressor are not forthcoming, the note makes it plain that the Geneva Disarmament Conference is at an end. It leaves the door open, however, for a new conference which would recognize and limit G

PARIS, March 24, (AP)—The missing Stavisky jewels—worth $650,000—were reported found today pawned in London. A secret service man followed the trail of the late Serge Stavisky's secretary, Romagnino, who went to London while Parisian newspapers were clamoring for his arrest. A detective discovered the jewels and the fact that they had been used as security for a loan of $40,000. The loan, it was said, was made after the police net started to close down on France's master swindler and before he died from a revolver shot in a villa at Chamonix.

By MELVIN K. WHITELEATHER Associated Press Foreign Staff PARIS, March 24—France, seeing her chances of keeping Germany disarmed slipping steadily away, is groping today toward a resumption of the old pre-war entente cordiale with England. With an answer to Britain's recent disarmament proposals — an answer which made clear France's refusal to disarm without adequate guarantees—Paris is known to have suggested in a secret communication that revival of the entente cordiale, with its unwritten but powerful implication of British assistance for France against Germany, would solve the problem. Feel Out Uncle Sam. In view of the startling nature of the French communication, which was published last night, it was reported in Paris today that Geneva disarmament circles and the British government are considering putting out feelers in Washington to determine the American position toward guarantee

A French note on disarmament to Great Britain, made public Friday, was received with noticeably different reactions today in every nation concerned. In Paris it was hoped that the note would result in the British government seeking the United States reaction toward the French request for guarantees of security. In London it was said that Great Britain would do nothing of the kind but that it was hoped France might modify her security demands. In Washington it was said flatly that the United States would not enter into any agreement guaranteeing security for France or any other nation.

LONDON, Mar. 24. — A somewhat funereal note from France on disarmament left Great Britain still willing today to seek further for a solution of the problem. As the note was published, the French War Ministry announced that beginning April 6 it would accept 18-month enlistments from men who had fulfilled their compulsory military training period of one year. League of Nations headquarters at Geneva announced that 4,000,000 men are under arms in Europe and that an additional 32,000,000 could be mobilized at any time, ready for war. The French note showed no real progress—rather a solidification of the deadlock that has existed for many months.

International News Service Staff Correspondent (Copyright. 1904, International News Service. Reproduction in whole or part Forbidden) LONDON, March 24.—French statesmen may be alarmed. Italian statesmen may be alarmed. A dozen European chancellors may echo with anxious prophecies. But when British statesmen are alarmed, it means dark days for Europe. Britain is alarmed today. She is alarmed as she has never been since Tirpitz and his navy league built the German fleet into a challenge to British security. Again today Britain is alarmed at Germany, this time not led by Wilhelm II, but by Adolf Hitler; this time not officered by Admiral Tirpitz, but by General Goering; this time not at the German navy league but at the Reich air defense league; this time not at German submarines but at German bombers. Openly declares Germany that Britain and France will fight side by side at the drop of th

London—Great Britain holds little hope that France will modify her security demands as a basis for a disarmament treaty and the British cabinet apparently is at a loss as to how to proceed with efforts to save disarmament. This was learned in official circles today as oral communications between the two governments proceeded in an effort by Great Britain to get a more definite statement on security from France than was given in the French note yesterday. It was stated in British official quarters that these exchanges through the respective ambassadors, which began Monday and were responsible for the delay in the publication of the note until yesterday, have been "inconclusive." France is expected to insist upon sanctions against an aggressor and on territorial guarantees as well as guarantees for the execution of disarmament. On these conditions only, it is understood, she would agree to

London, March 24 —(UF)—The drowning of more than a score of persons mostly children, when a pleasure boat capsized was reported today by an Exchange Telegraph dispatch from Tokio. There were 42 children in the excursion boat, accompanied by two teachers. Twenty-five children were rescued. Twenty bodies were recovered.

1934-06-02.text: LONDON, June 1—()—Frank L. Hutton found his daughter Princess Barbara Hutton Mdivani in a medical clinic here today and was visibly annoyed about something after he visited her. Hutton, who had been in a fine humor when his son-in-law, Prince Alexis Mdivani, greeted him at Southampton, appeared angry after he and Mrs. Hutton had been with their daughter for an hour and a half, Mdivani not being present. The Huttons did not reveal what had disturbed them nor would they discuss the health of the princess who earlier this week had been reported able to make shopping tours from her hotel.

(Copyright, 1934, by United Press) London — Proposal within the next 13 days for a series of definite conferences on war debts appeared today the sole possible alternative to general default of European nations to the United States. President Roosevelt's message was interpreted here as: 1. Formally inviting Europe to make full payment of the June 15 debt installment and in some cases arrears on former payments, or being declared defaulters under the Johnson act. 2. Leaving the way wide open for any nation before June 15 to seek a definite debt refunding conference and thereby avert default or annul previous default. Comment here and in other capitals varied but slightly. Nations not angry because of the president's broad hint that America’s debtors might pay their bills with the money they are spending on armaments, were cynical regarding his implied hope that substantial payment would b

(By The Associated Press) London, June 2—Prince Alexis Mdivani, his wife, Princess Barbara, and her parents, Mr. and Mrs. Franklin L. Hutton appeared really reunited today. They occupied adjoining suites in a swanky Dorchester hotel, and everyone was silent so far as the outer world was concerned. Sometime last night, Hutton called at the nursing home where he had found his daughter on his arrival from America yesterday and brought her back to the hotel they all are now occupying together. The prince prepared for polo as usual and his team “The Devils” went out to play its final game in the visitors’ tournament at Hurlingham.

| LONDON, June 4 (.—-Maybe, London society speculated today, the “affair Mdivani” was something of a molehill made into a mountain after all, All seems harmonious between Princess Barbara Hutton Mdivani and the Georgian prince she wed a year ago in Paris, despite reports that a split between them was what sent her parents, Mr. and Mrs. Franklyn L. Hutton, rushing to London to act as peacemakers, possibly to return Barbara to America. The frail young heiress has left a clinic and is in seclusion in a London hotel with Prince Alexis, London circles called her illness a “million dollar stomach ache.”

| LONDON, June 2. (UP) — King George, in uncertain health, will celebrate his 69th birthday quietly tomorrow. | The customary public observance will be held. | Flags will be flown all over the city and the King, on a military charger, will review his household troops on Horse Guards' Parade.

| Toulon, France, June 2—(P)—| Alert French gendarmes, ever on the lookout for spies around defense centers, nabbed an American in the naval arsenal here Friday afternoon and turned him over to judicial authorities. The prisoner, who said his name is Anulry Nikolajeski, 38, and that he was born in Chicago, insisted, police said, that he is not a spy, but merely a tourist who wandered into the arsenal with workmen. Nikolajeski is the third American taken into custody in connection with espionage charges in recent weeks. The others are Mr. and Mrs. Robert Gordon Switz of East Orange, N. J., and New York, who are under examination in Paris and are said to have confessed they are spies.

North Bay Ont., June 4.—(UP)—Marie, smallest of the quintuplets born to Mrs. Olivla Dionne, continued a game fight for life today, while her four sisters were apparently recovering from a light week-end attack of jaundice. The infants suffered a slight setback when a mild attack of yellow jaundice appeared to complicate their battle for existence, but 24 hours of treatment seemed to have cleaned up the disease which is common among very young babies. The quintuplets’ weight today, announced by their father, were: Emilie, 1 pound, 13 ounces; Cecil, 2 pounds, 1 ounce; Annette, 2 pounds, 4 ounces; Yvonne, 2 pounds, 6 ounces; Marie, 1 pound, 10 ounces. No definite conclusion regarding showing the babies at the Chicago fair has been reached, Dionne said.

NORTH BAY, Ont., June 2.—(WUP)— One of the Dionne quintuplets suffered a setback today and fears were held for her life. A definite report from the doctor attending was lacking pending completion of his examination. The quintuplets previously had thrived and were reported progressing favorably earlier this morning. Medical records show that survival of infants born as quintuplets is exceedingly rare in history and the doctor's report was anxiously awaited.

1934-09-10.text: GENEVA, Sept. 10.—()—Richard Sandler, of Sweden, was elected president of the League of Nations assembly at the first session of that body today. Backed by France, England, and Italy, an invitation for Russia to enter the league was circulated among the delegates and it was stated that some 30 countries were disposed to sign it.

TORONTO, Sept. 11 (4P).—Attorney-General Arthur Roebuck today announced identification of one of the suspects wanted in connection with the kidnaping last month of John S. Labatt, wealthy, London, Ont., brewer. Roebuck said the man was known variously as Albert Pegran, Albert Leon and Jack Snead. He said the man was a citizen of the United States, had a long criminal record and was believed to have driven the automobile in which Labatt was abducted.

Evidence that the British war office is disposing of surplus war stocks of such magnitude that the sale of even a part of these munitions could alter the balance of power in a small country was presented today to the senate munitions committee. This testimony came to light in a letter by the Soley Armament Co. Ltd. London, to the American Armament Corp., saying it acted as ‘agent for the British war office in disposing of small arms worth about $30,000,000. “The stocks we control,” the letter said, “are of such magnitude that the sale of a big block of them could alter the political balance of power of the smaller States, involving corresponding complications from the point of view of finance and in- j Gusizy.” State Department Mentioned. Testimony was given that the State department had advised Amer- "continued on Page 20

Washington, D. C., Sept. 10 (UP) —The British war office has turned over $30,000,000 worth of small arms, including machine guns, to a private company for sale, correspondence read into the records of the senate munitions investigation disclosed today. A letter from the Soley Armament Company, Ltd., to the American Armament Corporation, New York, dated February 3, 1934, told of disposal of the stocks. "AS we are really the sole selling channel for small arms, etc., which belongs to the British war office, and as we are to a very great extent controlled by the varying policies of the government, it is rather difficult for us to enter into firm and fast agreements with other armament firms." Alter Balance of Power. "The stocks we control," the Soley letter continued, "are of such magnitude that the sale of a big block of them could alter the political balance of power of the smaller states

COPENHAGEN, Sept. 9~ Great flight down from Norway. These Danes took nothing but a pig and a cow and common sense enough to stay out of war for 50 years. Today they, along with Sweden, Norway and Finland, are an example to the world of how to live neighborly and tend to your own business. There's lots to be learned from these Scandinavians. Yours,

SWAN RIVER, Manitoba, Sept. 10 — A mother and five children were burned to death last night at their isolated farm home in the Big Woody District, 15 miles west of here. The dead are Mrs. Walsh, 48, and her children, Kenneth, 14, Mabel, 13, Rita, 12, Dorothy, 8 and Mary, 2.
(Early Story on Page 12.) Geneva —(#)— The council of the League of Nations today reached an accord “in principle” to grant a permanent seat in the council to Soviet Russia.

(Editor’s Note: Senator Huey P. Long, central figure of a bitter primary fight in Louisiana in which the militia, private armies, and charges of graft and corruption have been paraded and reparaded, today granted one of his rare interviews to a United Press correspondent. It follows:) —By H. O. Thompsen— NEW ORLEANS, Sept. 10—(UP)—Huey P. Long, directing a hot political fight in a suit of peach-colored pajamas, said in an interview today that he thought the nation’s farmers and workers could combine to mold the future of America. The dynamic Long, dashing from bed to radio microphone and back again, said he had no ambition to lead that coalition but that given a few weeks of relief from other problems, he could fashion a new political force from those classes. All Long wants for himself, he said, is to get things running so well he can go back to “my little old law office in Shreveport.”

1934-05-04.text: London, May 3—4)—Great Britain is prepared to make a silver token debt payment to the United States in June, it was reported in financial circles today as a result of the recent drop in silver prices. While official confirmation was lacking it is believed probable the British government took advantage of the low price. Although the day of reckoning is only a little more than a month away there is still no official indication that Britain is making any kind of a payment on her debts to the United States, but it is believed it will be another token payment.

CRANWELL, Eng. May 1. (AP)— Four Royal Air Force officers were killed today when the two airplanes they were flying over the airdrome collided and smashed to earth. All four were dead when emergency squads reached the scene.

LONDON, (#)—Ibn Saud, ruler of Saudi Arabia, was reported today to have crushed the ancient kingdom of Yemen, captured Hodeidah, and sunk armed ships in Hodeidah harbor with his modernized army artillery. The Imam of Yemen, ruler of the country, was reported assassinated in a revolutionary outbreak. The British government moved rapidly to protect its nationals and British property and to prevent any organized uprising of Arabians. Warships including the sloop “Penzance” were dispatched to the area. H. M. S. Enterprise, a cruiser, was ordered from Mombasa, East Africa, to Aden, in Southwest Arabia. The situation in Arabia was regarded with grave concern by the British government. France and Italy, which possess colonies at the southern end of the Red Sea, also may become involved, it was said. Official dispatches did not confirm the reports of the death of the Imam, who had ruled with abs

New York—(#)—Harry Mozely Stevens, who created the American hot dog stand and built a fortune on it, is dead at 78. The English-born caterer to the hungry appetites of millions of this country’s sport fans succumbed to arteriosclerosis at his home here yesterday after a long illness. Starting in a small baseball park at Niles, O., Stevens lived to see his business develop until the far-flung Stevens’ concessions covered every major league ball park, many of the largest race tracks, old Madison Garden and the new Grand Central Palace. Stevens sold the first hot dog (so named by the late Tad Dorgan, sports cartoonist) at the Polo Grounds in 1900. Sausages had been sold in rolls before that time but the hot sausage in the hot roll with mustard or pickle was his own idea. The new delicacy met with immediate acclaim from hungry sports followers and quickly developed into a national

London, May 3. — Great Britain will present a virtual commercial ultimatum to Japan late today in an effort to halt the damaging encroachment of Nipponese trade in the dominions. As the result of a long cabinet meeting last night Walter Runciman, hard-boiled president of the Board of Trade—an important cabinet post in Great Britain—invited Tsundeo Matsudaira, Japanese ambassador to visit him at 3 p.m. today. Runciman’s instructions were to intimate diplomatically to Matsudaira that Britain was prepared to declare a trade war with Japan unless she yielded to the British demand to partition world markets on the basis of reduced Japanese textile exports. It was learned that before taking its decision the government consulted with the colonies, and found them ready to impose quota restrictions against Japanese imports.

LONDON, May 4 (AP).—British occupation of Hodeidah was threatened today because of the breakdown of the civil administration at that important south Arabian port as a result of the headlong flight of Yemen warriors before the conquering troops of Ibn Saud, ruler of Saudi Arabia. Apprehension over the future ambitions of the powerful Ibn Saud in other parts of the Arabic world were overshadowed in British official quarters by alarming reports that a state of anarchy exists in Yemen itself. At Rome, the Italian government ordered three light warships to Hodeidah to protect Italian subjects and property which may be endangered by the conflict in Yemen. The order for the dispatch of the warships to the danger area came from Benito Mussolini as premier and minister of the navy.

Rome, May 4. (AP)—The Italian government today ordered three light warships to Hodeidah to protect Italian subjects and property which may be endangered by the conflict in Yemen. London, May 4. (AP)—Italy’s extensive interests in the southern Red Sea area were regarded today as responsible for the dispatch of three Italian warships to Hodeidah. It had been rumored here that Italian agents had been backing the Iman Yahya, the ruler of Yemen, and that this accounted for the reckless manner in which he had flouted offers of peace by the powerful Ibn Sand. Such rumors were discounted, however, in government quarters which denied emphatically they had any such information regarding the situation there.

| Copyright, 1934, Associated Press BAGHDAD, Iraq, May 3.—The complete collapse of Yemeni forces in Western Arabia during bitter tribal warfare with the highly-efficient army of Ibn Saud, ruler of Saudi Arabia, was reported tonight simultaneously with rapid British, Italian, and French steps to protect nationals in the area. Ibn Saud, the most powerful Arab leader in this era, was said to have conquered the ancient kingdom of Yemen—bounded by the Red Sea, the desert, and British-controlled Aden—captured Hodeidah, and sunk armed ships in Hodeidah harbor with his fighting planes, armored cars, and well-trained troops. The Imam of Yemen, the ruler of his country, was reported assassinated in a rebellion; the British government hastened to send warships to the war-stricken area to protect its nationals and interests, and Italy and France, sharing with Britain a grave view of this border disp

1934-10-19.text: Mildenhall Airdrome, England. (AP) — Veteran fliers cocked anxious eyes at the skies today as they made final preparations for a race halfway around the world. Some twenty-one planes will soar away tomorrow in quest of the fat prizes that await the winners at Melbourne. The race is in two sections, speed and handicap, and several pilots have entered both. The entrants are fervently hoping for good weather, for the 11,023-mile trail will take them over sea, mountains and desert.

(Copyright, 1934, Associated Press) London, Oct. 18.--Great Britain stands with the United States, France and Italy—against Japan—in wanting to continue basic principles of the Washington and London naval treaties, an official British source said today. That was Britain's reply to Japan's demand that the treaties be scrapped and other means of limiting navies be set up. “Japan wants equality.” Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, Japanese delegate to tri-power naval talks starting here next week, said yesterday as he disclosed that he would ask for abolition of the 5-5-3 ratio, long irksome to Nippon, and seek limitation on the global tonnage basis instead. As the British and American delegates to the conversations established their first contact, the British spokesman said his government wants the treaties continued with only relatively minor changes. At the same time, he said, the British will fa

London, Oct. 17 (4)—Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, Japanese delegate to the tri-power naval conversations here, said flatly today that Japan will demand abolition of the ratio system of limiting naval armaments. Instead, he revealed, the island empire will seek to substitute the global tonnage basis. These proposals will be made to the representatives of the United States and Great Britain in the course of the talks scheduled to start here next week. Yamamoto’s announcement came soon after authoritative sources had disclosed that the Americans, Norman H. Davis and Rear Admiral William H. Standley, will suggest substantial reduction in general naval armaments and renewal of the Washington and London naval treaties. (Under the terms of the Washington agreement, the United States and Great Britain are granted naval parity, with Japan permitted three-fifths of the armaments each has—the so-called

By ROBERT C. DOWSON (United Press Staff Correspondent) | MILDENHALL, ENGLAND, Oct. 19—(UP)—Three American airplane crews, and 18 from other countries, were ready today for the start at 6:30 a.m. tomorrow on the greatest aerial race ever run—the Mac Robertson International—from Mildenhall, in Suffolk, northeast of London, to Melbourne, Australia. At 45 second intervals the 21 planes will start for Baghdad, Mesopotamia, 2,553 miles away, the first compulsory stopping place on the 11,300 mile air-line route to Melbourne. There are intermediate checking points, which also are permissible landing places, at Marseilles, Rome, Athens and Aleppo, Syria. James A. and Amy Mollison, heroes of many record breaking flights, are to start first in their De Haviland Comet. Next will come the Americans, Roscoe Turner and Clyde Pangborn, in a Boeing Transport, followed by Col. James C. Fitzmaurice in the

LONDON, Oct. 19.—(/)—There is no chance of Great Britain re- turning to the gold standard as a result of measures to be taken at today's meeting of gold bloc nations at Brussels, well-informed financial circles say. England has officially proclaimed a determination to maintain the independence of the pound. This policy is expected to be supported as long as there is any possibility of currency fluctuations in the United States or other countries. (Plans to protect the gold standard are to be made at Brussels by a committee composed of representatives from France, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, Switzerland and Luxembourg). Foreign trade officials here consider that France is in a particularly uncertain position now and expect the British government to pursue a watchful waiting policy as long as there is any possibility of devaluation of the franc.

WASHINGTON, Oct. 18 (AP) — On sandalled feet, Madeleine Slade, famed English woman disciple of India’s Mahatma Gandhi, walked into the White House today and emerged with a new friend. Brilliant brown eyes flashing beneath the white cotton sari that covered her erect shoulders and much of her rough skirt of pleated brown, Miss Slade proved herself as democratic as her hostess. “I was immensely delighted with the democratic atmosphere,” she told the Associated Press. “No pomp and ceremony. You could just walk up to the White House as to any homely establishment. “I found Mrs. Roosevelt so charming. I enjoyed talking to her like I enjoy talking to a dear friend. One cannot say more.” Downtown Washington, which gasped 18 months ago when Mrs. Roosevelt walked from the Mayflower Hotel to the White House for a pre-inauguration visit, cast even more amazed glances at the daughter of the British

Mildenhall Airdrome, Eng.—(/)—John H. Wright of Utica, N. Y., long had the ambition of seeing the Prince of Wales. He more than achieved this Friday, for it developed into a case of the prince seeing Wright. The air-minded prince came out to inspect the planes which will take off Saturday in the race to Melbourne. After the inspection, the prince stood back and watched Wright put on an aerial display. The American turned the nose of his ship almost straight up in a display of steep climbing, then went into a series of Immelman turns for his royal audience. The prince shook hands with all the competitors. King George and Queen Mary motored to the airdrome to see the contestants. Plane Approved The plane of Miss Jacqueline Cochrane, New York, was weighed Friday and given official approval. LONDON, Oct. 19.—Some informed observers said today they believe Japan may suggest a global tonnage naval basis giving her a position midway between the present 5-5-3 ratio and parity. This belief was advanced as diplomatic and naval circles speculated over the extent Japan might go toward a compromise with the United States. These two countries open bi-lateral conversations next week with Great Britain in an effort to lay the groundwork for the 1935 naval conference. The biggest problem is to bridge the wide disparity between Japanese and American views. Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto’s refusal to say Japan wants equality in actual tonnage as well as equality in principle led to the belief he may take a stand midway between parity and the 5-5-3. So far British and American delegations firmly oppose changing the present relative positions. Spokesmen for the three nations, however, said the hop

1934-10-05.text: Hollywood, Cal., Oct. 5—(P)—Cary Grant, English born leading man of the films, was removed from his apartment today in a police ambulance suffering from what he said was poisoning but as to how it happened the actor remained silent. After receiving attention at the Hollywood receiving hospital Grant was permitted to return to his home. The police surgeon, Dr. C. E. Cornell, said his condition was not serious. Grant and his wife, Virginia Cherrill, separated last Saturday after a quarrel. Dr. Cornell quoted the actor as saying he had taken a poison tablet "under the stress of great worry." The landlady of Grant's apartment house, who refused to give her name, said the actor had been putting in call after call during the night for Miss Cherrill asking that she come to him.

SR RA SS Copyright, 1934, by The Associated Press MADRID, Oct. 5.—(PY)—At least 22 persons were killed and more than 100 wounded as virtual civil war between extremists and government forces threw Spain into bloody turmoil today. Six villages and cities including the important firearms manufacturing town of Eibar were captured by the extremists, who compacted into their forces Anarchists, communists and socialists. All six of the localities were recaptured in gun battles by soldiers, police, and Spain's famous civil guard—the Texas rangers of this republic. Planes Participate Airplanes roared into the fray, dispatched from government flying fields at Madrid to bomb the rebels into submission. No one knows how many were killed by airplanes that flew over the Pyrenees, across the land of the Basques, with orders to direct both bombs and machinegun fire at strongholds of extremists. By 6 p.

Madrid, Oct. 5.—Total known dead in the revolutionary general strike late this afternoon were more than 25, with many more wounded. The casualty list mounted rapidly as reports came in from the provinces, and it was feared the total dead and injured might exceed 100. At Mieres, in Asturias near Oviedo, rebels armed with modern rifles surrounded the government building, took the town hall and courthouse and threw the records into the streets, burning them. They then hoisted the red flag on the town hall. Two civil guards were killed. Twenty-one storm guards in the Mieres barracks were then surrounded and four of them were killed when they resisted. The remaining were wounded. In nearby Santullano, civil guards fortified themselves in a private house to repel an attack and several were killed. The trouble spread across the Mediterranean to Africa when workers in Ceuta, Spanish Morocco, dec

MADRID, (Copyright by AP). Revolutionary outbreaks in which at least three were killed came on the heels of a general strike which is challenging the authority of the new Spanish government. Strikers stormed the Montana Savoie barracks, and were repulsed by vicious fire from soldiers of the republic. In the Prosperidad district on the outskirts of the city strikers barricaded in a building exchanged hundreds of shots with a detachment of assault guards. Here also the demonstrators were defeated, and about 200 were arrested. Meanwhile the rightist government of Alejandro Lerroux, only a few hours old, was making a desperate fight for survival. It was understood that the new ministers, conferring while the bloody clashes were taking place in the streets of the city, had drawn up a decree of martial law. It was ready for instant promulgation, it was said in quarters close to the ministry. “

Preliminary reports stated that many were injured. The fight with the troops followed upon the killing of an assault guard whose detachment exchanged shots with disorderly demonstrators in the Prosperidad district. Two strikers were wounded in this encounter. In the clash at Prosperidad, on the outskirts of the city, strikers barricaded themselves in a house. MADRID, Friday, Oct. 5.—(U..)—Fatal clashes marked the first hours of the general strike called last midnight as socialists and communists made a united gesture against the government which threatened to break into revolt. Three persons were killed in shooting affrays. The most serious was in the suburb of Prosperidad where one storm guard was killed and a man wounded when guards raided a building where 50 youthful radicals reportedly were receiving Other gun battles occurred at San Vicente and near the old race track. Complete casualties were not ascertained immediately. Another raid on a private home in Prosperidad revealed a cache of 14 submachine guns and many pistols, authorities said. All workers affiliated with trades unions were expected to have joined the strike by dawn. Madrid, Oct. 5. (P)—A radical strike with the overthrow of the government as its announced aim swept Spain today and by noon nine persons were killed and an unestimated number wounded. Three civil guards, one assault guard and one extremist were reported killed in Asturias during several gunfire clashes. Several extremists were critically injured when strikers assaulted a civil guard attachment near the Selguera mine. Rush Assistance, The extremists were repulsed and authorities rushed reinforcements for the guards. It was reported that the attackers wore red socialist arm bands and used army type guns. At Fibar, gun manufacturing center, one extremist was killed and ten were wounded in an attempted assault on a factory. The government dispatched an airplane squadron to Asturias which is considered one of the extremist strongholds following the recent discovery of an armed plot there. Th

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 5. (4)— A plea for industrial peace through arbitration was voiced at the American Federation of Labor convention today by Miss Frances Perkins, secretary of labor. Making it plain that the government would not coerce either side in a capital and labor dispute, she asked for voluntary use of the mediation machinery the Roosevelt administration had set up.

1934-08-25.text: NOVOSIBIRSK, Aug. 24. — These folks got an entirely different alphabet where there is telegraph operators that can send messages in English. We are still in Siberia. If you think it's not big we have been for days and haven't made a dent in it. Wish I had Wiley Post here, This is his old round the world trail. Beautiful country, They are just harvesting the wheat. Women doing the harvesting and the men are at the depot. You know these folks got some ideas at that. Say you know all these big beautiful rivers we cross “run to the Arctic ocean. Nine o'clock at night and the sun's shining. WILL,

Washington --- (?) — Secretary Wallace expressed belief today that the world is headed toward an international AAA for wheat. Despite the adjournment of the international wheat advisory committee in London with little apparent success, the secretary said he had “substantial hope” the international agreement for adjusting production to world demand could be extended into 1935 and subsequent years. He hopes the next meeting of the committee, in Budapest Nov. 20, will succeed in adjusting differences. “Should an agreement be reached by the exporting and importing countries, either at the November meeting or later this winter, to continue restrictions of wheat acreage for next year’s crop, the United States would, of course, take whatever action would be necessary to comply with its commitments under the agreement,” he said. The AAA has announced a relaxation of its wheat control program, al

'By The Associated Press. PHOENIX, Ariz., Aug. 24.—Great Britain intervened today in the case of M. Rahmatula, Hindu, charged with cultivating a cotton patch in violation of the Arizona alien land law. Disturbed by threats—now withdrawn—of Salt River valley white farmers to initiate a “night riding” campaign against alien truck and cotton farmers who did not flee this district by next Saturday night, Wentworth Gurney, Los Angeles British consul, came to Phoenix to confer with Gov. B. B. Moeur.

NEWPORT, PEMBROKESHIRE, Wales, Aug. 25.—(?)}—Once they get back to America, George Pond and Cesare Sabelli said today, they would fly the Atlantic again within two months. Hard luck has followed them since they were forced down at Moy, Ireland, in May, after spanning the ocean. They made Rome, their original destination, after being forced down several times. On their return trip they crashed into a mountain near here several days ago. Despite their misfortunes, the fliers are setting up something of a record in persistence. Pond, his side tightly strapped as a result of the latest crash, and Sabelli came here to decide the best method of breaking the wreckage of their plane into small bits and shipping it to the United States. What remains of the plane is perched on a mountainside where it can’t be reached by truck.

Berlin—(UP)—Mrs. Sinclair Lewis, who writes under her maiden name of Dorothy Thompson, today was ordered by the secret police to leave Germany within 24 hours. The banishment order against the wife of the Nobel prize winner was based on her alleged hostile attitude toward Germany. Mrs. Lewis recently has written many magazine articles on Germany and the Hitler movement. It was privately reported that an interview with Hitler which she published in a magazine before he came to power had much to do with the expulsion order. Although she has been here scarcely a week, she is leaving tonight by the North express for Paris.

BOLOGNA, Italy, Aug. 24—The idea of war “is floating in the air,” and it behooves Italy, in preparation for any development to become a ‘militaristic, even warlike nation.’ Premier Mussolini said today in an address to 5,000 officers and military attaches at the conclusion of Italian army maneuvers. No one in Europe wishes war,” he said, standing on the turret of a heavy assault tank as he spoke. “But the thought of it is all around us. At the end of July an unforeseen situation developed which was similar to that which prevailed in 1914,” he continued. “If we had not sent our divisions to the front, complications might have resulted that could not have been solved except by the voice of the cannon. It is not necessary to be ready for the war of tomorrow, but for the war of today.” The entire Italian people, he added, today is ready to respond as a single unit in case of need.

BERLIN, Aug. 24 (AP)—The Nazi government has decided to put marriage on a “rational basis.” Eugenics officials issued today a list of ten commandments for the guidance of German youth when they face the complex business of marriage. "It's all right to marry for love, but the young couple must consider whether their marriage helps the nation." “Seek a mate—not a playmate—for matrimony,” says one commandment. It is also undesirable, warns another commandment, for anyone in good health not to marry. Not to “Remember always thou art German,” says commandment one. Number two urges “thou shalt not, if eugenically fit, remain unmarried. He who without solid reason does so, breaks the chain of the generation.” “Hold thy body clean,” says the third, which concludes with the injunction: “Remember you yourself are a German ancestor.” Number four—“Thou shalt keep the spirit and soul pure,” warns aga

BOLOGNA, Italy, Aug. 24—Benito Mussolini today told Fascist Italy to get ready for war. Speaking, appropriately enough, from the turret of an assault tank to 5,000 cheering officers and military attaches at the conclusion of Italian war maneuvers, the square-jawed premier said, “War can break out from one moment to the other.” “No one in Europe wants war,” Il Duce asserted, “but the idea of war is floating in the air. “It is not necessary to be ready for the war of tomorrow, but for the war of today. “We must become a military nation, even a militaristic nation, even—I might add—a warlike nation.” While Capt. Francis Brady, United States military attache, listened with the rest of the throng, Mussolini said war will accompany the fortunes of nations throughout the centuries, despite international good will conferences and treaties. “At the end of July,” he declared, “an unforeseen situat

1934-08-17.text: Toronto..(AP)—Despite information from an authoritative source that no ransom was paid to effect the release by kidnappers of John S. Labatt, London’s brewer, information was made public in Hamilton today that “less than $50,000 ransom was paid for the release of John Labatt.” This statement, made a few hours after the wealthy London, Ont., brewer had been released from a gang which held him captive sixty-five hours, followed one declaration that “not a cent of ransom was paid” and another that the complete $150,000 demanded had been put up.

TORONTO, Aug. 17—(AP)—John S. Labatt, wealthy brewer, returned to his home in London, Ont., today after 65 hours in the hands of kidnappers. The $150,600 ransom the kidnappers demanded was not paid, for the abductors released their victim as the Canadian police, including the famous Royal Mounted, moved ahead with British tenacity, to get their men. “Cold feet,” commented an authority, who disclosed that officials were determined to make an example of these first “snatch” gangsters in Canada’s history. Labatt was unharmed — unharmed but in a highly nervous state which sent him to bed. Police surrounded his home where he was reunited with his wife and children and visitors were not admitted, but a friend said he had not been physically injured. The brewer suffers from a heart ailment. His family had suffered anguish in his absence, for they feared the strain of his experience would kill h

London, Aug. 11. (AP)—The United States was tentatively allocated a 1934-35 wheat export quota of 10,000,000 bushels by the international wheat conference today, the Associated Press was informed by an official source. Argentina’s export quota was placed at 150,000,000 bushels, this source added. It was extremely doubtful that these figures would be altered, he said, expressing confidence no appreciable change in them would be made at any rate. The low figure set for the United States was a startling one to observers, although it was known she was willing to accept a considerable reduction because of the drought. It had been said on good authority 30,000,000 bushels would be acceptable to Washington. Argentina had asked an allotment of 150,000,000 bushels for export.

Labatt, kidnapped London (Ont.) brewer, was believed to be held by his abductors in a farmhouse in western Ontario. Although he did not reveal the source of his information, the officer said the Labatt family had made two contacts with the kidnappers through Hugh Labatt, a brother, while he was in Toronto. The whole investigation took a new turn late Thursday when it was learned that Hugh Labatt had been absent from the hotel room here where he had been conducting telephone negotiations, presumably with the kidnappers, on a secret mission since early Thursday. Further revelations disclosed the discovery of witnesses to the kidnapping of the wealthy brewer, near Sarnia at the family’s summer home. TORONTO, Aug. 17—(Friday)—(AP)—An unconfirmed report early this morning said John Labatt, kidnapped Tuesday by gangsters, had appeared at a hotel in Toronto. Police refused to discuss the report, saying there were no developments. The unconfirmed rumors said the wealthy London, Ont. brewer had been seen at the hotel, a different one from where his brother, Hugh, waited for contact with the kidnappers, and was in a badly shaken condition. The report said he appeared about 1:00 a.m. E.D.T. this morning. Another rumor which followed the report Labatt had returned to a hotel here said at least one of his kidnappers had been caught. Police also refused to confirm this.

LONDON, Aug. 18, ()—Princess Trina Youssoupoff receives $250,000 under the terms of the settlement of her libel suits against Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, Ltd., Fanny Holtzmann, chief of the Princess’ American counsel, announced tonight. In addition, the motion picture producers are to pay the costs involved in prosecution of Princess Youssoupoff's suit based on the film “Rasputin and The Empress.” The costs were estimated at between $65,000 and $75,000.

New York, Aug. 16—(UP)—Mrs. James Roosevelt, 80 years old mother of the president, returned from the Ile de France today happy to be home again despite a triumphal visit to England and France, but somewhat concerned over whether "Franklin" will like the tweed suit she bought him: "I do hope he will like it," she said anxiously. "The cloth is lovely." As usual "my boy, Franklin" monopolized Mrs. Roosevelt's thoughts, conversing with an animation that belied her years, she told of the interest in the president manifested by persons she met in Europe. "There was a great deal in the papers about you when you were abroad," a reporter remarked. "Isn't that complimentary," replied Mrs. Roosevelt, "It takes the newspapers to say beautiful things about people." She was asked about her visit with King George and Queen Mary of England. "We chatted most pleasantly about different things," she said.

| By The Associated Press Seymour, Texas, Aug. 17—Miss Ruby Britain, 40-year-old member of a prominent West Texas family, remained silent today on a charge of murder filed against her in connection with the roadside slaying of H. Nichols, Seymour bank official. Nichols was shot as he sat in an automobile on a country lane with Miss Willie Mae Couch, 19. Another woman drove up to his car, opened fire with a pistol, and drove away. Miss Britain was charged with murder after a car identified as hers had been found abandoned half a mile from the scene. Nichols’ widow and two children survive.

1934-08-12.text: LONDON () — An exiled Russian princess who had, she says, an unwanted and implied role in the motion picture, “Rasputin and the Empress,” has collected a huge sum — some sources said $750,000 — from the producers. The fortune was paid to Princess Trina Alexandrovna Youssoupoff by Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer as balm for the film’s alleged libel of the former Russian noblewoman. Miss Fannie Holtzmann, American attorney for the princess, said today the settlement was the largest she “ever heard of” in a libel case. The company paid the money out of court to forestall threatened suits in a number of other countries, after Princess Youssoupoff won a $127,000 verdict here. Miss Holtzmann stoutly declined to name the amount of the settlement, which makes the film one of the most costly in Hollywood history. But she said published reports that the sum was $750,000 were erroneous. “They are all guessing
