HAVANA, Sept. 2 (AP) — Police and students, traditionally foes in Cuba, clashed again here Saturday. Several hours of virtual siege of Havana University, where some 296 students sniped at police drawn up along nearby streets, ended bloodlessly as the students surrendered in small groups. Police released all those students they found unarmed. Those with weapons were taken into custody. The students, said to be members of radical groups, assembled at the university to protest the death of Tiedolfo Fernandes Sanchez, 22-year-old "bad man", who was killed early Saturday, officers said, when his friends fired on police guarding him. Twice before Fernandez Sanchez had been taken from the hands of the law. He was wounded last July 17 when machine gunners attacking parading members of the A B C political society, killing 15 and wounding scores, and was identified as one of those participating in

WASHINGTON— (U.P)— America’s first nationwide labor strike of nearly 1,000,000 textile workers became effective at 11:30 p.m., Saturday, after failure of last minute peace negotiations. The walkout in reality was technical. Mills throughout New England and the south were dark. They were closed as a matter of course Saturday. Most of them will remain closed Sunday and Labor day. The crisis will begin when whistles summon spinners and weavers in the cotton, woolen,

MOSCOW, Aug. 30.—These Russians sure believe in mass production. Just come from the race meet and they had 36 races. They run the Soviet derby today. All the horses belonged to the government but are raised and entered by different parts of the army and the collective farms. Half of 'em running and half trotting races. When the trotters come out old David Harum wanted to come down and take over the ribbons. Tomorrow I am trying out Russia's commercial aviation, flying down through the Ukraine and Caucasus to the Black Sea. Yours, WILL.

WARSAW, Poland. (P). Two hundred and fifty persons were reported dead and 1,400 seriously ill in an epidemic of dysentery raging at Krzemieniec, city of 10,000 population near the Russian border. Public markets and assembly halls in the city were ordered closed in an effort to halt the spread of the disease. While the cause of the epidemic was not announced, unofficial reports ascribed it to contaminated fruit and other foodstuffs.

MOSCOW.--I met a guy today that could remember back to the time when there was a czar in Russia. Trotsky was pressing pants in New York and Upton Sinclair was away uptown, Texas steers had long horns and governments paid their debts. Flying south through Soviet Russia and the oil wells smelled like regular capitalistic oil. Yours, WILL ROGERS.

GENEVA, Sept. 1—(/)—Nazi Germany stood formally accused tonight of providing military training for 16,000 German residents of the Saar in preparation for the plebiscite in that region Jan. 13. The Saar will vote early next year to rejoin Germany, join France or remain under League of Nations mandate. Documentary Proof, The League of Nations’ commission now governing the Saar today advised the league's home offices that it had discovered documentary proof that Saarlanders are being given military training in German labor camps. So serious did it consider the situation, the commission said, that it has drafted an order banning the German labor organization from the Saar and instructing youths now enrolled to report to police for surveillance. A Nazi “Putsch” to force a pro-German vote in the plebiscite was hinted at in some league quarters here. Seize Documents, Documents seized in the off

1934-04-13.text: Dublin, Irish Free State, April 13 — Lady Ashley and the man her husband named as correspondent in his pending divorce action, Douglas Fairbanks, sr, were reported today as being members of a house party at Luttrellstown castle in Clonsilla, near Dublin. They were said to be the guests of the Honorable Brinsley Plunkett, owner of the castle. Fairbanks and Lady Ashley were seen together after their arrival in Dublin, Residents in the district said they were expecting the party to go hunting.

DUBLIN, Irish Free State, April 17 — (AP) — Over the same route by which American Minister William Wallace McDowell recently traveled from Cobh to Dublin, his body will be returned tomorrow by special train for shipment to the United States on the liner Manhattan. The American envoy, who died at a banquet given in his honor Monday night, is being returned to his native land for burial. The American legation and the Department of External Affairs completed arrangements today for the ceremonial removal of the body from the legation to the railway station. Full state honors due the representative of a great and friendly nation will be accorded the late minister. The coffin, borne upon a gun carriage, will be escorted by Free State troops with customary impressive observances attended by representatives of the government, the Dáil Éireann, the Senate, foreign diplomats and representatives of

BOSTON, April 12 (#)—Torrential rain and melting snow tonight had overtaxed many New England rivers. Caused floods and washouts and necessitated the rescue of persons in marooned homes. A flood warning was issued for the Winooski valley in Vermont as the Winooski river continued to rise. All over Vermont and New Hampshire, roads were reported either flooded or washed out.

ASCOT, England, (UP) — The Prince of Wales’ cairn terrier Jiggs was lost today and police were searching for it over a wide area. The dog strayed from the prince's country residence, Fort Belvedere. Wales telephoned today from Glasgow to inquire regarding the search for Jiggs.

PANDERMA, TURKEY, April 13.—(—Samuel Insull turned jokester today while en route to Smyrna, where a ship waits to return him to the United States for trial. To the surprise of fellow passengers he cast off his appearance of despair during the night voyage by ship from Istanbul to this Marmora sea port. He even joked about the seven-man Turkish escort. “It is remarkable,” he said in jest, “that I should need an escort of seven. I'm perfectly harmless.” The fact that he was beginning a journey against which he fought a year and a half before finally being jailed by Turkish authorities at Washington's request, did not disturb Insull’s sleep. He was sleeping soundly when the Adarm docked here at 3 a.m. He was taken ashore at 6:15. Half an hour later he was aboard the train, Smyrna-bound. The train was due at Smyrna, about 175 miles from Panderma, at 8:30 o'clock tonight. There, aboard the Am

En route to Smyrna, Turkey, April 13—A new and confident Samuel Insull, seemingly reconciled to extradition, was to be handed over to the American Federal Government in Smyrna Harbor today. Shaking off the depression that gripped him during his detention at Istanbul, the 74-year-old utilities man, facing trial on fraud charges, braced up on the ship rail journey to Smyrna and the American steamship Exilona. He chatted pleasantly and fired wisecracks at newspaper men. This was aboard the little passenger packet Adana, which took Insull from Istanbul to Panderma, where at 6:30 a.m. today he entrained for Smyrna and the Exilona, to be handed over formally to Burton Y. Berry, third secretary of the American legation to Turkey, and then to be entrusted for the 5,000-mile voyage to Boston to Major John A. Crane, American Military Attaché, and Captain Wensel Habel of the Exilona. Insull almost

Istanbul, April 13--Quietly and calmly, Samuel Insull started Thursday the long trip to the United States where the fraud and bankruptcy charges he has evaded 18 months await him. The 74 year old former utilities czar was taken under guard from the Istanbul house of detention to the steamer Adana bound for Bandirma. Later he will be taken by train to Smyrna and placed in the hands of Burton Y. Berry, of the United States embassy, aboard the S. S. Exilona, which sails Friday for America.

MOSCOW, April 12 ()—A saga of the sea, unparalleled in modern times, reached a dramatic conclusion tonight as Soviet pilots rescued the last six persons of a party of 102 marooned on an Arctic Sea ice floe two months ago. The aviators a few hours earlier conquered hazards of the far north and brought 22 to the mainland at Cape Van Karem, Siberia, from the dangerous ice pack on which they sought refuge when their ship, the Cheliuskin, was crushed in the ice Feb. 13 and sank. “Pilots Vodopianoff and Doronin, who effected the rescue of the last survivors, had flown by easy stages, from Khabarovsk to Cape Van Karem, from which point they made their flights.” A brief dispatch from Cape Van Karem said Professor Otto Schmidt, commander of the Wrangell Island Expedition aboard the Cheliuskin, had been taken by airplane to Nome, whence he might be flown to Fairbanks, Alaska, for treatment for a

1934-05-24.text: Cardiff, Wales, May 24. (AP)—Capt. George Pond and Lieut. Cesare Sabelli arrived at the airdrome here today with the engine of their transatlantic plane Leonardo da Vinci knocking and smoking. They had flown from Port Talbot, Wales, where they were forced down earlier in the day on an attempted non-stop flight from Dublin to Rome. The motor that failed them just as they reached land after flying the Atlantic cut out again at Port Talbot, disappointing the two fliers once more. They made emergency repairs at Port Talbot and reached Cardiff without mishap. General repairs will be effected here before they start out again.

WASHINGTON, May 24. The United States, Great Britain and Japan were said authoritatively today to be engaged in preliminary conversations concerning the feasibility of holding discussions on naval questions prior to the Washington naval conference next year. William Phillips, undersecretary of state, declined any official comment on the discussions, but it was understood the first overtures for an exploratory survey of naval questions came from Great Britain and Japan. Japan Wants Revision. Japan, through official spokesmen, has announced on numerous occasions that she would demand a revision of the present five-five-three naval ratio established at the London and Washington conferences. Japanese officials also have suggested that a preliminary discussion between the three nations on questions especially pertaining to the Pacific would go a long way toward clearing the atmosphere for the

BALDONNEL AIRPORT, DUBLIN, May 24 (Thursday) (®) — George Pond and Lieutenant Cesare Sabelli took off for Rome shortly after 6:30 a. m. today (12:30 a. m. Eastern standard time) to complete their flight from New York.

TOKYO, May 24 (A) — Secretary Swanson’s insistence on maintenance of the 5-5-3 treaty naval ratios as among the United States, Great Britain and Japan, evoked today a strong official expression of Japan's refusal to agree to an extension of present limitations and agreements beyond 1936. Japan insists that the Washington and London treaties be replaced "by new agreements fairer and more reasonable, and affording Japan genuine sense of security," said Rear Admiral Teuneyoshi Bakano, chief of the navy office's propaganda bureau, in a written statement to the press. "The Washington ratios menace the Japanese empire's safety," the statement said. "The Washington treaty was framed to meet special conditions immediately after the war and now long outdated. "Armaments compacts must be offered in accordance with changed political, scientific and technical conditions. The London treaty was a temp

Prestwick, Scotland, May 24.~(U. P.) —Johnny Goodman, of Omaha, American open champion and heavy favorite, was eliminated from the British amateur gold championship, in the fifth round today. Goodman's conqueror was L. G. Garnett, of Addington, a former tournament player. The score 2 and 1. Goodman was the second American casualty of the day, for Jesse Guilford, of Boston, passed out during the fourth round played this morning.

PRESTWICK, Scotland, May 4. (AP). Johnny Goodman, American open champion and betting-odds favorite, was defeated in the fifth round of the British Amateur Golf Championship today by Leslie Garnett, an Englishman, 3 and 2. The surprising defeat of the young Omaha star stripped the championship of the first two favorites. Jack McLean, crack Scottish Walker Cup player, was defeated this afternoon by James Wallace, an unemployed carpenter, by 1 up. The only Americans left in the championship were: George T. Dunlap, Jr., United States amateur champion, and W. Lawson Little, San Francisco husky, who are among the eight survivors for the quarter-finals to be played tomorrow morning. They are in opposite halves of the draw.

PORT DARWIN, Northern Australia, May 23—-(AP)—Petite Jean Batten, who refused to quit trying after two failures, today made a new aviation record for women by completing a flight from England to Australia in 14 days, 23 hours and 25 minutes. The 24-year old New Zealand girl brought her old wooden Moth plane, which has been in use for nearly five years, down at 4 p.m. local time (1:30 a.m. Eastern Standard Time), to cut four and a half days off the previous woman’s record, set by Amy Johnson, wife of Capt. James A. Mollison. “I had an adventurous trip,” she said upon her arrival, “the weather was frightful throughout — where can I get a cup of tea?” On the last stage of her trip, across the Timor Sea, headwinds blew her plane miles south of the course, she said, but she managed to battle through and had no difficulty in finally locating Port Darwin. Miss Batten, who acted as her mechanic,

LONDON, May 23. (UP) — British financial leaders were pictured in well-informed quarters today as being highly alarmed by the prospect that President Roosevelt's silver monetization program will blast their hopes for the return of Great Britain to the gold standard in the near future. Despite the nonchalant attitude they assumed toward the American president's message, financial circles were pictured as being thrown into gloom.

1934-04-27.text: - Boston, April 26.—(P)—The discovery in New England of a large portion of the $50,000 ransom money paid by Col. Charles A. Lindbergh after the kidnapping of his infant son was reported and denied today. Late editions of Boston newspapers announced that more than half of the $50,000 which Dr. John F. (Jafsie) Condon tossed over a Bronx cemetery wall as ransom for return of the kidnapped son of Colonel Charles A. Lindbergh had turned up through the federal reserve bank in Boston. The child was found dead after payment of the ransom two years ago. William W. Paddock, deputy governor of the bank, denied any knowledge of the recovery of the money, which was said in the published reports to amount to as much as $380,000, unloaded in amounts of $4,000 and $5,000 during the past six months. At Rutland, Vt., Boston newspapers said a group of thirty or more department of justice agents had been c

WASHINGTON, APR. 27, (AP).-—J. Edgar Hoover, director of the justice department's division of investigation, today described as “without a scintilla of truth” reports published in Boston that a large amount of the $50,000 Lindbergh ransom money had been found in New England. The reports, he said, apparently grew out of a visit to Vermont last weekend of ten special agents of the division in an investigation of an extortion case. The investigation had “nothing on earth to do with the Lindbergh case,” Hoover asserted. The extortion case failed to develop, (Earlier reports concerning the ransom rumors are published on Page 17)

LONDON, April 27.—Great Britain has warned Germany in strong terms against applying a transfer moratorium to the Dawes and Young reparations loans, it was learned today as Germany's creditors assembled at Berlin to discuss the situation. It was reported, but not confirmed, that both Great Britain and the United States communicated with the German government several days ago. In any event, Sir Eric Phipps, British ambassador at Berlin, visited Baron Von Neurath, German foreign minister yesterday and told him Great Britain would “take a grave view of any such proposal.” There was some expectation here that American Ambassador to Germany William E. Dodd might make a similar visit. It was intimated officially here that Phipps told Neurath that the Dawes and Young loans were raised under the auspices of foreign governments and are governed by agreements reached at London at the 1924 conferenc

TOKYO, April 21—(INS)—Fearing the United States, Great Britain, and other signatories of the Nine-Power Treaty might invoke the pact to force her to explain herself, Japan today capitulated and decided officially to elucidate her “unofficial” policy of “hands off China.” A formal statement will be issued and signed by Foreign Minister Koki Hirota fully explaining the unofficial statement issued by the foreign office spokesman to the press several days ago, startling the world with the declaration Japan would not approve of foreign military and economic aid to China. The decision to offer an official version of the Japanese policy followed a firm request by Great Britain for such a step, and a milder request for elucidation made by American Ambassador Joseph C. Grew. Previously, the Japanese foreign office had taken the stand that “enough had been said,” and that

Tokio, April 27—Japan will maintain silence until Great Britain announces its view of her far eastern declarations, it was indicated today. A statement from Sir John Simon, British foreign minister, is due in the House of Commons Monday. Some newspapers have suggested the advisability of a formal government clarification of the declarations, but Koki Hirota, foreign minister, was understood to believe that the issue will evaporate.

MADRID, April 27 (®)—President Alcala Zamora today named Ricardo Samper Ibanez, resigned minister of industry and commerce, to form a new government. The president’s action came after three days in which Spain was without a cabinet, and monarchists commented upon the fact that such a situation was unheard of in the days of the King. The appointment came while some factions still clamored for the reappointment of Alejandro Lerroux, who resigned with his cabinet Wednesday.

BUXAR, India, April 26 (@) — The Mahatma Gandhi narrowly escaped serious injury today when his automobile was attacked with stones and clubs by a crowd opposing his campaign to assist the “untouchable” class. Gandhi, who not so long ago was considered by many in this country as almost a god, was unharmed, but three of his followers were injured and the car was badly battered. The little nationalist leader, world famous because of his campaigns and fasts to achieve his point, was returning from a propaganda tour in Assam and Harijan, where he had met extremely strong opposition from orthodox Hindus known as Stantanists. On reaching Buxar the Gandhi party found excitement at a high pitch among the local Hindus. Resentment rapidly grew until it culminated in the attack on the automobile. The mahatma’s appeal for non-violence — a creed to which thousands subscribed a few years ago — brought

GENEVA, April 23 Indications that Japan may exert effort to block the heralded League of Nations’ ten-year plan for the reconstruction of China unless the powers recognize Manchukuo were reported today in reliable quarters. International circles spoke also of the possibility that the Japanese will charge Dr. Ludwig Rajchman—the League's envoy to China who is now returning here with a project for helping China financially and socially—in the belief he wields political influence over Chinese leaders. These reports formed a background to a Japanese statement of April 17 in which T. Kyu stated foreign aid to China that had political significance should be secured by force if necessary. Chinese Leaders Appeal Chinese leaders mean while sat on the “hands-off” pronouncement with the possibility of Japanese overlordship and considered appealing to signatories—including the United States—of a nin

1934-04-17.text: LONDON, April 17 (#)---Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the Exchequer, declared to the House of Commons today that he did not propose to make any provision for the payments of war debts to America or the receipts of war debts from Great Britain’s debtors. ‘His statement was made in the midst of a speech in which he said Great Britain now had “regained its place as the first exporting country of the world.” He told his listeners, who cheered him repeatedly, that the past fiscal year had shown a profit of £39,000,000—or about $200,000,000--and that “the atmosphere is distinctly brighter.” He listed sources of revenue in proposing his budget for the year 1934-35 and said that in the year past the beer tax had produced $5,000,000 more than expected but that there had been a deficit in the revenues from tea and sugar. Groans followed cheers with this announcement.

Chicago..-(AP)—His attorneys objecting in vain, John Factor was held by the government today to await a presidential warrant which would send him back to England for trial as the alleged perpetrator of a gigantic mining stock fraud. Federal Judge Philip L. Sullivan dismissed a habeas corpus writ and ordered his detention. While United States marshals were preparing to take him to the Sycamore, Ill., county jail, his attorneys succeeded in arranging for Factor to remain in custody at a Chicago hotel.

LONDON, April 17. — (UP)—Great Britain adheres to her policy of refusing to pay her war debt to the United States pending negotiations for revision or cancellation, Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, revealed in presenting the 1934-1935 budget to the house of commons today. Despite a treasury surplus at the end of the fiscal year on April 1 of $160,567,940 and a prospective surplus of revenue over expenses in the current budget of $149,350,000, Chamberlain made no provision in the budget for war debt payments nor for reparations receipts. He did the same thing in the preceding two years. Nevertheless, Britain has been making small “token” payments to Washington to avoid being openly in default, and it was generally assumed such a payment would be made this year, outside of the budget.

London, April 17,—No provision for a war debt payment to the United States was made in the British budget which was presented to the House of Commons today. In addition to making no provision for war debt payments, not even a token payment, Chamberlain said he was budgeting no receipts from reparations. Failure to budget for a token payment, however, was not taken to mean that Britain may not make such a payment, deriving the money from the treasury or other sources outside of budget revenues. Chamberlain pointed out he had made no provision for war debt payments or reparations receipts in either of the preceding two years. “In the absence of any fresh developments,” he said, “I propose to follow precisely the same course.”

CHICAGO, April 17—-(UP)—John (Jake the Barber) Factor, wanted in England on charges of swindling investors there of $7,000,000 in a stock company venture, today was ordered into custody of U. S. Marshal H. C. W. Laubenheimer for confinement pending his extradition. The one-time Halsted street barber who became a multi-millionaire won the privilege of becoming a prisoner in his hotel room with a plea that he feared violence from fellow prisoners if he were sent to jail. "I helped the state send four gangsters to prison for kidnapping me," Factor argued with Federal Judge Philip Sullivan. "The underworld hates me. If I am sent to a jail I'm afraid of what might happen." Judge Sullivan ordered Deputy Marshal to telephone Assistant Attorney General Joseph Keenan in Washington, Keenan consented to confinement of the speculator in his own hotel apartment and Sullivan so worded his order. Facto

Chicago, April 17 (AP)—John Factor, the barber who became an international speculator and promoter, was ordered removed to the county jail at Sycamore, Ill. today to await arrival of a presidential warrant for his return to England to be prosecuted. Factor had done his job of testifying for the state against the four Touhy gangsters sentenced to prison for kidnapping him. The state made no further effort today to defer his extradition to London, where he must face a trial for an alleged $7,000,000 coup in mining stocks. Technically, the charge against the erstwhile Chicago banker was that of receiving money he knew to have been obtained fraudulently by his Broad Street Press, Ltd., an investment house.

LONDON, April 17.—Improved conditions, internal and external, have led Josef Stalin, Soviet Russia's leader, to launch a plan for revolutionary reorganization of the country's judicial system. The change involves not only the abolition of the dreaded OGPU, the secret political police, but an important democratization of the entire method of conducting prosecutions. It had been known that the OGPU was to be abolished, but the United Press is able today to give for the first time an authentic outline of the changes. The government is to be deprived of the executive power to impose the death sentence, or to impose prison penalties or edicts condemning offenders to long exile. Perhaps even more significant is the fact that it is planned soon to put into effect a measure by which persons accused of offenses hitherto warranting summary punishment by the OGPU—even execution without trial—will b

WASHINGTON, April 17—(CUP)—The silver drive was resumed in the House today coincident with receipt from Spain of formal notification that the London conference silver agreement has been ratified. Peru remains the only non-ratifying signatory of the agreement. WASHINGTON, April 17—While administration leaders began whipping Congress into line for President Roosevelt's remaining legislative program, the Congressional silver bloc today sought Rooseveltian support for their silver remonetization program. The silver bloc took a page from Mr. Roosevelt's own notebook. They sent an emissary to the White House to arrange a conference with the President on silver legislation. The bloc’s leaders expressed hope of converting the President to their remonetization program. The Senate held the stage both for the President’s program and for silver legislation. After conferring with Mr. Roosevelt, the l

1934-06-08.text: Geneva, June 8 (UP) — France and Great Britain, making mutual sacrifices in an effort to save the disarmament conference from failure, today approved a resolution designed to bring Germany back to it. Tired and pale, a small group of conference leaders dispatched copies of the resolution to London and Paris in the early hours of this morning. On the decision of the British and French foreign offices, they said, the conference’s fate rested. Before noon the replies came back—favorably. Davis Gets Credit To Norman H. Davis, chief American delegate, went most of the credit. He worked unremittingly for nearly 24 hours to bring the British and French together as the sole means of saving the conference. Davis, wreathed in smiles, received the United States press and said the present agreement will be a serious disappointment to people who do not want peace in Europe. He said in substance that

WHIPSNADE, England. June 8 iP — Helpless spectators, led by a Catholic priest, prayed for a 200 attendant here yesterday as four lions tore him to death. The priest was among the crowd attracted to the pit when L. Stetson, 26, went into it to recover a hat blown from the head of a spectator. While Stetson was meeting a horrible death, unconscious of what was going on outside, the clergyman offered a prayer. Scores of those about the enclosure respectfully bowed their heads. Keepers at the open air zoo said they believed the lions first went for Stetson playfully, but having drawn blood, their natural instinct was to kill. One witness of the tragedy noticed that two other lions in the pit looked on unconcernedly. They had just been fed. Two lions were killed before — could recover the man's life.

GENEVA, June 7 (4)--After long discussion of their varying viewpoints, representatives of the United States, Great Britain and France agreed late tonight on a program for the disarmament conference. The nature of the agreement was not revealed further than that it is a compromise between the proposals of Arthur Henderson, president of the conference, for an adjournment while political differences are cleared up, and that of Louis Barthou, French foreign minister, for the conference to go ahead with certain studies. However, the Associated Press learned the compromise provides specifically for negotiations by governments for the return of Germany to the conference. It was understood France made big concessions in order to save the conference. Barthou and other French delegates were said to be in a conciliatory mood. "The study of international security will be based on guarantees for loya

LONDON, June 8.—(#)—The blackshirts of Sir Oswald Mosley, who wishes to place England under a dictatorship similar to that of Italy, engaged in a pitched battle last night with opponents they described as “reds.” Some of the fascists were dressed in evening clothes as they fought hecklers, armed with razors. More than 100 were hurt, some seriously, and 20 were taken to jail before police finally quelled the disorder.

GENEVA, June 7.—A compromise agreement was reached tonight by representatives of the United States, Great Britain and France on a disarmament conference program, providing negotiations for the return of Germany. After a long discussion upon varying viewpoints following a dinner given by the French foreign minister, M. Barthou, announcement was made that an agreement had been reached on a program to rescue the faltering conference. Although the nature of the agreement was not fully revealed, it was said to be a compromise between the proposal of Arthur Henderson, president of the conference, for an adjournment while political differences are cleared up, and that of Barthou for the conference to go ahead with certain studies. The Associated Press learned that the compromise provides specifically for negotiations by governments for the return of Germany to the conference.

WHIPSNADE, England, June 7 (*)—While horrified spectators looked on, four lions in an open air zoo Thursday killed a zoo employee who had gone into their pit to recover a visitor’s hat. The owner of the hat and several other persons who tried to save the victim, Stanley Lewis Stenson, were driven back by the lions. Stenson went into the enclosure between the outer barrier and the railing surrounding the pit in which the lions are kept. As he crawled along the top of the inside railing two lions reached through the bars and began mauling him. The two other lions joined in the attack through the bars. Stenson then fell into the pit, striking his head on the concrete about 16 feet below. The lions dragged him further into the pit and killed him as the horrified spectators screamed and several women fainted. The keepers had to shoot two of the lions before they were able to drive the others

New York, June 8 (AP)—Eight lives were lost, 500 persons were made homeless, as a hurricane that caused damage estimated at $1,500,000 swept San Salvador Thursday and last night Pan American Airways reported today. Martial law was declared as a result of the complete collapse of communication facilities, light and power lines and railroad travel. The reports, wirelessed to Pan American Airways, via its airport in Salvador, which escaped damage, said many large buildings in the capital were partially demolished. Homes in residential districts were washed away by heavy rains, the report said, while the highway to La Libertad was left impassable.

Washington, June 8 (A4) - President Roosevelt told Congress today that he is preparing a vast plan of special insurance for the security "of the citizen and his family." This, with another national plan for land and water resources, will be laid before Congress next winter. In his longest message to the national legislature, the chief executive said: "People want decent homes to live in; they want to locate them where they can engage in productive work; and they want some safeguard against misfortunes which cannot be wholly eliminated in this man-made world of ours." Mentions Housing Bill Regarding homes, he said the government has already appropriated millions for housing, and in a housing bill now before the legislature, can "stimulate the lending of money" — to modernize homes and build new ones. Of the "problem of readjustment of the population," he said "hundreds of thousands of fam

1934-06-22.text: VIENNA, June 22—(AP)—Ivan Poderjay, whose most recent wife, Miss Agnes Tufverson of Detroit and New York, is missing, was held in jail today on a suspicion of murder and bigamy. The wife whom he married March 22, 1933, in London, Marguerite Susanne Ferrand, is held on a suspicion of having profited by a murder. Despite these suspicions which, under Austrian law, are sufficient to hold both of the suspects in jail, the police said they were most anxious to hear some definite charges against the couple. The Austrian authorities are making it clear that they have no desire to conduct the entire investigation of Poderjay. Not only does the expense of the investigation worry the police, but they also pointed out that they are smothered with political offenses which should be cleared up. Some 2,700 cases are awaiting final disposition. Police Force Kept Busy The police executives are burning m

Kopervick, Karmoy Island, Norway, June 21. (#)—Capt. Peter Moeller of the wrecker German liner, Dresden, told authorities today that the rock upon which the Dresden struck yesterday was not marked on the English admiralty chart being used as his navigation guide. Testifying at an inquiry into the accident, which damaged the Dresden so badly that she sank after 1,000 passengers had been rescued from her, Captain Moeller said he was depending on a pilot in waters with which he was unfamiliar. Pilot Jacobsen, a Norwegian, informed the court that Capt. Moeller had not asked him whether he had a pilot’s certificate covering Rysylke fjord. Previously Jacobsen had assumed responsibility for the disaster. Today he said that when it was decided to enter Rysylke fjord instead of following an originally proposed route he told the captain he did not know those particular waters. He said he was sure

LONDON, June 22--The decision of Premier Ramsay MacDonald to take at least a three months rest, leaving Stanley Baldwin in command of Great Britain's national government, aroused parliamentary circles today over the future of the regime established as a result of the financial crisis of 1931. Downing Street confirmed MacDonald's holiday plan but announced doctors had advised the premier to go abroad. There is a possibility he will make a trip to the United States or Canada, but at least the first week is expected to be spent at Lossiemouth, Scotland, his home. Should MacDonald's health not respond to the rest treatment, informed observers consider his present retreat would provide a graceful means of political retirement. But that emphatically is not the premier’s present intention. His hope is to build up his strength for the autumn session of parliament, which will provide the greatest

London, June 22; Seven days of evidence in the society divorce action brought by Edward Frank Willis James, brother of Mrs. Marshall Field, against his wife, Tilly Losch James, the beautiful Viennese dancer, was completed today before a courtroom of brilliantly dressed spectators who twittered over scandalous tid-bits. James alleged that his wife was guilty of misconduct with Prince Serge Odolensky, a member of an old Russian family. Both Mrs. James and the Prince denied the allegations, and the wife entered a cross petition for a judicial separation. She alleged cruelty; her husband denied that. At the conclusion of the evidence, the correspondent’s attorney, Roland Oliver, addressed the jury on behalf of the Prince. Then the case was adjourned until Tuesday. The evidence revealed that, after the honeymoon, when Mrs. James was playing in the musical show “The Band Wagon” in New York, th

MANSFIELD, June 23 (UP) Praise of President Roosevelt echoed from a platform here last night as leaders of Democrats and aspirants to nominations for high public positions stepped into the primary campaign. Governor George White and Congressman Charles F. West, Granville, brought loudest applause as they took introductory bows in their race for the United States Senate nomination. The Richland-Jeffersonian elite planned and directed the meeting. West and Governor White made appeals for support of the administration recovery program in which liberalism rung out. West has been regarded as the national administration’s choice for the nomination and as most likely to defeat Senator Sircon Fess in November. Governor White launched into an extemporaneous talk that rivaled that of Congressman West in its defense of Roosevelt's work. Democrats are afraid of the dictatorship of a few high financi

READING, June 21.— () —A little band of Pennsylvania Civil War veterans, survivors of thousands who fought to preserve the union today approved the idea of passing to their sons the responsibility of perpetuating the ideals of the Grand Army of the Republic. By unanimous vote the handful of "Boys in Blue" at the annual encampment adopted the suggestion of the Sons of Union Veterans to make that organization the legal successor of the Grand Army. By their action they placed the proposal before the council of administration, governing body of the Grand Army. From that group it will go to the national convention at Rochester, N. Y., in August. The plan was presented to the veterans by J. H. Wentzel, of Uniontown, past department commander of the Sons of Union Veterans. Wentzel said that in many places where the G. A. R. posts have been reduced to a few veterans, the Sons of Union Veterans a

LONDON, June 22.— (A). Great Britain has invited Germany to “talk over” her debts and the six-months moratorium. The invitation is contained in a strongly-worded note from Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, to Baron Von Hoesch, the German Ambassador in London, in which the British minister declined to accept the German grounds for default on the Young and Dawes Loans.

LONDON, June 22 (AP)—The queen of the seas is abdicating. England's giant Cunard liner Mauretania, which smashed transatlantic crossing records with almost monotonous consistency for more than 20 years, is to be scrapped, it was reported today. She leaves June 30 on her final run to New York. When she goes to the graveyard the Mauretania leaves a colorful history—not all of it concerned with lowering minutes on the run between continents. She carried thousands of American doughboys to France during her varied World War service and brought them back again. She rose supremely to the test on two occasions when speed seemed vital. In covering the 160 miles between her and the sinking freighter Laleham in 1924 the Mauretania broke her own speed record, attaining 29 knots. Loaded with 5000 wounded British troops, she steamed from the Dardanelles to England in one week in 1915. The giant vessel

1934-06-20.text: WASHINGTON, () — President Roosevelt and the State Department are inquiring into the proposal of Great Britain to impound the trade profits of Germany to offset the refusal of that government to pay foreign debts. It has been decided definitely that the United States government has the power to do this, but whether it will take action has not been decided.

BRIGHTON, England, June 20 — Brighton police today announced that the woman whose torso was found in a local railway station in a trunk would have become a mother in five months and that "pregnancy" undoubtedly provided the motive for the crime. The announcement followed a coroner’s inquest over the remains whose dismembered legs were found in London and whose head and arms are still missing, close after another gruesome discovery in the Brighton railway station, It was the body of a newborn baby. Both the woman and the baby are still unidentified despite supreme efforts by Scotland Yard, assisted by Sir Bernard Stillbury.

Associated Press Foreign Staff LONDON, June 19—(AP)—The Japanese erected a diplomatic fence of secrecy today around their plans for the 1935 naval conference despite assurances of the fairest treatment by representatives of the United States and Great Britain. Tsueno Matsudaira, Japanese ambassador, declined to tell Norman H. Davis, American representative in preliminary bi-lateral discussions, what are the present proposals and hopes of the Tokyo government. After Davis had given Matsudaira an unreserved promise that there will be no sort of Anglo-American understanding against Japan, he questioned the Japanese ambassador at length regarding his nation’s plans. The American ambassador-at-large asked particularly about press reports from Tokyo containing what appeared to be an inspired outline of Japan’s conference program. Matsudaira replied that he received no information officially an

Paris (4) — Laura LaPlante, blonde heroine of countless films, was married here today to Irving Asher, director of Warner Brothers London studio in a five minute ceremony at city hall in the ninth district. James J. Walker, former mayor of New York, and his wife, the former Betty Compton, film actress, attended the wedding, Walker serving as Miss LaPlante’s official witness.

| BRIGHTON, ENGLAND, June 20—(?)—A baby’s body was found here today in a suitcase in the same railway station checkroom where a woman's torso was discovered Sunday night, creating England’s most gruesome murder mystery in years. Legs of the young woman, whose body had been dismembered with a saw, were discovered Monday night in a London railway station. Police announced that the baby was born dead and had been deposited in the checkroom Feb. 24, and they believed the two cases are not connected. A Scotland Yard nationwide broadcast this morning disclosed that authorities were convinced the young woman had been slain within the past three weeks. Brighton police, considering possible motives for the woman’s murder, announced that she would have become a mother in five months,

Brighton, England, June 19. —(Fj— The chief of police of Brighton, after another examination of a woman's torso found in a trunk in a railway station here, said Tuesday there was no possibility it was that of Miss Agnes Tufverson, missing American lawyer. LONDON, June 20 ()—Prime Minister J. Ramsey MacDonald today presented a long outline of Great Britain's naval problems to the American delegation here to discuss plans for next year's naval disarmament conference. It was said in official quarters that MacDonald stressed Great Britain's “enormous responsibility, and her position in world affairs.” It was reported he discussed both European and Far Eastern problems at considerable length. It was understood that, for the second day of the preliminary conversations between the nations, Great Britain did not offer a definite outline for the 1935 conference.

LONDON, (CP). The aces of Great Britain’s crime detection forces gave their best efforts to solving the mystery revealed by the finding in two railway stations of parts of a woman's body. Sir Bernard Spilsbury, pathologist of the home office, who has played an important role in every major murder case of recent years, began a detailed examination of the torso found in a trunk at Brighton and the legs left in a suitcase at King’s Cross station. At the same time Chief Inspector W. Donaldson, Scotland Yard's best known detective, was tracing down the meager clues and directing the search for other parts of the body. Pieces of brown paper, similar in texture, in which the torso and the legs were wrapped, together with the trunk and the suitcase themselves furnished the principal physical clues. 1934-05-22.text: London, May 22.——Indications were seen in circles closely in contact with the war debts controversy today that the British government may be planning a new approach to the problem in the June installment due the United States. Any such move, it was plainly seen, however, is contingent partially upon President Roosevelt's forthcoming message to Congress on the subject of debts. . . Should the British take such action as is indicated, it would represent a drastic change in the policy manifest in recent days: Until today, official circles stoutly maintained that the first move in the debt situation must come from Mr. Roosevelt. ‘ Now the same quarters hint strongly that there has been a relaxation of this attitude over the Whitsuntide holidays, leading to a strong belief that Great Britain may be formulating a new plan for submission to Washington. . Ambassador Sir Ronald Lindsay has report

(AP)— America’s golfing Johnnies—Goodman and Fischer, today led the invaders’ parade in the British amateur championship. Goodman, the U.S. open champion, defeated W. M. Robb of Moseley, 5 and 4, while Fischer conquered Gus Moreland, a compatriot, 3 and 2. Goodman, the betting-odds favorite, played sound but not spectacular golf and won much as he pleased against Robb in their first round match, which was postponed from yesterday owing to the size of the field. The Omaha youngster, who negotiated the first nine holes in 37 to establish a three hole lead, will not play his second round match until tomorrow. If he gains the third round he will be forced to engage in another match in the afternoon in order to catch up with the field. Ended on 16th Fischer, the tall and spare golfing son of a Cincinnati letter carrier, closed out his second round match with Moreland on the 16th green. The tw

PRESTWICK, Scotland, May 22—(UP)—Paced by their champions, Johnny Goodman of Omaha, the open title-holder, and George Dunlap of New York, kingpin of the amateurs, five ace American players today moved forward in the British amateur golf tourney. Advancing with Goodman and Dunlap were Johnny Fischer of Cincinnati, Jesse Guilford, veteran from Boston, and Jack Westland, Chicago's star amateur.

The coup d'etat in Bulgaria, placing in power a group considered pro-French and removing men regarded as influenced by Italy, was looked upon in most European capitals as furnishing the one link needed to isolate Nazi Germany in the middle of a military alliance. While no agreement has been signed, the projected alliance of friends of France has been widely discussed. If carried out the defense chain would touch every border of Germany and would be the strongest European combination since the Holy Roman Empire. Soviet Russia has given indications that she is just about ready to enter the League of Nations, and to join in a mutual assistance pact with France and other powers for the protection of European borders. The pact, of course, would be open to Germany, provided she returned to the league, but its purposes would be attained equally, regardless of the Nazi government's attitude. The

PARIS, May 22 Pi—An assertion that the Prince of Wales plans to fly the Atlantic to Montreal, Canada, was made today by Edwin Woodhall, representing himself to be a former Scotland Yard man assigned to the Prince, on the seventh anniversary of Charles A. Lindbergh's New York-Paris flight. Woodhall, writing in the newspaper Excelsior, said that Wales had charted a route to Montreal, and that despite attempts to dissuade him he had recently discussed his plans with aviators. Wales also, Woodhall asserted, had the ambition to make a round the world flight.

Tokyo, May 21 (#)—Strong precautions against terrorism were continued in all parts of Japan today as the authorities studied various aspects of the financial scandal in connection with which Kideo Kuroda, Vice-Minister of Finance, and 14 other persons have been arrested. The Cabinet of Premier Saito, whose members are being heavily guarded by police, gave no indication of its eventual action. It was generally accepted that the Cabinet would not resign unless the full investigation, which may require a month, establishes that Kuroda and his associates are guilty of corrupt practices.

VIENNA. May 22 (P).— Eighty Socialist leaders jailed in the February civil war were free today but bombings and disorders continued despite the government's move to conciliate at least a section of its opposition. Two auxiliary police were wounded when fired upon by unknown assailants at Forfontrann, Upper Austria, during the night. Scattered bomb explosions were reported.

BARCELONA, Spain. May 21 (UP) — Eleven persons were killed and 22 were injured in a train crash today between the towns of San Baudilio and Bellobregat. It was reported an engineer was confused by a whistle blown by a man with a picnic party. It was understood the engineer believed the whistle to be a special signal, and he stopped his train. A train from the opposite direction crashed into the standing train.

1934-01-30.text: LONDON— A British ultimatum threatening trade reprisals against France was formally announced in the House of Commons today by Sir Runciman, president of the Board of Trade. Mr. Runciman declared that unless France restored the recently reduced and withdrawn quotas on British goods within ten days, the British would put additional tariffs on French goods. Protests Without Result Britain has formally protested to France, without result, against the quota reductions. She particularly objected to the restoration of quotas to the United States, claiming discrimination. British industrialists have been aroused particularly by the favors shown to the United States. The government refuses to begin negotiations for a new Franco-British trade treaty until the restrictions are removed. Observers saw in the strained Franco-British trade relations another link in the chain of difficulties. Continued

CAMBRIDGE, England, Jan. 19 Over roads which once shook to the noble tramp of hooves of Sir Launcelot's charger rode Percy Titmous, Esq. today. His mount, however, was no prancing stallion: it was an automobile "in the lower price class." Nor did Titmous wear the armored trappings of chivalry: instead, as becomes one who works in a brewery, he wore an everyday business suit. Thus unromantically arrayed he spurred on, one might say, toward Ely from Cambridge. And beside the historic road, in the best manner of the round table legends, he found a queen in distress. He did not know it was a queen, however. All he saw was a large automobile whose chauffeur was unable to make it budge. "I say," said Titmous, with nonchalance, "having trouble?" Then he looked again and lost his nonchalance; the passenger in the large car was Queen Mary. Titmous explained later that he thought only he "might be

LONDON, Jan. 29.—(UP) Queen Mary and her lady-in-waiting, Lady Desborough, had to hitch-hike today when their limousine broke down near Ely. They were en route from Sandringham to Cambridge on a shopping expedition. A passing motorist, Percy Tidmouth, traveler for a brewing firm, offered them a lift and they accepted. They arrived in Cambridge in a humble 10-horsepower sedan.

PARIS, Jan. 29.—(4)—Edouard Daladier was entrusted today with the task of forming a sort of “public safety” cabinet for a vigorous house-cleaning of financial scandals and restoration of shaken public confidence in the government. Daladier, minister of war in the Chautemps government and a former premier, was summoned to the Elysee Palace by President Lebrun after two others had declined to accept the premiership. Seventy-one-year old Gaston Doumergue, former president, declined to accede to the president's request yesterday. He said he was too old. Then Lebrun turned to Jules Jeanneney, but he refused to attempt to form a government which could restore political tranquility—and asked by the president—because of ill health.

Moscow, Jan. 30.—(UP)—A Soviet civil aviation stratosphere balloon which took off on an unannounced ascent today was reported in a message from its crew to have reached the record-breaking height of 20,600 meters (67,585 feet). After the balloon attained that altitude a radio message from the bag said a descent was being started immediately. At that position, the crew reports the temperature outside was between 33 and 49 degrees below zero and 4 below inside.

ATHENS, Jan. 29—The formal appeal which he hoped would give Samuel Insull, Sr. former American utilities operator from 4 to 15 more days haven in Greece, was submitted today to the Ministry of the Interior by Insull’s lawyers. The appeal was based on what his lawyer claimed to be Insull's bad health. He said the patient's health did not permit travel.

PARIS, (4P) — Edouard Daladier, again premier of France, formed a “clean-up” cabinet today to guide his nation out of the mire of the Bayonne pawnshop scandal. It is a cabinet of “the center,” neither radical nor conservative. It is composed mainly of veteran statesmen and, significantly, Col. Jean Fabry, Marshal Joffre’s aide-de-camp during the war. Appointment of the one-legged Fabry, veteran fighting man, as minister of war, was regarded as a clear indication of the strong defense policy with which France will confront Chancellor Hitler of Germany. The new cabinet is the fourth which France has seen since Chancellor Hitler assumed the leadership of Germany just a year ago today. In selecting his ministers, the new premier dropped all the powerful names of the ministry of Premier Camille Chautemps, the man whom he replaces.

BERLIN, Jan. 30.—(AP)—Adolf Hitler, chancellor of Germany, described his Nazi movement as democracy’s bulwark against communism in a speech today signalizing the first anniversary of his assumption of power. He declared that now humanity has entered upon a period of “searching for timely ideas and realizations that might give humanity a new well-being.” His declaration was made in a speech to the Reichstag which assembled in the Kroll opera house shortly after Hitler had gathered his entire cabinet around him. Hitler praised his regime as having “removed, in one year, a world of conceptions and institutions and put others in their places.” He said there had been misery in Germany before his assumption to power, but that now humanity seeks timely ideas for a new well-being.

1934-01-12.text: LONDON, Jan. 12. U.P)—Japan, determined to have a larger Navy, has intimated to interested governments her intention of giving the necessary two years’ notice to terminate the Washington naval limitation treaty, it was learned today. The earliest date for notice is December 31. There is to be a naval conference in 1935 to revise both the Washington treaty covering large ships and the London Naval treaty covering smaller ones. The notice therefore will serve principally as a formal announcement of Japan's often expressed intention to bid for a navy equal, or more nearly equal, to those of the United States and Great Britain. Japan's last official demand, made at the Geneva disarmament conference, was for a navy about nine-tenths as strong as those of the two great sea powers. It was understood that at the 1935 naval conference, she would demand, at the outset, a navy of equal strength.

PORTSMOUTH, Eng., Jan. 12.—-(/)— The battleship Nelson, “wonder ship" of Great Britain’s navy, was still hard and fast this afternoon, hours after she went aground at the entrance of the harbor. Numerous efforts were made to float the 33,500-ton flagship of Admiral Sir William Boyle, commander-in-chief of the home fleet, but they were fruitless. The crew of 1,000 was mustered on the afterdeck at different times during the morning and in an effort to create buoyancy jumped up and down in unison, taking orders from a leader who waved his arms like a bandmaster. Half a dozen destroyers dashed out from the dockyard and one by one swept past the Nelson at high speed in an effort to create a wash. This finally resulted in swinging the stern around appreciably but the bows remained embedded.

| INVERNESS, Scotland, Jan. 12.— The Loch Ness lake serpent, apparently losing its natural shyness, seemed today to be showing off, in small boy fashion, for the benefit of sightseers. Creditable witnesses asserted that the serpent not only seemed perfectly at ease in their presence but actually disported itself, threshing up great waves with its eight humps. Two Inverness women, Miss Margaret Cameron and Miss Ila Tinnock, were the newest witnesses of the serpent’s manifestations. Sir David Hunter-Blair, formerly a resident near the monster's lair, announced that he had been investigating its presence quietly for many years, having a natural hesitance in letting friends know that he believed in the existence of a fresh water parallel of the sea serpent. He said he believed it was the lone survivor of an extinct race of Regios that had lived for countless ages in the depths of the lake.

LONDON, Jan. 11.—A 43-year-old unemployed engineer boldly stepped up to the solicitor’s table in historic old Bailey court today, told the judge he had proof he was the nephew of King George, and won the right to subpoena witnesses in his fight against a charge of attempting to blackmail his majesty. Justice Charles said he would not go into the matter of ancestry for the moment but gave permission for the issuing of subpoenas to witnesses who, the defendant, Clarence Guy Gordon Haddon, said would testify that his mother was secretly married to the Duke of Clarence, the late elder brother of King George.

PURLOMUC LH, BOBIANd (Eb) -— A thousand odd British bluejackets jumped grinningly up and down on the after deck of the great battleship Nelson Friday, trying to free it from the mud on which it went aground as it left Portsmouth harbor for its spring cruise to the West Indies. The ship went aground at 9 a.m., in water that has brought grief to many vessels of large tonnage. The crew was mustered at once on the after deck and told to jump up and down. It was unavailing, and it was feared that the $38,000,000 ship, one of the two most formidable on the seas, would remain fast until high tide Friday night. She apparently was in no danger.

PARIS, Jan. 12 (*)—Premier Camille Chautemps warned the nation today that the royalist riots over the Stavisky scandal held the threat of a coup d'etat to establish a “directory.” Thousands of troops were held ready to march on Paris if necessary to stamp out the disorders, which have occurred in a protest against alleged complicity by government officials in the Bayonne pawnshop collapse which cost the public more than $40,000. The president of the Chamber of Deputies adjourned the body suddenly this afternoon in the midst of a pandemonium which broke out when Deputy Jean Ybarnegaray charged that “the police assassinated” Serge Stavisky, founder of the pawnshop to hush the case and protect higher-ups. Premier Chautemps jumped to his feet, waved his arms, and protested that Stavisky killed himself when secret service operatives surrounded him last Monday and pleaded he would make a “pers

PARIS, Jan. 11 — Defending his regime from a barrage of corruption charges in the chamber of deputies, Premier Camille Chautemps tonight disclosed what he said was a plot against his government in connection with the $40,000,000 Bayonne bank scandal. While mobs rioted outside the chamber, the premier told of a coup d'etat which he said had been prepared three days ago to place the government in the hands of a directory of a few men “reputed for their energy.” In a fighting mood, Chautemps told the chamber that the Democratic regime was endangered when a resignation of the cabinet was envisaged last Monday following upon the suicide of Serge (Handsome Alex) Stabisky and the collapse of his huge underground financial machine. 1934-03-28.text: LONDON, March 27—(#)—A Reuters (British) news agency dispatch from Athens tonight said Samuel Insull had changed from the little Greek tramp steamer on which he left Greece more than a week ago to another vessel at the island of Rhodes, in the southeastern part of the Aegean Sea. The fugitive former Chicago utilities executive left Piraeus, the port of Athens, ten days ago aboard the freighter Maiotis to escape American authorities seeking his extradition on embezzlement and fraud charges. The destination of the second craft was not identified in first reports and was not determined. The Maiotis, however, was reported to be sailing for Italy. During the past week authorities in Port Said, Egypt, have been on the alert in the belief that the expensively-chartered Maiotis was heading for the Suez Canal and some Red Sea haven.

WASHINGTON, March 27 (UP) President Roosevelt today signed the Vinson-Trammell navy bill, which provides construction of new ships to bring the country's sea forces up to the limit prescribed by the London treaty. The Vinson-Trammell act authorizes construction of 102 warships and 1,140 airplanes over the next five years to replace obsolete ships and bring the United States' sea power up to treaty limits. If the president and congress carry out this authorized program in full, the cost is estimated as high as $750,000,000. High naval officers want to start this year twelve of the destroyers and six of the submarines authorized by the bill. They place the cost of the first year's work on these ships at $20,000,000.

BY MAKI BE. PLUTIE NEW YORK, Mar. 28—(AP)—The trouble with American women (you can take this from Kenneth Green, a young English portrait painter) is that they’re all trying to be Dietrichs and Garbos. American women's beauty is getting standardized because screen stars sway public taste, Green said today. “The unusual face, the face that stands out in a crowd, is beginning to disappear from the American scene.” The artist, whose first exhibition in this country has just opened, called American girls the world’s most slavish imitators of film stars. He deplored the trend, because, he said, “America has the most beautiful women in the world.” Only one woman in 2,006,060 should try to imitate Garbo, the artist said, “But about one in twenty try it. “It may be that one in 500,000 have a Garbo face; but most women never can move like Greta, and should give up trying.” Unnaturally arched brow

LONDON, March 27 (i--The extent to which Britain is willing to commit herself in taking extreme measures to enforce disarmament so as to satisfy France was expected to be decided at least tentatively tomorrow at a meeting of the whole British cabinet. France has replied to London's inquiries for further particulars regarding what she desires in the nature of security guarantees, and the subject was discussed at length today by Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, and Charles Corbin, French ambassador.

London, Mar. 28.—(P)—Plans for a German airship service linking the United States to South America, Europe and southwestern Asia were outlined here by Hugo Eckener, Count Zeppelin’s successor as head of the German dirigible enterprise. Eckener revealed the great dirigible now being built in Germany larger than the American Macon would be used to operate a triangular service from central Europe to North and South America. Eckener revealed his plans in a lecture last night.

DUBLIN, March 27.—(#)—By presenting his credentials directly to President De Valera today instead of the king’s representative, W. W. McDowell of Montana, new American minister to the Irish Free State, broke what one official called England's “ropes and chains.” He was the first foreign envoy to ignore a years-long precedent by not giving his papers to King George's governor general, who was absent from a gala ceremony attending the function. Sean O'Kelly, minister for local government, said, in referring to the change in procedure: “One by one we are cutting the ropes and cords. England wound around. Cheering crowds lined the streets.

ZARAGOZA, Spain, March 28. Syndicalists today declared a revolutionary general strike. The declaration came shortly after a great popular demonstration as four victims of bombings which occurred Monday and yesterday were buried. Several suspects were arrested in connection with the case. The syndicalists are an extremist political party composed mainly of workers which late last year organized a widespread rebellion which was put down with the deaths of scores of persons.

ISTANBUL, March 28 (&)—The S. S. Maitois, believed to be carrying Samuel Insull Sr., passed the harbor of Istanbul at 5:45 p. m. today without stopping and started toward the Black Sea through the Bosporus. The Maitois signalled a Turkish police motorboat controlling Istanbul harbor that she was en route to Rumania with a cargo consisting of one passenger. Police signalled back that she was free to pass and the ‘phantom’ ship, whose whereabouts had been a ten-day mystery, steamed through the dark and rainy straits into the stormy Black Sea.

1934-03-16.text: (Copyright, 1944, By AM) HONG KONG, China, Mar. 15. —A gallant tribute to British tars who saved 187 American sailors from fiery death on the flaming gunboat Fulton came today from the Fulton’s skipper, Commander Harry McHenry, U. S. S. While the Fulton, A. V. U. S. navy craft, still burned on pirate waters north of Hong Kong, Commander McHenry and his men—safe in harbor here—recounted their harrowing experiences. They were brought in early today by the British destroyer H. M. S. Wishart—which saved them—and the steamer Tsinan, a commercial vessel. All were taken off by 10 o'clock last night. The fire, which broke out in the Fulton’s engine room about 6:30 o'clock yesterday evening, was expected to roar for hours as tugs began towing her toward Hong Kong today. As he told the story of the thrilling escape to the Associated Press, Commander McHenry plainly showed the effects of the ordeal

LOUISVILLE, Ky. March 15 (7 —A demand from the Kentucky house that President Roosevelt recall Robert W. Bingham, United States ambassador to London, unless his newspaper revealed the author of “The Psalm of Politics,” burst from the house late today in a renewal of the warfare over whether a newspaperman should violate a confidence. The resolution was adopted, 44 to 29, after a day of battle that included the filing of a $50,000 damage suit at the house lobby investigating committee, and a barrage of ugly words from both sides. “There has been a lie,” Representative Robert E. Webb said referring to the resolution regarding Judge Bingham, “either by the paper which published ‘The Psalm of Politics’ or by a member of this house,” and he added, “the time has come to take drastic action.” The Louisville Courier-Journal of which Judge Bingham is president and publisher, indicated plainly it h

by the Associated Press Return of the Insull brothers, Samuel and Martin, to Chicago to face criminal charges appeared near today as the former was located on a Greek freighter, following his sensational dash from Athens. The 74-year-old fugitive, aboard the vessel Maiotis, will be returned to Greek jurisdiction for deportation, the government announced. Meanwhile, extradition of Martin Insull was ordered in Toronto by Chief Justice Sir William Mulock in denying an appeal from a previous ruling that the former utilities executive must return to the United States.

Athens, March 15 (4) — Mrs. Samuel Insull, Sr., wife of the American utilities magnate, today was taken to the police station for examination after it became known her husband had fled from his apartment here. She said she did not know where he had gone. Two maids and a manservant also were questioned. A report that the 74-year-old fugitive had fled through a police barrier outside his apartment became general after officers went to the apartment and failed to find him. The theory was advanced that he had left Athens disguised as a woman and was on his way to Paris.

Athens.—-(AP)—- Samuel Insull, Sr., wanted in Chicago on charges of embezzlement and grand larceny, fled from his apartment home early today and it was believed he was on his way to Paris. He was said to have escaped dressed as a woman. After hours of official silence and dozens of conflicting unofficial rumors, the government, through the department of alien control, admitted officially that the 74-year-old former utilities czar had escaped. Insull apparently made his escape through a police cordon that surrounded his home where he has been in refuge from American authorities for more than a year. The tale was told that he left dressed as a woman. A maid and a woman friend of Insull who has aided in nursing him were taken to the police station for questioning. According to the report, the man long sought by American authorities slipped quietly from the luxurious flat at 2 a.m. today. He

He probably will be placed on the first America-bound steamer, it was indicated officially tonight, or, if any delay threatens such a course he will be sent directly across the border within 24 hours. Located Near Crete Insull, aged former financier who is wanted in the United States to face embezzlement and larceny charges, was near the island of Crete when authorities established contact by wireless with his boat, the freighter Maiotis, and ordered its master to turn about. ATHENS, Greece, March 15 (UP). Samuel Insull disappeared under the noses of the Greek police today when they sought to arrest him for deportation. The director of police said Insull either had escaped or gone into hiding to avoid being deported. The disappearance was a startling turn in Insull’s desperate fight to escape deportation to the United States where he faces charges in connection with the collapse of his vast utility interests. The Insull drama, rapidly approaching a climax where Insull either had to take the Orient Express across Europe voluntarily or be ejected forcibly, was heightened when police surrounded his hotel apartments. Twenty officers, headed by the director, invaded his quarters and found their quarry gone. The hall porter and three other servants were arrested for questioning. A wide search was started for Insull. He had defied the orders of the Greek government

ROME, March 15. — A concrete plan for the economic independence of Austria was formulated today by Premier Mussolini of Italy, Chancellor Dollfuss of Austria, and Premier Goemboes of Hungary. The three premiers also laid plans for the improvement of the economic situation of the Danubian states. They met in Venezia palace with their respective diplomatic representatives and commercial experts. Circles close to the government said it was logical to hope that the plans being drafted by the three premiers would create a new era in southeast Europe. They reiterated that these plans will serve as a basis for an invitation to France, Germany and the Little Entente to participate in an economic agreement. The invitation will not be extended soon, it is said, but some time after the agreement made by Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss of Austria, Premier Julius Goemboes of Hungary and Premier Benito

Fully agreeing with Sir Stafford Cripps' assertion that “Japan is converting Manchuria - and Jehol into a vast military base,” the official told the Associated Press: China In Danger “China now is in the direst danger as a result of Great Britain's statement of policy,” as enunciated by Sir John, foreign secretary, before the House of Commons. “It looks,” the official said, “as though Britain is moving in the direction of an ally of Japan to counter-balance the Russo-American approach. LONDON, May 18 — Emphasizing the war peril behind economic pressure, Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, made it clear today that Great Britain will take no action against any treaty violator without the full co-operation of the United States. Armed forces will not be sent to the Far East to 'preserve' China's integrity, Sir John declared in a vigorous defense of the Cabinet's foreign policy, after it was charged in the House of Commons that Japan is "pushing her imperialistic expansion into North China for the purpose of creating Manchukuo Number Two." "Economic sanctions (pressure against a treaty violator) cannot be applied without the risk of war," said the foreign secretary in his speech. "And we cannot undertake any system of sanctions or effective action unless the United States co-operates." However, he declared, Britain intends to fulfill all obligations under existing treaties t

Lahinch, Irish Free State—(p)—Because of further delays in repairing their plane, it was believed today Captain George Pond and Lieut. Cesare Sabelli, New York to Rome fliers, would be unable to hop for the Italian capital before Saturday or Monday. Strenuous efforts were made by mechanics of the Free State air force to complete repairs on the plane, damaged when the airmen landed near here after their flight from New York. Damage to the plane was more extensive than at first was believed and the lack of workshop facilities here added to the difficulties.

Political upheaval in the troubled Balkans resulted in the establishment of a strong arm government named by the King as troops rule Sofia. During the immediate transition, communication between Sofia and the outside world was interrupted, and wild rumors spread over central Europe concerning the Bulgarian situation. One rumor said the royal family had been bombed. It was indicated that the change of government had been effected without violence and that the troops had been withdrawn from the streets of Sofia. Earlier dispatches said that Kimon Gheorgieff, former minister of, had been named premier in the new cabinet, with Peter Nidleff and Petko Ziateff, army generals, included in the cabinet. Army leaders in the Bulgarian capital have been restive and disgruntled for weeks and it was understood that their demand for a new and stronger form of government resulted in the change. Dispatch

DUBLIN, May 18—(AP)—President Eamonn de Valera welcomed the transatlantic fliers Captain George Pond and Lieutenant Cesare Sabelli to the Irish Free State today on behalf of the Irish people. He received them with outstretched hands, warmly congratulating them on their safe landing near Lahinch Tuesday after the arduous ocean crossing. Selection of Port Marnock Strand as the take-off point for the return flight to America, he said, indicated that it has great possibilities as an air traffic center.
London—(U.P)—Germany has developed the most efficient gas mask ever made, it was reported today. The new mask is said to have seven filters against gas fumes,

Developments in the war-frightened world included: London—U.S. warned Japan that if she abrogates the Washington treaty, a free-for-all naval building race will follow and America can and will keep far ahead of Japan in sea strength. Geneva--A new French move for friendship with Germany, hailed in Geneva as likely to lay the specter of war hovering over Europe, today gave Soviet Russia, France’s wartime ally, cause for concern. The Soviet commissar for foreign affairs, Maxime Litvinov, hurried to Pierre Laval, French foreign minister, to ask France's pledge that she would not enter any agreement with another nation without consulting Russia. Budapest—Hungary sends sharp protests to Yugoslavia over mass deportations as breach of diplomatic relations nears.

London—The dying arms conference received another staggering blow today when Great Britain indicated she was through presenting proposals. Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, told the House of Commons Britain would exert herself to the last minute and the last ounce to achieve disarmament, but would refrain from new initiatives at the May 29 meeting of the conference. The arms conference is expected virtually to die then. Britain, he indicated, would merely point to the British proposals and then ask the others what they intended to do.

1934-05-02.text: London, May 2.—Two men, in all the world, were known killed in May Day celebrations—a Cuban soldier who shot himself with his tear gas rifle in Havana and a worker killed in a street fight at Caquste, Spain. It was one of the most peaceful May Days in years. Hundreds of persons received wounds in serious riots in India, according to a London Daily Mail dispatch from Bombay. Casualties of a mass Nazi demonstration in Berlin amounted to 1,630, all minor.

London, May 2—(#)—The Chinese government has been assured by Great Britain it was learned authoritatively today that China's interest was uppermost in the mind of Sir John Simon Monday when he said Japan's “special rights in China are recognized by other powers.” The statement was made in the course of a speech before the House of Commons in which Sir John, British Foreign Secretary, reviewed diplomatic exchanges brought about by Japan's restatement of a policy toward China. It appeared likely today that assurances similar to those given China have been given the American government although this could not be confirmed owing to the aversion of both Britain and the United States to any appearance of acting together on Far Eastern affairs.
