A large organization of German spies, engaged in gathering vital frontier defense secrets, was said by police today to have been uncovered with the arrest of three agents of the band, including a French captain and a British army officer. Revelations made by one of the suspects, Stanislas Krouss, a Pole, were said to have shown the spy organization to be the most dangerous discovered in France since the World War. Krouss was arrested in Paris by secret service agents who claimed to have caught him in the act of handing documents dealing with new frontier fortifications to an accomplice. The disclosures by Krouss, who posed as a businessman, led to the arrest, police said, at Belfort of the French officer, Captain Froge, who has been under suspicion for a long time. The identity of the accomplice mentioned in connection with Krouss was not revealed, but it was indicated that he is an Engl

London, May 2.—Bernard Rubin and Kenneth Holler, young Australian aviators, today claimed anew Australia-England flying record of 8 days 12 hours, after their arrival from Port Darwin. They landed at Lympne airdrome last night in dense fog. They left Port Darwin April 23. - The previous record of 8 days, 22 hours, 25 minutes was held by J. A. Mollinson, British transatlantic flyer.

TOKYO, May 1 (Pf) — Ignoring Secretary of State Hull’s statement of the American position as merely a redeclaration of “generally accepted principles,” Japan today joined Great Britain in regarding the controversy over Japanese-China policy as a closed incident. A communique to the Japanese press, which reviewed the discussions started two weeks ago, did not include the communication in which the United States cabinet member called attention to the nine-power treaty and stated that America stands firmly on its rights under that pact. The only mention of the American latitude in the communique was a statement that the head of the state department indicated his country is unwilling to accept the Japanese “Hands Off China” policy. A foreign office spokesman said that Japan had no intention of replying to Mr. Hull’s note, “Because we already have given assurances that Japan has no intention

PARIS, May 2. (4)—Police fought a pitched battle with Communists in a “tough” quarter of Paris today as climax to “Red May Day.” Four police were wounded. Communists, entrenched behind flaming barricades in a blind alley and windows of the municipally owned apartment poured a stream of pistol fire into the ranks of the police. After four hours of siege, the police were able to storm the Communist citadel.

PARIS, May 2. (#)—Police announced that a huge "German spy organization" had been uncovered with the arrest of an agent in Paris and that warrants had been issued for other members of the group. Secret service agents were said to be searching for the spies, but even the name of the agent arrested was not made public. Calcutta, India, May 2 (Wednesday). (Twenty persons were killed, hundreds injured and a dozen reported missing early today after a tornado swept the town of Sythet in the province of Assam. Native houses were blown away and many small craft on the Surma river foundered. The town of Sythet, capital of the district of the same name, has a population of approximately 14,000 and is a center of river trade. The province of Assam is located in the extreme northeast of India. European residences are scattered about the river banks and on the neighboring hillocks of Sythet. A violent earthquake shook the town in 1869.

1934-06-15.text: WASHINGTON. (CP) A strongly worded note reminded Great Britain that its own credit standing was involved in its debts to this country and suggested that offers would be considered for readjusting the debt or for payment in goods and services. The note to Sir Ronald Lindsay, the British ambassador, from Secretary Hull, set forth three points in response to the British debts note of June 4. They were: 1. Great Britain would have to pay only the amount of the June 15 installment to avoid being considered in default under the Johnson law. 2. There is no connection whatever between the debt owed the United States by Great Britain and those owed Great Britain by other countries. 3. The United States government will be glad to entertain proposals for either readjustment of the debt or for payment in goods and services. Washington, June 10—(AP)— The state senate today ratified the nine-year-old Geneva treaty providing for strict supervision of international traffic in arms, ammunition and implements of war. A reservation was attached, however, that the other nine principal arms producing countries—the British Empire, Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Soviet Russia, Czechoslovakia and Sweden—must approve the pact before it takes effect as to the United States.

United Press Staff Correspondent. LONDON, June 5—Great Britain decided today to seize German funds in England to compensate British credit for the moratorium declared by Germany on all her foreign debts. Businessmen will receive compensation for commercial debts as well as holders of German bonds, including the "guaranteed" Dawes and Young plan loans. Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, announced the plan in the House of Commons, adding that if Germany voluntarily made good before July 1—in other words, abrogated the moratorium as far as Britain is concerned—it would not be put into effect. ACTION MAY HURT CREDITORS IN U.S. The seizure would be accomplished by establishing a Clearing House which could sequester German funds in London obtained through export balances, etc. Britain’s move, it was believed, would react unfavorably on the United States by making it more difficu

/ LONDON (UP)—Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, announced in the House of Commons Friday that Great Britain would soon establish a German-British clearing house because of the six months moratorium declared by Germany on all foreign obligations. The clearing house would seize German credits in England and apply them not only to the service of German loans held in Britain but to business claims, he said. It was frankly a reprisal measure intended by the chancellor to force Germany to pay, by one means or another, British creditors at least during the July 1 - Dec. 31 moratorium period, declared as a desperate means of saving the mark. He gave Germany one chance—to make an offer for payment before July 1.

By ARTHUR RRISANE Britain, owing the United States $4,713,000,000, has decided that the best plan for this spring’s installment is to pay nothing at all. They would have gladly handed in a “token,” something for Uncle Sam to play with, perhaps a few silver dollars, but President Roosevelt had said: “Pay the amount due this spring, or consider yourselves in default.” The British do not like to be in default. Refusing to pay what they owe this nation would justify other nations in refusing to pay them. On the other hand, the British feel that, if they buy our dollars to pay us, they might increase the value of the dollar and diminish that of the pound. The upshot is that our British friends decide to pay nothing, explaining with words well chosen that we ought to be grateful that Britain did not allow Germany to destroy the United States in the big war. And, anyhow, it is all our fault. Th

WASHINGTON, D. C., June 15 (INS)—Today was Europe's pay day to the United States but Uncle Sam found only one debtor at the paying teller’s window, little Finland. For the rest it was a payless payday. Great Britain, France, Italy, Belgium, Poland and practically all the others joined in united default. The acknowledged purpose of this default is to force this government into granting drastic reductions of the eleven billion dollars owed American taxpayers. The United States was to receive less than one-tenth of one percent of the amount of the June 15th installment bringing the total amount of which Europe has defaulted to nearly half a billion dollars.

Germany’s six months moratorium on all foreign obligations, effective July 1, met with quick reprisal today. In the British House of Commons Neville Chamberlain, Chancellor of the Exchequer, announced that unless Germany made a satisfactory offer to British bondholders and commercial interests before July 1 he would set up a clearing house to seize German credits in Britain and pay debt services that way. In Paris the government protested officially against suspension of payment on the Dawes and Young reparations loans and the foreign office prepared to ask the United States, Britain and other creditors to take joint action. It was thought France meantime would not imitate the British action of making arrangements for a clearing house to seize German credits and apply them to the sacred reparations loans.

(Copyright 1934, by the Associated Press Berlin, June 15—Competent observers professed to see today in Germany’s suspension of payments on all her foreign debts a significant move to end reparations, and ultimately, the treaty of Versailles. Doubt was expressed that the payments would be resumed at the expiration of the moratorium’s six month period, reliable sources pointing out that complete abolition of reparations is an essential point in the Nazi program. Swift reprisals by other nations against the Reich appeared likely, dispatches said. Great Britain and France were reported to be considering plans to protect their bondholders, possibly by withholding commercial payments due Germany. A British note in April warned Berlin any interference with the Dawes and Young loans would be taken most seriously.

1934-10-02.text: FOLKESTON, England, Oct. 2—An airplane with seven occupants crashed into the misty English Channel only three miles from shore today on a projected flight to Paris, killing all of them. Two of the passengers were women. The cause of the crash probably will remain a mystery since no one witnessed it although the captain of a German steamer heard the roar of the airplane’s engine followed shortly by the crash as the plane plunged into the sea. A doctor official said he thought there might have been an explosion, although there was no evidence to support his theory.

ABRIDGE, England, Oct. 2 (U.P) A London-Paris passenger plane crashed in the rain over the English Channel today, apparently after an explosion, and carried the seven persons aboard to their deaths. The dead included an American, Albert Desanno, Philadelphia. The others were the British pilot and three French and two British passengers. The explosion tore the plane apart and it dropped into a choppy sea. The passing steamer Biarritz took the wreckage in tow and brought it in here. The bodies were so mutilated by the crash that they were almost unrecognizable. Five of them were brought in by the Biarritz. The accident occurred three miles off shore, near Folkestone. Two women were among the dead passengers. Two of the seven bodies had been recovered.

ABRIDGH, England, Oct. 29 (OP)—An American named Albert Desanno, first name and home address unknown, was killed today in the crash of a London-Paris air plane over the English Channel, airport officials announced. Seven persons were killed altogether, the British pilot and six passengers. Three of the passengers were French and two English. The bodies were mutilated and hard to identify. Apparently the disaster was caused by an explosion before the crash, while the plane was flying in the rain over a choppy sea.

Folkestone, England, Oct. 2. (INS).— Six passengers and a pilot lost their lives to-day when a brand new air liner crashed into the English Channel while flying to France. Five bodies were recovered by the cross-channel steamer Biarritz. The ill-fated plane, in the service of Hillman’s Airways, left the line’s airport in Essex county at 10:00 o’clock for Le Bourget Field, Paris, with six passengers and a pilot named Bannister. Steaming in a downpour of rain through the choppy channel from Folkestone, the Biarritz passed close to the wreckage of the plane shortly before 11:00 o'clock, three miles South of Folkestone. A lifeboat was quickly lowered, but only the bodies of Bannister and four passengers could be found. Other ships are now standing by.

Madrid. Oct. 1 (*—Premier Ricardo Samper's Centrist government collapsed today coincidentally with the reopening of parliament. A wild scene in the Chamber of Deputies as one minister after another announced he was resigning was followed by the premier's hurried visit to President Alcala Zamora to present the cabinet’s resignation. He then announced that Alcala Zamora would begin conferences with party leaders tomorrow preparatory to forming another government. Samper expressed the belief that the new government would be based largely upon radical Republican support somewhat similar to the old regime. He said, however, that some new blood probably would be infused.

Ley 2440 shoved £Press) Tokyo, Oct. 2.—Brigands raided two schoolhouses near Feghuanghen, Manchukuo, and carried off three teachers and about 100 pupils, all of them Chinese, said a Rengo (Japanese) news agency dispatch today from Antung. Japanese and Manchoukuan troops set out in pursuit of the brigands, the dispatch added. The section is northwest of Antung (a port in southern Manchukuo).

Paris, Oct. 2. (AP)—France decided today to store metals needed in time of war. The government’s fear of the scarcity of materials to equip the army led President Lebrun to decree a prohibitive export tax on waste copper, aluminum, zinc, nickel and tin. Aluminum is the only one of these metals which is produced extensively in France. The action follows similar measures taken by Germany, officials said.

| PARIS, Oct. 2.—(P)—A balloon higher than the cathedral of Notre Dame and with a capacity of 113,000 cubic meters (147,000 cubic yards) when fully inflated will be used by Prof. Auguste Piccard in his next stratosphere flight, he said in a copyright article in Le Journal. Prof. Piccard estimated the balloon would reach a record-breaking height of 19 miles. It will weigh more than a ton and will have an aluminum gondola, shaped like a diving bell.

1934-10-23.text: | MELBOURNE, Australia, Oct. 24 | (Wednesday) (AP)—Two Englishmen, Charles W. A. Scott, 31, and Tom Campbell Black, 35, won the $50,000 speed race from England to Melbourne but their closest competitors, a Dutch team in an American plane, won a fight for their lives early today. The flying Dutchmen, K. D. Parmentier and J. J. Moll, with five other persons in their big transport plane, were hours ahead of their nearest rivals, Colonel Roscoe Turner and Clyde Pangborn, at midnight. Then they became lost in rainstorms which were sweeping over the high uplands north of the Australian Alps. Anguished Australians, on the ground, saw flares dropping from the great ship through the sodden skies as the pilots wandered in circles, trying to get their bearings. Worst of all, here at the race headquarters in Melbourne was the receipt of an SOS wireless message from the plane. No one could go out to

MELBOURNE, Australia, Oct. 24 (Wednesday) (UP).—Two veteran British aviators slept today like men half dead after the greatest airplane speed race victory ever won, while two trailing planes, Dutch and American, followed them across the Australian continent. The victorious De Haviland Comet of C W. A. Scott and T. Campbell Black, the American-built Dutch “flying hotel,” and the American Boeing transport of Col. Roscoe Turner and Clyde Pangborn, all had shattered by days the England-Australia flight record. Forced To Land The Dutch plane—an American airliner—was forced to land 162 miles short of its goal. Scattered back of the leaders in the England-Melbourne race from the Dutch East Indies to continental Europe were 12 other planes, still struggling to complete the 11,300-mile air line course. Black with grime, staggering with fatigue, Scott and Black climbed from their bullet-like Comet

MILDENHALL AIR-DROME, Eng., Oct. 22.—Burley C. W. A. Scott and dapper Campbell Black hobbled their brilliant Red Comet into the last 2,176-mile stretch of the Melbourne air derby today out of Port Darwin, with two Dutchmen four hours behind them and the Americans, Turner and Pangborn, in third place. The record-smashing pace makers, who sliced a generous two-thirds of all existing England-to-Australia speed records in 2 days, 4 hours and 22 minutes, limped into Port Darwin on only one engine but repaired it in a few haste-ridden hours and sped on to claim the $50,000 prize at Melbourne. The first fatality of the air race occurred when Harold D. Gilman of Great Britain and his co-pilot Baines crashed in flames in Italy, between Soggia and Bari, according to word reaching the royal aero club; both were burned to death. The disaster left only 13 planes competing in the derby out of an origi

Melbourne, Australia, Oct. 23 (Tuesday) (#)—C. W. A. Scott and Campbell Black, Englishmen, today won the 11,300 mile London to Melbourne air race, landing at the Flemington race course here ahead of all competitors. The fliers, who reached Melbourne from far-away London in less than three days, traveled the last lap from Charleville with a faulty motor. But they nursed it along, after hasty repairs at Charleville, and made the 787-mile lap in fast time to capture the $50,000 first prize. Crowd On Hand Thousands of Australians, who had thronged the race course since noon, were on hand to see the red De Havilland swing in from the North in the mid-afternoon. Approximately 1,300 miles behind them, also tearing along at a terrific pace, came the pair of determined flying Dutchmen, K. D. Parmentier and J. J. Moll. They reached Port Darwin, paused 38 minutes and then sped on toward Charleville

London—(#)—Japan advanced a far-reaching plan for a new naval treaty Tuesday, based upon the principle of equality in defensive armaments and substituting a maximum tonnage limitation for the present ratios. The eagerly awaited program was laid down in a bi-lateral conference with representatives of Great Britain. The two countries are conferring with the United States, preliminary to the 1935 naval conference. The main points Tokyo wants, it was learned, are as follows: 1. The powers should first agree on the principle of equality of armaments, based on needs for national defense. 2. Abolition of the present 5-5-3 ratio system and the substitution of a maximum tonnage limit, each nation to determine her own categories and to have freedom of action in building to the limit which is set. (No figures were suggested as a limit.) 3. Elimination of aggressive warfare by a drastic reduction of

LONDON, Oct. 23 (P)--Japan's determination to denounce the Washington naval treaty, with its 5-5-3 ratio between the United States, Great Britain and Japan, was conveyed to Great Britain today by Ambassador Tsueno Matsudaira, a responsible Japanese authority said. The announcement, he declared, was made at the opening of naval conversations here between Japan and Great Britain.

PORT DARWIN, Australia, Oct. 23.—A red flash speeding south, the powerful airplane of C. W. A. Scott and Campbell Black Tuesday was approaching Melbourne —and the end of the great England to Australia air derby. Victory seemed to be within the grasp of the Englishmen as they left Charleville, only 787 miles away from the finishing line, at 10:38 a. m. Tuesday (7:59 p.m. Eastern standard time, Monday). Approximately 1300 miles behind them, also tearing along at a terrific pace, came the pair of determined flying Dutchmen, K. D. B. Parmentier and J.J. Moll. They reached Port Darwin, paused 38 minutes and then sped on toward Charleville. U. S. Flyers Third, Somewhere over the Timor Sea, presumably, were the Americans, Roscoe Turner and Clyde Pangborn, hastening on to this control point, the first on Australian soil. Throughout Australia excitement raged to a high pitch when news spread that

MELBOURNE, AUSTRALIA, Oct. 23—Conquering motor trouble and a field of the world’s foremost flyers, C. W. A. Scott and Campbell Black, British veterans, rocketed across the finish line early today to win the $50,000 London to Melbourne race in the fastest, long distance flight aviation has known. They covered the 11,300 miles from England in 70 hours and 59 minutes, far outdistancing the original 19 competitors who were left scattered over two continents. Thirty thousand spectators who had waited eagerly in the rain sent up loud cheers as the Red Comet was seen approaching the airport—the end of the flight almost half way around the world. Deaf from the flying at 165 miles an hour, Scott managed to blurt out that he and his companion had slept only two hours in three days. The tumult of the crowd rose as the plane came into sight and then shot down on the finish. Meanwhile Parmentier and

1934-10-26.text: TOKYO, Oct. 26.—(7)—Japan disclosed today it has told the United States and Great Britain it is unable to ask Manchukuo to modify a proposed oil monopoly program and advised them to approach the Manchukuoan government directly. (Neither Washington nor London recognized Manchukuo, Japanese-sponsored “independent” state. Representations had been made to Tokyo by the two countries, along with the Netherlands, alleging the monopoly would violate the nine-power treaty and the “open door” policy and work serious hardships on foreign oil companies. The foreign office, in the summary made public today, said Japan’s position was outlined in informal notes handed to the Anglo-American embassies nearly three months ago. Japan asserted the measures will not violate the “open door.”

‘By the Associated Press) | Washington, Oct. 25. —) Vigorous blows were directed from Washington and London today against Japan’s plan to establish strict governmental control over the oil business in that country and its sponsored empire of Manchoukuo. As Great Britain followed the American representation with a protest against any Manchoukuan petroleum monopoly, it became apparent that oil—fuel for warships as well as industry—is aggravating rather than smoothing the troubled Pacific. The Netherlands were reported authoritatively here to have acted along similar lines. Although the representations were worded much alike, it was emphasized here that the three actions were not concerted. Both the London and Washington governments claimed a violation of the nine-power treaty, Objects to Two Proposals Joseph C. Grew, American ambassador to Tokyo, was reported today to have made a series of

By Associated Press. LONDON, Oct. 26.—Japan told Great Britain at the preliminary Naval Conference today that she is willing to accept any maximum tonnage limitation to replace the ratio system which is mutually satisfactory to three powers.

By United Press LONDON, Oct. 26—American and British delegations are agreed that negotiations must be broken off if Japan insists on actual naval equality, at conversations here, it was learned authoritatively today. It was emphasized, however, that the stage has not been reached where such a rupture is a real issue, and that both Americans and British believe Japan is prepared to produce proposals much more conciliatory than those outlined in the first talks. The British-American agreement, it was learned, was disclosed yesterday when Norman H. Davis, chief American delegate, talked to Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald. Japanese and British conferred again today. Japan was expected to answer British questions regarding its proposals, Japanese and Americans probably will meet again Monday. —HAVE A HEART— LIBBY BACK TO STAGE

NEW YORK. (Special) — Mayor Fiorello LaGuardia has vetoed a city lottery bill to provide funds for unemployment relief. The action was reported to have been taken solely on the ground of questionable legality of the measure, which had been approved by the board of aldermen and the board of estimate. Borough President James J. Lyons, of the Bronx, who proposed the bill, said he would go before the next session of the state legislature in an effort to get through laws which would legalize a lottery.

Melbourne, Oct. 26—(UP)—Colonel Roscoe Turner, American flier, denied report tonight that he was considering racing an English plane from Melbourne to England. He said he would go to Sydney Monday to arrange for shipment to the United States of the plane in which he and Clyde Pangborn flew here from England. The proposal was made by Cathcart Jones, who plans to take off, possibly tomorrow, in an attempt to cut the time made by his fellow countrymen in their record breaking flight to Australia which won the air derby.

| Melbourne, Australia, Oct. 27 (P) — Catheart Jones prepared his plane for a dawn takeoff today in an attempt to cut the time of C. W. A. Scott and T. Campbell Black in their record flight from England to Australia. Nine of the air derbyists still were en route to the finish line. | Col. Roscoe Turner, mentioned as a possible rival of Jones in the projected London flight, spiked the report and said he would not take part in a possible 1936 race, “This race has cleaned me out,” he said. “If I am to take part in any 1936 race I'll have to find a backer.”

TOKYO, Oct. 26.—The magnitude of the new crisis between Japan and the United States and Great Britain over the proposed state oil monopoly in Manchukuo was clearly revealed here today when Japanese newspapers defied a police ban and published full details of the diplomatic exchanges in the affair. There was no attempt made to disguise the fact that an acute situation exists due to the firm belief of Great Britain and America that Japan is sponsoring this monopoly in Manchukuo for purely militaristic purposes and has objected.

1934-09-06.text: TORONTO, Sept. 6 ().—A high police authority revealed today that the “hideout” where John S. Labatt, London, Ont. brewer, was held captive by kidnappers recently, has been discovered 10 miles northwest of Bracebridge in the Muskoka Lake region. The hideout was in a heavily wooded area, Labatt, who was kidnapped Aug. 14 near Sarnia, told detectives after his release that he had been held in a place smelling strongly of pine. The police said they had not

Washington, Sept. 4.-(AP)—A senate committee was told today that the Electric Boat Company of New London, Conn., and Vickers, Ltd., of England had divided the world into exclusive areas for the sale of submarines and that the two companies interchanged patents for building boats. Other testimony went into the record that the boats were sold to foreign countries and that the United States Navy used some of the basic patents owned by Electric Boat. Henry R. Carsey, president of the Electric Boat Company, said his firm made a profit every time Vickers sold a submarine because of the Electric Boat patents. He added his company lost about $40,000 a submarine on 400 German submarines during the World War because of patent infringement.

The first lives were taken Wednesday in the riotous spread of the general textile strike. As sporadic clashes throughout the south and in New England stiffened the strife between mill owners and the United Textile Workers of America, President Roosevelt at the summer White House at Hyde Park arranged for a board of mediation to seek peace. He named Governor John G. Winant of New Hampshire, Marion Smith, an attorney of Atlanta, Ga., and Raymond V. Ingersoll of New York, Brooklyn borough president. Impartial surveys showed that of some 625,000 workers in the three primary textile trades—cotton, silk and wool—upwards of 300,000 were out. Many persons were injured and wounded in frequent clashes in southern mill towns between strikers and guards or officers.

Ile Rousse, Corsica, Sept. 6 (UP) —Noel Coward, British dramatist, escaped with his life today when the yacht on which he was making a pleasure cruise was wrecked in a gale. One member of the crew was reported drowned. Coward, stranded, telegraphed to friends to send him money and then left for Nice by steamer.

Washington, Sept 6 —(7)—Evidence that the Electric Boat company, America's foremost submarine builders, maintained close “agreements,” not only with Vickers, Ltd., of England, but also with leading shipbuilding concerns of Holland, Belgium, Norway, Russia, France, Spain, Italy and Japan, were laid Thursday before the senate munitions committee. Featuring Thursday's session was evidence that the Turkish minister of defense in 1924 was to have received $12,500 if the Electric Boat company got a contract to build a submarine for Turkey. A letter put into the committee record from H. H. Johnston, a representative of the New London, Conn., company to L. Y. Spear, a vice president, spoke of $25,000, half of which was to go to the minister of defense if the company got the business. Bid Against Italian Firm It was bidding against an Italian firm. “I know that this is irregular,” Johnston wrote.

Washington, Sept. 6 (AP)—Testimony that the State Department refused permission in 1929 for an American concern to sell submarines to Russia was given today to the Senate munitions committee. L. Y. Spear, a vice president of the Electric Boat Company of New London, Conn., said Amtorg, the Soviet Trading Corporation in New York, had asked about the prospect of buying undersea boats from the American concern. “We referred the matter to the State Department,” said Spear, “and were told that we should not sell such equipment to Russia. Naturally, the thing went no further.” The testimony came amid an excursion by the investigators into the ramifications of European armament sales during which it was developed that agents of the Electric Boat Company had protested that German shipbuilders had “violated the Treaty of Versailles” by organizing companies in Holland to build submarines. A letter

To the News-Republican: Helsinki, Sept. 5 — This is Finland, integrity’s last stand. They told our minister, Mr. Albright, “you loaned us the money when we needed it and we are going to pay you back.” Them’s mighty scarce words. I tell you they got just about the most stable government right now of any of them. It's a beautiful little city and clean. When these Finns aren't running a 25-mile race they are scrubbing on something. Haven't seen Nurmi yet. He is out a couple of hundred miles but is going to run down and see me tomorrow morning. Yeh boy, don’t miss Finland. Yours,

LENINGRAD, Sept. 3 — Well we are finally on the track of Finland. Found a pilot who is going to leave here with us in the morning and take us by way of Estonia and land us in Helsingfors; that's the place I been looking for for a month. Just like these folks to move their capital from a beautiful city like this to Moscow. Saw the opening of the great opera in Moscow Saturday night, new drama last night there and tonight the ballet in the real home of the Russian ballet. Saw Leningrad’s old stock exchange today; would hate to tell you what it is now, boys you better behave. Yours, WILL,

1934-10-09.text: London, Oct. 7.—— (4) — Virtual termination of the Washington naval treaty and the breakdown of restrictions on all capital ships on Dec. 31 of this year was declared inevitable today by an official source in close contact with international naval negotiations. Japan is expected to serve written notice to the United States that it is renouncing the treaty as from that date. The United States, on receiving such notice, under the terms of the pact would be required to notify the other treaty signatories, Great Britain, France and Italy. After Two Years Technically, the treaty would not actually expire until two years after notice of termination is served by any signatory. But to all practical purposes renouncement of the treaty on Dec. 31, the earliest possible date, would mean the end of the 5-5-3 naval power ratio which it established, and which is so repugnant to the Japanese. Rear Admi

United Press Staff Correspondent. MOSCOW, - Oct. 9.—(UP)—Joseph Stalin, secretary general of the Communist party and ruler of Russia, does not believe President Roosevelt's new deal methods can result in planned economy or permanent relief of unemployment, he told H. G. Wells, British novelist. A transcript of their talk was obtained today, Stalin expressed admiration for the president's initiative and courage, but he said he believed the President’s aims could be realized only by the overthrow of capitalism. He said further that he was convinced President Roosevelt would fail of re-election if he tried actually to satisfy the interests of the working class, Stalin and Wells talked for three hours in the Kremlin, examining from different points of view the world economic crisis and the political results to be expected from it. WELLS DEFENDS Wells, in general, defended the thesis that soc

BELGRADE, Jugoslavia, Oct. 9. —UP— Crown Prince Petar, 11-year-old son of the slain king, will succeed his father on the throne. He is now in school at Eton, England. He probably will be proclaimed king within a few days.

MADRID, Oct. 8—(AP)—Oviedo, seat of a huge government arsenal, was taken by rebels today in a new outburst of revolt against the government cropping out simultaneously at several points. Reports from Barcelona said three towns on the outskirts of the city, Matorell, Sabadell, and Badalona were in the hands of anarchists. Troops were dispatched to the trouble centers. Reports reaching Madrid also said troops were bombarding Ugo and Gijón, in Asturias province, where the rebels were reported solidly entrenched. Warships were bombarding Gijón, laying down a barrage for advancing troops. The reports said the rebels were equipped with machine guns and light artillery and were well fortified within the city. Casualties were reported to be heavy.

The government of Premier Alejandro Lerroux Tuesday began mopping up the remaining vestiges of rebellion in several provinces while estimates of the dead in the six days of extremists’ outbursts ranged from 500 to 1,000. Gen. Ochoa concentrated the government army on the outlying areas of Asturias where fighting still went on. Fragmentary reports to the capital Tuesday said he had occupied Oviedo, going there from Aviles. Congress to Convene Attention here was centered on the reopening of congress Tuesday afternoon, the presentation of the budget, and the appearance of the chamber with all the deputies of the left opposition in jail, in protest or repudiating participation in rebellion. Leftists were spreading reports that they might make an attempt against congress, using this as an excuse for a last stand in the revolutionary movement. The government took elaborate precautions, searchi

MADRID, Oct. 8. — A military dictatorship for revolt-torn Spain was forecast in responsible congressional circles tonight as nobles of the erstwhile monarchy joined 12,000 retired army officers in offering aid to the right wing government of Premier Alejandro Lerroux. A high ranking deputy whose name could not be revealed told the Associated Press "this uncertainty, if continued, will end in military dictatorship. The government should take the most drastic steps to end the revolt since otherwise the dictatorship seems inevitable," he said. (A military dictatorship, that of General Primo de Rivera, ruled Spain from 1923 to 1929, in conjunction with the monarchy). As reports reaching the capital indicated the revolt’s heavy fighting with its estimated thousands of casualties had hammered rebels into mere sporadic activity today except in northern Asturias, the Viscount of Cubas for the No

MOSURTAled Press Foreign Staff. (Copyright, 1934. by The Associated Press.) MADRID, Oct. 7.—Catalonia's revolution for independence collapsed under heavy shell-fire early Sunday, and the Spanish government apparently was smashing down a three-day red revolt that cost more than 500 lives and 3,000 casualties throughout Spain. Leaders of the Catalonian secession, including President Luis Companys, were captured in a short-lived civil war and marched through silent crowds to a prison ship in Barcelona harbor where they are to be court-martialed and probably sentenced to death. They surrendered at 6:30 a.m., with Spanish destroyers and foreign legionnaires from Morocco converging on the Catalonian political citadel. Bursts of rifle fire continued in the rebellious city of Barcelona through the night. Spain continued under martial law and vicious clashes with socialist, communist and anarcho-

MARSEILLES, France, (UP).— King Alexander of Jugo-Slavia, French Foreign Minister Louis Barthou were shot to death today by an assassin. General George, a French officer, was the third man to die. The fatal shots echoed through Europe with a political repercussion that recalled the assassination at Sarajevo in 1914 of Archduke Francis Ferdinand of Austria, leading to the World War. Gen. Dimitriejevitch, marshall of the court of King Alexander, who was part of the king’s escort, died of bullet wounds received during the assassination. The shooting occurred as their automobiles drew away from the dock where the royal visitor had been welcomed to France. Fire Into Crowd. Cavalry, drawn up to provide an escort of honor for the visiting king, whirled their mounts and charged into the crowd from which shots came just as a band finished playing the national anthems of the two nations. European

1934-11-15.text: (Copyright, 1934, By The Associated Press) London, Nov. 15—Great Britain let it be known today that if Japan rejects her proposal for naval equality "in principle," she will not grant Japan equality in the actual tonnage of their fighting craft. This indication, from an authoritative source, was contained in a statement that Great Britain still seeks a method of approaching a compromise on the difficult question of a new naval treaty but that she will not go beyond the recognition of equality in principle for Japan. This decision was made independently by Great Britain some time ago and has nothing to do with any conversations her diplomats engaged in the present preliminary naval parley have had with the representatives of the United States and Japan. Both the British and Americans here for the conversations said officially that reports that Great Britain and the United States were cons

NEW YORK, () — Henry Russell Browne, 74, retired woolen commission merchant and descendant of an old New England family; his wife and two negro servants were burned to death today in a fire that destroyed the Browne five-story town house. They were trapped when the fire roared up the wooden front staircase and burned through the roof. The only survivor was a wire-haired fox terrier. A fireman found the dog in the basement barking wildly. Browne was widely known for his collection of books and engravings, including revolutionary and early American documents, old coins, paper money and historical relics.

SYDNEY, Australia, Nov. 15 (#)— An airplane of the newly-inaugurated England-to-Australia service crashed in central Queensland today, killing three Imperial Airways officers and a passenger. The four-engined plane was bringing mail from England. What caused the crash had not been determined. It was the third air disaster within recent weeks in Australia, none of which has been explained.

LONDON (WP) — Great Britain has outlined to the United States naval delegation suggestions envisaging the possibility of British-American naval cooperation regardless of the fate of present naval limitation treaties, the United Press was informed Thursday. The suggestions, it was said, were outlined at a meeting of the British and American naval delegations Wednesday. The meeting was described as “a rehearsal of possible bases for a British-American accord in every contingency—namely, with or without an international treaty of limitation.” Norman H. Davis, chief American delegate, was believed to have reported the suggestions to the state department in Washington. It was understood on reliable authority that he made no commitment to the British. Not an Alliance It was said specifically that cooperation was envisaged and in no sense an alliance. Three possible contingencies were understoo

JACKSONVILLE, Fla., Nov. 15 (AP) -—— The British steamship Seven Seas Trader reported to the coast guard here early today it was aground off the Cuban coast and needed assistance. The position given by the ship was southeast point, Long Island, in Crooked Passage off Cuba. The coast guard here said it had no information as to the number of persons aboard the ship.

PARIS, Nov. 15 (UP).—In a specially constructed cabaret at the Ritz hotel, 123 guests danced until dawn today in celebration of the 22nd birthday of Princess Barbara Hutton Mdivani, five and 10 cent store heiress. The guests came from the United States, France and Great Britain. The orchestra came in an airplane from the gay Casino De Paris in London, at a reported cost of $10,000. Prince Alexis Mdivani’s gift to his wife was a diamond bracelet. When they married June 20, 1933, he received an allowance from her, sometimes reported as high at $250,000 a year but probably much less as her allowance then, as a minor, had just been increased from $300,000 to only $400,000 a year. Princess Mdivani’s fortune as of May, 1933, was reported officially by her father and guardian, Franklyn L. Hutton, to be $42,077,328.53.

1934-10-03.text: SOUTHPORT, England, Oct. 2. (?)—Charges that Japan is making "deliberate preparation for war which the Japanese consider essential" were placed before the British Labor Party today by Jack Mills, former member of Parliament. Mills demanded that Labor "hammer" from the British government a "declaration that there shall not, in event of war, be any assistance, financial or physical, from Great Britain to help a state which has outlawed itself in the eyes of the civilized world. Mills declared, "Every trade represented here is slowly being battered out of existence by the slave conditions of the Japanese industrial world."

WASHINGTON, Oct. 3—The United States intends to seek soon the cooperation of Great Britain in a unified effort to eradicate rum running. The projects international conferences are part of the administration’s vigorous drive to end illicit liquor traffic and boost alcoholic beverage taxes above $500,000,000 this year. Decision to ask Great Britain's aid in the troublesome problem followed disclosure by coast guard records that 18 known rum running vessels lurking off the eastern seaboard and southern ports fly the union jack. They are carrying cargoes of bootleg alcohol and Scotch malt, coast guard officers said. The question of stopping possible rum running into Canada also may be discussed in the planned conferences. Recently, an airplane was seized in New England as it was about to take off on a flight to Canada with a bootleg cargo aboard. Veteran coast guard officials said the scene

Folkestone, Eng., Oct. 2.—A mysterious crash of an air passenger liner into the English Channel — Britain's third serious air disaster in eleven days — today took the lives of all its seven occupants, one of them an American. The tragedy brought to 15 the toll of dead. Albert Desanno, 66, manufacturer of Philadelphia, who had been visiting friends at Woodford, Essex, for the past two months, was the American killed. Three other victims were French, the rest British. What caused the crash none knew. A theory that the liner exploded was strengthened by the condition of the bodies and the fact that the plane was broken into bits of scattered wreckage.

NEW YORK, (#)—Hours passed in silence early today after a British freighter, trapped in a terrific north Atlantic gale, had sent out an SOS and two other steamers reported they had failed to find her. The call for aid came from the S. S. Millpool yesterday afternoon. It was bound from Danzig to Montreal with a crew of 26. Another British freighter which sent out a distress call yesterday, the S. S. Ainderby, apparently was outlasting the gale. Two other ships were standing by. Carrying a cargo of grain, the Millpool last reported its position as approximately 709 miles off Labrador. The Cunarder Ascania, out of Montreal for Plymouth and London, and the Canadian Pacific freighter Beaverhill, went immediately to her aid. They reported through Mackay radio at 7:21 o'clock last night that they steamed close to the Millpool’s supposed position without sighting it. Nothing further was heard du

(By the Associated Press) London, Oct. 3.—England’s recovery program, says Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, is an unquestionable success. Chamberlain told London bankers at their annual dinner last night, in what some interpreted as a veiled reference to the United States' New Deal: “The voices of criticism have been hushed almost to silence. Perhaps an explanation may be found in the fact that their favorite instrument of chastisement, namely comparisons between wretched conditions prevailing here and glowing prosperity elsewhere, has not been easy to discover.” “What is right and proper for an old highly-developed country like ours,” he continued, “may be quite unsuitable for a new community whose people are less serious and perhaps less patient than our own.” Chamberlain cited a jump of 100 million dollars in exports during the first eight months of 1934, an increase

| (Associated Press Leadsead Wire): - LONDON, Oct. 3.--King George and Queen Mary returned today to the royal court after several weeks at Balmoral Castle in Scotland. The British monarchs face one of the busiest of London seasons, with events including the state opening of Parliament November 20, and the wedding of Prince George and Princess Marina November 29.

Tokio.—(AP)—An official army pamphlet which urged Japan to make ready for a possible war with Russia, spread uneasiness among the nation’s economic leaders today. This was reflected on the stock exchange. Leading shares declined on an average of two yen (about 60 cents). Newspapers said members of the cabinet, as well as civilians, were taken aback by the army's surprising manifesto, which proposed drastic changes in the nation's economic life and in nonmilitary government departments. It asserted the United States has three airplanes to Japan's one and that America wanted a navy larger than this country’s in order to support vigorous policies toward the Orient. Newspapers asserted Gen. Senjuro Hayashi, minister of war, would be questioned at the next cabinet meeting about responsibility for authorship of the pamphlet. Political writers predicted the statement would be a grave political

1934-01-14.text: CALCUTTA, Jan. 15. (AP) — At least 21 persons were killed and many were injured in a protracted earthquake which rocked all India today. The wife and children of G. W. Brown, the British manager of the Railway Workshop, and the wife of the Indian district medical officer were killed in the collapse of the Jamalpur railway station. The additional number of casualties were not immediately determined. Eight persons were killed at Patna and nine at Gaya.

Units of the British and Japanese navies moved today to protect their citizens caught, apparently, between two fires in the Chinese coastal province of Fukien. The cruiser “H. M. S. Berwick” was ordered by British authorities to steam from Hong Kong to Foochow, the capital of Fukien, to see to it that no Briton was molested in the fight between rebel and national forces. Japan acted even before Great Britain, the traditionally prompt guardian of her subjects. A Japanese cruiser anchored at Manol, below Foochow and landed a company of marines there. They were withdrawn soon, however, when order was reestablished. Dispatches from various points in the Far East indicated that Nationalist forces were victorious everywhere in their operations, occupying Foochow and moving on southward in pursuit of the remnants of the erstwhile powerful 19th Route Army which had, until today, defended the reb

CHICAGO. (®) John Factor, staving off a little while his own trial before a British court, faces four Touhy gangsters in a Chicago criminal courtroom next Tuesday. He has sworn vengeance against those who kidnapped and imprisoned him last July, for a ransom of $70,500. This is his chance. Prosecutors boasted they had piled up evidence enough to blot out the leaders of this sinister Touhy gang, which sprang into dominance of the underworld as the Capones slipped into a forced retirement. Once Factor was the poor immigrant from London, born there of Polish and Jewish parents. He went back to England to attain wealth. Again he was an immigrant, but now a millionaire destined to cut a spectacular swath in market gambling and Chicago night life. Again he is to go back, now to meet British justice that says his wealth is ill-gotten. For his kidnapping, the state, hurrying before Factor is extr

| By The Associated Press Vienna, Feb. 14.—Socialist women fought grimly throughout the night beside their men against an overwhelming wave of government troops. It was estimated that 1,000 persons have been killed. Today after a short lull the battle was resumed through streets littered with the dead. The women fought like old pioneers of the American prairies. A government troop commander said they helped carry munitions and reload rifles of their embattled husbands and brothers who fought from the windows of their homes. Their resistance was smashed by artillery. The state of civil war between abused socialists and the government continued serious throughout the nation but in outlying regions the government appeared rapidly to be gaining the upper hand. Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss, determined to retain control of the government, declared the socialist fight was “madness.” “One may s

TORONTO, Jan. 15 ()—Martin J. Insull, former Chicago utilities operator, was jailed today when Justice Charles Garrow in weekly chambers court denied a motion to free him from custody. Previously he had been at liberty on $10,000 bail. Insull now stands under order of extradition to Cook County, Illinois, to face trial on charges of larceny and embezzlement involving losses growing out of the collapse of Midwest Utilities. It was indicated that Insull would make a further fight against a return to Chicago, appealing next from the extradition order issued last fall by Justice A. C. Kingstone. Insull has been living at Orillia, Ont., 80 miles north of Toronto for the past 18 months. He is free on bail of $10,000.

SHANGHAI, China, Jan. 14.—(Sunday)—(#)—A two months-old secessionist movement in war-wrecked Fukien province tottered today as nationalist marines were reported in possession of Foochow, the capital, and the rebels took to flight. The famous 19th route away retreated from the beleaguered city; nationalist troops were nearly at the gates; British and Japanese warships were ordered to proceed to the city, and 300 Japanese bluejackets were said to have landed in the capital. In the face of the smashing Nanking offensive against the insurgents, who two months ago set up an independent people's government opposed to the dominant nationalist administration in Nanking, the fate of six American missionaries trapped by the fighting two weeks ago remained undetermined. CHERBOURG, Feb. 14 (®).— About 342,000,000 worth of gold— the biggest shipment of its kind on any single liner since the present gold rush began—started for America in the holds of the S. S. Majestic today.

ROME, Jan. 13. GPi--After a speech by Premier Mussolini, in which he spoke of Americanism and communism and called American industrial codes “only collective contracts imposed by the president,” the Italian senate this evening overwhelmingly approved his revolutionary corporate law. Duce criticized inflation as “a road leading to catastrophe” and declared the American recovery program “interests me particularly because it involves the direct intervention of the state in the nation’s economic life.” Under the corporative project, law-making, price-fixing and competition-regulating powers are to be given thirteen corporations or guilds, working through a national council and Premier Mussolini. It now goes to the Chamber of Deputies and will be rushed through in time so the new system can begin functioning late this month. 1934-01-19.text: WASHINGTON, Jan. 18. -—(#) --The Reconstruction Corporation has purchased a total of $131,671,605 of gold abroad, $108,307,850 of which was bought in London and Paris. It ceased making purchases this week. Hereafter gold buying under the administration’s monetary plan will be done through the treasury.

LONDON, Jan. 19. (A')—Clarence Haddon, who claimed royal kinship behind the bar sinister, was bound over to keep the peace today on condition he shall abstain from making the statement that he is the son of the late Duke Clarence, King George’s brother, and shall not cause any other person to make a like statement. Haddon was charged with having attempted to blackmail the King through the assertion that he was the illegitimate son of the King’s brother.

NEW YORK, Jan. 18—The dollar got out of control and rose sharply in terms of the British pound sterling today. While Secretary Morgenthau said in Washington that the Federal Reserve was buying gold abroad as well as domestically for the Treasury, foreign exchange dealers said it was obvious that buying power adequate to keep the American dollar down was lacking, with the $2,000,000,000 American stabilization fund not yet in operation. The slump in the pound in relation to the dollar caused some hesitancy in stock and commodity markets, and prompted vague rumors of the start of a “war” of depreciation between the pound and the dollar, although important banking quarters said such rumors were, to say the least, premature. They found other obvious reasons for the strength of the dollar. The British pound in New York closed at $4.95, off 8 cents, after touching $4.95, which was the lowest si

LONDON, Jan. 18 ()—To remove the “dead weight of social inefficiency and individual misery entailed by the existence of more than 300,000 “mental defectives,” the legalization of voluntary sterilization was recommended tonight by a government committee. The recommendation, in the form of a bill for a law, was made in a report of a committee which the ministry of health appointed last year to study the problem. It suggests that mentally defective and some physically ailing persons shown to be carriers of transmissible disabilities be deprived of reproductive powers only under the written authorization of the health minister. American experience showed the lack of wisdom in compulsory sterilization, C. P. Blacker, secretary of the Eugenics Society, said, and for this reason the committee decided against forced measures.

London, Jan. 19 (UP)—Clarence Guy Haddon, accused of having written letters to King George asking for money as “the illegitimate son of the Duke of Clarence,” surprised the public today by pleading guilty when his trial opened in the Old Bailey. Haddon, who has persistently maintained he was a nephew of King George and that he wanted only his “just dues,” listened intently while the charge was read. Then, to the amazement of the court, he entered his guilty plea, adding, however, the words, “under extreme provocation.”

WASHINGTON, Jan. 18—(Fi)— Chairman Vinson of the house naval committee announced today his bill to build the navy up to the London naval treaty limits had been approved by Budget Director Lewis W. Douglass as not in conflict with the financial program of President Roosevelt.

SORT AUGUSTUS, Inverness Scotland, Jan. 19 ()—Come now four Benedictine Monks of Fort Augustus Abbey to add their testimony to that of persons who claim to have seen the Loch Ness "monster." Come they do, despite the taunts of the incredulous—despite too, the charges that the so-called sea monster, serpent, giant squid or what-have-you, is just a myth invented to intrigue simple tourists. Abbott Hunter-Blair questioned the Monks. "Not only have we seen the creature once," he said they told him. "We have seen it on several occasions." And the Abbott—himself familiar with Loch Ness for half a century—wrote that he was convinced the weird and mysterious monster actually haunts the deep waters of the Loch. MORGES, Switzerland, Jan. 16, (®)—Madame Helena Paderewski, wife of the noted pianist, Ignace Jan Paderewski, died at their villa here today. She was 74 years old. Paderewski was with her when death came after an illness of more than two years.

1934-11-28.text: LONDON, NOV. 28. (AP).—Lord Ashley was granted a divorce decree nisi today from Lady Ashley and costs of the action were assessed against Douglas Fairbanks, Sr., named as co-respondent. The decree, which gives the young nobleman a final divorce after six months if contrary cause is not shown, was handed down shortly after the case came before Sir Boyd Merriman. The suit was not defended and services of a jury were not required. Lady Ashley is the former Sylvia Hawkes, musical comedy actress. The court action today required exactly eight minutes' time. Neither Lady Ashley nor Fairbanks was in court, but Lord Ashley was there smartly attired in a grey suit.

LONDON, Nov. 28.— (7) — Winston Churchill, Conservative Party leader, declared in the House of Commons that the German air force is rapidly approaching equality with that of Great Britain and that the present defense forces of Great Britain are entirely inadequate. “Germany is re-arming on land and she is re-arming also at sea,” declared Churchill, “but what concerns us most of all is the re-armament of Germany in the air.”

Plymouth, Mass. — It was three hundred and thirteen years ago that the Pilgrims of Plymouth gave thanks for their first harvest in the new world and—whether the history books say so or not—for the first New England Thanksgiving. In memorials of bronze and marble, far lesser deeds than the creation of America’s Thanksgiving dinner have been preserved for posterity. The rock upon which the Pilgrims first set foot as they stepped from the Mayflower here on Dec. 21, 1620, rests beneath an imposing monument. A hungry nation a roast turkey, couchant upon a bed of flaming cranberries, the product of his genius, the New England Thanksgiving dinner, will grace the tables of the land Thursday, from the creator, is the true story of the origin of the traditional turkey-and-cranberries dinner of Thanksgiving day. LONDON, Nov. 28 (AP).—Fog plunged festive London into near-darkness today but an official announcement said there would be no change in arrangements for the wedding tomorrow of Princess Marina and the Duke of Kent. Cheering crowds swept across the mall in front of Buckingham Palace this afternoon, surrounded the automobile in which the Duke of Kent and Princess Marina were riding, and forced it to stop almost five minutes before police could clear the way for its passage. The couple were on their way to a lunch with the Duke and Duchess of York. Both the princess and the duke were up early to take care of a hundred and one last-minute details. The duke has decided against a bachelor dinner party tonight but instead will dine with Marina and his and her parents in a small family party. London —()— Cheering crowds swept across the Mall in front of Buckingham Palace this afternoon, surrounded the automobile in which the Duke of Kent and Princess Marina, whom he will marry tomorrow, were riding, and forced it to stop almost five minutes before police could clear the way for its passage. They were on their way to a lunch with the Duke and Duchess of York. Neither the duke nor the princess appeared upset under the avalanche of the crowd. Both sat back smilingly in the automobile and waved their hands as members of the throng offered their congratulations and good wishes for the forthcoming marriage. A reception at St. James’ Palace in honor of Marina topped prenuptial social activities today. London, Nov. 27. (P)—American quarters here tonight were confident Japan would get no support from France or Italy in her denunciation of the 1922 Washington naval treaty. The American delegates to tri-power naval conversations here, which have reached the point of break-up over Japan’s insistence on naval parity, understood both powers would back Great Britain and the United States in placing the responsibility for denunciation entirely on Japan. Tokyo's request for French and Italian support was made informally some time ago. The formal request was made today. Britain and America, too, have been similarly approached, but were cool to the proposal.

London, Nov. 28 (UP) — Trains, buses and motor cars poured thousands into London today as carpenters hammered the last nails into the street stands and flags and bunting were displayed in preparation for the wedding tomorrow of the Duke of Kent and Princess Marina. There was a fair of carnival. Everyone seemed interested in the popular, pretty Greek princess and the duke, the king’s youngest son. So great was the rejoicing that for comparison people were going back beyond other royal weddings of recent years to recall the day of King George’s coronation in June, 1911: True Romance. The great city seemed so eager to honor the bride and groom perhaps because there was no atmosphere of arranged wedding, only the appearance of a true romance. The columns of stories in the newspapers were read avidly. Today the printed order for the wedding service was made public. As they kneel at the altar

LONDON, Nov. 28—(UP)—A heavy increase in Britain's air force, almost double the present strength, was announced officially in the House of Commons today during debate on Germany's rearmament which was pictured as a grave menace to Great Britain. ‘After Winston Churchill, former chancellor of the exchequer had demanded that Britain prepare to defend herself before it is too late, and had described the danger of Germany's air force which he said would nearly double Britain’s by the end of 1937 at the present rate, Stanley Baldwin promised the house that the government would act. He revealed for the first time Britain’s official estimate of Germany’s air strength, placing it probably between 600 and 1000 aircraft. Earlier in the day the possibility of war in Europe had been brought closer by Lloyd’s insurance underwriters who announced they were tightening their war risk insurance regulatio

Although the conversations will continue, it was said that the Americans feel that there is no possibility of a compromise agreement being reached. The United States delegates believe that the next step will be a denunciation by Japan of the Washington treaty of 1922, forcing the five signatories of that treaty—the United States, Great Britain, Japan, France, and Italy—to start from scratch in a consideration of the idea of naval limitation. CHICAGO, Nov. 23.—(P)—Robert H. Cabell of London, England, today was unanimously elected general manager of Armour & Co., pioneer packing firm, succeeding the late T. G. Lee. Cabell, for the last 20 years managing director of Armour & Co., Ltd., in the British Isles, was chosen to assume the duties of president of Armour by resolution of the board of directors.

(By The Associated Press) Boston, Nov. 25—Donald R. Richburg, executive director of the national emergency council, said today “the time is ripe” for private industry to step in and help take up the slack of unemployment. Richburg came to Boston to address the New England conference and the statement was made in an interview before his speech.

LONDON, Nov. 22.—(P)—A fourth power was called into consultation in the preliminary naval conversations today by the Japanese. Ambassador Tsuneo Matsudaira, the Japanese envoy to Great Britain, held a long conference with Ambassador Charles Corbin of France on the naval situation in general. Naval and diplomatic quarters viewed the meeting of the Japanese and French ambassadors as highly important at this time because of the reported French uneasiness over the naval situation and the virtual deadlock in the conversations between Great Britain, the United States, and Japan. France and Italy, who with the first three are signatories to the Washington treaty of 1922 and to the London treaty of 1930, are not participating in the present conversations but they are observing them closely. Work for peace centered at Geneva and London, while throughout Europe nations were making their armies ready for any emergency. The League of Nations council is preparing to consider complaints made by Jugo-Slavia with the support of Rumania and Czecho-Slovakia alleging Hungarian complicity in the assassination of King Alexander of Jugo-Slavia and Foreign Minister Louis Barthou of France at Marseilles Oct. 9. London, Nov. 23—(4P)—Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, told the House of Commons Thursday Great Britain will continue her efforts to bring about an agreement for naval limitation. “A breakdown of the system of naval limitation” would be “a great disaster for everybody, not merely for the powers now in consultation, but for the world at large,” the foreign secretary declared. His statement to the house, promised by Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald when he was questioned from the floor several days ago, served to throw into sharp relief the impasse the three major sea powers—Britain, Japan and the United States—have reached in tripartite conversations here. “We are doing our utmost in the most amicable way,” Sir John added, “and while I do not disguise the difficulties of the problem, for it would be very foolish to do so, there is nothing this country is not prepared to do within the limi

LONDON, Nov. 23.—British and American naval delegates have agreed that security, and not equality of navies, must be the basis of any naval limitation treaty, it was understood today. This would mean Great Britain had agreed with the United States contention that Japan, lacking far flung possessions, does not need, for security from attack, a navy as large as those of Britain and America. Norman H. Davis, chief American delegate, and Ray Atherton, counselor of the embassy, talked for two hours with Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald and Sir John Simon, foreign minister. It was denied they intended to present any united front against Japan but it meant that, separately if not formally in unit, they would oppose the firm Japanese demand for absolute naval equality. It was understood the conferees decided the negotiations must go on despite the absence of effective agreement.

1934-09-13.text: CRISTOBAL, Canal Zone, Sept. 12. (A%—The British freighter, Bradburn, carrying a cargo of cotton and phosphate out of Tampa bound for Kobe, Japan, reported she is afire. The ship is returning full speed to Balboa, from which port she sailed Sept. 9. The Bradburn is the third ship afire at sea during the last five days.

Cristobal, C. Z., Sept. 12. (P)—The British freighter Bradburn, playing the Caribbean, was racing toward port tonight with flames in her hold. The ship’s wireless message did not ask for assistance nor did it indicate the seriousness of the blaze. Carrying a cargo of cotton and phosphate and bound for Kobe, Japan, the Bradburn passed through the canal and sailed from Balboa, September 9. The Bradburn’s radio message gave the ship’s position as lat. 10, long. 87. That placed the vessel approximately 550 miles from Balboa off the coast of Nicaragua. The captain of the port at Balboa said the Bradburn’s speed was 10 knots. Hence he calculated that the ship would require 55 hours to return to Balboa, reaching that port some time Friday. An oilburner of 4,736 tons gross register and 400 feet long, the steel freighter was built in 1930 at West Hartpool, Eng. Its port of registry is Biddeford,

TAINDON, Ont., Sept. 13—About $25,000 was reported to have been extorted from half a dozen London businessmen as police sought to smash an alleged blackmailing ring. Many citizens viewed the revelation of blackmailing in the community as alarming evidence of the growth of a type of crime from which the Dominion regarded itself immune. Energetic police action was demanded. Three persons, Mr. and Mrs. Frank Tayler and Mrs. Mae Turnbull, were under arrest, held without bail. Other arrests were forecast. Arrangements were made not to disclose the names of complainants even at trials. It was understood that one payment to the blackmailers was made in the office of a London bank.

WOONSOCKET, FR. IL. UP— The first killing in the New England textile strike occurred here early today in a savage clash between National Guardsmen and 5,000 strikers in which six other persons were shot. The man slain was identified as Jude Courtemanche. He was found on Social Street, where the rioters had stood ground against volley after volley of rifle fire, with a bullet wound in his abdomen. He died at a hospital. Four of the other six wounded were reported in a serious condition at the hospital. In addition to these casualties, scores of combatants, both strike sympathizers and militiamen, were injured by clubs and brickbats. The street fighting here, which flared suddenly, was even more savage than that at riot-torn Saylesville, a few miles away, where three pickets were shot, two perhaps fatally, and a guardsman severely injured. SARNIA, Ont., Sept. 13 (P)—With the issuance of warrants for two men, the search for the kidnappers of John S. Labatt, brewer, of London, Ont., took definite direction today here and in the United States. Police of both countries were asked to look for Albert Pegram, also known by several aliases, and David Meisner, named in the warrants issued last night.

WASHINGTON, Sept. 13.—Evidence that the E. I. DuPont De Nemours Co. and Imperial Chemical Industries, Ltd., of England, in 1922 entered into an agreement for “sales cooperation” for disposal of their products in Europe, Asia and South America, was presented today to the senate munitions committee. This agreement superseded a previous arrangement of 1928, and continued a plan DuPont had originally entered in 1907. Under it the two companies agreed to use joint sales agencies which would offer products of both companies indiscriminately, with freedom of choice being left to the purchaser. It provided for suspension, during a war of major proportions where its continuance might prove embarrassing either politically or commercially. OKLAHOMA CITY, (AP)—Wiley Post, globe flier, said early today that his famous plane, the “Winnie Mae,” was so badly damaged in his recent stratosphere test flight that he will be forced to abandon plans to compete in the London-Melbourne air derby. He said his test flight assured him of success in setting a new airplane altitude record.

WOONSOCKET, KM. I, Sept. 1j--National Guardsmen and local police today regained control of the city after the worst rioting in the textile strike in the New England section during which a mob of more than 4000 out of control, looted stores and one bank, and destroyed property. Many of the stores looted, according to police, were sporting goods stores and pawn shops where guns and ammunition were stolen. One man was killed, six others were dying from injuries received in the rioting and five others were shot and wounded in the bitter conflict which raged all night and early today. The number of persons injured by stones, clubs and other missiles could not be estimated. The situation was brought under control today when the rioters themselves, apparently weary, drifted away and five truck loads of National Guardsmen arrived to reinforce the militia and local police already on duty.

1934-10-22.text: DARWIN, Australia, Oct. 22,—(UP)—Tragedy marred the England-Australia air race today as three speedy planes roared toward the finish line in the greatest aviation contest in history. In Italy, more than 10,000 miles behind the leaders, one of the laggard planes, carrying Flying Officer Harold D. Gilman and James Baines of Great Britain, crashed near Foggia after leaving Rome—and the fliers were burned to death. Of those still in the race, C. W. A. Scott and T. Campbell Black of Great Britain were dashing along the last stages of the race, flying over Australia and well in front. They had smashed the record from England to Australia by more than 100 hours. Their new mark is 52 hours, 33 minutes and 15 seconds. They left Darwin, on the northern coast of Australia, at 8:34 a.m., E.S.T., for Charleville, Australia, 1,389 miles away and 787 miles from Melbourne, the final goal. Closest behind

W. A. Scott, and his co-pilot, Campbell Black, rocketed into Singapore before dawn today. By United Press WASHINGTON, Oct. 22.—Criticism of President Roosevelt for praising British bankers and an attack on Government economic methods brought the first rumblings of controversy at the start of the American Bankers Association convention today. The critical appraisal by Robert M. Hanes, a North Carolina banker, came at the opening session of the convention, which met in a surface atmosphere where, at least, of cooperation with the Administration for business recovery. Hanes said the implied criticism of American bankers by the President in his last “fireside” talk was “totally uncalled for and unfair.” The President, in his speech, had praised British bankers for cooperating with their government for recovery. President Francis M. Law of the association, in a pre-convention statement, had sought to start the convention off in an atmosphere of harmony. He called for wholehearted

London, Oct. 22.—(/P)—Reports from Madrid to a British news agency today said twenty-seven mounted soldiers had been killed and many others wounded in the explosion of a motor truck loaded with dynamite in the Langreos mining district. Rebels had abandoned the dynamite which was being collected by troops.

At that time their nearest competitors, the Dutch team of K. D. Parmentier and J. J. Moll, at Rangoon, were at least 1,300 miles to the rear. The Dutchmen left Rangoon at 10:47 p. m. LONDON, Oct. 22 (40)--The London Mail says Howard Carter, co-discoverer with the late Earl of Carnarvon of Tut-Ankh-Amen’s tomb, will leave London for Egypt Oct. 25 in an attempt to find the tomb of Tut-Ankh-Amen's wife, Queen Ankh-Esen-Amen. The queen's burial place is believed to be near her husband’s but Carter said some months of research may be necessary before actual digging begins.

LONDON, Oct. 22—(UP)—Flying Officer Harold D. Gilman and James Baines of Great Britain were killed by a crash in Italy after leaving Rome in the England-Australia air race, the Central News reported. The plane was said to have crashed near Foggia after leaving Rome, and both fliers were burned to death. DARWIN, AUSTRALIA, Oct. 22—(UP)—C. W. A. Scott and T. Campbell Black, flying their British De Havilland Comet airplane, "Grosvenor House", arrived on the Australian continent today, days ahead of the England-Australia Flight record and hours ahead of their competitors in the Mildenhall Melbourne air race. They arrived at Darwin, after the most astonishing speed flight in aviation history, at 11:07 GMT (6:07 a. m. EST). The British flyers landed with but one of their twin Gipsy motors working. DARWIN, Australia (UP)—C. W. A. Scott and T. Campbell Black, flying their British De Haviland comet airplane "Grosvenor House," arrived on the Australian continent today, days ahead of the England-Australia flight record and hours ahead of their competitors in the Mildenhall-Melbourne air race. They arrived at Darwin, after the most astonishing speed flight in aviation history, at 11:07 G. M. T. (6:07 a.m. E.S.T.) Scott and Black took off again for Charleville and Melbourne at 1:34 p.m. G.M.T. (8:34 a.m. E.S.T.) after hasty repairs to one of their motors. The British flyers landed with but one of their twin Gipsy VI motors working. Work of repairing the damaged one was commenced at once. It was a dramatic last stage of the greatest air race ever held.
