1934-06-16.text: WIMBLEDON, England, June 16. (U.P) — America’s women's tennis squad today retained the Wightman Cup, symbolic of Anglo-American team tennis supremacy. The issue was decided when Sarah Palfrey of Brookline, Mass. defeated Peggy Scriven of England, 4-6, 6-2, 8-6 in the fifth match. This victory gave the United States team the series four matches to one, a much more impressive triumph than in 1933 when the Americans won four matches to three. It marked America’s eighth series victory against four for the English women, during 12 years of play.

Wimbledon, Eng., June 18—(AP)—A pair of singles victories by Helen Jacobs of Berkeley, Calif., and Sarah Palfrey of Brookline, Mass., today gave the United States the Wightman tennis cup for the fourth straight year and the eighth time since the international competition with England was inaugurated in 1923. Going into the final day with a lead of two matches to one, Miss Jacobs, American champion and team leader, added to America’s advantage by winning in two hard-fought sets, 6-4, 6-4, from Dorothy Round, first ranking British player. The cup was clinched for the fourth consecutive year by Little Sarah Palfrey who rallied gloriously to conquer Miss Margaret Scriven, 4-6, 6-2, 8-6.

Europe interrupted its funeral dirge over what it considers the corpse of the war debt issue Friday to shout a battle hymn against Germany for declaring a moratorium on external obligations, particularly the Young and Dawes loans. In London and Paris the international financial situation was the chief topic of discussion in the press and in official and business quarters. Attention was divided between assertions that sums due the United States, already formally defaulted by all nations except little Finland, should not and cannot be paid, and equally emphatic declarations to the effect that Germany must be compelled in some way to meet interest payments on her bonds. Both France and Great Britain contemplated setting up clearing houses to handle transactions with Germany through which funds from commercial accounts could be taken for payments to the British and French bondholders. While

HUNION, June 16 (UP).—The newspaper Daily Sketch reported today that Mrs. Thelma Raye Colman had petitioned for divorce from Ronald Colman, motion picture star, and that the suit would be heard soon, probably at the end of July. Colman has been separated for some time from his wife, whom he married in 1920.

LONDON. June 16. -P!—The Evening News said today that the English wife of Ronald Colman, motion picture actor, has brought suit for divorce and that Colman is not defending the case. Mrs. Colman, who was formerly Mrs. Thelma Victoria Maud Dawson, has been living on the Riviera for several years. The Colmans were married in London in 1920.

BARBIZON, France. — (4?) — Leon Trotsky, fearing an attack on his life by White Russians, fled Monday from his newly uncovered hiding place in Barbizon. Neighbors said the Communist leader, in exile from Soviet Russia, and his wife left their secluded villa at daybreak in a black automobile. Their new destination is unknown. Their place of exile was discovered Sunday by gendarmes who raided the place expecting to find spies.

PARIS, June 15, (PI)—A bomb exploded in the office of Andre Citroen, the “Henry Ford of France,” today in the campaign of terror by the “three judges of hell” which has frightened all Paris. The bomb was addressed to Citroen personally but was opened by the librarian of the motor plant. His hands were badly torn and the office was slightly damaged. Four other infernal machines which failed to explode were received in the morning mail today, bringing to 10 the total of bombs mailed by the terrorists in the last 48 hours. Four persons have been injured by them.

Warsaw, June 15. Bronislaw Pieracki, minister of the interior of the Polish cabinet, was mortally wounded late today by assassins who attacked him as he was leaving a club. He died a short time later in a hospital. Two shots were fired from a group of men who had waited some time for Pieracki to come from the building. The assassins escaped in the confusion which followed. A policeman who tried to hold one of them was wounded. One of the bullets struck the minister in the head. One theory held by the authorities is that the assassination was provoked by the arrest of a large number of Ukrainian terrorists yesterday at Cracow and Lwow.

1934-01-02.text: LONDON, Jan. 2 (UP)—Richly-gowned women in fashionable Hyde Park walked in front of their automobiles to guide their chauffeurs homeward before London's worst fog in years lifted early today. Conductors did the same, carrying torches ahead of slowly moving trains. The fog, which tied up highway, rail and air services, vanished this morning under a rainfall which brought a grey, bleak dawn but allowed transportation to resume. During yesterday's fog, which covered 8,000 square miles of England, three persons were killed in road accidents and three drowned.

State Department today instructed Ambassador William E. Dodd in Berlin to make representations to the German government against the announced intention of the Reichsbank to reduce interest payments on foreign loans other than the Dawes and Young loans. The British government already has taken action.

(By the Associated Press) - London, Jan. 1—England’s new year was dulled today by a cold, gray fog which blanketed London and the southern counties and caused six deaths and numerous injuries in accidents. Road, rail, air and water traffic in all directions was paralyzed or crippled. Not a single airplane could leave or reach Croydon airport. One airliner managed to creep through the murk from Poitiers as far as Lympne airdrome. Horse Races Cancelled Shipping in the Solent and other coastal areas was at a standstill. The annual horse races in Manchester were cancelled. Nine young Americans en route to Milan, Italy, to defend America's ice hockey championship, reached London at the height of the fog’s greatest density. “Gee, your fog has given us a nice New Year's welcome,” said their manager, Walter Brown. “Even the old trophy is affected. It needs some polishing,” he remarked as he disp

Dublin, (AP) -- Gen. Eoin O'Duffy, co-leader of the United Ireland party, won the first round today in his fight against a charge of inciting to kill President Eamon DeValera. A military tribunal decided today to obey—for the time being, at least, the high court's conditional order prohibiting it from proceeding with the case against the militant blue-shirter, Justice Byrne granted the court order yesterday on the ground the charge was outside the tribunal's jurisdiction. O'Duffy was accompanied by his chief lieutenant, E. J. Cronin, and Solicitor P. F. O'Reilly.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 2.—(#)—The government’s gold price remained unchanged today at $34.06 an ounce. It represented the tenth repetition of this quotation for newly mined domestic metal. In London, bar gold was worth $32.73 on the basis of a sterling opening of $5.154.

— Berlin, Jan. 1 (4)—Chancellor Adolf Hitler told President Paul von Hindenburg at a New Year's reception today that the German nation entered a brighter future when the aged President on last Jan. 30 entrusted to him the office of the chief executive. Crediting Von Hindenburg with having initiated a long absent unity in the nation, Hitler said, "the power issuing therefrom enabled us to cement the Reich firmly together, call a halt in the religious, moral, and cultural decay, and to improve the country’s economic position. “Thanks to your confidence in me and the government, we have been enabled, while guarding our honor and rights to equal treatment, to pursue a policy whose ultimate aim is, was, and will remain a true and sincere peace."

SUMMERSIDE, Prince Edward Island (4)—Born in a snowbound open sleigh with the temperature at 10 below zero, an infant boy was described as “thriving” in a hospital here today. Mrs. Kenneth Lecky gave birth to a child about three-quarters of a mile from the hospital after farmers had worked for hours getting the sleigh through six miles of snowdrifts between the Lecky home and the town.

ROME (£) — Complete severance of alliances between politics and business is among the proclaimed purposes of the new corporative system to be inaugurated in Italy this month, a system based on the new Fascist philosophy of state. The separation is to be accomplished by giving business its own law-making institution, where it may openly and directly enact the legislation it considers necessary for its protection. Legislative privileges vested in the new institution — the National Council of Corporations — will be shorn from the powers of the chamber of deputies, and instead of being subjected to approval by a political body the laws will be enacted by the businessmen themselves.

1934-12-20.text: LONDON, Dec. 20—Gales over the north Atlantic flung up further barriers for shipping today, several liners bound from America to Europe reporting they would be many hours late. The Orient liner Orford, upon her arrival at Plymouth from India, reported a member of her British crew was swept overboard in the Bay of Biscay and drowned. The storms which wrecked the freighters Sisto and Usworth also were responsible indirectly for the sinking of the Dutch steamer Orania yesterday in Portuguese waters. Her 280 passengers were removed safely. Published reports said the Orania was rammed by the Portuguese freighter Loanda in Leixões harbor as the Loanda raced for shelter. The Sisto went down after a battering by the raging seas near the Azores, but all aboard were saved by the rescue work of the crew of the S. S. New York. Seventeen were lost in the sinking of the Usworth. The liners New York an

A spokesman for the United States Naval delegation said tonight that Great Britain and the United States are likely to sign a naval accord between themselves after 1936 if there is no general international naval treaty by that time. The statement was made following the close of the naval conversations which have been carried on for the last two months among delegations from the United States, Great Britain and Japan. These conversations, designed to pave the way for a new naval treaty, did not result in an agreement. He said the American delegation feels that Japan at the present time has been prevented from agreeing to the continuance of the Washington treaty of 1922 because she is going through an internal constitutional revolution. He said the Washington treaty, which puts Japan on the short end of the 5-5-3 naval ratio, has been a political issue in that country for so long that, wit

LONDON, Dec. 19. New evidence was given tonight that Great Britain and the United States stand steadfastly together against granting Japan naval parity as tri-power conversations here adjourned after two months of fruitless negotiations. In an address broadcast in England and rebroadcast in the United States, Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, said: "Our view, the British view, is—and I think it is also the American view—that equality in security is not necessarily reached by an agreement allowing the three powers equality in naval armaments." Earlier American quarters indicated their belief that it would be futile to call an open conference of the world sea powers next year unless Japan surrenders her demand for equality. Looking beyond the naval treaties themselves, delegates believe that of the Pacific political treaties, weakened as they were when Japan seized Manchuria in 1931, only the hollow framework remains. British delegates were inclined to view pacifically the end of the 'preliminary' conference here. The Americans were not. LONDON, Dec. 19--(#)--A naval conference of the world's three greatest sea powers will be held next year only if Japan surrenders her demand for equality, American quarters indicated tonight as tri-power preliminary conversations here formally ended after two months of fruitless negotiations. Simultaneously Japan, in effect, abrogated the 1922 Washington treaty which assigned her the short end of the famed 5-5-3 ratio, the privy council at Tokyo unanimously recommending to Emperor Hirohito that the agreement be denounced. Tonight nothing was in sight to keep Japan, Great Britain and the United States from building their navies to the limit of their national resources after the denouncement of the treaty, together with the accompanying London treaty, expires two years hence. Hull, England, Dec. 19.—{}— English justice today exacted a woman's life for the murder of her husband—the first time in eight years a death penalty had been imposed on one of her sex. The woman, Mrs. Ethel Lille Major, 42-year-old mother of two children, was hanged in Hull prison. LONDON, Dec. 19.—(P)—The world's latest effort at limitation of armaments ended like its predecessors in utter failure tonight with the break up of the preliminary naval conversations among Great Britain, the United States and Japan. Prime Minister J. Ramsay McDonald, as host, told the American and Japanese delegates at the final session, however, that Britain was not content to let matters rest, and intended to continue her efforts for a solution of the naval problems facing the three great sea powers. MacDonald reportedly reaffirmed Great Britain's support of Washington's insistence upon the present 5-5-3 ratio of naval strengths among the three powers, with Japan on the small end. End of the depression, rise of the dollar and brilliant diplomacy that will overcome danger of war with Japan are among the main events predicted for the United States. There also are in the crystal murders, floods, transport accidents and the possibly voluntary retirement of President Roosevelt as having done all he could for the country. But this last, she said, was vague, and probably would not happen in 1935. “The menace of war will hang over Europe like a pall and there will be skirmishes in the Far East, involving the Russians and the Chinese, but actual war will not break out during the coming 12 months. 1934-01-04.text: Washington, D.C.—The government Thursday again offered $34.06 an ounce for newly-mined domestic gold. It was the twelfth repetition of this figure. On the basis of a sterling opening of $5.1074 to the pound, London's bar gold price was $32.54 an ounce.

London. Jan. 3, ()—The death list of persons connected with the opening of the tomb of King Tut-Ankh-Amen in 1922 in Egypt was brought to 20 today with the death of Arthur Edward Pearse Brom Weigall. Weigall, who was present when the tomb was opened, died yesterday at the age of 53, after a long illness. Friends said it was “extraordinary” that he had died so comparatively young, and they recalled the tradition of Tut-Ankh-Amen's curse against those who should violate his last resting place.

NATAL, Brasil, Jan. 4—(UP)— The French navy seaplane Southern Cross, with its crew of five, arrived at seven-ten a.m. today after a 2010-mile flight from St. Louis, British West Africa. The plane left St. Louis in midafternoon yesterday, and Commandant De Bonnet, in charge, reported his progress frequently by wireless. The flight was somewhat longer than the recent one of Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh. They flew 1834 miles from Bathurst, further down the African coast than St. Louis, to Natal.

‘Copyright, 1934, by United Press | LONDON, Jan. 4 (UP)—Japan, | fast outdistancing all rivals in | the race for world trade, consolidated her successes in the orient today with the successful conclusion of a trade treaty with India which it was feared will have far-reaching effects on English textile mills. Dispatches relating this reached London from New Delhi, the Indian capital, late tonight. The negotiations, in process for four months, were concluded and the treaty dispatched to Tokio for early ratification, the United Press learned. The trade accord between Japan and India is for a period of three years. It allows Japan to supply India with a maximum of 400,000,000 square yards of cotton piece goods under a 50 per cent duty. In return Japan is to buy 1,500,000 bales of raw cotton from India, rather than the United States, where the Japanese have been buying much of their raw mater

| LONDON, Jan. 4.— President Roosevelt turned British criticism to praise by his earnest message to the reconvening of congress, newspaper comment showed today, Skeptics, who have been many, admitted with good grace that he had stirred the United States out of discouraged lethargy, Editorials, in sum, constituted the warmest British tribute to the President in many months. Distrustful of the methods the President has chosen to speed recovery, British opinion joined in eulogizing his qualities of leadership and courage. Of all comment, perhaps the most significant was that of the financial news, representing the most hostile section of the President’s British critics, bankers and financiers, “He has succeeded in stirring the American nation out of the morass of apathetic discouragement into which it had sunk,” it said. “Even if measures otherwise harmful, and a certain amount of pure ball

Rome, Jan. 3.—()—A revision of arms figures calculated to strike a satisfactory balance among national armaments, rather than a wholesale slash previously favored by Italy, was said authoritatively today to have been suggested by Premier Mussolini to Sir John Simon, the British foreign secretary. An official communique issued tonight said they had a "cordial colloquy" and will meet again tomorrow morning. In the absence of a more complete account the exact nature of the talk could only be conjectured, but well-informed circles believed that Il Duce has practically abandoned hope in the present situation of winning France over to a thesis of an immediate and radical cut in arms. Steps to build up a force of 100,000 officers to supervise the military and moral training of 2,000,000 boys, members of the Balilla and the Avanguardisti youthful Fascist organizations were announced today by Ren

Paris, Jan. 4.—(4)—France was shaken today by charges that ten to twenty-million-dollar frauds have been revealed by the collapse of the credit municipal bank of Bayonne, which was the city’s pawnshop, and the disappearance of its mysterious founder, Serge Stavisky. The manager of the institution was jailed December 30 and a warrant was issued for Stavisky in connection with the recent alleged issuance of unauthorized bonds. Premier Camille Chautemps, with names high in French governmental quarters involved in the affair, declared Stavisky, who police said had many aliases, will be brought to justice and the case sifted thoroughly. Insurance companies were reported by investigators to have been the principal victims of the sale of fraudulent pawnshop bonds, which Stavisky—operating under the name of Serge Alexandre—is charged with issuing for from three to ten times the pawnshop’s legal

PARIS, Jan. 4—(UP)—A major financial scandal, threatening to involve high government officials, developed today from the collapse of the Crédit Municipal Bayonne, a private bank. Liabilities were estimated at 500,000,000 francs ($31,000,000). Police sought Alexander Stavisky, its head, who was reported to have fled to Greece, Mexico or Venezuela. Gustave Tissier, a director, was under arrest charged with having given several jewels pawned at the institution—which also was an official pawn establishment—to his mistress. Names of two cabinet ministers were brought in to sensational French reports of the bank’s affairs when it was charged that Stavisky had received a mysterious tip from a government department to leave the country and had been aided in his flotation of bonds by another. The scandal started with the failure of the Municipal Credit Bank of Stavisky, one known as Serge Alexand

1934-04-11.text: HAVANA, April 11—(CP)—Cuba has declared a 2-year moratorium on about $50,000,000 in loans from American and British houses and leaders said today it may be extended even longer. It was a case, government officials explained, of letting national obligations, including salaries of public employees, go unpaid, or of suspending payment on certain international obligations. Cuba chose the latter course. Under the moratorium, approved by the cabinet of President Carlos Mendieta last night, nothing will be paid on the principal of bonds floated through Speyer and Morman from 1904 to 1927. Officials emphasized that the interest will be paid. Although the moratorium was announced for two years, Treasury Secretary Joaquin Martinez said "it really will be effective until when Cuba can sustain the burden without danger to its economic structure."

Dublin—The body of American Minister William W. McDowell lay today at the United States legation which he took over officially only two weeks ago on his first diplomatic mission. After an active career as a mining man and political leader in Montana, McDowell was given the post of minister. Last night there was a government dinner in his honor. As he was responding to a speech by President Eamon de Valera he fell dead. Irish Free State officials, diplomats and persons from many countries carried in their minds today the tragic picture of McDowell's collapse as they watched him, the center of interest at the brilliant state dinner at grim old Dublin castle, making his first real diplomatic speech.

London, April 11—(4)—Sir Gerald Du Maurier, 61, noted actor, died in a nursing home today after an operation for an internal disorder. Famed as an actor, producer and manager, Sir Gerald was born at Hampstead, England, March 26, 1873. He was the son of the late George Du Maurier, who won renown as an artist on the staff of Punch and as author of “Trilby.”

GENEVA (UP) — A warning that peace is menaced by a general armament race was given to the world Tuesday by Arthur Henderson of Great Britain, president of the world arms conference in opening a meeting of the steering committee of the conference. Henderson appealed to the delegates to facilitate framing of a treaty to check the movement, The delegates met in the hope of revitalizing the sagging conference and to consider a meeting of the full conference for May 23 in an effort to find a way out of a complete deadlock, Sensing a political angle, Norman H. Davis, American disarmament delegate, announced from London that he would not be present Tuesday.

LONDON, April 10 — Walter Runciman, British Board of Trade president, turned thumbs down today on immediate tariff talks with the United States, indicating that Britain may consider American recovery efforts insufficiently developed to make commitments desirable now. "I do not think commercial conversations between the two governments should be usefully considered at this time," he told the House of Commons in reply to a member's question regarding tariff changes to encourage employment. A belief that London wants to await further developments in Washington before proceeding in matters of tariff gained weight through the fact that Great Britain in recent months has engaged in trade discussions with other countries, including France, Russia, and a number of smaller continental nations.

Istanbul April 11 (INS)—Samuel Insull, indicted former utilities magnate of Chicago, will be extradited to the United States on Friday. This information, revealed exclusively in an International News Service dispatch from London yesterday, was confirmed here today, although American Ambassador Robert P. Skinner remained silent on details of Insull’s departure from Turkey. Insull will leave Istanbul aboard a small boat which will take him to Port Panderma Thursday. He will then go by train, an overnight ride, to Smyrna, where the Turkish government formally will turn the Chicago fugitive over to Burton Y. Berry, young third secretary of the American embassy who has been designated to return Insull to the United States. (Continued on Page Six)

WV Bt. PUGH CAMBRIDGE, England, April 11—Another “dead sea” has been discovered. Unlike the one in Palestine, it is not open to the sky and in its murky and mysterious depths no living thing moves. It is far down in the ocean between Arabia and India. To depths of from 50 to 100 feet below the surface, the waters teem with marine life. Below those levels life does not exist. The discovery is due to the research of the expedition financed by the late Sir John Murray. The commander sent today a fresh report to Prof. Stanley Gardiner, expedition secretary. Prof. Gardiner expressed the opinion that the lack of life in the depths may be laid to the petroleum which has been seeping for ages from the land into the sea, producing an effect similar to the familiar Palestinian Dead Sea. The secretary received from the expedition samples of water and one from other parts of the ocean between Arabia

Havana, April 10.—(?)—The cabinet tonight approved a two-year moratorium on the principal of about $53,000,000 in foreign loans granted by American and British financial houses to the Cuban government between 1904 and 1920. These were known as the Speyer and the Morgan loans. It was made clear that the moratorium was only on the principal of the Speyer and Morgan loans, and that interest payments would be made regularly.

1934-03-27.text: WASHINGTON, March 27—(CUP)— President Roosevelt today signed the Vinson-Trammell navy bill which provides construction of new ships to bring the country’s sea forces up to the limit prescribed by the London treaty. Cameras clicked as Mr. Roosevelt, in the presence of Rep. Fred Britten, R., Ill., and Rep. Carl Vinson, D., Ga., signed the document. The President issued a statement in which he said “it has been and will be the policy of the administration to favor continued limitation of naval armaments. It is my personal hope that the naval conference to be held in 1935 will extend all existing limitations and agree to further reductions.” The Vinson-Trammell act authorizes construction of 102 warships and 1,140 airplanes over the next five years to replace obsolete ships and bring the U.S. sea power up to treaty limits. If the president and Congress carry out this authorized program in fu

Paris, March 26, (i France's hopes for a tri-power defense alliance of France, Great Britain, and Belgium will be broached at a conference tomorrow between foreign affairs minister, Louis Bartou and Count Charles de Broqueville, the Belgian prime minister. An apparent breakdown of the disarmament conference and what Paris statesmen call the steady rearmament of Germany are worrying the French, who are launching diplomatic calls to England and the little entente.

SPY se SsEPesteR Ve Sees (Associated Press Foreign Staff) LONDON, March 26 (?)—How far Great Britain is willing to go in coercing nations to live up to a disarmament treaty was considered tonight by cabinet leaders. This issue, raised by France in an arms note last week, opens a new and possibly a deciding chapter in months-old disarmament negotiations. The British government was said to view the subject with an open mind but requires further communications from France before taking any definite stand. U. S. Attitude Is Factor The attitude of the United States and the extent to which nations would disarm if Britain obligated herself to take military and economic measures against a violator of a treaty were viewed as deciding factors. The question of military and economic sanctions heretofore had only been raised as a possible retaliation against an aggressor in the event of a breach of p

LONDON, Mar. 27. ()— The President Roosevelt from London morning newspapers today — congratulations on settling the dispute in the American motor car industry! Predicted the Times: "It will increase the enormous prestige he already enjoys and strengthen him in dealing with disputes which reach a critical stage in other industries." And the Telegraph said the present terms "will become a new chapter in the whole of American labor. ... It is a great personal triumph for Roosevelt. His intervention administered the greatest blow that individualism in American big industry has sustained."

PARIS, March 27 (—French police smashed at political factions which, they said, are arming themselves against the government, in a widespread series of raids today throughout Paris and the suburbs collecting hundreds of rifles and pistols and a huge stock of ammunition, swords, and bayonets. The raiders searched for evidence that the extremist groups of the Right and Left political parties were arming in anticipation of a papers have repeatedly charged. The details of the raids were kept secret, although various incidents seeped out. It was reported that 40 guns were found under beds and behind cupboards in an apartment in Saint-Quen, a working-class suburb where many radicals are known to live. In another haul, 36 automatic pistols, a quantity of bayonets and swords, and a number of rifles were taken. Two persons were known to be arrested in the earliest raids of the day. Of these two,

By Associate, SHANGHAI, March 27. — Miss Leonora Levy, weak and pale from an attempt to kill herself with C. G. Julian, unfolded today what she called the “inside story" of the former American oil millionaire’s death Sunday. “He was broke,” said Miss Levy, Julian’s secretary and confidante. “Saturday night was the last night he could have had a roof over his head. Hotels where he had registered had ordered him out. "In addition, he had proposed marriage to me and I had turned him down. With all this, he said life wasn't worth living. He checked out. (Meaning, Julian committed suicide by swallowing the powerful potion from which Miss Levy later drank.) “‘I never will attempt suicide again, but damn the doctors! I wanted to die.” “I attempted suicide,” she said, “because I felt I was indirectly instrumental in his death.” Miss Levy and Julian, who fled to China in default of $25,000 bail i

Shanghai, March 27.--(A.P.) — General Chiang Kui-Shek shipped four of his high ranking air officers to the United States today to study the latest American aeronautical advances and bring new ideas back to China. The Chinese fliers are due in San Francisco April 11 on the President Coolidge. They are General K. Y. Wong and Colonels T. S. Chang, C. S. Ding and J. O. Mov.

PARIS—Robert G. and Marjorie Switz, young Americans held as leaders of a great international spy ring, may win freedom on bail on the ground that because they betrayed comrades they are entitled to clemency, it was indicated today.

1934-02-03.text: Washington, D. C.—(AP)—A series of private money talks with Great Britain was indicated authoritatively today to be either underway or about to begin, as officials here investigated actions in London and Paris to determine their own course. In the intricate web of European governmental high finance, authorities saw possibilities that might determine the future of President Roosevelt’s dollar program. Reactions abroad yesterday to the 40.94 percent devaluation and the new high for gold were not considered highly satisfactory here. High sources conceded the Roosevelt gold policy could be hampered by a French embargo on gold which would eliminate this heavy source of the world market supply and simultaneously act against the effect of America’s fixed $35 an ounce price. Officials watched particularly for movements that might affect the gold standard position of France, such as continued hea

LONDON (#) - The sixty-cent dollar was a knockout blow for many Americans who work for a living abroad. Many of them fear they'll soon be roving up and down the streets of Europe saying, “Brother, can you spare me a sou, penny or farthing?” American government employees abroad, convinced they are the “forgotten men” of the new deal, were jolted in the pocketbooks again today with the notification that their pay checks will no longer be cashed at the old parity rate of $4.86 to the British pound, but on a basis of the ruling exchange rate. From the French capital the devalued dollar has started homeward the last of the foot-free traveling Americans who hoped the dollar would rise or that the French franc would decline. The American Chamber of Commerce in Berlin sent a cablegram to the National Chamber of Commerce in Washington, protesting the action of the House Appropriations Committee i

Southampton, Eng., Feb. 3 (AP)—The trans-Atlantic gold rush in the wake of American devaluation moves began today. The great liners Bremen and Berengaria sailed with cargo stacked with gold bars of an estimated value of more than $30,000,000. By special train, airplanes and trucks the gold arrived at the port and was stacked in heavily guarded cases until safely aboard the ships. The Berengaria carried about $20,000,000 worth of gold and will pick up another $5,000,000 at Cherbourg tonight, while the Bremen had $7,500,000 worth in its strong rooms. The precious cargoes consisted of gold bars weighing about 60 pounds each. The bars were packed two to a box and each box was worth roughly $50,000.

LONDON, Feb. 2. — (P) — Emily Smith, a solitary old woman who lived in one of the lowliest districts of Paddington on the upper reaches of the Thames river, left a will which revealed today an estate of more than $250,000. It all started from pennies. She was the daughter of a veteran of the Crimea who was in charge of the famous garden maze at Hampton Court Palace, with the privilege of charging for admission. The charge was a penny, and persons from London and the world over thronged the palace every summer for the thrill of trying to find their way out of half a mile of strange labyrinthian passages formed by hedgerows planted in the days of Charles I. The last ten years the government has taken over the maze—and likewise the pennies.

(By the Associated Press) Paris and London experienced a gold rush Friday, and dollar quota- tions ascended. - London operators bought French gold francs heavily for resale in the United States at a profit; the unpre- cedented price of 139 shillings, six pence a fine ounce approximated the United States’ offer; a flood of gold was started to America. One London newspaper used the big headline: “City Goes Mad on Gold.” Reasons for the excitement were found in operators’ desires to partici- pate in what they predicted would be a Wall Street boom in response to the American devaluation of the dol- lar and the meeting of the French normal adverse balance of trade. In the British capital the American currency closed at the day's best rate $4.92 3-4 in relation to the pound— a rise of nearly five cents to the pound—after a weak opening. The after-hours rate was even better, $4.90 1-2. The doll

LONDON, Feb. 3.—(P)—Hiroshi Saito, who at 47 has been rewarded with one of the two most important assignments in the Japanese diplomatic service—the ambassadorship at Washington—left for his new post today firmly convinced that nothing stands in the way of bringing about the most friendly basis of understanding between the two countries. “There is no real outstanding difficulty” between the United States and Japan,” the new ambassador said as he walked through Waterloo station to entrain for Southampton to embark on the Berengaria. “It is absurd to say that Japan and America now or ever will be at loggerheads.” Saito called attention to the recent expressions of opinion in America on matters in which the Japanese are concerned, such as the Manchurian problem, immigration and trade. These expressions, he said, indicated Americans are beginning to understand Japan’s position in these matte

London.---(UP)—London’s world market gold rate, major factor in intricate international monetary maneuvers, was reduced sharply today as the American dollar continued its firmness despite devaluation. The pound opened at $4.89½, and closed at $4.93¼. French franc opened at 77½ to the pound and closed at 77 23/32. As against the American treasury rate of $35 an ounce, the London rate today was fixed at $38.95, down 85 cents from yesterday's record price of $34.80. More than $7,000,000 in gold bullion was aboard the fast liners Berengaria and Bremen, which left Cherbourg today for New York. The gold will be offered for sale at the treasury price in order that speculators may gain the difference between the London and American prices. The gold rate today was set at 438 shillings’ three pence. Yesterday’s rate of 139 shillings 6 pence, a record, was set with the pound at $4.96, and the equiv

CHICAGO, Feb. 3 (UP).—John (Jake the Barber) Factor will be permitted to remain in the United States to appear at a second trial of three Touhy gangsters charged with kidnapping him, attorneys for the British government indicated today. The first trial of Roger Touhy, Albert Kator and Gustav Schaeffer on the kidnapping charges ended last night in a deadlocked jury, which was discharged by Judge Michael Feinberg. The date for the new trial was set for February 13.

1934-06-29.text: Sandwich, Eng. June 29.—(P)—Henry Cotton, 27 year old British professional, today won the British open golf championship with a 72 hole aggregate of 283, tying the record for the tournament created in 1932 by Gene Sarazen. After setting a record-breaking pace for his first two rounds, with a 67 and a 65, Cotton struck his third round this morning in par 72 and faltered on the final round, taking a 78. He missed a three foot putt on the final green and his bid to break Sarazen's record, but his victory nevertheless ended a 10-year winning streak by Americans. Trailed by a gallery of 5,000 stampeding and cheering Britons, Cotton went into the final round with a ten strokes lead over the field. The pressure of the terrific pace of his previous rounds coupled with the shouting, bothersome crowd combined to almost cause the Briton's collapse. Far off the gain he maintained on Wednesday, Thurs

Sandwich, Eng. June 29, (U2) —Henry Cotton, lanky British professional attached to the Waterloo Club of Brussels, Belgium, today captured the British open golf championship. The 27-year-old Britisher, who shot some of the most spectacular rounds ever witnessed on this difficult course, scored a 79 this afternoon for an aggregate of 283. Cotton owed his triumph to the brilliant 67 he scored in the opening round, and the record-breaking 65 recorded in yesterday's second round. He faltered somewhat in the third round played this morning when he scored 72, but slumped desperately in the final round this afternoon. Despite the near blow-up in the final test, Cotton equalled the record low score for the British open. It was estimated by Gene Sarazen of New York when he won the title at Prince's in 1932. The previous record was 285 by Bobby Jones in 1927. Cotton's victory broke the ten-year hol

(Copyright, 1934, by the Associated Press.) BERLIN, June 28.—(#)—Adolf Hitler stood today at a crossroad marked “right” and “left.” Germany seethed while he debated his choice. The chancellor came back to Berlin after several days of quiet reflection in his mountain home—reflection following growing outbursts against radical Nazi policies. Two groups began powerful efforts to have him take their side. It is a struggle for “the capture of the soul of Hitler,” one cabinet minister said. Urge of the Radicals. On the one hand there was the radical young wing of impetuous revolutionaries, typified by Joseph Goebbels, minister of propaganda, and Dr. Alfred Rosenberg, philosophic dictator of the Third Reich whose books on religion have been proscribed by the Vatican. They insist the Nazi revolution has just begun and that no loyal German can be satisfied until the Nazis exclusively control ever

- Vienna, June 28—(UP)—Widespread bombing outrages broke out in Austria today, one of which was said possibly to have been directed at Louis Barthou, French foreign minister. The main line of a railroad near Bludenz was shattered by a bomb. Trains were delayed for several hours, but one bearing Barthou to Paris missed the explosion. Widespread property damage accompanied the disorders on the 20th anniversary of the assassination of Archduke Ferdinand at Sarajevo, Bosnia. A police captain died of injuries received in a political clash at Graz.

ISTANBUL, Turkey, June 29 (AP).—Death caught up today with Zaro Agha, Turkey’s Methuselah who once boasted he would live forever. The picturesque old man who claimed 160 years and felt deeply hurt when anyone doubted it died—by a quirk of fate—in the children’s hospital. For two months Zaro Agha, whose longevity brought him from obscurity to world fame and Broadway when he was “past 150,” had been ill. He was suffering from a variety of ailments, including Bright's disease and gland and bladder disorders. Probably his proudest possession was a certificate purporting to show he was born in 1774—before the American colonies declared war on Great Britain. Zaro had buried 10 wives and had another desert him. Number 11 got angry six years ago when her aged husband decided he wanted a twelfth wife—one young and pretty—and refused to come home. The number of children? Zaro boasted that at 96 hi

5 RR KR PRA EE RA VEIN | United Press Staff Correspondent | (Copyright 1934 by United Press) BERLIN, June 29—-(UP)--Chancellor Adolf Hitler fought for his political life today amid rumors of an impending reactionary coup and a general strike. Though the situation was serious, competent, unprejudiced German opinion saw evidence that he would win. There were half a dozen circumstances that might lead to the overthrow of Hitler and national Socialism, but Hitler seemed unexcited, unhurried, and determined to find a solution for what promised to be a finish fight between radicals and conservatives. More important, both sides expressed publicly and privately confidence in him personally as the only man at the moment who could remain in power. ISTANBUL, Turkey, June 29 (UP).—Zaro Agha, the ancient Turk whose life bridged two epochs in history, died today, painlessly and looking forward to an eternity in paradise, attended by the entrancing houris of Islam. For several days he had been sinking, suffering from a hopeless combination of uremia and arteriosclerosis. Between periods of coma, sometimes delirious, he reviewed the little events and triumphs of his life, and occasionally mumbled: “I am 164 years old.” His age was his pride, his age and virility that took his six feet of thick bones covered by wrinkled brown skin to New York and London only four years ago, to go to night clubs, ride in an airplane and bounce up resiliently after being hit by a Broadway taxicab. Dr. Bedjet Sait Bey told him he was going to die. “I have lived longer than any man,” he said, “I am all ready.” He took a sip from a glass of milk beside his be

BOMBAY, India, P)—Pieces of iron, laid by wreckers were removed from a crossing at a wayside station near Poona Friday just before a train bearing Mahatma M. K. Gandhi passed. Last Monday a bomb was thrown at a car at the Poona municipal hall, where Gandhi was due to make a speech. He arrived five minutes after the bomb exploded. It injured five people.

1934-10-16.text: COBH, Irish Free State, Oct. 16 The American liner Manhattan set a new post-war speed record of 5 days, 6 hours, 19 minutes today for the crossing from New York to Cobh. Her average speed across the Atlantic was 22.78 knots.

BOSTON, Oct. 16 (AP).—Surgeons heard today how Daphne Muir, English novelist, saw after nine years of total blindness that was ended by a modern surgical miracle. She is attending the meeting of the American College of Surgeons as the guest of Sir Harold Gillies, a British surgeon, and his wife. Dr. Tudor Thomas, the Welsh surgeon who restored her sight, is not here, but in his absence her visit fitted into the ‘show me’ clinics of the surgeons, where they gather at hospitals to see surgery. Daphne Muir was blinded nine years ago in an automobile accident. The blindness was in both eyes and in both of them it was in the cornea, the outer covering, just in front of the pupil of the eye. Normally the cornea is clear as glass. It may become opaque from injury or acid or disease. That shuts off all light, and that happened to Mrs. Muir. This darkening of the cornea is not the same as a catar

Muskegon, Mich.—()—An “Enoch Arden” case, with reverse English, neared its legal conclusion today with the issuance of a marriage license to a couple whose first marriage was terminated when the first wife of the husband let it be known she wasn’t dead, after all. Louis Crenno, of Muskegon Heights, who got a divorce last week from the wife he had believed dead, obtained the license to wed “Ella N. Start,” the maiden name of his second wife. They were married several years ago after a body taken from Lake Michigan at Chicago had been identified as that of the first Mrs. Crenno by Mrs. Fred Savoy, of Bessemer, Mich., her mother. They separated when the first Mrs. Crenno wrote her mother from Eggertsville, N. Y., to say she was alive. Crenno and the wife he now is to re-marry have two children.

HAWARDEN, Ia., Oct. 15 (7) — The First National Bank of Hawarden was robbed here this afternoon by three unmasked men armed with a machine gun and automatic pistols. The bandits escaped with $1,200 to $1,500 in counter cash, but arrived five minutes after a nighttime lock on the vault safe prevented them from obtaining an additional $6,000 in currency. Three hostages taken with them in flight north on State Highway 12 were released unharmed a short distance in the country.

MILDENHALL AIRDROME, Eng., Oct. 16 —Col. Roscoe Turner and Clyde Pangborn, in their big twin-engined airplane, swooped to a fine landing here today despite a wind with practically gale force and intermittent storms which swept across the airdrome. They were reporting their readiness to start Saturday in the 12,000 mile England to Australia air race, the world’s longest. The American team had flown Marthlesham where their machine was weighed and checked. In Wintry Weather When they piled out of the ship, Turner called and shouted at Pangborn: “Come along, boy, let's go somewhere and get warm.” Both the men were shivering in the unseasonable icy blasts. Their arrival attracted a great deal of attention for the team is regarded as one of the favorites in the race. Their machine was the fifteenth to report at Mildenhall, and was to be followed today by seven more bringing the total in readin

PARIS, Oct. 15 (4)—Raymond Poincaré, one of the last of France’s great World War figures, died quietly at 3:30 o’clock this morning. The wartime president and “savior of the franc” ten years later, was 74 years old. The shock of the Marseille assassinations may have hurried the end. M. Poincaré grieved over the disastrous event, for he knew King Alexander well and Louis Barthou was his life-long friend. Death came at his home here after a short illness which doctors thought was not serious. The elderly statesman had expected to leave shortly on his annual winter trip to the Riviera. Although virtually in political retirement since he resigned as premier in 1929, Poincaré had just been reelected to a departmental council seat after a spectacular physical comeback. Doctors two years ago gave him up for lost. “Just Worn Out” “He was just worn out,” they said today. All last night his wife a

MELUN, France, Oct. 16 — The French National police announced that Mio Kraj, alias A. Chamley, had confessed he was sent to Marseilles with Petrus Kalemen to assassinate King Alexander of Yugoslavia. Kalemen whose real name was Georgies, a Macedonian revolutionary leader, actually killed the king and was slain by police. The French police said that in his confession Kraj declared that a delegate of Dr. Ante Pavelich, head of the revolutionary secret society, Ustashi, gave Kalemen instructions on the killing. “I am going away,” the delegate was said to have told Kalemen and Kraj. “You know the king is arriving. You also know what you must do—go to Marseilles and fire on the king.” Kraj admitted that he and Kalemen arrived in Marseilles on the day of the assassination and picked a favorable spot where the king would pass. Two bombs and an automatic pistol were found in a search of the hote

PARIS, Oct. 15 (AP)--The body of Raymond Poincare, who served the France he loved with passionate patriotism as wartime president, will be buried Saturday in the little family cemetery at Nubecourt near Bar-Le-Duc. Poincare, broken by long illness, died early today at the age of 74. His labors for his country had taxed too greatly, he himself said, his physical resistance. Like Poincare, the little cemetery where he will be buried, while the notables of France and the world pay him honors, suffered in the war. Its tombstones still bear the scars of shell fragments. Paralysis Fatal A stroke of paralysis which reached his heart ended the life of the man who was described as the last of France’s war great and the savior of its money. His health had long been poor, weakened, as he once said he was, “by the succession of emotional shocks” he experienced as president during the war and his bat

1934-09-18.text: ANEGNWY DRE a, IN, Te, OPT, Le (P)—In one of the swiftest and most dramatic races ever waged for the famous America’s Cup, the big blue challenger from England, Sir Thomas Sopwith’s Endeavour, overcame a succession of sail-hoisting difficulties today and administered an unexpected but sound beating to the defending sloop, Harold S. Vanderbilt's Rainbow. Endeavour demonstrated conclusively that she is a superior heavy weather craft, completely reversing her sorry showing in Saturday's drifting match that wound up “no contest,” and today was one up in the first conclusive test of the 1934 series. The British yacht was roaring full-throated defiance to American sea supremacy for the first time since 1920. After chasing the Rainbow over the outgoing half of the windward-leeward course through heavy seas and rain squalls, Endeavour overtook the defender at the outset of the run home, with a f

NEWPORT (AP) — Driving his yacht Endeavour through choppy seas, T. O. Sopwith scored a second straight triumph in the America's Cup series Tuesday and took a commanding lead in an effort to get the cup held by America for 83 years. The Britisher sent the boat over the finish line 51 seconds ahead of the Rainbow. Endeavour broke the America's Cup record for the 30-mile triangle course after overcoming difficulties such as a torn sail and unfavorable position on the first leg of Tuesday's race.

Rome, Sept. 18 (AP)—Italy’s farming industry will be brought into a strong national organization under the corporative state system, to be inaugurated November 19. The working class will be welded together in one group and the owner-manager class in another. The two classes will be united in the central corporations. Two major national coordinating bodies have been created for the separate groups. These are the Fascist Confederation of Agriculturists, for the owner-managers, and the Fascist Confederation of Agricultural Workers.

(By United Press) GENEVA, Sept. 14.-Admission of Soviet Russia to the League of Nations was voted formally tonight by the assembly. The assembly voted Russia a permanent seat on the council. The vote on admission was 39 to 3. Voting 'no' included Portugal, and Argentina.

United Press Staff Correspondent GENEVA, Sept. 18 (UP) -—A meeting of the League of Nations assembly was called today for 6 p. m. to admit Soviet Russia to the league. Seventeen years after the Bolshevik revolution, the Union of Soviet Republics has been invited to join the league, and was assured the necessary two-thirds majority. The steering committee, which called the assembly session, decided that Salvador de Madariaga, Spanish delegate, should submit the political commission's resolution recommending Russia’s admittance, and then the assembly should vote the Communist republic into the league and a permanent seat on its council. After that, it was planned that the Russian delegation, headed by Maxim Litvinov, brilliant foreign minister, should enter and take seats. Litvinov was expected to make his maiden speech at once. That his speech would be a memorable one, no one doubted. Tha

EDMONTON, ALTA., Sept. 18.—(?) A woman, it has often been said, may change her mind, but the appellate division of the supreme court has ruled that she may also change her husband's mind. W. Fraser, Bonnyville farmer, traded his cow for a buggy and took the vehicle home. Mrs. Fraser objected to the deal, and he marched back to his neighbor, with whom he made the trade, and left the buggy and took the cow. Charged with theft of the cow, Fraser was fined $1 by a magistrate. However, when the appellate division heard all the facts, it ruled that under the circumstances there was insufficient evidence to support a theft charge, and quashed the conviction.

Geneva, Sept. 17.—(?)—Five nations opposed to Russia's admission to the League of Nations lashed out today at communist propaganda but the league's political committee nevertheless voted to recommend the Soviet for membership. Inasmuch as all countries entitled to vote at tomorrow's session of the assembly which will formally decide the Russian issue had the right to vote in committee, the result was deemed a safe indication that Russia's election is certain. Delegates representing Portugal, Switzerland, Holland, Belgium and the Argentine assailed Moscow's political philosophy before the committee voted 38 to 3 in favor of Russia’s admission. There were seven abstentions. France Heard With the question already decided in Russia's favor save for the formalities of the committee's recommendation and the assembly's formal vote, Louis Barthou, foreign minister of France, which has staunchly

Geneva, Sept. 18 (P)—Communist placards distributed in Geneva welcomed Soviet Russia into the League of Nations as the assembly prepared today to admit her formally into the international family. The signs, pasted on windows of many stores during the night, said: “welcome to Union of Socialist Soviet Republic, which brings us peace.” Leon Nicole, head of the socialist Geneva government, issued an order to police to interfere no longer with persons wearing red caps. The action of the League’s political committee in recommending Russia for entrance clinched matters yesterday but the assembly must make a formal vote. The Netherlands, Portugal and Switzerland voted against a favorable report.
