The forthcoming visit of Louis Barthou, French foreign minister, also was mentioned. Baldwin answered with a curt negative when Morgan Jones, labor

London, July 6—(4)—Technical collaboration from Great Britain in the event Belgium is ever invaded is all that France is asking of England, and indications are that she may get it, The Associated Press was informed today. France has not asked and does not expect, it was learned, any sort of political or defensive alliance with Great Britain, not because the French would not want it, but because months ago Britain plainly informed Paris that the Locarno pact was the only one to which she wished to adhere. The technical collaboration would consist of purely military cooperation which is a matter affecting the general staffs of the two nations’ military forces, and not a political point. In return for technical cooperation, France would have to divorce herself entirely in any military way from the Belgian general staff and reconstruct a French defense policy on the basis of a strictly neutr

WIMBLEDON, Eng., July 7 (P)— Helen Hull Jacobs, twice a finalist but never a winner of the most prized title in tennis, again was turned back today in her bid for the women’s singles crown of the all-England championships by Dorothy Round, ranking English player, who defeated her 6-2, 5-7, 6-3 in the final round.

MAGNOLIA, Mass., July 7 (UP).— The “machine-gun” with which five sportily-garbed bandits engineered the biggest gem robbery—about $400,000—in New England’s history here yesterday, was no more dangerous than John Dillinger’s wooden pistol, investigators decided today. Police said there was every indication that the “machine-gun” carried by the leader was a wooden dummy, painted black. Under threat of death from this “weapon,” three employees of the Magnolia branch of Hodgsen-Cennard & Company, long-established Boston jewelry house, submitted to being bound and gagged while the robbers cleaned out the exclusive shop. After itemizing the loot, company officials estimated its wholesale value at $327,377 and its retail value at $500,000 to $550,000. It was insured for a half million dollars. While they checked their losses, police and private detectives sought a regular summer resident of thi

Copyright 1954 United Press BERLIN, July 7.-A pause seemed today to have come in the rapid pace of events which in the last week have centered the eyes of the world on Germany. In that belief dozens of foreign correspondents who sped to Berlin are leaving for London, Paris, Moscow and other points. In Berlin remain a hundred provocative questions — and nobody can answer them. There is the riddle of Adolf Hitler and why he, who has always been first to make a leader's declaration at the moment of crisis, has made no public statement since last Saturday. Many people say there are factors in the investigation of the Schleicher-Roehm revolt which would be jeopardized if any public statement were made at the moment. What will be the relative position of Herman Goering, the former "Iron Fist"; Vice Chancellor Franz von Papen and Minister of Propaganda Paul Joseph Goebbels and the Reichswehr in

Hollywood, July 6 (Alec Francis, old time character actor of the motion pictures, died late today at Hollywood Hospital. Francis, whose death came unexpectedly after an illness of only three days, was 64 years old. Born in England, he had been in motion pictures since 1910. Among some of the better known pictures in which Francis played were “Mata Hari,” in which Greta Garbo played the lead; “Arrowsmith,” “Smilin’ Thru,” “Outward Bound,” “The Return of Peter Grimm,” and “The Music Master.”

LONDON, July 6.—Military collaboration of a technical nature in view of a Franco-British defense alliance emerged today as a possible answer to French attempts to gain security guarantees. The Associated Press was informed France and Great Britain already have exchanged private views on the matter. French Foreign Minister Louis Barthou will raise the point officially next week on his visit to join in preliminary naval conference conversations, and expects to carry home a formal affirmative reply. Barthou also will ask the British to state formally whether they still stand by all that the Locarno Pact implies, and the British will make an affirmative reply.

ALTON, England, July 7.—(UP)— Because of the long drought, Chesterfield Lane, proprietor of the Swan hotel, had lines painted five inches from the bottom of all bathtubs, with a notice asking guests not to fill the tubs beyond that level:

1934-05-15.text: Paris, May 15, (R)—Airport crews of three nations watched today for the orange colored airplane Leonardo Da Vinci to flash across the Atlantic coastline, bearing Cesare Sabelli and George R. Pond on their New York-Rome flight. Weather conditions were reported generally good with favorable wind. The two World War veterans, Italian and American, were believed approaching the French coast between Brest and Bordeaux on their 4,600-mile flight. It was hoped that during the afternoon the Leonardo would cross the coast and speed on to the Italian frontier and down the peninsula, to arrive at Rome at dawn tomorrow. Though Sabelli and Pond, realizing an ambition of years standing, intended at their start from Floyd Bennett airport, New York, at 8:24 a.m. yesterday, to cut the corner of the Canadian coast and shorten their flight by 250 miles or so, reports indicated that they had taken the safer

Tokio (/P)--A Japanese army report said today that rifle fire from Russian military positions on the Russian bank of the Amur river Saturday killed one Manchukuoan sailor and wounded another aboard a steamer. The army report made no mention of advices from Tsitsihar to the newspaper, Asahi, that a detachment of Japanese troops bound for duty at Heiho was aboard the vessel. The war office declined to comment. A spokesman said the government of the Japanese protected empire of Manchukuo was investigating. He said a protest might be made to Moscow. Tokyo government officials expressed the opinion that serious Russo-Japanese friction because of the affair was unlikely in view of the serious efforts being made by both governments recently to arrive at a friendly solution of the Russo-Japanese issues.

BERLIN (WP)—Dr. Hermann Victor Masuch, meteorologist, was found dead Tuesday in the wreckage of Germany's largest non-dirigible balloon "Bartsch Von Sigsfeld," 12 miles east of the Latvian town of Boenaburg, on Russian soil. The body of Dr. Franz Martin Schrenck, balloonist, with whom he set out from here Sunday on a flight into the upper air, was found ten miles from the wreckage. An international search was instituted for the balloonists Monday. They set out to go to an altitude of 32,800 feet (10,000 metres) to study the effects of cosmic rays on gases. The Bartsch Von Sigsfeld was a balloon of stratosphere type. Three tanks of oxygen, flags and other articles were found undisturbed in the balloon's gondola. Condition of the balloon's scientific instruments, which might give a clue to the flyers’ fate, was uncertain. The balloon went up at 8 a.m. Sunday and disappeared eastward.

Fontainebleau, France, May 18. - (4P) - Five men and two women were killed and six persons were injured today as the driver of an automobile in a hill race tried to avoid hitting a stray dog and plunged into a group of spectators. Spectators waved to the driver, Eric Cochin, a military aviator, calling his attention to the animal. Cochin pulled quickly on his steering wheel to miss the animal, and the speeding car went out of control. Cochin died a short time later in a hospital. One of the women was decapitated as the car struck her. Two of those killed were soldiers from the artillery school here. Fredericksburg, Va., May 13. - (P) - John Harding O'Donnoghue, Sr., of Washington, was instantly killed today, and Mrs. Dorothy Swift, also of Washington, was injured when her car struck the north end of the Falmouth bridge, near here, as she swerved to avoid hitting a dog.

Berlin—(—Hermann Wilhelm Goering, minister of aviation, today ordered a commission to go to Russia at once to investigate the deaths of two German balloonists found dead on Russian soil. The dead men were the crew of Germany's biggest balloon, the Bartsch von Segsfeld. They were Dr. Hermann Victor Masuch and Martin Schrenk. They took off Sunday from Bitterfield, Germany. No more was heard from them until today when the Soviet government announced the wrecked balloon had been found last night 22 miles east of the Soviet frontier station of Sedesh. One balloonist lay dead in the gondola. The body of the other pilot was found nine miles farther east. German experts said they were sure that a faulty oxygen apparatus caused the death of the two men who had sought to make substratosphere studies.

FONTAINEBLEAU (France), May 14.—Eight persons—six men and two women—are dead and five injured because of an automobile racing driver's efforts to save the life of a dog. The driver, Erich Cochin, an army aviator, lost control of his car and it hurtled into a mass of spectators when he swerved during a race in Fontainebleau Forest to avoid hitting the animal. Cochin died in a hospital, one of the women killed was decapitated. The spectators had attracted Cochin’s attention to the dog, waving to him and crying out when it dashed out upon the speedway. The dog apparently escaped unhurt.

CIUDAD REAL, Spain, May 15.— Women and children were used as shields, it was charged today, in Socialist rioting in which several persons were wounded critically at Villarubia De Los Ojos. Fighting broke out when Civil Guards attempted to disperse Socialists demonstrating in front of the Town Hall against the removal of the Socialist mayor. The rioters hurled sticks and stones. A battle ensued.

Tokyo, May 14.---(4)—The slaying of a Manchukuoan sailor and the wounding of another on the Amur river Saturday was laid by Japanese army reports today to a burst of rifle fire from military positions on the Russian bank of the river. An investigation of the incident was begun by the newly-formed state of Manchukuo. Japanese reports said the sailors were felled while aboard a steamer. Comment was declined by the war office, but a spokesman said that officials of Manchukuo, a Japanese-dominated state which recently enthroned Henry Pu Yi as emperor, were seeking to get to the bottom of the affair. Protest Predicted A protest to Moscow appeared likely, especially in view of the strained relations between Japan and the Soviet in the Far East.

1934-02-09.text: A cold wave struck the eastern United States today and sent a score of persons to death in the bitterest temperatures ever recorded in many cities. The sub-zero wave reached west to Wisconsin but was most intense in New York state and New England. In New York City an all-time low record was set with a reading of 14.3 degrees below zero which came on the 64th anniversary of the founding of the U. S. weather bureau. In slum districts families suffered severely. Lodging houses were stormed by transients seeking refuge. Traffic in New York harbor was hampered by floating ice and upper reaches of Hudson river were frozen from shore to shore. The lowest temperature in the east was recorded at Mt. Washington, N.H., where a 99 mile northwest wind dropped the mercury to 40 below zero. Boston established an all-time cold record of 18 degrees below zero and six deaths were reported in Massachusetts

MANSFIELD, Feb. 9 (UP)—Greater use of the parole law to relieve overcrowding at the Mansfield reformatory will be recommended by State Welfare Director John W. McSweeney in a report to Gov. George White on conditions at the institution. The welfare director made this statement Thursday night after a thorough inspection of the prison. He had been sent here by the governor and remained until after all prisoners had retired so as to be able to report on sleeping facilities at the institution. "The parole is the only possible means" of relieving overcrowding at the present time and in view of changed economic conditions is more advisable now than at any time in the past few years, McSweeney said. "There is little chance of enlarging the reformatory or of building a new penal institution to house the overflow. Transfer to other institutions is impossible because they are crowded." McSweeney s

| Paris, France, Feb. 9.—()—Gas- ton Doumergue, 71-year-old premier- designate, turned his back on youthful enthusiasts this afternoon to name a cabinet of experienced veterans banded together by the crisis threatening their France. Some half a dozen former premiers were named in the ministry which Doumergue planned to present later in the day to President Lebrun for approval. Two of the strongest political veterans in France today—former Premiers Andre Tardieu and Edouard Herriot—agreed to serve in this time of need as “ministers of state” without portfolios. They will both have the title of vice premier. The cabinet is slightly leftist or advanced liberal in complexion with only the communists and the socialist faction headed by Deputy Leon Blum left out. Street disorders as a prelude to the general strike called for Monday, again threatened Paris. Soldiers were moved toward the worker

Paris, Feb. 9 (UP)—Gaston Doumergue completed his “salvation” cabinet today as 8,000 troops marched into the capital and camped at public buildings and barracks. Doumergue completed his cabinet at 1 p.m. He decided to take only the prime ministry instead of occupying also one of the ministerial portfolios. The 71-year-old Doumergue planned to announce his cabinet list this afternoon after President Albert Lebrun decreed it as official. It will be published in tomorrow’s official journal as final. The troops, symbols of the republic’s authority, came to reinforce the Paris garrison in anticipation of a 24-hour general strike called by labor unions in protest against the possibility of a dictatorship under the concentration government. Doumergue’s cabinet, as unofficially outlined, was regarded as perhaps the strongest France has had—even stronger than the “save the franc” cabinet of Raymo

(Copyright, 1934, By The Associated Press.) PARIS, Feb. 8—P)—The aged and venerated Gaston Doumergue led anxious France along the path to peace today after 48 hours of violence, but the Premier-elect met difficulties as he sought a “cabinet of political truce.” A veteran of political strife as former minister, premier and president, Doumergue worked to perfect his “salvation government” in an atmosphere of sadness, with flags everywhere at half mast in honor of victims in Tuesday's and Wednesday's nights of terror. His smiling arrival from his peaceful country home this morning brought a happy rush of affection by a greatly-relieved citizenry, who acclaimed him with fond shouts of “Vive Doumergue!” and followed his automobile almost worshipfully. He hoped to build his “ministry of premiers” in 12 hours, but his secretary tonight admitted that the task would have to continue tomorrow. Pol

MOSCOW, Feb. 9. (UP)—Soviet Russia is ready to defend her borders, Kliment Voroshilov, commissioner of war, assured the red army today at one of the greatest military demonstrations in Soviet history. A vast display of military strength was given in Red Square in connection with the congress of the communist party, now in session. It significantly displayed the recent great technical and mechanical improvements in the red army, displaying more than 500 tanks, heavy tractor-drawn artillery, and anti-aircraft equipment.

Paris (P) — Premier-elect Gaston Doumergue struggled grimly to bring about political truce in France today while troops were concentrated in Paris for a threatened shock tonight. His new cabinet is expected to be formed by the time communists, defying police, planned to occupy the Place de La Republique in the heart of the workers’ district. Company after company of provincial forces were thrown around public buildings and 14,000 police were braced for a fight.

Athens.—(AP)—The Balkan non-aggression pact, which it is hoped will change the whole history of this stormy peninsula, was signed today by representatives of Turkey, Greece, Yugoslavia and Rumania. The pact was seen as offering an opportunity for economic collaboration by the long non-cooperative 55,000,000 inhabitants of these four countries. The absence of envoys from Bulgaria and Albania cast a shadow over the ceremony in the historic audience chamber of the Greek academy, but it was said Bulgaria might accept later. Signatory nations agree among other things to guarantee one another’s frontiers for five years.

1934-09-25.text: ABOARD ARGO, OFF NEWPORT, R. I. (UP). Harold Vanderbilt sailed across the finish line Tuesday in his big white defender, Rainbow, to retain the America’s Cup for the United States—providing the protest signaled from the halyards of T. O. M. Sopwith’s defeated British challenger, Endeavour, is not sustained. A red protest burgee also was flying from Rainbow's rigging. Vanderbilt trailed Endeavour over the first leg, a 10-mile broad reach to the southward. But the American skipper hauled his Class J sloop over the second leg, a beat to windward, in brilliant style, outguessing the challenger on tacks, and tore around the corner leading by nearly three minutes. The situation of protests was without precedent in the history of cup racing. Both protests will be heard separately. The first to be registered by either of the rival skippers will be the first one considered. Endeavour came home af

was a new champion today of Hollywood's many one-punch “battles of the century.” He was John Monk Saunders, the writer, who was crowned unofficially after he claimed a knockout over Herbert Marshall, English actor, at a party attended by many film personages. The one-punch encounter occurred at the home of Ernst Lubitsch, the director, during a party honoring Max Reinhardt, noted German producer who is staging the “Midsummer Night's Dream” in California. Accounts differed but it was agreed that Marshall was knocked to the floor in the presence of Gloria Swanson whom he escorted to the Lubitsch home. Saunders said he struck the English actor after the latter called him a name and neglected to smile, “If he had read ‘The Virginian’ he never would have used that word without smiling,” Saunders observed, “He didn't, so I felt it necessary to let Mr. Marshall have ‘one on the chin.” But Marsh

HOLLYWOOD, Cal., Sept. 25.—(*)—Herbert Marshall, English film star, didn’t smile when he said it, so John Monk Saunders floored him with a right to the chin, the novelist and scenarist related today. Hollywood’s latest one-blow battle was fought at the home of Ernst Lubitsch, screen director, where the elite of the motion picture colony gathered early yesterday to honor Max Reinhardt, German producer of Shakespeare’s “Midsummer Night’s Dream.” “He forgot to smile when he made a remark,” Saunders, World War flying ace and once winner of the academy award for the best film story of the year, declared. “Although regrettable, I found it necessary to let Mr. Marshall have one on the chin. We were the best of friends and had been for years. I’m sorry this had to happen.” Spectators asserted the “battle” lasted only long enough for Saunders to uncork a long uppercut and Marshall to hit the floo

Newport, R. I., Sept. 25—With both yachts flying protest flags as a result of the pre-start maneuvering, the British challenger Endeavour today led the defending sloop Rainbow around the first ten-mile mark of the sixth race of the series for the America's Cup. After bolting over the starting line with a 40 second advantage, the challenger rounded the turn at 11:51:37. The Rainbow came around at 11:52:45, giving the challenger an advantage in time at the mark of a minute and eight seconds. The elapsed time for the first splurge of the course was Endeavour 1:11:37—Rainbow 1:12:45.

ABOARD U.S.C.G. CG, ARGO, Of Newport, R.I., Sept. 25—(UP)—With red protest burgees flying from their halyards, T. O. M. Sopwith’s blue, British challenger, Endeavour, heeled around the first turn in the America's cup race today with Harold Vanderbilt's big white cutter, Rainbow, snapping at her heels. The two racing sloops had hoisted the red signals almost as they crossed the starting line, following a tangle back of the buoy, in which Sopwith rode the defender off her course, came swiftly about and headed for the line 100 yards ahead. Vanderbilt had completely lost way due to this brilliantly executed maneuver. Endeavour roared over the line on the first 10-mile leg to the outer turn, with Rainbow boiling along in her wake. Sopwith brought his craft to windward, forcing Rainbow off her course, and then bore down on the turn with the American several lengths behind. Endeavour rounded th

ABOARD U. S. C. G. CUTTER ARGO OFF NEWPORT, Sept. 25.—(AP)—The American defender Rainbow today overcame a one minute 8 seconds advantage the British challenger Endeavour had built up on the first 10-mile leg of the 30-mile triangular course and flashed across the line a winner in the sixth and deciding race of the America’s Cup series. The victory was clouded, however, for both skippers flew protest flags from start to finish and the argument must be decided by the judges before possession of the ancient trophy is certain.

ABOARD COAST GUARD CUTTER ARBO, Sept. 25.—In an ultra dramatic race with the red flag of protest flying from each ship, the Rainbow, America defender, defeated Endeavour of England today in the sixth and deciding race for America’s cup. Rainbow won by a margin of 55 seconds. Rainbow won her fourth consecutive victory, and apparently closed out the most sensational race of the series by four wins to go.

DUBLIN, SEPT. 25. (AP).—The Marquis of Waterford was found shot dead today in the gun room of his ancestral home after an early morning rabbit hunt. A sporting gun lay near the body. The Marquis was only 33 years old and was one of the most popular Irish peers. He succeeded to the title when he was ten years old. Lord Tyrone, year-old son of the Marquis, succeeds to the title.

1934-11-14.text: London, Nov. 14.—A joint American and British effort to concentrate disarmament work on a world treaty for control of the arms traffic seemed foreshadowed today. The meeting of the steering committee of the World Disarmament Conference at Geneva Thursday, it was indicated, may mark the tacit abandonment of present efforts for a general treaty in favor of an arms control pact as the sole hope of progress. Secretary of State Cordell Hull's announcement at Washington of the United States’ advocacy of an arms control treaty was in accord with the British view, emphasized by Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald in a speech last night at Southampton. “The only solution,” he said, “is control of sale of armaments by the license system. We want to make the British system of export licenses international, so that what we do every country will do. Therefore we are going to Geneva to get that done.” His

Reno, Nev., Nov. 14—(@)— A hasty Reno divorce trial today ended the marriage of pretty English-born Audry James and Marshall Field III, millionaire grandson of the late Chicago merchant prince. A charge of extreme mental cruelty, details of which were not disclosed, won the decree for Mrs. Field at a private hearing before District Judge Thomas F. Moran. Field did not contest the case.

by Littetut Press London, Nov. 13. — A demand by General Jan Smuts of South Africa, one of the empire’s most respected men, for fairness toward Nazi Germany, and a warning that the Pacific naval problem far overshadows European ones in importance caused a sudden shift in land and naval disarmament talk today. Demanding the revision of the Versailles treaty, Smuts said: “There is only one way to remove the inferiority complex that is obsessing and poisoning the mind and the very soul of Germany; namely recognize her complete equality with her fellows. ‘But the naval ratio treaty now seems the danger. If that goes, the other issues settled at the Washington conference may also be reopened and the whole Pacific concert collapse.” He appealed to Japan to pause before starting anything that would imperil the concert in the Pacific. Smuts’ demand, and his warning, came just after the following

LONDON, Nov. 14.—()-—An authoritative British source expressed the belief today that some sort of an arms control plan will be approved at Geneva as the result of British and American initiative, He indicated the British had received assurances that other countries are likely to support the plan.

London, Nov. 15 (4?)—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald and Neville Chamberlain, Chancellor of the Exchequer, between them today placed an effective quietus on any efforts to bring the war debts question up for consideration. After MacDonald told the House of Commons he planned to call no new conference to deal with the matter, the lanky Chancellor declared that the whole question of international debts was in abeyance at the present moment. That statement, he said, applied equally to the international debts discussed at the Lausanne conference and to the war debts owed to the United States. MacDonald was questioned from the floor as to whether he intended to redeem his promise to call another conference of the powers because the creditor nations had failed to obtain settlement of their obligations to the United States. He replied: “I do not consider that circumstances calling for a new con

LONDON, Nov. 14.— Thousands were arrested in sweeping political roundups in central Europe today as Balkan governments pressed their investigation in the background of the slaying of King Alexander. The principal arrests, comprising the greatest roundup of political extremists in many years, were conducted in Roumania and Bulgaria, it was revealed in dispatches reaching London from Pucharest and Sofia. More than 3000 including 500 women were arrested in Bucharest alone.

LONDON, Nov. 14.—(#)—Tangled naval negotiations between the world’s three greatest sea powers, with no two thus far apparently able to agree, brought an unexpected Anglo-American conference today. British delegates sought the “mystery meeting.” Americans said they had received no indication of its purpose, while the Japanese appeared perplexed by the development. Observers assumed the British would discuss further their compromise proposal to Tokyo, which is understood to involve granting Japan tonnage equality in principle but not in effect. Details of the plan have not been announced. Americans have opposed the compromise, holding firmly for the present 5-5-3 ratio, which Japan wants to scrap. Although the Japanese delegates are awaiting instructions from Tokyo, it was indicated they too are against the London scheme. The decision to confer with {Please turn to Page 6, Column 7}

London, Nov. 14 (INS)—Outlawing the Irish hospitals sweepstakes, the House of Commons today passed the betting and lotteries bill by a vote of 206 to 38. The formality of royal assent is expected immediately. Distribution of tickets for the Irish sweep, French, Spanish and other government lotteries, will henceforth be prohibited in England, Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland. Publication of the results of the drawings, which packs the newspapers for days several times a year with the names of lucky ones, will be prohibited. There is nothing to prevent Britons sending their ten shillings to Dublin to buy tickets, but it is believed that interest in the sweepstakes will wane when bettors are not able to secure immediate news of the drawings, but will have to depend on the radio or Dublin or Paris newspapers for winners. The Irish sweep alone took millions of pounds out of Britain each

1934-03-02.text: LONDON, March 2—(#)—The defense wound up its case in the “Rasputin libel suit” today in a blaze of new sensations — including the revelation for the first time by a member of the British parliament that he had been invited to join the party which poisoned, clubbed and shot to death Rasputin, the Russian imperial court’s “Mad Monk.” It remained for Com. Oliver Locker-Lampson to supply the dramatic climax to the day’s testimony in the $2,000,000 libel suit of Princess Irena Youssoupov against producers of the film “Rasputin and the Empress.” The testimony already presented gave intimate details of the gruesome murder which took place in the cellar of the St. Petersburg palace. Locker-Lampson, a member of Parliament for 25 years, and distinguished for his services during the war—said he had been asked to join the “murder party” and had taken part in an unsuccessful scheme to save the Russia

References LONDON, March 2.—An official American source informed the United Press today that President Roosevelt was eager to have a world non-aggression treaty effect, ed simultaneously with, or parallel to any disarmament agreement. This desire, the informant said, was behind the American proposal, made this week in reply to a British disarmament memorandum, that signatories to any disarmament agreement pledge themselves to refrain from sending armed forces across their neighbors' borders. It was explained that the President was convinced that besides limiting, or abolishing, large offensive weapons it was essential to insure that remaining armaments were not used for invasion. This news came a few minutes after Great Britain, in publishing its air force estimates for 1934-35, offered Europe a clear choice between reaching a disarmament agreement and matching her in vast expenditures o

LONDON, March 1—(P)—New details—piling horror on horror—regarding the death of the sinister monk Rasputin in the St. Petersburg imperial palace were recited by Prince Felix Youssoupoff today in an excited London court. The descendant of high Russian nobility, appearing in a damage suit hearing, told how he was partly hypnotized by the mad monk, how he gave his victim poisoned cakes and wine, and then shot and beat him to death before a crucifix. Prince Youssoupoff testified in his wife's $2,000,000 suit against a film company for allegedly libeling her in a film depicting Rasputin and the Russian czarina. Passages from a book by the prince were read to show the picture historically inaccurate. The case for Princess Irena Youssoupoff was concluded this afternoon, and Sir William Jowitt, for the defense, told the jury it must be proved that the film referred to her. Sir William asked the p

Paris, March 2 (AP)—The French cabinet decided today that Chancellor Hitler’s request for rearmament of Germany could not be accepted unless adequate assurances were given that new armaments limits shall be observed. Great Britain will be asked to come to the defense of France if Germany should break such an agreement. High army, navy, and air chiefs, forming the national defense council responsible for France’s armed strength, are to give their opinion to the cabinet. An official note to Great Britain then will be drafted by Premier Gaston Doumergue’s “military directory,” composed of War Minister Petain, Air Minister Denain and Naval Minister Pietri with Foreign Minister Louis Barthou attending.

By RICHARD D. McMILLAN (United Press Staff Correspondent.) PARIS, Mar. 2 — Great Britain intends soon to present to European nations a revised disarmament memorandum with the intimation that its acceptance is the only alternative to an arms race," it was said authoritatively today. Indications were that the memorandum would be along lines which Britain, Italy and Germany already have approved, and that France, if it rejected the program, would find itself isolated as recalcitrant. It was indicated further that the present national government, strong and enjoying wide popular support, would feel itself forced at whatever cost to refuse acceptance. France’s way out seemed to be acceptance of one proposal in the prospective memorandum — a non-committal conference of European powers. At this conference, as things stood, the chief hope seemed to be a meaningless agreement that would lead anyw

February 26—Henry W. Longfellow, great U.S. poet, born 1807. 27—England sees its first game of baseball, 1874. 28—Great comet visible by day over United States, 1843. MARCH 1—Napoleon returns to France from Elba exile, 1814. 2—Texas declares independence of Mexico, 1835. 3—U.S. Navy is founded with 13 active ships, 1801. 4—Chicago, with population of 4,170, made city, 1837.

Valetta, Isle of Malta (4) Lieutenant Commander H. Thornton Jones of the British battleship Royal Sovereign was found shot to death in his cabin today. Pending inquiries by naval officers, no details of the affair were revealed.

London, Mar. 2 (INS)—Great Britain today announced her 1934 program for air defense at home and abroad, calling for creation of four new airplane squadrons "in the interest of national and imperial security." The new program calls for a gross expenditure of 20,165,600 pounds sterling (approximately $100,828,000), an increase of 527,000 pounds ($2,635,000) over last year. Net expenditures are put at 17,561,000 pounds ($87,805,000), an increase of 135,000 pounds ($765,800) over 1933. Britain will build two new squadrons for the home defense force, one new flying boat squadron for overseas work, and one new squadron for operation from aircraft carriers. 1934-09-22.text: ABOARD U. S. C. G. CUTTER ARGO OFF NEWPORT, Sept. 22 (AP).—In as thrilling a race as ever was sailed for the America’s cup the defending Rainbow today defeated the British challenger Endeavour in the fourth race of the current series to even the count at two victories each. Rainbow regained the lead from the British challenger Endeavour, which she had trailed by 27 seconds at the first mark, to show the way around the 20-mile buoy by 59 seconds. The times at the second mark were: Rainbow 1:00:39. Endeavour 1:01:38. Rainbow had made the second leg, a broad reach of 10 miles, in 54 minutes 46 seconds, a minute and 26 seconds faster than had Endeavour. Endeavour overcame a 300-yard lead Rainbow built up in the first few minutes and led the American defender by 27 seconds at the end of the first 10-mile leg. The challenger made up most of her early disadvantage in the last mile of the course

WREXHAM, Wales, Sept. 22.—(P)—Hope was abandoned at dusk today for 100 coal miners caught in an explosion and fire in Gresford colliery. Rescuers worked all day to enter the pit but were unable to reach the lost miners. They were trapped nearly two miles from the mouth of the pit in which they were working. Rescuers, despite heroic efforts, were unable to penetrate the wall of flame and the floods of poisonous gases which barred their path. Two men of a rescue party were carried out unconscious and died at the surface. Sixteen bodies of miners who were overcome near the pit entrance were recovered. Nearly three-quarters of the 400 miners below the surface at the time of the explosion escaped. Five of the men who escaped from the blast spent nearly an hour climbing a narrow airshaft the 200 feet to the surface from the level on which they had been working. At the pit mouth stood the miner

AULESBURY, Buckinghamshire, Eng., Sept. 22. (F)—Four fliers were killed today when their airplane with which they had refueled Sir Alan Cobham’s plane as he started out on an attempted non-stop flight to India, crashed in flames on the main London highway near here. Twenty miles out from Portsmouth—over the English channel—the fliers had poured about 100 gallons of gasoline into Sir Alan's ship. The death crash occurred as they returned to England.

Aboard S.S. Ile de France, Sept. 22.—I tell you, you can't beat England for her justice. Brought some English papers on board and it tells of a man who killed his nagging wife and the judge gave him a year, but apologizes for it. Said he was compelled to do it under the law. Europe's awful quiet now. Don't hear much war talk so I guess that means one will break out. That's when they have ‘em, when there ain't any reason. Sure hate to miss that polo game tomorrow. In Russia, if they send you on a mission and you don't perform it, you better not come back, so if you birds lose this game don't come home, letting a lot of dudes beat you. Yours, the Rape @ 1086. MeNeught Sy te, fea.

A thing we were pre-eminent in. Can't make 'em believe we've been wanting to lose that cup for 40 years. What's this about my western boys losing a polo game. I got to get home and start brain trusting for 'em. Hold 'em cowboys. Yours, WILL ROGERS ©

WREXHAM, Wales, Sept. 22. (UP) Blackened, broken bodies, raised one by one to the pit head of the Gresford Colliery while horrified, sobbing women stood by, today told the story of the latest disaster in the great Welsh coal fields. It was feared that more than 250 men were trapped hopelessly behind raging flames in the mine galleries, and that the shaft would have to be sealed, despite statements of mine officials that they believed only 100 men were imprisoned. A thousand men of the night shift were working in the pit when at 2 a.m. there was an explosion. Immediately afterward flames began roaring through the galleries. Seven hundred of the men reached the surface. Most of the rest were trapped behind fire-swept debris. At noon 15 bodies had been brought up by rescuers. A sixteenth body brought to the surface was that of one of the many rescue men who braved the flames in an effort to

I., Sept. 22.--Heading off the challenge of Britain's royal blue sloop, Endeavour, Harold Vanderbilt drove his Rainbow home today to deadlock the America’s Cup series at two victories each. Rainbow won by 1 minute, 16 seconds. Losing the lead only once, when Endeavour outraced her to the first turn, Vanderbilt piloted his big white cutter home in one of the greatest racing duels in cup history. He recovered the lead halfway to the second mark, bore down on the turn nearly a minute ahead and drove into the finishing stretch with Sopwith in hot pursuit. The two sloops raced through bucking seas, Sopwith trying every maneuver to cross to weather of the defender, but Vanderbilt luffed him off, outfooted him on the closing reach and heeled over the line, victor in one of his most brilliant racing efforts. 1934-11-10.text: WASHINGTON, Nov. 9. (AP) — Mincing no words, the United States formally protested to Persia today against the reported discourtesy shown there recently to two American entrants in the England to Australia air derby. In a note detailing the treatment accorded John H. Wright and John Polando when they made a forced landing October 23 between Mohammerah and Abadan because of minor engine trouble, the United States said it was “at a loss to understand” the action of the Persian authorities. “The lack of consideration shown to these two American fliers under the exceptionally difficult circumstances in which they were placed has made a most unfavorable impression in the United States,” said the note. Although granted Persian permission to fly across that country and land there if necessary, Wright and Polando were detained 24 hours and subsequently withdrew from the race at Karachi, India, be

London, Nov. 9.—A brilliant gathering at the annual Lord Mayor's banquet in London's historic Guild Hall tonight heard Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald declare Great Britain's effort to promote world peace by setting an example in disarmament has proved fruitless. The premier’s address was the climax of colorful ceremonies that marked the accession of the new Lord Mayor, Sir Stephen Killik.

LONDON (UP)—Nine hundred fishermen, in 130 boats, have been missing off the Korean coast since a gale Wednesday night, and two destroyers from the Chinkai naval base have sought them in vain, the Tokyo correspondent of the Exchange Telegraph reported today. LONDON (UP)—Two hundred and fifty miners were buried in the Yayoi coal mine on Hokkaido island by an explosion, the Exchange Telegraph Tokyo correspondent reported today. Thirty-seven bodies had been recovered, the dispatch said. ALBUQUERQUE, N. M. (UP)—Ellen McAdoo, daughter of Sen. William Gibbs McAdoo of California, and Raphael De Onate, screen player, were married.

NEW YORK, Nov. 9—()-- Simon Lake, on the eve of one of history’s greatest submarine treasure hunts, asserted tonight he was more interested in a successful test of his oddly-shaped undersea salvager than in recovering the $4,800,000 gold reputedly aboard the British Frigate “Hussar” under the swirling waters of Hell Gate. Nearing the climax of his long career as a submarine builder and designer, Lake was only doubtful of finding a treasure trove in the hulk of the ship which has gripped the attention of salvagers ever since it was sunk in the East River in 1780. For the veteran Milford, Conn., engineer, the “Hussar” adventure promised achievement of a boyhood dream, inspired 60 years ago by the reading of Jules Verne’s “Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea.”

The finance ministry ordered an inquiry into charges brought against Charles Levy and his cousin, Joseph Levy. They were accused of floating several hundred million francs worth of bonds and juggling accounts through a network of firms.

Rome—(#)——-Premier Mussolini called upon the world today to recognize the international value of his new fascist corporative state, which he launched with an historic address. He said the world value of his new system, which is to replace Italian parliamentary government, must be affirmed, “because it is only on this international ground that the worth of nations and races will be measured when Europe, despite Italy's efforts toward peace, shall have arrived at another crossroads in its destiny.” He predicted that his experiment in “self-administration” for industry, commerce and business would lead to worldwide repudiation of old political methods. The Italian premier said the corporative state will work evermore for social justice “so as to shorten the distance between maximum and minimum income. We cannot admit the inevitability of social misery.” When he spoke of the “equality of man

(Copyright, 1944, Associated Press) Paris, Nov. 9 (4?)—Pierre-Etienne Flandin, newest “truce” premier promised the nation tonight to fight the depression as aged Gaston Doumergue went back into the retirement from which he was called to rescue France from civil war. The strapping Flandin’s program, with which he hoped to win the backing of France's watching millions, included these important points: 1. Continuation of the policy of political truce inaugurated when February's bloody Stavisky riots seared politicians into agreement. 2. A fight against poverty and unemployment. 3. Economy in government. 4. Rapid adoption of the 1935 budget. 5. Strengthening the authority of the state. His program, in general, resembled Doumergue’s. There was, however, one important difference. ROME, Nov. 9.—The wheels of Benito Mussolini’s new corporative State start turning tomorrow. A reform designed to tear out the roots of parliamentary government, the long-prepared state, in which industry, commerce, business and the professions are to make their own laws, will be formally set up by Il Duce himself. Tonight he and his formidable propaganda machine were advertising it to the whole world as something new in modern-day government, something soon to be copied by other states. The Duce is expected to make one of his most important speeches of recent years at the opening ceremony.

1934-09-27.text: Clydebank, Glasgow, Scotland, Sept. 26—(P)—Queen Mary today christened the giant new Cunard-White Star liner as the great ship started down the ways to the water. The Queen Mary, which Great Britain believes will be the queen of the seas, slid down successfully for a perfect launching. The choice of the name of a living queen for a christening was most unusual. Right up until the moment of the actual christening, no one had announced what the great ship’s name was to be and the suggestion “Britannia” ruled a favorite. The launching followed a short speech by King George. The Prince of Wales was present. So was Ambassador Robert W. Bingham of the United States, Mrs. Bingham, and many other notables.

CLYDEBANK, Scotland, Sept. 26 —(— Queen Mary of England, defying precedent, today gave her own name to the great Cunard-White Star liner which King George described as “the stateliest ship now in being.” Christened the “Queen Mary” by the queen, the 40,000-ton hull, Britain’s bid for supremacy of the seas, slid smoothly, majestically, almost noiselessly down the ways into the basin of the river Clyde. The roar of pelting rain on thousands of umbrellas and the volley of cheers from the throats of 250,000 spectators echoing from the hull’s red and gray sides made the queen's christening words almost inaudible.

Wrexham, Wales, Sept. 20.—(A)—One hundred coal miners, entombed half a mile underground by a blinding explosion in the Gresford collieries, were given up for lost tonight. The blast sent the roofs caving down upon them while fire which followed trapped them in a roaring subterranean furnace, a mile and a half from the mouth of the pit where rescuers were powerless to reach them. Bodies Found Among the nine bodies recovered from the explosion area two were those of rescue workers overcome while battling the scorching flames and clouds of poisonous fumes from fire damp. There were about 400 men in the mine at the time of the blast.

SEYMOUR, Sept. 26.--A 39-year-old widow, Miss Ruby Britain, related in her trial today on murder charges that she had a love affair with Horace Nichols, Seymour businessman lasting several months, but that he had been having 'other dates' before he was shot the night of last Aug. 15 while sitting in his automobile near Vernon with Miss Willie Mae Couch. Miss Britain insisted she fired only because she thought her life was in danger. Date Is Arranged She said Nichols who was married tried to make a 'date' with her in September, last year, and in November they finally arranged one. From that time until last June they were together as often as once a week, she said. Two letters she said Nichols wrote to her while she was on a visit from Seymour, last January, were introduced in evidence. Each was headed 'my darling' and spoke of strong affection for her. Perfect Gentleman Miss Britain said

CAMBRIDGE, Mass., Sept. 27. (WP) Meteorites were reported today to have fallen in at least five places in Massachusetts as the aftermath to the brilliant daylight meteor that raced across New England yesterday.

SEYMOUR, Sept. 27.—(P)—All testimony was completed today in the trial of Miss Ruby Britain for the fatal shooting of Horace Nichols, Seymour banker, and the state and defense rested. Arguments were scheduled to begin at 1 o'clock this afternoon. The greater part of the morning was taken up with cross-examination of the defendant. C. C. McDonald, special prosecutor, was unable to shake Miss Britain's story that she shot Nichols when she believed that he was about to carry out threats she claimed he had made against her. The cross-examination brought out that the defendant was married for five years to Bob Grossman and took her maiden name after his death eight years ago. She denied having important relations with other men and insisted that Nichols meant much to her. GENEVA (#) -— A permanent peace conference in which the United States could participate is still a goal of Soviet Russia, Maxim Litvinoff, her commissar for foreign affairs, told the assembly of the League of Nations today. Litvinoff took from the rostrum to discuss his surprise resolution yesterday asking the league council to secure a report on whether the world disarmament conference could be resumed with a possibility of success. In resonant English Litvinoff, whose country was admitted to the league only last week, announced he had not abandoned the idea of a permanent conference devoted to the consolidation of peace movements—a proposal which was not accepted by league leaders earlier in the year.

Rome, Sept. 26.—(4--Italy ought to have more babies, Benito Mussolini believes, so today he set out to deprive all marriageable maids of their jobs. The result, Il Duce himself has predicted, will be that they'll have to find themselves husbands. Mussolini, determined to boost Italy's birth rate, took another step calculated to promote weddings. Henceforth every single man who tries to get work with the government will have to prove his intentions to be married, and private industry will be requested to set up similar requirements.

1934-03-31.text: MIAMI, Fla., March 31 (4)—President Roosevelt was away from land again today, fishing in well chosen waters of the Bahamas near the Great Abaco island for the gamest of fish, bonefish. He dropped into harbor yesterday at Nassau, capital of the British Bahamas, amid salutes from a cruiser of the English navy, but did not land. American sailors aboard the accompanying destroyer Ellis manned the rails and dipped the flag. Mr. Roosevelt later received Governor Bede Clifford of the islands aboard ship. He and his party were well out to sea by nightfall and today were casting about for big game.

Paris, March 30.— (2) — John Francis Amherst Cecil and his wife, who as the former Cornelia Vanderbilt was one of the most wealthy American heiresses, let it be known today that they have instituted “friendly” divorce proceedings. The marriage of Mr. Cecil, son of Lord William Cecil of London, and Miss Vanderbilt, daughter of the late George W. Vanderbilt, in Biltmore, N. C., April 29, 1934, attracted the attention of international society. A financial arrangement has been concluded and the Cecils have agreed to share equally the custody of their two children.

NEW YORK, March 30.—(AP)—The dangers of a European war, at least in the immediate future, have been greatly exaggerated, in the opinion of James Truslow Adams, historian and Pulitzer Prize winner, who paused here today on his way from London to Washington. “And it's not because several nations of Europe might not want to make war,” Adams said, “but because they cannot. “England can't make war because at present the people wouldn't stand for it. Unless it were perfectly obvious to every man in the street that the life of the British Empire was at stake, the first result of any declaration of war would be a general strike.

Istanbul, March 31.—()— Turkey today ordered the arrest of Samuel Insull, but the 74-year-old Chicago fugitive flatly refused a police request that he quit his floating haven, the tramp steamer Maiotis which flies the flag of Greece. It was Greece which gave him a year and a half's asylum from United States authorities who seek to try him on charges of grand larceny and embezzlement growing out of the collapse of his Midwest utilities companies. The Turkish order followed a request by the United States government that Insull be arrested, but Insull apparently clung to the hope that the Greek flag would continue to give him protection. Complications in Turko-Greek relations as a result of the incident were feared in some quarters, for Capt. Ioannis Mousouris, the master of the Maiotis, protested to the Greek consul here against the detention of his vessel in the straits of the Bosporus, a

ATHENS, March 31.—Foreign Minister Demetrios Maximos today cabled the Turkish government, demanding release under international law of the Greek steamship Maiotis, which has Samuel Insull aboard as passenger. Turkish authorities have held the ship since Thursday, seeking a way to extradite Insull to answer charges of fraud in the United States. Maximos cabled the master of the Maiotis to refuse to surrender Insull if police demanded him, and to ask for indemnities for the Maiotis’ detention, which he holds to be without warrant in international law.

ROME (#) - Cardinal Franz Ehrle, for many years librarian of the Vatican, died last night of a pulmonary affection which reduced his health to a critical state several days ago. He was 88 years old. Pope Pius sent the cardinal, a German, his blessing Monday and the last sacrament was administered.

PARIS, March 31.—(#)—The pinch of gold prices and fears of further riots are exercising a depressing effect upon business in France. Tourists, France’s great “hidden exports,” have been almost eliminated as a result of the riots. Many tourists fled from Paris during the violent disorders in which police and anti-government demonstrators battled in the streets. Others, apparently despairing of an immediate improvement in conditions, have left since owing to the political unrest which precipitated and has trailed the rioting. Amid this unrest arises the voice of Premier Gaston Doumergue insisting that the franc must be maintained, but admitting that taxes must also be diminished if business is to survive. Officials freely admit that devaluation of the franc, king of gold bloc currencies, is a possibility unless public finances are put in order. Deflation Sought: In an effort to offset the

ROME, March 31 (1).--Paschal candles were lighted in nearly 500 churches and basilicas this morning as priests and laymen alike celebrated Holy Saturday. Church bells silent since Holy Thursday rang out, sacred images somberly draped in commemoration of Christ's passion and death were uncovered, and joyful organ music once again was allowed to resound through the churches. The ceremonies marked the end of the 40-day Lenten mourning. Today's services held a note of joyful anticipation for tomorrow's anniversary of Christ's resurrection. (Cardinal Pacelli lighted the Easter fire in St. Peter's this morning by striking sparks from a flint. The "new fire" as it is called was suggestive of the resurrection. 1934-05-03.text: LONDON (4) — Walter Runciman, president of the British Board of Trade, is expected in well-informed circles to inform Ambassador Tsuneo Matsudaira of Japan at a conference late today that Great Britain has completed proposals to restrict the importation of Japanese goods into British colonies. It was indicated that the interview was regarded as most serious in the face of world competition between Great Britain and Japan for trade markets. In many areas, Japanese goods are underselling the British and others considerably and Japan has made rapid strides forward in the textile business, long a mainstay of England. The British are understood to be alarmed at the spread of Japanese trade through the colonies and Africa, one of the chief centers affected. | London, Max 3.—(AP)—A well-dressed burglar robbed the home of Greta Nissen, actress, of $35,000 worth of jewels early today.

London, May 3 (AP)—Restrictions which Great Britain contemplates placing upon the importation of Japanese goods to crown colonies and to the British Isles were given to the Japanese ambassador, Tsunedo Matsudaira, today by Walter Runciman, president of the board of trade. The restrictions are intended to prevent underselling of British manufactured goods by Japanese importers. The ambassador was understood to have said that no immediate reply to the proposal could be given. MOMBASA, Africa, May 3.—(UP).—In connection with the war in Arabia, the British cruiser Enterprise altered her course today and started full speed for Aden.

PARIS, May 2? (4)-Police announced today the arrest of a “dangerous spy,” who they said bought French defense secrets for Germany through want ads and gained information by communications worded like love letters. One of his alleged agents also was taken into custody. Secret, police said the prisoner is Stanislas Krauss, a former Polish army officer, and that his confession of an ingenious espionage system led to the arrest of Captain Froge of the French army. Two Germans have been arrested in the case, police said. One, unidentified, is held at Metz on a charge of espionage and another German, Josef Peter Moeller, was convicted and sentenced to two years in prison and fined 1,000 francs (about $68). PARIS, May 2. — Communist hatred of police flared anew in street battles tonight among the teeming slums where May day rioters had rained pistol fire and bricks on guards a few hours earlier. Several hundred manifestants after a meeting at the "Joan of Arc City" municipal apartment which rightists say is a revolutionary center — ripped up newly repaired pavements and attempted to build barricades. Police reinforcements again besieged the huge tenement block which served as the red citadel during sharp encounters between last midnight and 5:30 a.m. today, in which 20 communists were injured. Police swinging their clubs energetically, dispersed the bands. Then the officers, numbering 2,000, withdrew to motor buses surrounding the block, leaving one street occupied by 100 menacing youths. The police subsequently settled down to a night of watchful waiting following a practice they used earl

1934-07-14.text: GENEVA, July 14.—(UP)— Soviet Russia will officially ask for admission to the League of Nations within two weeks, league officials reported today. It was said the Soviets were virtually certain of election to the league in September, with support of France and Britain. Entrance of the Communist state into official membership in the league has long been considered a vital factor in peace and disarmament negotiations in Europe. The Russian delegates, usually headed by the blunt-speaking Maxim Litvinov in recent years, have participated in various conferences sponsored by the league, especially the disarmament conferences. Frequently, Litvinov criticized the league in speeches at Geneva sessions.

Douglas, Isle of Man.--(AP)— Kaye Don, British racing driver, was found guilty of a charge of manslaughter today growing out of the death of his mechanic, Francis Taylor, in a crash during a test run here. The trial judge postponed delivering the sentence until Monday. Don insisted today, under cross-examination, that he thought he showed no carelessness during the test run which resulted in the crash.

EDINBURGH, July 14. (UP) — A man stepped out of a crowd of coal miners today and threw a beer bottle at the king and queen of England. The bottle apparently was aimed at a window of the king's automobile. It missed its mark but created the most sensational affront to the British monarch in many years. The king and queen have been residing at Holyrood Castle for the past week. They had attended the races at Hamilton Park and were en route to the castle.

GENEVA, July 14 (AP).—The world powers were committed today to another serious fling at disarmament next September by the official convocation of the steering committee of the disarmament conference. Arthur Henderson, conference president, encouraged by the recent Franco-British conversations and the boom given to security pacts, officially called the committee meeting for the early days of the League of Nations assembly beginning Sept. 10. The Eastern Locarno pact which France is fostering and which England and Italy have endorsed was regarded as a major factor in determination to carry on conversations in furtherance of world peace.

(Copyright, 1934, by the Associated Press) BERLIN, July 14—(4)—More firing squads and more “purging by blood” await any who challenge Adolf Hitler's rule of Germany. This was the warning Germany pondered today as it digested the chancellor’s Reichstag defense last night of the June 30 “liquidation” of 77 traitors. “Everyone is to know for all future times,” he said, “that if he raises his hand for attack against the state, certain death will be his lot.” The speech, to which many parts of the world (including America) listened, stood today as a definite marker on Hitler's road to the building of a new Germany. Nazis Cheer Hundreds of Nazis rose and cheered when the address—an explanation of the execution of storm leaders and others June 30—was ended. The chancellor scarcely noticed them. A plot of Ernst Roehm, executed Storm Troop leader, he said forced him to “act with the speed of lightning,” in the early morning hours of June 30 when “mutineers” were shot summarily by firing squads. “In this hour I was responsible for the fate of the German nation,” Hitler declared. VIENNA, July 14. (®)—A squad of men entered the apartment of Cornelius Zimmer, alleged Nazi, stood him against a wall and shot him to death today. Public conjectures were aroused whether the killing inaugurated ruthless vigilante action against the Nazis. - Bombings continued. At Mosern in Tyrol, a bomb exploded in front of a church, tearing a huge hole in the wall and destroying the altar and the church's interior.

BERLIN, July 14.—Fourteen days after a crisis that threatened civil war, Germans awoke today realizing clearly for the first time just what had threatened them and just what they escaped. Many realized also for the first time the caliber of the man whom millions call “The Leader.” Chancellor Hitler, remembering how those in the Kroll Opera House galleries sprang spontaneously to their feet, shouting hysterically when he addressed them last night and the thunderous cheers from crowded streets when he drove back to his chancellery, may have realized also what seemed an undoubted fact—that he had won a revitalized support from his party and revitalized confidence in himself. His speech was what Hermann Goering, his chief aide in the cabinet, called the final accounting of his handling of the plot of storm troop leaders to organize the government and, failing his personal approval, to assass

1934-07-13.text: Berlin, July 10.—(#)—Paul Joseph Goebbels, Nazi minister of propaganda, read the riot act to the press of the world tonight, especially the French and English press, in a message internationally broadcast. “I call you all to witness,” he said to an invisible audience of many millions in describing the suppression of the second revolution, “that there have been cases of lies, slander and misrepresentation of the true facts, such as are almost without parallel in journalism.” “A large part in the foreign press,” he charged, “has embarked upon a campaign of lies which in its maliciousness can be compared only with the campaign of atrocity tales that were set in the scene against Germany during the war.”

LONDON, July 13 (P)—Great Britain has reinforced the pact of Locarno but has not entered any "select alliance with any country," Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, declared today before the House of Commons. In his anxiously awaited statement of position on continental affairs, Sir John said the recent Anglo-French conversations had resulted in a greater feeling of peace and security in Europe and will greatly improve conditions on the continent if powers affected fully enter the proposed eastern regional agreement. He added that Premier Mussolini of Italy agrees with Britain as to the necessity of an eastern pact—"eastern Locarno" as it has been called—and fully approves of it. Sir John supported the statement of Louis Barthou, French foreign minister, when the latter left London, that Britain and France were cooperating in trying to effect permanent peace in Europe. NEW YORK, July 12—(4)—The early downfall of Adolf Hitler as chancellor of Germany was predicted today by George E. Earle, the democratic candidate for governor of Pennsylvania. Earle arrived on the U. S. liner Manhattan from London, where he has been observing the European situation. He expressed himself freely on his dis-taste of the Nazi movement in Germany and Austria. “I am certain,” he said, “that the Germans will rid themselves of Hitler in the near future. The only reason the Nazis have managed to stay in the saddle so far is by virtue of their absolute control of the press, the radio and the pulpit. “That control is beginning to crack up. There have been definite signs of it in the last two weeks. Hitler's passing is simply a matter of time, and then the Germans will act as a great people have always acted.”

London, July 13.—(UP)—A firm declaration of Sir John Simon, foreign minister, that Great Britain's foreign policy was for the good of the British, not of Europe, marked today a House of Commons debate on foreign affairs that seemed to indicate a cabinet split on rearmament. “We are not going to undertake any new obligations in Europe at all,” Simon said. “Nor will we lend ourselves to support any arrangement among European states under which one group builds up a combination against another. That was made quite clear to M. Barthou (Louis Barthou, French foreign minister) on his visit here this week. He accepted that.” Simon's speech came soon after the disclosure that Britain had urged in Berlin, Warsaw and Rome the advisability of an Eastern European security treaty, in an apparent effort to forestall a speech by Chancellor Adolf Hitler in the Reichstag tonight. London, July 13 ()—Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, discussing recent Anglo-French conversations, told the House of Commons today Great Britain has made “no select alliance” with any power. “We are undertaking no new obligations at all,” Sir John said. He made clear an eastern security pact, the goal of France, must not be used as an instrument against any one people such as Germany. Simon said the chief mission of Louis Barthou, French foreign minister, on his visit here earlier this week was to outline reasons for the necessity of a pact of mutual assistance in eastern Europe, embracing the Baltic States, Russia, Poland, Czechoslovakia and Germany. LONDON, July 11. (UP) — Lloyd has declined to insure the life of Chancellor Adolf Hitler, it was learned tonight. The agency which recently gave policies on the life of President Roosevelt to those interested in his continuing as head of the United States government also has declined to issue policies on the lives of President von Hindenburg, Vice Chancellor Franz von Papen and Gen. Hermann Wilhelm Goering, Hitler's chief aid.

London, July 10. (®)—Louig Barthou, French foreign minister, who came to England seeking assurances of British cooperation in event of war, left tonight expressing far more satisfaction than could be accounted for by official reports of the conversations he had with cabinet members here. Britain and France, he said, reached a “friendly understanding” and found that they are “agreed on the European situation.” His enthusiasm was not supported by British comment, and doubt was expressed in informed quarters that any extensive assistance was promised in event of invasion of the Franco-Belgian area. British cabinet members have stated repeatedly that no pact will be entered into beyond the Locarno agreement, under which Great Britain, France, Italy, Belgium and Germany undertook to preserve the peace of western Europe. London. — (U.P) — King George stopped playing golf because he “got so damned mad,” the Prince of Wales told the Lucifer Golf Society in a speech last night.

1934-07-11.text: LONDON, JULY 10, (AP).—Louis Barthou, French foreign minister, indicated today on his departure that Britain will go to the aid of France in case the Franco-Belgian area is invaded by a foreign power. Leaving for Paris after two days of momentous conversations with British officials, he indicated further that Great Britain had sanctioned in principle the Eastern security pacts in which France is participating although Britain was not a signatory. The great statesman departed declaring that France and Britain “are agreed on the European situation.” He expressed high satisfaction with the results of his visit, reiterating that no formal pact of any kind had been signed but that the two nations had reached a “friendly understanding.”

LONDON, July 11.—Europe’s political situation was believed to be the best in many months, if not in years, today after a conference between French and British diplomatists. Most reliable information here and in Paris indicated that as the result of conversations between the French, led by Foreign Minister Louis Barthou, and British, headed by Sir John Simon, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, Germany would be asked to rejoin the League of Nations and France, with Britain's approval, would try to work out security treaties covering Eastern Europe and the Mediterranean. The Eastern European treaty, Moscow as well as other information disclosed, would lead to an immediate application by Russia to join the League—a move second only in importance to an American application. Barthou was back in Paris today, reporting to his government. He sent the Minister of Marine Francois Pietri, who p

BERLIN, July 11. (4j)—Foreign Minister Konstantin von Neurath today received the ambassadors of Japan, Italy, England and France to impress upon them the necessity of intervention in the Memel territory of Lithuania by powers signatory to the Treaty of Versailles. Von Neurath declared that conditions in the territory were untenable. The situation in this Lithuanian territory, detached from Germany by the Treaty of Versailles and constituting a largely autonomous unit, has been increasingly difficult of late because of Lithuanian and German differences.

Certain unreported sub-rosa shenanigans have been going on in foreign exchange. For one thing, the British have been secretly trying to bid the dollar up. For another, several of the largest European financial syndicates have been quietly transferring their accounts to America. These two moves are behind the recent strength of the dollar. They have been noted by those in charge of the government exchange stabilization bureau, but by few others. The British are probably buying dollars for exchange advantage. LONDON, July 10,—P)—His lips sealed for two years about the sunken British cruiser Hampshire and the $10,000,000 golden treasure possibly hidden in the wreck, Charles Courtney, New York’s deep sea locksmith, sailed for home today on the Leviathan. Courtney arrived in London Monday after a mysterious trip through Europe including a visit to Moscow and Leningrad. He says the Hampshire search is not closed, both his backers and the British admiralty having asked him to “pipe down.” He took a vow to keep mum about the matter for two years. The cruiser Hampshire was the vessel on which Lord Kitchener went to his death during the World War in the North Sea. The vessel struck a German mine. Vienna, July 11.—(4)—Engelbert Dollfuss, Austria’s fighting little chancellor, announced a huge new drive against Nazis today after concentrating in his own hands all the military and police power of the nation. The death penalty will be dealt out for the mere possession of explosives, Dollfuss announced, in an effort to stop widespread bombing outrages. Follows Mussolini's Lead In a cabinet shake-up, Dollfuss presented the resignation of the whole group to President Wilhelm Miklas and then submitted a new list for approval by the president. Dollfuss appeared determined to stamp out the whole Nazi movement in Austria. Taking a leaf from the notebook of his neighbor and friendly protector, Benito Mussolini, Dollfuss will add several cabinet portfolios to his active duties. He will be chancellor, foreign minister, minister of defense, public security, and agriculture. All military and poli

Berlin ()—Germany threatened today to expel foreign correspondents whose accounts of the bloody “second revolution” aroused Nazi ire. Hitler's own newspaper editorially underscored the warning given journalists by Paul Joseph Goebbels, sharp-tongued minister of propaganda, in an address last night. Germany otherwise was comparatively quiet following days of bullets and then of oratory. It awaited the account of his stewardship from the lips of “der Fuehrer,” Hitler himself, who has called the puppet Reichstag to meet Friday night. Hitler is expected to explain his ruthless suppression of the ‘Roehm revolt' of June 30. Foreign correspondents, many of them angered by Goebbels’ bitter attack, considered the possibility of making formal remonstrances. They pointed to the difficulty of getting confirmation of reports and rumors.

BERLIN, July 10—(AP)—The 100 percent Nazi Reichstag, inactive survivor of the republican days, was ordered today to assemble Friday evening for what is expected to provide a dramatic carry-over from the tension and confusion of the “second revolution.” From the lips of Adolf Hitler himself the Reichstag, the German people and the world are likely to hear an explanation of the summary executions and other bloody events of June 30 and the days immediately following. As if in preparation for this “authentic” explanation from the highest source in Germany, Propaganda Minister Joseph Goebbels in a worldwide broadcast this afternoon lambasted the foreign press for its reports of Hitler's “purge.” While Goebbels lashed out vigorously against numerous European newspapers, he made no charge of faking against any American paper or agency. “Campaign of Lies” A large party of the foreign press, he s

1934-06-05.text: LONDON, June 5.—(AP)—Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, told the house of commons today that Great Britain—who announced yesterday she would pay nothing on her forthcoming war debt instalment—would have paid at least a “token” June 15 but for the fact that President Roosevelt could not guarantee that Great Britain would not be classed as a defaulter. His statement was heard by an eager audience which jammed the chamber. The treasury bench was crowded with ministers and so were the seats allotted to foreign ambassadors and distinguished strangers. The treasury head said that the British debts note, made public last night in Washington, had been intended to be published simultaneously here and in Washington today. “Owing to a misunderstanding for which the American government was in no way responsible,” said Chamberlain, “the terms of our note which was delivered at 8 p.m. b

Astrom, the Finnish minister, informed the State Department that the Finnish government would, as usual, make full payment in cash of its war debt installment, amounting to $166,538 in New York on June 15. Johnson Act Cited The British note was delivered to William Phillips, under secretary of state, by Philip Mainwaring Broadmead, first secretary of the British embassy, acting for Sir Ronald Lindsay, the British ambassador. Paris, June 5 (AP)—Paris newspapers hailed Great Britain's decision to suspend war debt payments to the United States today as proof that France was right all along in defaulting and that henceforth a united Europe will oppose America on the question. “France was right, war debts are dead,” said headlines in the papers. France, now that she has Great Britain for a companion as a debt defaulter, is expected to press new efforts to liquidate her huge war debt to the United States. A basis of ten cents on the dollar appeared today to be a likely proposal for settlement of the $3,960,772,238 fortune France owes America. Any likelihood the French would pay something on the $59,000,000 due June 15 appeared remote following publication of the British note to Washington announcing that nation would default. The sentiment of parliament is against payment as apparently is that of a majority of the

Great Britain’s blunt announcement that it would “suspend” its June 15 war debt payment to the United States appeared the forerunner today of a general default by European nations to edge their cost by so much as a small token payment. Developments included: London — Members jammed the House of Commons in hopes that Chancellor of the Exchequer Neville Chamberlain would explain the debt note. Paris — French cabinet members opposed to debt payments appeared confident that France would follow Britain’s example. Washington — United States apparently contemplated no action for the present. Finland announced intention to pay her debt promptly and in full. Following the British note to Washington, the dollar strengthened sharply in terms of the shy pound, but in Paris the dollar was weaker in relation to the franc.

LONDON, June 5 (UP) — The British Government proclaimed its intention to Parliament today of suspending war debt payments to the United States and indicated its earnest desire for a general revision of war debts between all nations. The announcement by Neville Chamberlain, Chancellor of the Exchequer, was an apparent bid to Washington to take the next step and start conversations. He was careful not to propose a general conference, however, in deference to Washington’s refusal to deal with its debtors collectively. There was nothing in his speech which intimated that Britain would insist on conferring with other nations, or would not be willing to discuss a separate settlement with the United States. His reference to all intergovernmental debts, however, reflected the desire for a settlement all around.

There was a possibility the government might address a note to the United States, signifying its willingness to participate in debt negotiations leading to definite settlement on a fractional basis. But it appeared that growing sentiment in the cabinet to try to remove the stigma of three debt defaults by offering a token payment was halted by the strong British note. Andre Tardieu, minister without portfolio, and Pierre Laval, minister of colonies, both former premiers and leaders of the anti-payment faction were openly joyful. WASHINGTON, June 4 IL... Great Britain, first of the debtor nations to undertake payment of vast funds borrowed in time of war, joined the defaulters' bloc today with notification to this government that on June 15 it will not pay millions due the treasury. The British debt note reiterated the view expressed 18 months ago that debt payment agreements "cannot be revived without disaster." With British debt default on June 15, a problem which has plagued the world since the war goes into deadlock. Want Conference The debtor objective appears to be a general conference to adjust the $12,000,000,000 obligations advanced by the United States when allies had their backs to the wall. This government rejects the general conference idea. There is no intention in Washington of permitting the United States to be "ganged" by its debtors.
