1934-06-18.text: Shanghai—(A)—Six British citizens, including two British naval officers, were kidnapped together with 20 Chinese by pirates this afternoon from a British commercial steamer off the mouth of the Yellow River. The sea wolves took over the ship, the Shuntien, which was on its way from Tientsin to Shanghai, apparently after boarding it in Tientsin and awaiting the opportunity to overpower the crew and passengers. The capture was effected without opposition. The pirates forced the captives into a fleet of five junks which stood by. Besides the captives, the pirates removed all the most valuable merchandise. Then the steamer proceeded to Chefoo. The Britons captured, beside the two naval officers, were one commercial traveler and three members of the steamer’s crew.

Basingstoke, England (AP)—The Duke of Wellington, 85, a grandson of England’s distinguished military leader, died at his home near here on the 119th anniversary of the Battle of Waterloo. The nobleman, who was the fourth Duke of Wellington, died of pneumonia on the great estate given to his forebear for the notable victory over Napoleon.

BRIGHTON, Eng., June 18.—(P)—The torso of a woman’s body, from which the head, arms and legs were severed, was found today in a trunk in the luggage office of the Brighton Railway station. The woman was thought by police to have been about 40 years old. Her height possibly was 5 feet, 2 or 3 inches. The body appeared well nourished. It was wrapped in two kinds of brown paper and bound with a window cord. The body, which was unclothed, bore no wounds other than those incurred in the severing of the head, arms and legs. The paper bore the letters "Ford," which police thought might be part of the name of a town. Investigators discovered that the trunk, of "cabin" type, in which the body was found was left at the station after noon on June 6. Scotland Yard was not communicative concerning either the discovery of the torso or the strange case of the missing Miss Agnes Tufverson of New York an

LONDON, Eng.—(#)— Prime Minister Ramsay McDonald announced Monday in the House of Commons that the British government proposes to reply to the United States’ war debt note regarding the suggestion that Britain make payment “in kind,” that is, goods and services. Replying to a query from the floor as to whether he would consider handing over Bermuda or other island territories no longer of defensive value to this country as payment, the prime minister said: “There could under no circumstances be any question of such an arrangement.”

London, June 18.—/P—It is almost unusual—even irregular, Lord Merrivale, that famous judge, actually discarded his wig in court today. The most dignified police in the world, as represented at the bobbles at Rochester, discarded their tunics and directed traffic in their shirtsleeves. As England steamed through another humid day with no rain in sight to relieve the countrywide drouth, 500 police armed with birch brooms guarded the Ascot heath and race course from the danger of fire. At 1 p.m. the temperature in London was 81 degrees in the shade, 1 degree higher than yesterday. A guard was kept everywhere against wastage of water. Critics of the Crystal Palace fountains were quieted by a public announcement that the water there is used over and over again, being pumped into the air from the reservoir to which it returns. Sir William Prescott, one of London’s five water “dictators,” said

London, June 18 (UP)—Great Britain plans to reply to the latest United States note on war debts, in which payment in kind was suggested as a possibility, Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald told a questioner today in the House of Commons. MacDonald was replying to a question by Captain Arthur Evans, Conservative, who asked whether the government would reply to the United States note and whether it would consider handing over Bermuda or any other island territories adjacent to the United States which no longer have defensive value to the British Empire. MacDonald said that as he had told a previous questioner on March 6, there can under no circumstances be any question of such an arrangement as handing over Bermuda or other islands.

Basingstoke, England, June 18.—(U.P.)—The Duke of Wellington, grandson of the iron duke who crushed Napoleon, died today—on the 120th anniversary of the battle of Waterloo. An attack of bronchitis brought on a heart attack and pneumonia. The duke was unconscious for two days before his death. Today he was to have presented King George, at Windsor Castle, with a silk flag representing a year’s rent on his estate of Strathfieldsays.

WASHINGTON, June 18 (UP). —President Roosevelt's vacation plans are askew again due to congress’ failure to adjourn. He had planned to leave Washington Wednesday, receive an honorary degree from Yale University and then go to New London, Conn., to see the Harvard-Yale crew races. If congress adjourns today, Roosevelt may be able to go as he planned. Otherwise he probably will be forced to abandon the Yale trip.

1934-06-07.text: LONDON, June 7.—(#)—Official quarters said today that the British government will not accept disarmament proposals made by Louis Barthou, French foreign minister, in Geneva. The government, said these sources, has instructed Captain Anthony Eden, Lord Privy Seal and British representative at the disarmament conference, to attempt to get the French to agree to the original suggestion relative to arms levels made by Arthur Henderson, the president of the conference. It was stated that Great Britain will not be turned from her self-imposed role of umpire in the tangled disarmament controversy.

WHIPSHADE (England), June 7, L. Stetson, 26, a member of the staff of a big open air show, was mauled to death today by four lions when he tried to recover a hat which was blown into the lion cage from a spectator’s head. Keepers had to shoot two lions before they could recover the body.

Reading, Today—(AP)—An automobile crashed through a heavy barricade at the dead end of a street and toppled down a 30 foot embankment today, killing four men and seriously injuring a fifth. The dead: Morris L. Koller, 23; William T. Kittinger, 22; Harold J. Spatz, 18, and J. H. Schaeffer, 22, all of Reading. Lawrence Kuhns, 22, of Boyertown, driver of the car, was taken to a hospital where it was said his condition was critical. Police were forced to go three blocks out of their way to reach the railroad tracks to which the car had gone. They found the bodies of the four victims buried under the wreckage. All were badly mutilated. Kuhns was thrown clear of the car.

DUBLIN, IRISH FREE STATE, June 6 (4)—Twenty-one percent of the $9,010,875 in prize money distributed by the Irish Hospital Sweepstakes on the result of the Derby at Epsom Downs today will go to the United States. Statisticians went to work within minutes after Windsor Lad thundered under the wire and announced that $1,901,854 would go to holders of tickets in the United States. No announcement was made as to the amount of money which Americans contributed to the $14,175,190 taken in by the Irish Hospital Fund but if buyers in the United States spent the same proportion as they won their contribution would have been $2,976,750—something more than $1,000,000 above the amount they got back. There were four American tickets on Windsor Lad and the holders of each ticket will get $151,200. On Euston, the second horse, there were likewise four American tickets, each of which will pay $73,600. T

LONDON. June 6. (?)—The opposition to Great Britain's decision to make no war debt payment to the United States on June 15 began to find its voice today after the first burst of general approval. “I regret that Britain did not decide to pay the June 15 installment,” said Lord Strabolgi, labor peer, in the house of lords, “We should avoid the possibility of default.” In other quarters similar expressions were heard, but the supporters of the government plan remained quite clearly in the majority.

(By The Associated Press) Brussels, June 7—Belgium, plunged into sorrow three months ago by the death of King Albert, rejoiced today at the birth of his grandson, to be named Albert. The child was born last night to Queen Astrid and King Leopold II in the Royal Castle at Laeken. Her Majesty and the infant son were reported to be well. All Brussels was awakened at 6 a.m. today by the boom of 101 guns, announcing the joyful event and the news was communicated officially by Burgomaster Max.

Brussels, June 6.—(P)—Queen Astrid of the Belgians gave birth tonight to a son, the third child in the royal family of King Leopold. The child was born at 11:35 p.m. in the royal castle at Lacken. Both mother and child were reported well. A salvo of 101 guns will announce the event to the citizens of Brussels at 6 o'clock tomorrow morning. An informal christening, which is customary within twenty-four hours of birth, will be performed privately by a court chaplain Thursday. The formal christening will be at the royal palace in Brussels a month later. It is understood the baby will be named Albert, for the late king, father of Leopold, who fell to his death while mountain climbing. King Leopold and the queen, a member of the Swedish royal family, were married in 1926. They have two other children, Josephine Charlotte, born in 1927, and Baudoin, born in 1930.

Madrid, June 7—(/P)—Guards surrounded the home of President Niceto Alcalá Zamora today as a precaution against an alleged plot to assassinate him while sanguinary disorders reddened by a farm strike splotched Spain. A newspaper was fined after publishing a report that Rightists were implicated in an uprising and planned to kidnap the president but authorities took extraordinary precautions at the executive mansion against any attempts on his life. The assassination of Gen. Ferdinand Berenguer, brother of a former Monarchist premier, and at least ten deaths and scores of injuries in the farm strike spread fears of an uprising. It was believed the assassins of Berenguer had mistaken him for his partagan Gen. Damaso Berenguer, who served as premier under former King Alphonso. 1934-07-10.text: London — Refusal by Italy to modify her naval construction plans cast a shadow today over Anglo-French naval conversations proceeding in the presence of the French foreign minister, Louis Barthou. It was understood in informed quarters that the British told the French of their concern over the Italian program of two 35,000-ton battleships, and it was reported the French may feel unable to pursue extensively their pre-conference discussions in preparation for the 1935 naval parley. They will be retarded, it was indicated, until the full extent of Mussolini’s exact plans is revealed. Lendon, July 9.—(#)—The general political situation in Europe including the French sponsored eastern security pact were discussed at an opening conference today between Louis Barthou, French foreign minister and Sir John Simon, foreign secretary of Great Britain. Disarmament in all its phases was aired at a luncheon given by Sir John in honor of Barthou. The only person present not directly connected with the Anglo-French discussion was Arthur Henderson, president of the world disarmament conference. French circles expected Barthou and Norman H. Davis, American ambassador-at-large, to confer sometime tomorrow if time permits before Barthou leaves London at four p.m.

The conversations were regarded as having achieved a vital step in the consolidation of European peace. Reliable quarters said the following results had been attained: 1. Britain agreed to assume a benevolently neutral attitude toward the Franco-Soviet scheme for an eastern European pact of mutual assistance to include Germany, 2. (By the Associated Press) London, July 9 A friendly “understanding” between Great Britain and France fortifying and bringing up to date provisions of the Locarno pact, was believed to have been reached between Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, and the French foreign minister, Louis Barthou. While the actual results of the important sessions were bound up tight in official secrecy, it was understood France was warmly assured Great Britain has every intention of fulfilling all her obligations under the Locarno treaty. LONDON, Eig.—(/P)—Louis Barthou, French foreign minister, indicated Tuesday upon his departure for Paris that Britain will go to the aid of France in case the Franco-Belgium area is ever invaded by a foreign power. “We French and British are agreed on the European situation,” Barthou said as he departed, indicating that the British had acceded to most of the points of the French proposal. He reiterated that no formal pact of any kind had been signed, but that the two nations had reached a “friendly understanding.”

BERLIN, July 9.—(AP)—Germany plans to push vigorously a friendlier foreign policy, it appeared today, fearing other countries will build political fences completely shutting her out. Her hand was figuratively stretched out in mingled friendship, apprehension and defiance to France and the world. A ringing pronouncement for Franco-German understanding, and at the same time a warning that Germany will fight “as no people ever yet fought for liberty,” by Rudolf Hess, trusted Hitler lieutenant, was considered something of an about-face from a firm Nazi policy. Addressing 12,000 Nazi chieftains at Koenigsberg yesterday; Hess said a defenseless country endangers peace and that Germany would be satisfied with the minimum of arms. BERLIN, July 10. (4)—The reichstag was convoked today for Friday for a speech by Chancellor Hitler on events which made the executions of June 30 necessary. Chancellor Hitler, who since June 30, the date of climactic events marking the beginning of the “second revolution” has kept silent, once more will use the forum of the so-called national parliament to address the nation and the world. His speech is calculated to answer innumerable questions that German citizens and foreigners have been asking in explanation of the executions of June 30. The reichstag has not met since January 30, this year, when Chancellor Hitler gave an exhaustive account of the first year of his stewardship. 1934-12-17.text: LIVERPOOL, Dec. 15 (/).—Seventeen men perished during attempts to rescue the crew of the British freighter ‘Usworth as wild seas reduced the ship to a helpless bulk. Advices to the Cunard-White Star line from the liner Ascania said today that fifteen members of the Usworth’s crew had been lost, along with two members of the crew of the Belgian liner Jean Jadot, which, with the Ascania, went to the rescue of the stricken freighter. The master of the Ascania informed the line that eleven members of the freighter’s crew had been rescued, nine by the Ascania and two by the Jean Jadot. The Usworth was abandoned and was drifting helplessly with a heavy list to port, the Ascania’s message said. Describes Rescue Attempts. Heroic attempts to rescue the helpless members of the Usworth’s crew were described by Capt. Sadie Gonthier, master of the rescue ship Jean Jadot, in a wireless dispatch to the

Saarbruecken, Saar Territory, Dec. 7—(AP)—Rigid precautions to prevent clashes between international troops and Saarlanders were adopted Monday after bitter resentment was aroused by an Anglo-native street fight. A resident of the Saar was wounded by a British police officer's pistol Sunday, and in the resulting scuffle the officer and an English nobleman were beaten. The incident created alarm, with the Saar already tense over the January 13 plebiscite which will decide its future. It came as the League of Nations moved an international army into the territory to preserve order during the vote. When news of the shooting and subsequent beatings filtered through the Saar, the German Front, a Nazi organization, called special meetings of protest. LONDON, Dec. 17. (#)—The United States delegation to the naval conversations with Great Britain and Japan indicated today, just in advance of the conversation's break-up, that it would leave possible future conversations up to the British and Japanese. All three delegations studied the wording of the declaration of formal adjournment which probably will be issued Wednesday or Thursday at about the time Japan denounces the Washington naval treaty of 1922. These same quarters said that this modification would remove the last obstacle to an agreement with Great Britain on the question of the freedom of the seas. Great Britain contended in the last war that she had the right to search ships suspected of trading with enemies and it is understood that the proposed new American policy would remove official protection from such ships. AARDKULCIEN, Saar Territory, Dec. 16--(PJ)—A bullet from the pistol of an English Member of the international police force here Sunday to prevent trouble in the plebiscite struck a man in the stomach, and a hostile crowd beat and injured the Englishman. Serious trouble threatened for a time between the Saar residents and the foreigner, whose automobile had struck a woman. The Englishman, James Justice, was one of the volunteers recruited for the Saar police in accordance with a plan of the League of Nations’ Saar commission, which controls the territory under a mandate. When an angry crowd gathered about him, Justice drew a pistol. The crowd closed in, menacing him, and hands reached out to seize the weapon. During the scuffle the gun went off twice, one bullet striking an electrician named Neumeisterer. He was not seriously injured. The crowd, numbering about 30 persons, immediately clo

HULL Ene, Dec. 18.--Mrs. Ethel Lillie Major, 42, will be hanged Wednesday morning. She will be the first woman to go to the gallows in England since 1926. The home secretary's office reported inability to discover any grounds for the reprieve of the woman, who was convicted of poisoning her 46-year-old husband, Arthur Major.

Saarbrucken, Dec. 17 (UP) Resentment spread throughout the Saar today against foreign supervision of the January 13 plebiscite as the result of two clashes between British members of the international police and civilians. Tension was perhaps greater than at any time during the anxious months of preparation for the plebiscite, in which the Saarlanders are to determine by ballot the status of their territory. Feeling spread to the officers who are supervising the territory under the League of Nations governing commission. Local newspapers launched attacks on the international police and said the clashes showed the people could not depend on them. The incidents came as a British army advance contingent, part of the British-Italian-Swedish-Netherlands military force which will take over the policing, left on its way to the Saar, and as Major General John E. SEATTLE (#) — The British steamer Cape Ortegal, which sent out SOS calls last night 400 miles off the coast, reported it was limping back to Puget Sound today for repairs. The ship apparently was safe, despite a bad list caused by a shifting deck load of lumber. “It should be able to return safely,” said David R. Girdwood, president of the Girdwood Shipping Company, under whose charter the vessel was sailing.

LONDON, Aug. 14 (UP).—Austria has sent a note to Britain, France and Italy asking permission to enlarge its army because it fears another Nazi putsch is imminent, it was learned today. The note seeks an agreement permitting Austria to maintain a special auxiliary armed force of 9,000 troops beyond the existing 20,000 in the regular army. The powers are considering the request and are expected to reply favorably. Advices from Vienna indicated Prince Ernst Rudiger Von Starhemberg, Austrian vice-chancellor, who has been conferring in Rome with Premier Benito Mussolini, would go to Paris shortly to seek French support of the army plan. Well-informed sources here were ready to credit the Austrian fear of another revolt. It is known the abortive uprising of July 25 was premature and ill-planned. LONDON, Ont. Aug. 14. Pp John S. Labatt, president of the Labatt Brewing Company, was kidnapped today while traveling by motor between London and Sarnia. While members of the family, apparently as the result of a warning, would not discuss the details of the kidnapping, it was reported that a note was found inside Labatt's abandoned automobile demanding $150,000 ransom. The automobile was left by the kidnappers in front of St. Joseph's hospital. The note was said to have threatened death if police and the public were informed of the kidnapping. The family was en route to Sarnia, where it was indicated that the brewer was being held. Labatt was known to have left the residence of Harry F. Holland, 10 miles north of here, this morning, and the finding of his car, together with other circumstances, was said by police to leave no doubt but that he had been kidnapped.

Cork, Irish Free State, Aug. 14—(AP)—A woman's heroism was credited today with saving many lives in savage fighting yesterday between 5,000 farmers, enraged by a tax sale, and 300 civil guards. Mrs. Eamonn O'Neill, wife of a member of the Dail, rushed between the combatants, risking her life in heavy gunfire, and pleaded with them to stop. Both farmers and officers ceased shooting, fearing they would hit her. The woman then helped Jeremiah Lynch, a critically wounded farmer, outside a yard where the battle took place. Lynch later died. More than 100 others were injured. The farmers had attacked the guards, surrounding the yard where cattle taken from two farmers who did not pay land taxes were to be sold. First aid doctors established a dressing station nearby to treat the injured. Disturbances broke out in other sections of the city and police used clubs to disperse demonstrators. Troop

LONDON, Eng. --(/P)—- The former Empress Zita, described by diplomats as “a fast worker” was said Monday by an authoritative source to be going ahead with her efforts to bring about restoration of the Hapsburg throne in Austria despite objections from the Little Entente nations. Italian officials were said by the same source to have suggested that Zita go slowly in her negotiations on the continent looking toward making her son the Archduke Otto, a king. While British officials declined to discuss the monarchical plans, they ridiculed reports that Otto, now in Sweden, might try to marry a Swedish princess. “An Italian princess still remains the probable consort if his plans for the throne ever get anywhere,” one diplomat said. Another high source described Otto's present journey in the Scandinavian countries as mere “dust in the eye” to cover Zita’s real negotiations in Italy, France and

LONDON, August 14 (4% — That necessity still exists for government measures to bring wheat farmers a satisfactory margin of profit was stressed at the opening session today of the International Wheat Conference. A review of the current situation disclosed that the wheat "diplomats" met the 1,000,000,000-bushel glut of world stocks will be considerably alleviated as a result of the universal drought. This, they estimate, will cut normal production this year by 300,000,000 to 400,000,000 bushels. "But we still have far to go if we want to safeguard the world against the danger of grave crises in the future," said a conference spokesman. A summary of drought results made at the meeting brought out that Argentina alone of the big producers will have a good crop. But big carryovers were found still to be a serious menace. CORK, Irish Free State, Aug. 14.— Soldiers wearing helmets and armed with bayonets patrolled the streets tonight after gaining the upper hand in a fierce fight with 5,000 farmers, in which one man was slain and upward of 100 injured. Jeremiah Lynch, a farmer, died of wounds as his determined companions battled to prevent a tax sale. Police, later reinforced by soldiers, at first believed only a couple dozen had been injured. But tonight it was learned eight doctors had set up a private dressing station near the farm where the fight occurred and that many injured were attended. The courage of a woman, Mrs. Eamonn O'Neill, whose husband is one of the county court members of {Continued on Page 3. Col. 3.}

CORK, Irish Free State, Aug. 13. —(AP)—Farmers of County Cork, 5,000 strong, took the offensive against police today in an effort to prevent a tax sale and were repulsed only after a terrific battle in which one farmer was killed and 25 others were wounded seriously enough to require hospital treatment. The policemen were attacked as they were guarding a yard where cattle taken from two farmers for failure to pay land taxes were being sold. Ultimately the defending force was augmented by a military detachment. A feature of the battle was a spectacular charge of twelve men in a motor lorry, which plunged at top speed through a cordon of police around the barricaded cattle-yard. One of the wounded men was in a serious condition tonight with a bullet wound in the lungs. Five others were shot, and the rest were injured by police clubs. When the 5,000 farmers came to town to protest the sales

VIENNA, Aug. 14—Fifteen more Nazis were marched into a courtroom today to be tried for treason, a grim procedure which has left eight of their fellows dangling on the gallows. They are accused of participation in the seizure of a radio station and the chancellery July 25, in an uprising which resulted in the assassination of Chancellor Dollfuss. More than 100 other Nazis are awaiting their turns to go on trial here. Austria's hangman, although he is having a busy season, observes the formalities. Not even the weather interferes. He wore faultless evening dress and a high silk hat when he executed four policemen last night a few hours after they were convicted of participation in the Nazi revolt. A steady rain fell as the four went to their deaths in the yard of the district court building. They went through the ordeal stoically, rejecting the opportunity to make a final statement. Five o

1934-01-08.text: WASHINGTON, Jan. 5.—UP— There are so many pigs in Denmark that there’s a serious shortage of Scotch whisky in the United States. Here’s the plot: Great Britain has signed a contract to buy 62 per cent of her pork from Denmark. And Great Britain wants to sell the United States Scotch liquor by the boatload. The United States replies, through the federal alcohol control administration: "You buy our pigs, or we won't buy your whisky." Great Britain retorts: "We’re sorry, but we don’t need any more pigs." The United States insists: A Warning to Britain. "Better find a way to buy American pigs, or we'll drink gin." That is as far as the international dialogue, couched in diplomatic language, has progressed. The initial British quota of 607,000 gallons has been exhausted. The FACA says that no more import licenses will be granted until Great Britain diverts some of her pig business to the Unit

Chamonix, France, Jan. 8.—(>)— Serge “Handsome Alex” Stavisky, alleged $40,000,000 swindler, shot himself in the head today when police surrounded him in a hidden villa. He was at first thought to have died instantly but a hastily summoned physician found a sign of life. A battle immediately was begun to save Stavisky from death in order to turn him over to trial. Application of restoratives brought an apparent consciousness to the man who had been sought for two weeks following the collapse of the Bayonne pawnshop which he founded. Later, however, he lapsed into a coma and the doctor said he feared the wound was mortal.

Tokyo—(#)—Deaths of 71 persons and injuries to 56 in a panic-stricken crowd were reported today by the Rengo News Agency correspondent at Kyoto. The crowd was in the Kyoto railroad station to bid farewell to a group of recruits for the imperial Japanese navy. The cause for the sudden panic and stampede in which the victims were trampled underfoot was not immediately explained.

PARIS, Jan. 8.—(”)—France agreed today to increase threefold the quotas on American products as announced at the first year. The United States embassy announced the conclusion of this arrangement whereby the United States will be exempted from the French policy to reserve three-quarters of its imports quotas for bargaining. While the announced arrangement does not give full satisfaction to American business interests, it restores the quotas as they affect the United States to the figures of 1932. The automobile imports still are hit as the quota is based on 1932 figures which were smaller than the 1933 motor imports. The agreement excludes apples, pears, mechanical tools other than those for agriculture, lamps, and radio apparatus from the bargaining quotas.

Berlin, Jan. 7.--Police swooped down on 1000 German Sunday school boys today, broke up their meeting and arrested their leaders as the mailed fist of the state came to the defense of Reichbishop Designate Ludwig Mueller and his Nazi church regime. In defiance of Bishop Mueller's suppressive church decree, opposition pastors in hundreds of reich churches meantime went into open revolt and disclaimed allegiance to Mueller. The Sunday school lads, members of the German Bible circle, were just coming from the Church of St. Paul the Apostle. They had been listening to a fiery sermon from the Rev. Martin Niemoeler, national opposition leader, a former submarine commander and Iron Cross war hero. Protests Are Read Up Niemoeller read defiant protests to the 1,000 assembled youths, aged from 14 to 20. The protests had been issued by insurgent pastors of the emergency federation. The police were w

GENEVA, Jan. 5.—(AP)—A world-wide improvement in the employment situation, led by the United States, was noted today in a communique of the international labor office. “In the United States,” the statement said, “the rise in the employment Index is very marked—73.5 in October, 1933, as compared to 59.6 in October, 1932.” (Continued on Page 2, Col. 8.)

PARIS, Jan. 8- (UP)—The United States embassy announced today it had been advised by the French foreign office that United States import quotas for the first quarter of 1934 have been increased 100 percent. Hundreds of American products are affected, and millions of dollars. Just before the new year, France reduced import quotas on all industrial goods by 75 percent. The government hoped to force other nations to grant France reciprocal advantages in order to bring their quotas back to the previous level. "The United States now becomes the first country to obtain an increased quota.

Berlin—(4)—One hundred pastors who protested from their pulpits Sunday against the suppressive decree issued by Reichbishop Ludwig Mueller may face suspension for insubordination, it was believed today. Led by the Rev. Martin Niemoller, head of the opposition to the Reichsbishop and his Nazi church regime, the pastors read from a statement distributed by the insurgent ministers of the emergency federation. After the meeting at which Dr. Niemoeller spoke, police broke up a throng of 1,000 German Sunday school boys as they left the church. The youths attempted to parade, but were dispersed. Hundreds of other pastors throughout the nation also read the protest. Assuming dictatorial powers over the Evangelical church to “restore orderly conditions,” the Reichsbishop in his decree set up regulations providing for the dismissal of pastors and disciplinary action against officers “who misuse th

1934-02-22.text: Perlin, Feb. 21.—Chancellor Adolf Hitler will join forces with Great Britain in a supreme effort to start a new movement for disarmament, it was reported here tonight. The chancellor, according to well-informed persons, today approved an English memorandum "in principle" following a long and cordial conversation he had with Captain Anthony Eden, British lord privy seal at the British embassy. It was understood Herr Hitler decided to bury whatever doubts he is reported to have had about certain features of the proposed British plan in order to strengthen Captain Eden's hand in the latter’s negotiations with Premier Mussolini in Italy shortly. Il Duce May Join

LONDON. (Special) — The love of the young Swedish Prince Sigvard for a blond German film actress prevailed today against the strenuous opposition of his family. Sigvard sent a special envoy of his father, Crown Prince Gustaf Adolf, back to Sweden with a firm declaration that he and Fraulein Erika Patzek will be married in the Caxton hall registry office here March 8. Laughing gaily at royal persons who believe princes should marry princesses, the young couple planned to obtain a special license.

By United Press Bad flying weather throughout the Fast today brought the United States Army Mail service its fourth fatality, & forced landing in Pennsylvania winds and curtailment of service in New England and parts of the South. A plane flying mail between Chicago and Toledo crashed in the woods near Deshler, O., killing Pilot Lieut. Duward Lowry of Milwaukee. Lieut. Frank Hollenstein was forced down by fog and haze in a small clearing near Haydentown, Pa., but was uninjured. All planes at Memphis were grounded by the weather. The westbound Cleveland plane was halted at Louisville. At Newark Airport center of the storm area, all schedules were being maintained with the exception of the Boston runs. Airmail service was crippled in the Rocky Mountain area. Snow and low ceilings prevailed throughout the district with several scheduled runs cancelled for the second successive day.

| BERLIN, Feb. 22—(7)—German newspapers charged today that France is trying willfully to prolong the world disarmament crisis, The charges were hurled editorially at the height of negotiations between Capt. Anthony Eden of Great Britain and German government leaders which many observers believe will result in a new movement toward an agreement on arms,

London, Feb. 22 (AP)—With or without royal consent, the wedding of Prince Sigvard of Sweden and his pretty German commoner will proceed as planned, it was reported reliably today—and the parents of the trim, blond Fraulein Erika Patzek will be on hand for the nuptials. So far as is known, the only guests expected at the simple wedding planned for March 8 are Erika’s father, Anton Patzek, Berlin businessman, and her mother. Both Prince Sigvard and Miss Patzek remained in seclusion after the prince, son of the Swedish crown prince, had turned a deaf ear to Count Folke Bernadotte who flew to London to dissuade them from marrying. Prince Sigvard, who like his bride-to-be is connected with the UFA motion picture company in Berlin, was induced to talk briefly last night. He shied when the marriage was mentioned. A questioner was referred to his lawyer. Neither added anything to published repor

PAY SASS B4 AIS SATE PRAT 6S ORES London, England, Feb. 21.—Stubbornly refusing to renounce his plan to marry a pretty German motion picture actress over the protests of the Swedish Royal family, Prince Sigvard, second son of Crown Prince Gustaf of Sweden, was located today living in seclusion in a small exclusive hotel in the West End. The prince, who is 26 and third in line for the Swedish throne, was found after an intensive search of Berlin and London, after it was reported he had “eloped” with his commoner bride-to-be, a beautiful 22-year-old blonde. The prince was firm in declaring his intentions to wed the girl, the daughter of a wealthy Berlin merchant.

BRUSSELS, Feb. 19.—(4)—Belgium mourned today her hero-king and prepared for the coronation of his sorrowing son. Albert I, king of the Belgians and the commander-in-chief of their army when, ragged, ill-fed and suffering, it stood off the forces of Kaiser Wilhelm during the World War, was killed late Saturday in a fall while mountain climbing. It was his favorite sport, and he was an expert; but a bit of frost-bitten rock broke in his hand, and he plunged 26 feet to death. They found him where he had fallen, 10 hours later. Death must have been instantaneous. At all events the 58-year-old king did not suffer. His skull was fractured. With all the pomp of royal ceremony the state funeral of Albert I will be held Thursday. To Be Crowned Within 24 hours of the announcement Crown Prince Leopold will become, at the age of 32, the fourth king of the Belgians—Leopold III. Prince Leopold and the

(Copyright, 1934, By the Associated Press) : Brussels, Feb. 22. (P)—King Albert I was buried today in the crypt of a little gray church near the royal castle at Laeken. He was laid to rest beside the bodies of his predecessors Leopold I and II after one of the most impressive funerals given a national leader in modern times. Eight hours of military processions and religious rites in two churches were ended at 3 p.m. when the body was placed in its last resting place after a brief, private benediction before the royal family. Tens of thousands of persons took part in the processions and hundreds of thousands more witnessed the pageantry under heavily overcast skies. Rain fell slightly for about half an hour while services were held in the thirteenth century cathedral of St. Gudule. The rain stopped again when the mourners resumed their march toward Laeken. One of the most spectacular scen

1934-01-17.text: Washington, Jan. 17 (AP)—Rum boats—163 of them—were riding the Gulf Stream today toward the Spanish Main in a race with the law that brought no frowns to the federal government. The flotilla, bearing around 2,500,000 gallons of liquor, is bound for Belize, British Honduras; the Bahama Islands, and other foreign ports in the south in an effort to get the liquor consigned for legal shipment into the United States before February 9. The government announced the movement and made no mention of disapproval, indicating rather that the move would decrease the smuggling menace and increase the supply of available liquor in this country. Rum row had lingered long off New York and New England even after repeal.

CHICAGO, Jan. 16 () — Roger Touhy and three members of his gang went on trial today charged with the $70,000 kidnapping of John “Jake the Barber” Factor who faces extradition to England on charges of swindling British investors of $7,000,000. The four marched before Judge Michael Feinberg and found themselves in a courtroom almost bare of spectators. It had a small garrison of guards, but their weapons were concealed. Neither guns, shackles nor uniforms were in sight, and the four, described by the state as notorious desperadoes, were escorted by an equal number of deputies. Touhy, Gustav “Gloomy Gus” Schaefer, Albert Kator, and the gray-haired Edward McFadden, known as “Father Tom,” each entered pleas of “not guilty.” Touhy, curly-headed, slouched in his chair, watching the selection of the jury closely. Spectators were kept to a minimum by orders that anyone who entered must submit to

SOUTH BEND, Ind., Jan. 16. —Of all things—William Shakespeare is having trouble with his English! Not William Shakespeare of Stratford-on-Avon, but William Shakespeare of Notre Dame. William is a promising halfback, a good student in other studies, but not so hot in his English course. With mid-semester examinations at hand, Elmer Layden, Notre Dame's new athletic director and football coach, today urged William to bear down on the English so he won't become ineligible.

LONDON, Jan. 17 —(AP)— Gilding Clarke, “Iron Man” of the famous Old Vic theatrical company, who collapsed when given a friendly slap on the back during a rehearsal of “Orpheus” yesterday, died in a hospital today. Friends said they believed the unexpected slap caused a shock that affected the actor’s heart. A man of great strength, Clarke weighed more than 256 pounds.
WASHINGTON, Jan. 17.—(U.P)— President Roosevelt is not seeking an agreement with Great Britain on monetary matters or trade, it was stated at the White House today.
LONDON, Jan. 27 (AP).—The admiralty today awarded contracts for eight destroyers to cost $11,250,000 under the normal replacement program of 193.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 16.—Word reached the Government this afternoon that 163 rum running boats, concentrated off the northeast coast, had left for Belize, British Honduras, with 2,000,000 gallons of American type whisky ultimately to reach the United States through legal channels. Officials here tacitly approved the efforts of the erstwhile rum runners to get their cargoes into the United States through legal methods. There are expectations that some of the vessels would stop at the Bahamas Islands and other points in the Caribbean and have the liquor consulated from there. On Jan. 13, the Government lifted import restrictions on American type whiskys—rye and bourbon. It was explained that this meant importers would have to have their merchandise cleared through consuls in foreign ports by Feb. 12, but the consignments did not have to reach the United States by that date. Officials said the

Calcutta..-(AP)—The estimates of India’s earthquake dead leaped into four figures today. Some observers said 2,000 was a conservative estimate of those killed in Monday's catastrophe. The paralysis of communication lines made accurate information most difficult to obtain. Officials were confining their statements to the list of known dead, still standing at 112; but reports from aviators flying over parts of the shaken area were much more horrifying. Hundreds were reported killed at Muzaffarpur. Some said the streets there were littered with corpses and that the town lay in ruins, (The correspondent of the London Daily Mail cabled his newspaper that fliers who had viewed Muzaffarpur from the air estimated the dead there would exceed 1,000. Hardly a house remained standing, the airmen said, and water, spouting from fissures in the earth, had created a wide flood area. Neighboring towns of

1934-03-20.text: by Dale Harrison Associated Press Staff Writer Two men who came to America from England and (1) made good and then (2) made not-so-good, faced precarious and definitely adventurous futures today. One is Samuel Insull, a rogue at the age of 74 on the face of the earth, hunted by his adopted United States, shooed from Greece, and unwanted by any other country of the world. The other is John Factor, speculator and gambler wanted in England much as Insull is wanted here to answer — for what happened to other people's money. Both were English-born and American naturalized, each wrote his name with gold upon Chicago—and American—affairs. Insull wrote with the pinched penmanship of a Croesus, for the well in which his pen dipped was the American investing public. Factor stroked with a Wellingford flourish. Each started poor, seeking wealth. Each got what he wanted, together with trouble he had

DUBLIN, — Many cans: yere among the ticketholders today as the drawing began in the Irish Grand National sweepstakes. A final analysis of counterfoils dumped into the huge mixing drum preparatory to the beginning today of the three-day draw showed 67 percent of the tickets were held by residents of the British Isles, 16 percent by Americans, and 17 percent by Canadians. Total receipts for the Grand Richborough; Marty D’Napoli, on Thrumster; John O'Neal, Worcester, on Cantilling; William McLean, Bridgewater, on Libour; The Horseman, Arlington, on Tron. Saint; Elizabeth Harrington, Middleboro, on Forrium; Portia; certificate of F.C. Dougherty, Newton, on Coolinolagh; and Johannar, North Bennington, Vt., on Inverse.

(Copyright by United Press) PARIS, (UP).—Robert C. Switz, young New Yorker, was revealed by his own confession today as the Paris chief of an international spy gang which they said operated on behalf of Soviet Russia and Germany to learn the military secrets of France, Great Britain and the United States. With Switz is held his wife, the former Marjorie Tilley, Vassar girl. After a merciless cross-examination lasting far into the night, Switz broke down and made admissions which led to five more arrests, in addition to some 20 already made. American and British agents were said to have co-operated in uncovering the ring. The youthful Switz succeeded to leadership of the conspiracy a year ago, police said, after the original chiefs had been nearly trapped and fled France. His confession disclosed that he met agents of the international spy syndicate in the United States where he and his w

(Copyright, 1934, by United Press.) PARIS, March 20 (UP).—Two young Americans, Robert and Marjorie Switz, breaking under a merciless cross examination, were declared by police today to have revealed details of the greatest espionage ring in history, reaching across the Atlantic to the United States. Jubilant, the secret service asserted officially after months of reticence that police charged the ring operated in behalf of Germany and Soviet Russia against France, Great Britain and the United States. Switz, an aviator, and his wife, a Vassar graduate, held in separate prisons for three months, were taken last night before Magistrate Ernest Benon, who is in charge of the espionage investigation. They were questioned for hours. Police said they involved themselves in contradiction after contradiction. As a result, armed with names of persons never before suspected in the long inquiry, sure

ASSOCIATED PRESS ATHENS, March 19.—A raging storm on the Mediterranean endangered the life of Samuel Insull tonight as the world speculated on his ultimate destination. Huge waves pummeled and tossed his expensively-chartered little tramp steamer which creaked and groaned in the terrific wind, and it was feared the most famous of all present-day fugitives from justice might collapse with another heart attack. Insull, a poor sailor on a fair day, was believed facing grave danger. On his first flight from Greece last week, the 74-year-old former utilities czar suffered a heart attack in good weather, was seasick and could not eat, requiring medical attention. The freighter was believed well off the coast, cruising in a zigzag course, awaiting final instructions from the shore as to the possible places Insull might use as a haven from arrest for American authorities. He is sought for grand

PARIS, Mar, 20 (UP)—The first evidence that Alexandre Stavisky, banker whose $30,000,000 scheme collapsed and led to one of the gravest scandals France has ever known, did not commit suicide but was slain by secret hirelings to close his lips, was offered today. Members of the parliamentary commission investigating the Stavisky scandal demanded a new autopsy of his body after viewing films taken immediately after his death, when he was trapped by police. The films revealed blood streaming from Stavisky’s nostrils and mouth and also apparently from his chest. Deputies in the audience failed to perceive powder burns which would inevitably be caused by a close range suicide shot.

Paris, March 20—Apprehensive over the demands of Chancellor Adolf Hitler that Germany be allowed to rearm, the government announces a plan to swell the army’s ranks by inducing young conscripts to re-enlist in order to avoid the hazards of job hunting at the present time. The army also invites all unemployed young men in France who have left the ranks in the last five years to enlist for new short terms until labor conditions improve. The announced purpose of the government is to reinforce the army with short-term recruits because the regular conscript classes are beginning to slack off in numbers, due to the low wartime birth rate. Special recruiting will begin in April, an official communique said. Certain “specialists” will be offered 18-month terms and others may enlist for six months. All enlistment requirements will be lowered. Ordinarily conscript troops of the Chamber of Deputies

ADDIS ABABA, ABYSSINIA, Mar. 20—(UR)—One of Samuel Insull’s hopes as a place of refuge seemed illusory today when authorities told the United Press he had not obtained a passport visa and would be refused one if he asked for it. It was said that Insull would not be permitted to enter the country without a visa and that it had been decided not to give him one because of the legal complications involved. The American legation had said previously that if Insull arrived here he could be arrested and sued in the consular court as an American citizen. It was admitted that the question of actual extradition to the United States might prove a difficult one.

1934-02-28.text: LONDON, Feb. 28.—The dramatic story of the death of Rasputin, lecherous “mad monk” of Russia, was told to a breathless, packed courtroom today by the man who helped kill him, Prince Felix Youssoupoff of Russia testified in the suit of his wife against the Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer company, charging that she was libeled in a film in which one of the characters, intended to represent her, was seduced by the monk. Poisoned and Shot. The prince, once one of the great nobles of the Russian empire, in almost monosyllabic replies to the questions of Sir Patrick Hastings, counsel for his wife, told the story of the assassination. He said after Rasputin had been given poisoned cakes and wine, he shot him once with a revolver he obtained from Grand Duke Dimitri Paviovich. Then Puriskevich, the third of the conspirators, shot him three times. “In the end,” Hastings asked, “did you do anything to kill him

LONDON, Feb. 26 — (AP) — In short crisp sentences, Prince Chegodieff Youssoupoff told a tense courtroom today in the trial of his wife's libel suit that he killed Rasputin, Russia's “mad monk,” for the good of his country. The descendant of one of old Russia’s most noble families took the stand after the defense had intimated that he had not slain the powerful monk in St. Petersburg during the stirring days of the World War. His wife, Princess Irena Youssoupoff, is suing the Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures, Ltd. for $2,000,000, alleging the picture “Rasputin and the Empress” libeled her by linking her objectionably with Rasputin. Youssoupoff claims he killed Rasputin when the latter told him he was in the pay of Germany and planned to seize the czar’s throne. It was his first narration of the event in court, although he had written of it. “In doing what I did, I thought I was acting in the

| LONDON, Feb. 27 (UP).—Justice Horace Avory began hearing today the suit of a Russian princess who charges she was libeled by being portrayed in an American movie based on the life of Rasputin, the mad Russian monk. The suit is that of Princess Irina Alexandrovna, niece of the murdered Czar Nicholas II and wife of Prince Youssoupoff, who killed Rasputin. The princess charges that in the film she was portrayed as Princess Natasha, who was represented as being seduced by Rasputin and becoming his mistress.

LONDON — (AP) — The House of Commons early today defeated a motion challenging Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald’s refusal to receive the British hunger marchers or to allow them before the bar of the House. The vote was 270 to 62... The premier participated in a rough-and-tumble debate in defending his refusal to receive deputations. He reiterated the charge that, “These marches have been organized by a body notorious for attempts to spread unconstitutional propaganda.” Angered by the prime minister's stand, John McGovern, who led the hunger marchers from Glasgow, and Labor Member George Buchanan had interrupted proceedings frequently to fling pertinent pieces at MacDonald.

TOKYO, Feb. 22—(4)—The Japanese foreign office sent a sharp protest today to Moscow demanding flights of Soviet planes over Manchuria and Korea be stopped. The spokesman said “we consider such incidents highly dangerous. It is always dangerous for children to play with fire.” The Japanese government sent the demand for guarantee against any further flights over Manchurian territory.

Paris, Feb. 27.—(#)—An air, sea and land reorganization plan to strengthen France in troubled Europe will be presented soon at a special cabinet session it was learned today. Premier Gaston Doumergue tentatively has approved the program. It would be part of a vast military and economic rehabilitation scheme. The huge sum necessary to finance the plan would be raised through a loan possibly in England. A strong professional "shock" troops army is the idea the minister of war is said to have approved as part of a move toward strengthening the navy. Further, the navy would speed authorized construction of ships, and roads probably in the Alps would be built as part of a general plan to relieve unemployment.

VIENNA, Feb. 28. (AP)-- Vienna was sensationally quiet today- the date of expiration of the so-called Habicht ultimatum. Up until mid-afternoon, three hours after the expiration of the “truce” extended by Theodore Habicht, exiled leader of Austrian Nazis, there had been no demonstration nor disturbances in the capital, none reported in the provinces, and no new incidents on the Austro-German border. The University of Vienna students attempted no demonstrations and no unusual street gathering was discernible.

ASTRAKHAN, U. S. S. R., Feb. 28 (7)—With the help of an airplane, 20 of the 500 fishermen marooned on the ice floes of the Caspian Sea reached shore safely today. The rescue plane landed on an ice floe which bore more than 100 men. It distributed food to the marooned fishermen, then, after an aerial survey, guided 20 of them to land across the drifting ice. The ice-breaker Ettwo and more airplanes now are making efforts to reach the other men. If the present favorable weather continues, the rescue parties hope to save all.

1934-07-31.text: TOKYO (#)—Premier Keisuke Okada, in the first meeting with representatives of the foreign press, said Tuesday Japan was undecided whether to abrogate the Washington treaty, which established the five-five-three ratio in capital ships of the United States, Britain and Japan. “In order to reduce the burden of taxation,” Okada said, “naval armaments must be reduced to the smallest proportions possible. Such naval limitation must come from reduction of part of the heaviest armed nations. I cannot favor the present ratio principle, which hurts itself in respect to certain nations. I hope a better method will be discovered.” “Asked whether the means of Japan would demand a parity with American and Britain, requiring them to reduce to Japan's level, the premier said: “I do not expect such radical changes so suddenly.” He expressed confidence that the 1935 naval conference would succeed.

WIMBLEDON, ENG., JULY 31. (AP).—Great Britain today retained the Davis Cup, historic international tennis trophy, as Fred Perry, ace of the British forces, defeated Frank X. Shields, 6-4, 4-6, 6-2, 15-13, in a desperately fought fourth match to clinch the series with three victories. One more match remains to be played between Sidney B. Wood, Jr. and Henry Wilfred (Bunny) Austin, but the outcome can have no bearing on the five-match series. Perry won out in one of the longest and most bitterly fought sets of cup play, the long fourth, to register Great Britain's seventh victory in over a quarter of a century of Davis Cup competition. They won the cup from France last year, halting a tri-color reign that had extended since 1927, when the United States lost the cup to France. It was the fifth time the United States had been in the challenge round since the cup was lost.

LONDON, July 31—(/)—A divorce court today granted a decree nisi to Mrs. Ronald Colman against her husband, the motion picture star, in an undefended suit. Mrs. Colman said that she and her husband were married Sept. 18, 1920, at St. George's register office in London but have lived apart since 1924 when Colman left her. She said she was now living in a London hotel.

London—(C.P.)—Great Britain went ahead today with her plans for a stronger air force. Approval of the expansion program was voted overwhelmingly by the House of Commons after Stanley Baldwin, acting prime minister, expressed belief Germany may greatly enlarge her armaments in the air. A laborite motion to censure the air plans was rejected by a vote of 404 to 60. “If we do not act now,” Baldwin told the House, “we may find ourselves later on in terrible jeopardy.” Great Britain has already served notice she intends to ask for a bigger navy at the 1935 naval conference. Baldwin, in one of the most sensational foreign policy speeches heard by Commons since the World War, said rapid advancement in the air had made Great Britain foresee a new frontier extending beyond its own borders. “Let us not forget,” said the acting premier, “that since the day of air old frontiers have gone and when yo

LONDON, July 31 (UP).—Acting Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin's frank declaration Great Britain's frontier now lies along the German Rhine brought the country to a realization today of the danger of new war. Political correspondents of newspapers called the declaration the most important, in European affairs, since 1918. There was no effort to conceal the popular or governmental view that the potential enemy of Great Britain was Germany. Baldwin's statement was made in a House of Commons debate on the plan to increase the number of fighting planes from 844 to 1304. What he said was: “Since the days of airplanes, the old frontiers have gone. When you think of the defense of England you no longer think of the chalk cliffs of Dover. You think of the Rhine. That is where our frontier lies.” Seldom can there have been so frank a statement that a nation with which Britain enjoys supposedly frien

LONDON, July 30—(*)—The possibility of German rearmament in the air was emphasized in the House of Commons today by Stanley Baldwin, acting prime minister, in a strong plea for the British government's program of air force expansion. Following Baldwin's revelation of concern over the German plan, Winston Churchill, conservative member, charged that Germany "in violation of the peace treaty has created a military air force now nearly two-thirds as strong as our home defense force." Churchill added that Germany is increasing her force. Baldwin expressed the belief that Germany intends a big expansion of her air armaments if she obtains the right or "seizes the right to rearm."

Wimbledon, England, July 31, U.P) — America’s quest to return the Davis Cup to the land of its donor failed today for the seventh time when Frederick J. Perry, ace of England's squad and No. 1 in world rankings defeated Frank Shields, fighting New York tennis star, 6-4, 4-6, 6-2, 15-13 in the fourth match of the challenge round. The final set of the deciding match was one of the most thrilling in all Davis Cup history, and was decided in one of the largest scores of a challenge round match. Beginning at the ninth game there were eight consecutive service breaks. Both players were exhausted at the end. Shields’ showing against the mighty Perry thrilled the partisan crowd to the point where the spectators not only cheered him for his game stand, but led them to “boo” the foot-fault umpire for repeatedly calling errors on Frank.

London—U.P)—The divorce court granted a decree nisi today to Thelma Victoria Maud Colman against Ronald Colman, movie star, on the ground of adultery in Paris. Mrs. Colman testified that at first their marriage was ideally happy, but the rift came more than ten years ago. They last lived together in London in 1924. She went to California in 1925 and an agreement was concluded in April of that year under which she got a lump settlement and also a monthly payment for the next ten years. Colman did not contest the suit.

1934-07-01.text: LONDON ()—The Duke of Marlborough, the ninth holder of the historic title and former husband of Consuelo Vanderbilt, American heiress, died suddenly in London today. Formerly active in public life, the duke was under-secretary of state for the colonies from 1903 to 1905 and joint parliamentary secretary to the board of agriculture in 1917-18. He married Miss Vanderbilt, a daughter of William K. Vanderbilt, in 1895, when she was only seventeen. They were divorced in 1920.
HENDON, England, P)—Stanley B. Collett, son of the Lord Mayor of London, was killed Saturday when an airplane he was observing crashed at an aerodrome. The Prince of Wales witnessed the tragedy.

TOKYO, June 30.—(P)—The Japanese navy feared a loss of at least 13 men today in the crash of two warships and what appeared to be another tragedy, this one in the air. Four men were known dead, two were missing and four were injured after the new 1,700-ton destroyers Miyuki and Inazuma rammed together last night. Three naval airplanes had been missing for more than 30 hours with a crew totaling nine. Planes and warships have been searching for them since last night. BERLIN. (Copyright by AP.) Chancellor Adolf Hitler, ruthless and uncompromising, smashed a revolt in the Third Reich Saturday with swift retaliation that took the lives of high oppositionists to his rule. Over all Germany by night, however—with troops and machine gunners, rifle carrying police and guards on patrol—there was suspense, fear, apprehension over a civil war or at least a revolution of the nationals. For the present, Hitler held undisputed power. In a day of summary punishment for those who challenged his authority, the denouncement of the crisis of recent weeks, hastened by the disclosure of immoral orgies indulged in by leaders of his own Nazi storm troops, the chancellor “liquidated” leaders of a threefold opposition—the reactionary monarchists, the “Catholic Action” group and the left wing storm troopers who plotted his end. Captain Ernst Roehm, national chief of the Nazi storm troops, committed suicide when Hitler had him arrested as a conspirator. “Catholic action” party, was killed in his office by one of Hitler's special black-shirted guards, a Schutzstaffel member. Berlin, June 30—Chancellor Adolph Hitler today rode roughshod over foes attempting to overthrow his regime. Former Chancellor Kurt Von Schleicher, reactionary and monarchist, was killed by police when he resisted arrest as a conspirator. Captain Ernst Roehm, national commander of the Nazi storm troops and one of the most advanced radicals, was deposed from power and ejected from the Nazi party. Premier Herrmann Wilhelm Goering of Prussia announced that he was carrying out drastic police action on Hitler's personal orders against Nazi storm troop leaders attempting to force a second German revolution. His measures, he said, were extended in two directions—against absolute reactionaries and absolute radicals.

PARIS, June 30, UP)—Benjamin and Joseph Adamowicz, Brooklyn bottlers, landed at Flers d'Orne, near Alençon today, far short of their goal, which was Warsaw. Neither of the brothers was injured, although they were obliged to make a forced landing and their plane was damaged in the descent. They had left Harbor Grace, N. F., yesterday, in their Bellanca monoplane, “The City of Warsaw.”

FLERS, France, June 30 — (AP) — Fog, foul weather, and fuel shortage ended another brave aerial venture near here today, hundreds of miles short of its goal. A rough field at Saint Andre de Messel, a tiny village three miles west of Flers, provided haven for the giant tri-colored Bellanca monoplane in which Benjamin and Joseph Adamowicz, flying brothers from Brooklyn, took off boldly yesterday at Harbor Grace, N. F., in an effort to fly non-stop to Warsaw, Poland. After 22 hours and two minutes in the air they found the twin threat of dwindling gasoline and murky weather too much, and eased their big ship down just after dawn had cleared away the haze at 7:00 a.m. GMT (2:00 a.m. EST). While worried watchers searched the sky at Dublin, Paris, and Berlin, the two tired soda-pop manufacturers, who came right back to try again after a crack-up in Newfoundland spilled their hopes last year, c

1934-09-26.text: CLYDEBANK, Scotland, Sept. 26 (UP)—The Queen Mary, mightiest liner afloat, was launched today with Queen Mary bestowing her own name as she christened it before 250,000 of her madly cheering subjects. The costliest experiment in the history of maritime navigation was set afloat in the Clyde with a smoothness which was a tribute to the engineering skill of the builders. It was sent on its way with a speech by King George in which he expressed the fervent hope that it would play an important part in the revival of international commerce and promote friendship between nations, especially Great Britain and the United States. He prayed that it might carry the people of the two lands to and fro to learn about and understand one another.

NEWPORT, R. I., Sept. 25 (P) —Britain’s newest and perhaps most gallant bid for the famed America's Cup ended drably tonight far from the open seas where Tom Sopwith’s challenger Endeavour and the snow white defender Rainbow fought through six races. Sopwith, so bitter he said he never again would challenge for the battered old mug, withdrew his protest of Rainbow's 55 second victory today—fourth straight after the Endeavour had won two races. His withdrawal of the second charge of foul he has made in the series automatically removed the necessity for hearings of the race committee had ordered tonight after Harold S. Vanderbilt broke out the red flag of protest and Sopwith followed suit a few minutes later at today's starting line. There was no questioning Sopwith's bitterness as he explained his withdrawal of the protest tonight. “I protested for the same reason I did Saturday,” he said

NEWPORT, R. I, Sept. 26. (AP)— The America’s Cup, won 83 years ago from the fleetest of English schooners, remained today safely in the possession of the trustees of the New York Yacht Club, once more successfully defended against British invasion. Its retention, however, by virtue of a four-to-two victory by Harold S. Vanderbilt's yacht, Rainbow, over Thomas Octave Murdoch Sopwith's sloop, Endeavour, left bitterness, dissension and some dissatisfaction which may never be eradicated. It was almost certain that the Royal Yacht Squadron, whom Sopwith represented, will not challenge for the cup for many a year. Sopwith himself said he would never race for it again. The climax of the race series off Rhode Island coasts came four days ago when the British skipper declared he had been fouled by the defender. His protest against illegal racing received scant consideration from the committee des

CLYDEBANK, Scotland, Sept. 26. —With King George's blessing and Queen Mary's name, a mammoth new British liner, the Cunard-White Star 534, slipped into the Clyde today amid driving rain, thunder, and the cheers of a quarter of a million spectators. In his launching speech, King George made a friendly gesture to the United States. Speaking of the great new ship, although without mentioning the United States by name, he said: “This one is built to carry the people of two lands, in great numbers, to and fro, so that they may learn to understand each other. “Both are faced with similar problems, and they prosper and suffer together. May she, in her career, bear many thousands of each race to visit each other as students and return as friends.” The choice of the name of a living queen for a christening was most unusual. The completed vessel will cost an estimated $30,100,000. She was started

LONDON, Sept. 24.-- (U.P) — The most colossal ship the world has ever seen, a Cunarder 1018 feet long, costing more than $40,000,000, will be launched on the River Clyde tomorrow. Queen Mary will christen the vessel, the name of which has been kept a secret. The tonnage will be about 73,000. Financial circles regard the ship frankly as a great gamble and do not believe it possibly can make money, because of its initial cost and the cost of operating it.

NEWPORT, R. I., Sept. 25. (AP)—Victory in defense of the America’s Cup automatically went to the Rainbow tonight when T. O. M. Sopwith’s British Challenger withdrew its protest of the American sloop’s fourth victory today. Thus the victory is official tonight, three hours after the finish of the deciding race, when the Englishman announced his decision. America’s margin of victory in the 15th series for the historic trophy was four races to two. Both Sopwith and Vanderbilt hoisted their red protest flags shortly after the start of the sixth race this afternoon, won by Rainbow by a margin of only 55 seconds. Vanderbilt’s protest automatically disappears inasmuch as he won the race anyway.

SEYMOUR, Sept. 26,—(P)— Miss Willie Mae Couch, 18, of Portales, N. M., today identified Miss Ruby Britain, 40, as the assailant of Horace Nichols at Miss Britain's trial on a murder charge. She testified she had not known the defendant before the shooting, but she identified her as Miss Britain sat in the courtroom. Miss Couch testified that Nichols was shot by a woman on a side road as he sat in his automobile with her and that neither he nor his assailant said a word. The witness started her testimony with the statement that she had known Nichols, a businessman here, for about a year and that on the night of August 15 she went for a ride with another man. She said she later entered Nichols’ automobile and they drank beer at a filling station. Then they went to a side road and parked, listening to

MOSCOW, Sept. 25 (Ten contestants for the Gordon Bennett Cup, coveted prize of free balloonists, were reported down today, six of them in Russia. Others of the 16 balloons which started from Warsaw Sunday possibly were drifting eastward over Central Russia. The American Navy balloon and that of the Buffalo Courier Express, only entries from the United States, were safely down on Soviet territory near the Estonian boundary.

1934-08-11.text: Halifax, Aug. 10—Archbishop C. I. Worrell, primate of the Church of England in Canada, died in a hospital tonight. He had been ill for three weeks. Archbishop Worrell was elected primate of all Canada by the house of bishops of the general synod of the Church of England in Canada on Sept. 23, 1931. He succeeded Rev. S. F. Matheson of Winnipeg, who retired a year previous. He became a bishop of Nova Scotia in 1904 after 23 years of service in the church. He held the post of archbishop of Nova Scotia since 1915.

| LONDON, Aug. 11—(UP)—The Daily Herald said today that the Princess Youssoupoff had received 150,000 pounds sterling (approximately $762,000) from Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, in payment of all claims for libel. The princess, who claimed her reputation was damaged by the picturization of a woman of the Czar’s court, in the film “Rasputin and the Empress,” won her damage suit against the producers in the British courts. Suits were threatened throughout the world. The film company announced yesterday they had been settled for an undisclosed amount.

VIENNA, Aug. 11 (AP).-—Prince Ernst von Starhemberg, vice chancellor of Austria, left by airplane today for Rome where it was generally believed he would discuss the question of his country’s independence with Premier Mussolini. Von Starhemberg’s announced purpose was to visit Austrian youths now on vacation near Rome as guests of the Italian government. The possibility of foreign financial assistance to Austria was another subject that the vice chancellor may talk over with Il Duce, who is determined that Nazis shall not seize control in Vienna.

MOSCOW. (4). Wholesale murder and sabotage along the right-of-way of the Chinese eastern railway—subject of a long-standing quarrel between Soviet Russia and Japan—was charged in the report of the Russian director of the line. He declared a reign of terror centering in the region divided by the railroad had resulted so far this year in the death of 46 persons, including nine officials of the road, and the wounding of 102. The newspaper Pravda, organ of the Communist Party, pointedly warned Japan that the Soviet government could not be bullied into sacrificing the railway either by the terrorism of "bandits" or threats of the Japanese press.

Moscow, Aug. 11.—(P)—A reign of terror on the eastern line of the Chinese Eastern railway, attributed by the Soviet press to Japanese and Manchurian efforts to force Soviet Russia to sell the railroad line cheaply, was described today in a report by Russian Manager Rudi of the railway. Rudi’s report, made to the joint Manchukuo-Soviet board of directors, stated that conditions had grown alarmingly worse between June 17 and August 6, enumerating 12 train wrecks, 43 bandit raids, two murders, 24 railway employees wounded, 14 robberies, 28 cases of damage to the road bed, two fires, nine cases of sabotage to telegraph and telephone lines. He said the worst train wreck occurred July 28 when many members of the train crew were victims. Rudi said that, in spite of the armored trains and railway guards at its disposal, the railway board was unable to check the bandit and outlawry and that, desp

BERLIN, Aug. 10. (AP) — Definite shortage of feed grains in Germany was reported today by foreign agricultural observers returning here from a tour of the provinces. This shortage and the consequent fear that farmers would use bread grains to feed livestock, in the opinion of these observers, prompted the new system of compulsory delivery of cereals introduced by the Nazi government. The compulsory delivery is closely patterned after the Russian methods, requiring farmers to deliver by specified dates at the beginning of the new crop year fixed percentages of the cereals delivered in the old crop year. Rumors already are current here, however, that the farmers are beginning to balk at this coercion, delivering only cheaper qualities of bread grains for the time being. Since German farmers are accustomed to feed a certain amount of rye to livestock, they can make ready use of bread grains

ROME, Aug. 11—(AP)— Prince Ernst Von Starhemberg, vice chancellor of Austria, arrived here today from Vienna. It was generally believed his trip was made in order that he might confer with Premier Mussolini on Austrian security, although this explanation was denied in official quarters. The official explanation is that the purpose of the trip was to visit the camp of several hundred Austrian youths on vacation at Ostia as guests of the Italian government. Pulvio Suvich, under secretary of foreign affairs, planned a dinner tonight in honor of the prince.

Rome, Aug. 10 (2) — Paul Block, the publisher, asked Premier Mussolini today if he did not think the world would applaud if il Duce gave Italy a free press. “But we have a free press,” was the reply of the Premier, who smiled broadly. Mr. Block's interrogation came at the end of a 30-minute talk at the Venezia Palace. “I assure you we now have a free press,” Mussolini said in reply to Mr. Block's question. “But if a newspaperman writes what we know would hurt our people and our government we call his attention to it.”

1934-07-03.text: LONDON, July 3—(UP)—Charges by the Hitler government that the late Kurt Von Schleicher and his fellow conspirators were dealing with an unnamed foreign power received substantiation today from the diplomatic representative of an important European power. “On the basis of sensational information now available,” he said, “the Schleicher conspiracy, designed to overthrow Hitler, had wide ramifications and indications point to connections in France.” The official German version of the plot failed to name the nation alleged to have been involved, although the entire account was regarded as a thinly veiled reference to France. The report was ridiculed abroad and the French government, after demanding that Hitler name the power, issued a categorical denial of any association with the alleged conspirators. LONDON, July 3 (#) — Stanley Baldwin, Lord President of the Council, told the House of Commons today international political conditions are so serious it is imperative for the 1935 naval conference to “achieve some end.” Baldwin spoke as acting Prime Minister in the absence of Ramsay MacDonald, and as acting head of the British naval delegation. He evaded all questions from the opposition regarding Great Britain's maximum naval demands as presented recently to the American delegation. It was the second time since naval conversations began here that Baldwin has declined to reveal British plans, but he did emphasize the efforts of the cabinet to obtain a new international naval agreement. “World conditions,” he said, “in many ways are more difficult than at the time of the London conference, and therefore it is more than ever necessary to survey the entire ground before the conference. “De

London, July 3. (AP)—Urging English speaking peoples all over the world to unite in a fight against compulsion in government, Nicholas Murray Butler, president of Columbia University, New York, today addressed a Pilgrims banquet here. Butler bitterly attacked both fascism and communism. “If liberty is crushed by compulsion in the generation which lies ahead of us,” he said. “it can only be because the English speaking peoples have failed in their great task.”

of Detective Albert Bush, was today denied a new trial and sentenced to be electrocuted Oct. 15, LONDON, July 3—(UP)—The former crown prince of Germany arrived at Doorn, Holland, by airplane this afternoon to see his father, the ex-kaiser, according to an Exchange Telegram dispatch from Amsterdam.

THE HAGUE, Netherlands, July 3 (?)—Henry prince consort of the Netherlands, died suddenly this afternoon of heart disease, the end coming before Queen Wilhelmina could reach his side. While the 58-year-old husband of the queen had been ill for several days, he had shown improvement until shortly before his death at 3 p.m. The prince consort was stricken in his office at Red Cross headquarters June 28, and the queen hurried home from Switzerland where she was on a holiday. She was at another palace today when word came that her husband's condition had suddenly taken a turn for the worse. She hurried to the royal palace, but arrived too late to see the prince consort alive.

By The Associated Press, Today's developments in Ger- many: Chancellor Hitler in a special order put an end to extreme measures for the control of the “second revolution,” announcing that effective July 1 all offenders against the party would be dealt with by the regular court. The eyes of the Nation were focussed on Berlin where a cabinet meeting was in session, slated to accept the resignation of Vice Chancellor Franz von Papen and to replace him with Hermann Wilhelm Goering, the Prussian Premier. From Amsterdam a British news agency reported the former Crown Prince had been expelled from Germany and had arrived by plane at Doorn. Munich was stirred by strong rumors of the death of the Bavarian premier, Gustav von Kahr, who turned against Hitler after plotting with him in his 1923 “beer putsch.” It was said he was shot Saturday.
