BERLIN, July 16. —(P)— Adolf Hitler, following a defense of his execution of Nazi rebels, turned today to problems of the church, a source of much unrest. The chancellor was to confer with Reichsbishop Ludwig Mueller, in charge of the government program for a unified German Protestant Church which has aroused the ire of thousands of clergymen and members of their congregation. There have been repeated reports that Dr. Mueller would resign, after intense opposition to him on the grounds the state was attempting to run the church. He suspended many pastors. After the conference Hitler may go on a vacation. This may include a visit to Bayreuth for the W: music festival and to see Winifred Wagner, the composer's daughter-in-law and a close friend of the chancellor.

VIENNA, July 15—(4#)—Four persons were killed in turbulent political disorders in Austria as several battles flared up and dynamiters continued a widespread destruction of property. Three were killed in a spirited clash between gendarmes and the outlawed Republican Guardists who were attempting to hold a meeting in the picturesque Vienna woods near Kaltenleutgeben. Nearly a thousand Socialists participated in the woodland gathering. It was a secret session, but was discovered by two Fascist volunteers. The Fascists were overpowered, but the disturbance attracted attention and a company of gendarmes rushed to the forest. A menacing crowd quickly surrounded the officers. Fearing capture, the gendarmes opened fire. Three Socialists fell mortally wounded. Among those seriously injured was a Fascist sympathizer. As the shooting started the crowd dispersed, its members seeking shelter in the w

SHANGHAI, July 16 (4)— An American missionary and a Swedish explorer, reportedly seized by brigands, are safe again. Dispatches from Hankow said the Rev. Howard Smith, formerly of Washington, Pa., had been released by his captors after two months of captive. Dr. Sven Hedin, noted explorer, notified associates he was safe in Turkestan, Details of Smith’s release were lacking but he was reported to be in good health. A ransom of $35,000 had been demanded for him.

(By the Associated Press) Berlin, July 15.—Germany turned from considering the after-effects of Chancellor Hitler's party cleansing today to another nationwide Nazi “tag day.” This was Rose Day, in contrast to two weeks ago when armed guards held sway in Berlin. The Sunday before that, grey-uniformed youths had solicited funds on the streets for “air day.” Today, the rose—mostly blood red—was the center of attraction in German life. Girls and buxom young women—some 1,200,000 of them—were called from the sphere of activity the Nazis have set for them, kitchen and nursery, to sell the roses. There were 20,000,000 blossoms for distribution at 20 pfennings (about 6 cents) each. Each rose had a ribbon bearing the legend “Fuer mutter und kind” (For mother and child). The money raised is to be spent to send mothers and children on trips for health and recreation, under the scheme of the Nazi bu

1934-08-24.text: NEW YORK, August 24 ()—Word came from London today that a Kansas farmer's daughter -- rosy-cheeked, dimpled Gene Dennis—is figuratively knocking the Britishers for a bally loop. Gene has been in London since early spring and is known all over England as the American “girl psychic.” She has appeared at three London theaters, has given “readings” at the afternoon teas of a big London hotel, has been interviewed on coming events by most of the large newspapers of England and, in addition, has written a weekly article for the London Sunday Dispatch at a pay rate of $250 an article. An Associated Press dispatch from London today attributed her present fame to her sensational prediction that Windsor Lad would win the derby—which he did. Miss Dennis named Windsor Lad on a London stage when the horse was a rank outsider, five weeks before the race. She repeated the prediction several times, in t

London, Aug. 23. (AP)—The international wheat conference adjourned today until November after approving a recommendation of the governments concerned that new systems for quarterly export quotas be adopted this year. The conference failed to reach an agreement on the amount of quotas for each country which are to be decided at the next meeting if the governments have approved the plans.

- PHOENIX, Ariz., Aug. 24.—(P) —A conference between Governor B. B. Moeur and the British consul in Los Angeles was called here today to discuss the status of Hindu farmers in the Salt River valley where a farmers’ group has announced an ouster drive against alien agriculturists, particularly Japanese. Less than 24 Hindus are in the valley where an estimated 1,000 Japanese reside and the consul, Wentworth Gurney, said he wished to discuss the Hindus' status as they are British subjects. Fear of possible violence in the ouster campaign was met by statements from the farmer group that no outbreaks were contemplated in the attempts to make alien farmers leave the valley. The farmers said their only interest was in seeing enforced the alien land law, which prohibits aliens leasing or owning agricultural land.

MESSINA, Sicily, Aug. 24— (UP)—Sicily was shaken by a strong earth shock today, followed by two milder tremors, while Mt. Stromboli poured forth threatening clouds of smoke. The volcano continued belching spasmodic streams of lava, but the molten waste streamed towards the sea along the northern slopes, which are neither inhabited nor cultivated. No losses have yet been reported. Smoke clouds at the summit of the volcano are so dense that her fires are hidden, although at night an intense glare is visible.

Berlin, Aug. 23.—()—The revival of pagan faith in Germany was laid today at the door of Hitlerism. Said P. Oriowsky, a paganist leader, at a convention of the pagan group: “The Nazi revolution created the prerequisite for a revolution of lofty values known as religion. Acknowledgement of the sacredness of the German race and blood has alone made possible an objective attitude toward Christianity.” Striking parallel utterances by Reichbishop Mueller tend to confirm advances made by the pagan faith movement. The Reichbishop, who is charged with unification of the German Protestant church, praised the Nazi revolution for having “opened new prospects for eternal folk values, above all for ties of soil and blood.”

By The Associated Press Moscow, Aug. 24—Years of differences between Russia and Japan over the Chinese railway, key to a great slice of the Orient, come close to a showdown today. Eyes of the Soviet and embassies here intently following the incident were on Tokyo to which Moscow addressed a blunt protest for the arrest of scores of its citizens along the railway. A note given Japan by the Soviet ambassador said "similarly and of late repeated demonstrations of the Japanese war ministry paralleled with action in Manchuria testify to the aggravation of the aggressive intentions of some official Japanese circles." Russia demanded steps toward the release of 88 Soviet officials and employees of the Chinese Eastern railway in the note presented at Harbin.

| MOSCOW, Aug. 24.-(UP)—Soviet Russia holds Japan responsible for a month-long series of incidents in the Chinese Eastern Railway zone of Manchukuo. It was revealed today with publication of a sharp protest note sent to Tokyo. The note protested the arrests, over a period of many weeks, of 88 Russian employees of the railway, of which Russia owns a half share. Diplomatically it was of importance because it ignored the repeated Japanese assertion that Manchukuo, the state it made out of Chinese Manchuria, is solely qualified to deal with incidents in its territory.

MOSCOW, Aug. 23—(AP)—The Soviet government has protested directly to the Japanese government arrests of Soviet citizens along the Chinese Eastern Railway in Manchukuo, it was learned tonight. The protests were made yesterday. The Soviet protest coming hard on the heels of an earlier communication addressed to the Manchukuo government, was delivered by Ambassador Yureney to the Tokyo government, it was learned.

1934-06-14.text: WASHINGTON, June 13—(CP)— President Roosevelt is willing to consider payments in goods by European war debtors only on a partial basis. This was made known at the President’s semi-weekly press conference in comment on the United States note to Great Britain yesterday pertaining to the payments due next Friday. The suggestion for this manner of payments made in the note was declared not to be an offer for full payment on such a basis. Reaction abroad was divided, with indications of disfavor in London and possibly favor in Paris. Mr. Roosevelt emphasized that the American note was simply a reply to the British default, pointing out a way of payment rather than making an offer. In other words, the United States said it was willing to discuss the war debts if asked by Great Britain and is willing to consider ways of avoiding obstacles raised by the British of making full payments in cash.

LONDON, June 14—Great Britain will pay nothing on the war debts installment due the United States tomorrow, it was stated officially today. The cabinet has not yet written its reply to Washington but it was announced that Secretary of State Hull’s note suggesting payments in kind would not change Britain’s original decision to default. Because of the pressure of other matters, including the question of the policy toward India and the Fascist-Communist situation, the cabinet has not yet had time to consider the recent American debt note fully. A reply may not be written before early next week, with the possibility existing that an official reply may not be sent, a point on which the cabinet is undecided since the Washington note was in reply to one from Great Britain. No instructions have been sent as yet to Sir Ronald Lindsay, ambassador to Washington, but he may be asked to inquire exac

LONDON, June 14.— (UP) — Sophie Tucker, the famous American "blues" singer, was the heroine of a street accident today when she risked her life to save a child from under the wheels of an automobile. As the car bore down on the child, another woman who saw the accident screamed, and Miss Tucker dashed to the rescue and shoved the child out of danger. In leaping aside herself, Miss Tucker's leg was slightly injured.

- Plymouth, England—(/)—Sir Hubert Wilkins, arriving today from New York, announced he would make a submarine exploration trip in 1935 to Spitzbergen and the Bering Straits. He will be accompanied by Lady Wilkins. Sir Hubert said 1,500 miles of the trip would be made under Arctic ice. An order for a submarine has not yet been placed.

| WHIPSNADE, England, June 14. —The story of how Stanley Stenson, who, a few years ago was one of London's rare gun-toting bandits, lost his life in a lion’s den as the result of a one-shilling bet was unfolded at a coroner’s inquest. The inquest, held within hearing of the roars and cries of animals in the open air zoo which was the scene of the tragedy last Thursday, resulted in a verdict of death by “misadventure” at the claws of the lions. Stenson died, the jury held, from the mauling and tearing of two lions while rescuers tried to pull him away from the bars of their pit, rather than from a 16-foot fall into the den. Horace Myhill testified. Stenson offered to bet a shilling (about 25 cents) that he could retrieve a hat from the open air pit, and that Myhill then threw in his hat. Then, he said, Stenson went to the top of the inside railing around the pit and the lions seized him.

Subsequently, the suggestion to Great Britain that her debts might be paid “in kind” fell upon hard soil, but dispatches Wednesday from Rome and Paris indicated the suggestion might be received there more favorably. Hope of collecting anything on next Friday's installments dwindled in Washington with receipt of notes from the French, Belgian and Czechoslovakian governments explaining they cannot pay. Great Britain has made no official statement concerning the possibility of paying in goods, but the general view in political circles was that the proposal will not be found acceptable. In France, however, where a similar offer is expected, it was pointed out that some such plan would meet the objection to depleting the French gold supply, and it was anticipated that France might pay partially in wine and potash. In Rome, it was indicated the Italian attitude, strictly against payments, may

LONDON, June 13 (4)—The suggestion from Washington that war debts might be paid in goods instead of gold was given a cool reception in Great Britain today, and while France and Italy appeared somewhat interested, there was no evidence that immediate action will be taken. Downing Street maintained the usual secrecy after a cabinet meeting which lasted for an hour and a half, but the general view in political circles was that the proposal of Secretary of State Hull will not be found acceptable.

Unless their plans change, Hitler and Mussolini will meet today for a talk, each flying to meet the other near Venice, Hitler from Berlin, Mussolini from Rome. It will be as interesting a meeting as any that has happened since Francis the First of France went to meet Henry the Eighth of England on the “field of the Cloth of Gold,” on the French side of the channel, and more important than that meeting. Henry and Francis are said to have indulged in wrestling bouts. Hitler and Mussolini will do the same, only mental, not physical wrestling. The French and the English governments would like to know exactly what the two dictators, the original and the copy, say to each other. The meeting may be historical and in its results as important as the meeting between Attila and the Pope, Leo the First, nearly fifteen hundred years ago, when the Pope persuaded the Asiatic Barbarian to cross the Alps

1934-02-27.text: Washington, D. C., Feb. 26.—(7)— Rear Admiral Richard E. Byrd and “Little America” may again be the chilly subject of an exchange of notes between Great Britain and the United States. Great Britain was reported today in unofficial but usually reliable quarters to be thinking of “reminding” the United States again that King George has claimed three large sectors around the South Pole, including the ice and snow of “Little America.” Indications were that Great Britain would assert British claims “by right of discovery” should Byrd “discover” and lay American claims to any land which England says its flag is on. On November 17, 1928, the British government addressed a note to the State Department in which it asserted that in addition to the Ross dependency and the Falkland Island dependencies there were “certain areas in the Antarctic to which British title already exists.” The areas were l

London, Feb. 27 (#) —A British admiralty report cites the United States as leading world powers today in the number of cruisers planned or being built. The figures, as given in the official report, are: United States, 11 cruisers under construction, six projected; British Commonwealth, seven building, three definitely planned; France and Italy, six each under construction; Japan, two building and two projected. Far out in front in the number of completed cruisers, the British Commonwealth was revealed as having fifty—the maximum accepted under the London naval treaty. Compared with this number, the United States was listed as having 21, Japan 31, Italy 24, France 15, Russia six and Germany eight.

Rome, Feb. 26 (4?)—Premier Benito Mussolini and Captain Anthony Eden, special British envoy, agreed today on the possibility of finding a basis for a general agreement on disarmament, an official communique announced. The communique, issued tonight after a long conference, said: "The head of this government received the British Lord Privy Seal, Captain Eden, at Venezia Palace this afternoon. "Captain Eden informed him (Mussolini) of conversations he (Eden) had had at Paris and Berlin. This information enables them to examine afresh the British and Italian memoranda. "They find themselves in accord as to the object to be reached, particularly as to the possibility of finding a basis for a general agreement." Premier Mussolini and Captain Eden discussed all phases of the European disarmament problem during their long conference. It was understood that several large points of difference sti

WASHINGTON, Feb. 27.—(AP)— Opposition to the Fletcher-Rayburn stock market regulation bill was expressed today by Charles A. Collins, president of the Boston Exchange, who contended it would “work a hardship on the New England public as a whole and on the small houses serving New England. Before the House interstate commerce committee, he registered “an emphatic and strong objection against the provision of the legislation “which makes it unlawful for a concern to be both a dealer and a broker.” Michael J. O’Brien, president of the Chicago Stock Exchange, warned against too strict Federal regulation of the exchanges.

London, Feb. 27. (UP) — Hunger marchers forcing their way into the one-mile prohibited zone surrounding the House of Parliament today sent a deputation into the Prime Minister’s residence to demand that Ramsey MacDonald, Labor Premier, hear their complaints. Several hundred marchers wearing red scarves, many hatless, marched into Downing Street where MacDonald has his official residence and his offices. MacDonald’s private secretary received the invading deputation. He advised them that MacDonald “unfortunately” was absent attending the British Industries Fair. “His absence is a grave insult,” the fiery leader of the marchers said. “Please ask him to see us when he returns.”

| VIENNA, Feb. 26 (AP)—Troops of the Fascist heimwehr were marching to all sections of Austria today—and the increase of rumors was major. The most sensational of these rumors was that they were preparing to meet Archduke Otto, claimant to the Austrian throne, at the Swiss border and escort him triumphantly to Vienna. Another, equally unsubstantiated, said 40,000 members of the heimwehr were concentrating along the Austro-German border. Both the foreign office and heimwehr headquarters vigorously and indignantly denied these tales. The foreign office stated there was no concentration of armed men on either side of the Austro-German border. A government spokesman said all these troop movements of the heimwehr were really propaganda marches. The Socialists have been crushed, he explained, and now the heimwehr is following up its victory by parading its force in all provinces.

VIENNA (U.P.) (By Telephone to Berlin)—Heavy troop movements along both sides of the Czechoslovakian frontier coincided Tuesday with sudden imposition of a censorship of all messages. The censorship, applied in the early hours of this morning, resulted in elimination from dispatches of any reference either to the troop movements or to reports that Archduke Otto of Hungary or some other Hapsburg might be made king of Austria. Governments of Czechoslovakia, Roumania and Jugoslavia have announced that they would regard any such restoration of the Hapsburgs as a cause for war. Travelers from Czechoslovakia reported great military activity along the Czechoslovakian side of the border, and 2,000 heavily armed members of the Schutzbund, the auxiliary mobile police force, were sent to the Austrian side, in addition to troops. These men were part of the troops sent during the weekend to the Germa

Moscow — () — Facing death from drowning or exposure, 545 fishermen and 330 horses were drifting helplessly on two separate ice floes in the Caspian Sea today while an airplane from Moscow sped to their assistance. A sudden rise in temperature yesterday caused the ice to break up, catching 400 men and 190 horses in the vicinity of Dolgiy Island and 145 men and 140 horses near Kulali Island on ice packs which rapidly were swept out to the open sea. Their plight was described as extremely perilous because of a lack of food supplies and the fact that the ice upon which they were marooned was soft. An airplane which left Moscow with food and medicines yesterday was due in Astrakhan, a city at the mouth of the Volga River on the Caspian Sea. From that point it was planned to conduct rescue operations. Meanwhile, a government rescue commission was continuing efforts to find a way of saving 101

1934-03-13.text: New York (A) — Refusing to discuss London reports that she and Doug Fairbanks had patched up difficulties, Mary Pickford announced today that she expected to return to Hollywood and pictures within a week or 10 days. Copyright 1934, Associated Press | London Douglas Fairbanks, Sr., and his wife, Mary Pickford, have practically patched up all their differences and are near a reconciliation, the Associated Press learned from indisputable sources today. Fairbanks and Miss Pickford have talked over transatlantic telephone during the last few days with the result that their reunion on the old basis of married life is practically assured. It is just a matter of time now, the Associated Press informant said, but reconciliation will require several months.

(Dy £4 Mave LI oo) London, Mar, 13.—Laura La Plante motion picture actress, said today she is suing her husband, William Seiter film director, for a divorce and that she has filed the suit in Riga, Latvia. At the film studio here where she is being starred in an English picture, Miss La Plante said: “The proceedings have been taken on the ground of incompatibility. There is no other reason and we still are very good friends.” She said her husband was sending a waiver from Hollywood and on its receipt she would sign it, after which she supposes the divorce will be granted under the law of Latvia. “I'm going to stay in England for a while,” she said, “I will make another picture after the present one, and then probably I will appear in a stage show in the provinces.”

LONDON, March 13 (UP) —The Daily Herald, organ of the labor party, reported today that former Kaiser Wilhelm and members of his family would confer at Doorn this week on plans for his own funeral. It was said the family would discuss Wilhelm’s failing health, his funeral and plans for the family’s future after his death. Negotiations were progressing, the correspondent asserted, between German Nazis and representatives of Wilhelm for permission for him to be buried in Germany.

(Copyright, 1934, by United Press.) NEW YORK, March 13 (U.P) — Official odds against a European war within the next 12 months are 100 to 7. Yet odds against such a war within two years are 100 to 40. Lloyds of England will take no bets at any price that there will not be a war within five years. A manufacturer or a commercial firm whose business would be ruined by a European war can take out insurance with Lloyds’ underwriters today by paying a premium of seven guineas for every 100 guineas on the face of the policy. If he wants to extend the period for two years, it will cost him 40 guineas. He can, however, obtain a reduction on the premium by naming in the policy those nations which will become involved in hostilities. War fears, expressed in such high rates for insurance, have been stimulated by reports of tremendous armament activity. Not since the fiery forges of the great Krupp ca

European politics entered a new phase today. France prepared a note rejecting a despairing last attempt by Great Britain to reach agreement on the present basis. Fearing both a naval race and the collapse of land disarmament negotiations, Britain was reported reliably to be considering inviting European powers to an air power conference, hoping to obtain some measure of agreement by limiting the scope of its hopes. Premier Benito Mussolini started a new lead of practical diplomacy, of which an air conference would be a part, by inviting to Rome the chancellor of Austria and the premier of Hungary to discuss the future of central Europe without the cumbersome formality of a full dress conference of powers. Before he left Vienna for Rome, Austrian Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss made his most significant appointment in many months when he named Prince Schoenburg-Hartenstein, Fascist-Monarchi

The British conclude, sadly, that war must come, and, wisely, decide to be ready. Intensified warship building begins, with seventeen major warships, including three powerful submarines, in the program. Britons hate submarines, because Britain has so many ships afloat, and submarines sink floating ships, but if others have them, Britain must have them. It will interest our financial wizards, printing billions in bonds, paying as many billions in interest, to learn that Britons feel able to build because their budget shows a surplus of more than $125,000,000 this year. No surplus in our blessed country, thanks to sending to friends in Europe billions that will not return. Next in interest to British warship building comes the birth of a child in London with a ‘tail’ two inches long. This should have happened while William Jennings Bryan and Clarence Darrow were arguing evolution in Tennes

LONDON, March 13—The familiar old controversy over the value of big battleships beats again today about the ears of Great Britain’s leaders. Sir Bolton Eyres-Monsell, first lord of the admiralty, reawakened the argument through his advocacy of the battleship in presenting the 1934 naval estimates to the House of Commons. Although he carried the support of the majority in Commons last night, strong criticism of his stand followed. Only 35 votes were recorded against the estimates as adoption followed debate during which Sir Bolton assured his hearers that the new program contemplates building up to treaty limits. As the naval estimates call for expenditure of 56,550,000 pounds (now about $282,750,000)—an increase of about $15,000,000 over last year. Besides winning approval for his contention in regard to battleships, Sir Bolton also was given hearty support in his stand for the interdepe

(Copyright, 1934, Associated Press) LONDON, March 12—Lady Ash- ley, whose husband named Douglas Fairbanks, Sr., as co-respondent in a recent divorce action, when told tonight a reconciliation between the actor and Mary Pickford was virtually assured, said she knew he was going to return to the United States, but ‘I do not expect that will be for some time.’ “I know he is going back for the opening of his picture, which he is just starting to make here,” she said when told by the Associated Press as she reached her Mayfair flat that Hollywood's erstwhile “real couple” was about to get together again. “As for my own plans, they are rather indefinite for the moment.” Lady Ashley, the former Sylvia Hawkes, a London actress, refused to discuss reports that she and Doug, in whose company she was seen frequently in recent months, were ever considering marriage. That the acrobatic Fairbanks and

1934-08-22.text: LONDON, Aug. 21 (*) —The International wheat conference which failed to achieve its two principal goals — agreements for quotas for the present crop year and additional acreage reduction —prepared tonight to wind up its work tomorrow by giving final approval to a series of general proposals for submission to the 21 governments adhering to the 1934 wheat pact. Through failure to reach agreements on quotas for the year which began August 1, 1934, the conference established the first “open season” in wheat shipping since August, 1933, leaving exporting unrestricted at least until November. The acreage reductions aimed at but not obtained would have affected Argentina and some European countries. The general proposals which will go to the governments are intended mainly to keep alive for another year the advisory commission established here last year. Settlement Expected The refusal of Argen

Reykjavik, Iceland, Aug. 22 ()—John Grierson, British aviator forced down in a fjord while attempting to cross the North Atlantic in a light plane, was found today. He was uninjured and he planned to take off again later in the day for Angmagsalik, Greenland. Grierson took off from here yesterday and soon afterward broadcast a radio message asking for help. Numerous vessels joined in the search for the aviator.

Toronto, Ont., Aug. 21.—The actual kidnappers of John S. Labatt, wealthy London, Ont., brewer, are known to police, it was stated this afternoon in a story received by the Toronto Star from its London correspondent. The question now facing police, the story added, is to apprehend the gang involved in the Canadian “snatch.”

Toronto, Aug. 18.—()—While pressing their investigation of Canada's first kidnapping, Ontario officers took steps today to create a province-wide system designed to prevent the spread of abduction for ransom. Information gained in dealing with the case of John S. Labatt, London, Ont., brewery president, who was held by kidnappers for nearly three days, will form the basis of a discussion by police officers who will meet with Attorney General A. W. Roebuck. The question of whether ransom was paid remained undetermined. Talk of murder came after the kidnappers were alarmed by reports they received, apparently regarding police activity, this source said, but later new reports lessened their fright and nothing more was said on the subject.

Reykjavik, Iceland, Aug. 22. John Grierson, British flier en route to Canada, was found by searchers on an isolated fjord in Iceland today, and announced he would leave for Angmagsalik, Greenland, late today.

GENEVA, Aug. 21—(4)—Rabbi Stephen S. Wise of New York in a statement today declared before the third world Jewish conference that the boycott against Germany by Jews will not be abandoned until Adolf Hitler’s regime cancels every law or practice “violating human freedom, political equality, and the ideals of civilization.” BERLIN, Aug. 21—(P)—Nazi propaganda guns fired an anti-Christianity barrage today which caused grave apprehension in Roman Catholic and some Protestant circles. Gravely apprehensive leaders said developments in the troubled church situation indicated fresh tension, despite Chancellor Hitler's acknowledgment of “positive Christianity” in a recent declaration at Hamburg. Heading the developments was an appeal for abolition of Christianity, apparently inspired by Hitler youth leaders. Paul Joseph Goebbels, minister of propaganda added to the fears with a veiled threat aga

HARBIN, Manchuria, Aug. 21--I see by the papers that Huey Long decided in favor of Paraguay and got a fort named after him down there. I guess these folks heard about a big island near New York named for Long where there was a battle not long ago. If Huey will intervene over here right quick I think I can get a country and two miles of railroad named after him. Yours.

BUDAPEST, Aug. 21.—(/)—Mrs. Antal Krammer, a peasant woman living near Budapest, today was awarded the government's first prize for having more children than any other mother in Hungary. Mrs. Krammer, who is only 48 years old, now has 21 children. She was married at 16. Gold medals were awarded 6,000 other Hungarian mothers, who, combined, have a total of 80,000 children—an average of 13 1-3 children each. For her championship, Mrs. Krammer received a state prize of 100 pengoes in cash—which is approximately $21, or $1 for each child. In addition, the city of Budapest conferred a gold medal upon her and various associations and private individuals gave her numerous presents.

1934-04-26.text: Boston —(#)—The Boston Globe says that a large quantity of the money which Colonel Charles A. Lindbergh paid to the kidnappers of his 16-month-old child who later was found dead, has been recovered in New England. The amount recovered totals more than half the $50,000 paid and was found in blocks of $4,000 and $5,000, the Globe says.

President Roosevelt's move to expand the navy was linked today with Japan's “hands off China” policy. Although officials gave no basis whatsoever for the connection, administration aides were informed that in London and other world capitals the two developments were mentioned in the same breath. The state department, however, held to the strict silence it has maintained since the Japanese semi-official pronunciamento was issued nine days ago. In this deliberate silence, the best informed observers found intimation that the United States plans no immediate diplomatic move in Far Eastern affairs. In accordance with the plan to increase the navy to full (Continued on Page Fifteen)

BPS SSSAS VAIN SSS London, April 26.—Billingsgate, London's famous fish market which bows to none in age, smell or language, may be enlarged. A scheme is being considered by the city for a new building and a 50-foot quay to cost $5,000,000.

Tokyo, April 26. (AP)—American concern over Japan's declared intention to oppose Occidental dealings with China which from Japan's own viewpoint "endanger the peace of eastern Asia," found official expression today. The United States' attitude was carried to Foreign Minister Koki Hirota by the American ambassador, Joseph C. Grew. Although the ambassador, according to the foreign office version of the interview, delivered no note and made no representations, merely requesting an authoritative version of Japan's restatement of policy toward China, the visit profoundly impressed Japanese officialdom. Tokyo government leaders were impressed particularly because Grew's visit indicated Washington intends a further thorough study of the declaration, made public April 17, before deciding on its course. Additional significance was attached to the call in high circles here because it followed clos

By The Associated Press Madrid, April 26—President Zamora, fighting to avert civil war, will resign today, it was indicated, if such a step is deemed necessary in the governmental crisis gripping Spain. With a state of alarm in effect throughout the nation, threats of strikes and riots flared on many sides.

Buxar, India, April 26—(7)—A rock smashed the windows of a car in which Mahatma Gandhi was riding today but he escaped uninjured from a clash with persons opposing his campaign to assist India’s untouchables. It was the first time the mahatma ever had been made the object of a physical attack. Three nationalist congress volunteers accompanying Gandhi were injured in the attack, said to have been made by orthodox Hindus who bitterly opposed the Indian leader's long campaign to succor the oppressed classes. Gandhi was reported today to be threatening to undertake another period of severe penance because of growing opposition to his movement for the untouchables.

Buxar, India, April 26 (UP)—Caste Hindus savagely stoned a motor car in which Mahatma M. K. Gandhi was driving today and then demolished it. Gandhi escaped uninjured, though the other three occupants were hurt. Gandhi threatened to do penance—probably a three week hunger strike—because of the attack. The attack was the first ever made on Gandhi. Those with him were members of the Indian nationalist congress. Gandhi said he thought he would undergo penance, if not for the attack because of his failure to break down the opposition to his demands that the stigma be removed from the untouchables, scorned by caste members; he took the attack as meaning that caste members were unmoved by his pleas.

HAVRE, France, April 26. (UP)— Information of importance regarding the Lindbergh kidnapping ransom may be obtained from Stewart Donnelly, international confidence man, it was intimated today as he sailed under arrest in the liner Washington for New York. Donnelly was handed over by French police aboard the Washington just as it was ready to leave. Detectives Martin Hayes and Frank Ralph took custody of him in behalf of New York police department and at once placed him in the ship's brig where he will remain until he reaches port. It was learned that Herman Leffert of the American secret service talked with Hayes and Ralph before he sailed on the Ile de France yesterday for New York and said afterward: "We believe Donnelly can enlighten us on the Lindbergh ransom

1934-08-10.text: London.— (AP) — The Trail of the Caribou landed here today after a flight of 30 hours and 58 minutes from Wasaga Beach, Ont. The fliers, James Ayling and Leonard Reid, had set out to establish a new long distance record, with Baghdad, Iraq, as their goal. Their landing means that they only covered a little more than half of the 6,300 miles they had set as their objective. The Canadian airmen set their black biplane down here after covering approximately 3,700 miles. They were sighted at 4:55 p. m. G. M. T. (10:55 a. m. C. S. T.) over Stag Lane airdrome. They hopped off from Canada at 5:00 a. m. (E.D.T.) yesterday. Their rapidly diminishing supply of gasoline forced the fliers to change their plans and to decide to land in England, Reid said. They brought their plane down on a private flying field in Middlesex a short time after circling over the Hendon airdrome on the northern outskirts

LONDON, Aug. 9.—(UP)—Leonard G. Reid and J. R. Ayling, attempting a non-stop flight from Ontario to Bagdad, landed at Heston airdrome at 6 p.m. today (noon, Uniontown time). The fliers completed a successful crossing of the Atlantic, but their attempt to set a new world non-stop distance record was spoiled. They had been in the air approximately 31 hours since leaving Wasaga Beach, Ont., early yesterday. After landing at Heston, near London, the fliers took off almost immediately for Hatfield airdrome, about 20 miles northwest of here.

London, Aug. 10. (AP)—After a sound night's sleep Leonard Reid and James R. Ayling appeared fully recovered today from their fatiguing flight over the Atlantic, in which they battled fog and dense clouds. Their future plans were undecided. The two landed at Heston airdrome late yesterday, having travelled approximately 3,700 of the 6,300 miles from Ontario to Baghdad, their goal. Since their dream of breaking the distance flight record has been shattered, it was assumed Reid and Ayling would not continue on to Europe and Asia Minor. Sir William Ayling, "Jimmy’s" father, said he was "delighted with the flight." Carburetor trouble, the fliers said, used up their gasoline supply at a rapid rate. The engines consumed 17 to 18 gallons an hour instead of the usual 10 and they had only about 200 gallons left when they landed. This and weather conditions forced them to give up the Baghdad goal.

LONDON, Aug. 9.—(AP)—James Ayling and Leonard Reid, adventuresome Canadian fliers, completed a trip across the Atlantic Ocean today, but storms defeated their effort to set a new non-stop airplane flight record. They landed here this evening, abandoning their effort to fly from Wasaga Beach, Ont., to Baghdad, Iraq, after ocean storms had buffeted their sturdy black biplane for many hours. Ayling and Reid came down at Heston airport, a little disappointed but still cheerful, at 5:07 p. m., G.M.T., 9:01 p. m. B.B.T. They had come from the shores of Lake Ontario, had crossed eastern Canada and the North Atlantic Ocean, in 31 hours and 7 minutes. The controls of their plane, the "Trail of the Caribou," jammed dangerously several times, and there were indications they might cause more trouble. And ahead weather was becoming increasingly unfavorable. Over England the fliers made a hasty calcul

LE HAVRE, France, Aug. 10 (P) - Mrs. James Roosevelt, mother of the president, sailed for home today on the S.S. Île de France after a month’s visit in London and Paris. She waved her goodbye to a cheering crowd with a bunch of violets.

LIVERPOOL, N. S. ()—A battle for nearly three days and nights with a giant tuna fish, the dream of every deep-sea angler, was the happy realization today of Thomas Howell, Chicago grain market operator. Landed after a 62-hour tussle, said to be the longest on record, the tuna weighed 792 pounds. This beat by 12 pounds the local record breaker caught off here a few years ago by Zane Grey, the novelist.

SOUTHAMPTON, Eng., Aug. 10. —One of the largest shipments of bullion in recent months was embarked today on the American liner President Roosevelt, for delivery in New York. Included in the shipment were 4,000 bars of silver and sixty boxes of gold. The movement was regarded as the first response to the Washington government's announcement that silver would be nationalized. The shipment, consisting of 400,000 pounds of sterling in silver and 600,000 pounds sterling in gold, was valued at approximately $5,082,000 at today’s rate of exchange.

LONDON, Aug. 9. (P)—James Ayling and Leonard Reid, adventuresome Canadian fliers, completed a trip across the Atlantic Ocean today, but storms defeated their effort to set a new non-stop airplane flight record. The controls of their plane, the "Trait of The Caribou," jammed dangerously several times, and there were indications they might cause more trouble. Ahead weather was becoming increasingly unfavorable. Over England the fliers made a hasty calculation and concluded they did not have enough fuel to break the existing long distance flight record of 5,657.6 miles.

1934-08-07.text: Santa Rosa, Calif.—(AP)—Mrs. Charmian London, widow of Jack London, the author, was reported to be in a “very serious” condition today as the result of injuries suffered when a horse she was riding stumbled and fell, pinning her to the ground. Physicians said her left side was badly crushed, five ribs broken and her left lung injured.

WASHINGTON (AP) — The heat got Pal, last of the White House dogs. Pal, an English bull terrier owned by Gus Gennerich, the President’s personal attendant, began acting queerly some days ago, and so today he was in a dog hospital for treatment. About two weeks ago Winks, a setter puppy owned by President Roosevelt, ran headlong into an iron fence and was killed.

CARDROSS, Dumbartonshire, Scotland, Aug. 7, (P)—The British drought is rapidly making this village the most popular spot in Scotland. There's whisky in its drinking water—and the drinking water is free. When the town’s water reservoir went dry from lack of rain, reserves were brought from other points in the great casks in which this region abounds. It abounds in them because they are used for maturing whisky, the Scotch variety. Local temperance organizations protested strenuously against having to drink water with a distinct highbally flavor but the village authorities answered that the water is perfectly safe.

TANNENBERG, Germany, Aug. 7—(*)—Germany buried Paul Von Hindenburg in a shrine it holds sacred today after Adolf Hitler in an emotional eulogy at the bier said the late president “opened the door” to Naziism. Brief and simple was the funeral, as the old warrior-statesman had wished, but thousands of uniforms gave it a military atmosphere. The body of the 86-year-old leader was placed to rest in one of the towers of the national war monument, erected on the scene of Von Hindenburg’s great triumph over the Russian army in 1914. Thousands of mourners were turned away, but the entire nation paused during the funeral hour in a farewell tribute to its revered leader. Hitler Silent on Policies Hitler, as on yesterday at a memorial service of the Reichstag, eulogized in glowing terms the man whose power he took over, but he failed to give the expected indications of his future policies. Von Hind

LENS, France, Aug. 1.—(AP)—Two hundred miners were trapped today in the 1,000-foot level of a coal mine where they were imprisoned yesterday by a group of 20 Polish miners protesting against the discharge of two comrades. The group blocked the galleries and cut air, water, and electricity connections, entirely paralyzing the mine. A foreman, who descended the shaft last night to negotiate a relief, was also held below. Heavy police guards surrounded the shaft but communications ceased at 10 p.m. yesterday.

(By United Press). Tannenburg, East Prussia, Aug. 7.— President Paul von Hindenburg was returned today to rest forever in the soil he made historic by his victory of Tannenburg over the great Russian 'steam roller' in 1914. Over his body Adolf Hitler, who became supreme ruler of the nation when Hindenburg died, called him the guardian of the nation’s rebirth. His funeral cortege, which had moved throughout the night from his chateau at Neudeck along roads strung with garlands of grape-draped pine boughs, between lines of eerily flaring torches held by Nazi storm troopers, arrived at 6 a.m. at the great memorial of his victory. On the plains around the memorial lay the graves of German soldiers who fell at Tannenburg, symbolic eternal guards for their chief. They are the only isolated Soldiers’ graves in the country. Those who fell in obeying Hindenburg’s orders and winning some of the gr

‘Rome, Aug. 7 (4)—The departure of the Archduke Otto, pretender to the Austrian throne, from Brussels today strengthened reports current here that he will meet Premier Mussolini, despite denials by government attaches. Since the assassination of Chancellor Dollfuss many believe that the return of a Hapsburg to the Austrian throne is needed as an assurance against the final triumph of the Nazi in Austria.

VIENNA, Aug. 7. (AP)---Court martial today sentenced two members of the Nazi putsch against the government of Chancellor Dollfuss to be hanged. Karl Kostelnig was sentenced at Klagenfurt, Ernst Feicke, the first regular army soldier brought to trial in connection with the putsch, was sentenced in Vienna.

1934-08-20.text: NEWPORT, Pembrokeshire, Wales, Aug. 19 (George Pond and Cesare Sabelli, turned back by a raging storm over the Irish Sea on a Rome-to-Dublin flight, attempted to land near here this morning but crashed into a mountain in the darkness, ruining their hopes for a return Atlantic flight. Miraculously they escaped serious injury. Pond said “I'm afraid the plane is damaged almost beyond repair. It will certainly not be fit for an Atlantic flight this year.” The two fliers, who started from New York last May on a flight to Rome, crashing in Ireland and finishing their flight by easy stages, were only slightly injured and suffered from shock. They were on the return journey, only a few hours’ flying distance from Baldonnel airport, Dublin, their first goal. The crash occurred about 4 o'clock this morning, after the fliers had experienced normal conditions almost all the way from Rome to the coas

NEWPORT, Pembrokeshire, Wales, Aug. 20.— nf Bg Pond and Cesare Sabelli sadly surveyed today the wreckage of the airplane they had hoped would carry them on a return flight across the Atlantic. While they were flying at a fast speed, the plane crashed into a hillside early yesterday when they attempted to make a forced landing on a hop from Dublin to Rome. The fliers escaped serious injuries but were shaken up and bruised; Their plane was burned near the top of a 1,200-foot mountain. An inspector is to go over it to see if salvage is possible. Pond and Sabelli, who were forced down at Moy, on the west coast of Ireland, after flying the Atlantic in May, spent all day Sunday in bed recovering from effects of their crash. Pond, who was piloting at the time, was worse shaken than Sabelli and decided to submit to an X-ray examination to make sure his injuries are not serious. “We were lucky to

LONDON, Aug. 20.—(P)—Rumors and threats to kidnap the princesses Elizabeth and Margaret Rose of Great Britain's ruling house were denied today by sources close to King George. Col. Bowes Lyons, brother of the Earl of Strathmore, said no special precautions are being taken to guard the granddaughter of the king, and that an outbreak of scarlet fever was the reason the girls had not been out on shopping trips. They are staying at Glamis Castle in the highlands of Scotland.

Newport, Pembrokeshire, Wales — A rather serious dislocation of one of George Pond’s ribs as a result of the crash of the Pond-Sabelli trans-Atlantic airplane was disclosed by an X-ray examination at a hospital here today. Arrangements were made for the American aviator to be treated by a specialist at Cardiff. Pond, meanwhile, was able to move about and both he and his flying companion, Cesare Sabelli, visited Newport Castle where they were congratulated by the occupant, Lady Lloyd, on their escape from death when their plane crashed into a hillside early Sunday. The fliers, who had started from Rome and intended to fly to New York from Dublin, were undecided today as to their plans for the immediate future. After examining the airplane an expert said "it can be repaired but not here."

- LONDON, Ont., Aug. 20.—(®)— There were unconfirmed reports today that arrests would be made in the case of John S. Labatt, London brewer who was held three days last week by kidnappers and then released. Police authorities refused to make a statement. They were believed to be concentrating a search for the abductors along the border area of Windsor and Detroit. Labatt, who is staying in the apartment of his brother here, was said to have recovered sufficiently from his experience to “be up and around the house.” A police guard placed around the building after Labatt’s return has been withdrawn,

London, Aug. 18.—‘After we turn you loose in Toronto and you talk and any of our gang is arrested we will come back and kill you,” was the death threat given to John Labatt by his abductors as they left him on Thursday night in Toronto. This fact became known here today through channels close to the police and Labatt’s family. Labatt told the police he knows he was in a house but has not the faintest recollection where he was. He was blindfolded all the time.

NEWPORT, Wales, Aug. 20, — Cesare Sabelli and George R. Pond, trans-Atlantic flyers, began dismantling their wrecked airplane Leonardo Da Vinci on a mountainside today, all hope of an early westward Atlantic flight dissipated. Caught in fog on a flight from Rome to Dublin, the flyers turned back toward Great Britain from the middle of the Irish Sea, and seeing the lights of Newport decided to circle until dawn. At 4 a. m. yesterday they crashed into 1,200 foot Garn Ingli mountain.

LONDON, (UP). Proposals for a gigantic international wheat pool to control exports and prices provided a sensation Monday at a session of the drafting committee of the world wheat conference. Plans for the super-pool were presented by representatives of the seven major wheat-producing countries involved in a session at the United States embassy. The meeting lasted three hours and a half. Some details of the scheme were permitted to become known. A fixed percentage of the world’s exports of wheat would be diverted to the pool as a reserve. The committee will meet Tuesday in an attempt to draft by-laws which will be submitted to the interested governments.

1934-12-07.text: LONDON (#) — A Warsaw dispatch to the London Daily Express said today wholesale executions of suspected enemies of the Soviet government had taken place in Russia within the past 24 hours. The lives of more than 200 persons, including Leonid Nicolieff, accused assassin of Sergei Kiroff, and many women and children, were snuffed out by firing squads, the dispatch said. Nicolieff’s wife, sons, two daughters and 85-year-old mother were reported to have been among the victims. Fourteen officials of the Moscow OGPU, the Union State Political Administration, the story said, also were executed in the grim warning to disloyal citizens. The members of the OGPU were said to have been slain in Leningrad following a clash between Moscow and Leningrad OGPU detachments. The fighting, it was said, occurred after Joseph Stalin, convinced of disaffection in the Leningrad group, dismissed Chief Yagoda and

LONDON, (AP).—In the first public statement of United States policy since the tri-power naval conversation began, Norman Davis, United States ambassador-at-large said today that abandonment of the Washington and London naval treaties “would lead to conditions of insecurity, international suspicion, and costly competition with no real advantage to any nation.” This statement, regarded as a warning to Japan, was made before the American Correspondents’ Association at a luncheon. Heretofore, all statements on the American policy have been released through a delegation spokesman.

The United States served notice today that this country will not agree to Japan's demands for naval parity. If Japan persists in her determination to abrogate the Washington and London naval limitation treaties, she may expect a free-for-all naval construction race, with the strong implication that the United States can and will outstrip her in building warships. The pronouncement of American naval policy was laid down in London by Norman H. Davis, chief American delegate to the naval conversations now going on in London. Although Davis spoke informally, and on his own responsibility, there was little doubt that his remarks had the full approval of Secretary of State Cordell Hull and presumably, President Roosevelt. AIMED AT JAPAN It was evident also his remarks were directed to Japan. He took occasion to answer specifically the principal arguments of the Japanese. The American naval pos

London, Dec. 7.—(Friday)—(P)—A Warsaw dispatch to the Express said today that Thursday a red terror ran riot in Russia, with more than 200 persons, including women and children, summarily shot within a few hours. The dispatch said that the sound of shooting was heard every few minutes in the law courts and that among those executed was the assassin, Leonid Nicolaieff, who slew the communist leader, Sergei Kiroff. Others reported shot were Nicolaieff’s wife, son, two daughters and 85-year-old mother. Fourteen officials of the Moscow OGPU, the union state political administration, also were executed, according to the Warsaw report. Joseph Stalin was reported ruthlessly purging the country because of the slaying of Kiroff. Having discovered a serious split in the ranks of the OGPU he dismissed Chief Yagoda and ordered the widespread arrests and executions and called in the red army to prote

TOKIO, Dec. 7 ()— Japanese naval propagandists were quoted today as accusing the United States of desiring to expand its armaments "for subjugation of the world." The comment was inspired by the speech of Norman H. Davis in London yesterday in which he sounded the warning that a costly naval race would result from abrogation of the Washington treaty. The newspaper Jiji Shimpo attributed to anonymous naval authorities the statement that the speech shows the intention of the United States "to establish an overwhelmingly superior navy both in the Atlantic and Pacific for subjugation of the world. If such ambitious plans are unchecked, world peace will be endangered."

ORTO, Dec. 7. — Japan turned a deaf ear today to an American warning that a costly naval race would follow abrogation of the Washington treaty. Discussing the London speech of Norman H. Davis in which he gave the United States’ views, a foreign office spokesman said: “No government could last a day in Japan that compromised with the established decision to terminate the Washington treaty. On that the government's decision is fixed completely and is supported by public opinion. “We already knew Mr. Davis advocated maintenance of the present treaties, and his speech contains nothing new. “We are not seeking a naval race. It is Mr. Vinson (Carl Vinson, chairman of the American house naval affairs committee), who declares the United States will build five ships to Japan's three.”

LONDON, Dec. 6.—Japan was warned by Norman H. Davis today that by scrapping the Washington Naval Treaty, she would endanger security, create suspicion and force the world into a costly naval race. The American ambassador-at-large also announced that President Roosevelt has proposed “a substantial all-around reduction in naval armaments.” Since no agreement to reduce has been reached, the envoy said in a speech before the American Correspondents Association, the United States strongly advocates continuing the Washington and London treaties with the assurance of “equality of security.” (Japanese spokesmen have served notice that Japan will denounce the Washington treaty, which gives the Far Eastern nation the smaller end of a 5-5-3 ratio.) Washington: The United States Supreme Court refused Monday to interfere with the conviction of Oscar M. Hartzell of Iowa for collecting funds from people on representation that they would share in a vast estate supposed to have been left by Sir Francis Drake, Elizabethan English explorer. Hartzell, who lived on a farm near Des Moines, went to England, the government contended, and directed agents in this country in collecting between $700,000 and $800,000 in cash during the last 10 years. He was convicted in northern Iowa federal court at Sioux City, of using the mails in promoting the alleged fraud, sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment and fined $2,000. The Supreme Court has refused to review the conviction, which had been affirmed by the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals. Hence it stands. 1934-07-23.text: LONDONDERRY, NORTHERN IRELAND, July 23.—(4)—John Grierson, British pilot, took off today on a flight to Ottawa, Canada, via Iceland and Greenland. Weather conditions were ideal. Grierson attempted a flight to New York over a similar route in 1933 but his plane cracked up at Reykjavik, Iceland, as he was taking off for Greenland. Col. Charles A. Lindbergh, there at the time, aided Grierson in salvaging the plane.
Reykjavik, Iceland, July 23. (F)— John Grierson, British flyer, arrived here at 11:30 a.m., E.S.T., today after a flight from Londonderry, Ireland, on his way to Ottawa by the north route.

By The Associated Press Warsaw, July 23.—Outbreaks of typhoid fever in some sections of Poland were reported today as drinking water was polluted and 200,000 persons were estimated nearly destitute because of floods. The threat of a typhoid epidemic throughout the flood area caused apprehension while Warsaw awaited a fourth flood crest moving down the Vistula river. The known dead already number 240. The lack of drinking water is pressing because the rivers have been polluted by bodies and are unfit for use.

| By The Associated Press Chicago, July 23—Dillinger’s dead! | He swaggered from a neighborhood theatre last night into the raking fire of government guns. Too late he saw the gleaming steel of the trap set for him. His hand went for his gun. Three bullets tore into his body—one in the neck, two in the body. He staggered and fell. It was the end of John Dillinger. The place was just outside the Biograph Theatre, a neighborhood movie house on the Northwest side in territory where the blood of many a Chicago gangster has flowed before. Attempted Disguise Dillinger, his hair dyed a darker hue, tell-tale scars on his cheeks lifted by plastic surgery, gold-rimmed spectacles framing his shifty eyes, his nose straightened, a carefully-groomed black mustache adorning his lip and fingerprints obliterated by acid, strode through the lobby and sauntered down the street. For the safety of Rear Admiral Richard E. Byrd was felt today. The trail leading to his lonely weather observation outpost was lost. A tractor party which set out Friday to bring him back to the main base reported it could not pick up the trail. The group was fifty miles out on the 123-mile run. Orange flags with which the trail had been marked could not be found at that point, the relief party reported yesterday. Byrd followed the trail four months ago to take up his lonely duty. Dr. Thomas C. Poulter in charge of the group said it had battled in bitter weather to reach the fifty-mile station. Temperatures ranged from fifty degrees below zero to seventy-one degrees below. The expedition traveled 130 nautical miles to attain the fifty nautical miles, Dr. Poulter reported, zigzagging back and forth over the ice barrier. The three, who overpowered unarmed guards and scaled the walls in a hail of bullets while most of the prison population was attending a Sunday baseball game, were Raymond Hamilton, one time run- Walker, Thompson's companion in several crimes, was shot to death as he attempted to scale the walls. Charlie Frazier, leader of a recent Louisiana prison break, was wounded; and Roy Johnson, bandit, wounded. All Texas, Oklahoma and Louisiana haunts of the men were being searched. State and Texas rangers were guarding areas near the Mexico border. A few hours after they...

MRE VEE, S0G.,, JUV <0 (*—John Dillinger sr., respected farmer of this neighborhood, today went about the business of arranging for the burial of his son and namesake today as calmly as he had awaited the day he knew was coming when bullets would end the notorious bank bandit’s life. Momentarily shaken by the announcement of Johnny Dillinger’s death at the hands of federal agents last night in Chicago, the elder Dillinger quickly regained his composure and looked after the minutest details of the funeral. At his side, Mrs. Audrey Hancock, sister of the bandit and who virtually reared him, upheld the family reputation for calmness in exciting moments. At first she would not believe that her brother was dead. Convinced finally, her first thought was of her father. Both said they had been “expecting something like this to happen to Johnny,” and in the next breath strongly upheld him as a pe

Ossining, N. Y.—()—At least 16 persons—men, women and children—rode to flaming death in a big motor bus Sunday, and the burned and twisted wreckage was searched today for more bodies. The bus, carrying more than fifty persons from Brooklyn to a scheduled baseball game at Sing Sing prison, plunged wildly down a sharp hill in Ossining, dove off a 40-foot embankment and burst into flames as it landed in a lumber yard. Sheets of blazing gasoline shot in all directions from the vehicle’s exploding fuel tanks. The flames raged over two square blocks of lumber and coal yards and docks. Twelve seared bodies were removed as soon as the fire could be checked. Four of those rescued alive died in hospitals. More Missing. Half a dozen passengers still are unaccounted for. They are feared dead. Many of the rescued are not expected to survive. Six persons, their clothing ablaze, ran from the roaring fu

1934-03-15.text: CHIPPINGHURST, England, March 15—(—The Duke of Gloucester was heavily thrown today when riding in the South Oxfordshire point-to-point steeplechase here and was badly shaken. The horse fell on a fence. The duke is the third son of King George and is considered a fine horseman.

LONDON, March 14. (AP)—Captain Anthony Eden, British lord privy seal and arms expert, told parliament today that he rejected any idea of the imminence of war. 'I do not believe,' he asserted, 'that, anxious as it is, the situation is desperate. It is not so.' Captain Eden, who returned recently from arms discussions in Paris, Rome and Berlin, pictured the Franco-German situation as one of mistrustful apprehension, but maintained that 'while there is a glimmer of light we cannot admit defeat.'

English-born Samuel Insull, who fled to ancient Athens for refuge after his utilities empire collapsed in modern Chicago, spent nearly a year and a half fighting return to the land of his adoption. The business leader and patron of arts was in Paris when a Cook County, Ill., grand jury indicted him for larceny and embezzlement on Oct. 4, 1932. Three days later he disappeared and the United States asked France to arrest him. On Oct. 9 he fled to Athens from Milan, Italy, and then opened the long and tedious battle of United States authorities to return him for trial. Ruled Against Treaty. The Greek government held him for a United States writ and then announced an extradition treaty between the two countries was invalid because it had not been ratified. In November he was seized for extradition and pleaded illness. (Continued on Page Nine)

HONKONG, March 15.—The U. S. Navy gunboat Fulton, almost a total loss from a mysterious fire which swept it from bow to stern, was towed toward Hongkong today from the pirate-infested waters of Bias Bay, where British warships and merchantmen had rescued its crew of 180 officers, sailors and marines. Eight seamen from the ill-fated gunboat required hospital attention for slight burns when they were brought here by the H. M. S. Wishart, British destroyer, and the S. S. Tsinan, a merchant steamer. The Fulton was on pirate patrol in the Bias Bay section, forty miles north of Hongkong, when the fire broke out. It was believed that oil had ignited in the vicinity of the Diesel engines with which the craft had been refitted. Ships in the vicinity raced to the Fulton’s side. The Wishart, first to arrive, daringly drew alongside. Sailors leaped from one ship to another. Others were picked up fro

LITTLE AMERICA, via Mackay Radio, March 14 (Delayed) (A) Admiral Richard E. Byrd's monoplane, carrying Lieut. Com. Isaac Schlossbach, U.S. Navy, retired, and three passengers crashed at 12:30 o'clock today. No one was seriously injured. The plane cracked up 500 yards south of the expedition camp here. In the plane besides Lieut. Com. Schlossbach were Arthur A. Zuhn, Mt. Pleasant, Ja., Fred J. Dustin, Revere, Mass., and Harry Young, New Zealand.

BRISBANE, Australia, Mar. 19. (UP)—A storm described as of appalling character swept the northeastern Australian coast today. Fifty men, crews of three coastal ships, were known dead. Ten persons were known to be missing. Many small craft along the coast were unreported. The storm, said in dispatches to be of cyclonic nature, was asserted to be the worst in the history of Northern Queensland. It struck over a 500-mile area between Cape York, at the northern tip of the east coast, and Cairns, 850 miles north of Brisbane.

Paris, March 15 (AP)—Former King Alfonso of Spain and his companions on a lion hunt in the Sudan narrowly escaped death in an exchange of gunfire with a Sudanese patrol, reports from Egypt said today. Each group mistook the other for bandits. The hunters, who left Cairo early in February, were plodding over a desolate stretch of desert when they were fired upon. The former monarch and his party promptly returned the fire. Both sides continued firing several hours before the mistake was discovered.

Tokyo, March 14.—(/P)—A complete investigation of the landing of two Soviet airmen in the Japanese-protected empire of Manchukuo was ordered today by the government. The flyers, who made a forced landing March 11 and have been held by Manchukuoan authorities, will be taken at once to Hsinking (Changchun, the capital) for questioning. War department officials as well as the foreign office manifested considerable perturbation over the incident and demanded to know why the plane, a bomber of the Soviet air forces, descended on 'forbidden' territory.

1934-06-12.text: Paris, June 11 —(AP)— Reports that Germany may be on the verge of suspending payments on Young and Dawes plan loan bonds as well as commercial debts alarmed British and French financial quarters today. Rumors concerning the Dawes and Young loans arose soon after receipt of French information that payment on the commercial obligation had been suspended. This news resulted in a long talk at Basel, Switzerland between Montagu Norman, governor of the Bank of England, and Dr. Hjalmar Schacht, president of the German Reichsbank. Great Britain and France are trying to get assurances that the payments will be met.

Washington, June 14. (4°)—Belgium and Czechoslovakia joined today in the parade of European war debtors who have informed the United States they will default on debt installments on June 15. Great Britain, as previously announced, will “defer” payment of installments of $261,791,011 it has falling due on that date. Finland, which has always paid promptly and in full, is the only nation to announce it will pay its installment of $166,538 in cash in New York City on Friday. Ten other nations are to be heard from before the semi-annual due date on June 15. Italy owes $2,088,108, of which $23,428,605 is due on Friday. Belgium reported inability at this time to pay anything on the $18,468,907 due on June 15. Of that amount, $11,309,453 is past due on previous installments and $7,159,454 becomes due on June 15. Belgium has defaulted on its last three installments due. Czechoslovakia owes the U

ALFORD, Lincolnshire, England, June 12, (AP).—John Twigg, a farmer, while joy riding in an airplane over this little market town the other day dropped a rotten egg with unerring aim on the police station. The amateur air bomber in police court today was fined $10, with an additional $7.50 in costs for this affront to local authority. The case, one of the oddest ever brought in England, ended abruptly when Twigg pleaded guilty.

LONDON, June 11. (AP) — Bilateral discussions in preparation for the 1935 naval conference, which are regarded with frank pessimism by Japanese quarters here, will begin late this week with talks between British and American representatives. Norman H. Davis, United States ambassador-at-large, and Rear Admiral Richard H. Leigh, will assist Ambassador Robert W. Bingham in discussing the subject with British statesmen, probably Captain Anthony Eden, lord privy seal, and members of the American section of the foreign office. Anglo-Japanese conversations will follow, and American-Japanese discussions will then take the center of the diplomatic stage. Officials in close touch with the situation reiterated that Russia and Germany will not be invited either to the preliminary discussions or to the 1935 conference.

Rome, June 12 (UP)—The wan, weak spotlight of disarmament activities shifted from Geneva to Italy today as Premier Benito Mussolini prepared to confer with Chancellor Adolf Hitler in a curtain-raiser to the British-Japanese-American naval talks at London. Mussolini was at his summer home at Rocca Delle Caminate, near Forli. His conference with Hitler, scheduled for Thursday, is to be held at the historic castle at Strà. halfway between Venice and Padua. Under Secretary for Foreign Affairs Fulvio Suvich and other officials are due in Venice tomorrow to prepare for the arrival of Hitler and his entourage by airplane. Hitler and Mussolini are expected to discuss the whole range of European problems, but particularly Mussolini is expected to make a bid for leadership in European peace work by trying to form a basis for Germany’s return to international discussions. Then will come the naval t

Rome.--(AP)—The trans-Atlantic airplane, Leonardo da Vinci, bearing Capt. George Pond and Cesare Sabelli, landed here at 8:12 p.m. today after a flight from Lympne, England. The fliers were welcomed by General Valle, undersecretary of aviation, and a committee of high generals of the air corps. The two will be entertained by the government.

Paris, June 11.—(UP)—Fredrick Delius, British composer and one of the greatest musicians of his generation, died last night at Grez-sur-Loing on the edge of Fontainebleau forest, blind and nearly paralyzed.

PARIS, June 12.—France decided officially today to default on its $59,000,000 war debt installment due to the United States June 15. The decision was reached at a cabinet meeting at the Elysee Palace over which President Albert Lebrun presided. It had been expected that France would default the installment—its fourth default since December, 1932, when the government of Edouard Herriot fell because Herriot insisted the debt must be paid. Since the British default notice, however, there had been some consideration whether France might not make some gesture that would lead to early debt negotiations and avoid further default.

1934-11-26.text: CARLISLE, Pa., Nov. 26.—(CP)—The first definite clue to the identities of three fair-haired little girls, found dead in a rain-dampened mountain thicket, turned authorities toward New York and New England today in their investigation. The information came from Paul White, Harrisburg bus driver who, after viewing the three linen-swathed bodies at the morgue, said he was certain they were the three children who accompanied a woman from New York to Harrisburg in his bus last Wednesday. White also positively identified a suitcase, picked up two miles from where the girls’ bodies were found, as one of three carried by the woman on the trip. The party had tickets from Boston, he said, and the woman, who seemed “very tired,” led the group from the bus at the state capital. On the four-hour trip from New York to Harrisburg, White said the woman never left the bus. She was about 35 years old, wit

(Copyright, 1934, Associated Press) London, Nov. 25.—An atmosphere of warlike excitement prevailed in Europe at the beginning of a new week tonight as nation after nation joined in the cry "Who’s your ally?" In the last few days new shouts of discord have echoed across the borders of European nations. Like children seeking shelter from an approaching storm, countries big and small were hunting new security under the skirts of alliances with powerful neighbors or distinctively strategic countries. Even the United States figured in this new phase of world politics when the question of a new Anglo-American understanding was reported to have been under contemplation to offset Japan's insistent demands at the London naval conversations for parity in armaments. London, Nov. 26.—()—Three kings—George of England, Christian of Denmark and Haakon of Norway—with their queens will sit down together tonight in Buckingham palace at a dinner given by King George in honor of Princess Marina and the Duke of Kent. The king and queen of Denmark and Prince Waldemar arrived in London today for the wedding, which takes place Thursday. A busy round of engagements faced them.

LONDON, Nov. 26. — American delegates to the naval conference have suggested to the British the possibility of an informal agreement by which, if the Washington naval treaty lapsed, they would not build against each other but might be free to match Japan's level, it was understood today. It was said that the British showed no desire to enter into any such agreement. As outlined, it was understood the proposal was that Britain and the United States would pledge themselves informally not to race against each other. They would inform each other regarding their building programs. Neither would object to the other building up to any strength to which Japan took its navy. The reported proposal, it was said, was made on the theory that if Japan denounced the Washington treaty, and no other was negotiated, it was withdrawing from what amounted to a pacific league. London, Nov. 25.——(AP)——Princess Marina had a thrill this afternoon when with her princely fiancé she visited the spacious house in Belgrave Square which the couple will occupy after their marriage next Thursday. The Duke of Kent and Marina spent 20 minutes inspecting their future domicile. It was only one incident in a busy day which began with a journey to the private chapel in Buckingham Palace for services during the forenoon, accompanied by the king and queen and other royal personages. After church the couple took a drive in a black sports car with the duke at the wheel, returning to the palace for luncheon.

London, Nov. 26.—-(UP)—Central London today is bright with flags and varicolored paper chains after a weekend of work in preparation for the wedding Thursday of Princess Marina of Greece and the Duke of Kent, King George’s youngest son, .. Shopkeepers, dressmakers, milliners, beauty specialists, enjoy a boom business. Newspapers are subordinating all news to that of the wedding festivities and people in the streets are watching for the royal couple, eager to cheer them whenever they are seen. The king and queen of Denmark and Prince Waldemar came by special train today to attend the wedding. The Duke of York welcomed them at the station. Buckingham Palace has a theoretical “house full

LONDON, Nov. 25,—CUP— George Bernard Shaw, 178, playwright, was recovering today from a heart attack which at first was believed serious. His physicians, however, said that while the grey-bearded Irish humorist was in bed with a nurse in attendance, his condition was not serious.

' London, Nov. 26 (INS)—A modern Cinderella without the rude awakening. A simple, unspoiled young girl rushed into wealth and glittering prestige with no clock to strike the fateful midnight hour. This is Princess Marina of Greece, the pretty young Balkan girl who on Thursday will become the bride of George, the Duke of Kent, and at the same time the Fourth Lady of the United Kingdom. Wooed and won by the 31-year-old English prince in a Balkan castle in Yugoslavia, Princess Marina comes to England wide-eyed and awe-struck by the splendor of her new position as bride of a member of the British royal family. Since the day her engagement was announced, Princess Marina has lived in a giddy whirl of social functions and the joyous but arduous task of choosing her trousseau. With her arrival in London for the ceremony, her duties and her pleasures have increased a hundredfold. From the moment

1934-08-16.text: TORONTO, Aug. 16. (P)—As the 48th hour after the kidnapping of John S. Labatt, wealthy London, Ontario brewer, passed today, silence enveloped the hotel room where Hugh Labatt awaited word of his missing brother. It appeared certain that no personal contact was made between Hugh, who was supposed to have $150,000 ransom with him, and the kidnappers. In an early morning telephone conversation, over a period of two hours, he talked three times with the kidnappers. After the third call it was indicated that Hugh made a rendezvous with the kidnappers today.

| SEYMOUR, Aug. 16.—(4)—As the result of a nocturnal roadside shooting, H. Nichols, assistant cashier of the First National Bank of Seymour, was dead today and Miss Ruby Britain, member of a pioneer Baylor county family, was in jail charged with murder. Miss Willie Mae Couch, 19, was placed under an appearance bond as a material witness. According to the story Miss Couch told officers, she and Nichols rode around in his car for a while last night and finally parked on a road a few miles from town. A few minutes after they parked, a car containing another woman was driven up beside theirs and the woman, without saying a word, opened fire on Nichols. The 38-year-old bank official stumbled out of his car and staggered down the road some 70 yards before falling dead. Hysterical, Miss Couch drove the car back to town and told officers of the shooting. Deputy Sheriff Pat Taliaferro, City Marsh

| LONDON, Aug. 16. UP)—A new draft world wheat agreement, under consideration by the international wheat advisory committee, would slash the United States export quota almost to the vanishing point, it was learned today. | Whereas the United States was allotted a 7,000,000 bushel quota for the last crop year and a prospective quota of 84,000,000 bushels for the new crop year, the agreement would give America a quota of but 15,000,000 bushels. This quota would compare with the following allowances for other countries during the year terminating July 31, 1935: Canada 250,000,000 bushels; Argentina 140,000 bushels; Australia 120,000,000 bushels; Russia 20,000,000 bushels; Hungary 12,000,000 bushels, and Bulgaria and Yugoslavia 4,000,000 bushels each. Thus the total world quota for the 1934-1935 year would be 565,000,000 bushels.

DINGWALL, Scotland. (UP) A ten-second earthquake shook Dingwall early Thursday morning. Bedsteads and other furniture trembled, plaster cracked and fell and woodwork began to crack, arousing the startled residents. There was no serious damage.
