London, April 24. (4)—Concerted action by the United States and Great Britain, or any other combination of powers, against Japan's hands-off China policy is firmly opposed by the British government, it was learned tonight. Such a move, even in the form of the mildest inquiries to Japan, was described emphatically by an authoritative British source as “entirely out of the question.” This information was taken as adding significance to a conference this evening between American Ambassador Robert W. Bingham and the Chinese minister here, at the latter’s invitation. In American quarters it was said Mr. Bingham was simply the listener at the parley. He had nothing to say for publication afterward, but it was indicated the Chinese envoy wanted to explain to the American the Chinese viewpoint. It was said no proposals are being made on behalf of the Washington government.

(Copyright 1934, United Press.) Washington, April 25.—Japan is suspected today of synchronizing major announcements of Chinese policy with unusual naval developments in Great Britain and the United States. Two striking coincidences are causing observers to ponder. They are examining the Oriental problem to determine whether British and American naval movements were related to Japanese decisions on: I. Military invasion of Manchuria. II. The new “Oriental Monroe doctrine.” Japan’s Manchurian invasion began Sept. 18, 1931. Twenty-four hours earlier an embarrassed British admiralty revealed mutiny aboard the Atlantic battle fleet at Tavergorodon, Scotland. The Japanese announced they were invading Manchuria to protect their railroad and to disperse bandits. From that modest beginning grew a new state con- {Continued On Page Five

(By United Press). Tokio, April 25.—Foreign Minister Koki Hirota today dismissed imperturbably as “a friendly inquiry” Great Britain's request—received today—for information regarding Japan's startling declaration of Far Eastern policy.

1934-01-24.text: LONDON, Jan. 24—(4)—The British government today recognized the new government of Cuba under President Carlos Mendieta, MADRID, Jan. 24—(#)—The Spanish government today announced its recognition of the Cuban government of President Carlos Mendieta.

London, Jan. 24—(7)—Nearly 7,000 square miles of London and surrounding territory were blotted out today in the worst fog of this winter. Tens of thousands of commuters were delayed as trains, buses and trams were compelled to move slowly. More than a score of persons were injured in collisions which were numerous despite the cautionary pace imposed in the murk with visibility down as low as a couple of yards. Water traffic was equally demoralized or completely tied up, notably on the Thames from which the harbor master reported: "Nothing is moving on the river except the tide."

PARIS, Jan. 23—(P)—A warning that Premier Chautemps, himself and three members of his endangered cabinet would be named in documents on the Stavisky pawnshop scandal, was served them today by Deputy Henroit. Henroit advised the Premier that ministers of finance, justice and commerce be ready to defend themselves before the chamber of deputies. Charges have been hurled by angry deputies that Serge Stavisky, alleged late leader of pawnshop operations in which the public was fleeced of forty million dollars, received protection in high circles. Meanwhile, four thousand police patrolled the area near the chamber, battling hundreds demonstrating against pay cuts.

ATHENS ()—The Supreme State Council rejected Samuel Insull’s appeal today and thus placed the official stamp of legality upon the government's order that he must seek another refuge at the end of this month. The council ordered the former Chicago utilities operator to pay the costs of the proceedings. Insull appealed after the minister of the interior refused to extend his residence permit beyond January 31 and thus enable him to continue evading extradition to the United States by remaining in his Athenian retreat. Twice before, Greek courts had held in Insull’s favor in cases through which the United States sought his extradition to face charges of larceny, embezzlement and violation of bankruptcy laws. The formal announcement said today that the minister of the interior’s decision constituted in itself an administrative act and therefore was a matter which could be dealt with by the c

Calcutta, Jan. 24. (UP) - An appalling toll beyond any previously hinted may be reached in India’s earthquake dead, it was indicated today when the Rajah of Monghyr said deaths in Monghyr alone have reached 25,000. It will be weeks, he added, before ruins can be removed to reveal the incalculable bodies buried by the earthquakes last week which shook the region during the important Moslem festival of Hidul Fitr. The Rajah predicted two generations will pass before the devastated areas can be rehabilitated. (The district of Monghyr is in northeastern India in the Bhagalpur division of Bihar and Orissa. It has an area of 3,927 square miles and is divided by the Ganges.) An unnamed engineer was quoted today as having declared after a survey that the names of both Monghyr and Muzaffarpur might as well be erased from the map. Authorities generally appear anxious to conceal the true proportion

Tokyo—UP—An anti-militarist tenor marked the first interpellation in Japan’s imperial diet today when members of the cabinet completed their statements of policy and declared questioning in order. It was a spirit in tune with the plea for peace and “understanding” voiced by Foreign Minister Koki Hiota upon whom greatest attention was focused as the diet was reconvened today. Count Yoshinori Futaara opened by criticizing the government for permitting publication of inflammatory articles and predictions of war without specifically mentioning a recent magazine interview with Vice-Admiral Nobumasa Suetsugu (Continued on Page 4. Col 1)

MADRID, Jan. 24—(#)—The attorney general of Spain recommended to the supreme court today a pardon for four Americans held in jail at Palma, Mallorca, for assaulting two civil guards. The four Americans are Mr. and Mrs. Clinton B. Lockwood, of West Springfield, Mass., Roger F. Mead, of New York, and Edmund A. Blodgett of Stamford, Conn. They have been held in custody at Palma since last Sunday, when they were arrested following a supreme court reversal of a military tribunal verdict. The military court had acquitted them of the charge, but the supreme court found them guilty and sentenced them to six months and a day in jail. Intercession for their pardon was made directly to the Spanish government by Ambassador Claude G. Bowers of the United States.

PARIS, Jan. 23 (#)—The French cabinet wrested a vote of confidence from a riotous chamber of deputies this evening while all available police battled with street mobs shouting “Stavisky cabinet, resign!” A vote of 386 for and 201 against was given Premier Camille Chautemps after a bitter struggle over opposition charges of official corruption in connection with the $40,000,000 collapse of the Bayonne pawnshop and the operations of its founder, the late Serge Stavisky. Republican mounted guards rode the sidewalks of Boulevard St. Germain repulsing the largest crowd of the three days of rioting and preventing them from marching on the chamber building. The rioters chanted “Out with Chautemps!

1934-02-10.text: London, England, Feb. 9.—(AP)—Virginia Cherrill, American movie player, and Cary Grant, also of the films, were married today at the Caxton Hall registry office. They will sail from Plymouth, England, for the United States tonight aboard the liner Paris. “We are both very happy,” said Grant, who is a native of Bristol, England, after the simple ceremony. “Now we are going straight to Hollywood,” he added. “We have got to get back to work.”

Paris, Feb. 9—Gunfire spurted anew tonight in the working quarter of Paris where Communists battled police, set fire to two churches and besieged public buildings. A policeman was gravely injured. Four others were seriously hurt and 22 less seriously, some of them struck by bullets. Five hundred were arrested as bands of shouting men ran through the district, smashing windows and looting stores. By midnight, calm seemed to have been restored. The rioters, who were demonstrating against a "wave of Fascism," enticed police to wide streets where women threw flower pots upon the struggling masses from upstairs windows. The working-class district near the Place de la Republique—a mile square in area and the home of the notorious Apaches—was thrown into an uproar. The Churches of St. Joseph and St. Ambroise were set afire. The big and new Fast Railroad station was sacked and the North station

| ATHENS, Feb. 8—(U.P.)—Samuel Insull, Chicago utilities magnate, was informed unofficially today that he must leave Greece within five days. | The notification from the government that he must leave his refuge here and take his chance of further evading the effort of the United States to extradite him to answer charges in connection with the collapse of his utilities empire, came after two government physicians reported he was able to travel without danger to his life. At first the physicians were inclined to report that he ought to be permitted to remain here, on the ground that the strain and humiliation of prosecution would endanger him. The government asked them to confine the report to his ability safely to travel. As soon as the report was made Insull was placed under closest police surveillance, though he is at liberty to leave the country—and welcome when he likes. Insull, most

Berlin, Feb. 9 (?)—A near-hurricane swept Germany and roared across Scandinavia during the night and early today killing several persons and injuring scores. It was one of northwest Europe’s worst storms in years. Three were known to be dead in addition to an undetermined number of sailors drowned when the fishing vessel, Condor, sank with all hands on board in the estuary of the Weser river. Baltic and North Sea shipping was driven to harbor by the storm. Widespread damage was caused along the seashore. Hamburg, Breslau and Stettin all reported heavy damage from the high winds. WARSAW, Feb. 10. (Py) — A strong wind spun a windmill too fast in the village of Kostary in the province of Polesie today. The windmill burst into flames. The flames were carried by the gale into the village. Fifty-four buildings were destroyed by fire.

Vienna, Feb. 9.—()—The belief that the Austrian government will follow the sensational expose of an alleged Marxist plot with the dissolution of the socialist party was expressed today in socialist circles, where it was said a general strike would thereby be precipitated.

OTTAWA (#) — One reason for President Roosevelt's good health after 11 strenuous months in office is — “he likes the job.” “That,” smiled no less an authority than Franklin D. Roosevelt's own mother, “always helps anyone.” Mrs. James Roosevelt, 79 years of age, came here for the wedding today of her grand-niece, Irene Helen Robbins, daughter of the United States minister to Canada, and Alexander Cochran Forbes of Boston. “It's some excuse — his being President of the United States; but still, Mrs. Roosevelt said, “he does not write me often enough.”

Paris, Feb 10.—Gaston Doumergue makes two sacrifices in becoming premier of France, but he has at least two compensations. He is a man without a fortune and his principles require him to resign from the lucrative directorship of the Suez canal. This position, to which he was named only a year ago, was estimated to pay him between 200,000 and 400,000 francs annually. He also will be forced to forego the life of peace, quiet and rest that he loves at the age of 70. His compensations are the great honor of having been chosen as the saviour of France in a dark hour and his pleasure at sharing this honor with his wife, whom he married in 1931.

1934-01-10.text: LONDON, Jan. 10—(4)—Foreign minister Dimitri Maximos of Greece declared in an exclusive interview granted the Associated Press today that his government’s decision that Samuel Insull must leave Greece by the end of January is final and irrevocable. The former American utilities operator, given an extension of his police residence permit to allow him to remain until Jan. 31, is wanted in the United States to face charges growing out of the collapse of his utilities empire. Greek courts twice have held against United States attempts to obtain Insull’s extradition. Maximos said the government expects the high court of Greece to summarily dismiss Insull’s appeal from the ruling against further extension of his stay in Athens on the grounds that it has no authority to interfere.

INVERNESS, Scotland, Jan. 10. The Loch Ness Lake serpent was given a material aspect today by eyewitness statements of five more persons and the mute evidence of a human body found near its reputed lair on the north shore. The body was that of a man of rd, apparently wealthy. It was washed up on the shore near the spot where Arthur Grant, son of a Glen Urquhart land owner, reported he saw the monster Friday. To Scots, the body, though pending an inquest, there was no evidence of death by violence, was impressive. Loch Ness, in Scots tradition, never gives up bodies. Two policemen, a woman and two members of a newspaper investigating party said they had seen the serpent, making a total of 155 persons who believe their eyes did not deceive them. The policemen and the woman said they saw the monster yesterday morning. They saw a long black object travelling in the direction of Dores. The ot

London.--(AP)— The proposed pig-and-liquor swap between the United States and Great Britain appeared today to be assured. Official quarters said that the "American offer" to double the British liquor quota in return for an increase from 6.3 to 7.6 per cent of the British import quota on American pork products was received by the British government today. Simultaneously, Great Britain is considering a vigorous protest to France because that nation has increased her quota on imports of American goods by 30 per cent while Great Britain remains on a reduced quota basis. Pending the clearing up of this issue, it appeared likely that Great Britain would withhold announcement of a definite agreement with the United States on liquor and pork. In this connection, observers noted that the liquor-pork swap was called an "American offer" today, whereas previously it was said that Great Britain had i

London, (4°)—It was understood today that the United States will double its import quotas on British liquor immediately for the period ending March 31. An official announcement that the British quota on the United States pork products will be increased is not expected for the next several days, however. The increased quota on American pork will be a permanent allotment when fixed. Official quarters indicated that no trouble was expected from other nations whose pork products quotas will have to be reduced in order to permit the increase on the American importations from 68 to 76 percent of the total British importations. The increase in the American pork quota permitted to enter the United Kingdom results from the American government's decision to increase the British liquor quota. Each nation used its respective product as a bartering means.

| BWAMPSCOTT, Mass., Jan. 10. —UP— A dog chased its tail here until it dropped dead from exhaustion. Patrolman Frank Bailey saw the dog, an English setter, whirling in circles after the elusive tail. He said the dog continued the “chase” for an hour, and still was circling when he left. Later the dog was found dead in the field.

Leipzig, Germany, Jan. 10—(>)—Marinus Van Der Lubbe, 24-year-old Dutch stonemason, was beheaded today for firing the German Reichstag building in Berlin last February. He had repeatedly confessed to setting the fire, but steadfastly refused to divulge any information as to whether he had any accomplices. Van Der Lubbe had been under sentence of death since December 23 when the supreme court convicted him and acquitted four co-defendants. Steps through which the Dutch government sought to gain a lighter sentence for the young Hollander were unavailing. Late last night Van Der Lubbe was informed by the Leipzig prison governor that justice must take its course, but the announcement failed to rouse him from the stupor in which he remained virtually throughout the long trial. Van Der Lubbe did not reply to the question of whether he wanted a clergyman to attend him on the last walk to the gui

LEIPZIG, Germany, Jan. 10—(UP)—Marinus Van Der Lubbe, a Dutch stone mason convicted of burning the Reichstag building, was beheaded today at Leipzig prison. A plea by Queen Wilhelmina of Holland, sent through the Dutch minister, for commutation was unavailing and the 24-year-old Lubbe went to the block at 7:30 a.m. The silk-hatted, frock-coated executioner severed Lubbe’s head just after daybreak in the inner court of the Saxon state prison. The beheading in Nazi eyes was a concession. He was to have been hanged, a death considered less honorable. Lubbe went to the scaffold like a dumb animal and placed his head on the block. The executioner released the knife of the guillotine and Lubbe’s head was severed. Had the execution occurred anywhere else in Germany, the executioner would have used a battle axe, which by tradition is the usual instrument of death. News of the execution was unexp

PARIS, Jan. Royalists rioted near the Chamber of Deputies this evening in angry protest against what they alleged to be the part of high-placed officials in the $40,000,000 collapse of a Bayonne pawnshop and in the death of its founder. Shouting "Down with the thieves! Down with the assassins!" and swinging canes, the irate crowd launched a series of attacks on policemen stationed as guards in the district, ripped up iron tree protectors, broke lamp posts and blocked traffic over a mile-square area. Scores of persons, including many women, were taken to police stations, but were released shortly, and hundreds of spectators were massed in the big Place de la Concorde to watch the bitter demonstrations which taxed police facilities to the limit. Inside the parliament halls an air of almost equal tension prevailed. Cabinet Seeks Truce The reorganized cabinet paced the lobbies, trying to neg

1934-04-28.text: By The Associated Press. LONDON, April 27.—A British authority’s answer to the “Asia for Asiatics” doctrine came today from a source close to the British Indian administration. Japan, the authority said, may dominate China by force and may gain some influence in Siam through intrigue—though this latter is doubtful—but she will never exercise even minor influence in India and other areas of Southern Asia. “Asia for Asiatics” is rapidly becoming the slogan of all Eastern peoples, he added, “but only the Japanese conceive of this new Asia as being run by Japan.” — The authority attributed the popularization of the slogan to Japan's rise to power and imperialistic expansion. A doctrine of “Asia for Asiatics under the leadership of Japan, acting in close collaboration with other Asiatic powers,” has been enunciated officially by the Tokyo government through Masayuki Yokoyama, consul general a

BERLIN, April 27.—(Ur)—French and British warnings against any German plan to postpone payments on the Dawes and Young loans startled the German foreign office today as representatives of foreign bondholders conferred with Reichsbank officials regarding service on medium- and long-term German obligations. The British ambassador told Foreign Minister Von Weurath that a "grave view" would be taken of any moratorium on the post-war Dawes and Young loans, and the French envoy was close behind with similar representations. The American embassy, however, said no instructions had been received from Washington on this point, although Americans hold more of these obligations than any other nation. Given Preference A German foreign office spokesman said the British and French communications were given due attention and called them in keeping with previous efforts of the two.

LONDON, April 28.—Great Britain considers the Japanese “hands off China” incident closed, it was officially intimated today. Newspapers were informed that Sir John Simon, foreign minister, would announce in the House of Commons Monday that assurances made to Sir Francis Lindley, British ambassador, by Koki Hirota, Japanese foreign minister, were considered most satisfactory. Further indication that Japan has succeeded in diminishing foreign anxiety reached an important embassy today. In effect, it was said, Hirota retracted the April 17 statement of a Japanese foreign office spokesman which roused worldwide anxiety. Japs Win Point. It was reported here that as a concession to Japan, the League of Nations secretariat agreed that Dr. Lena Rajchman, sent to China to plan continuance of League reconstruction work, would not be sent back there; Japan strongly objects to him. TOKYO, April 28.—(Saturday) (P—An official statement of Japan's China policy, asserting that Japan “cannot remain indifferent” to the efforts of foreign powers to aid China has been furnished to the American and British ambassadors here. The statement was delivered to Joseph C. Grew and Sir Francis Lindley, American and British ambassadors, respectively, after they had requested Foreign Minister Koki Hirota for an authoritative translation of the “hands off China” declaration of the foreign office of April 17. The official statement, which was revealed here today follows the main lines of the earlier declaration but contains what diplomatic circles regarded as more conciliatory language. Certain foreign efforts to help China, the new declaration says “endanger the peace of East Asia.” Japan, however, it continues, has no intention of violating China's sovereignty and integrity; desires t

LONDON, April 27.—British-Indian administration quarters affirmed today that the white man’s leadership is become discredited in the eyes of far-eastern peoples, but described as “absurd” any Japanese hope that this will engender a Japanese “Monroe Doctrine” for Asia. They unhesitatingly modified Masayuka Yokoyama's official picture of a future Asia only for Asiatics with the phrase, “but not dominated by Japan.” Yokoyama, Nipponese consul general in Geneva, this week enunciated a doctrine of "Asia for Asiatics led by Japan, acting in close collaboration with Asiatic powers" since “Japan must fulfill her duty as defender of peace in eastern Asia.” Claim Prestige Lost The decline of western prestige in the far east, said an authority in close touch with the government of India, “is due mainly to these two reasons: “First, the humiliating defeat of a western power in the Russo-Japanese War

TOKYO, April 23 (UP)—Japan was represented today as sharing the reported British view that its latest clarification of its "hands off China" declaration had "closed" the incident which created worldwide anxiety. A foreign office spokesman said Japan as well as Britain felt the incident was closed. Any further statements from this government, it was indicated, depended on the British House of Commons reaction to an announcement Sir John Simon, British foreign minister, is expected to make Monday relating to Japan’s policy toward China. Official Statement Foreign Minister Koki Hirota has given foreign diplomats an official statement of Japan’s "hands off China" policy, thus providing a basis for future diplomatic discussions of the world-shaking declarations. In conversations with U.S. Ambassador Joseph Clark Grew, the Japanese foreign minister submitted a written explanation which duplica

Associated Press Foreign Staff TOKYO, April 28.—(?)—Japan issued an “official” interpretation of her restated policy toward China today. Foreign Minister Koki Hirota said in a statement that Japan “cannot remain indifferent” to foreign efforts to aid China that “endanger the peace of Asia.” Japan has no desire to interfere with the rights of other powers in China, the statement added, and will welcome other nations’ dealings with China provided such dealings rebound to China’s benefit. Hope was expressed that the statement would convince governments alarmed by the April 17 declaration that there never had been any intention to assert Japan’s right to censor the relations of occidental nations with China. Rome, April 28.—(4)—King Victor Emmanuel declared today that while Italy ardently desires peace, she will increase the strength of her military in the conviction that this is the best guaranty of peace. The King was cheered roundly as he made the declaration in opening the 29th parliament since Italy became a united kingdom in 1860. “We sincerely and ardently desire for Italy and Europe the longest possible period of peace,” the king said, “but the best guaranty of this peace is the efficiency of our armed forces.” “My government will augment and perfect this efficiency, which rests on three points—officers, materials and unity of preparation.” Joining in the enthusiastic cheering were senators and deputies—including Premier Mussolini and Guglielmo Marconi, members of the Italian cabinet and Crown Prince Umberto. Elaborating on his “three points of preparation,” King Victor said Italy’s

1934-03-08.text: London, March 28—A romance like a fairy tale of fiction came true today with the wedding at noon of Sigvard, Prince of Sweden and grandson of the Swedish king, to the beautiful Erika Patzek, 22-year-old daughter of a Berlin industrialist. In taking his commoner bride at a registry office in the heart of busy London, the 26-year-old prince—like Lennart, his cousin—abandoned his princely rights for a romantic union with the girl of his dreams. Ceremony Is Brief Obviously happy, the two were wed by the “marrying” superintendent of the registry office, aided by the assistant registrar. The ceremony was of only a few minutes’ duration. Each had only two sentences to say. Both smiled nervously as they drove up to the registry office in a big limousine for the ceremony. Erika was wearing a smart navy blue tailored costume with a hat to match, and a spray of lovely white orchids on one of the la

| LONDON, March 8 (4)—Great Britain plainly served notice upon the world today she is determined to have parity in the air as long as other nations cling to their aircraft building programs. She is unwilling, Sir Phillip Sassoon told the House of Commons, ‘to accept a position of continuing inferiority in the face of rapidly expanding air forces in the United States, Japan, Russia and other nations.” Sir Phillip, the undersecretary for aviation, declared Britain has concluded she must, as long as air forces exist, “have parity in the air, howsoever that parity is attained.” “The world has reached a critical point of extreme delicacy in the matter of disarmament,” he said, during debate on estimates for increasing the British air force by four squadrons. “Far from accepting our proposals other nations have steadily increased the strength of their respective air armaments until they far ou

LONDON, March 8.—Prince Sigvard of Sweden, grandson of King Gustav V, today married Erika Patzek, beautiful blonde German motion picture actress, at Caxton Hall Register Office near Westminster Abbey. In so doing he made great sacrifices on the altar of love. As the brief ceremony was conducted, the Swedish Riksmarskalk—Lord High Chamberlain—was on his way to Stockholm to issue decrees depriving the prince of his royal status for marrying a commoner. He will be deprived of the right of succession to the throne. He is third in line as the second son of Crown Prince Gustav Adolf. The ceremony was most simple—dramatic in contrast to the solemn ceremonials to which royal princes such as Sigvard are destined if they obey the laws of their countries restricting their choice of wives to officially approved princesses. There was no best man and no reception. The bride’s brother, George Patzek, s

LONDON, March 8 — (2 — EL. bow-benders may well doff hats to Tom, the man who sat at the bottom of the ocean and drank whisky, with water under his chin and 60 feet of it on top of him—drinking when a slip would have drowned him like a rat in a trap. The story of Tom was told to the Royal Society of Arts by Sir Robert Davis, noted authority on deep-sea diving, and here it is: “Tom, a diver working on a wreck, had sent up no cargo for the last couple of hours and everybody became anxious about him. At last he shot to the surface and was dragged to the ladder. Then it was seen that he was drunk. Yet he went down as sober as a horse at a funeral, and the chief salvage officer set about clearing up the mystery. “This is how Tom did it: As the ship sank she had heeled over slightly to one side. London, Mar. 8 ‘UP)—The government gave its pledge in the House of Commons today that Britain would have an air force on a par with other nations. Sir Philip Sassoon, Undersecretary of the Air Ministry, in introducing the air estimates, said he realized the additions made would be considered disappointing to many, “but we do not want at this stage to put forward a program that might prove to be the starting gun in a race of air armament.”

London, March 7 (4)—Plainclothes men, from famous Scotland Yard and police in faraway Cape Town were called in today to solve the mystery of a box containing 930 fine ounces of gold when it left South Africa and nine cents worth of cement when it reached London. Their problem had many elements of a detective yarn. Police knew that the box had gold in it when it started for London, that during the trip it was in a strong room that was not opened en route, and that police themselves watched it hawk-like when it was transferred from Southampton by train here. They saw in the mystery a new kind of racket which has sprung up as a result of the flight of gold to the United States. The discovery by bank attendants that the gold—worth $32,300 when it left Cape Town—was missing showed that the gang had done some careful research in how the precious metal is shipped. The box had been re-sealed so

WASHINGTON, March 3. — Amid talk about a “British spy” house naval affairs sub-committee decided today there had been no excessive profits made on or collusion involved in navy airplane contracts. Representative McFarlane (D-Tex) objected to approving the report prepared by chairman Delaney (D-NY), until “all the evidence is in.” He contended the committee should not act until the printed hearings were available.

CINCINNATI, March 5. (UP) A brother of Princess Irina Youssoupoff, who was awarded $126,800 in London this week in a suit against the Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Company on grounds that the picture “Rasputin” constituted libel against her, works in a beauty parlor here. He is Prince Vassili. His wife, a princess in her own right but not a member of the Romanoff family, works with him. Vassili is the nephew of Nicholas, late Czar of Russia. His mother and Princess Youssoupoff's mother were sisters of the Czar.

1934-12-16.text: HOLLYWOOD, Calif., Dec. 13.-- Another disarmament conference wending its way home labelled “no hak.” ‘In London in 1930 we had 100 writers and 50 on the delegation from here. We are getting a little wiser. Roosevelt hired a fellow named Davis, (Norman Davis) and he just pays him so much a conference, and gives him the contract to attend all there is. They all go home sore at each other now. That's one thing that conferences always succeed at, each nation, finding out just how “honery” the others are. I bet you that history don’t record any two nations ever having war with each other unless they had had a conference first, Yours, /

LONDON, Dec. 15. (4) — The Marquess of Donegal, writing in tomorrow's Sunday Dispatch, says Adolf Hitler recently was attacked from the air while flying over East Prussia. A traveler who just returned from Germany told him the tale, the marquess writes, An unidentified plane swooped down from the clouds on der Fuehrer's craft, his account said, spraying it with bullets and then fled in the direction of Lithuania. The marquess' story says neither Hitler nor his pilot was hurt but those in charge of the realm leader's safety were greatly alarmed and precautions to protect him thereafter were redoubled. In his article he also says that Paul Joseph Goebbels, Nazi minister of propaganda, is in terror of being poisoned and has his wife, Martha, prepare all his food with her own hands.

LONDON, Dec. 15.—David Lloyd George, liberal leader and wartime prime minister, today revealed plans to embark early next year on a reconstruction campaign designed to make him the Roosevelt of Great Britain and give to Great Britain a Rooseveltian New Deal. Nearly 72, chief figure in a party all but crushed between conservatives and laborites, Lloyd George said he intends to go. Finance, industry, agriculture, shipping, housing, transport, communications and electric power are included in his plans. He calls for complete nationalization of the Bank of England, now operated privately under government control. "Get something done," Lloyd George said, will be the slogan of his campaign. His proposals, he said, are the result of talks with eminent economists, financiers and business men. He intends to publish them early in the new year. "The American New Deal," he said in discussing his pro

Aboard SS. Jean Jadot, Dec. 15—(Radio to United Press)—A lifeboat upset by high waves in an coated sea cost the lives of 15—most of whom choked on fuel oil—in the destruction of the British freighter Usworth by a storm. The ship Ascania, both standing by to take 25 exhausted men off the sinking Usworth some 650 miles off Newfoundland, rescued 11 survivors from the British freighter. Huge waves which capsized a lifeboat from the Jean Jadot after several attempts to reach the Usworth accounted for most of the victims. (A radio message from the Ascania to the Cunard White Star line offices in New York said that the Ascania had nine survivors and the Jean Jadot ten others.)

LONDON, Dec. 15.—(#)—Dressed in wet and soggy golf togs after a friendly game in a pouring rain, delegates of the world's three great sea powers reached another impasse in naval matters today. After a round on the famous Walton Heath golf course, in which the Americans, Norman Davis and Admiral William H. Standley, lost a foursome match to Ambassador Tsuneo Matsudaira and Sir John Simon, they repaired to the clubhouse. Davis told the British foreign secretary and Matsudaira that resumption of naval conversations next year depends on a marked change of attitude in Tokyo during the next few days. Incidentally it was the first discussion in which all three delegations had participated simultaneously. They had a great game of golf albeit a wet one. Batteries of news and sound cameras and a gallery of spectators accompanied them. The Americans sloshed to defeat on the first hole.

Terse wireless messages crackling in from mid-Atlantic Saturday told of a foundering ship, a capsizing lifeboat and the dying gasps of 17 men. Stark realism was added to earlier advices of how the British freighter Usworth was battered so helplessly by a howling winter gale that she had to be abandoned, and how two rescue vessels, tossed by mountainous seas, were able to save only eleven of her 26 men. Two members of a lifeboat crew put out by the Belgian liner Jean Jadot died in the attempt, and their names were added to the 15 from the Usworth. "It is a terrible tragedy," concluded a message from the Jean Jadot, describing how the victims choked in the heavy fuel oil that had been pumped into the water in an effort to save them. The Jean Jadot, bearing two survivors, and the Cunard-White Star liner with nine, were steaming on their respective ways, having left the lifeless Usworth to b

Shanghai, Dec. 15 (P)—cold-blooded, public execution of two American missionaries by the Chinese bandits who looted Tsingteh was described in reports received today by the China Inland Mission station. Details of the fate which befell Mr. and Mrs. John C. Stam, young victims of the outlaws’ brutality, were communicated to the mission headquarters by the Rev. George Birch. Mr. Birch, a Canadian missionary, was one of a group which brought the Stams’ orphaned daughter, three-months-old Helen Priscilla, to Wuhu after the pillage of Tsingteh. The missionary said the Americans were slain by the bandits, apparently with the object of embarrassing the Chinese government in its relations with the United States. Their bodies, abandoned on a battlefield 15 miles from Tsingteh, were discovered by Chinese, who risked their lives in the search for the family. A Chinese Christian pastor, Mr. Birch rel

Geneva, Dec. 15.---(/P)—Fear was expressed in League of Nations circles tonight that Italy may refuse to recognize the league's jurisdiction in her controversy with Ethiopia. League officials foresaw the possibility that Benito Mussolini might follow the precedent set in 1923, when Italy declined to admit the league's right to interfere in her dispute with Greece over the Island of Corfu. The Italo-Ethiopian issue, nominally growing out of frontier clashes between Ethiopian and Italian forces in Africa, was attributed here indirectly to the clash of Japanese and Italian commercial issues in Africa. Because Tokyo's withdrawal from the league becomes effective soon, Geneva was following the African dispute with close attention. A report that Japan plans to send a military mission to Addis Ababa to heighten the efficiency of his majesty Emperor Haile Selassie’s army increased apprehension,

1934-03-23.text: Paris, Mar. 23. (AP)—France flatly declares that Germany is violating the Versailles treaty by rearming, in a note sent by the French government to Great Britain and made public today. In the note France says she refuses to sanction this rearmament and at the same time join other powers in disarmament. “Germany is bringing up her armaments to a much higher level than that authorized by the treaty,” says the note. One paragraph of the note makes the suggestion that another form of conference—which the French privately call a “rearmament conference”—be called among the powers concerned. The paragraph in question says the disarmament commission “is entitled to say in conjunction with all other interests at stake whether these principles be departed from,” referring to the covenant on disarming provisions. The note says five vital problems must be settled: “1. The status of semi-military org

PARIS, March 21.—(4)—French secret police were hot on new trails today in their broadening investigation of what authorities call the greatest spy ring in history—a ring they say ferreted out naval and military secrets of the United States, England and France. Fresh angles were uncovered in the first examination of documents seized yesterday when six persons were arrested as a result, authorities said, of revelations drawn from the two American prisoners, Robert Switz and his wife, Marjorie. Judge Andre Benon, the investigating magistrate, led in a further scrutiny of the confiscated documents today. Additional sensational disclosures were predicted. Police said more arrests are in prospect—perhaps as many as 25. However, they maintained the utmost secrecy regarding those under suspicion. Including the Switzes, natives of East Orange, N. J., and New York, 16 are in jail. Judge Benon main

AINTREE, England, March 23.—Dorothy Paget’s Golden Miller fought his way to victory in the Grand National Steeplechase today defeating a field of twenty-nine other great jumpers in the world’s most difficult race. J. B. Snow’s Delaneige was second. John Hay Whitney’s Thomond II, an American owned entry, was third. William Parsonage’s Forbra, the 1932 winner, was fourth. It was a magnificently run race, at a terrific pace, with the lead alternating constantly between Golden Miller, Delaneige and Forbra. During the early running Southern Hue had set the pace, but folded up under the terrible grind. F. Ambrose Whitney, whose wife won the Kellsboro Jack last year, had high hopes for victory with Sorley Boy, but he fell. Southern Hero also went down.

New York, Mar. 23 (UP)— Mrs. Margaret Meringer disclosed today she held a ticket for approximately $153,000 on Golden Miller, winner of the grand national steeplechase at Aintree, England. She was doing her housework when news of her good fortune came to her over the radio. Confused and happy, Mrs. Meringer, wife of a New York restaurant chef, said she had no immediate plans for using even a part of her fortune. The Merringers have a son and daughter, both attending public schools.

DUBLIN, March 23.—President Famon de Valera, charged with attempting to set himself up as a dictator, drove ahead determinedly today in his fight to abolish the Irish Senate. His bill was passed on first reading in the Dail Eireann last night, 79 to 43, but since the measure will be scorned in the Senate it was believed the government might go to the voters for support—possibly in June or July. President de Valera sponsored the bill after the Senate blocked a measure to ban the wearing of blue shirts, symbol of the anti-government organization led by General Eoin O'Duffy.

CHICAGO, Mar. 1L—(AP)—Birth of a baby with a two inch tail has been reported in the Journal of the American Medical Association by its London, England correspondent. “The rare condition of a baby born with a tail has been observed at the Metropolitan Hospital,” the correspondent reported, “the tail is about two inches long, tapers to a point, and is curly and normally sensitive. Removal is proposed. “Prof. Julian Huxley has remarked about the case, that different parts of the body develop at different rates during embryonic life. Usually the tail does not develop at all, but in this case apparently it has emerged at almost the same time as the other parts of the body.

Athens, Greece, March 23--Lincoln MacVeagh, United States minister, telephoned the British legation today, requesting that Mrs. Samuel Insull be granted a British visa on her passport. The request followed a move on the part of Mrs. Insull and her counsel to obtain permission for the wife of the fugitive Chicagoan to go to England. M. Pop, one of her lawyers, indicated she hoped to acquire a permanent domicile in England.

Paris, France, March 23—France rejected the latest British disarmament proposal because of suggestions that Germany be allowed to rearm, it was disclosed today. Exchanged notes were published, further diminishing the hope of a European agreement on arms.

1934-06-01.text: (Copyright, 1934, by The Associated Press) LONDON, May 31 --(AP)—Three attempts to kidnap members of his family from his home at Beverly Hills, Cal, have been graphically described by E. L. Cord, American automobile and airplane magnate, to English acquaintances. One of the attempts, involving the use of a mysterious airplane, was said to have resulted in the advice of a California police chief to the “American millionaire to take his family out of the United States for an extended visit abroad. SINCE APRIL It was learned definitely today that Cord has been in England since the middle of April, a date corresponding to the sensational kidnapping cases of William F. Gettle in California and June Robles in Arizona. Cord has taken a home in Surrey for the summer and it was said he does not intend to return to the United States until the kidnapping panic has died down. On one occasion, accord

SOUTHAMPTON, Eng., May 31. (AP)—Franklin L. Hutton, American 10 cent store millionaire, has arranged stateroom accommodations for his daughter, Princess Barbara Hutton Mdivani to return to New York with him June 6 but has not provided accommodations for her husband, Prince Alexis Mdivani. Hutton will arrive here tomorrow. His arrangements for the return became known today. The millionaire is coming aboard the S. S. Bremen and is said to have made his arrangements by radio telephone from the ship itself. He was understood to be planning a quick trip to London where his daughter now is staying with the prince. There he is expected to join her and bring her with him back to re-embark upon the Bremen for the return voyage.

CROYDON, England, May 31 (AP). A French freight airplane struck a wireless mast in a heavy mist near the airport today, skimmed several houses, crashed into another and then demolished two garages, crushing automobiles inside them. Captain Raymond de Fives, the pilot, and Rogert L’Huilier, mechanic, were killed.

(By The Associated Press) Following a tiff between French and British representatives, the disarmament conference was in recess today at Geneva. The disarmament leaders spent their holiday trying to save the parley from collapse. Meanwhile: The biggest display of naval power in the history of the United States— 96 warships— passed in review before President Roosevelt. A French fleet set out from Orient to determine the effectiveness of coast defenses. Germans Celebrate Germany celebrated the anniversary of the naval battle of Jutland which both that nation and Great Britain claim to have won during the world war. Japan launched its new cruiser Mikuma which carries fifteen 6-inch rifles and is expected to do 33 knots. The war in the Chaco Boreal between Paraguay and Bolivia went right on, although Bolivia asked the League of Nations to fix responsibility under article 15 of the covenant a

London, - June 2 (UP)—Fast talking by Alexis Mdivani, worthy of the diplomacy with which his forbears held sway among the goat herders of their native Georgia, seemed today to have won reprieve if not pardon from Barbara Hutton, his five-and-ten-cent store heiress wife. Mr. and Mrs. Franklyn L. Hutton, Barbara's father and mother, arrived on a rescue mission on the Bremen yesterday to investigate their marital rift. Alexis was at the dock to tell his story. He motored them the 75 miles through the beautiful aunts and surrey countryside to London, talking all the way. At the Dorchester hotel he diplomatically left them, kissing Mrs. Hutton’s hand with Georgian gallantry, and they went after leaving their bags to a nursing home where Barbara was under treatment. The talk, apparently, had won the day. The United Press learned on unimpeachable authority that Hutton persuaded Barbara to meet

SOUTHAMPTON, England, May 31.~(AP)--Revelation that accommodations have been reserved for Princess Barbara Hutton Mdivani to sail for New York with her father on June 6 heightened interest today in reports the young American heiress and her Georgian husband are about to separate. The father, Franklin P. Hutton, who is on his way here on the S. S. Bremen, made reservations for himself and daughter, it was learned, but none for the husband, Prince Alexis Mdivani. The reservations, it was said, were made by telephone from the Bremen, which will arrive here tomorrow. The father is expected to go to London, where the princess and her husband are staying, immediately upon arrival here.

London.—(AP)—Great Britain's initiative in arranging preliminary conversations makes London the logical site of the 1935 naval conference, authoritative sources said today. Washington and Tokyo, it was understood, studied the matter before replying to Britain's invitation to preliminary discussions and each decided it has no objection to holding the conference here if officially invited.

LONDON, May 31—The British war debt proposal, based on the idea of future bilateral discussions between London and Washington, was authoritatively stated today to have been transmitted to the American capital. Whether it had been delivered to the State Department to await President Roosevelt's return was not indicated, but it was clear the government expects it to be published shortly. It was categorically denied in the highest possible quarters that Great Britain had approached either France or Italy in the matter, and it was pointed out this country has always opposed the idea of a general conference. (In Rome, the foreign office officially denied Italy had been consulted by Great Britain in the subject or expected to be, and in France officials made similar statements.) The note is understood to propose that a conference consider the debts question, either with or without a token paym

1934-06-30.text: LONDON, June 30 (UP).—Airport crews of half a dozen countries watched today for the red, white and blue Bellanca monoplane City of Warsaw in which Benjamin and Joseph Adamowicz, Polish-American brothers of Brooklyn, N. Y., were due to pass over Western Europe on their way from America to Warsaw. A special air ministry weather report said that the weather from 400 miles west of Ireland to the coast was mainly good. There were moderate south to southwesterly winds. It was cloudy. Visibility was good. When they left Harbor Grace, Newfoundland, at 4:57 a. m. EDT yesterday the brothers estimated they would make the trip to Warsaw in 30 to 32 hours. Their course lay over Ireland, 2000 miles from Newfoundland; England, Holland and Germany.

LONDON (P)—Outbreak of a bitter British-German trade war at midnight seemed almost certain when delegates failed Saturday to make progress toward agreement on the German foreign debt moratorium. At noon negotiations were threatened, after three days of futile work with complete collapse. Spokesmen for both sides were pessimistic. Germany's complete moratorium on foreign debts is effective at midnight. The declaration of trade war would come when the Nazi government failed to deposit in the bank for international settlements, the reparations bank, the July installment of the Young reparations loan, due Sunday. Great Britain is prepared to operate as from midnight its clearing house system to seize German credits to pay holders of the Young and Dawes loans, in addition to some others. Seizure would be effected by imposing a 20 percent levy on all imports from Germany. Germany, it was learn

| LONDON, June 30—(UP)—The 9th Duke of Marlborough, who 'wooed, won and then lost two ‘American society beauties, died today. | The duke died at his London house in Carlton House Terrace at 10:30 a.m. | The first duke married Consuelo Vanderbilt of New York, one of the most brilliant matches of an era when American wealth and 'English lineage was considered, in society circles, the ideal combination. They were divorced in 1920, and later the duchess obtained an annulment from the Roman Catholic church at the request of her Catholic second husband, Col. Jacques Balsan of France. In 1921 he married Gladys Deacon of Boston.

London, June 30 (UNS)—Some apprehension was felt here today for the safety of Joseph and Benjamin Adamowicz, brothers, flying from New York to Warsaw. At 11 a.m. (6 a.m. EDT) they had not been reported, although it was estimated they should have passed over the British Isles sometime during the early morning. Berlin, June 30 (INS)—All airports throughout Germany and Poland were keeping a sharp watch today for Benjamin and Joseph Adamowicz, the Brooklyn soda pop manufacturers, who were believed nearing Europe on a flight from New York to Warsaw. No word had been received from them at an early hour this morning, but little anxiety was felt, since the flying brothers themselves had estimated it would require at least thirty hours, perhaps longer.

LONDON, June 30 (Saturday) — aPp—Coast guards and airports were instructed to be on the lookout for two Brooklyn flyers, expected over the British Isles some time today in an effort to fly non-stop from Harbor Grace, Newfoundland, to Warsaw, Poland. The flyers, Benjamin and Joseph Adamowicz, will have good flying weather as they approach Ireland, the air ministry announced. For 400 miles off Ireland, the brothers probably will encounter moderate to fresh south or southwesterly winds, with visibility mainly good. HARBOR GRACE, Newfoundland, June 20.—(4)—Two Brooklyn businessmen who took up flying for sport were far out over the north Atlantic tonight in their second attempt to make a non-stop flight from North America to Poland, land of their birth. Benjamin and Joseph Adamowicz, soda-pop manufacturers, had a westerly wind to speed them in their big, high-winged Bellanca monoplane, after

By Associated Press PARIS, June 30.—The monoplane "City of Warsaw" bearing two Brooklyn fliers, landed safely today at Saint Andre de Messei, Although their goal was Warsaw, Poland, they were forced to land because of a shortage of gasoline. The fliers, Benjamin and Joseph Adamowicz, brothers, hopped off from Harbor Grace, Newfoundland, yesterday at 3:58 a.m. in an effort to fly their big, bright-hued monoplane, the "Warsaw," veteran of one trans-Atlantic crossing, non-stop to Warsaw, The silent flying pair, whose hopes for a successful flight to Warsaw were dashed last year when they cracked up in Newfoundland, set their big plane down safely. Saint Andre de Messei is a village of 234 inhabitants, 150 miles northwest of Paris.

Hitler suppressed a Nazi storm troop mutiny, before it was well started today, at the cost of the lives of Gen. Kurt von Schleicher, former chancellor and Reichswehr commander, and several of his own best men. Schleicher was shot as he resisted arrest as a conspirator against the government. Leaders of the mutinous element in the storm troops were also killed, or committed suicide as they faced arrest and court martial. Thus came to a head a series of sweeping and bloody maneuvers which have marked the unrest and sporadic grumbling that has tested the strength of the Nazi regime in recent times. Storm Troopers Under Arrest Storm troop headquarters all over the country were occupied by state police or gendarmes — the picked black uniformed bodyguard unit of the storm troopers — and Reichswehr soldiers. There were reports from some places of disturbances which meant resistance of the mutin

Captain Ernst Roehm, national chief of the Nazi storm troops, committed suicide when Hitler had him arrested as a conspirator against the government. Former Chancellor Kurt Von Schleicher, leader of the reactionary Conservatives and Monarchists, was killed "resisting arrest" as a conspirator. Heinrich Klausmer, chief of the "Catholic action" party, was killed in his office by one of Hitler's special blackshirted guards, a Schutzstaffel member. When Von Schleicher was killed, his wife, Frau Elizabeth Von Schleicher, also was slain in the fracas that went with the arrest. Roehm Led Radicals Roehm was regarded as the most extreme leader of the radical Nazis; Von Schleicher was the extreme reactionary who favored the restoration of the monarchy to Germany. Vice Chancellor Franz Von Papen, the man who two weeks ago warned Hitler that a second revolution led by extremists was impending, was ta

1934-10-27.text: London, Oct. 26.—(AP)—A bell was voiced in some American quarters tonight that Japan is trying to wreck tri-power naval talks in progress here. Refusal of the Japanese delegates to fix the maximum figure to which they would be willing to limit defensive ships gave rise to the belief that they were seeking so to entangle the conversations that compromise would be impossible, thus giving them an opportunity to abandon the discussions. These American sources were convinced that Japan would excuse her walkout on the plea that the other two participating powers, Great Britain and the United States, would not give her sufficient rights under the new treaty she proposes to make her defensively secure. This, it was expected she would contend, she was forced to take matters in her own hands. Counter-Plan Once the conversations were at an end, the Americans believe, Japan would propose a non-aggre
SINGAPORE. (AP)—King Prajadhipok of Siam has abdicated his throne at Bangkok, said report reaching here today. The king is in London.

LONDON, Oct. 27—Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, Japanese sea dog delegate to the three-power conversations, said today he will stay here a year if necessary to get a satisfactory naval agreement. That was the outspoken admiral’s reply to reports the Japanese were building up a situation which would enable them to walk out on the English and Americans. Ambassador Tsuneo Matsudaira arranged a golf engagement with Norman Davis to discuss the situation and iron out difficulties which have arisen during the week. Admiral Yamamoto believes the Japanese proposals for a new naval treaty constitute an epoch-making plan for ending all aggression and bringing about real peace.

- MELBOURNE, Oct. 27—(Saturday)—(AP)—Cathcart Jones and K. W. Waller, fourth place in the London-to-Melbourne air derby not good enough for them, took off at dawn today to follow the 11,500-mile trail back in an effort to set two new records. The English pair believe their green (De Havilland) Comet was the fastest ship in the race and hope to better the record-smashing 70 hours, 59 minutes, 50 seconds the derby winners, C. W. They also wanted to set a mark for the round trip that would give other airmen something to shoot at. As Jones and Waller set out jauntily along the course leading back over half the world and across the equator, four-fifths of the 20 planes that left Mildenhall airdrome last Saturday still had not reached Melbourne. John H. Wright and John Polando, who were delayed by their arrest in Persia, planned to continue the flight from Karachi, India. They were earlier rep

LONDON, (AP).—King Prajaanipok of Siam apparently did not intend to comment on reports from Singapore that he intended to abdicate his throne. The king at present living quietly in a Surrey retreat and is having his eyes treated by London specialists. He has given no indication of his future plans nor has he made any official remarks about abdication. His secretary said the first he knew about the latest abdication rumor from the Straits Settlement was through inquiries made of him. The Siamese legation knew nothing of the report.

Darwin, Australia, Oct. 27. (12) — Cathcart Jones and Kenneth Waller arrived here at 6:15 p.m. today (2:15 a.m. EST) to complete the second leg of their race flight to England. They made the 1,384-mile flight from Charleville in 63 4/5 hours, averaging 205 miles an hour in their attempt to cut the London to Melbourne time of C. W. A. Scott and T. Campbell Black, who covered the distance in 70 hours, 59 minutes and X seconds. Storms over the dangerous Timor Sea prevented the fliers from taking off on the next leg of their trip and they decided to wait until dawn, Sunday. Squadron leader Malcolm MacGregor of New Zealand landed at Charleville at 3:28 p.m. (12:28 A.M. E.B.S.T.) on his way to Melbourne. Thus the English racers on their trip toward England are passing the still-contending derbyists, going in the opposite direction. John H. Wright and John Polando left Karacht, India, continuin

DARWIN, Australia, Oct. 27. (UP) —Lieut. Cathcart Jones and Ken Waller, British fliers, arrived today on their way from Melbourne to England, trying to better the time of C. W. A. Scott and Tom Campbell Black in the Mildenhall-Melbourne race. They planned to remain here overnight because of storms in the Timor Sea. Scott and Black made the flight in 71 hours 18 seconds. The record for a flight from Australia to England is eight days, nine hours. This record was made in September by James Melrose of Australia, flying to England to compete in the Mildenhall-Melbourne race. Jones and Cathcart left Melbourne at 6:35 a. m. today Darwin time (4:05 p. m. yesterday E. S. T.). They averaged 194.877 miles an hour on the 2,176-mile flight from Melbourne, including the 40-minute halt at Charleville.

- LONDON, Oct. 27.--(AP)--Rumors spread through London tonight that a revolt had occurred in Siam, but these were not confirmed in advices from Bangkok which followed a report from Singapore early today that King Projadhipok, now in England, had abdicated.

1934-10-10.text: (Associated Press Foreign Staff) London, Oct. 10.—(4)—Yugoslavia's new king, young Peter II left London at 2 p.m. today to pay homage at the bier of his murdered father, Alexander I, and to embark upon his new monarchial duties. The 11-year-old boy monarch, snatched from sleep in the quiet of a countryside English school, walked courageously to the train in Victoria station here, holding the hand of his maternal grandmother, the Dowager Queen Marie of Rumania. They had gone to the station from a west-end hotel where hurried plans for a trip to France were completed about noon. A cheer arose from the sympathetic English spectators as the world’s youngest king left the hotel walking at the side of his grandmother, but an impressive quiet fell over the crowd at the station as the royal party boarded a train. Peter, who yesterday wore a school cap of the Sandroyd school, today wore a brown h

(Copyright, 1934. by United Press.) LONDON, Oct. 10 (UP)--Europe today awaited the subsidence of shock over the Marseilles assassination to start anew its race to consolidate alliances in preparation for armed peace or bitter war. For months an all round shift in European diplomatic alignments had been pending, statesmen were going to and fro from capital to capital, sometimes secretly, to negotiate. Alexander himself went to France on one of the most important diplomatic missions in months. Since the World War, Jugoslavia, with its co-members of the Little Entente, Czechoslovakia and Roumania, had been closely allied with France. In recent weeks Jugoslavia had shown leanings toward Germany, and the protective cordon which France had thrown around Nazi Germany was threatened. Jugoslavia was on terms of near-hatred with Italy, and Barthou was going at the end of this month to see Premier

LONDON, Oct. 10 (4).—Peter Karageorge, 11 years old, tumbled into bed last night a carefree schoolboy at Sanroyd school. Today he arose as King Peter II, ruler of Jugoslavia. The news of his father’s tragic death at Marseille, kept from him all last night, was imparted early this morning. Before Peter could realize the significance of the news, he was en route to Belgrade. Last night the housemaster was notified to arouse Peter earlier than his dormitory mates. With sleep still in his eyes, he was awakened; a message was whispered in his ear that urgent news awaited him in the headmaster’s office. Dressing hastily, Peter followed the housemaster to the school office where his tutor, C. C. Parrott, and the headmaster were seated. Probably still wondering what school rules he had broken, the news was imparted that changed him from Peter Karageorge to King Peter II. Breakfast was hastily se

San Francisco, Oct. 9.—(4’)—An appeal for the assistance of American labor in building up “a mass of hostile opinion” against such dictatorships as those of Italy and Germany was made to the American Federation of Labor convention here today by Walter M. Citrine, secretary of the British Trades Union Congress. Citrine referred to the fascism of Italy and Germany as “the greatest danger to democratic institutions today.” He said not less than 2,000 persons had been killed in a “reign of terror” accompanying the rise of fascism in Italy and that similar things occurred in Germany. “But for the financial help of reactionary employers,” he said, “fascism would not have been possible in either country.” Row Due Delegates said they expected the building trades dispute to come before the convention shortly for a finish fight. A skirmish heralding a possible battle in the federation over the des

WASHINGTON, Oct. 9.—The coming London naval conversations already are heading toward the same old game. The delegates seem to be practicing ventriloquism and imitations, as usual. Your hair will stand on end when you hear the Japanese proposal. If the U. S. diplomatic grapevine is still as trustworthy as it used to be, the Japanese—these same Japanese who have been slyly hinting that they want naval parity with Britain and the United States—are going to take the lead for disarmament—yes, disarmament. That should be the best peace-loving imitation yet offered of the international The explanation, of course, is that the proposal will be grossly unacceptable. It will be the kind of disarmament which might help Britain and Japan, but would pinch us. At least that is what President Roosevelt's naval experts have heard. They understand that the Japanese offer will be based on a reduction in th

MADRID. (Copyright by AP.) Spain's six-day red revolt was a dangerous mass of embers Tuesday night, flaring into gunfire here and there as the conservative government of Premier Lerroux remained in power. Former Premier Manuel Azana, one of those sought at Barcelona following the smashing of a separatist revolt Sunday, was arrested Tuesday. He was found hiding in Barcelona at the home of a Dr. Gubernes, and had taken refuge on a balcony while police were searching the house. With him was arrested a syndicalist leader, Senor Pestena, friend of the imprisoned Catalonian president, Luis Companys. Tenaciously the socialist and communist rebels held on in northern Spain, rallying at Oviedo, Asturias province, and barricading themselves against attack in the city’s labor district. The army was waiting reinforcements before attacking. A column of troops under General Ochoa was moving into the m

The body, dressed in the stained fighting uniform the king wore in the World War, was carried in state from the Marseilles prefecture, where it had been lying, to a waic- (Turn to Page 10—No 17)

to Marseille to claim her dead, while all Europe waited, tense, to measure the effect of King Alexander's murder. Even as Queen Marie, arriving by special train, went to the place where her husband's body lay, another death resulting from yesterday's tragedy occurred. Madame Duprec, a widow, who was wounded by bullets from the same gun that killed King Alexander and France's Foreign Minister Louis Barthou, died at a hospital. Others who were killed were a police officer and the assassin himself, Petrus Kalemen.
