General Alfonse Joseph Georges of AIX EN PROVENCE, France, Oct. 10. — Two fugitive companions of Petrus Kalemen, assassin of King Alexander, were the objects of a wide police hunt today when it was discovered they stayed at a hotel

1934-10-13.text: | NEW YORK, Oct. 18 (AP).— King winter sent his advance agent into the northeastern part of the country today with snow and low temperatures prevalent over a wide area, Chill blasts were felt throughout the New England states where snow fell in many places. Maine was the hardest hit. At Caribou 10 inches of snow was reported. In many sections the potato crop was threatened unless the snow melted. Presque Isle, Me., reported a 14 inch snowfall and telephone and power lines were laid low by the storm, Snow and freezing temperatures were reported also in New York state. The temperature in the Adirondacks hovered around 20 degrees, New York city felt sharp weather with the mercury close to the freezing point.

BOSTON, Oct. 13.— (UP) —The most severe early-season blizzard in New England's history raged today, with far northern sections already knee-deep in snow. Maine was hardest hit. Nearly every portion of the six northeastern states felt effects of the unpredicted storm. Shipping was hampered and small craft clung snugly to harbors. Highways were blockaded by snow with hundreds of motorists marooned in stalled cars on isolated roads. Neither official forecasts nor the long-range predictions of the almanacs had carried a hint of the impending blizzard. Weather-wise New Englanders, who have experienced many “green” Christmases in recent years, were astonished by a “white” Columbus Day. (Snow flurries began at mid-day yesterday and it was still snowing this morning, flakes in Boston being almost the size of half dollars.) Snow fell Oct. 2, 1899 and Oct. 10, 1925, but in each case the fall was r

LONDON, Oct. 12 (UP).—The government-operated telephone service announced at 9:30 a. m. today that telephone communication with Spain was temporarily suspended in both directions. The Spanish authorities told the United Press Madrid bureau that the telephonic prohibition was the result of false news sent abroad by certain correspondents, who were not correspondents of the United Press.
EASTBOURNE, Eng. Oct. 18 (UP).-William Kemp, 29, was summoned to police court today for driving his 28-year-old automobile “without due care and attention.”

(Copyright, 1984, by The Associated Press) Belgrade, Oct. 12.—The boy king, Peter, came back to his native Yugoslavia tonight, his carefree schooldays in England over. While the country waited in deep mourning for the arrival at Split of the body of King Alexander, assassinated Tuesday at Marseille, Peter's special train crossed the border and the 11-year-old ruler set foot once more on Yugoslav soil at the frontier station of Tasinica.

By the Associated Press The Yugoslav situation Saturday: Belgrade—King Peter II acclaimed by huge crowd on arrival from England, Yugoslavia tranquil, Paris—Police hunt Czech “gun girl” in Marseille assassination plot. They accused the terrorist band “Ustashi,” of Hungary, as the power behind the assassination of King Alexander. London—Great Britain disclosed as wanting League of Nations to investigate Marseille slayings. Fears tension between Hungary and Yugoslavia. Rome—Mussolini handling Italo-Yugoslav relations cautiously to prevent breakdown in peace structure. Paris—Funeral of Foreign Minister Louis Barthou, slain with Alexander, draws world leaders.

A snow storm and low temperatures brought early winter scenes to New England Saturday while most of the nation enjoyed sunny autumn weather. Louisiana sweltered under a hot sun. Three ships were in trouble off the New England coast. New England states reported the most severe early blizzard in history, with Maine and other states having snowfall which blocked highways in some sections. Temperatures were in the lower thirties in Boston and snow was 18 inches deep in some parts of Maine. The temperature was 86 in New Orleans. Upper New York state reported the mercury in the lower thirties and the weather forecast was for continued cold tonight, although tomorrow will be warmer. Snow flurries fell at Scroon Lake and elsewhere in New York. Many mountain peaks and some football gridirons were snow clad.

LONDON, Oct. 8 (P)—The British government wants the League of Nations to have full responsibility for investigating the Marseille assassinations should international relations become strained, it was said authoritatively today. Leaders of the government are anxiously watching latest disclosures indicating an international terrorist organization with members from Italy, Hungary and other nations was linked to the assassinations of King Alexander and Louis Barthou, and the possible effect on relations between Yugoslavia and Hungary and Italy. If proved the plot originated in Hungary it was feared a political situation might arise. It was pointed out that earlier information that the arrested men carried Czechoslovakian passports, now established as forgeries, was not so serious, as Yugoslavia and Czechoslovakia have been staunch allies since the war. But Hungary has consistently demanded r

1934-05-23.text: Port Darwin, North Australia, May 23 (AP)—Jean Batten, 24 year old New Zealand girl flier, reached this city today after a solo flight from England on which she set a new women’s record for the distance. Miss Batten made the long, hazardous air jaunt in 15 days, 23 hours, 25 minutes, eclipsing the former woman’s mark of nineteen and one half days, held by Amy Johnson, wife of Capt. James A. Mollison, British flier. Miss Johnson completed her flight and set the old record May 24, 1930. Miss Batten was making her third attempt at the flight when she soared away from Lympne, England, May 5. Her first effort was in April, 1938. Then her machine broke down beyond repair at Karachi, India. Last month, trying again, she crashed in Roma. She received severe face lacerations. Nevertheless, as soon as her plane could be repaired, she flew back to England and began preparations for the third try wh

LONDON, May 22 (?)—A complete about-face by Great Britain on the war debts question was hinted strongly in informed circles today, with the possibility that the government may approach Washington for a discussion of the subject. Heretofore, the official attitude has been that the United States must take the initiative in any reopening of the debt question.

May 23.—(UP).-—Four ace American golfers — Johnny Goodman, of Omaha, George Dunlap, of New York, Lawson Little of San Francisco and Jessie Guilford of Boston — today moved into the fourth round of the British amateur golf championship. Meantime three members of the original overseas delegation of 14 were eliminated. The losers were Johnny Rischer of Cincinnati, Jack Westland of Chicago and Douglas Grant of California and London.

DUBLIN. (#). Overcoming the jinx which harassed them on the west coast of Ireland, Capt. Georg Pond and Lieut. Secare Sabelli brought their orange monoplane safely to Dublin. The fliers will refuel at Baldonnel field Wednesday and expect to take off no later than Thursday morning for Rome, the destination of the flight which started in New York on the morning of May 14. The plane landed at Baldonnel airdrome one hour and forty minutes after taking off from a muddy field near Lahinch where it had made a forced landing after the trans-Atlantic flight.

Lahinch, Irish Free State, May 21. (4)—Presently forced into inaction as repairs are being made on their Trans-Atlantic monoplane, Capt. George Pond and Lieut. Sabelli made plans to enter the coming race from London to Melbourne, Australia. The filers will first, however, carry out their project of visiting Rome and then flying back to New York from Ireland, Capt. Pond.

World capitals turned a speculative eye Wednesday on President Roosevelt's proposal to Congress for a bi-metallic basis for currency. The London Post said: “Events alone can show whether the whole project is anything more than a dexterous maneuver to put silver on the shelf.” The London Times said: “It is extremely doubtful how far prices will be affected by manipulating the metallic content of the currency unit.” Rome was interested in how the new metallic standard might affect war debt payments. Paris affected not to be interested at all. Official comment was withheld in Berlin.

Port Darwin, Australia, May 24 — Miss Jean Batten, 24, of New Zealand, who sold her piano to pay for a course in flying, set a new women’s record for the England-Australia flight by arriving here yesterday in 14 days, 23 hours, 53 minutes. The former record, held by Amy Johnson Mollison, transatlantic flyer, was 19½ days. A Gypsy Moth light plane brought attractive Miss Batten to Port Darwin to better Miss Johnson’s record by nearly five days. She had also three mascots—a lion's bone, a medal of St. Christopher, and a silk Union Jack. It was her third try at flying to Australia;

Dublin, May 22 (AP)—Capt. George Pond and Lieut. Cesare Sabelli landed their transatlantic airplane at Baldonnel field here at 8:50 p. m. (2:50 p. m. E.S.T.), after a flight from Lahinch on the west coast.

1934-02-23.text: LONDON, Feb. 23. U.P)—Sir Edward Elgar, master of the king's music and a composer of world renown, died today. He was 76 years old. Many critics believed him one of the greatest of modern day composers. He had been in practical retirement for 13 years, grief stricken at the death of his wife. Elgar died at his Worcester home, Marl Bank, to which he was removed early in January after he seemed to be recovering from an abdominal operation he underwent here in October. On Saturday his condition became worse, and his death had been expected at any time. Only two weeks ago, using two telephone lines from his sick bed, he conducted an orchestra which was making a phonographic record of his composition “March From Caractacus.” Immediate plans to pay national honors to Sir Edward were halted when his daughter revealed, a few hours after his death, that frequently, in recent months, he had asked

BERLIN, Feb. 23. ()—There will be no devaluation of the mark Dr. Hjalmar Schacht, president of the Reichbank, has promised German bankers. Such a move, he told a group of bank executives yesterday, would only result in further devaluation by the United States and Great Britain. The central bank president warned his hearers they would be out of a job unless they catch the Nazi spirit. “The men who today head German banks,” he said, “can fulfill their tasks only if, with a full heart, they devote themselves to the spirit of the new state.”

WASHINGTON, Feb. 23 (AP).—Investigation of the holdings of the Pennsylvania Railroad company and the Pennroad corporation in New England railroads was ordered by the interstate commerce commission today on complaint of six New England governors. They charged that the holdings of the Pennsylvania railroad and its holding company, the Pennroad corporation, in the Boston and Maine railroad and the New York, New Haven and Hartford railroad might have the effect directly or indirectly of substantially lessening competition.

LONDON—Lady Mount Temple, wife of a former minister of transport, wants the plain gold wedding band abolished. She told the National Jewellers’ Association at their annual dinner that it was a “monstrosity,” and she appealed for its deposition in favor of the much more beautiful gem-set ring or the plain platinum circlet.
WORCESTER, England, Feb. 23 (—Sir Edward Elgar, British composer, died at his home early Wednesday. He was 77 years old. Sir Edward had been ill since an operation in October.

BRUSSELS, Feb. 23. (2.—The new king of the Belgians, Leopold III, was enthroned today when the former Crown Prince took the oath to defend the constitution before both houses of Parliament. He officially became king, succeeding his father, the late King Albert I, at the conclusion of reciting the oath today. The young monarch spoke the oath before the legislators and assembled dignitaries. The public mourning for the dead Albert was suspended for two days as a medley of church bells pealed for his son. Only minor communist and separatist disturbances interrupted the beginning of Leopold's reign.

Paris, Feb. 23.—Premier Doumergue called today for the capture, dead or alive, of the mysterious slayer of Judge Albert Prince, “the man who knew all” in the Stavisky banking scandal. The premier’s order went out after Minister of the Interior Albert Sarraut declared he believed France in the grip of a “mafia” gang determined to block the investigation. The government offered 100,000 francs (about $6,500) for the arrest and conviction of the slayer. Relief grew in official circles today that the judge was murdered because he knew too much. Still, police said they were baffled by conflicting tales of the killing. Bound and mutilated, Judge Prince's body was found on a railway track near Dijon Wednesday. Nearby lay a bloody knife. His briefcase had been rifled. He had been brutally slain just one day before he was to have testified in an investigation into the collapse of Serge Stavisky’s

Brussels, Feb. 22.—(#)—The body of the knightly King Albert lay in peace tonight in the crypt of a little gray church near the Laeken royal castle and plans went forward for the enthronement of his son, Prince Leopold. Albert was buried with the pomp of courtly custom; Leopold will be made king with similar circumstances, but without the tears that marked the cortege of princes, diplomats, clergymen and commoners honoring the dead monarch. As Big Guns Boom Eight hours of military processions, religious rites, and cannons’ solemn salutes ended this afternoon with the lowering of the body into its last resting place beside the coffins of Leopold II and III. One man was killed in a fall from a tree in the royal park and two men were seriously injured as they fell from a balustrade while watching the funeral processions. Several score others were injured in accidents along the route. Members

1934-05-08.text: LONDON— A grim fight to restrict world trade proceeded today while British and other statesmen continued statements that restoration of the flow of international commerce was essential to economic recovery. The cabinet, after having declared a trade war against virile, ambitious Japan, endeavored to work out measures to impose import quotas in the crown colonies on Japanese goods. It awaited anxiously expected tariff reprisals from Japan. Rubber men of the principal producing countries were perfecting the details of a plan designed to restrict sharply the export of rubber, hoping for higher prices — principally to American consumers, by far the greatest users of rubber. Grain Experts Meet Wheat experts of the United States and other producing states meeting here as the international wheat advisory committee sought to work out an agreement to fix minimum export prices for the whole world,

LONDON, May 7.——An open trade war with Japan was declared today as the British government announced an “intensification” of commerce within the empire. The House of Commons applauded while Walter Runciman, president of the Board of Trade, outlined concisely his government's decision to take whatever action “the government believes necessary” to halt Japanese competition with British goods, particularly textiles, within the British Empire. He hinted that the “battle might be waged in other parts of the world as well. In the debate following Runciman's announcement, J. H. Thomas, secretary for Dominions, replied to attacks by Sir Herbert Samuel, Liberal leader, by reiterating the government’s empire free trade policy and declaring that every effort will be made to intensify the exchange of products among dominions and colonies. U. S. Policies Attacked Thomas sharply attacked American econo

DARJEELING, Bengal, India, May 3 (P)—Two Bengali assassins fired revolvers at Governor-General Sir John Anderson at a race meeting at Lebong today. Sir John was uninjured, but police killed one of the Bengalis and seriously wounded the other. A British woman was wounded slightly by one of the assassin’s bullets.

(Copyright, 1934, United Press) WASHINGTON, May 8.—The United States appears today to be headed for debt stalemate with the Soviet Union similar to that which disrupted Moscow's negotiations with France and Great Britain. Ten years after those countries recognized the Soviet Union their respective debt claims remain unsettled. Attorney General Homer S. Cummings has formally proclaimed the Soviet Union to be in default. Ambassador Alexander Troyanovsky protested to the State Department, contending his government had signed no obligation to pay debts incurred by previous Russian governments. Further complicating the debt muddle is the Rappallo Treaty between Moscow and Berlin in which Germany waived all claims against the Soviet Union with the stipulation that Germany must be paid if Moscow ever pays any other claimant. France and Great Britain recognized the Soviet Union in 1924. Great Br

LONDON, May 8. — Reports of a British cabinet break on the question of disarmament gained momentum rapidly Tuesday. Some newspapers went so far as to describe the situation as a The crux of the differences is said to be whether in view of failure to arrange a disarmament convention, the British government shall attempt again to harmonize its actions.

WASHINGTON, May 8. -- The United States is through accepting "token" payments from the European debtor nations, it was learned today. This government will declare Great Britain, Italy and the other former “token” payers in default under the Johnson Act the middle of next month unless they meet their unpaid obligations in full or a new debt agreement is reached in the meantime. Both possibilities are considered doubtful and indications are increasing the United States will receive absolutely nothing from the debtor nations with the exception of the little republic of Finland, which is expected to continue meeting its obligations in full. Official announcement of the government's view that under the Johnson Act it cannot continue to exempt those nations which make “token” payments from the defaulting class may be made within the next few days. This action is expected to terminate the so-ca

* TOKYO (#)—A high foreign office official said today that Japan believes the British import quotas against Japanese competition infringe upon the most favored nation clause of the Anglo-Japanese treaty. However, he added, Japan will withhold retaliatory action—seeking first to protect her treaty rights through diplomatic methods. At Osaka, textile leaders expressed the opinion the quotas, announced in London yesterday by Walter Runciman, president of the British Board of Trade, would do little harm to Japanese trade. These authorities declared that if British action to place restrictions on Japan’s exports to crown colonies, starting Wednesday, goes no further than Runciman indicated it will not be necessary for the Tokyo government to act. Nevertheless, Saburo Kurusu, chief of the commercial bureau of the foreign office, was assigned to pave the way for a possible Japanese course of ac

TOKIO, May 8. (?)—Japanese government officials and industrialists quietly organized their resources today to defend their far-flung commercial empire against the first onslaughts of the trade war declared by Great Britain. Activity in official and commercial circles belied the intimations of a government spokesman that Japan’s textile leaders, most affected by the British move, are not disturbed by the order imposing quota restrictions on Japanese goods in British colonies. Fusajiro Abe, chairman of the Japanese Spinners Association, insisted that there is no need for immediate retaliation. There was much talk here that the cabinet would invoke against the British the extraordinary powers granted by the tariff authority law. The statute, which became effective May 1, was framed to meet such an emergency. It gives the government power to revise or revoke foreign import allotments and to

1934-10-01.text: (World Copyright, 1934, United Press) PARIS, Oct. 1—Premier Gaston Doumergue of France, in an exclusive interview today with the United Press, declared that the safeguarding of world democracy is in the hands of three nations—the United States, Great Britain and France. Himself engaged in a fight to preserve the last of the great strongholds of European democracy, Premier Doumergue drew a parallel between his own efforts and those of President Franklin D. Roosevelt—taking a definite stand as an advocate of sound gold money and against inflation and artificial tampering with currencies, and pointing to his opposition to Socialism and Communism, France's suave leader directed my attention to the similarity of efforts by the French and American governments to find a way out of the world crisis without sacrificing the principles of democracy which were born of their two revolutions. The Associated Press, in a series of seven articles starting today, will describe the status of feminism in foreign nations. The series will include reports from Buenos Aires, Madrid, Amsterdam, Oslo, Vienna, Paris, Montevideo, Rome, Berlin, Shanghai, Rio de Janeiro, London, Dublin, Moscow and Tokyo... the A.P. By The Associated Press In a world in which old foundations are shaking and revolutions are chasing each other across the frontiers, how are women faring? In the rush of more spectacular events what has been the fate of feminism? Answers to these questions were sought from the foreign bureaus of the Associated Press. In some places the cause of women's rights has made notable advances. In others it has lost ground. In numerous nations feminism has been forgotten for the moment, lost in the surge of other affairs. The Associated Press will present the reports of its foreign bureaus

Vienna — Austria with “regrets” declined today to the demand of the United States government for the extradition of Captain Ivan Poderjay, husband of Agnes Tufverson, Detroit and New York woman who has been missing since January. Under the extradition treaty between the two governments, it was pointed out, perjury does not constitute an extraditable offense. A perjury charge against Poderjay was filed by the New York district attorney's office, which wanted to question him in his wife’s disappearance. Poderjay, who has been in jail in Vienna for several months, married Miss Tufverson in New York last December shortly before she disappeared. Poderjay later revealed he had been previously married and the perjury indictment was returned against him in connection with the marriage license granted him in New York. Miss Tufverson was a successful New York lawyer before her marriage.

Hametin, Germany. Sept. 30.- Adolf Hitler was accorded comparatively scant applause today by 700,000 farmer folk, gathered for the national harvest thanks festival on storied Bueckeberg Hill, for his assurances that better days are coming. Der Fuehrer exhorted his hearers to put forth greater and greater efforts in the fatherland’s financial struggle, and laid down renewed claims that the Nazis had helped the farmers' lot immeasurably. “Because of a single will and through a single power we are gathered here,” Hitler proclaimed in an increasingly hoarse and rasping voice to farmers and their families mingling with Reichswehr men and Storm Troopers on the sun-bathed Weser hills. “Before January 30 last year we could not hold our hands together in peace to make life quiet and peers. A single cry of despair came from the whole Reich. A third of all Germans were jobless. Outsiders predicted

TOKYO, Oct. 1.—(%)—The Japanese military command in Manchukuo reported to Tokyo today it planned to protest to Soviet Russia after an exchange of rifle fire between Soviet and Japanese troops last Tuesday. No casualties resulted from the shooting which took place on the eastern border of Manchukuo. The boundary line there has long been in dispute. The Japanese report said the Russians shot at a Japanese surveying party near Sanchakou, a military guard over the party returned the fire, the report added, and the Russians withdrew. The Russian version says about 25 Japanese cavalrymen fired on six Russians, who were on Soviet territory. The Russians retired without firing, their explanation says.

HAMELIN, Germany, Oct. 1.-(4-- The Nazi program has achieved “Success,” says Adolf Hitler. The chancellor told a gathering of 700,000 farmers and their families here yesterday that “We have taken over a bankrupt business which others had destroyed in 15 years. Success has come, and people today again have faith.” Hitler spoke at the national harvest festival.
LEOBEN, Austria, Oct. 1—(AP)— Another Austrian Nazi, Peter Pfister, was sentenced to death today at a courtmartial for participating in the July insurrection in which Chancellor Dollfuss was slain.

MADRID, Oct. 1—(P)— The resignation of Richard Samper Ibanez as premier of Spain will be placed before congress today, throwing the young republic into another major crisis. Samper Ibanez, who took over the leadership only five months ago, is quitting because he does not have a majority backing in congress. Many observers believed President Niceto Alcala Zamora will call Alejandro Lerroux, Samper Ibanez’ predecessor, to take over the government.

1934-10-04.text: | NEW YORK, Oct. 3,—(INS)— | Grave fears that the British freighter Millpool, carrying a crew of 26, had sunk with all on board lost, 700 miles off the coast of Newfoundland, were expressed early today in dispatches received here by Mackay Radio. The steamer Black Gull reported that it and the Canadian Pacific freighter Beaverhill had reached the ‘last given position of the distressed Millpool, which sent out several S. O. S. signals, but were unable to find any trace of her.

San Francisco, Oct. 3.—(/P)—A call to the workers of the world to “unite solidly in order to prevent what seems to be an approaching war” was voiced before the American Federation of Labor convention here today by William Green, its president. In doing so, Green introduced John Stokes of London, fraternal delegate from the British Trades Union Congress, who told the convention “the socialist principle has become the obvious and sole solution of our economic industrial crisis.” Organized workers were warned by Joseph A. Padway, Milwaukee labor attorney, against dropping their weapons in an industrial truce with employers. He criticized the Department of Justice and the National Labor Board for their alleged unfairness to labor. William Dunn of Toronto, fraternal delegate from the Canadian Trades Union Congress, told the convention there appeared to be a growing number of workers in the sl

-NEW- YORK, Oct. 3 (#)—The British freighter Millpool, crippled by a storm 700 miles off the coast of Labrador, was still missing tonight, with a crew of 26. Two ships that raced to her rescue gave up the search after the waters of the Atlantic revealed no trace of her, but a third ship was still circling the angry sea. The last distress message from the Millpool was described in a wireless from another ship as “unreadable.” A second British freighter, the Ainderby, also was battered by the storm. Her bridge was carried away and she was unable to heave to, but she was afloat with two vessels standing by.

New York, Oct. 3.—(4)—Distress and SOS signals flashed from two British freighters battered by storms in Mid-Atlantic waters Tuesday and sent nearby ships speeding to their aid. The SOS came from the freighter Millpool, which reported that its after-hatch had been stove in, its top mast broken and three men injured. Distress messages were sent out by the freighter Ainderby, about 1,500 miles northeast of New York. The messages said the No. 1 hatch of the vessel has been flooded.

WEST HARTLEPOOL, England, Oct. 4 ().—The British freighter Ainderby, in distress in the North Atlantic, is making for an Irish port, said a message received from the captain today by the Ropner Company, owners of the ship. “Impossible to reach Newfoundland,” the message said. “Water is filling the number two hold * * * through a defective bulkhead. Pumps working incessantly. Doing everything possible to cope with the situation.” The Ainderby, bound to Montreal from Wales, sent out a call for help Tuesday afternoon. Part of her bridge was carried away by a gale and she was believed to be drifting helplessly. Later the vessel reported her hatch, which had been stove in, was temporarily secured and two ships were standing by.

Rainbow has won the fourth face and the America’s Cup remains in America, unless a protest made by the British should be upheld by the yacht club committee. Both yachts came in flying protest flags. Next time, perhaps, our patriotic millionaires, instead of building a toy sailboat, will set this government a good example by building a really fast and powerful flying ship, and go over and show Europe that the country that invented the airplane does not propose to remain forever last in the air. Percy Rockefeller, second son of the late William Rockefeller, who was John D. Rockefeller's brother, died yesterday, only 56 years old. He was a highly intelligent man and a hard worker. London, Oct. 4 (#)—The delegations of the United States, Great Britain and Japan, meeting here for preliminary naval conversations about October 17th, were said by authorities today to be likely to consider a plan for a general conference of a large group of powers in 1935 instead of those three with France and Italy. The forthcoming conversations also will decide, it was said authoritatively, whether the political aspects of naval problems will be placed in the agenda of the 1935 conference. The British government, it was stated, “has an open mind on both matters.” If the powers want the Washington treaty extended, political problems might well creep in. Japan’s reported plan to denounce the Washington treaty as of December 31, 1936, was expected to be the first question to come up.

VIENNA, Oct. 4—(AP)—Dr. Franz Sonnleithner, chief of the secret code bureau of the Austrian government, has been arrested on charges of informing German nazis in advance of all security measures planned by the Austrian government. The government's disclosure that Sonnleithner had been jailed for

1934-03-09.text: London, Mar. 8—Prince Sigvard of Sweden surrendered his royal rights today and married the beautiful German actress Erika Patzek in one of the most exciting civil ceremonies held in London in a long time. It was one of the rapid-fire weddings, by special license, for which old Caxton Hall is famous, but the accommodating and efficient officials in the registry were unable to work as smoothly as customary. Several hundred persons jammed the streets in front of the hall and twice broke through police lines—the first time when the dark-haired and slender prince and the petite golden-haired fraulein arrived, just as Big Ben nearby tolled the noon hour, and again when the couple left a few minutes later. A municipal election almost disrupted the routine inside the hall, but the wedding was moved upstairs to a big council room. Sigvard is the Duke of Uppland and the grandson of the Swedish kin

- LONDON, March 9 (AP).—Great Britain is prepared to call a convention of western powers immediately in an attempt to regulate air forces in this part of the world if the disarmament conference at Geneva finally breaks down. Stanley Baldwin, lord president of the council, said this in the House of Commons last night in the debate of British air estimates for 1934. “Supposing our convention fails,” he said, “I would not then for a moment, nor would the government, delay our efforts to start work the next morning to get an air convention alone among the countries of western Europe for saving our own European civilization.” The speaker added that he had not given up hope for an arms convention and said he was not prepared to admit the disarmament situation is hopeless.

LONDON, March 8. (AP)— Prince Sigvard of Sweden and his beautiful actress-bride, like many less famous honeymooners, gave a final romantic touch to their wedding tonight by departing secretly for Berlin just a few hours after their marriage. “After Berlin I can’t tell you anything except that I hope to continue my chosen vocation as a film director,” said the dapper young prince who surrendered his royal rights by marrying the blonde Erika Patzek in the Caxton Hall registry here at noon. “We did not want anyone to know about this,’ he said, smiling genially, in an exclusive interview with an Associated Press representative shortly before the departure of their train. It was announced previously the couple would leave for Italy tomorrow on their honeymoon. An Exciting Ceremony The wedding ceremony was one of the most exciting civil marriages in London for a long time. It was rapid fire, t

Great Britain and France made it known Thursday that their desires for security have forced them to new attitudes regarding armaments. Sir Phillip Sassoon, British under-secretary for air, told the house of commons the British government must have parity in aviation as long as other nations cling to their aircraft building programs. Leaders of the French armed forces agreed it was impossible for France to disarm and permit Germany to rearm without further security guarantees. On the other side of the world, in China, Japanese military chieftains questioned increasing Chinese orders for American airplanes.

NEW YORK (U.P) — The government of the United States “still functions under the constitution” and the national debt, including the vast emergency expenditures for recovery, still is lower than England's, Postmaster General James A. Farley said Thursday night in a speech at the New York Drug Trade dinner. “From time to time,” he said, “partisan critics of the administration complain that the Roosevelt recovery program is costing vast sums of money and that Congress is giving too much power to the president. They forget, or rather they prefer not to remember, that the terrible depression through which the people of this country have struggled has been as disastrous and far-reaching as a war would have been. All of us know that money is not spared when it comes to prosecuting a war. Why should money be spared in fighting such a depression?

LONDON, Mar. 9. (U.P) — Labor candidates, running on a platform dovetailing with the socialistic one with which they will enter the next general election, have been swept into control of the London County Council, returns in the municipal election showed today. Labor leaders jubilantly regarded the returns as an indication that the party will gain tremendously in the next parliamentary election, when it plans to seek a majority in the House of Commons on a platform involving nationalization of essential industries. Returns today in the election for councilmen who will administer city affairs for three years, showed the following representation: Labor 61, Conservatives 37. Of 26 outstanding seats, many are for labor strongholds, and the labor men were conceded a majority in the new council, for the first time. Conservatives—running as municipal reformers—have controlled the council for 27

KAMAKURA, Japan, Mar. 9—(U P)—Police investigating the attempted murder of Sanji Muto here tonight, worked on the theory the millionaire industrialist and newspaper publisher may have been another victim of the dread “blood brotherhood.” Muto was shot by an unidentified assassin this morning as he motored from his villa to a railway station to take a train to his offices in Tokio. A stray bullet struck the millionaire’s secretary who was killed. The assassin then shot and killed himself. Surgeons at Kamakura hospital tonight were giving the wounded millionaire blood injections. They reported his condition improved. Muto was head of the influential Tokio daily newspaper Jiji Shimpo. He was active in politics.

SHANGHAI, March 9.—(®)—The suspicions of the Japanese military have been aroused by American airplane salesmen and instructors in China. It is rumored here that Japanese agents are keeping close tab on American fliers who come to China, seeking to determine if they have any connection with the United States government. 1934-11-04.text: Nottingham, an air-force flier who set out to sprinkle confetti from their plane over the country church where a friend was being married were burned to death today when their plane crashed. En route to the scene of the wedding they were seen to pitch suddenly to the ground. Showers of confetti they had intended to embellish the wedding shot into the air as the machine hit the earth and then burst into flames, incinerating the occupants. The two fliers were Frank Dalton and Philip Rook, members of the Nottingham squadron of the auxiliary air force. Observers said a wing of their machine, which was a private one, hired for the occasion, appeared to collapse while they were stunting.

Davis, United States ambassador-at-large, Sir John Stevenson, British foreign minister and Tsuneo Matsudaira, Japanese ambassador to Great Britain, will begin diplomatic explorations of the difficulties in the way of an agreement among the three nations, it was understood. Quip Helps Meanwhile, some stir was caused by Admiral William H. Standley’s jest offer, made Thursday, to swap the United States fleet for Japan’s and still lick them. His quip, it was said, helped considerably to ‘clear the air during the discussions.
| LONDON, Nov. 3-(?)-—-Completely deadlocked after one more week of negotiations, naval delegations of Britain, the United States, and Japan today postponed further discussion until next week.

RAVENNA, O., Nov. 3—(AP) Two men who accosted Miss Doris Morton, 25, cashier of the Ravenna Evening Ledger on the street today, took the newspaper's payroll amounting to about $600 and fled in a waiting automobile. Miss Morton was returning to the office from the bank with the money in a wallet under her arm when the two men stepped up. One put his hand over her mouth, and the other shoved a revolver to her side. One of the men grabbed the wallet and the pair ran to the curb and sped away in the auto, driven by a third man.

VEN DOUNG, France, Nov. 3 (4) The first French gold shipment since the United States dollar passed the point where it is profitable to export gold was loaded today on the S.S. Bremen for New York. Forty cases of gold valued at approximately $2,610,000 were dispatched to the Chase National Bank of New York by the bank's Paris branch. The Bank of France has made successive weekly gains in its reserves and France has recently begun again to ship out gold.

BERLIN, Nov. 8.—The Reichsbank will not pay any interest whatever on bonds held abroad during the year which began July 1, it was announced today. Until the announcement some foreign holders held faint hopes that the Reichsbank might pay 40 per cent of the interest. It was recalled Germany made a conditional offer at a transfer conference in May that if her foreign exchange situation improved appreciably, 40 per cent cash would be paid on the interest coupons maturing between July 1, 1934, and June 20, 1925.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 3 (UP).— President Roosevelt's truce between capital and labor faced an important test today with chances apparently good that it would win. The test was labor's reaction to renewal for 90 days of the unchanged automobile code. While not overly enthusiastic at the failure of the administration to open the automobile code for possible amendments desired by labor, union opinion was expected to go along with the President in view of his intention to investigate conditions thoroughly prior to expiration date of the renewed code February 1.

Chicago, Nov. 2 (#) — Caught up by the cross-examination he fought angrily all day, Samuel Insull admitted today a $10,000,000 "mistake" in one statement to stockholders of the Corporation Securities Company. His defeat on this point came after he had parried questions from Prosecutor Leslie E. Salter for three hours, battling for his financial reputation against government charges of mail fraud. The 74-year-old Chicagoan, while Prosecutor Salter pursued him with questions, had complained twice to Federal Judge James H. Wilkerson they were "double barreled." The Judge ordered Insull to answer, but said he might explain, Statement Read Salter produced a financial statement which said the securities held by the Corporation Securities Company, under fire as a "hundred million dollar swindle," were carried at $86,000,000, their purchase price. 1934-05-26.text: London, England, May 26.—(7)— Scotland Yard took official notice today of reports that it was searching for John Dillinger, American bad man. Its notice was a flat denial. “The report which appeared in a morning newspaper today saying Dillinger is in London is entirely without foundation,” announced the famous police headquarters. “No search has been carried out and none is contemplated.” The official statement was made after the Daily Mail declared a man who knew Dillinger “well” in the United States had given Scotland Yard a statement saying he saw the criminal in London two days ago.

London, May 26-(%)—The divorce case in which Lord Ashley named Douglas Fairbanks, Sr., as co-respondent will be defended in court by Lady Sylvia Ashley, it was announced Friday. The case was set for trial at the summer term of court, but an exact date has not been fixed.

SERED ne eg, Ae Re, eA TORYO, May 25—fA--The Japanese government was understood today to have accepted a British invitation to carry on diplomatic talks with the United States and Great Britain separately preliminary to the 1935 naval conference. High Foreign Office authorities said Ambassador Matsudaira, who represents Japan in London, was invited by Sir John Simon, British Foreign Secretary, to ask his government whether it would enter into frank preliminary talks on the subject of disarmament.

Prestwick, Scotland (AP)—W. Lawson Little of California defeated James Wallace, Scottish carpenter, 14 and 13 today for the British amateur golf championship, smashing all existing records for this classic tournament. After gaining a 12 hole lead in the morning round by shooting a sensational 66 to break all records for this strenuous, seaside course, Little put an end to the one-sided match at the 23rd hole with another display of sub-par golf. He was three under par for the five holes of the afternoon round and eight under par for the match.

LONDON, May 25—(AP)—The United States government, it was learned authoritatively today, has instructed Ambassador Robert W. Bingham to inform Great Britain that the United States is prepared to carry on preparations for the 1935 naval conference through normal diplomatic interchanges and discussions. Ambassador Bingham has informed the British government of Washington's attitude, which was reported as being ready for a broadening of the conference to questions of technical naval aspects if such broadening should seem advisable. Last week the British foreign office asked Ambassador Bingham, and presumably, the Japanese, French, and Italian ambassadors to inquire of their governments what steps they were willing to take looking forward to the preliminary preparations for the conference. | Manila, May 25. (4) — Once the ruler of an insular kingdom of 500,000 warlike Mohammedans, the Sultan of Sulu, whose power under the American flag has been fading year by year, waited today for an apology from the government of British North Borneo for its failure to salute him on his visit there last February. Still clinging to the belief he is entitled to the honors of royalty, the Sultan recently asked North Borneo authorities why they did not fire the customary twenty guns for him and his adopted daughter, the Princess Dayang Dayang. North Borneo, once a part of the sultan’s realm, still technically recognizes his spiritual authority, but all the secular power that once was his now belongs to the United States and Great Britain. LONDON (#) — The Daily Mail said today a man who knew John Dillinger “well” in the United States has told Scotland Yard he saw America’s No. 1 public enemy in London two days ago. The newspaper said it had received a cable from Washington saying American authorities are convinced Dillinger still is in the Midwest, but added Scotland Yard nevertheless was hunting him here. Detectives have extended their search to palatial homes in London’s fashionable west end, it was added, in the belief wealthy international criminals may be hiding Dillinger. There are many such criminals living in London unmolested because of the inability of authorities to disprove their claim to British nationality. At the same time, the underworld is being combed, The Mail said. 1934-04-08.text: LONDON, Apr. 7.—James Fullarton Muirhead, editor of Baedeker’s famous guide books for 35 years, died today at the age of 81. Muirhead wrote in particular Baedeker’s volumes on London, the United Kingdom, United States and Canada. He had traveled extensively in Canada and the United States.

GENOA, Apr. 7. (U.P.)—Mrs. Thalia Massie, central figure of a sensational assault and murder case in Hawaii, lay in hospital today under close guard of nuns and insisted calmly and tirelessly: “I am going to die. You may stop me now. You may think you are more clever than I. But I will show you.” Her wrists gashed deeply but not dangerously, Mrs. Massie was at the hospital of Dr. Emilio Porelli, head of a clinic for nervous diseases, after an apparent suicide attempt Sunday night aboard the line Roma as it entered the Mediterranean.

OSLO, Norway, April 7 (7) — A huge crag weighing thousands of tons fell into the sea off Norway’s west coast early today and caused huge waves that trapped sleeping residents of two villages, at least 50 of whom drowned. Many other inhabitants of the fish-hamlets, Tafjord and Pjoraa, on opposite sides of Korsnaes Fjord, were still missing tonight and were believed victims of the sudden, terrifying disaster. First a small part of the cliff, long regarded as a menace, fell, throwing up a small wave. Two other falls followed in rapid succession and sent a wall of water as high as 30 feet sweeping over the flimsy houses. Many of the small structures were carried off like doll houses. Others were reduced to splinters by the heavy impact of the water. Boats in the harbor were tossed upon the land. Motor cars and other vehicles were borne far inland. ISTANBUL, April 7.—(P)—The expulsion of Samuel Insull within a week for trial in the United States on fraud charges seemed certain tonight because of a decision forbidding his appeal from a Turkish extradition ruling. Attorney General Kenan Bey announced the aged former utilities executive cannot question Turkey's stand on the legality of plans to relinquish him to American officers, and simultaneously a Turko-American extradition treaty moved toward final approval. Nevertheless, the one-time Chicagoan’s attorneys were still determined tonight to go before the courts with what they called an iron-clad argument in favor of their right to appeal.

OSLO, April 7.--The worst disaster Norway has experienced in several decades occurred today when two little west coast fishing villages were overwhelmed by huge waves and a crag overhanging the fjord on which they lay crashed into the sea. More than 50 persons drowned, among them 20 children, as waves rushed over the village of Tajford and Fjoraa and swept a half mile inland, beating down everything in their path. The helpless villagers were taken unawares as they were asleep in their homes, which were mainly of timber. Most of the houses were carried off entirely. When the waves retreated the shores were littered with debris and bodies. Many dead were believed buried under the ruins of other buildings. A steamer was dispatched from Aalesund to help the survivors, and the government telegraphed offers of aid. All boats in the harbor were flung up on the shore, while at several points mot

GENOA, Italy, April 7. (4)—Mrs. Thalie Fortescue Massie was guarded closely in a clinic today lest she attempt suicide again. The young woman, principal in the Honolulu attack and murder case of two years ago, was confined to the clinic Thursday night when the liner Roma brought her here. Officers of the ship said she had slashed her wrists and jumped from the top deck to a lower deck en route from New York. Her injuries were slight, but she was highly nervous. Dr. Darrio Borelli, clinic director, said Mrs. Massie insisted at first that she would “do it again at the first opportunity” because of her regret at having “got a divorce from my husband.” She and Lieut. Thomas Hedge Massie, U.S. N., were divorced at Reno in February. The director diagnosed her case as melancholy and acute sadness.

ISTANBUL, April 7. (?—Samuel) Insull’s lawyers announced today they would file either tonight or tomorrow morning an “iron clad argument” for an appeal against his detention for American authorities, While these new plans were laid, the fugitive remained secluded in his room at the house of detention, attended by his 12 cents a day wallet.

Budapest, Hungary, April 7. (AP) A new plot to assassinate Romanian state leaders, including possibly King Carol, was reported uncovered in Bucharest today. Several officers and civilians were arrested, among them the well-known Colonel Prekup. Reports said the projected killings were to have taken place at a midnight service marking the Orthodox Easter. Late last month police said a conspiracy to assassinate Premier Tatarascu and other government leaders had been revealed.

1934-11-12.text: GLASGOW, Scotland, (UP).— Betty Gow, former nurse for the Lindbergh family, has been asked officially by United States authorities to be ready to leave for the United States at a moment’s notice to testify in the trial of Bruno Richard Hauptmann, alleged kidnapper of the Lindbergh baby, her relatives said today. “She is ready and willing to go to the United States at any time, although to the best of her knowledge she never saw Hauptmann,” her brother said. “However, if her evidence will be in any way helpful, she will go gladly. In Constant Touch. “She has been in constant touch with American authorities ever since she came home.” She refused to indicate whether a sailing date had been picked. Miss Gow is closely guarded by relatives and is not permitted to leave home without an escort. FLMINGTON, N. J., (UP).— Betty Gow, nursemaid for the murdered Charles Lindbergh, Jr., will be a rout

LONDON, NOV. 12. (AP).—There will be no defense to Lord Ashley's suit for divorce in which Douglas Fairbanks, Sr., is named co-respondent, and “the case should be all over in about half an hour,” it was learned today from lawyers engaged in the case. Although there were persistent reports that Lady Ashley will go to the United States, she has made no move to indicate she intends to give up her residence here.

LONDON, Nov, 10 (Py) — "David Lloyd George, Britain's wartime premier, told an audience today at an exhibition of gruesome wartime photographs that a wager on the possibility of war would be an expensive proposition. "If you want to know whether there is any danger," he said, "go to Lloyds and ask what it would cost you for a policy insuring against the risk of war for five years." He said he was not among those who considered war was imminent but said it was lurking in the path along which humanity has got to tread, and intimated that it would be impossible to set insurance against war occurring within ten years. Lloyd George, his large white hair tossing, put a warlike interpretation on Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald's speech last night at the Guildhall in which he said disarmament never could be accomplished by example. | WASHINGTON (I#—The American tax-payer may have eventually to answer the question “little man what now?” which was put to the Japanese this week by the British naval delegation in London, it was indicated Monday in naval and administration circles. He may eventually have to put up a lot of extra money in taxes to pay for new ships for the navy if the Washington and London naval agreements are scrapped, as now appears likely. Navy officials here, anticipating a fizzle of the London conversations and 1935 naval conference, have gone ahead with tentative plans for new ships. They did not speak openly of a naval building race. They advocated only maintenance of the present tonnage ratios. There is little difference, No Compromise Neither naval nor administration opinion here believes that Japan will accept a British compromise proposing the right for Japan in principle, of naval equality. LONDON, Nov. 12 (UP).—Workers in the Vickers works at Crayford observed two minutes of silence yesterday in commemoration of Armistice day. Then they returned to their benches, turning out machine guns, rifles, and poisonous gas projectors.

London, Nov. 12.—The word “obey” is included in the marriage service for the Duke of Kent, the king’s youngest son, and Princess Marina of Greece at Westminster Abbey, where Dean Foxley Norris officiates. The king and queen and the Prince of Wales will accompany the Duke of Kent to Victoria station on Nov. 21 to meet Princess Marina on her return to England. They will drive with her to Buckingham Palace, where she will stay with her parents, Prince and Princess Nicholas, until the wedding on Nov. 29. A choir of seventy will sing at the ceremony an anthem especially composed by Dr. Bullock, the abbey organist.

(United Press Leased Wire) PARIS, Nov. 13.— High commands of the French, British and Belgian armies have concluded an air defense agreement in the event of war, the newspaper Paris Midi reported today, which envisages exchange of information and mutual reinforcement. British airplanes have been assigned bases in France and Belgium in case of attack, Midi reported.

LONDON, Nov. 12. (UP)— The United States moved today to sound out Japan's opinion on the advisability of a treaty to establish international control of the arms traffic. Hugh Wilson, representing the United States, called on Ambassador Tsuneo Matsudaira at the Japanese embassy. They were understood to have discussed whether it would be advisable to embody such a treaty in a general arms agreement or draft a separate agreement. Because of difficulties entailed in reaching a comprehensive agreement among the powers, it was believed the latter course was favored. At the meeting of the steering committee of the arms conference at Geneva on November 20, it was expected the United States and Great Britain would propose rigid regulation of the arms traffic under supervision of an international committee. Wilson recently sounded out the French and Italian attitude on the proposal.

1934-04-14.text: VIENNA, April 14—(4)—Train wreckers who derailed the Vienna-Paris-London express Tuesday were trying to kill Emil Fey, vice chancellor of Austria, it was learned today. Fey was traveling to Salzburg in the saloon coach of the train when the locomotive, mail car and baggage car plunged into a ditch between Wels and Linz, capital of Upper Austria. Authorities announced that the Left Radical group was suspected of carrying out the wrecking plot. Police were trailing suspects and indicated they expected numerous arrests soon.

Victoria, B.C. Apr. 13. (#)—A “new Klondike” gold strike, reported to average almost $12 a cubic yard for coarse gravel, sent prospectors rushing to the Squaw Creek area of British Columbia today. The new price for gold in the United States—$35 a fine ounce—gave added impetus to the trek of mining men over trails made perilous by the melting snows of an early spring. Reports from the area said three men worked for a few weeks on one claim and recovered more than $7,000 in gold, based only on the former United States price of $20.67 an ounce. Most of the claims at Squaw Creek have been staked by Indians, who sought only nuggets. The white men, with their better methods of reclaiming gold and the new high price, expect to reap a rich harvest. A few white men went in last year. The district is in the pocket formed by the Yukon-British Columbia boundary line and the Alaska Panhandle. In addi

WINDSOR, England, April 14. (4) —Found: One dog, Cairn terrier. Name of owner: Edward Albert Christian George Andrew Patrick David Windsor, Prince of Wales, Name of dog: Jigs. Found by: Unidentified motorist. Received by: Southampton police who had been driven madly looking for Jigs since Thursday night when he ran away from Wales’ country house, Fort Belvedere. Charge: A. W. O. L. Disposition: Lodged in jail awaiting royal equerry.

DUBLIN, Irish Free State April 13.—(4)—Crowds lined the street for two miles today as the body of William Wallace McDowell, United States minister, was carried on a horse-drawn carriage from his legation to a railroad train, starting the trip back to the United States. At the Kingsbridge railway station it was placed on the train for Cobh to be transported to the S. S. Manhattan and home.

| ISTANBUL, April 12—(4)—Samuel Insull, Sr., today was started on his long, involuntary journey from a Turkish jail back to the United States. He was removed under guard from the Istanbul house of detention to be taken to Smyrna where he will be placed on board the SS Exilona, sailing Friday. Formal extradition will be made on the steamer when Turkish police hand over the former Chicago Utilities magnate to an American diplomat, Burt Y. Berry, third secretary of the United States embassy to Turkey.

MOSCOW, April 13.—The last six men of the Cheliuskin Arctic expedition, stranded on ice for fifty-eight days, have been rescued by airplane it was announced officially today. The news meant that aviators who had braved without glory for years the rigors of the Siberian wilds on routine jobs had evacuated 107 men, women and children left adrift at sea when the icebreaker Cheliuskin was crushed in the ice February 13. The aviators saved not only all the refugees but, after they had brought off the last six today, went back and got the sledge dogs who had been taken off the Cheliuskin with its human complement.

Alessandria, Italy, April 13, UP—A landslide at the hamlet of Grondona during the early hours of today killed ten persons, caused grave injuries to two and made 200 of the town's population homeless. Grondona is 27 miles from here. About midnight the inhabitants heard a loud rumbling. Then a mass of earth, boulders and trees crashed down the mountainous slopes and into their homes. The dead included one man, seven women and two children.

8. S. EXILONA. UP. Samuel Insull dropped his role of man without a country and fugitive from American courts and sailed for the United States, a prisoner at last of an American official. The head of the wrecked Insull utilities was formally delivered to Burton Y. Berry of the Istanbul American embassy sixteen months after he fled from fraud charges at home and two weeks after Turkish officials arrested him. In an extremely brief and simple ceremony the Turkish police commissioner, Nail Bey, handed the former multimillionaire over to Berry, who gave the officer a receipt, signed by himself and the Exilona’s captain, for Insull's delivery, and a copy of the presidential warrant for the Chicago detention. Insull was formally extradited aboard the ship at 10:50 p.m. Thus the extradition Insull had fought against for so long was effected. He stood, disconsolate, witnessing the ceremony. It wa

1934-05-07.text: - LONDON, England, May 7. (UP) Great Britain declared a tariff war against Japan in the British Empire today and also threatened to increase the tariff on silk imports into the United Kingdom. Goaded into action by the heavy inroads of Japanese cotton and rayon textiles into British trade, the government took its drastic step without even waiting for Japan's reply to the recent British demand for a reduction of such exports. At the same time he made his announcement, however, Walter Runciman, president of the board of trade, did not close the door to trade peace and invited Japan to compromise. He said it was not necessary to denounce the Anglo-Japanese trade treaty and added: “The government is ready at any time to give the most careful consideration to any proposals which the Japanese government may desire to bring forward.”

LONDON, May 7. (‘UP)—Great Britain opened her long-threatened trade war on Japan today. Walter Runciman, president of the Board of Trade, announced in the House of Commons that he would ask the British colonies to impose import quotas against Japan, effective from today.

LONDON, May 7—(#)—Great Britain plans to make another token payment in June on her war debts to the United States but is hopeful that President Roosevelt will submit a new plan for a final settlement of the question before then. It was officially and emphatically denied Monday that there have been to the present any British proposals or any sort of diplomatic negotiations in reference to the matter.

London, May 4. W.P.—Hopes of hundreds of American girls and women were rewarded today or were dashed, to their despair, when the American embassy announced the names of 21 who are to be presented at the first two Royal Courts of the social season, May 15 and 16. Mrs. Robert Worth Bingham, wife of the American ambassador, will present the debutantes—for the purpose of London society, they are all “Debs”—to the king and queen at Buckingham Palace. Among those to be presented is Mrs. Cecil B. Seiberling, Akron, O.

London—(A)—Walter Runciman, president of the British board of trade, told the House of Commons today that the British government is preparing to utilize import quotas as a weapon in the battle against increasing Japanese trade competition. His statement came in a review of the British trade negotiations with the Japanese. In the face of Japan's apparent unreadiness to reach a basis of understanding, Runciman said: “The British government has come to the conclusion it would no longer be justified in postponing such action as is open with a view to safeguarding the trade of this country.” He said, be told the Japanese ambassador “that in the circumstances the British government is obliged to resume the liberty to take such action as is deemed necessary to safeguard our commercial interests,” with the assurance that it would be taken “in no unfriendly spirit.” Runciman said that colonies an

..CAIRO, Egypt, May 8.—(A~—~Assurances British subjects will be safe in Hodeidah, captured Yemen seaport, came today from the Emir Feisal; as the troops of his father, King Ibn Saud of Saudi Arabia, pushed on to complete the conquest of Yemen by attacking Sana, the capital. The emir sent a messenger to Kamaran island, where a number of British Indians had been taken on the sloop “Penzance.” The Emir Feisal was placed in command of Hodeidah, the messenger said, and his forces had restored order in the city disturbed by the disorganized retreat of Yemen defenders. Messages from the war zone told of the capture by the Saudi soldiers of a consignment of arms and ammunition sent from Europe to the Imam Yehyi of Yemen, who has been reported to have been assassinated as his army met defeat. | LONDON — The Prince of Wales, renowned for his appreciation of a good story, tells one of his own. The yarn, related by his Royal Highness at a dinner of the Welsh Guards, tells of a man who complained to his doctor of pains, but was unable to locate them. The patient was ordered to place a piece of paper under his vest and make a mark wherever he felt the pain. But when the doctor called later, the paper was missing. The man’s daughter, asked if she knew its whereabouts, replied: - “Do you mean that piece of paper with all the holes in it? We put it in the pianola and it played, ‘O God, Our Help In Ages Past.”

LONDON, May 7 (®)(4)—The London Post suggested today that some leaders abroad—‘not excluding Hitler’—should read President Franklin D. Roosevelt's new book if they would “learn how it’s done.” The British edition of the American president's work, “On Our Way,” appeared today. It was greeted with the most cordial recognition by London newspapers. The Post, sometimes a severe critic of America, printed an editorial which said: “Whatever verdict history may pass on the president's work as a whole, it may be anticipated with certainty that it will account him without controversy the saviour of his country at one of the darkest hours in her annals.” After citing striking passages from the book, the Post concluded: “if fellow aspirants abroad—not excluding Hitler (Chancellor Adolf Hitler of Germany)—would learn how it’s done, let them study ‘On Our Way’ and see.”

1934-12-27.text: The Arctic blast which swept across the country struck with renewed fury at many points today, leaving behind a steadily mounting list of fatalities. Shipping along the North Atlantic coast was endangered as the storm whipped across the eastern states, The British freighter Quebec City was wrenched loose from her anchorage and driven aground on the mud flats of Brooklyn, while the rudderless Belgian freighter Emile Franqui, bound for Antwerp from New York with a crew of 35, was battling a gale off the coast of Nova Scotia. New England Gale Heavy seas battered the main shore when a 57-mile-an-hour gale howled across New England with rain, snow, sleet, hail and lightning following in its wake. San Francisco felt the tail end of the storm in the form of a hard rain while the Pacific Northwest was raked by 70-mile-an-hour gales. A hangar at the Portland, Oregon, airport, was demolished. London—()—The Japanese unofficially advised the British today that the Tokyo government would denounce the Washington naval treaty of 1922 this Saturday at Washington. The delegates to the preliminary naval conversations among Great Britain, the United States and Japan long have been given to understand by the Japanese that the Washington treaty will end Dec. 31, 1936. By the terms of that treaty, any denunciation must take place before Dec. 31 of this year, consequently the Japanese have been expected to make their formal move toward ending the treaty before the end of this month. Admiral Yamamoto of the Japanese delegation is taking steps to obtain a conference with the British in the next day or so.

TORONTO, Dec. 27.--(2)--W. A. Kingsland, general manager of the central region of the Canadian National Railways, issued an official statement today saying E. S. Lynch, forward brakeman of the London-Toronto passenger special which was wrecked Christmas night with a loss of 15 lives, threw the switch which sent the Detroit-Toronto express into the standing special. The statement, in part, follows: *The company’s investigation of the accident at Dundas on Dec. 25 shows after the passenger extra had entered the siding, Rear End Brakeman Phelps properly set and locked the switch for the main line and turned the marker lights on the rear of his train from red to green to indicate to the enginemen of any following train.

Washington, Dec. 27 (P)—Henry J. Allen, former U. S. senator from Kansas, returning from a 2-month trip through England, asserted today that British recovery from the depression has been more rapid than the movement toward better times in America. Presenting detailed figures on employment, return of salary cuts and other elements he interpreted as heralding recovery in Great Britain, the former Wichita publisher offered three reasons: The balancing of the budget, the use of protective tariff and a new building program. “The government was forced to raise the already high taxes cutting for every pound,” said Allen, “but in the 3-year period, the budget was balanced and taxes reduced. England, of course, is as enthusiastic about the protective tariff as we were in the McKinley administration.” He asserted business in this country needs more confidence and more reason for confidence. “We ne

HAMILTON, Ont., Dec. 26. (*)—The splintered wreckage of a Christmas excursion train was searched Wednesday for additional victims as officials of the Canadian National Railways opened an investigation of a collision Tuesday night which took at least 15 lives. More than a score of persons were injured, some critically, when the Detroit to Toronto Express tore into the rear of the stationary excursion train on a siding at Dundas, seven miles from Hamilton. Five women were among the mangled victims of the disaster whose bodies have been recovered but as yet are unidentified. Additional deaths were feared. Officials of the railway said the cause of the accident apparently was an open switch and promised an intensive inquiry. Laden with merry holiday travelers, the excursion train was bound from London, Ont., to Toronto. Most of the victims, all of whom apparently were Canadians, were residen

WELLINGTON, New Zealand, Dec. 26. (#)—Lincoln Ellsworth, Antarctic explorer, and his pilot, Bernt Balchen, were reported Wednesday to have made a successful airplane flight across the Antarctic from Deception Island to the Bay of Whales. The flight was made Tuesday, Christmas Day. The report did not say whether Sir Hubert Wilkins, the partner of Ellsworth on the expedition, was in the plane with Ellsworth and Balchen. It did, however, say that the members of the expedition intended to have a great time in their encounter with the expedition headed by Admiral Richard E. Byrd at Little America. The steamers Bear of Oakland and Jacob Ruppert of the Byrd expedition and the S. S. Wyatt Earp of the Ellsworth-Wilkins group will meet at the Bay of Whales in the next few weeks.

Berlin, Dec. 27—Reports in newspapers in the Saar territory and elsewhere that hundreds had been arrested in Berlin in another “June 30 purge” were officially and emphatically denied here today. The reports were termed “ridiculous and regrettable propaganda” and “malicious, cowardly and baseless propaganda and manufactured lies” designed as an anti-German blow just before the January 13 plebiscite. A secret police officer said there had been no arrests for sexual abnormalities in at least the last 10 days. Government activities here have generally been quiet through the holidays. Many government, party and military leaders are still outside the city and there has been little going on in Berlin since Saturday except social affairs.

1934-10-07.text: MONTREAL, Oct. 6 (AP)—A red-haired Spanish-American night club dancer named Dolores Morel, held in the slaying of William Owen, British broker's assistant, admitted Saturday night according to police that she plunged a knife into him in self-defense. Owen bled to death early Saturday in Dolores’ apartment while a physician the woman had called tried to save his life. She had fled from the place and was injured when she ran Owen's automobile into a tree at Longueuil. “We were alone in the apartment at the time,” she was quoted in a statement made public by Inspector Armand Brodeur. “Two men who were with us had previously left. “William Owen, a hard man to deal with when partly drunk, tried to argue with me in a thoroughly drunken condition, I would not give him the answers he expected so he started beating me and suddenly commenced to choke me.” The statement issued by Brodeur then quote
