| MADRID, Oct. 6—(P)—The death toll in Spain's extremist rebellion mounted to 104 persons at noon today, with at least 350 wounded, as machine guns, rifles, and pistols obliterated a government statement that tranquility had been restored. At dawn the death list stood at 93 and the government of Premier Alenandroux, against which the anarchists, Communists and Socialists had declared war, stated the general strike was a failure and that troops were being withdrawn from most of the battlefronts of the last two days. Strike Again Suddenly the extremists renewed battle. Eleven more persons were killed in clashes during the morning. Trouble in the mining regions of Asturias accounted for six of the morning's dead. In Madrid, a boy of 14 on his way to school and an unidentified laborer were killed when caught in a crossfire between extremists and Civil Guarda in the Cuatro Caminos district. E

MADRID, Oct. 7 (Sunday)—Secession in the northeast, bloody revolt in the far north and utter confusion in this seat of government faced the young Spanish republic today. Blood flowed in dozens of towns the total of the dead being between 200 and 300. The most menacing development of a riotous day was Catalonia’s formal declaration of independence and the sharp fighting which followed in the streets of Barcelona. Luis Companys, president of that state, appeared on a balcony of the Barcelona town hall and solemnly announced: “Catalonia is breaking off relations with the rest of Spain. . . .I demand complete discipline from everyone. Long live liberty.” Demands Army Support Companys demanded of General Domingo Batet, commander of the Spanish garrison at Barcelona, that he swear allegiance to the new regime. “Batet asked for an hour to think over the matter.” But in less than an hour the aut

MILAN, Italy, Oct. 6. U.P)—Premier Benito Mussolini announced to a cheering crowd in Cathedral Square today a Franco-Italian agreement—considered one of the most significant accords in recent years—would be signed at the end of October. The announcement by the Fascist Premier, who stood alone on a 30-foot tribune before a crowd of 200,000 in the square and side streets, confirmed United Press dispatches of last week forecasting the accord between the two nations. “With our nearest neighbors we can have but two policies: either friendship or hostility,” Mussolini said. “Yesterday, we defended the independence of Austria and we will continue to defend it. “European development is impossible without Germany, but it is necessary that some trends in Germany’s politics be changed. Germany cannot be estranged from the course of European history.”

Milan, Italy; Oct. 6 (4)--Half a million Italian mouths opened in uproarious laughter today at a declaration of Premier Mussolini that relations with neighboring France in the last year "have been notably better." Whether or not the laughter was originally by a wink of Mussolini's eye, it was probably the most dramatic interruption ever accorded a public address. Five hundred thousand persons jammed into the immense cathedral square roared at what seemed to them a huge joke. They laughed again when il duce in a momentous policy address coinciding with the thirteenth anniversary of his decision to march upon Rome, paused to let the laughter die down and then told them "your attitude indicates that you are a very intelligent people." He began his reference by saying "there is no doubt that for at least a year, until now, our relations with France have been notably better." Then he said: "Y

MONTREAL, Que., Oct. 6 (CUP)-- Dolores Lopes, Montreal cabaret entertainer, confessed today, police said, that she killed William Owen, 40-year-old stock broker formerly connected with the Lloyd George secretariat. Police quoted her as saying that she killed Owen in self defense after a midnight drinking party in her apartment. He died of a knife wound in the shoulder.

1934-12-28.text: LONDON, Dec. 28.—(AP)—An authoritative diplomatic source stated that Great Britain, with the cooperation of France and Italy, will propose a general security pact embracing almost all the countries of Europe immediately after the Saar plebiscite. The suggested convention, it was said, will be submitted at Geneva, the seat of the League of Nations. The plebiscite itself is to be held Jan. 13, and the council of the League of Nations is to meet just two days before the balloting by which the Saarlanders will express their desire as to the future sovereignty of the Saar basin territory. The suggested pact would be a joint pledge and guarantee of the independence of Austria. It also would pledge the signatory nations not to make any moves against one another involving Austria or any other question in which two or more countries had an interest. Germany, it was stated, has given assurances th

Rising temperatures in the east, middle west and southwest today gave most of the country a mid-holiday respite from storms and sub-zero temperatures. Meanwhile New England points were cleaning up the debris that marked the path of a howling gale that killed three persons and reached a velocity of 175 miles an hour atop Mt. Washington, N. H., where the temperature sagged on Thursday to 30 degrees below zero. A moderation of temperatures in the stricken areas along the northeast coast aided in the work of repairing the damage wrought by the gale, described as the worst in many years. Frame dwellings in the wind’s path were reduced to splinters, and other structures were badly damaged. The loss was unofficially estimated at half a million dollars. While temperatures moderated in the central west yesterday there were additional deaths to swell the total of fatalities indirectly attributed t

(By Associated Press) London, Dec 28—The Japanese today made a surprise move to obtain one more discussion of the naval relationship of Japan, the United States and Great Britain before the United States delegation sails for home. Adm Isoroku Yamamoto of Japan requested Admiral William Standley to join him late tomorrow in a last talk. The Americans plan to leave tomorrow night. This unexpected move, American quarters said, may be actuated by a Japanese wish to make it appear that the Washington delegates are leaving when the Japanese are willing to discuss further steps toward a compromise. — NANCE REFUSAL LEADS TO TRAGEDY son was killed and nine seriously injured when exiled Austrian Nazis and Germans fought after a Bavarian girl refused to dance with an Austrian. Ellsworth R. Hodgdon of Rye is at the Portsmouth hospital recovering from an appendicitis operation.

A winter hurricane lashed the New England seacoast with destructive fury Thursday and swept over the White Mountains with a velocity of 175 miles an hour. It was the last phase of a winter storm that had brought sub-zero temperatures, snow and high winds in a wide sweep across the northern states. Tragic accompaniments of the wintry weather were the deaths of seven little girls—three of them daughters of Harry Hammon, truck driver at Mishawaka, Ind. They died in flames in their one-room house when a pot of oil, warming on the stove to thaw the car, boiled over. Four other little sisters, 2 to 8 years old, drowned in icy Hughes River at Harrisville, W. Va., when their rowboat capsized. A mile-a-minute gale tore into New England, wrecking communication lines, destroying trees and unroofing buildings. Boston clocked the wind at 66 miles an hour, Springfield, Mass., at 75 and the instruments

London. Dec 28 (AP).—Admiral William H. Standley, of the United States, and Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, of Japan, met today to discuss the naval situation, as it appears now that the tri-power discussions have broken up. Yamamoto, among others, has been Standley's guest at a luncheon. Yamamoto suggested that the two meet tomorrow just before the American delegation sails for home but the luncheon gave them an opportunity to hold their conference today instead. It was understood that the Japanese admiral outlined Tokyo's instructions that the Japanese delegation is to discuss with the British a possible approach to a compromise. These instructions, however, did not indicate that there would be any change in Japan's demand for equality. Yamamoto’s desire for the conference with Standley was a surprise.

CHICAGO, Dec. 28—(UFS)—Snow and another cold wave from the Rockies swept down on the middle west today while gales that lashed both coasts swept out to sea and temperatures rose. New England, cleaning up debris and counting casualties of a hurricane, was threatened like the midwest with more snow and cold after a day of respite. Scores of persons were injured in Boston and Springfield, Mass., New York and cities to the north when the wind reached 66 miles an hour in Boston, 75 in Springfield and velocities passing 50 miles in almost every New England state.

LONDON, Dec. 27. (7)—George Bernard Shaw won't do any soothsaying concerning 1935--at least, not unless he's paid for it. "I'm sorry,” the writer said when asked what he thought the new year held in store for the world, “but I'm not God Almighty.” “Haven't you even a little idea about what the year might bring?” he was asked. “Young man,” came the shavian reply, “I never have little ideas. All my ideas are big ones. It would take me a month to write them down for you. How much will you pay me for them?”
DUBLIN, Dec. 28. (UP)—The Irish Free State literature censor has banned Mae West's novels “She Done Him Wrong” and “The Constant Sinner” it was announced today.

1934-02-14.text: VIENNA, Feb. 14—(UP)—(By telephone to London)—Slaughter of Socialists continued on an appalling scale today when the government relentlessly advanced its war to wipe Socialism out in Austria. The United Press estimate of 1,000 dead appeared to be conservative but, beyond that, any figures must be guesswork. The most tragic part was that many women and children apparently were victims in the shelling of crowded socialist apartment houses. Semi-official sources estimated roughly that at least 20 to 25 women had been killed in Vienna. Five of them were not identified. Casualties among children were not known. Ash Wednesday and St. Valentine's Day will long be remembered in the history of Vienna. Few of the devout braved the bullet-torn streets to visit church and have the traditional cross of ashes marked on their foreheads. The government forces, overwhelming the dauntless but poorly-equip

(World Copyright 1934 by United Press) VIENNA—(By Telephone to London)—Austria’s Socialist revolution soon will be history, Engelbert Dollfuss, four foot eleven inch “vest pocket chancellor,” told the United Press today in an exclusive interview. Dollfuss, always confident, never on the retreat, spoke as if he regarded the revolution as over already, though artillerymen then were shelling socialists just across the Danube. Forty-one, gray eyed, mustached, wartime hero as a peasant first lieutenant of machine guns in an aristocratic army, shot once by a would-be assassin during 21 purple months in office, Dollfuss’ tone was eloquent of his character. Austria, he said, would continue his political and economic recovery. “Events of the past few days in Austria,” he said, “have been followed with great interest abroad. I am glad to be in a position to inform you that order has been re-establ

(By the Associated Press) Concern lest the ultimate result of the uprising in Austria be its union with Nazi Germany was expressed today in the capitals of Great Britain, Italy and France. London, through Captain Anthony Eden, Lord Privy Seal, is expected to inform Chancellor Hitler of Germany within a week that it insists on Austrian independence. The French cabinet decided to give the Dollfuss government economic aid and plans to enlarge quotas on Austrian goods and join other countries in extending credits. Official comment was lacking in Rome but many Italians expressed fears Nazis would gain the upper hand in the little neighboring country. An unofficial proposal by Henry Berenger, chairman of the foreign affairs committee of the French Senate, that France, Italy and Great Britain intervene to protect Austria's independence should the socialists win had drawn no response from London

(By The Associated Press) CIVIL WAR in Austria with hundreds dead, strikes in Spain, a trade conflict between Great Britain and France were features Tuesday of a dark European picture. Government forces bombarded socialists’ strongholds in Vienna. Estimates of the number dead ranged from 500 to 2,000. In a dozen other Austrian cities civil war raged. Order Returning Nine were hurt in street clashes attending a general strike in Bilbao, Spain. Student disorders flared. Premier Alejandro Lerroux said “danger at certain focal points has not been entirely eliminated,” but order was returning. A trade war between France and Britain was in effect with the imposition of an extra 20 percent duty on most French imports and reduced French quotas on British goods. Premier Gaston Doumergue’s new French cabinet was “silently working” to restore order and economic well-being. A general strike Monday w

London, Feb. 14.—(7)—As the trade war between France and England got into full swing yesterday, it was considered probable here that it might become a long and bitter commercial fight between the two nations. In political quarters, it was thought likely that it may be a long time before any definite move is made to end it. While the British government is certain to reply to the latest French note, the dignity of officials here and in Paris, well-informed persons believed, will not permit either country to back down in the near future. Meanwhile, the British government searched for new commercial ties. The Associated Press was informed by members of the Russian trade delegation that a new Anglo-Russian trade pact will be signed Thursday by the British Board of Trade. British shipping interests today feared a considerable loss in business with the French colonies as a result of the trade w

Rv Associated Press, London, February 1—Amid rumbling rumors of war there came intimation today that the world disarmament conference may be resumed within two months. Officers of the conference met privately today to decide if and when the conference

Vienna, Feb. 14.—(By telephone to London) government forces, definitely on the offensive, opened the third day of the Socialist revolution today with a war scale attack on the principal rebel stronghold here and confidently predicted early victory. As the attack opened a Socialist prisoner was sentenced to death by court martial for his part in the revolt. A gallows was erected at Linz, principal Socialist center of revolt in the provinces. The wartime hangman of army deserters was impressed to execute any condemned there. Soldiers under the personal command of Major Emil Fey, a veteran vice chancellor, moved against the great apartment on the Danube across the Vienna-Dorf bridge to attack Socialists there. Fighting proceeded at other points here, at Linz, at Steyr and other industrial towns. In regiments, in small bands, even single-handed, their women sometimes in front ranks, the Soci

Portland, England, Feb. 13—Twenty-seven men of the crew of the Greek steamship Meandros, feared drowned, were landed here today by the coastal steamship Eleth. A 28th man was landed at Southampton and but two were missing of the entire crew. Those picked up by the Eleth, including the captain, were taken from an open boat in the English channel, where the British steamship Dartford collided with and sank the 4303 ton Meandros.

1934-10-30.text: LONDON, Oct. 29—(#)—Japanese proposals for a new naval treaty to supplant the London and Washington pacts are not acceptable to the British and American delegates, it was learned today. The Japanese, it was understood, have been informed that the two powers are unable to accept Japan's flat declarations of the principle of equality and their proposal for a maximum or global tonnage basis of limiting armaments. The next move in the vital discussions was therefore up to the Japanese. It was understood that unless they modify their attitude, there is virtually no possibility of a compromise. An American spokesman indicated the belief that tearing up the Washington treaty of 1922 may mean the end of collateral pacts which now guarantee the open door in China and non-aggression in the Far East. The delegation understands that the Japanese would seek to change the pacts or end them entirely sh

LONDON, Oct. 3 — American hope for unequivocal British support against Japanese demands on naval equality seemed quashed today. British delegates made it plain to America that they opposed Japan's demand for an allotment which would allow a nation to build ships of such size and class as it desired within a specified total maximum naval tons. However, it was learned that the Japanese were conferring on technical points with the English. United States experts have not been approached in this respect. This leaves the United States alone against the other two nations in the conversation.

LONDON, Oct. 28—(7)—King Prajadhipok, five-foot, wiry monarch of Siam, is willing to take back his threat to quit the throne if the home government knuckles down to an ultimatum demanding withdrawal of a measure curbing his royal prerogatives. The Bangkok government, Prajadhipok’s private secretary disclosed today, has asked the diminutive ruler to reconsider his intention to abdicate. Advices direct from Bangkok, the first since establishment of strict censorship, disclosed meanwhile that the king’s 10,000,000 subjects are completely in the dark about what is going on. There is no resolution, it was indicated, but those in power are keeping from the public the information that the king has threatened to abdicate, waiting until the thing is settled one way or the other. The king and queen spent the week-end quietly at the private re- (Continued on Page 2, Col. 1)

LONDON, Oct. 28.—(#)—The 16,000,000 subjects of the king of Siam did not know today their ruler had threatened to quit, but his representatives here said the government had asked his majesty to reconsider. While King Prajadhipok was on the continent, it was revealed the government at home amended some of his prerogatives, principally that of life and death over his subjects. Prajadhipok threatened to resign. The monarch let it be known today he would withdraw this intention if his government abandons the measure limiting his powers.

- London, Oct. 20.—()—In an effort to cool a disagreement which has deadlocked naval negotiations among the world’s three largest sea powers, a meeting tentatively scheduled for today was called off. Japanese delegates had hoped to meet with the Americans but it was understood these delegations along with the British decided it would be best to postpone the talk until tomorrow. Japan held her ground in the face of American and British opposition to her proposals for a new naval treaty based on the principles of tonnage equality. The delegates from Tokyo are convinced that they can dent the opposition by further conversations. As a result, they asked for a new meeting with the Americans. But the Americans feel concessions must come from the Japanese. Norman H. Davis and Admiral Wm. H. Standley told the Japanese delegates that junking of the Washington and London naval treaties would not g

LONDON, Oct. 29.—()—Catheart Jones and Ken W. Waller landed at Allahabad at 9:55 a. m., G. M. T. today after a flight from Singapore. They said they would not take off toward England until tomorrow morning. The fliers reached Singapore non-stop from Port Darwin, Australia, yesterday, covering the 2,084 miles in less than 11 hours, averaging 201.7 miles an hour. A delay at Port Darwin badly hurt their chance of beating the time of 70 hours, 59 minutes and 50 seconds made last week from England to Melbourne by C. W. A. Scott and T. Campbell Black. Eight of the original 19 starters from Mildenhall airdrome in the Melbourne derby still have to reach that city.

—CALCUTTA;—India, Oct. 30 (NP) —John H. Wright and John Polando, Americans, today abandoned their effort to finish the England-Australia airplane race in their Lambert monocoupe, Baby Ruth, smallest entrant in the event. A cracked cylinder caused the decision. The plane will be shipped back to the United States.

LONDON, Oct. 30.—(4—King Pra- padhipok, a spokesman disclosed today, is calmly reading books while the government of Siam debates issues which may mean his abduction. The king, in Surrey, is awaiting a reply from Bangkok to his latest communication. He has threatened to give up the throne if the government does not withdraw a measure limiting the monarch’s power of life.

1934-11-08.text: London, Nov. 7.—(UP)—Curiosity of Crown Prince Michael of Roumania concerning operation of an army tank endangered his life, and that of his father, King Carol, and several army generals recently according to a Bucharest dispatch printed by the Daily Express. The king and crown prince were attending army maneuvers. Michael, unobserved, jumped inside a tank and manipulated some levers which set it in motion, straight for the king and his generals, who fled. The crown prince, attempting to stop the tank, touched some more levers and started a machine gun firing. He shouted for assistance to halt the tank and an officer finally got it stopped. Michael crawled out of the machine smeared with oil and before his father could reprimand him, said: "You can't do anything to me. I've got a motor car driver's license."

TOKYO, Nov. 5.—Japan rejected in effect today a British compromise offer in the deadlock London naval negotiations. Naval spokesmen said the government “cannot accept any naval formula which, theoretically allotting parity, actually asks Japan to accept inferiority.” The statement was made after dispatches came from London telling of a compromise proposition. “We are unable to conceive of an acceptable scheme which will grant the principle of equality we have already demanded and contain at the same time restrictions giving something less,” the spokesmen said. “Whether Japan will build up to full parity with America and Great Britain is another question, but that question must be left to Japan’s own decision and not subject to agreements with the other powers.”

LONDON, Nov. 17.—UP—Great Britain today intimated for the first time her willingness to recognize Japan's nominal naval equality, the United Press learned on excellent authority. The British at a meeting with the Japanese delegation to the preliminary naval conversations here, advised Japan she would compromise on the equality demand on the basis of a “gentleman's agreement” obligating each of the major sea powers—Britain, the United States and Japan—to declare the level to which one intends to limit naval construction. It was learned that Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald was on the verge of the meeting with the Japanese. (Continued on Page 2, Col. 7.)

PARIS, Nov. 8.—(UP)—Premier Gaston Doumergue’s ‘salvation’ cabinet, formed after the bloody riots of February, was wrecked today on the rocks of party politics and a grave crisis was precipitated. Police and Republican guards were stationed at public buildings, ready to suppress any disorders after the cabinet had resigned. By agreement, Pierre Laval, Doumergue’s foreign minister, was delegated by President Albert Lebrun to form a new cabinet. It was taken for granted that he would succeed, and some members of the Doumergue government accepted their old portfolios. But within little more than an hour, Laval went back to the Elysee palace and told the president he was unable to form a cabinet. Lebrun delegated Pierre-Etienne Flandin, public works minister, leader of the left Republican party of the Centrist group in parliament, to try where Laval had failed. The situation was an anxious o

The aged premier, his nine-month-old true cabinet wrecked by radical socialist opposition to his plans for reforming the nation’s constitution, announced tonight he would present his cabinet’s resignation to President Albert Lebrun. Doumergue came to power amid storms, the Binody Bier riptide in January and February. He steps down amid political reforms and amid dire forecasts of new strife to come, Feels Blameless. His mind is at rest, however, and he feels that the blame is not his, 'the situation is clear,' he said tonight, after announcing his cabinet 'would meet for the last time at the Elysee Palace tomorrow. '“The responsibilities for breaking the political tense are established and I am more at ease. I go to the cabinet meet

PARIS, Nov. 8 (INS)—Pierre Etienne-Flandin, former minister of finance, late today formally accepted the task of forming a cabinet to succeed that of Premier Gaston Doumergue. Flandin accepted provisionally immediately after being summoned by President Lebrun but deferred formal acceptance until he had opportunity to confer with party leaders.

TOKYO, Nov. 8,—(P)—Fear that the Japanese freighter Ranan Maru, with a crew of 42, was destroyed by fire was expressed today in a Rengo (Japanese news agency) dispatch from Niigata, North Honshu Island, Japan. The vessel earlier today sent out a radio call for help, saying she was afire and drifting northwest of Niigata. No further messages have been received from her and rescue ships were unable to locate her.

ROME, Nov. 5,—(#)—All school teachers, male and female, will wear uniforms from now on in Premier Mussolini’s compulsory military culture courses. These lessons will be taught in every high school and college. The innovation is a part of Il Duce’s plan to militarize Italy. The school “marms” will wear the uniforms of instructors in the girls’ section of the Balilla (Fascist youth)

1934-10-17.text: London, Oct. 17.--(7P)—A substantial reduction in general naval armaments and the renewal of the Washington and London treaties will be suggested by the United States delegation in the forthcoming naval conversations, it was stated authoritatively today. This authority said the Americans would be willing to eliminate the word “ratio” from any future agreements if Japan so desired, replacing the word with the term “relative security.” May Eliminate Fight A certain amount of belief was expressed that such a change might eliminate any fight over the action parity between the United States, Japan and Great Britain. The representatives of Japan and the United States came to England Tuesday to attempt to chart the course of the 1935 naval conference. Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, Tokyo's delegate, said at Southampton Japan will decide at the conclusion of the conversations whether to denounce the

LONDON, Oct. 17—(4)—The American defenders of the Schwab bridge trophy continued play against a mounting English lead today in the third session of the five days of play. But Ely Culbertson and his teammates were still confident they would retain the most eagerly sought prize in international bridge. Before play opened today the British team, after 120 hands, led 40,430 points to America’s 35,860 points.

LONDON, Oct. 17—Japanese representatives began preparation today of a draft of proposals for the 1935 naval conference while American and British delegates eagerly awaited Tokyo’s plans. Since the Japanese expect to make a lengthy study of the situation before showing their hand in the three-power talks preliminary to next year’s naval meeting, it is probable their proposals will not be disclosed until next week. One of the first problems facing the three countries is to determine whether the conversations will be bi-lateral or participated in simultaneously by all three. America, it is known, is ready for tri-power discussions if they are desired, but so far the Japanese are fighting shy of the method, claiming language difficulties are too great for general conversations. Great Britain planned to have bi-lateral discussions and unless they change their view, it is unlikely that either

Paris, Oct. 16.—(4’)—France tonight was striving desperately to keep the Marseilles murders from becoming another Sarajevo as police at Melun tore from Mio Kraj, third terrorist suspect jailed, an admission that he was sent to Marseilles to kill King Alexander of Yugoslavia. While the French determination to have Hungary clean up the alleged terrorist ring that plotted Alexander’s death equalled that of the Little Entente, France nevertheless was eager to keep tempers even and prevent the Balkan powder keg's flaring up again. Yugoslavia was expected here to demand explanations from Hungary of its alleged tolerance at Danka Puszta of the Ustashi, Croat revolutionaries.

Assassinations of King Alexander of Jugoslavia and Louis Barthou of France may start Europe not toward war but toward a more solid basis of peace, it was indicated Wednesday. Statesmen of several European nations, who after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand at Serajevo in 1914 were talking war, now talk peace. By their acts in the eight days since Alexander and Barthou were shot down—by tactful speech and tactful silence—they have maintained a diplomatic atmosphere which makes possible constructive negotiation. Diplomatic Move Jugoslavia was outraged by the assassination of its forceful popular king. There were anti-Italian riots, and anger against Hungary, alleged to have sheltered the Croatian terrorists who murdered Alexander, was open and intense. But Jugoslavia's first diplomatic move, the United Press learned on most reliable authority, was a temperate request through i

(By Associated Press) Paris, Oct. 17—French diplomats have the full support of Benito Mussolini in their efforts to keep the Marseilles assassination from disrupting the peace of Europe. Diplomatic circles said today they were informed Il Duce is more than ever bent on pushing a policy of conciliation despite the years of ill feelings between Italy and Jugoslavia. As the threads of the assassination plot are gradually being unraveled, the French foreign Office is just as busy as the French police have been. Plans to scatter the clouds which gathered eight days ago were laid in Benes, Czechoslovakian foreign minister and leader of the Little Entente and League of Nations, with Pierre Laval, France's new foreign minister. Laval planned to pursue the vigorous policies of his predecessor, Louis Barthou, a victim at Marseilles with King Alexander. He will soon visit Rome.

PARIS, Oct. 17.—(UP)—Police today named Anton Pavelle, famous Croatian nationalist, as the probable master mind in the astonishing international plot which led to the assassination of King Alexander and Louis Barthou. They sought him, Gustav Perchee, who, they said, was his first lieutenant, and Egen Kvaternik, “the delegate,” alleged to be the liaison man sent with the four who were designated to kill Alexander. Secret police have information that both men are in France, and they are to answer to charges that would share the guilt of the assassin squad.

By The Associated Press Paris, Oct. 17—The hunt for Dr. Ante Pavelich and Gustave Perec, alleged leaders of the terrorist band blamed for the assassination of King Alexander of Yugoslavia and Louis Barthou of France, turned to Switzerland today in the belief they are hiding there. The two alleged higher up "delegates" Kvaternik and a "gun moll" are suspected of having escaped to neutral territory because of the revelation of the recent hiding places in Hungary and Italy of the two chiefs threatening diplomatic complications. Diplomatic circles say they are informed Premier Mussolini is more than ever bent on pushing a policy of reconciliation. Plans to scatter the clouds which gathered eight days ago when the assassins' pistols were fired were laid in a talk between Dr. Edouard Benes, Czechoslovakian foreign minister and leader of the little entente, with Pierre Laval, France's new minis

1934-12-11.text: WASHINGTON, D. C., Dec. 11— Great Britain has formally notified the United States that she will default on war debt installments, totaling $379,461,776, due Saturday. Ending a general revision of the entire inter-governmental debt structure, the British note made public by the State Department today said Great Britain considers it useless and unwise to make the payment. They consisted of regular $117,000,000 due Dec. 15 and the $261,000,000 on which Great Britain already is in default. Finland is the only country expected to pay. She is the only debtor nation not in default. Paris dispatches said the French cabinet is drafting a note explaining that she would default, totaling $163,176,000. The United States expects the other 10 debtor nations to default.

STOCKHOLM, Sweden, Dec. 10.—(#)—Four Americans and one Italian were honored here today in the 1934 Nobel prize awards while at Oslo, Norway, the peace prize went to Arthur Henderson, Great Britain’s president of the world disarmament conference. The award in medicine is shared by three Americans. The fourth award to an American was for accomplishments in chemistry. The other award goes to Luigi Pirandello, Italian novelist and playwright. Three of the Americans who received the honors are here for the presentation. They are Doctors George Minot and William P. Murphy of the Harvard University medical school, and Dr. George H. Whipple of the University of Rochester, joint winners of the award in medicine. Dr. Harold Clayton Urey of Columbia University, whose discovery of “heavy water” won him the chemistry prize, was unable to attend the ceremony, Lauren Steinhardt, United States minister

LONDON, Dec. 11.—(CUP)—Great Britain not only is defaulting on her war debt payment due to the United States on Friday, but is turning down a suggestion from Washington that she talk over the prospects of reaching a settlement, it was revealed today in the House of Commons. Neville Chamberlain, Chancellor of the Exchequer, told the House it would be useless and unwise to start debt negotiations at present. A note from Washington on Nov. 22, he added, had announced that the United States was ready, through diplomatic channels, to discuss any British proposals for settlement.

(By The Associated Press) Greystones, Irish Free State, Dec. 11—Joseph O’Leary, well digger who has been imprisoned in a shaft since Saturday, has given up his brave fight for life. “Say bye, I am dying,” was the message he sent out last night. A fresh slide of earth apparently sealed the doom of the man whose fortitude during his ordeal had aroused the admiration of the country. Troops continued to work today, however, taking over digging operations from tired civilians. Continued falls of earth and sand hindered operations and hope that O’Leary still lives was abandoned.

-10.—(AP)—The well which has held Joseph O’Leary prisoner since Saturday became his tomb today. All hope of rescuing the plumber whose fortitude inspired the admiration of the countryside was abandoned when the side of the well collapsed further as diggers brought their tunnel into the shaft. The rescuers themselves had to flee to safety. Troops who were called to the scene continued to dig for O’Leary’s body. Shortly before the last cave-in a priest was lowered into the well by ropes, giving the entombed man conditional absolution while the crowd gathered at the mouth of the well kneeled in prayer. O’Leary had been working in the well, perched on a ladder, when the walls caved in on him. That was Saturday at 8 p.m. The rungs of the ladder were broken, crushing his limbs, and only his head and neck were visible from above. Rescuers working from above managed to free his arms and get food

COLUMBUS, O. — Governor White today commuted, to expire at once, the sentence of Louis Mazer, convicted of manslaughter in the slaying of Don R. Mellott, Canton editor, in 1926. Mazer, who was admitted to the Ohio penitentiary in June 1927, to serve 3 to 20 years, has been at the London prison farm since June 1925. The governor cited the recommendation of trial judge Alger and prosecutor D. W. Harter, now a judge, that Mazer had given the state valuable testimony in the Mellott case convictions.

Washington, Dec. 11—(P)—Great Britain has told the United States she will default on the $379,161,776 War debt payments due Saturday, while Finland—the only nation which has paid in full—has given notice she will present her $228,538 in cash. The British said in a note made public today by the state department that it was considered “useless” and “unwise” to make further payments pending a general revision of the entire intergovernmental structure. The state department also announced that L. Astrom, the Finnish minister, had communicated officially that Finland would continue her usual practice. The state department expects the other debtor nations to default. Paris dispatches said the French cabinet is drafting a note explaining she would default on installments totaling $163,616,841. The British made token payments of $10,000,000 in June, 1933, and $87,900,000 in December, 1933, but “d

| PHILADELPHIA, Dec. 12. | (AP)—The Evening Bulletin today quotes Hirosi Saito, Japanese ambassador to the United States, as saying in an interview Japan will pursue her plan of establishing peace in the Far East ‘even if she has to fight both Great Britain and the United States.’ Ambassador Saito granted the interview after his talk to the Philadelphia Lecture assembly, the paper said. He is quoted as asserting “Japan will commit national suicide, if necessary, to pursue her plan of establishing peace in the Far East. “She will pursue this policy, even if she had to fight both Great Britain and the United States, and regardless of the whims of these two countries. “However, Japan has only peace in mind. If we feel it necessary for our purpose of establishing the peace in the Far East, Japan will gobble up Northern China for that purpose, and we will do so regardless of what other powers

1934-11-18.text: CAPE TOWN, Union of South Africa, Nov. 17 (4)—Sixty-one natives participating in a beer-drinking party near East London were instantly killed when lightning struck the hut in which the party was held, dispatches reaching here said today. Only three of the 64 natives who gathered for the party survived.

London. -- (AP) - Ambassador Tsuneo Matsudaira of Japan today, on behalf of his nation, rejected the British suggestion for a compromise in the proposed naval treaty. The ambassador told Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, that Japan could not accept the British offer of a treaty which would recognize only equality in principle for Japan. Japan wants the right to equalize in actual tonnage. At the same time, Matsudaira urged that the British consider new ways of approaching a compromise which would recognize Japanese equality.

London, Nov. 17 "(#)--England was echoing today with the grave warning that she was in “mortal danger” from an air attack by Germany. Winston Churchill, British statesman-soldier-author, last night told his countrymen that Germany was "re-arming with the utmost speed" and vigorously urged that Great Britain make herself “the strongest air power in the European world” without delay. “This,” he said, “was necessary to avert another war. “Only a few hours away from us by air,” Churchill, former chancellor of the exchequer, declared in an address, “is a nation whose people are being taught from childhood to think of war as a glorious exercise, and death in battle as the noblest fate of man.” The English statesman described England as “an inviting prey or bait to the ambitions and appetites of hungry powers.” Churchill did not directly name Germany as the source of England’s danger from the a

DARIEN, Conn., Nov. 17. (UP)— Police directed a search throughout New England today for John D. Lewis, escaped convict, alleged brains of what officers said was a plot to kidnap Robert Lewis, 12, step-son of Gustave U. Westheim, wealthy head of a travel bureau. Three additional persons were arrested in Providence, R. I., last night and were being questioned there by Darien police. They were Lillian Borg, 23, and David Borg, 18, wife and brother of Joseph Borg, one of three men arrested after a fight with police in the Westheim home here yesterday. The third person arrested in Providence was Joseph Frovall, whom police said owned the car that took the gang to Darien. All denied any knowledge of the crime, but Mrs. Borg admitted her husband had entertained strange men in their Providence apartment. Police said Lewis was the member of the gang that fought police in the Westheim home who esc

LONDON, Nov. 17 — In the wake of Japan's rejection of the compromise plan for naval limitation, British participants in the power naval conversations here tonight were more hopeful for ultimate agreement than at any time since negotiations began. The Japanese delegates, Ambassador Tsunco Yamamoto and Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, will deliver Tokyo's formal reply to the British compromise proposal next week. Japan stands as firm as ever on her demand for equality on the high seas. At the same time, it was learned, the Japanese will request further conversations as to the possibility of meeting Japan's desire for equality with the other two powers engaged in the conversations, Britain and the United States. Britain's plan, put forward in an effort to end the deadlock holding conferences, involves recognition of Japan's right to equality in principle, whereas the Japanese want actual tonnage e

I commented LONDON, Saturday, Nov. 17 - UP Personal advertisement in the Morning Post: "Man aged 106, active as at 40, needs employment." Qualifications included a "youthful appearance" and ability as a linguist.

(Associated Press Foreign Staff) Rome, Nov. 17.—(4)—The prospect of black shirts in swaddling clothes greeted Italy today. A new and far-reaching government order enrolls the man-child in the ranks of Premier Mussolini's balilla organization from the time of birth. The premonition of the drumbeats and bugle-calls thus is injected into the rattle shaking of Italy’s infant, while the press warns of “a crucial year” approaching for Europe. Coincident with the announcement that the new-born babies will be enrolled in the black shirt pre-military organizations, Il Duce’s newspaper Popolo D'Italia said tension on the continent is becoming grave. “It is necessary to be strong to meet and dominate all events,” the newspaper said. “The situation in Europe about us is grave. . . as was the case twenty years ago dissensions, menaces and struggles for hegemony, blocs, alliances and armament races di

GENEVA, NOV. 17, (AP). — It was officially announced today that the League of Nations Chaco consultative committee had reached an agreement on means to end the savage warfare between Bolivia and Paraguay. The agreement will be embodied in a report to be presented to the special assembly of the League which meets next week to consider the Chaco dispute.

1934-06-27.text: London, June 27.47) — A new British note was cabled to the British embassy in Washington today in which the British government emphasized its desire to negotiate a permanent war debts settlement with the United States. Foreign office officials declined to reveal the exact nature of the note except to say, “it is quite short.” The British policy of the past in reference to the desire for a discussion of a full settlement of the debt question was understood to have been restated as part of the communication. The note is in reply to one by Secretary of State Cordell Hull suggesting payment “in kind,” but it comes with Great Britain already in the defaulter class. She entered that status June 15 when she refused to pay an installment. British circles pointed out that the day following the Hull note President Roosevelt took the position that payments in kind could be only “very partial” ones.

London, June 30. — Adam and Eve had a lot of trouble over an apple, but evidence is put forward to show that it really was gout that put the first man in his grave. This theory was advanced by an ancient manuscript put on display in London's historic College of Arms. The exhibition was opened in celebration of the 450th anniversary of the association known as Kings, Heralds and Pursuivants of Arms Organization. The lowdown on Adam was offered in an ancient vellum pedigree of a Saxon king who had proudly traced his family tree back to Adam. The king asserted that the ancestor of all mankind 'dyed of gowte.'

LONDON, June 27 (AP)—Matchmakers who have been worrying about the single state of the Prince of Wales had something new to talk about today. Wales, who turned 40 Saturday without so much as an inkling that he was even thinking of matrimony, attended a dinner dance last night at the Dutch legation in honor of Princess Juliana of Holland, who is in London for the season. The prince and the princess, who is 25, have been linked in marriage rumors before. For that matter, both have been mentioned by matchmakers with nearly every royal house containing an eligible heir.

| LONDON, June 26—(4’)—A British jury decided today that Tilly Losch James, pretty Viennese dancing star, was guilty of adultery with Prince Serge Obolensky, and a divorce decree nisi was granted to her wealthy husband, Edward Frank James. The dancer, pale and trembling, looked around the crowded courtroom and clutched her bottle of smelling salts as the verdict was read. The decree nisi means that the divorce will not become absolute for six months. Mrs. James had sought a judicial separation.

(BY 2228 ARBOUR LOG, Press Sandwich, Eng. June 27--Shattering all first round records in the history of the British Open golf championship, tall Henry Cotton, a native professional, today scored a sub-par 67 over the Royal St. George's course to take a three shot lead in the first 18 holes of the 72-hole title grind.

Lendon, June 27,—The cabinet meeting today as hopes for naval disarmament dwindled, was reported to have endorsed supplementary estimates to strengthen the navy, army and air force. Increases for the navy and air force were said to be large, and for the army, small. It was reported that a bill incorporating the supplementary estimates would be introduced in parliament next week and would signalize the opening move in an impressive plan for rearmament in view of the serious world political situation. Reliable information was that the government had determined to go ahead with its plan—based on the certainty of failure of the land disarmament conference—to make Britain's air force as large as that of the greatest one within striking distance. This plan would mean building up to the level of France and Italy. But it is really, and frank (Continued On Page Two

London, June 27 (UP) — An Anglo-United States diplomatic incident arose today over disclosure of the contemplated increase by Great Britain in her naval, air and land forces. The foreign office was understood to have made a strong oral protest to Norman H. Davis, United States ambassador at large, alleging that a certain official attached to the United States delegation to the current naval conversation, had been guilty of gross indiscretion in an effort to maintain friendly contact with the press.

LONDON, June 27.—Tilly Losch, famous dancer divorced yesterday by Edward F. W. James, received a second blow today when she was ordered to pay a share of the cost of her defense. Sir Boyd Merriman, president of the divorce court, decided that Miss Losch must pay the cost of investigating cruelty charges which she brought against James, wealthy Briton and former diplomat. Prince Serge Obolensky, with whom a special jury decided yesterday, Miss Losch had committed misconduct, was ordered to pay the costs of the rest of the suit. Miss Losch, protesting to her friends that her friendship was an innocent one and commenting sadly that she was penniless, was not in court. She was planning, she said, to resume her dancing career to restore her finances.

1934-08-08.text: Toronto, Canada, Aug. 5— James Ayling and Leonard Reid, hopped off from Wasaga Beach early today on an attempted non-stop flight to Baghdad. Their plane, the “Trial of the Caribou” in which James and Amy Mollison, British fliers, once intended to make a trans-Atlantic flight, took to the air at 6:12 a.m. and immediately headed northeast. The plane was heavily loaded, having aboard 600 gallons of gasoline. The fliers believed this supply would carry them through to their goal without stopping if they did not run into headwinds for any considerable period of time. Both the fliers are Canadians, Reid, 36, lived for years in Newfoundland, where his father is manager of a government railway. Ayling, 29, is a former member of the Royal Air Force.

TA ROSA, Calif. Aug. 8. (*) she left side crushed in a fall with her horse Mrs. Charmian London, widow of the author, Jack London, remained in a critical con- dition and could not be out of danger for at least a week.

WASAGA BEACH, Ont., Aug. 8 (AP)—James Ayling and Leonard Reid took off today in an attempt to fly non-stop to Baghdad, Iraq, and break the world’s long distance flight record. The heavily loaded plane ran a mile and a half down the beach before soaring away at 4:12 a.m. CST to the east. Ahead was the dangerous north Atlantic hop, the biggest hazard along the 6,500 miles route to Baghdad. The plane, “the Trail of the Caribou”, is the same one in which Captain James Mollison and his wife, Amy, British fliers, attempted to take off from the same beach last year on a long distance flight, only to crack up at the start. The fliers have been prepared for the test for months. Cross winds balked an attempt July 24. They preferred to start from central Canada instead of from Harbor Grace, Nfld. where most of west-to-east hops have been inaugurated. Six hundred gallons of gasoline was aboard the p

BERLIN, Aug. 8—(4)—Adolf Hitler put aside the role of general orator today and turned to the task of guiding Germany through grave problems which enmesh it in one of its most critical mazes since the World War. The chancellor, president in all but name, returned to the capital by airplane yesterday immediately after he had spoken a eulogy at the bier of the late President Paul von Hindenburg. Germany's economic situation is grave. A sharp decline in foreign trade and ensuing foreign exchange difficulties have necessitated a program of rationing raw materials which recalls war-time measures. This, economists say, is bound to result in a curtailment of production and the problem of keeping factories going is imminent. The financial dilemma was re-emphasized yesterday by the announcement that registered marks would be barred to foreigners living in Germany.

By United Press QUEBEC CITY, Que., Aug. 8.—The black biplane, “Trail of the Caribou,” en route from Wasaga Beach, Ont., to Bagdad, Iraq, was sighted over Quebec City shortly before noon today. The fliers were headed due east. A short time later the fliers passed over Isle Verte.

TANNENBERG, Germany, Aug. 7. (P)—In a tower room of the national shrine erected in memory of his greatest military victory, the body of President Paul von Hindenburg rested tonight while thousands of his fellow-countrymen waited patiently in flickering torch light for a glimpse of his coffin. Funeral services in which his successor, Chancellor Adolf Hitler, with deep feeling said Von Hindenburg, "opened the door" to the present regime delivered the old soldier into his monumental shrine. The final rites, brief and simple as the field marshal had wished, were conducted on the very spot where 20 years ago he stopped the Russian invasion. After the coffin had been brought here from the Von Hindenburg estate at Neudeck, along 60 miles of torch-lighted road, there was prayer, music, a short talk by an army chaplain and Hitler’s fervent speech in which he declared the name of Von Hindenburg ca

VIENNA, Aug. 8. — (#) — Nine members of the Vienna police force went on trial for their lives today before a court martial, charged with high treason for participation in a raid on the chancellery July 25 which resulted in the assassination of Chancellor Dollfuss. Seven Are Married. Seven of the men who may go to the gallows before the day is over are married. One of them is an inspector and two are surgeons. The government placed its campaign against nazis in the hands of Major Emil Fey. Fey, who performed yeoman service for the late chancellor in the suppression of socialists last winter, is under orders to wipe out nazi influence. To achieve this end he is given sweeping powers, including the right to discharge private employees suspected of nazi sympathies. Cabinet Awaits Reaction. While Fey plans his drive, the cabinet awaits reaction to its approval of Franz von Papen as Germany's

Lens, France—()—One hundred and eighty Polish miners who held 11 French miners captive during a 36-hour novel strike today were threatened with expulsion. Forced by hunger and thirst to emerge from the mine, the Poles made a condition of surrender that nobody would be prosecuted. But police opened an inquiry, which is expected to result in a number of the strikers being asked to cross the border. French miners were angered and police were alert throughout last night, fearing clashes. The French general labor federation sent a protest to the ministry of labor as a result of the affair, demanding more effective efforts to protect French miners. The Poles came from the 1,000 foot coal pit last night with their 11 hostages while citizens of Lens shouted curses at them. They struck because two of their fellow-countrymen were fired for engaging in political activities. The Poles grappled with

1934-09-19.text: ABOARD U. S. C. G. CUTTER OFF NEWPORT, Sept. 18 —(#)— Endeavour, T. O. M. Sopwith’s British challenger for the America’s Cup, today won her second straight victory over the American defender Rainbow in a 30-mile race over a triangular course in a fresh breeze. Beaten over the starting line and handicapped with a torn sail the blue-hulled challenger quickly made the start and made each mark a winning one as she boiled home winner by 51 seconds. In her victory she added new laurels as she broke the record for a triangular course set by Enterprise in 1930, and set a new time of three hours, nine minutes and one second.

GENEVA, Sept. 19.—(4)—With Russia occupying her permanent seat in the League of Nations council for the first time, France and Great Britain today denounced the bloody war between Paraguay and Bolivia as a debacle which must stop. Louis Barthou, French foreign minister, told the council the time has come for action in the Chaco dispute and "this conflict threatens to affect the prestige of the league."
