WASHINGTON, D. C., Sept. 19,—(U, P.) The death toll in the general textile strike mounted to 15 today as violence flared in New England and the South. A striker died of bayonet wounds at Belmont, North Carolina, to add the latest fatality. Georgia state troops maintained martial law over many textile centers. Approximately 150 pickets were interned in a barbed wire camp. Six more mills were reopened, Maine guardsmen arrested ten pickets from a contingent of 225 girls who had marched to Lewiston to force the closing of a plant. Several were injured in the riot at Waterville, Maine. In Saylesville, Rhode Island, scene of recent strike warfare, the Sayles Furnishing Plant reopened. Pickets were peaceful and state troops had no trouble maintaining order. Other plants in the state opened under similar conditions. In Washington further peace negotiations were held in abeyance, pending a report

New York, Sept. 18 (4) — John Barrymore is in London negotiating with producers for a series of British-made films. The actor slipped into New York three weeks ago from Hollywood, stayed a few days and sailed quietly on the Berengaria for conferences with the British producers. His attorney, M. Hotchner, said Barrymore had been asked repeatedly in the last few years to make pictures in England.

ROME, SEPT. 18. (AP) — Compulsory military service for Italians beginning at the age of eight and continuing to the age of 33 was decreed today by the council of ministers in probably the most sweeping military law ever passed in history. Declaring “the functions of a citizen and of a soldier are not dividable in the fascist state,” the council created the three following categories of compulsory military training. 1. Preliminary—Beginning at the age of eight years. 2. Military—Beginning at the age of 21 years. 3. Post-Military—Continuing for ten years after the military phase is concluded. With reference to the youth, the council declared that by this decree boys from the time they are eight years old until they are called to arms at 21 years will be prepared spiritually, physically and militarily by the civic organization of the fascist Balilla and by the fascist youths of combat. Thus

THE HAGUE, Sept. 18.—(?) — Police dispersed a communist demonstration with severe fighting today when ten automobile loads of demonstrators tried to upset the royal procession in which Queen Wilhelmina went to the opening of parliament. When the queen spoke from the throne inside the house of parliament, communists created another scene. Three communist members of parliament were ejected from the chamber and then arrested. Contrary to general expectations, the queen made no reference in her speech to rumors that the betrothal of Princess Juliana was forthcoming.

GENEVA, Sept. 18 (AP) — The League of Nations assembly officially voted Russia into membership today and Maxim Litvinov, Russian commissar of foreign affairs told the delegates that Russia was entering the league as a representative of a new social system which would renounce none of its attributes. The Russian diplomat praised his nation as a kind of League of Nations by itself since it includes 200 nationalities who "co-exist in peace while enjoying their own culture and languages."

GENEVA, Sept. 19 — Soviet Russia, the League of Nations’ newest baby member, promised today to take a leading role in future activities. By admitting Russia, the League added to its membership 8.28 per cent of the world’s population, covering 14.5 per cent of its land surface. Maxim Litvinov, Russia's foreign minister and chief delegate, seemed ready to start at once on a fight to preserve peace and to use the League insofar as he could to offset possible threats from Germany and Japan, both of which have given notice of withdrawal from it. Within two hours after admittance, Litvinov in a joint statement with the Polish delegation asserted that a series of treaties between two nations, rather than one all-embracing treaty, gave hope of preserving eastern European peace. The statement was regarded as Poland's price for withholding its opposition to placing Russia in a permanent seat on th

1934-12-01.text: SANTA MONICA, Calif., Nov. 20.—Reading the list of guests at a big wedding in London, Grand Duke Dimitri of Russia, Grand Duchess Xenia of Russia, Grand Duke Vladimir of Russia, Moscow will get a kick out of that. Then there was a big It was really a pre-war gathering. It was a very gracious gathering of King George of England to dig up all these old has-beens and let 'em live over again past glories, even if it was just for a day. Not a Stalin, a Hitler, or a Mussolini to mar the proceedings. Yours, WILL.

TOKYO (#) — The United States and Great Britain today, for the third time in five months, had concertedly notified the Japanese government of their objection to the Manchoukuo oil monopoly in diplomatic representations. It was officially admitted today that Sir Robert Clive, the British ambassador, gave a note on the subject to Foreign Minister Koki Hirota November 24, and, although the United States embassy and the foreign office declined to give out information, it was authoritatively learned that Ambassador Joseph C. Grew of the United States delivered a similar note to the foreign minister’s residence this weekend. With these diplomatic moves, the Anglo-American oil controversy against Japan was regarded by observers as having entered a more tense stage.

LONDON, (UP)—John Cecil Lawrence, barrister, today petitioned for divorce from Elissa Landi, motion picture star of Hollywood. He charged misconduct. Abram Chasins, of the Curtis Institute of Music, Philadelphia, was made a party to the suit. Miss Landi announced last May that she had sued Lawrence in Los Angeles charging mental cruelty. She had informed Lawrence of her decision, she said. "My husband used to try to do everything to insure the success of my acting and writing," she explained. "But now he seems afraid that he may be called 'Mr. Elissa Landi.'" Miss Landi, in private life Mrs. Elizabeth Marie Lawrence, is 27. Lawrence is 31. They were married in London Jan. 28, 1928. After starring in "Farewell to Arms" in New York two years, she went to Hollywood.

REDS, England, Dec. 1—A 62-year-old mother who painfully put to death an imbecile son because she faced a serious operation and feared she wouldn't survive, was sentenced to death today on a charge of murder. The frail little mother, Mrs. May Brownhill of Pennal, who had devoted the last 30 years of her life to nursing the son, Denis, heard the verdict of the jury and the sentence of the judge stoically, standing with her head erect. Asked if she wished to address court she replied, “I did it in love.” There were tears in the eyes of many in the audience. According to testimony at the trial, the mother, upon being told she could live only six months unless she underwent a dangerous operation, put her son to bed and gave him 100 sedative tablets, then turned on the gas. Next day she calmly told the family doctor who came to investigate: “I just put Denis to sleep.” Later, when police char

Japan proposed new efforts to reach an agreement on naval limitation—but insisted that agreement must give her full equality in naval armaments. Tsuneo Matsudaira, the Japanese ambassador to London, told Norman H. Davis, United States ambassador-at-large, Tokyo was willing to try to reach an understanding on the basis of recent British compromise proposals. A ten-year treaty was envisaged in the British suggestions. Matsudaira, however, said Japan would insist that the treaty provide full equality for the Japanese navy, refusing to accept the British thesis that the principle of equality might be recognized and equality in naval armaments. LONDON, Nov. 30—(4)—Japan to-

LONDON (AP) — The possibility of a new tri-power ten-year naval treaty began was seen today as a result of new proposals made by Japan. Ambassador Tsuneo Matsudaira of Japan told Norman H. Davis, the American representative to the naval parley, that Japan was willing to try to reach an understanding on the basis of recent British compromise proposals. However, the British suggestion that Japan’s right to equality in theory only be granted and that equality in fact be withheld was flatly rejected by the Japanese.

READING, Nov. 50—-(AP)—The bodies of an attractive young divorced mother and her 7-year-old daughter were found clasped in death today in a gas-filled bedroom. The victims were Mrs. Cora Catherine Schoenly, 25, a brown-eyed brunette knitting mill worker, and Carmen Rae, who was six months old when her parents separated in 1928. Coroner S. B. Glick described the case as murder and suicide. The owner of the apartment reported to police that Mrs. Schoenly had been despondent. Glick said he believed the mother took her daughter to bed as usual without telling the child of her intentions.

LEEDS, England, Dec. 1 (UP)-- Mrs. May Brownhill, 62, today was sentenced to be hanged for the “mercy murder” of her imbecile son, Dennis, 30. According to testimony at the trial, Mrs. Brownhill was suffering from an ailment. She feared she would not recover from the operation because of her advanced age. It was these circumstances, the defense contended, which prompted her when she gave her helpless son 100 grains of aspirin and turned on a gas jet in order that she might not leave him alone in the world after her own death.

1934-04-04.text: Mid-summer heat in the east, a howling blizzard over part of the west and threatening floods in New England feature the variegated current bill offered by that veteran impresario, the weather man. The south enjoyed balmy, springtime temperatures. In New York he offered odds that today would break the all-time high for April 3—73.4 degrees, set in 1892. That should be cheering to the citizens of Montana and Wyoming as they dig themselves out of ten-foot snowdrifts piled up by a storm last night. The thermometer reached 75 in New York yesterday, while Washington reported 84 and Boston 72. Massachusetts and Connecticut were keeping anxious watch on the Connecticut River, which had reached flood stage at several points. The present situation is not dangerous, but it is feared that the continuing warm spell will cause a further rise. Other New England rivers were reported in the same conditio

London—(L.P)—Just when the Swedish royal family apparently was drawing a deep breath of re- lief at assurance that another prince is not altar-bound with a pretty commoner, word reached London today that a union they all can approve is in prospect. The London Daily Mail, in a dispatch from Stockholm, says the engagement of Princess Ingrid, daughter of Crown Prince Gustaf Adolf of Sweden, to 35-year-old Crown Prince Frederick of Denmark, is "impending." Princess Ingrid is a sister of 22-year-old Prince Bertil whose rumored romance with Christina Brambeck almost upset the vacation of King Gustaf at Cannes, France. The tennis-loving king stopped packing his bags and returned to the courts at the French resort yesterday when assured Prince Bertil still hasn't "made up his mind." Prince Bertil’s brother, Sigvard, married a German actress a few weeks ago and their cousin, Prince Lennart, took

ISTANBUL, April 3 (P)—Samuel Insull renounced United States citizenship today and claimed he was a British subject in his battle against extradition to America on charges of fraud. His attorneys took this step after Turkish authorities rejected the Chicago fugitive’s appeal from a court decision holding him for U.S. authorities. Prosecutor Kenan Bey said no appeal was in order. Insull’s legal aids revealed they intended to carry the fight to the highest authorities. The prosecutor's declaration that Insull's appeal could not be considered was regarded as ending his chances of prolonging the legal fight here against being turned over to United States officials.

ISTANBUL, Turkey, April 4.—Samuel Insull, querulous, despairing but still fighting extradition, moved to replenish his empty war chest today unknowing that Mme. Zehra Couyoumdjoglou, mystery beauty, had tried to land here to aid him and had been turned away. Calling on the remnants of his $100,000,000 utilities fortune to save him, Insull through his lawyers cabled to London for $10,000. It was revealed that when he landed here he had but ten Turkish pounds —$8.20. He kept up his spirits by conferring with his attorneys on plans to defeat plans of the Turkish and American government to send him to the United States for trial for fraud. The lawyers gave him some hope, but all government and judicial authorities seemed agreed that he had made his last stand and lost. Ignoring efforts to appeal in his behalf, officials awaited a warrant from American Ambassador Robert P. Skinner and were re

ISTANBUL, Turkey, April 3—(AP)—Samuel Insull, beaten in his long fight against extradition to the United States, expressed his readiness tonight to return to America if he could be assured he would not be persecuted by his "enemies." Jurists declared he could appeal from a decision of a penal court on which Turkey’s decision to send back the fugitive was based; the government kept him in jail and considered his case closed; and American officials prepared to come and get him. Disconsolate in the drab surroundings of a prison hospital room and depressed because of the latest developments in his dramatic fight against three governments, Insull cabled to his London representative for funds. It is generally believed that the former millionaire financier and patron of the arts is financially poor. During a conversation with an attorney the white-haired, 74-year-old man said he would not hesit

By United Press ATHENS, Greece, April 4—A request of George Pop, counsel for Samuel Insull, that Insull’s forcible seizure by Turkey be submitted to the World Court at the Hague was rejected today by Premier Panayot Toaldaris.

PARIS, April 3. — Fears that street fighting might be resumed and charges that rightists and leftists are preparing for a revolution led authorities today to redouble their searches for hidden arsenals. The accusations of secret arming the extremists camps hurled at each other were taken so seriously that Minister of Justice Henry Cheron ordered a vigorous investigation despite denials by the police and secret service operatives that rifles and pistols were being smuggled across the French borders. Thousands of rifles and automatic pistols were reported smuggled into France. Large quantities of the latter were said to be arriving in Paris daily, consigned to big armament firms.

Paris, April 3 (/P)—Reports of a German Nazi expedition laden with arms to aid rebellious Moroccan tribes caused the French government today to warn military posts in North Africa to be on the alert. Spanish authorities were asked to guard against the landing of a shipload of munitions supposedly en route from Rotterdam with a German agent and 10 Nazi storm troopers.

1934-11-01.text: London, Ky., Nov. 1.—A windstorm which twisted over the northern edge of Laurel county left five members of a family of seven dead today, and an unidentified amount of damage. The dead are Mrs. Emma Robinson, 32, and four of her children: Robert, 12; Vergie, 10; Ralph, 8, and Wilma Jean, 3. Her six-year-old son was found near the door of their house, unhurt, and the father, who was a mile away on business, also escaped uninjured. The bodies of the five dead were found huddled together on a bed, in the charred remains of what had been a roadside filling station, garage and dwelling. The building apparently was fired by the heating stove after being wrecked by the wind. The storm wrecked the mess hall of a CCC camp across the Rockcastle River in Rockcastle county last night, and twisted other buildings in the neighborhood from their foundations.

TOKYO, Nov. 1. —The Manchukuo government, it was learned today, has already moved to effect the oil monopoly despite the representations by the United States, Great Britain and the Netherlands. Disregarding foreign charges that the scheme is discriminatory and violates the open door principle, Manchukuo instituted steps to assume early possession of the extensive marketing installations made in Manchukuo by the Standard Oil of New York and the British Asiatic Petroleum Company. They are to be eliminated from profitable distributing and retailing business built up in recent decades.

London, Ky., Oct. 31 (AP)—A cyclone which wrecked two dwellings seventeen miles north of here tonight caused the death of Mrs. Emma Robertson, 32, and four of her five children. They apparently were burned to death in a fire which started when the storm wrecked their home. One child, a 6-year-old boy, escaped death in some unexplained manner. The father of the family, Robert Robertson, was away from home with a truck when the storm hit. The storm struck about 6:30 o'clock tonight, residents of the vicinity said. It wrecked the Robertson dwelling, which was in connection with a roadside filling station, leveled a store about 100 yards distant, and blew down the mess hall at a CCC camp located near the Rockcastle River, known as the Walnut Grove camp. The terrific wind was accompanied by a heavy downpour of rain.

LONDON, Oct. 31.—(#)— The British government has decided to establish an inquiry into the private manufacture and sale of war materials, it was stated in political quarters tonight. Official confirmation, however, was lacking for the present. The Daily Mail said the government's decision was partly a result of the senatorial inquiry of the United States at Washington and also partly because of a deadlock in the disarmament conference. It was believed the government also would propose that other nations join a conference to discuss the manufacture and exportation of arms with a view of obtaining a convention establishing international control. Such a conference, it was suggested, might take the place of the disarmament conference.

LONDON, Nov. 1 (AP).—Great Britain, political quarters said today, plans an investigation of the private manufacture and sale of war materials. The government also will propose an international conference to discuss manufacture and exportation of arms with a view of joint control, it was believed. Although official confirmation was not given, the Daily Mail said the government's decision was a result in part of the inquiry held by the United States Senate and because of the deadlock in the World Disarmament Conference. During the Washington munitions probe several references were made to Great Britain and Vickers-Armstrong, a powerful British munitions and shipbuilding firm, which figured in the testimony. Sir Bolton Eyres-Monsell, First Lord of the Admiralty, denied before the House of Commons yesterday allegations that Vickers-Armstrong had a “friend in the Admiralty” who was helpful i

London, Nov. 8.—(/P)——Japan tonight stood as pat as ever on her demand for equality on the high seas, Japanese delegates here for tri-power naval conversations have decided tentatively not to accept informal British proposals intended to break the existing deadlock, even though these proposals went far toward embodying Tokyo's schema for new methods of limiting navies, it was learned authoritatively.

LONDON, Oct. 31--(P)—Japan tonight stood pat on her demand for naval equality, and tri-power conversations seeking an agreement for limiting sea weapons were at a stalemate. The negotiators representing the United States, Great Britain and Japan decided, however, to continue their conference indefinitely, hoping something unforeseen may develop to break the deadlock. Nippon’s delegates, Ambassador Tsuneo Matsudaira and Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, were firm in their assertions that Japan will not abandon her insistence that she is entitled to equality with Great Britain and the United States on the high seas.

land, Nov. 1.—(P) — Winston Churchill, former chancellor of the exchequer of Great Britain, declared today in a speech to members of his constituency that Germany was rearming "secretly, legally, and rapidly." LONDON, Nov. L—(?)—President of the Board of Trade Runciman today announced settlement of the Anglo-German commercial debts controversy by special cash and earmarking funds, and revealed Germany has agreed to continue to pay interest on the Young and Dawes loans held in Britain. The Reichsbank will immediately provide 400,000 pounds sterling for aiding in the liquidation of outstanding commercial debts. In addition, Germany guarantees to earmark 55 percent of the value of German exports to Britain for payment of British exports to Germany. This allocation, Runciman said, should according to the usual trend of Anglo-German trade be sufficient to enable British exports to be paid in

1934-07-20.text: London..—(AP)—Charges of continued misconduct by Douglas Fairbanks, Sr., and Lady Ashley since they were named February 5 in Lord Ashley's suit for divorce were filed shortly before noon today in the Somerset house registry office. “The supplementary petition requires an answer within fourteen days if the correspondent (Fairbanks) and the respondent wish to resist it,” said an attorney for Lord Ashley. Notice is to be served on lawyers for both Fairbanks and the former London cabaret performer, Fairbanks and the bobbed-haired Lady Ashley flew to Paris together July 7 and are now at Monte Carlo with her sister. “We do not care where they are,” said the attorney. “Their attorneys will take care of services.” The supplementary petition, it was learned, cites “various places and various dates” when the alleged misconduct took place.

Santa Monica, Calif., July 19.— In 1926, I was in England during their world famous general strike and brother, it was general. Not a paper printed, not a train, not a bus, not a wheel turned. Well, I never got through telling of the composure of those level-headed people. Well, I went to San Francisco. And I tell you we are not so "nutty" under stress as you might think. It was as quiet as the British. The only thing went haywire was the headlines in the out-of-Frisco papers. There is lots of sense in this country yet. Copyright McNaught Syndicate.

LONDON, July 19—Stanley Baldwin, lord president of the council, informed the house of commons today that the British government has decided on a program of increasing its air force by 41 squadrons during the next five years. Of the new squadrons, he said 33 would be allowed for home defense, raising the existing 42 squadrons at home to a total of 75. The remaining squadrons would be for service with the fleet as an air arm or for use abroad.

LONDON, July 19—(4)—Outlining the plans for British air defense expansion, made necessary, the government believes, by failure of the powers to agree on disarmament, Stanley Baldwin told the House of Commons today that 41 new squadrons will be created. Baldwin, Lord President of the Council and acting Prime Minister, explained that 33 of the squadrons will be added to the home force, bringing the total to 85, and that the others will be for service with the fleet abroad. The program is to be carried out, he said, during the next five years. Since the average squadron is composed of 12 planes, the expansion will mean the addition of nearly 500 planes to carry out the British plan to make this country equal in air strength to any power within striking distance. A prominent air authority said that the number of first line aircraft of Great Britain at the end of 1933 was 840, and that the 41

Edinburgh—(/P)—A man who hurled a bottle or large glass at King George and Queen Mary was discharged today at a police court hearing and, it was believed, had the king to thank for it. The object was thrown Saturday as their majesties were motoring to Edinburgh for Harthill. It struck the pavement a few yards behind the royal car. Police immediately seized the man; King George expressed a wish that the man be freed, it was understood.

WASHINGTON, (UP) — The administration’s conciliation forces in the San Francisco strike emergency were strengthened Thursday by the return of Jonald R. Richberg, recovery coordinator, who had been on vacation. Richberg arrived by special plane from New England at midnight and conferred with Secretary of Labor Frances Perkins and Marvin McIntyre of the presidential secretariat. President Roosevelt was seen here Thursday wielding a powerful if indirect influence toward speedy and peaceful settlement of the strike. The hand of the president was observed behind the strengthening of federal mediation on the Pacific coast by the addition of Gen. Hugh S. Johnson and Sen. Robert F. Wagner.

BOSTON, July 20. —(P)— Fire crept stealthily through miles of New England's famished forests today and smouldered threateningly in the scrubland of her coastal plains. Farmers, campers and CCC men fought the devastating blazes with no hope of early aid from the elements. A forest fire which started yesterday in Mooslameo Mountain, East of Lake Dunmore, in Vermont, was beyond control and was burning over a wooded area a mile square. The blaze was believed to have started from a hiker's camp. Flames licked at the borders of Battell forest, a tract of first growth trees owned by Middlebury College. With hundreds of acres of brush and woodlands already burned over, one more in the Cape Cod area of Massachusetts were destroyed by fires at Mashpee, Bourne and Falmouth. At North Andover, Mass., a blaze swept across approximately 1,000 acres of swamp and crept onward in the direction of Boxford.

Associated Press Staff Writer Unless the "liberals" center on a gubernatorial candidate, there is danger of the "drys" ruling Texas, Maury Hughes, who would be chief executive, warned a Georgetown audience last night. "The combined dry forces of Texas will rule the state unless the liberals consolidate their strength behind their strongest candidate," Hughes said, arguing he was the man to select. He said should the "drys get command, it would not be rule of the majority." Tom Hunter told his Beaumont audience it was the task of the state to see that every child in Texas has a proper education. "The safety of any self-governed people depends upon its educational facilities, a well-grounded planning of the trained mind," he said. "And the availability of opportunity in independent competition." Attorney General James V. Allred, in a Temple speech, stressed the need of regulation of electr

1934-07-17.text: | BRIGHTON, Eng, July 16.—UP) A stuttering waiter who mysteriously disappeared over the week-end was sought today for questioning in the bizarre trunk murders of two women. A woman's body, jammed double into a trunk, was found last night. In the trunk also were the head and arms of another woman, believed to be those from the torso found in a trunk at a railway station here June 18. A description of the waiter, known as “Toni Mancini,” an Italian, was flashed by telegraph and telephone to police of the entire country and inquiries for him were made at French ports on the English channel. He was known to have spent a few hours late Saturday night at a Brighton dance hall after a lengthy grilling by police before the discovery of the latest body. At dawn Sunday he was seen walking toward London. Authorities closely guarded details, but the newest body was said to be that of Violette Kaye,

LONDON, July 17—Tony Mancini, a stuttering Italian waiter, was charged today with the willful murder of Mrs. Violette Kaye—also known as Mrs. Violett Saunders—a professional dancer. She was the victim of “the Brighton trunk crime No. 2.” Her body was discovered jammed in a trunk with the head and arms of another woman, believed dismembered from the torso discovered a month ago in a trunk in the Brighton railroad station. Mancini was arrested early today in southeast London and questioned by Scotland Yard detectives. At the end of their grilling, they charged him with murder and arranged for his appearance in police court tomorrow.

DOUGLAS, Isle of Man, July 16 - (AP) — Kaye Don, British motor and boat racer, was sentenced today to four months in prison on a manslaughter charge and then was released on bail pending appeal. Leaning on a cane, Don was pale as the judge pronounced sentence based on his conviction Saturday of responsibility for the death of his mechanic, Francis Taylor, in an automobile crash during a test run.

LONDON, July 16 (AP).—Great Britain and the United States decided today to suspend Thursday bilateral conversations preliminary to the 1935 naval conference for the remainder of the summer. Norman H. Davis, ambassador at large, and other American delegates will then leave for Washington,

BRIGHTON IS SCENE OF SECOND TRUNK MURDER IN 2 MONTHS; BODY OF ONE IS IDENTIFIED. BRIGHTON, LONDON, July 10.—(4)—Local police and Scotland Yard Monday pressed a nation-wide "hue and cry" for a stuttering waiter "with well-greased hair" after a new trunk murder was discovered here, complicating an old mystery in a manner seldom found outside fiction. Scotland Yard cautiously refrained from certainly connecting a woman's body and the head and arms of a woman found Sunday night with a torso discovered June 18, although the arms and head were said to have been tentatively connected with the earlier crime. In that case, the entire body of the first woman victim now has been discovered, though not identified, since legs were found in King’s Cross station in London. The Yard officially referred to the two cases as "Brighton trunk crime." (Continued on Page 2, Column 5.)

Istanbul, Turkey, July 17.—(P)— Eight British warships arrived here today as the British government requested a joint Anglo-Turkish inquiry into the killing Saturday of a British naval officer by Turkish soldiers. The British asked that their own naval authorities be allowed to join the investigation under way by the Turkish government and likewise search for the body of Lieut. J. W. Robinson, the naval surgeon who was shot as he paddled in a skiff off the island of Samos. He fell into the water and his body has not been recovered. Admiral Sir William Fisher, commander in chief of the British Mediterranean fleet, and the British consul of Smyrna already are on the scene. The flagship of the fleet is expected momentarily.

(By The Associated Press) London, July 17—The court of appeals today dismissed the appeal of Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, Ltd, from the verdict of a lower court which awarded damages of $125,909 to Princess Irena Youssoupoff, who charged she had been libeled by the portrayal of a character in the motion picture, “Rasputin and the Empress.”

London, July 17.—(UP)—The appeal of Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, Ltd., against the $125,000 libel verdict awarded Princess Irina Youssoupoff because she was portrayed in the film “Rasputin and the Empress,” was dismissed today with costs. The court granted a stay of execution pending an appeal to the House of Lords on condition that M-G-M pay the princess an additional 5000 pounds (about $25,000) if the appeal is not sustained.

1934-08-03.text: HONOLULU, Aug. 3--With Dolifuss, the conservative, gone, and that fine, level-headed patriot, Von Hindenburg, gone, it looks like it takes a radical to live. England saying that her borders reached to the Rhine was good news to these islands, for that means that ours at least reach our own possessions. The army and navy have to be — this hop all the time. It's like carrying the mail. We ask ‘em to do something right now and then blame ‘em because they have had no practice. If we ever had to fly here we would have to ask ‘em to postpone the emergency till we learned it, so don't blame the boys. They will have to wait now till commercial lines do it first. Yours.

SHANGHAI, Aug. 3 (UP).- Warships of three foreign nations rushed today toward Foochow, where a communist army reportedly is menacing the city. The United States sent the gunboat Sacramento to the scene. The British authorities ordered a destroyer to proceed from Hong Kong. A Japanese warship already was under way. Reports said an army of 500 Chinese communists was within a short distance of Foochow, which has many foreign residents.

LONDON, Aug. 2 (AP).—Many diplomats gasped today at the suggestion of Secretary of the Navy Swanson for a cut in naval tonnage power. Naval experts showed little apparent surprise, however, at the possibility America may propose a 20 to 80 percent reduction at the 1935 naval conference. They viewed the American secretary's statement as the first definite proposal of reduction offered by any nation. There has been a feeling here that the United States would make a reduction proposal after ambassador at large Norman H. Davis returned to Washington and discussed the status of preliminary conversations in London with Washington officials. Expected Plan. The British confidently expected Davis to reveal some such plan while he was here and were surprised that he did not. Swanson's views were regarded in some quarters as an adroit way of giving the other powers something to think about during t

London, Aug. 2 (4) — Great Britain's apprehension over Germany's future, now that von Hindenburg is dead and Adolf Hitler has become the sole arbiter of that nation’s affairs, is sharpened by a noticeable “cooling off” in Anglo-German relations the last few months. A series of incidents, including the German debts controversy and the Austrian situation, has caused differences to increase at the moment the one man regarded as the greatest stabilizing influence in Germany passed on. Sources close to the British government pointed out today that foreign powers cannot possibly repose confidence in Hitler to the degree they did in von Hindenburg.

(COPY PUBLISHING Liveat, UME Fess) Neudeck, East Prussia, Aug. 2. — President Paul Von Hindenburg, soldier and statesman, died at 9 a.m. (8 a.m., EST.) today it was announced officially. The mantle of power that slipped from his shoulders falls to Adolf Hitler, Bavarian house painter who became Chancellor and dictator of Germany. He died on the 20th anniversary of the World War I in which he was a leading figure. Before his death, the 86-year-old idol of the Republic, while clinging staunchly still to his lifelong monarchism, was understood to have imparted his blessing to Hitler as Germany’s leader. Hindenburg fought death as he had fought in life. It took him two days to die, days in which doctors marvelled at the strength of the heart that kept blood pumping through his great frame while uremia poisoned him. At the end, only members of his family were at his bedside. The President's f

BY 29S ASSWULALE PAE} BERLIN, Aug. 3.—(/P)—Germany gazed across the bier of her dead president today into an uncertain future of super-Hitlerism. Complexities within the fatherland and without confronted Adolf Hitler, the corporal who, by the death of the aged Paul Von Hindenburg Thursday, has become master of the destinies of 65,000,000 Germans. His weapon for successfully overcoming these problems is a dictatorial power without parallel in all Europe. The "free plebiscite" he has ordered to be held August 19 to determine a successor to Von Hindenburg is, as all Germans recognize, but a ceremony. It will rubber stamp Hitler’s assumption of presidential powers in addition to those he exercises as chancellor. Seem Bewildered Many Germans seem bewildered over the suddenness of events, even though nothing unexpected has occurred. The Nazis, however, have moved with a nice regard for public

Associated Press Foreign Staff, VIENNA, Aug. 2.—(A)—Paul Hudl, fifth Nazi to go on trial for implication in the Nazi putsch in which Chancellor Dollfuss was killed, today was convicted of high treason and sentenced to life imprisonment. The sentence was imposed after a brief trial before a court martial, which had been generally expected to sentence Hudl, a former officer in the Austrian army, to death on the gallows. Three other Nazis were hanged this week for implication in the putsch. Hudl was wounded twice and decorated five times for bravery in the World War. He is 42 years old. The former officer created a sensation in his testimony by stating that the federal employees of the chancellery did not have the feeling of being prisoners after Nazis seized the building. Most of them yelled “Heil Hitler” when the putschists took charge, he said. “The personal adjutant of Emil (Continued o

By United Press. BERLIN, Aug. 2.—Adolf Hitler, former Austrian house-painter, became sole dictator of the German people today on the death of President Paul von Hindenburg. Hitler’s cabinet made him president-chancellor, absorbing all the powers of both offices. He has control of the powerful Reichswehr army, whose members are to take an oath of unswerving loyalty to him. Hitler thus has greater sway than any dictator on earth. Even Mussolini has a king who outranks him, albeit with little authority. Asks Referendum The chancellor wrote to Dr. Wilhelm Frick, minister of interior, asking him to submit to a referendum as soon as possible today’s law conferring the president’s functions on him. He said he did not want to assume the title Reichspräsident because it was inseparable from Hindenburg’s name. He added that he wished to be addressed as “Fuehrer and Reichschancellor” in the future.

1934-03-19.text: CHICAGO, March 18. (P)—A showdown appeared imminent today in the fight of the British crown to remove John Factor, international speculator, to England to face a charge of involvement in a $7,000,000 stock swindle. The one-time immigrant boy who started on a “shoe-string” to run up his fortune—reputedly to some $5,000,000—finally faced the possibility of hearing Federal Judge Sullivan order him placed in the custody of a United States marshal for return to England by operatives of Scotland Yard. The hearing was called on the request of Franklin R. Overmyer, counsel for the British crown, for cancellation of orders delaying Factor’s extradition which were issued so he could testify against the men who kidnapped him for $70,000 ransom. If Factor loses it will mark the end of a three-year struggle and he will go back to his native land, reputedly “broke” after a stormy career in America, cl

CHICAGO, (4)—Another day of freedom was given John Factor today as extradition proceedings against the stock speculator were held in abeyance pending a conference between the secretary of state and the British ambassador at Washington. Representatives of the British crown were in the federal court of Judge Philip Sullivan to oppose Factor’s motion to dismiss the extradition order against him, but District Attorney Dwight H. Green requested the day's continuance.

WASHINGTON, March 19 (AP).— Sir Ronald Lindsay, the British ambassador, called at the state department today and sought ways of hastening Great Britain’s requested extradition of John (“Jake the Barber”) Factor, wanted in England for alleged defrauding of investors involving $3,500,000.

Boston, Mass. Mar. 18. (AP)— Edward A. Filene, prominent merchant and chairman of the New England District Recovery board, today issued an appeal to the American Federation of Labor and the General Motors corporation to come to an agreement and avoid a threatened strike. “This strike must not happen,” said Filene. “All America looks to the great American Federation of Labor and the Great General Motors corporation to prevent any such nation-wide calamity, which would not only be a dangerous blow to the president's recovery program, but seriously injure the morale of the whole nation. “Industrial statesmanship of the highest order is needed on both sides; for the situation is unprecedented and calls for a courageous breaking of precedents on the part of both employers’ and employees’ organizations. “I am hoping for something much better than a compromise. I am hoping for a solution which

ATHENS, March 19 (AP)—A rumor that Samuel Insull is at the mercy of gangsters who slipped aboard his little Greek freighter in Piraeus harbor aroused excitement in Athens today. It was said the gangsters intended to kidnap the 74-year-old runaway from American justice and hold the former Chicagoan for ransom in Cretan caves or on islands nearby. Commenting on this latest and wildest of all the sensational stories which accompanied Insull's most recent escape on the sluggish vessel Maiotis, police denied that any kidnappers could have boarded the ship while it was in the Athens harbor. The story was widely “played” in the Greek press. Aside from this, there seemed no foundation for the rumor other than the Piraeus harbor master's announcement that he had received no messages from the ship, in which Insull has been bound for some unknown asylum, since 5 o'clock Sunday afternoon. The Associ

ATHENS, Mar. 19. (U.P)—Samuel Insull, seeking a refuge from American law in the little tramp steamer Maiotis, was understood today to have instructed "influential" friends in the United States to intercede with President Roosevelt in his behalf. Free for the time being as he steamed across the Mediterranean, Insull was beset by fears of being kidnapped. Before he left here early yesterday, after his brief return at the demand of the government, Insull expressed the fear that American authorities might charter a ship to kidnap him or to "exterminate" him in a simulated collision. His statement showed the hysterical condition in which events of the last few days had left the aged utilities man, interested only in avoiding a return to the United States to face trial on the charge of irregularities in connection with the collapse of his industries. But there were reports here that Insull's f

Edmonton, Alta... March 19.-(AP) Fragments of a huge meteor which last night illuminated the heavens in Alberta and Saskatchewan and was viewed in some parts of Montana were sought near here today. At Saskatoon the light from the meteor far outshone the municipal airport's beacon. It was believed to have exploded and disappeared in dust somewhere about 100 miles southeast of here, where houses were reported rocked by the explosion. Reports of the brilliant meteor, a flaming light and then an explosion, came from a score of towns southeast of here. The flash was seen in Helena and other Montana cities. Fiery Ball It was described by motorists as a fiery ball emerging from a cloud and illuminating the sky to almost daylight appearance. It resembled a full moon in size and its speed appeared terrific, those who saw it said.

ROME, March 18.—(4)—A 60-year program of internal and external expansion which in the 21st century will give Italy the “primacy of the world” was outlined today by Premier Benito Mussolini in a speech to 5,000 cheering chief Fascists of the kingdom. That century, he said, will be a “Blackshirt era.” The dictator spoke in the Rome opera house to the so-called quinquennial assembly of the regime one week before the five-year election. In the audience were virtually all of Italy's noted men, including Guglielmo Marconi, the inventor, the cabinet, provincial prefects and other officials. 1934-04-09.text: London, April 9—(4)—Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, told the House of Commons today the British government is giving very serious consideration to Germany's contemplated increased expenditures on her army, navy and air forces. Sir John was cheered by the legislators as he made the announcement. He declared: "I have instructed our ambassador at Berlin to make inquiries of the German government on the subject." The Commons was reconvening after its Easter recess for the session which will end in July. The German budget for 1934 made public Mar. 27 showed large increases in military appropriations for the Reich. Among the items which attracted attention was a $10,000,000 grant to the Nazi storm troopers, the first time in the history of the German republic that appropriations have been made for the political army. The German budget showed that in the coming fiscal year the army a

London, April 8.—(AP)—Despite official denials, it was learned today from persons closely associated with Scandinavian royalty that the announcement of the engagement of the Danish Crown Prince Frederick to the beautiful Swedish Princess Ingrid is expected to follow upon the return of King Gustaf to Stockholm from the Riviera. The fact was reported in well-informed quarters both at Copenhagen and at Stockholm. It was said that the royal couple already are engaged, but are pledged to delay official announcement until the king's return from his long winter vacation.

OKLAHOMA CITY. (4) The Daily Oklahoman in a copyrighted story says Wiley Post, globe-circling record holder, has fixed for his twin goal in 1934 a new airplane altitude record and the winning of the international air race from London to Melbourne, Australia, next October. Post has invested thousands of dollars and more than eighteen months of engineering and experimental work in the new ventures. The intrepid flier’s new program will continue to team Post with his veteran flying companion, ‘The Winnie Mae of Oklahoma.’ Post's objective will be to better the world’s airplane altitude record of 44,819.418 feet, held by G. Lemoine of France. In the second, the international air race, he will be matched against the world’s greatest pilots in ships built especially for the race.

———_—_————— ES EE: Se ee SHANGHAI, April 9.—(4)—An undertaker is beginning to wonder what to do with the body of C. C. Julian, former Oklahoma and California oil operator who killed himself. Upon order of British Authorities, after the Canadian-born fugitive from Oklahoma justice took poison March 25, the firm prepared the body and arranged for a simple funeral. Then came instructions from Julian's sister in Los Angeles, Mrs. Viola Greenhow, to have the body cremated and the ashes sent to America. The undertaker today, however, said that no money had been received for expenses, despite repeated queries sent to Los Angeles. The wife of the one-time millionaire who died in poverty, was said to have sent funds from her home in Winnipeg, Canada, to "insure burial." Yet the body now lies in an obscure corner of the undertaker's parlors, giving the sister in Los Angeles time to claim the ashes

Vancouver, B. C., April 9—America’s first Sasquatch-catching expedition headed into the mountains of British Columbia Sunday on a hunt for the horrible, hairy, naked bogeyman of Indian legend. J. F. Blakeney and C. K. Blakeney, medical students at the University of California, read reports of frightened tribesmen that the giant baby snatcher of old had been seen recently in the mountains north of Harrison Lake, and determined to attempt to photograph or lasso a Sasquatch. The fabled Sasquatch, as described in Indian lore for hundreds of years, is supposed to lurk in caves and glades coming out in the twilight to peer into Indian teepees, to slither and snatch at children, to steal food, play diabolical tricks and even kill warriors. “Our professor of anthropology will be much interested,” said the Blakeneys.

LONDON, (?). British disarmament hopes were buoyed by the receipt of a French note which is understood to imply that France now is willing to “talk turkey” about an agreement envisaging the controlled rearmament of Germany. While the French communication was not made public, it was learned France recognizes the disarmament ground is shifting and is prepared to carry on discussions based on this new concept. An exploration of possibilities for a new arms convention on an altered basis, however, was predicated on the understanding that the ultimate decision must be taken by the world disarmament conference as a whole.

ISTANBUL, April 9—(®)— United States Ambassador Robert P. Skinner announced today that Samuel Insull may be placed aboard a vessel sailing for America Wednesday. He said American agents expected to reach a final decision within a few hours. If the Chicago fugitive is started on his homeward voyage Wednesday, it probably will be aboard the American export boat Executive.

Brussels, April 9. (7?)--One person was slain and more than a score were injured in a week-end political clashes which threatened to break out anew in and near Brussels today. A communist was killed in rioting which broke out in connection with the inauguration of Brussels headquarters of the nationalist blue Shirts. Clashes spread throughout scattered sections of the capital between the uniformed nationalists and bands of communists. In Brussels, ten communists and 15 nationalists were wounded and injured in hand-to-hand fighting. The rioting then was carried into other localities. Fears that the fighting would be renewed led police officials to order extraordinary precautions throughout the capital today. Official apprehension were heightened by a communist statement which warned the nationalists that plans were being made to avenge the death of their comrade. Nevertheless, the new kin

1934-08-19.text: BLED, Yugoslavia, Aug. 18, ().— King Alexander's object in inviting Prince George of England to be his guest in the royal summer palace here was learned on high authority today to be directed toward promoting a marriage between the British King’s fourth son and Princess Marina, the third daughter of Prince Nicholas and Princess Olga of Greece. This authority stated that Prince Paul, Alexander's nephew, who is very close to the King, has been designated as matchmaker because he speaks fluent English.

LONDON, Ont., Aug. 18.—(UP)—A trusted employee of the Labatt Brewery, headed by John E. Labatt, millionaire Canadian, was mysteriously slain during the night, it was reported here today. The man was Gordon McKenzie. He was found on the street by a London taxi-cab driver. His skull had been crushed in some unexplained manner. He was taken to Victoria hospital but died shortly before noon without regaining consciousness. Detectives were summoned immediately from police headquarters and started an investigation of the death to determine whether there was any connection with the John S. Labatt kidnapping case. Coroner Dr. J. C. Wilson received a report from the hospital that the man undoubtedly had been a victim of foul play. The hospital reported that the probable cause of his death was a fracture of the skull. His neck might have been broken, a Dr. Arnett, of the hospital staff, who attend

LONDON, Aug. 19 (Sunday) —Anxiety grew here and in Paris and Dublin as the midnight hour passed and no word or sign had been received from George Pond and Cesare Sabelli, who hopped off from Rome this morning with Dublin their goal on a trip back to New York.

Rome, Saturday, Aug. 18.—(AP)—George Pond and Cesare Sabelli hopped off at 7:02 a. m., today (1:02 a. m., E.S.T.) for Dublin, en route to the United States on a return flight. The flyers were bade farewell at the field by General Giuseppe Valle, under-secretary of air, and members of Sabelli's family. The hop-off from Montecelio military air-drome had not been announced because of the air ministry's desire to avoid a crowd. The flyers have been guests of the Italian Aviation corps since their arrival here several weeks ago. Pond and Sabelli crossed the Atlantic in May, making a forced landing at Moy, on the west coast of Ireland, May 15. They proceeded by stages to Rome, their original destination.

To the German fatherland belong also the life and soul of the German Jews who do not know any other fatherland.” The surprising and carefully-worded statement continued “in the spirit of the late president's will, we also approve the joining of the chancellor’s and president's offices.” The statement said that after the post-war troubles “we welcome the national awakening since January, 1933, although it had brought us

_ BERLIN, Aug. 18. (UP)—Exhorted by speakers, goaded by party workers, Germans prepared today to write a page in their history by massing at the polls in millions tomorrow and voting in a national referendum to confirm Reichsführer Adolf Hitler as their dictator-President, Chancellor, war lord combined. Hitler's goal was a vote of more than the 40,588,000 by which the 45,000,000 electors—of a population of 65,000,000—approved last November his withdrawal from the League of Nations and disarmament conference. He sounded the keynote of his appeal himself in his speech at Hamburg last night. It was absolute unity, without question, without criticism, under Hitler, the Nazi party and the army, for a Germany that would rise through sacrifice and struggle to its old time glory despite foreign enmity and internal depression. His references in his speech to foreign nations were those of any orat

Toronto, Ont.—A second Canadian kidnapping was threatened today, after the solution of the John S. La Batt case when Harry C. Hatch, one of Canada’s richest brewers, received a note, threatening him with abduction. Police were immediately informed of the note despite a threat of bodily harm, contained in the message. Text of the letter, which was delivered through the mail to Hatch’s office in Toronto, was not made public. Hatch is head of the consolidated distillers, reportedly the largest whiskey manufacturers and brewers in the Dominion. He is several times over a millionaire. The new kidnap threat was credited directly to the fact that the gang which abducted John S. La Batt, London, Ont., brewer was still at large. No amount of money was mentioned in the letter to Hatch, it was reported. Hatch could not be located immediately but it was assumed police had furnished him with a guard

TOKYO (#) — No casualties were reported from a strong earthquake which struck the Nagoya district, almost in the center of Japan, a few minutes before noon today. Communication lines were destroyed to the north but were rapidly restored. Damage was less heavy than had been feared after first reports. The quake’s center was 40 miles north of the city of Nagoya, which is 160 miles from Tokyo. Damage to railway tunnels and bridges was reported and the city of Kyoto was badly shaken.

1934-09-11.text: Washington, Sept. 10 (4)—Senate investigators into high pressure munitions sales methods today uncovered a frank proposal that the United States government buy war stuff from a firm in England—described as a “semi-official” agency—to help arm the Chinese against Japan. Along with this went testimony—afterwards denied—that state department officials had advised the American Armaments Corporation of New York to “obtain an injunction against the government” to overcome the embargo on arms shipments to Bolivia and Paraguay. Senators were told also that Representative Britten, Republican, of Illinois, accompanied representatives of the corporation to the state department in mid-June to seek approval of an arms shipment to Bolivia outside the presidential ban. Once more talk of bribery in connection with munitions sales was heard. At one point testimony was presented that “fifty grand”—$50,000

John Ball, the Irish director of the Solely Armament company, today. [By The Associated Press] More than 40 persons were injured or overcome by tear gas and two others were shot yesterday as violence flared at two points in the New England sector of the textile strike front. Three state policemen were among 15 hurt in a riot at the Powder Mill and Alexander Curtain Plant at Danielson, Conn. when troopers hurling tear gas dispersed 1,506 pickets. Boston, Sept. 10 (/P)—Two men were shot and more than two score others either bruised or overcome by tear gas in the most serious textile strike rioting in New England since the strike was declared. The shooting of two members of a crowd of Saylesville, R.I., was the first strike shooting in this section of the country. More than 25 other persons were injured including the 10-year-old son of a Rhode Island jurist unwittingly caught in a crush before the Sayles finishing plant. A few hours later 15 persons were injured, several seriously in a riot at the Pawtucket and Alexander curtain plant at Danielson, Conn., as 1,500 picketers were dispersed by State Police hurling tear gas bombs.

ALLIANCE, O., Sept. 11—Two gunmen Monday secretly planned to hold up the England drug store here. They carried their plans out last night and authorities counted the cost as follows: Three innocent persons dead. One of the bandits dead. The second bandit suffering from broken legs. The robbers fled from the drug store in a stolen automobile and drove northwest at high speed. At an intersection ten miles away they crashed into another car. All its occupants were killed and both bandits were critically injured, one of them fatally. The dead are Eugene Quilter, Jane Ann Quilter, 18, and Hugenta Nimereala, 18, all of Louisville and all en route to enroll in Kent State College. Geobel was driving the car which was struck by the robbers’ machine. One of the bandits, unidentified, died in Alliance Hospital of his injuries. The other, identified as Ward Wobadask, suffered broken legs. Herded Cus

(Copyright, 1934, By Associated Press) HAVANA, Sept. 10.—(4)—Four sections of the Cuban government tonight speeded their investigation into the disastrous fire aboard the liner Morro Castle as Havana's chief of port police, Capt. Oscar Hernandez, charged flatly communists set the fire. At the same time secret police searched every passenger and every piece of baggage leaving on Pan-American airways planes after the aviation company had received anonymous threats from terrorists. George Grant Mason, Jr., Pan-American’s representative for the Caribbean, confirmed the fact that the threats had been made. Such anonymous warnings were not unusual, however, Mason said. A mysterious telephone call brought the latest warning, Mason revealed. “This is X-247,” the caller was quoted as saying. “Remember the number. Search every piece of mail leaving on today’s plane because I learned through a woma

| BOSTON, Sept. 11 (AP).—Idle mill operatives in New England increased slightly today as national guard troops were mobilized in three States—Rhode Island, Connecticut and Maine—to cope with rioting and to relieve local police on strike duty. Suspension of operations in a Pawtucket, R. I. romper factory forced 400 out of employment and increased the total idle to 153,926 in the six States with 77,819 still employed. Two companies of State Militia stood guard in the mill village of Danielson, Conn. as picketing threatened further violence, officials said, in the drive to close the only plant operating there—the Powdrell and Alexander Lace Curtain factory. Meanwhile, Companies F and K, 169th Infantry, Connecticut National Guard, were under secret orders to move into Willimantic, Conn. It was believed they would report for duty at the American Thread Company plant. The Guardsmen were ordere

BERLIN, Sept. 11.—UP—All importations into Germany were declared subject to state control today when Dr. Fritz Sarnow, representing Hjalmar Schacht, economy dictator, outlined Schacht’s new plan described to save the government's depleted currency reserves through the restoration of imports. The nation’s 10 import control departments will be increased to 25, thus putting the whole import system, including the field of farm products, into the government’s hands. Five decrees, three of which will be issued in the near future, define the functions of the control departments. The ministers of economics and agriculture will supervise the departments for distribution of foreign currency permits. Requests for imports for use in the manufacture of products to be exported will be given first consideration. The value of materials which may be imported without a permit was radically reduced from 15

1934-03-12.text: LONDON, March 13,--(UP)— The court of appeals today granted the application of the Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer company for a stay of execution of judgment obtained against it by Princess Irina Alexandrovna, pending hearing of an appeal. However, the court ordered that the company should pay the princess at once 5000 pounds ($26,387) of the 35000 pounds ($129,376) awarded her by a jury which ruled.

LONDON, (®). The Daily Mail said the marital breach between Douglas Fairbanks and Mary Pickford was less wide than is generally assumed, and that their friends expected an early reconciliation. The paper's film correspondent added that the Pickford divorce proceedings in the United States would be discontinued and that she had cancelled her projected sale of Pickfair, their home in Los Angeles. The paper said Fairbanks had regularly telephoned to Mary since he came to London, and represented him as being greatly upset at alleged distorted reports concerning himself and his wife. NEW YORK. (?). Mary Pickford’s secretary said the actress had no comment on reports from London that she and Douglas Fairbanks might become reconciled.

LONDON, March 12.—Former Mayor James J. Walker, denying that he ever ducked income taxes, announces that he plans to go home and practice law. A bit of the old Walkerian nonchalance cropped out in a statement with which the New Yorker greeted news that the United States is moving to sue him, Andrew W. Mellon and others for income taxes. “Even in this doubtful position,” he said yesterday, “I am glad to be in the same list with Mr. Andrew Mellon.” Walker, who is stopping at a Surrey Hills hotel with his wife, the former Betty Compton, said he was “not altogether surprised.” “It is now nearly two years since the American authorities decided that my income tax return was incorrect,” he said. “They spent three months investigating my financial position, both privately and in my capacity as a public man. They found nothing in either case that would enable them to bring a charge of tax evasion

ATHENS, March 12—(UP)— Bulgaria, Jugoslavia, Roumania, Luxembourg, Great Britain and Canada, were rumored today as possible destinations of Samuel Insull, Chicago utilities man, apparently doomed at last to seek refuge elsewhere against the efforts of the United States government to make him stand trial on charges of irregularities in the collapse of his companies. ‘Through the network of American extradition treaties now covers most of the world, Insull might hope to plead in some country, that he was a victim of persecution and could not be extradited because the offenses with which he is charged in the United States were not an offense in that particular country. It was a decision by the great high courts that Insull was guilty of no offense in Greek law that permitted him to remain here for so many months. The government finally decided to oust him because it felt his presence endang

New York, March 12. (UP)—A note of caution was injected today into an otherwise optimistic annual report of the United States Steel corporation which termed the present outlook “encouraging.” “It is gratifying to note that operations in January and February of 1934 showed improvement over operations in the corresponding months of 1933,” Myron C. Taylor, chairman of the board, said in the report. “The outlook is encouraging, present indications being that sales in 1934 will exceed those of 1933.” Taylor’s report emphasized that the company’s subsidiaries have carried out the law and the code in respect to collective bargaining and that the plan whereby employees select their own representatives to deal with officers of the corporation had proved “eminently satisfactory.”

| LONDON, March 12 (UP).-—Dr. Khalid Sheldrake, British missionary and son of a London pickle manufacturer, may soon be crowned king of the Chinese province of Sinkiang, the Daily Express reported today. There was no confirmation of the report,

London, March 12, — By the end of 1936, the British navy will reach maximum tonnage permitted by treaty, Sir Bolton Eyres-Monsell, first lord of the admiralty, told the House of Commons today in presenting naval estimates for the year. Practically all warships, he said, will be under the treaty age limit at which they can be replaced, although the navy will have 50,511 tons in the destroyer category and 4,000 tons in submarines which will have reached the age limit.

SASEBO, Japan — The Japanese torpedo boat Tomozuro, a new and secretly designed naval vessel, capsized during maneuvers today and authorities abandoned hope of finding any of its 106 officers and men alive. The accident was the second disaster in the Japanese navy since December 1932, when the destroyer Swarabi capsized off Formosa with loss of 105 officers and men. The Tomozuro capsized during early morning maneuvers in heavy weather. The destroyer Tatsuta later reported it had taken the overturned craft in tow. Cause of the disaster was a mystery for the time being, at least.

1934-08-21.text: GLASGOW, Scotland, Aug. 21.—(7)— More than 30 passengers were injured and one seaman was washed overboard and drowned when a terrific gale struck the liner Cameronia in mid-Atlantic, it was learned on the ship’s arrival at Clyde today. Passengers said some waves 60 feet high broke against the anchor liner, which sailed from Boston, Aug. 12, and from New York the previous day. A team of Penn State football players was aboard but escaped injury. Boats and furniture were smashed and tables were torn from their fastenings. The ship hove to for eight hours to wait for the gale to moderate. It heeled at an angle of 35 degrees, passengers reported.

London, Aug. 21.—Attempts to reach an agreement on export quotas were definitely abandoned today by the world wheat conference which had been in session for a week. Unrestrained shipping of wheat by all countries is assured at least until November. This means the first "open season" in wheat shipping since the 1934 wheat agreement was signed last August, although during the year Russia refused to accept her quota and Argentina exceeded her allotments when negotiations for an increase fell through. The refusal of Argentina to accept less than 150,000,000 bushels coupled with a favorable world wheat situation because of the drought, led the conference to abandon a plan for establishing annual quotas during this session. A discussion of the allotment was postponed until November.

GLASGOW, Scotland, Aug. 21 (UP) — The Anchor Line steamer Cameronia, deck battered and furniture splintered, and 30 of her passengers suffering from injuries after being hurled across her cabins by 60-foot waves, arrived here today from New York with the loss of one life. A seaman on duty on a storm-torn deck was washed overboard during the 70-mile gale and carried to death. Meanwhile below deck and included in a heavy passenger list were members of the Pennsylvania State College soccer team. The passengers at one time seemed to be approaching panic, but were quieted.

GLASGOW, Aug. 21.—The Anchor liner Cameronia arrived from New York today with thirty passengers injured as the result of a two-day gale in which the big ship rolled and pitched alarmingly in sixty-foot waves lashed by a seventy-mile wind. American passengers included one who, undivulged, suffered a double fracture and injured ribs. - William Rich, a Californian, was home during the gale Friday.

LONDON, Aug. 21.--(N$)-The Italian schooner Efisia Serra was sunk today in a collision with the American export liner Kxochorda off Leghorn, according to an Exchange dispatch from Turin. The schooner’s crew was rescued.

By 126 AMGCCIAICG Fess COLUMBUS, O., Aug. 21.—A reprieve until Nov. 27 was granted today by Gov. George White to Serafino Sinatra, alias Joe English, convicted of the killing of Jack Kennedy, Toledo night club operator, and awaiting execution in Ohio's electric chair.

FLORENCE, Italy, Aug. 21 (P. —Unconfirmed reports said today that Premier Mussolini of Italy and Chancellor Schuschnigg of Austria, meeting here, were drafting a military clause for the Italo-Austro-Hungarian accord. The clause would be one of mutual assistance among the three countries and would permit Italy to march into Austria if necessary to aid that nation. Certain it was, however, that Mussolini and Schuschnigg confered together with Fulvio Suvich, the Italian under-secretary of state, after Schuschnigg’s arrival by train from Austria this morning. They talked in the magnificent old Villa de Marinis, set deep in a park of trees overlooking the city. Because Florence is the center of military maneuvers, the city is under strict wartime measures and the heads of neighboring governments entered it under cover of darkness. Paris, Aug. 20. (AP)—The newspaper Paris Soir charged today that the will of the late President Paul Von Hindenburg of Germany had been falsified so as to eliminate a recommendation that former Kaiser Wilhelm should "succeed" him. The newspaper said the last section of the will was written by Paul Joseph Goebbels, Nazi minister of Propaganda. It based the story written by its central European correspondent on an "authentic source," the paper stated. The newspaper said the original will was much longer than that published last week, lauding Chancellor Hitler, and advised Germany to make Wilhelm president and Franz Von Papen, now special envoy to Austria, as chancellor. Charges were made by the Soir that Von Papen, then vice chancellor, was named in the will before Hitler's "purging" of Nazi ranks June 30 and for this reason attempts were made to kill him. 1934-07-30.text: LONDON, July 30 (4)--A reliable source stated tonight that the British government has learned that an official statement was issued in Berlin last Wednesday evening proclaiming the overthrow of Chancellor Dollfuss of Austria in "a great popular revolt as important as it is welcome." This statement, according to the same source, was withdrawn a half hour later before it could be published in any of the newspapers of Germany. Quarters close to the British government attach great importance to the fact that this statement was purported to have been issued by the official German news agency in Berlin in view of protests emanating from the German capital disclaiming any connection with Bavarian activities and Austrian internal affairs. LONDON, July 30.—Stanley Baldwin, acting prime minister of Great Britain, said in the house of commons today that there is no immediate danger of war in Europe despite the difficulties and perplexities of the present situation. He made his statement in defending Great Britain’s recently announced plans to increase its military force. He opposed the labor party’s motion of censure, declaring: “There is no cause at all for a panic of any kind. As far as I can see, there is no risk in the immediate future of peace being broken. “It might well be that peace will not be broken and there are a great many people in Europe who will do all they can to see to it that it is not broken.” Declaring “the question of imperial defense and disarmament had occupied the minds of the government and the house of commons itself for many years,” Baldwin continued: “In the Saar, in Memel, and in Danzig, there h

Wimbledon, Eng., July 20. ()—George M. Lott, Jr., and Lester Stoefen today defeated Harold G. N. Lee and George Patrick Hughes in the doubles encounter of the Davis Cup challenge round 1-6, 6-0, 4-6, 9-7 to give the United States a fighting chance against Great Britain in the five match series. Their victory in the third encounter sent the decision to the two singles matches tomorrow between Sidney B. Wood, Jr., and Henry Wilfred (Bunny) Austin and Frank X. Shields and Fred Perry. Perry defeated Wood in a bristling five-set encounter Saturday in the opening singles and Austin humbled Shields in straight sets. Lott and Stoefen received unexpected opposition from the makeshift English team, Lee having been substituted for Perry at the last minute to save the latter for singles duty.

LONDON, (UP).—Ominous preparations for “the next war” were revealed in the House of Commons today when Stanley Baldwin, Lord President of the Council, announced Britain's plans for building up her air force as part of an imperial defense plan. Baldwin startled the House by making the following points: 1. The air force will be built up over four years from 844 to 1,304 planes, an increase of 460 fighting ships. 2. The civilian population will be drilled for defense against air raids. 3. The acting Prime Minister virtually sanctioned Germany's right to re-arm because of her absolute defenselessness in the air. 4. He expressed his expectation of another war, although he does not expect it in the immediate future. Rome, July 30.—(#)—Premier Mussolini passed the 51st anniversary of his birth sweltering in Rome, going over reports and telegrams from troubled Austria and from his Ambassadors at Berlin, London and Paris. Important reports from his military ministry also were laid on his desk. Premier Mussolini had planned to pass the anniversary bathing in the Adriatic Sea at Riccione with the! LONDON, Jul. 30—Evidence has been submitted by the Austrian government showing the extent of German activity in fomenting trouble in Austria, Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, told the House of Commons today. Sir John said that not only during the February trouble but also recently, there had been received from the Austrian government "A collection of material indicating considerable German influence in propaganda against the Austrian government and in the series of outrages committed in Austrian territory." He added he was not aware of any intention of summoning a special meeting of the League of Nations Council to consider the situation. Impartial disapproving German influence in Austria, Sir John indicated Britain preferred that Austria make a direct demand of Germany to cease interference, rather than for outside powers to act.

BERLIN, July 29—(AP)—Rumors originating in Czechoslovakia that Italy, France and possibly England are considering a joint demarche to the Hitler government, alleging implication and responsibility in the Austrian crisis, filtered into Berlin tonight. From Munich came even stronger rumors regarding Italy’s attitude. Well-informed sources there said Italy will demand dissolution of Hitler’s storm troops and the Schutz Staffel, black-shirted picked guards. It was said Italy’s demarche will take the form of a sharp note demanding an answer within 48 hours. Mussolini, it was understood in Munich, has instructed his ambassadors to notify the interested powers of his intention and to suggest to them that Nazi organizations such as the storm troops are a constant menace to Austria’s independence. The Hitler government, meanwhile, continued to concentrate its energies on its international reputat

BERLIN, July 31.—(UP)—President Paul von Hindenburg, Germany’s war hero and beloved peace time leader, was critically ill today. The cabinet was summoned hurriedly from all parts of Germany. The 86-year-old warrior, although weakened by months of serious illness, refused to bow his head to the enemy. He left his bed this morning, took a little nourishment and showed lively interest about in his surroundings. Then he returned to his bed, his doctors announced, and “entered a peaceful sleep.” For months he has suffered from a bladder complaint.

1934-01-29.text: Cambridge, Eng., Jan. 29 (A P)—Percy Titmous, who works for a brewery, drove into town this morning with Her Majesty, Queen Mary, riding in his little automobile. The townsfolk stared in amazement from the sidewalks. Queen Mary’s automobile had broken down between Ely and Cambridge while she was motoring from Sandringham to shop for antiques. Titmous saw Her Majesty’s plight as he drove down the road. He offered his aid. The Queen accepted.

Washington, Jan. 29—-(P)—Administration officials today carefully outlined plans for throwing the $2,000,000,000 stabilization fund into gear, at the same time seeing possibilities of a stern currency war with Great Britain. It is stated authoritatively that the treasury has reached no understanding with London on the relative position of the pound and dollar. In other words, this government will employ what Secretary Morgenthau terms its $2,000,000,000 of “blue chips” independently of England's use of her equally large equalization fund. When asked the direct question of whether a currency struggle with Great Britain is imminent, Morgenthau’s frank reply was “I don't know.” In other quarters, however, it was indicated that while a money conflict stands as a possibility it is not looked for immediately. LONDON, Jan. 29 (UP).—Britain is ready to resume war debt negotiations with the United States "whenever, after consultation with the president of the United States, it appears it could be done," the House of Commons was informed today. The announcement was made by Leslie Hore-Belisha, financial secretary of the treasury.

LONDON, Jan. 28,-4)—A drastic measure aimed at world-wide rehabilitation of wheat by establishing a minimum scale of prices and exports is the most important proposal of the agenda of the international wheat advisory commission, which begins its third session here tomorrow. There was considerable doubt on the eve of the opening whether 21 nations adhering to the international wheat pact can be persuaded to approve the project. Agreement Essential. - PARIS, Jan. 29.—Former Premier Edouard Daladier accepted President Lebrun’s invitation to form a new French government today. Daladier’s acceptance of the post, involving a grave task of political reconstruction in the face of the greatest national crisis since the war, came as a surprise to many politicians. - The former premier was called to the presidential palace at 10 a.m., after Jules Jeanneney had refused a perfunctory offer of the premiership. When he went in to talk to the president, it was announced that his mission was purely one of “political consultation.” Less than an hour afterward he had been commissioned to build a new government on the wreckage of the old Chautemps cabinet, which disintegrated under the pounding of politicians and the people angered by the Stavisky banking scandals.
