Paris, Jan. 28.— (AP) — France seemed ready to turn to the veteran former Premier Édouard Herriot today to lift the nation from the riot-ridden crisis which toppled the Chautemps government into the discard. President Albert Lebrun asked the aged former President Gaston Doumergue to form a cabinet in his first move to reorganize the government, but Doumergue refused. “Moral Crisis” The hurried resignation of the Chautemps cabinet Saturday, driven from power by popular indignation over the Stavisky bank scandal, faced Lebrun with the task of solving a ‘moral crisis’ instead of a mere political problem. Herriot was generally predicted to be chosen for premier. The streets of Paris were comparatively quiet today after a night of intense rioting which capped eight days of open disorder; At Rouen, however, government employees, encouraged by the success of Paris mobs, staged demonstrations ag

(DY The Associated Press; Athens, Jan. 29.—Two official physicians examined Samuel Insull sr., fugitive former utilities operator of Chicago, today and decided “he was capable of traveling. They had been assigned by the government to determine whether Insull’s plea of illness, by which he sought an extension of his Greek haven from United States justice, was true. His lawyer, P. Rhallis, had asked an extension of Insull’s permit to remain in Greece from five to 15 days after the permit expires January 31.

ATHENS, Jan. 28 (4%) A frightened and sick man, in bed gasping for breath, was how persons having entree to his apartment today pictured Samuel Insull, once powerful utilities executive, as he waited a decision on whether his stay here would be extended. A medical commission appointed by the minister of interior will visit Insull tomorrow to examine him. If they agree with findings of Insull’s private physicians that he is too ill to travel, his permit to remain in Greece will be indefinitely prolonged, M. Montzourimis, the interior minister, said. If the commission does not agree with the other physicians, Insull will be deported within three days, it was understood. Members of the Insull entourage said his condition was worse today and he was unable even to read a newspaper. 1934-01-27.text: COLUMBUS, Ohio, Jan. 27 As I got to the field in Tulsa yesterday morning “Gypsy” Smith, great English evangelist, came out to the airport, and we had a fine chat. He talks to ten thousand people a night there. A very earnest, fine man, who advertises no particular route to salvation. I asked him, in saving Oklahoma for the Lord, to save Alfalfa Bill Murray, him and Jim Ferguson for there ain't any more like those two, and I just kinder like ‘em. Missouri, Indiana and Ohio all passed under us in order. Three great old states, whose statesmen have made history. Yours,

CHICAGO, Jan. 27 (1).—A charge that John Factor made up his kidnapping story in an attempt to evade extradition to England for an alleged stock swindle appeared today as a major part of the defense plan to save Roger Touhy and three reputed associates from the electric chair. Touhy's attorney, William Scott Stewart laid the foundation for this attempt when he began his cross-examination of Factor after the latter had made a dramatic identification of Touhy and two other defendants as members of the gang that took $70,000 in ransom to free him last July. “It's a good story, if it's true,” said Stewart, who charged that Factor had “swindled widows and orphans in England out of their life savings and that “someone in authority” had led Factor to believe the United States Supreme Court's order for his extradition would not be carried out if he identified the defendants. (By The Associated Press) Reykjavik, Iceland, Jan. 27 — Twelve British seamen drowned when the British trawlers Sabik and Kuthamia collided near Dyrafjord Friday. The Sabik sank almost immediately. The Kuthamia, badly damaged, succeeded in reaching Dyrafjord harbor.

Washington, Jan. 27—The Pittman amendment to the administration money bill, authorizing the issuance of certificates against silver purchased from domestic producers under the London agreement, was adopted today by the Senate. The amendment, which was approved without a record vote, is permissive, permitting the President to exercise the powers conferred within his own discretion. It is not mandatory. The amendment also would permit the issuance of silver certificates against any silver held in the treasury, and would allow the President to make a larger coinage against foreign bullion. Administration leaders accepted the Pittman amendment after the Senate had rejected the Wheeler silver purchase amendment by the narrow margin of 45-43.

PARIS, Jan. 25. — At dawn today, in the cold, grey stadium of the Parc Des Princes, the first duel growing out of parliamentary insults following debate on the Stavisky banking scandal was fought to a draw. Nobody was hurt, not even bystanders or seconds. The deputy Andre Hesse, a maitre of the law courts and former minister, and the Lawyer-Journalist Joseph Beineix met with primed pistols and were placed an ample distance apart. Each fired four shots. Where the shots went nobody knew and nobody seemed to care. Afterwards the principals refused to become reconciled, although the honor of each had been nobly maintained. Beineix was accused by Hesse of writing a derogatory newspaper article about him.

PARIS, France — (P) -- Premier Camille Chautemps and his cabinet resigned Saturday following a series of demonstrations against the government as a result of the recent collapse of the Bayonne municipal pawnshop (bank) and the resultant mud bath for government officials who were accused of conspiracy and fraud in the financial scandal by the Chamber of Deputies. Chautemps’ was the fourth cabinet to collapse in a year.

ATHENS, Greece, Jan. 26—(AP)—Samuel Insull has chartered a hydro-airplane and ordered it held ready for a flight to an unknown destination, it was rumored today. . . With the circulation of this unconfirmed report, it also was rumored that his destination if such a flight were undertaken possibly would be Abyssinia. The possibility that he might attempt to make a clandestine departure before the date of his scheduled expulsion, Jan. 31, had been discussed earlier. It was stated officially that Insull will be permitted to remain in Greece until his health is satisfactory, provided he applies for a prolongation of his police residence permit and an official physician certifies that deportation would be dangerous.

Paris, (4)—Premier Camille Chautemps and his cabinet resigned today and royalist rioters smashed through thousands of police packed into the huge Place de L'Opera. The mob rioted despite all precautions which the authorities of Paris mustered to prevent their demonstrations. The battling monarchists plowed into the ranks of the gendarmes repeatedly. Previously the head of the police force had announced that his precautions would “nip in the bud” future riots but the solid blue ranks of the police broke on the second attack. The Place de L’Opera was by that time a wild turmoil. The orderly police ranks were broken. At least 2,000 royalists were in their midst, swinging their fists. Groups of 50 to 100 men struggled, shouting wildly, all over the pavement. Royalists introduced magnesium flares into the battle. They threw them in among the police horses. 1934-09-28.text: SEYMOUR, Sept. 27. (P)—A district court jury tonight weighed the fate of Miss Ruby Britain, 40-year-old Seymour resident accused of the roadside slaying of Horace Nichols, businessman. At 11 p.m. the jury was preparing to retire and it was not likely a verdict would be reached before morning. Long and fervent pleas for conviction and acquittal were made by five attorneys in arguments during the day. Defense attorneys hammered on the contention that Nichols, married and father of two children, was “a debaucher of women.” They also argued that the defendant acted in self-defense when she killed Nichols.

(Associated Press Leased Wire) SEYMOUR, Texas, Sept. 28.—A District Court jury today convicted Miss Ruby Britain, 40, for the slaying of Horace B.E. Nichols, Seymour businessman, and fixed her sentence at 12 years in the penitentiary. Nichols, sitting in his parked automobile last August with Miss Willie Mae Couch, was killed by bullets fired from a passing machine. Miss Britain said she shot when Nichols made a move for his gun. She testified Nichols “meant much to her.”

Rome, Sept. 28-Benito Mussolini, who regards disarmament as “utopian,” drove ahead with vigor today to make Italy a super-militaristic nation. Il Duce took personal charge of the program, which will put boys at the age of eight and upward in uniform. A new department created by Mussolini will direct the training of Italians between the ages of eight and 33. To head this bureau, called the inspectorate of pre and post military training, Mussolini called General Francesco Grazioli, veteran of campaigns against rebel tribesmen in Libya. The inspectorate is to coordinate activities of the air, navy and army ministries—all of which are headed by Premier Mussolini. Official inaugural ceremonies will be held October 29, a day after the 12th anniversary of the Fascist march on Rome. Mussolini will be the “keynote” speaker. In this address he is expected to outline reasons for his announced inten

Kamenz, Germany — Detective Arthur Johnson of the New York police department today entered and searched the home of Frau Hauptmann, mother of the suspect in the Lindbergh case, in the aged woman’s absence. Guarded by a solid wall of local police and accompanied by plainclothesmen from Berlin and Dresden, Johnson had the small apartment opened by a locksmith, according to police, and entered to search for clues that might lead to further evidence concerning Bruno Richard Hauptmann, held in New York. Frau Hauptmann was visiting another son in Dresden. A throng of curious citizens filled the narrow street to get a glimpse of the “famous detective.” Coming by automobile from Bautzen, Johnson took local police by surprise. After stopping an hour and a quarter, he left again for a destination which was not made known.

Sy United Press GENEVA, Sept. 28.—The United States, non-member of the League of Nations, refused today to join the league's conciliation committee, set up in an effort to end the Gran Chaco war between Bolivia and Paraguay.

(Copyright, 1934, by United Press) SHANGHAI, (UP).—The Chinese national government, in a note to the United States, intimated strongly that it may be forced to adopt the gold standard because of the American silver policy, the United Press learned exclusively today. This intimation was contained in the second note dispatched by H. H. Kung, finance minister, to the United States demanding an immediate clarification of the administration plans regarding silver, the basic metal of the Chinese currency system. Authoritative circles said the note, sent September 24, makes the astonishing offer to sell to the United States all of China’s vast silver holdings in exchange for gold. This could be accomplished by placing an embargo on exports and paying banks a premium for delivering their holdings to the government, it was explained in financial circles. The United States practice of buying silve

(MGCC eS £ SSS S40erwm tees TOKIO, Sept. 28.—Authorities today believed R. B. Terry, Berkeley, Calif., was drowned in the typhoon which swept over southern and central Japan last week. Searchers found wrecked on the shores of Shikoku island, Ehime prefecture, the motor yacht in which Terry had set out from Imaharu port just before the storm. No trace of the American, a representative of a foreign firm at Kobe, was found. No other foreigners are listed among the 2300 persons killed in the storm.

Tokyo, Sept. 23—(AP)—The yacht of B.B. Terry, American, missing since last week's typhoon, was found drifting today without an occupant, said a Rengo (Japanese) news agency dispatch from Hiroshima. Police of Ehime prefecture expressed belief today that Terry, formerly of San Francisco, had been swept overboard and drowned. The yacht, "Hope," was in a badly damaged condition near Yosaka, island, off the coast of Ehime, in Japan's inland sea. Terry was sailing from Matsuyama to Kobe when the destructive typhoon struck. An extended search had been carried on for him at the request of the United States embassy.

1934-02-20.text: NEW YORK, Feb. 20.—UP—An intense blizzard engulfed eastern states today, causing at least five deaths and doing incalculable damage. Two vessels were reported in distress off the New England coast, with the freighter Northern Sword flashing repeated S.O.S. signals from off Winthrop, Mass. 3 States Blanketed. New York, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania were blanketed under a deep layer of snow. Dozens of communities were snowbound. Offices in Boston, New York, Buffalo, Philadelphia, and other cities were handicapped because crippled transportation systems prevented employees from reaching them. The Northern Sword was aground off Winthrop and her last radio message, picked up by both MacKay and Radio Marine, said she was being pounded heavily. Grave fears were felt for the safety of her crew, believed to number about 20 men, although two coast guard cutters were in the immediate vicinity and ru

London, Feb. 20 (AP)—Describing President Roosevelt as a remarkably adroit politician, Sir Arthur Steel-Maitland, former minister of labor, said today “he can give Lloyd George five yards start in a hundred-yards dash and beat him.” “There is no question of whether American recovery will come,” said Sir Arthur, speaking to the American chamber of commerce, “the only question is when Roosevelt will make it come.” He termed Mr. Roosevelt a “sphinx of a remarkable kind” and compared him to “the driver of a team of huskies.” Mr. Roosevelt, Sir Arthur asserted, is like Columbus except “Columbus did not know where he was going, where he arrived and when he got back to Spain did not know where he had been.”

Washington, Feb. 20 (AP)—Mrs. Franklin D. Roosevelt went down the line again today for the child labor amendment, taking issue with all opposed to it—including the Ambassador to Great Britain and her own son in Massachusetts politics. Everybody is entitled to his own opinion, she told her press conference, but just the same she wrote to son James and asked him his reasons for opposing the amendment. She disclosed that she had written in response to questions, which arose, when she said that Ambassador and Mrs. Bingham would be White House guests this afternoon. “Are you going to ask the ambassador about the child-labor amendment?” a reporter asked. Mrs. Roosevelt had no doubt that she would.

| BOSTON, (AP). — Violent gales and heavy snow Tuesday cut off Boston and other New England cities from all rail communication with New York City, imperiled ships and lives at sea, and caused serious collisions on land and demoralization of motor and railway traffic. | The New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad announced cancellation of all train service between Boston and New York and Springfield and New York after revealing that no train had gotten through from Boston to New York since Monday. All service on these lines to New York City was canceled, railroad officials said until further notice. | Meanwhile, a 2,500-ton collier, the Northern Sword, was aground in shallow water off Winthrop, Mass. Coast guardsmen stood by with breeches buoy apparatus, prepared to take off the crew. | Two coast guard patrol boats fought their way to the aid of a leaking, rudderless and drifting schoon

BY ALBERT W. WILSON. Copyright, 1934, by The Associated Press. Brussels. -- The Belgians once more had their beloved King Albert I today. He came to them in death, but once again they were permitted to gaze upon his face. His body lay in state in a small room on a wing of the second floor of the grand palace. Thousands upon thousands passed in slow file beside the bier. It was the first time the citizens had seen their monarch since Saturday, the day he departed from Brussels on the mountain climbing expedition that was to bring him death. As the body lay on its black-shrouded resting place, the head was wrapped in a heavy bandage. The face was much paler than when I saw it Sunday, only a few hours after the embalming. Only the face was exposed to view, for a Belgian flag entirely covered the body below the head. Hundreds of women left the mortuary chamber weeping. There were delays in t

BRUSSELS. (Copyright by AP). A caisson draped in black bore the body of King Albert between solid rows of war veterans with bowed heads, back to the capital city to lie in state for three days. It will be King Albert's last stay in the royal palace, from which he was driven at the outbreak of the World War, for he will be buried on Thursday in the royal crypt at Laeken. Solemnly the populace gathered along the black route of march, still stunned by the shock of the accident that cost the monarch his life Saturday while mountain climbing in his native hills. A detachment of cavalry bearing torches rode at dusk before the coffin. The streets of Brussels were draped with flags of black, yellow and red—the national colors—surmounted with black crepe. A mist mantled the city, as if in sympathy for the most sincere grief of Belgians of all classes. Street lamps were veiled. The youthful Crown

BRUSSELS, Feb. 20—(%)—Thousands upon sorrowing thousands of Belgians passed today before the body of King Albert as it lay in state on its catafalque in the Chapelle Ardente of the royal palace. Clad in a general's uniform, the face bruised by a fatal fall from a mountain rock face, the hands clasping a crucifix, the dead body lay in a setting of silver ve black draperies and green foliage. Candles flickered eerily in the little palace chapel, near the ballroom in which only recently the king and queen had given a gala court ball. Grenadiers in khaki, with crepe draped swords, stood guard, as had done all night while first in line outside the royal palace waiting, from midnight on, to pay homage to the monarch who led them in war and peace. War veterans, war widows, children of war dead, men and women who could remember all of the 34 noted years of his reign; top-hatted men from the citi

BRUSSELS—(AP)—Brussels today was a mecca for the mourning. Sorrowing subjects of Albert I, king of the Belgians, poured by the thousands into the black-draped capital and to the palace where lay the body of the monarch, who fell to his death while mountain climbing Saturday. Royalty from other lands came, too, and knelt at the bier to which the body was borne in the fantastic light of torches last night. Persons of all ages and social circumstances formed a silent, sober line outside the palace, to be examined by police for a last glimpse of one they knew as the "Knightly King." The palace will be open for the same purpose Wednesday. The body will be removed Thursday to the old cathedral of Saint Gudule for the funeral services. Queen Elizabeth, broken by grief, visited alone the body of her beloved husband and king before it was removed from the royal chateau at Laeken in the gathering

1934-11-02.text: London, Nov. 3—(AP)—Cathcart Jones and Ken Waller, English “boomerang fliers,” returned to England today, completing a round trip to Melbourne, Australia. They left Mildenhall airdrome on the morning of Oct. 20 and set their trim monoplane back on British soil at Lympne airdrome at 1:14 P. M. today, exactly 13 days, 6 hours, 42 1/2 minutes from the moments they left. In that length of time they covered a route 22,646 miles long. In making the return flight, the boomerang fliers set a new record of 5 days, 15 hours, 54 minutes from Port Darwin, Australia, to England. The previous record was 8 days, 9 hours made in September by C. J. Melrose. They made the last leg of their journey non-stop today from Athens.

“A reign of terror in Germany” to keep the world ignorant of her “feverish” rearmament was the accusation Winston Churchill, Great Britain's former chancellor of the exchequer, levelled at the Nazi government Thursday as Europe's governments worried over the outlook for peace. London — Churchill, addressing members of his constituency, asserted Germany was rearming “secretly, illegally, and rapidly” and assailed the National government for failing, he said, to speed up its program for air defense. National Defense Stressed Paris—The fear of war overshadowed visits of the French people to graves in connection with All-Saints day, as the government stressed the necessity for national defense and made ready to throw troops into the Saar if the League's governing commission so requested. Berlin.—The government newspaper Deutsche Diplomatische Politische Korrespondez warned France she “is pla

Woodford Bridge, England—(?)— Winston Churchill says Germany is "secretly, illegally and rapidly preparing." "A reign of terror exists in Germany in order to keep secret the feverish and terrible preparations they are making," said the former chancellor of the exchequer in an address to his constituents. "Vice Premier Stanley Baldwin has said 'our frontiers are the Rhine.' Can we be sure that the men now in control in Germany will not reply to that: 'Our targets are the Thames?" Churchill warned his hearers Germany will have "overtaken us before another year has passed" in "organized military machines alone." He asserted the Reich has "gigantic civil aviation with enormous reserves of pilots and airplanes, many of them faster than our fastest military machines." Churchill said England must face the future "with energy and courage if a safe, coherent and peacekeeping policy is to be found

NORWICH, Eng., Nov. 2.—(UP)—Harry Stanley Green, 42, a bank clerk, began a year prison sentence today because, grieved for depression-hit customers, he transferred $80,000 from accounts of wealthy clients to the accounts of the poor. Green admitted he was responsible, and it was shown that he had used none of the money for himself. In charge of the books, Green was able for a long time to continue without detection because there was no alteration in totals.

LONDON, (AP)—Members of the labor party exulted today over the outcome of balloting in municipal elections yesterday. Spokesmen said the party had a net gain of 419 seats already recorded with 575 results still to be announced. The victory was largely at the expense of the conservatives.

(Associated Press Foreign Staff) - ROME, Nov. 2 (*).—The foreign office expected France today to seek in Rome for her decision to send troops into the Saar if a German outbreak follows the Jan. 13 plebiscite. The step would be similar to one taken by France in London. Italy will be consulted with England, a foreign office spokesman said, because this country likewise is a signatory to the Locarno pact. Asked what would be the Italian attitude, the spokesman replied that Italy's chief position is that the Saar problem should not lead to war. He said it was logical, however, that France should place troops at the disposition of the League of Nations’ Saar Commission because it would be difficult to obtain soldiers from a disinterested country. The newspaper Tevere, the only one to comment editorially on the situation, accused France of being willing to disturb the peace of all Europe over

Hsinking, Manchukuo, Nov. 2.—(UP)—The Manchurian government today announced the creation of a state oil monopoly which the United States, Great Britain and The Netherlands fear will drive out foreign companies and close the "open door" to Manchukuo trade. Forecast by some observers as the first of a series of state monopolies planned by a government not recognized by any nations except Japan and El Salvador, the Manchurian oil control plan extended to the sale, exportation and importation of all volatile lamp, heating and light oils, benzol and oil fuel substitutes. In announcing the monopoly program, the government of Emperor Kang-Teh, once a high emperor of China, sought to assure foreign firms now doing business in Manchukuo that they would not be molested and that every effort will be made to have them continue in business as wholesale agents licensed by the government agency control

Lympne, Cathcart Jones and Ken Waller, British aviators, arrived today after a round trip flight to Melbourne, Australia, in 13 days, 6 hours, 43 minutes, 30 seconds—record. They flew more than 800 miles.

1934-09-15.text: Seneva —— () — Great Britain, France, and Italy took turns today reproving Poland for her denunciation yesterday of the general minorities treaty—fearful, nevertheless, that an embittered Poland might still block Russia’s admission to the League of Nations by refusing to vote the Soviet Union a permanent seat in the league council. The chiding was administered by Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, Louis Barthou, French foreign minister, and Baron Pompeo Aloisi, Italian delegate to the league. They directed their oratory in answer to Joseph Beck, foreign minister of Poland, who had told the league that Poland henceforth would look out for her minority populations under her own laws. Sir John told the league assembly that Poland cannot disregard her obligations to minorities and that “article 93 of the Treaty of Versailles, dealing with the Polish minorities question, cannot be ove

BALBOA, C. G. 4 SCR. 42 YT), ~~ Five and smoke bursting forth as the hatch cover of the British freighter Bradburn was removed late today led port authorities to take hurried precautions to protect other shipping in the harbor. A Canal Zone tug tied up to the ship, ready to tow her to sea if the blaze increased. The docks in the immediate vicinity of the freighter were closed to traffic. Dense clouds of smoke poured from the Bradburn’s hatch, three ventilators, the crew’s issue, and the quarterdeck. Firemen, after abandoning earlier efforts to quench the flames with steam under pressure, decided to use water despite the danger of ruining the cargo of 4,200 tons of cotton aboard. Racing 550 miles back to Balboa after fire was discovered in her hold, the Bradburn tied up at Balboa docks this afternoon with her cargo of cotton smoldering stubbornly down inside her.

Aboard U. S. C. G. Cutter Argo, Off Newport, R. I—(#)—Rainbow, the American defender, was leading the British challenger Endeavor by two minutes 40 seconds, as they rounded the halfway mark in the first of their series for the America's Cup. Rainbow rounded the windward mark at 1:42:40 and Endeavor at 1:45:25. Beating to windward in a light breeze that never exceeded nine knots, Rainbow required three hours, two minutes and 40 seconds to negotiate the first 15 miles of the 30 mile course. Soon after the boats rounded the mark, the spectator fleet began closing in astern. It seemed certain some of the big power craft would interfere with the breeze and that Endeavor, being astern, would suffer most.

ABOARD U.S. C.G. CUTTER ARGO OFF NEWPORT, R.I., Sept. 15 (AP).—Harold S. Vanderbilt's Rainbow, defending the America’s cup against the challenge of T. O. M. Sopwith’s Endeavour, was leading by six lengths at 12:10 p.m. (E.S.T.) one hour and thirty minutes after the start. At 12:05 p.m. (E.S.T.) Rainbow went on the starboard tack and crossed Endeavour's bow. Then she came about again on the port tack and took up a position directly ahead of the challenger. There was a good chance both yachts could fetch the halfway mark without taking another hitch. The American yacht had better way on at the preparatory signal. Rainbow was out at the buoy while Endeavour was close under the stern of the committee boat. Throngs of yachting enthusiasts filled the city and almost everything that would float was pressed into service to carry spectators out to the open ocean course, nine miles southeast of Br

BROOKLINE, Mass., Sept. 15.—Lawson Little of San Francisco, British amateur titleholder, held a lead of 5 up over David (Spec) Goldman of Dallas, Tex., today at the end of their morning round in the 36-hole final of the national amateur golf championship.

CHESSINGTON, England, Sept. 14.-Ben Turner, parachute jumper, floated smoothly down from Surrey's skies this afternoon to land safely smack in the lion's den. Suspended precariously on the bars at the top of the cage, Turner's emotions were—to put it mildly—mixed, as two full-grown growling beasts leaped time and time again at his legs, just out of their reach. Firemen quickly manned hoses to subdue the animals and trainers fired pistols, driving the lions to the corner of the cage, while Turner unharnessed himself and clambered down to safety.

--* PROVIDENCE, R. I., Sept. 15 (?)—Rhode Island—storm center of the textile strike in New England—appeared calm today after four days of rioting in which three persons were killed and more than 300 injured.

By the Associated Press. Textile strike violence in New England subsided yesterday but President Roosevelt, still concerned, sped to Newport, R. I., for conferences on the possible necessity for federal troops. The scene of disorders had shifted to the South, with scattered outbreaks in North Carolina, Georgia and Maryland. More guardsmen were ordered out in North Carolina, Maine, Connecticut and Georgia. National strike leaders appealed to Atlantic longshoremen to back their fight by refusing to handle textile shipments. Francis J. Gorman, chairman of the strike committee, claimed that the number on strike yesterday was the largest since the walkout began. Independent estimates placed the total at slightly more than 400,000. Conference Roosevelt will discuss the Rhode Island situation today with Secretary of War Dern and Major Fox (Continued on Page 2)

1934-07-26.text: Aboard S.S. Malolo.—The big thing you hear about the Pacific side of the world is the great exposition at Melbourne, Australia, in October. It's the tourists’ next great roundup. It's where that greatest of all air races is to end. A $50,000 prize from London to Melbourne, 12,000 miles. We have over a dozen of our crack fliers and over half the ships in it will be American made. Wish the army and navy would put a boy apiece in there, Wiley Post hopes to make it in fifty hours, keeping the championship in Oklahoma. I sho’ would love to be with Wiley. I could be his navigator. I have flown that very same route ten thousand of the twelve from Singapore to London on the Dutch line. Hope to see lots of aviation on this trip. (Copyright, 1934, McNaught Syndicate, Inc.)

WIMBLEDON, Eng., July 25—(AP)—Sydney B. Wood, Jr., and Frank X. Shields, playing magnificent tennis, today won the final two singles matches from Australia in the interzone final of Davis Cup play to advance to the challenge round against England. Wood first defeated Jack Crawford, ace of the Aussies, 6-3, 9-7, 4-6, 4-6, 6-2, in a match postponed from yesterday by rain and Shields then put over the clincher against young Viylan McGrath, 6-4, 6-2, 6-4. They meet England for the historic cup in a five-match series starting Saturday and continuing next Monday and Tuesday. It was the fifth time the United States had won to the challenge round since losing the cup to France in 1927. Only in 1931 and last year, when England defeated them in the interzone, had they failed to gain the final round of the international tennis competition.

London, July 26 (P)—An authoritative British source said today that the governments of Great Britain, France, and Italy were convinced that no new action by the three powers to defend Austrian independence was necessary. This source said the governments named felt assured that a death blow had been dealt the Nazi movement in Austria by the action of the Austrian Nazis yesterday. A denial by the Italian government that it plans any action was followed closely by a declaration of Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, in which, before the House of Commons, he belittled the Nazi strength in Austria. Another source revealed that earlier today Great Britain, France, and Italy lost no time in preparing to take action in the Austro-German situation. On the basis of more complete information from Vienna, however, he predicted they would keep their hands off. France Gives Warning.

With the anti-nazi Prince Ernst Von Starhemberg heading the government of Austria, succeeding the anti-nazi Engelbert Dollfuss, other European capitals, concerned over who controls the powder box nation, breathed easier today. A British authority in London said that Great Britain and France believed the Austrian nazis had killed their hopes for popularity when they killed Dollfuss and that none of the three nations would take new action to defend the independence of Austria. The reaction in other capitals was: Rome—Italian troops were ordered to the Austro-Italian border, but it was explained that this was merely a precautionary measure since the authority believed the Austrian government would be able to handle its internal situation without outside help; at the same time, the authoritative newspaper Giornale D’Italia, in an apparently “inspired” editorial, declared Chancellor Hitler of

The peace of Europe hung in delicate balance today as the nations lined up on either side of the fulcrum—Austria—where civil strife between Nazis and government troops followed the assassination of Chancellor Dollfuss. The World War alignment was again approximated—Italy, France, England and the Little Entente all reported ready to take steps against Anschluss or union between Austria and Germany. Germany essayed a strictly neutral course, recalling her minister for unauthorized intervention at Vienna and closing her borders to political refugees from Austria. French sources, which have regarded Nazism as a war menace since Hitler came to power, professed nevertheless to see the hand of Germany and Der Fuehrer behind the Austrian Nazi putsch. Mussolini gave assurance that Italy will defend Austrian independence “even more strenuously in these exceptional and difficult times,” and all Ita

London, July 26 (Thursday) (4) A dispatch from Vienna in a late edition of the London Mail said today that Heimwehr troops and civilians had sought during the night to lynch the assassins of Chancellor Dollfuss. The dispatch said police, heavily armed, had repulsed all attempts to get at the prisoners by threatening to fire into the approaching crowd.

(Copyright, 1934, Associated Press) BRATISLAVA, Czechoslovakia (Via Telephone to Berlin and London), July 25.—A band of 300 Nazi conspirators, wearing the uniforms of the historic Devtschmeister regiment, raided the federal chancellery at Vienna this afternoon, killed Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss and held two other Cabinet members imprisoned for more than six hours. Shortly before 1 p. m., 300 uniformed men closely resembling the soldiers regularly on duty at Ballhausplatz motored into the chancellery courtyard. Firing a volley of shots, they yelled “Close the doors,” and the big doors of the chancellery building swung to. The conspirators then deployed themselves along the various corridors of the building, disarming the guards as they went. 1934-10-31.text: PARIS, Oct. 31.—France has notified Great Britain she has made preparations to crush any attempt at a Nazi putsch in the Saar region. Charles Corbin, French ambassador to London, outlined to Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, steps taken by France to place at the disposal of the League of Nations all forces necessary to prevent any subversive action. The Saar votes January 13 on whether to rejoin Germany, unite with France or remain under the league's mandate. Rumors in France of activities of Nazis in the Saar were intensified. The French general staff has ordered garrisons in Alsace-Lorraine to be prepared for duty protecting French interests. Recruits have been trained swiftly in the area. Several regiments are regularly stationed near the Saar frontier. Anti-Nazis in the Saar heard rumors that 17,000 Nazis now in labor camps across the German frontier planned a putsch on the

LONDON, Oct. 31 ().--The Japanese delegation to the naval conversations, it was authoritatively learned, will inform the Americans late today there can be no surrender on the question of the principle of naval tonnage equality. The Japanese will make it clear, it was learned, that unless the British and Americans are willing to concede equality there is virtually no hope for an agreement.

CALCUTTA, INDIA, Oct. 30.—(?)— John N. Wright and John Polando, American entries in the England to Melbourne air derby, abandoned the race today because of a cracked cylinder which has held them in Calcutta since Sunday. The airmen expect to sail shortly for America, shipping their plane home.

London, Oct. 30 (4P)—A House of Commons labor opposition in a fighting mood was apparent today when Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald allotted two days for the discussion of the sedition bill. Few measures in recent years have aroused more comment than the bill, designed to check the distribution of seditious literature among the forces of the crown. The critics’ main objections to it are that possession of such literature without lawful excuse is made an offense and a justice of the peace may issue a search warrant if there is reasonable ground for suspicion that an offense has been committed. The reassembled House cheered as George Lansbury, veteran labor leader, hobbled to the opposition bench, leaning heavily on a stick. Labor cheered itself hoarse as the labor victors in the recent by-elections in North Lambeth and Swindon took their seats. Lansbury pressed for more time as MacDonald

Newmarket, England, Oct. 3 Spilling huge fortunes into the laps of American sweepstakes ticket holders, "Wyehwood Abbott" today won the historic Cambridgeshire handicap, the great Fall classic of the English turf. "Commander II" finished second. "Highlander" was third. None of the American-owned horses in the race finished in the money. "Wyehwood Abbott," owned by O. P. Whitney and ridden by Jockey Perryman, was the last-minute favorite in the betting. The entry carried a weight of 118 pounds. The race itself paid little more than £1,090 to the owner of the winning entry, but something more than $10,000,000 in sweepstakes prizes will be distributed to ticket holders throughout the world. "Commander II," ridden by H. Beasley, carried 116 pounds; "Highlander," with Jockey Weston up, carried only 114 pounds. LONDON. (FP, Tsuneo Matsudaira, Japan's ambassador to Great Britain, moved to break the deadlock gripping five power naval conversations here. He visited Sir John Simon, British secretary of State for foreign affairs and member of his government's naval delegation, at the House of Commons to propose another approach to an agreement. Although the visit was secret, it was learned the ambassador indicated that the Japanese might give some guarantee that they do not want naval armaments equal to those of the United States and Great Britain in return for recognition of the principles of Japan's proposals for new methods of naval limitation. Prime factors in the deadlock have been Japan's insistence on her right to equality. WASHINGTON. NEWMARKET, Eng., Oct. 31. U.P.) O. Watney’s Wychwood Abbot won the Cambridge handicap today, showering $3,000,000 to 20 lucky holders of tickets on him in the Irish sweepstakes. A. B. Briscoe's Commander the Third, an outsider, was second, and Lord Derby's Highlander third. Other millions of dollars went to holders of tickets on the other horses and to bettors who had wagered heavily in “doubles” on the winners of the recent Cesarewitch and this race. Three Americans held tickets on Wychwood Abbot, netting them $150,000 each or a total of $450,000. Wychwood Abbot was nine to one in the betting, Commander the Third was forty to one, and Highlander twenty-two to one. Thirty-three ran. Eight Americans held tickets on Commander the Third for $75,000 each for a total of $600,000. Four Americans held Highlander for $50,000 each or a total of $200,000. French soldiers will move in, said the foreign office, only if the League of Nations requests it, but the army was bracing itself to protect French mines and citizens of the Saar and to prevent border disturbances. 1934-12-30.text: WASHINGTON, Dec. 29— (GP) Japan today formally abrogated the Washington and London naval treaties, effective Dec. 31, 1936. Notice that Japan is freeing herself from the limitations imposed by the naval treaties was delivered to the State Department by Hirosi Saito, Japanese Ambassador, upon cabled instructions from his government. Japan called for a new “equitable agreement” that would impose the same limitation on armaments of all nations instead of Japan having the short end of the present 5-5-3 ratio with the United States and Great Britain. This common upper limit should be fixed as low as possible, the Japanese foreign office said in a statement distributed throughout the world. “In order to render it difficult for any power to attack another, but easy to defend itself, the offensive arms should be totally abolished or drastically reduced, and the defensive arms adequately provided

Washington, Dec. 29.—The National Association of Manufacturers today stepped into the approaching congressional battle over social security with a denunciation of any unemployment insurance system involving compulsory contributions by industry. It made public what is termed an analysis of British experiments in this field of sociology and asserted the major conclusion to be derived therefrom was that "no system of unemployment insurance has any chance whatever of success unless it is on a contributory basis." The association is on record as favoring the general idea of such insurance, but is ready to campaign against any plan, such as that advanced by prominent administration advisors, for a tax on payrolls to provide a fund for payments to the jobless. This idea was the kernel of the Wagner-Lewis bill—subject of a protracted dispute at the last session of Congress—which had the outspoke

LONDON, Dec. 29.—American and British spokesmen asserted Japan’s formal denunciation of the Washington treaty today reversed the clock a dozen years. Deepest regret was expressed that the only successful disarmament pact would be junked, and the British and Americans were convinced that only a change in Japan’s attitude in equality would make possible a new treaty.

| WALDMOHR, Germany, Dec. 29.—(P)—Miss Elsa Sittell of New York was under arrest here today as a result of derogatory remarks the young woman is alleged to have directed at the Hitlerite storm troopers and picked Nazi guards. Miss Sittell disappeared while traveling in Germany near the French border. It was learned she stopped at Schoeneberg en route to ff and entered a restaurant where she had the conversation which apparently resulted in her arrest. Miss Sittell went to Europe several weeks ago and was planning to sail for home next week. Officials of the American University Women's club in Paris received a telegram from her yesterday indicating that she had been detained at the frontier. The message asked that her baggage be held for her in Paris. Friends of the New York woman said they planned to notify the American consulate today of her predicament.

It seemed improbable she could be released even on parole to await trial before next Wednesday. It was understood G. A. Makinson, American consul general, was on his way here in an effort to see her. Miss Sittell has received no visitors since her arrest Monday. Requests for release have been made to the state's attorney but no decision in her case is expected until after the New Year's holiday. Miss Sittell was arrested last Monday, the day after she left Paris to seek the parents she had not seen for 10 years. Moscow, Dec. 24—A Leningrad firing squad today ended the lives of 14 asserted anti-Stalin terrorists convicted of plotting and carrying out the assassination of Sergei Kirov, powerful communist, Dec. 1. Leonid Nikolaieff, who the Soviet said had confessed to firing the shot, and 12 associates were shot in the city where the murder was committed. The execution took place immediately after the military collegium of the supreme court found them guilty. Court sits secretly. The court, sitting secretly, needed only two days to hear the evidence.

(Copyright, 1934, by Associated Press) WALDMOHR, Germany, Dec. 2 (AP)--Miss Elsa Sittell of New York, held in jail here for a week, was revealed here tonight as an American Saarlander en route to vote in the Jan. 18 plebiscite against the Saar territory’s return to Germany. The girl, held incommunicado in the village’s one-room jail, was taken into custody by the town’s one policeman and was charged with making derogatory remarks about the government of Reichsführer Adolf Hitler. She dances light-heartedly in jail. American Vice Consul George Madkinson at Frankfort arrived tonight at Zweibruecken en route to aid the American girl. Miss Sittell was born in the northwest part of the Saar territory. Soon after her arrival, the townspeople said, “she started talking rather freely.” Word soon spread to the sole police officer, who promptly locked up the girl. That was Dec. 2. She has remained

WALDMOHR, Germany, Dec, 29.-(P)—Elsa Sittell, a New York girl arrested here for alleged derogatory remarks about Adolf Hitler's Nazis, danced about merrily in her prison cell today to show her complete lack of concern over her plight. She was awaiting without worry the arrival of United States Consul General George A. Makinson, who left Frankfort-on-Main early in the afternoon by automobile. The Waldmohr criminal police said "Fraulein Sittell is in excellent spirits. She has plenty of food and all possible conveniences." "There is no occasion for any 'atrocity' story," the police asserted, declaring "her dancing around merrily in her cell is the best proof she is being well treated." 1934-11-21.text: (Copyright. 1934, Associated Press) Lendon, Nov. 20..-Japan will decline to enter any separate agreement guaranteeing peace in the Pacific and the integrity of China if there is no new naval treaty, it was learned tonight. A pact to that effect was proposed by the British to save the principles of the nine-power and four-power treaties should they be junked. This would occur if no naval agreement was made to replace the Washington and London treaties which Japan intends to denounce. The Japanese delegates to tri-power naval conversations here rejected the proposal because, they claimed, it would further complicate the negotiations which are at an impasse because of Japan's insistence on equality in naval armament. LONDON, Nov. 21.—(AP)—Beautiful, blue-eyed Princess Marina of Greece returned to London today for the last few days of hurried preparations for her wedding November 29 to the Duke of Kent, the youngest son of King George and Queen Mary. She found the city blanketed with a choking fog, the worst this autumn, but she also found a warm welcome from the royal family and the public. The Duke of Kent traveled down to Dover early this morning to accompany his future bride to London from her channel crossing, while the King and Queen braved the yellowish, acrid mist to greet her at the railroad station. Thousands of spectators packed every inch of space in the station and along the route from the station to Buckingham Palace where Marina and her parents will be guests until the wedding. Waves of cheers echoed through the murky station where flowers and powerful lamps made a brave show in brighte

LONDON, Nov. 21.—A crisis approached in naval limitation talks today when Tsuneo Matsudaira, Japanese ambassador, arranged a conference with Sir John Simon, foreign minister. Matsudaira had fresh instructions from Tokyo, calculated to put the conference on a new track or make its present near-deadlock absolute. Simon came from a cabinet meeting which considered the naval situation in the light of an expected firm Japanese demand for naval equality and United States refusal to concede it. Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, chief Japanese technical negotiator, was reported to have said that if Japan were not granted equality she would build ships of whatever type and size she thought fit, and would not agree, as Britain suggested, to limit sizes. The United States delegation was reported authoritatively to be determined that if the conference fails, America will take the right to extend its zone of

Bucharest, Rumania, — (4) — King Carol, it was learned today, resents a royal slight offered him by the King and Queen of Great Britain through their failure to invite him to the wedding of Princess Mariana and Prince George. Carol was said by friends to feel that since the British rulers invited Princess Helen, his estranged wife, to attend the wedding, royal etiquette required them to ask him also. Although Carol is Mariana's uncle, he is not sending her a wedding present. The Rumanian king, friends asserted, feels double piqued because the British royal family also ignored his sister, Princess Elizabeth, whose husband, the former King George of Greece has been invited to the London nuptials. (By The Associated Press) London, Nov. 21—The joint parliamentary committee on Indian reforms advocated an all-India federation comprised of self-governing units in its long-awaited report made public today. The report urges this system be substituted for the present centralized government. Eleven provinces of British India, two of them new, would be linked in the federal system with the native Indian states, which would enter the federation by voluntary act of their rulers. These recommendations in the main follow the proposals laid down in the governmental white paper of last year for the reform of Indian government in the direction of granting self-rule “with safeguards.” This is, in other words, still reserving control over vital questions of defense, external relations and the like. Inasmuch as the Washington and London naval treaties expire late in 1936 either the United States or England normally would be expected to call the 1935 conference. London, Nov. 21. (AP)—The season’s worst fog, which for the last three days has plagued most of England, closed again around London today, thicker than ever. It tied up traffic in the Thames and snarled land traffic throughout the metropolis. The Cunard liner Alaunia was fogbound a quarter mile offshore in the Thames, already 48 hours behind schedule. Flares and other devices, coupled with increased police control, failed to cope with growing traffic tangles in London. Hundreds of motorcars and buses were stalled at the curb, and many of their occupants passed the night in the vehicles.

London, Nov. 21,—14—"Outside" questions dominated tri-power naval negotiations Wednesday, negotiations which naval and diplomatic circles said are on their deathbed. A British-Japanese meeting was probable for a further discussion of questions outside the main naval problems on which the two and the United States might be able to agree. It was considered unlikely the British would make any move toward suggesting a new compromise plan for a naval treaty until after discussions with the Japanese. Both Washington and Tokyo rejected the previous English compromise plan. Great Britain is trying to get the powers to approve a separate agreement stating each would notify the others of all building plans in case they are unable to agree upon a treaty. 1934-01-18.text: LONDON, Jan. 18.—(CUP)—Authoritative dispatches from world capitals, bearing on the far eastern situation and the tension between Russia and Japan, led diplomats today to forecast a world crisis by the time of the 1935 naval conference. With neither Russia nor Japan apparently ready for a showdown, months of political maneuvering are in prospect before the conference is held. But the United Press was informed in Moscow on unimpeachable authority that Russia believes the crisis cannot be long delayed. Russia seemed bidding for French, Polish, League of Nations and American support, Japan for German support. French and British viewpoints complicated by their tremendous far eastern interests. The situation apparently was that Russian-Japanese suspicion remained though nervousness was decreased as to the immediate future. WASHINGTON, Jan. 18. (#)--Formally reporting approval of the administration’s currency measure, the house coinage committee said today that Great Britain forced the United States off the gold standard and the proposed $2,000,000,000 stabilization fund was intended “to prevent a repetition of this experience.” With the dollar giving below $5 to the pound on the foreign exchange market, democratic house leaders were rushing pens to bring the monetary legislation up in the house tomorrow. Great Britain's operation of her equalization fund, the committee formally reported to the house, “was so effective in driving our dollar up that we were forced off the gold standard.” “It is to prevent a repetition of this experience that we create the stabilization fund preparatory to the return to gold redemption.” The proposed stabilization fund was termed “the most ingenious instrument ever developed

LONDON, Jan. 17—A secret mission to London recently by a member of President Roosevelt’s “brain trust” was reported here today as the basis of an informal currency agreement which may hold the British pound around a five-dollar ratio. Americans in close touch with official circles in London had various reports of an American monetary expert who came here soon after the resignation of Oliver M. W. Sprague as financial and executive assistant to the Secretary of the Treasury on November 21. The expert was said to have had conferences with Bank of England officials and to have arrived at an understanding about methods by which London and Washington would be kept informed of each other's policy. HAVANA, Cuba, Jan. 18, —(ks —Selection of Col. Carlos Mendieta as president was confirmed at a meeting of the leading political parties today. The native states of India, not part of British India, number

Dover, O., Jan. 18, U.P.)—Marjorie Ann Seikel, five years old, may have to learn to talk again, because of a fall from a piano stool more than a month ago. Unconscious for 26 days, Marjorie had emerged from the coma today and showed some improvement. She was unable to talk, however. Physicians believed a blood clot on the child's brain had affected her memory. She did not lose consciousness for five days after the accident.

LITTLE AMERICA (Via Mac- Kay radio), Jan. 18.—()—Admiral Richard E. Byrd and his antarctic expedition arrived here at 12:39 s. the @. & T.. today. (Unusual static interference made it difficult for the Byrd flagship to communicate with civilization). The flagship was forced to travel at a reduced speed Tuesday night owing to a blizzard. But yesterday the sky cleared slowly and the waters of the Ross sea became deep blue. The expedition intended to determine the state of the old camp at Little America, which Byrd left four years ago, immediately.

BERLIN (#) — The German worker will hereafter be in relation to his boss what a private in the army is to his captain. Unquestioning obedience is enjoined upon the worker as the first commandment of a new labor law, announced by Chancellor Adolf Hitler last night, and effective May 1. "It is the most advanced labor legislation in the world," declared Minister of Propaganda Joseph Goebbels before a gigantic labor mass meeting. Under the law, if a factory owner or captain of industry is benevolently inclined, workers may enjoy a patriarchal regime in which the employer and the government, working hand in hand, will give him all material comforts — and even spiritual diversion.

Paris..-(AP)—-France has informed Germany that “automatic, periodic and equal supervision” of all armaments must be the foundation of any disarmament agreement, it was learned today. The stand was taken in a memorandum submitted to Berlin January 1. The German answer is expected daily. ~~ The memorandum, it was learned on highest authority, makes the following points: 1. Any new nonaggression pact must offer additional guarantees of security without weakening the old ones. 2. Supervision of armaments must be accepted by all nations signing the pact. 3. Any consideration of German army strength must take into account police and other organized forces, such as the Nazi storm troops. 4. France is willing to reduce her army on a parallel with transformation of the German army to a short-term conscript army. 5. 1934-05-13.text: LONDON (AP) — The United States has notified Great Britain that a token payment on the war debts installment due in June would be regarded as evidence of default, it was learned officially today. Notification was given through the British ambassador at Washington, Sir Ronald Lindsay, by Secretary of State Cordell Hull. Sir Ronald informed his government of the United States decision in a lengthy cable received just before noon today. Secretary Hull notified the envoy, he reported, to the foreign office, that the Johnson bill makes it necessary for America to regard token payments by any nation as default.

As a result two alternatives face the cabinet, which early next week will tussle once more with the persistent debts problems. First, to make a token payment anyway as evidence of good faith and willingness to negotiate for a solution, and, second, outright default, in the hope of forcing a quicker solution. The matter was put squarely before the London government by American Secretary of State Hull through the British ambassador in Washington, Sir Ronald Lindsay. The Johnson bill, said Mr. Hull, makes necessary a new American policy by which token payments in lieu of full installments June 15 could only be regarded as evidence of default. (Copyright, 1934, by United Press) LONDON, May 12.—A prophetic nightmare in which fleets of airplanes, droning through moonless nights at great altitudes above sleeping cities to drop one and two-ton bombs on women and children, brought Europe to the starting line of an aerial armaments race today. It was agreed generally that general disarmament has become merely a hope for the future—possibly after another World War. A naval armaments race, limited only technically by the expiring naval treaties of Washington and London, has begun in fact. 10 Factors Ten factors, developed during the last 14 months, preceded the impasse today. They are: 1. The Nazi government determined to end the humiliation of the Versailles peace treaty, which sharply limited German armaments and entirely forbade military airplanes. 2. Athens, Ga., May 12—(AP)—Secretary of Agriculture Wallace warned today that unless the international wheat conference in London can be patched together the United States may virtually remove domestic wheat control and compete vigorously with other nations for the world’s markets. Collapse of the London conference will not have serious effect on American growers but other exporting wheat nations will feel it greatly, he said. Here for a speech before the University of Georgia Institute of Public Affairs, the agricultural secretary told newspapermen: “I was exceedingly disappointed in the collapse of the conference. Athens, Ga, May 12.—The wheat-growing nations of the world today were put on notice by Secretary of Agriculture Wallace that an agreement must be reached unless they wish the United States to go into production on a big scale and battle for the world’s markets. Reviewing the collapse of the London conference which was designed to increase export prices by 10 percent and aid the farmers of the world, Wallace said that he was “exceedingly disappointed” by the failure of the conference and that it was a serious matter for the world although it was not so serious from the viewpoint of the American farmer. Unless the conferees can work out an agreement, he said, the United States may give up crop control and compete in outside markets. BY ARTHUR BRISBANE By the president's decision France and England, not having paid their debts, are officially declared in default, and will not be allowed to borrow in this country even from private sources. This will not be alarming to England or France or to international American bankers, but it will suit the American people. Europe may not hold American dollars at so low a price, now that it is no longer able to borrow them by the carload, or import our United States gold by the neat little barrel. After the president announced the default and this country’s refusal to accept any pretty little token, the London Evening Star, in big type, called the president’s announcement a “highwayman act by the United States.” Considering that the British government is bullying Germany over a miserable little debt of $120,000,000, the British watchers should not object to the president telling th

The cleanest inside job of political guillotining in many a day was the one done on the innocent professor from New England, Dr. Thorp. Not a fingerprint was left anywhere to tell who lopped off the head of the director of foreign and domestic commerce. Everyone knows the trigger man was Senator Stephens, of Mississippi, but he is strictly a trigger man. In his long career he has never been known to plan a job of such proportions as this one. There was a master mind behind Stephens, but no one knows who, although some people have suspicions. If the Senate of the United States should hold a secret vote today awarding a medal to the man who got Thorp, a majority probably would vote, rightly or wrongly, for none other than James A. Istanbul, Turkey, May 2—(UP)—Wrinkled, shriveled Zaro Agha, called the oldest man in the world today, disclosed the secret of longevity, "The answer? Lots of frequent wedlock, that's it," he said, as he paced the grounds at the hospital where he has been under treatment, stretching his legs tentatively and waving his arms to bring back the circulation. His eyes, after his serious illness, had regained the sparkle that used to enliven them when on his visit to New York several years ago he entered a night club and watched the chorus. Zaro is the aged man feeling that he agreed to permit Dr. Rejat Sabit Bey to make the radiographical tests of his bone conformations as recommended by Dr. Serge Voronoff, monkey gland expert, to determine whether he really is 164, as he claims, and how he got that way. Zaro opposed the tests fiercely when they were proposed.

1934-04-06.text: Turnbridge Wells, Kent, England, April 6—(AP)—Sir Robert Peel, husband of the actress, Beatrice Lillie, died today on the eve of his 36th birthday. Death came after an appendicitis operation. Sir Robert was a great-grandson of the famous prime minister, Sir Robert Peel, who founded the metropolitan police force. From him, London got the names “Bobby” and “Peelers.” His 18-year-old son, Robert, is to succeed to the baronetcy created.

By United Press LONDON, April 6.—The Daily Telegraph reported today that Samuel Insull’s funds were coming from almost inexhaustible sources. Friends in Great Britain had raised many thousands of pounds for him as did persons in the United States, likely to be involved if he were tried in the United States, and hence willing to send any reasonable sum to keep him away. The newspaper added that if he were returned there would be plenty of money for his defense.

LONDON, Apr. 6. — (>) — How the United States stands on a proposal for punitive measures to guarantee execution of a disarmament treaty today was explained to Great Britain. Norman H. Davis, American ambassador-at-large, outlined Washington's views in a forenoon conference with Sir John Simon, British foreign minister. Davis made plain, it was understood, that the United States categorically refused to commit itself to punitive action but would not interfere with the carrying out, even through military or economic measures, of a program to enforce disarmament of any European nations. The United States is still determined, Davis was reported to have stated, to remain aloof from the power of negotiation until European countries have settled their political questions and are ready once again to talk about making a definite reduction of armaments. Perranarworthal, Cornwall, England, Apr. 5.—Rembrandt’s priceless painting, “Pontius Pilate” was destroyed in a fire which wrecked the palatial country mansion “Carclew” owned by the noted polo player, Capt. Charles Tremayne, early today. Several members of the Tremayne family and their guests were trapped in various places in the mansion but escaped without injury. Both the Captain and Mrs. Tremayne were driven back by the flames when they tried to escape in their nightclothes over the roof. They finally got out down the back staircase. Rembrandt's painting was not the only old master to be destroyed; two paintings by Murillo were burned as were many valuable books. Captain Tremayne is noted as an art connoisseur as well as for his horsemanship. It was he who headed the British polo challengers to America in 1930 to play for the Westchester cup.

Genoa, Italy, April 6 (AP).—Ships’ officers of the S. S. Roma said today that Mrs. Thalia Fortescue Massie, principal figure in the sensational Honolulu assault case of 1932, attempted suicide by slashing both wrists and throwing herself from the liner’s top deck on the voyage to New York. Prof. Dario Borelli, director of the nervous ailment clinic in Genoa, where Mrs. Massie has been since the ship's arrival yesterday, confirmed the officers’ report. The director said that Mrs. Massie told him she attempted suicide when the steamer was three days out from Genoa because: “I wanted to die. I regretted having got a divorce from my husband.” Mrs. Massie and Lieutenant Thomas Hedges Massie, of the United States Navy, were divorced at Reno, February 23. Dr. Borelli told the Associated Press she would have to remain in the clinic from 30 to 40 days before she could recover completely. Ships’ o

SHANGHAI, April 6. (®)—Laying feudal siege to the walled city of Kingyu, 300 miles north of here, 2,000 Chinese bandits scaled the walls, looted and ravaged the populace and applied the torch to the town, reports reaching here today said. The renegade Mongolian General Liu Kwel-Tang, known as China's most sensational bandit leader, commanded the tattered outlaw horde which scaled the walls with ladders, carrying flaming brands. Like medieval armies which once sacked Europe’s embattled towns with catapults and fiery arrows, Liu's forces swept out of the mountain fastnesses of Shantung province to within easy traveling distance of Shanghai, one of the world’s most modern cities. ISTANBUL, TURKEY, APR. 5. (AP).—Samuel Insull spent today writing notes for his memoirs so that the world will have his side of a spectacular story. Sitting under guard in a hospital ward, he jotted down data on his desperate sea flight from American authorities. The Turkish government, which stopped the flight unceremoniously, sought to sweep away the last legal cobwebs and have him ready for the United States when it comes to get him.

GENEVA, April 6—Chinese circles alleged today that Japan plans to seize Peiping and put Emperor Kang Teh of Manchukuo on the throne there as emperor of the northern provinces of China. At the request of Wellington Koo, Chinese delegate to the League of Nations, the league distributed to all its members China's protest against the enthronement of Pu-Yi as emperor of Manchukuo, the Japanese-created state. The action was considered a diplomatic move on the part of China against Japan. The protest, which was made by Wang Ching-Wei, foreign minister of China, on the occasion of the enthronement ceremony, calls Pu-Yi a puppet and his assumption of the imperial title high treason against China. Koo particularly was asked by his government to protest to the committee handling the problem against recognition of Manchukuo. 1934-11-27.text: LONDON, Nov. 26.— ‘4 —Princess Marina—who the British learned today was a headstrong and even sometimes naughty little girl during her childhood in Athens—was guest of honor tonight at the most brilliant dinner party in Buckingham palace since the war. Three crowned heads were among the gathering of royalty at the function, the first of a series preceding Marina's marriage on Thursday to the Duke of Kent. A book called “The Authorized Story of Princess Marina,” published today, revealed to an amused public that Marina once sat down on the street car tracks in Athens and refused to budge because her will had been crossed. Then, according to the book, she repeated the performance a couple of days later despite a personal warning from her father, Prince Nicholas, that she would be spanked. Another time she “threw her Greek grammar out the window, then wept tears of repentance, not because s

London, Nov. 27 (P)—Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald announced in the House of Commons today that Great Britain will not propose to the United States negotiations for a pact of mutual assistance in the Pacific along the lines of the Locarno treaty. The Prime Minister reiterated Great Britain's desire to maintain friendly cooperation with both the United States and Japan. His statement was in response to a question by Geoffrey Mander of the Liberal Party as to whether the government (Continued on page 2)

LONDON, Nov. 26.—Certain naval quarters tonight suggested that when Japan junks the Washington naval treaty of 1922 a “naval race of technical improvements” may follow, resulting in new types of powerful warships which would make Germany's pocket battleships look like the galleons of old Spain. The United States’ plans, it was indicated, would be made in general cooperation with Great Britain, thereby conforming with the American hopes for an accord on general policies. Such an accord, it was believed, probably will be suggested to Great Britain if there is no new naval treaty. The accord would not bind either nation to concerted action on all types of ships, but would eliminate open competition between the two powers and keep both ahead of Japan.

London, Nov. 27. (AP)—It was rehearsal day today for the wedding of Princess Marina and the Duke of Kent. Seven high-stepping Windsor greys went through their paces in a practice jaunt for Thursday’s task of drawing the honeymoon coach of the Grecian princess and the fourth son of the King of England. Arrangements were made also for a wedding rehearsal today at Westminster Abbey, attended by the bridesmaids, and for a rehearsal later of the Greek wedding ceremony in the chapel of Buckingham Palace. Four greys will draw the royal coach Thursday, attended by two outriders in full scarlet and gold liveries with cockaded hats. On this drab morning, the horses pulled a plebeian luggage carriage. There were seven of them—one just a substitute in case a member of the first team becomes temperamental. Marina and her fiancé had a private rehearsal last night at the abbey.
