London, Nov. 27. (UP)—Refusal of France and Italy to join Japan in abrogating the Washington naval treaty was regarded as a foregone conclusion in Anglo-American quarters today. Foreign Minister Koki Hirota of Japan has invited France and Italy to join in the move. The Japanese previously sought British cooperation but Britain declined. Not Satisfied France’s refusal, it was believed, would be mainly due to the general French policy in favor of the status quo of treaties. Although France is not satisfied with her naval ratio under the Washington treaty, she was believed to feel that the assistance of Japan in scrapping the treaty would morally aid Germany’s efforts to abolish the Versailles treaty. Italy also has expressed a desire to increase her relative naval strength but the Italian government last December on presentation of the naval budget, expressed opposition to Japan’s policy.

London, Nov. 27 (4#)—The petition of Lady Vera Hodge, the former Countess of Cathcart, for a divorce from Sir Rowland Hodge, Tyneside ship owner, on charges of alleged adultery, was dismissed today by a court. Lady Hodge, who had two previous husbands, was detained in 1926 at Ellis Island by immigration authorities who refused her admittance to the United States on grounds of "moral turpitude."

Developments in Europe failed to improve the outlook for international peace today. In London, Japan's suggestion that France and Italy join her in abrogating the Washington naval treaty was met with statements that the two European nations would not be willing to side with Japan against Great Britain and the United States. Anti-Czechoslovakian demonstrations occurred in Vienna, Austria, and Cologne, Germany, in sympathy with German students in Prague who have been clashing with Czechs. Advices from Saarbrucken indicated that League of Nations authorities had decided to close the Saar frontier for two weeks in advance of the plebiscite, to avoid clashes between French and German elements. The French chamber of deputies passed large naval and air force budgets, on the top of the sizeable military budget passed last week. Raids on foreign terrorists continued in the French capital.

Tokyo, Nov. 27 (4)—Formal expression of American dissatisfaction with Japan’s “hands off” policy in the Manchukuo oil monopoly dispute was strongly indicated today, following Great Britain’s example. The American embassy is keeping in close touch with Great Britain which set forth its views in a note handed Foreign Minister Koki Hirota. It was learned oil companies who face loss of their business in Manchukuo because of the monopoly have reached an agreement on a joint plan of action. American, British and Dutch interests are involved.

1934-06-23.text: LONDON, June 22.--Military dictatorship in Germany in September was predicted by a “personage” close to former Kaiser Wilhelm, the Daily Herald correspondent at Doorn, Holland, asserted today. Wilhelm, the Herald's informant said, learned during the last few weeks that plans for proclamation of the dictatorship, which would oust the Nazi government, were formed and ready for execution. “The former Kaiser will be back in Germany before the beginning of 1935,” the informant was quoted as saying. “It may be as a private citizen or it may be in an official capacity, but he will be back. “There never has been an official contact between the Nazi movement and Doorn castle (where Wilhelm is in exile). On the contrary the relationship has been bad. Wilhelm never has met Chancellor Adolf Hitler and each has refused to see representatives of the other. “We here do not expect to see Hitler last thr

London, June 23. (P)— He doesn’t look it, but the Prince of Wales is 40 years old Saturday. Busier than ever and graver of mien, the heir to the throne of the British Empire does not get much relaxation these days. Content with his modest bachelor apartments at St. James’ Palace and his country place at Sunningdale, he has devoted himself in recent months to the campaign for removing slums throughout the British Isles.

HYDE PARK, N. Y., June 23—(UP)—President Roosevelt arrived at the Summer White House at 5 p.m. today after a five and a half hour motor ride from New London, Conn. Mr. Roosevelt and his party motored. He disembarked at the Coast Guard Academy in the Connecticut port. He will return to Washington Tuesday morning. The Longshoremen’s strike paralyzing shipping on the Pacific Coast was expected to be No. 1 on his agenda when he reaches his desk. The President last night dispatched to Governor Frank F. Merriam at Sacramento, Calif., a telegram advising him that appeals for Federal intervention to halt the strike had been laid before Miss Perkins. The Summer White House also was expected to announce either late today or tomorrow Presidential action on a number of important bills that were passed in the closing hours of Congress. While no official information was available there were reports in

LONDON, June 23--(UP)—Unmarried, and apparently unlikely to be, the Prince of Wales celebrated his 40th birthday quietly today. He had lunch with his parents at their palace, and received his birthday gifts, including those from his little nieces, Princesses Elizabeth and Margaret Rose. The birthday revived popular discussion as to the Prince’s persistence in enjoying—or enduring—a bachelor’s life. For a long time there has not been even a rumor regarding a marriage, and many people are convinced that he intends never to take a wife and provide an heir to succeed him on the throne. Some people even think he will not be King—that he will renounce the throne in favor of his brother the Duke of York. In that event, barring the possibility that a son is born to the Duke, Princess Elizabeth would be heir to the throne and would ascend as Elizabeth II. However, he has a high sense of state dut

LONDON, June 22—(AP)— New demands that Great Britain pay her war debts to the United States were made on the floor of the House of Commons Friday. Members of the labor and conservative parties joined in an attack. Col. Josiah C. Wedgewood, laborite, took advantage of a debate on the finance bill to declare: "I want from the chancellor a definite assurance that, be difficulties what they may, England is going to meet her bond in the long run and see fit to pay back to America." Capt. Victor . Conservative, suggested that the government (Continued on Page Eight)

New York, June 22—-(AP)—The Whitney Museum of American Art announced today that Mrs. Juliana Force, director of the museum, at present in London, has sent an agent to Venice with instructions to withdraw the entire American exhibit at the current Venice biennial exhibition unless the portrait of Marion Davies, movie star, is removed. Mrs. Force’s objections to the painting were not announced. It was painted by Tadestyka, a Polish artist. The Whitney Museum has charge of the American division of the exhibit which is held every two years and is considered important in the world of art. The exhibit opened May 12 and will close October 25,

Los Angeles, 1 June 22.—Ida Lupino, young English actress, fell victim to the epidemic of infantile paralysis here today. She was confined to her home in Beverly Hills. Physicians said she had contracted the disease some time

Berlin, June 23—(IP)—Great Britain’s invitation to the government to send a delegate to London in an effort to avert the trade war threatened for July 1, when Germany is to impose a moratorium on foreign debt payments, was accepted today. The announcement that the invitation had been accepted did not disclose who would be sent or the date of the conference. Great Britain announced that it would impose a clearing house to seize German credits in sufficient value, if possible, to meet services on German gilt edge securities, but it offered to negotiate. Germany announced it might retaliate by barring imports from the entire British empire—a move that would penalize the dominions. Britain has an unfavorable trade balance with Germany. Those of the dominions, which are separate units for trade purposes, are heavily in their favor. Germany's acceptance of the offer to negotiate came less than

1934-08-30.text: LONDON, Aug. 29 — England welcomed the news today that her Prince George would desert in bachelorhood his elder brother, the Prince of Wales. Announcement that George, 32-year-old fourth son of the king, would wed the beautiful Princess Marina of Greece, caught London off-guard. But approval of the match, the first in the royal family in 11 years, was quickly forthcoming. Marina, who is 27, has one qualification among others which will be welcomed by the British folk. She speaks English perfectly, and has spent much time in this country. May Wed In Autumn. A courtship in the romantic Alps of Yugoslavia, culminating five years of friendship, resulted in the match. George, who is visiting with Princess Marina at the summer home of Prince Paul of Yugoslavia, her cousin, wired his father for consent. It was speedily given. The palace announcement said: “It is with the greatest pleasure that

London, Aug. 30 —(P)— When young Prince George strolls to the altar with his pretty princess, Marina of Greece, the Prince of Wales—that perennial bachelor—may be his best man. Still agog over Tuesday night's announcement of the youngest English prince’s engagement to Marina, court circles Wednesday heard that Edward of Wales, of the British throne, might be present at the ceremony as his brother’s second. The close friendship known to exist between the two lent substance to the reports. Wales, it was learned, was among the very first to share Prince George’s romantic secret, revealed to the surprised but approving capital in Tuesday night's court circular. As George and Marina left Salzburg, Austria, where they had been visiting secretly the past three days, to return to Yugoslavia, where their five years’ friendship flowered into romance, the excited capital began discussing probable p

By Associated Press BOHINSKO LAKE, Yugoslavia, Aug. 30.—Prince George of England and Princess Marina of Greece will be married in Westminster Abbey some time this winter, the Associated Press learned today. The exact date of the ceremony will not be decided until the prince has conferred with his father, King George. The princess plans to go to the altar attired in a wedding dress worn by her mother when she was married to Prince Nicholas at the Russian emperor's palace 32 years ago.

London, Today.-- (P)- The foreign office announced today that Great Britain, Italy, and France were campaigning actively for the entrance of Soviet Russia into the League of Nations with the likelihood they will be successful. An invitation is expected to be issued to Russia shortly after the league assembly meets Sept. 10 at Geneva and the Russian acceptance is understood already to be assured. "The British, French and Italian governments," said the official statement, "are making inquiries through their representatives in various capitals with regard to the attitude of the governments to which they are accredited toward the entry of the Soviet Union in the League of Nations." High British sources said this statement would not have been issued here if the preliminary steps were not already completed and the successful culmination of these efforts virtually assured. While there has been

(By The Associated Press) The temperature was below freezing at Owls Head, N. Y., today and there were snow flurries in parts of the Adirondacks. A thin carpet of snow covered the vicinity of Crystal Lake in Maine. Elsewhere in New England killing frosts and near freezing temperatures were reported. Boston's suburbs registered as low as 45 degrees. New York City at 52 degrees, was colder than it had ever been on any previous August 30 of record.
BEET SET SO FAR IN HER BORING London, Aug. 29. (#)—Lily Damita took time off from the filming of ‘Brewster’s Millions’ here today to announce her engagement to marry real millions.

BOSTON, Aug. 30 (4°)—Killing frosts and near freezing temperatures arriving nearly a month ahead of schedule were reported in New England today, while Boston’s temperature of 50 was within one point of equalling a 22-year record, and suburbs reported thermometer readings as low as 45 degrees. At localities reported that the mercury dipped to 36 and 38, damaging beans and corn usually withstand considerable cold. Flower beds of that kind blackened and died. The coldest in seven years, points behind normal for August alone. Provided the weather continues next month, experts said, it would be the coldest summer on record. Fair and continued cool was today’s forecast, with slightly warmer predictions for tomorrow. Average rainfall for the period of June 22 to Aug. 30 has been 3.55 inches compared with the normal figure of 7.66.

Moscow, Aug. 30. — Ambassador Bullitt just flew in aboard a good old army plane from Odessa, down on the Black Sea. What a live bird this Bullitt is, and a tremendous favorite here. He did a smart thing, he picked George Hanson, our crack consul general from Harbin, to come here and assist him. The Soviet writers are holding a convention here. They are the richest people in the U.S.S.R. Maxim Gorky's royalties last year were seven million roubles. I am trying to learn to write in Russian. Yours, at. . 4s.

1934-01-11.text: LONDON, Jan. 11.--Clarence Guy Gordon Haddon, 43-year-old unemployed consulting engineer, won the right to call defense witnesses when he went on trial today charged with threatening and attempting to blackmail King George. Agreeing to subpoena witnesses, but reserving decision on whether he will hear them, Justice Charles of Old Bailey—London's famous criminal court—adjourned the hearing until either January 19 or 23. Haddon, who claims to be the illegitimate son of the late Duke of Clarence, elder brother of King George told the court: “I have witnesses to say that my mother was secretly married to the Duke of Clarence.” “We won't say anything about that,” the justice replied. “I will allow the subpoenas. I only want to indicate that if I find that they have no relevance to the charge itself, although they may be relevant to other matters, you will, I know, expect me in pursuance of my

WASHINGTON, Jan. 1—[?]—The price of $34.06 an ounce was continued by the government today for domestic gold. It was the 18th posting of this same quotation for newly mined domestic metal. In London, Sterling opened at $5.19 to the pound. At this level, bar gold was worth $32.44 an ounce.

(By the Associated Press) The jockeying of the United States, Great Britain, and France for more favorable trade positions with each other aroused sharp protests Wednesday in two of the capitals, The United States Senate adopted a proposal to place excise taxes on liquors from foreign nations behind in their American debt payments, Great Britain demanded of France the same "preferential" treatment for British products as France gave the United States in increasing by 300 percent the quotas on certain products in return for higher allotments on French liquors, In London it was said the United States immediately would double the import quotas on British liquors for the period ending March 31 in exchange for an increased allotment of American pork products allowed to enter Great Britain, France and Russia, meanwhile, reached an agreement for increased transactions.

LINGFIELD, Eng. Jan. 11 - American-owned Grand National Candidates today ran one-two in the southeastern handicap steeplechase over a three-mile course. F. Ambrose Clark's Eorley Boy won with J. H. 'Jock' Whitney's Lone Eagle II in second place.

LONDON, Jan. 11.—(4)—The report Sir John Simon brought back from his conversations with Premier Mussolini at Rome has created a more hopeful outlook toward disarmament negotiations, it was apparent today in informed political quarters. The cabinet’s disarmament committee held an exhaustive discussion of the situation, and although it was not suggested there had been any definite development, there was talk of distinctly brighter prospects. Postponement of the meeting of the Arms Conference steering committee at Geneva from January 22 to January 29 to allow further progress in diplomatic exchanges was among the possibilities discussed informally. The Times, editorially supporting the idea of postponement, said “There can be no doubt that to break into Franco-German negotiations, which are making some progress, would be far more likely to hinder than to help them.” Advocating that a soluti

Te tae aoa ean ae NEW YORK, Jan. 11 ()—Ethel Barrymore sailed today aboard the Aquitania for England where she will appear in London in Sir James Barrie's ‘The Twelve Pound Look.’ She plans to stay abroad two months.

Paris, France, Jan. 11—(4)—The Stavisky scandal storm broke full force on the government of Premier Camille Chautemps in the chamber of deputies today. The cabinet went before the chamber and sought to avert its overthrow by a frank admission of "faults and negligence" and promises of drastic reforms and punishments in police and judicial procedure. Deputies opposing the government charged that corruption in the government, in the parliament and in the press enabled Serge "Handsome Alex" Stavisky, who killed himself Monday when police caught him, to fleece the public of more than $40,000,000. Stavisky founded the Municipal Pawnshop of Bayonne, and disappeared three weeks ago leaving it without assets.

Leipzig, Germany, Jan. 10.—(AP) The beheading of stolid Marinus van der Lubbe today for the burning of the Reichstag last February closed one chapter of that sensational case, and brought to the fore the probable fate of his four fellow defendants. The emotionless young Dutch brick mason was executed at 7:30 o'clock after refusing, as in a coma, to reply to final questions whether he had anything to say and whether he had any last wishes. In two or three days the German government is due to decide what to do with three Bulgarians, who have been in jail since Dec. 23, when the supreme court convicted Van der Lubbe and acquitted the other four.

1934-06-03.text: London.—(AP)—Reliable sources said today that Great Britain apparently has reached an understanding with President Roosevelt on the war debts question, and will make a token payment June 15. The only comment from official quarters, however, was: "We are studying Mr. Roosevelt’s message with much interest." Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, arrived here today from Geneva, where he left the world disarmament conference yesterday. He will spend his weekend at his home in the country in private talks with other cabinet members. Sir John in his trip from Switzerland had the opportunity to be fully informed of the content of Roosevelt’s message. It is known that the message occasioned the British government no surprise of any kind and indicated both Washington and London knew each other's views before Mr. Roosevelt's message was sent to Congress. A formal communication regarding Great

Associated Press Foreign Staff LONDON, June 2.—While no official statement was forthcoming, the belief persisted in informed quarters today that Great Britain has reached an understanding with President Roosevelt on the war debt question. The understanding was described as providing a token payment on the June 15 installment, followed by bi-lateral conferences. “We are studying Mr. Roosevelt's message with much interest,” was the only official comment on the president’s message to congress. The British government apparently was not surprised at the nature of the message, and found nothing in it not already known here regarding Mr. Roosevelt’s views. While officially the document was regarded as not unfriendly to Great Britain and as nothing more than a historical resume of the subject for congress, some newspapers were critical. Instead of agreeing with these newspapers, officials pointe

LONDON, June 2 (#)—Princess Barbara Hutton Mdivani had recovered sufficiently today from the ailment that sent her to a medical clinic to return to the hotel where her parents are staying, but neither she nor her parents went out to see her husband, Prince Alexis, play polo. A spokesman for the Hutton entourage explained today that “the ailment which brought Mr. and Mrs. Franklin L. Hutton to London to visit their daughter was a stomach disorder.” The princess was said to have contracted the illness while in China on her round-the-world honeymoon trip and to have suffered a recurrence recently. There was no indication that the friendly relationship in evidence between the prince and his (Continued on Page 2, Col. 1)

ROME, June 2 (4.—Premier Mussolini told 10,000 war volunteers today that Italy will fight her next war for herself alone and not on behalf of any other nations pretending to be her allies. “Italy’s volunteers, if war is necessary, will shed their blood only for Italy,” declared Il Duce. “Experience has shown them that it does not pay to help by land and sea the people who pretend to be our allies.” Mussolini was interpreted as referring to France and her World War ally, Serbia, now part of Yugoslavia.

NORTH BAY, Ont., June 2 (U.P.) -- Marie, the smallest of the famous Dionne quintuplets, was in a serious condition today after a setback suffered this morning: “Not much better,” reported Dr. A. R. Dafoe, the country physician who attended the five girl babies since they were born to Mrs. Olivia Dionne on Monday. “We have hopes, however.” Medical records do not show any quintuplets of which all survived. The progress which had been made by the Dionne infants, however, had raised hope that they would all live. The quintuplets slept peacefully through a minor excitement at their home last night when a stove pipe caught fire. The fire was nothing serious.

ROME, June 2. UPR—Premier Mussolini made a fighting talk today before 10,000 war volunteers, and was given an enthusiastic shout of affirmation when he asked if they are ready to fight again if necessary. He promised them, though, that if they do fight, it will be for Italy alone and not on behalf of other nations pretending to be allies. “Italy's volunteers,” he said, “if war is necessary, will shed their blood for Italy alone. Experience has shown them that it does not pay to help by land and sea the people who pretend to be our allies.”

Saturday June 16 looks to be another zero hour for President Roosevelt and his National Recovery Administration. Sufficient activity has been noted in the opposite trenches already to have the White House ‘shock troops’ standing by for a major attack. At midnight that day the licensing provision of the Industrial Recovery Act expires and the administration loses its major punitive weapon for code enforcement. Democratic strategists chose not to ask Congress to renew it for fear the whole NRA organization would be opened up to intensive debate and possible disruption. Although he has never resorted to it, this provision empowered the president in any industrial crisis to license an industry and deny all plants the right to operate that fail to observe Blue Eagle rules one hundred percent. Industrialists have chafed under the threat of the licensing provision. They were pretty certain Mr.

PARIS, June 2.—(#)—France considers building a defense against Nazi Germany far more vital to her safety than smoothing relations with America, officials indicated today. Thus the country was expected to prefer another war debts default June 15 to sacrificing her military strength, as much as she had hoped President Roosevelt would show her some acceptable way out of the debt controversy. The Chamber of Deputies, which is master of the government on the war debts issue, has shown no inclination to make the “substantial sacrifice” suggested by Mr. Roosevelt in his war debts message yesterday. Instead, the French cling to the contention that a scaling down of reparations requires the same trimming of war debts. Officials indicated that the message had left France’s policy of default unchanged.

1934-09-05.text: [BY ASSOCIATED PRESS] The first big day of the general textile strike was hailed by union leaders today as a “tremendous success” while employers declared that a poll of the industry in New England indicated the majority of workers were opposed to the strike. In New England, where the mills were closed yesterday because of the Labor Day holiday, in mills employing an aggregate of 125,000 it was reported that at least 50,000 were idle. Half and Half In the great textile centers of the Carolinas a survey indicated that approximately 80,000 were idle and the same number working. In the dozen or more other textile states affected by the strike indications were that at least half of the workers were idle. The most disorder reported in the strike today was at Macon, Ga., where fist fights were numerous, there were several arrests and many threats of warrants. One automobile load of mill office

WASHINGTON, Sept. 4—L disclosures that two American and British armament makers had combined to dominate world submarine building, with Sir Basil Zaharoff as their super-salesman, were written today into the open records of the Senate munitions investigating committee. The story, studded with hints of international intrigue, was unfolded during the day-long questioning of three officials of the Electric Boat Company of New London and New York. This concern, now building submarines for the United States Navy, was shown to have an arrangement with Vickers, Ltd., foremost of British armament companies, through which business was divided and few submarines were constructed throughout the world without one or the other getting a share in the profits. Washington, — (UP) — Electric Boat company officials informed their British associates in 1927 that the business of selling warships in South America was based on “graft,” it was disclosed today at the senate’s munitions investigation. The statement was made in a letter from L. Y. Spear, Electric Boat vice president, to Commander C. W. Craven, managing director of Vickers Ltd., on March 3, 1927. Payment of special commissions to various interests by Luis Aubrey, Peruvian representative of Electric Boat, represented “bribery,” Sen. Bennett Clark, D., Mo., charged. LONDON, Sept. 5.— (UP) —The British government was represented today by a well-qualified spokesman as welcoming the revelations of the United States Senate investigation of a secret armaments pact between Vickers-Armstrong, Ltd., of Great Britain and the Electric Boat Company, of Groton, Conn. A full report of the hearing will be transmitted by the British embassy at Washington for the consideration of government here. It was stated that there was no resentment by responsible leaders of the fact that the name of the British government was brought into public discussions and it was stated that Norman Davis and other American disarmament delegates made it clear in their recent conversations in Europe that they felt much could be done for peace by exposing the tremendous political influence of private armament firms. The London Herald quoted Sir Charles Craven, director of Vickers-Armstrong

Havana, Sept. 4.—({#)—To the bursting of bombs, the rattle of rifles and the shouting of rioters, Cuba today celebrated its first "Fourth of September" holiday. One man was killed. A year ago tonight, Top Sergeant Fulgencio Batista and his little band of conspirators staged their "enlisted men’s revolt," ousted their officers, removed the provisional government of President Carlos Manuel de Cespedes and in its stead put five executive commissioners of their choosing. President Ramon Grau San Martin succeeded the commission; President Carlos Hevia replaced Grau; President Carlos Mendieta followed Hevia, but Batista, elevated to the rank of colonel and keeping his grasp on the army, remained. His Day So today was his day and, little mindful of the ruction raised by groups he and his henchmen regarded as radicals, Batista made the most of it. Early today he sent his army musicians marching

Textile strike disorders flamed from New England to Alabama today as President Roosevelt moved for peace. Tear gas bombs, stones and clubs figured in the scattered clashes between pickets, police and mill guards. Sabotage reports came from southern mill towns. “Flying squadrons” of union pickets in the south found their mill shut-down drive bringing martial law threats in North and South Carolina. Troops were held in readiness. Scores Injured Scores were injured in a wild shot that was fired, causing a melee between police and pickets at Macon, Ga. State police in Connecticut were ordered to quell strike demonstrations. An angry crowd of strikers demanding the surrender of a strike chief was repulsed by Nashua, N.J., police. Three women were injured in Atlanta. A Spindale, N.C., textile worker was stabbed. Another was beaten at New Bedford, Mass.

Viarregio, Italy, Sept. 4. (P) — Italy's king and queen met Austria's erstwhile empress here today, and decided to link the two dynasties in matrimony. The royal conclave, it was learned, approved the engagement of Archduke Otto, pretender to the Austrian throne, to marry Princess Maria, youngest daughter of King Victor Emanuel and Queen Elena of Italy. No formal announcement of the oft-rumored engagement was issued, but Prince Felix, prince consort of the grand duchess of Luxembourg, who is visiting former Empress Zita of Austria here, confirmed to The Associated Press the fact that the match had been made. The official announcement, it was understood, would be delayed pending clarification of Otto's position in reference to the restoration of the monarchy in Austria and Hungary.

NUREMBERG, Germany— “By this revolution, the German form of life is definitely settled for the next thousand years,” Reichsfuehrer Adolf Hitler declared today in a proclamation to the opening session of the Nazi Party Congress. District Leader Adolf Wagner read the proclamation to a cheering assemblage of National Socialists. “The will of the National Socialist government leadership is unfaltering and unshakeable,” the President-Chancellor declared. “If the face of this our enemies—especially those beyond our borders—are prone to consider 4,000,000 votes as a menacing opposition, then we can only smile to ourselves.” Hitler declared the opposition was not united, “either in a faith or a program.” “Our next attack,” he said, “must also disperse this last remnant of a non-Nazi philosophy. . . . National Socialism knows what it wants and wants what it knows. The National Socialist revolutio

1934-11-30.text: (Copyright, 86%, Associated Press) | London, Nov. 29.—In the grandest, most gorgeous show London has seen in many years, beautiful Princess Marina of Greece became the bride today of the Duke of Kent, King George's handsome youngest son. A half million persons who packed this staid old city to the chimney-tops roared cheer after cheer as the young couple, parading in glittering processions from Buckingham Palace to Westminster Abbey and back, plighted their troth in two separate ceremonies. Feverish, happy excitement, not at all blighted by early morning rain, fog and mist, gripped the capital from the moment Marina, waking early, peeped out between the curtains of her Buckingham Palace suite until shouting throngs saw the newly-weds off for their country honeymoon. Carnival Spirit The mood of merry-making still held the city tonight and the spirit of carnival reigned at all London's pla

LONDON, Nov. 30.—(UP)—The Duke and Duchess of Kent embarked on their honeymoon at Himley Hall in Worcestershire today while thousands of Londoners nursed headaches acquired in making the royal wedding the gayest celebration since the armistice. While Londoners crowded hotels, restaurants, night clubs, cabarets and theaters last night, the young couple arrived at Snowhill Station, walked through a triumphal arch erected in their honor, and motored to Himley Hall. They had left London with cheers and the peals of bells ringing in their ears. They arrived at the tiny village at the estate to find it in darkness. There are no street lights. Policemen with torches and servants with flares guided their motor car to the estate. Only the butler and the housekeeper received them. They dined at once, and then watched a motion picture of scenes of their wedding. In London was the occasion of celebr

By The Associated Press London, Nov. 30—London celebrated until an early hour today the wedding of Princess Marina and the Duke of Kent while the pair were in honeymoon retreat at the country home of Earl of Dudley. They were received only by servants after the trip through the English countryside before cheering throngs. Crowds in London kept up the celebration until long after midnight. Once or twice groups of “rowdies” clashed with police but there were no further disorders.

PARIS, Nov. 30,—(UP)—Joachim Von Ribbentrop, special German disarmament envoy, arrived today for conferences which it was hoped might make possible a new deal in European politics through direct negotiation by Germany, France and Great Britain. Ribbentrop will talk with Foreign Minister Pierre Laval. It was understood he hoped to present a basis for solution of the question of German rearmament and future control of armaments. May Return To League Such a solution would leave the way open for Germany to return to the League of Nations and disarmament conference, from which it announced its intention a year ago to withdraw because of dissatisfaction with the powers’ stand on German armaments. The German negotiator was expected to ask France to accept as legal the German rearmament which is known to be progressing, and to offer assurances that Germany should return to the League and disarma

LONDON, Nov. 29,—(!™%—Great Britain's big royal wedding was not without its casualties. Ambulance men attended 750 cases along the wedding route, where crowds were most densely packed. Ten persons were taken to hospitals, but most of the other troubles were minor. Many women fainted. A few persons suffered fractured bones.

LONDON, Nov. 30 (UP).—Prince Paul of Jugoslavia, closely guarded by Scotland Yard men who feared an attempt on his life by terrorists, left today for Belgrade after a breakfast conference with Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald. It was understood that MacDonald and the prince discussed the Jugoslavian-Hungarian dispute that arose from the assassination of Prince Paul's nephew, King Alexander. Prince Paul is chief regent for five-year-old King Peter.

(By the Associated Press) London, Nov. 29.-The British capital was packed with throngs made happy by the marriage of the Duke of Kent and the Princess Marina of Greece, but London was not the only place where British celebrated. British warships all over the world fired a 21-gun salute at high noon. Their sailors had an extra tot of rum with which they toasted the royal couple's health. Millions of people lost sleep in order to hear the wedding ceremony broadcast all over the world. The ceremony in Westminster Abbey was witnessed by 1,500 invited guests. It was a typical London November day, with dull gray skies and occasional drizzles of rain that absolutely failed to dampen the enthusiasm of the vast crowds that patiently waited hours to catch a

Tokio...(AP)--Japan's foreign minister, Koki Hirota, told the diet today the government is "endeavoring to establish firmly the principle of nonmenace and nonaggression." "It is according to this principle," Hirota said in a long-awaited speech, "that Japan proposes abolition of the ratio principle hitherto in force and establishment of a common upper limit for the powers concerned (Japan, the United States and Great Britain)." In insisting upon abolition of the ratio principle in naval disarmament, Hirota declared the country is actuated by "the spirit of disarmament." "In consonance with the spirit of disarmament, we desire to bring about thorough and drastic naval reduction and to lighten thereby the tax burden of nations in the future," he said. "To that end we desire to bring down this common upper limit to the lowest level possible and at the same time through drastic reduction and

1934-09-08.text: Militant efforts of strike leaders to force shutdowns in the textile industry focused in New England today and met with scant success as the number of estimated idle workers increased 10,000 to almost 370,000. Peter Van Horn, leader of the silk manufacturers, said in New York City that if protection could be obtained for the industry all possibility of the success of the strike would be removed by Monday. Secretary of Labor Frances Perkins, after conferring with members of the president's textile strike board in Washington, expressed confidence that the board would be able to arrange a settlement of the walkout. Francis J. Gorman, chairman of the union strike committee in Washington, declared that the strike was already “85 per cent effective” and denied that a general strike of all labor unions was imminent. Situation in South Quiet The situation in the South was comparatively quiet aft

TOKYO, Sept. 7 (P)—Japan definitely committed itself today to a policy of being second to none in naval armament. The empire determined to renounce the present scheme of naval limitation, and demand in naval matters a ranking in all respects equal to that of the United States and Great Britain. The formal policy received the approval of the nation's highest authorities. It was stated that the program now definitely drawn up will be the guide for Japanese negotiators at the naval conference next year, and at conversations in London preliminary to the conference. There was no official disclosure of details of the policy, but newspapers unanimously asserted that one of the fundamentals is a demand for the abolition of the ratio principle for limitation of navies.

Washington, Sept. 7.—(#)— King George V, of England, and the United States war department were portrayed before the senate munitions committee today as competing salesmen in the armaments marts of the world. There were gasps of amazement from a little group of spectators when the committee was told that England’s ruler, in 1932, personally intervened in an attempt to stop the sale of guns to Poland by a New York firm. The war department, it was testified previously, had actively aided the Driggs Ordnance Engineering company of New York in its efforts to sell the Polish government weapons that deal death. Day of Drama Testimony portraying the English king as an armament salesman almost overshadowed other startling developments uncovered during the day’s rapid-fire hearing, the last until Monday. Among them were: Photographs showing Turkish officials aboard the U.S.S. Raleigh in 1929 to in

TOKIO, Sept. 8—(%--Japan is ready to demand equality on the high seas. The Island empire, latest addition to the world's major powers, is determined to chuck overboard present naval limitation schemes and insist on parity with Great Britain and the United States. Details of the new policy were not officially announced, but it was learned it has the approval of all the nation's highest authorities. Recommendations of high naval officers were incorporated in the program, prepared by Admiral Mineo Osumi, minister of the navy, and the cabinet gave its unanimous approval. Then Premier Keisuke Okada carried the document to the palace, where it was reported the emperor also endorsed it. Subsequently, Japan's highest ranking admirals, members of the supreme war council, assembled to approve the policy which, it was stated, will guide Japanese representatives at next year's naval conference and a

Geneva, Sept. 7 (#)—Extraordinary police precautions will be taken to protect the French delegation to the League of Nations and also later the Russian delegations, if Russia is elected to the League of Nations, it was revealed today. Local authorities were advised by the central government at Berne of rumors that manifestations were being prepared by Fascist elements against both the French and Russian representatives.

(Copyright, 1934, by Associated Press) VIENNA, Sept. 7.—Rumania’s famed “red-headed woman” tonight was reported ready to retire from the spotlight. Diplomatic quarters here heard that Mme. Magda Lupescu, titian-haired beauty for whom Prince Carol once foreswore his throne, was urging Carol to seek reconciliation with Princess Helen, his former wife. King Carol's friend, the reports said, recommended the reconciliation as the best way to silence growing criticism of Carol. (A group of Rumanian army officers recently was convicted of plotting against the lives of Carol, members of his court and Mme. Lupescu). All the one-time junk dealer's daughter asks as the price of her withdrawal, the reports said here, is the right to reside quietly in Rumania as one of Carol’s royal subjects. The diplomats here understood too, that Dowager Queen Marie of Rumania was striving to untangle

TARANTO, Italy, Sept. 7.—Premier Mussolini declared today that he personally would march at the head of the Italian people if “we are called upon to take the field.” Mussolini made his declaration in a speech to a great crowd which welcomed him on a visit to his naval center. “The Italian people must be ever on the alert,” said Il Duce. “They must be ready for any event!” He declared that Taranto’s functions should be that of a “capital among seafaring nations.” Taranto, he said, should stand as a symbol “to keep the Mediterranean open for the liberal expressions of the commercial and economic will of the people.” He was loudly cheered when he recalled that Napoleon once said the people's bread depended largely on their bayonets.

Geneva, Sept. 7. —(#P)— Louis Barthou, French foreign minister, today failed to persuade Poland, Portugal and Argentina to support Russia’s admission to the League of Nations. He spent the day conferring with delegates representing those nations, the most potent opponents of the Russian candidacy, but admitted afterwards that further negotiations would be necessary. To Sit Today A secret session of the council has been convoked for tomorrow afternoon when the French hope the Russian problem will be solved satisfactorily.

1934-07-27.text: London, July 26. -—- (4) —- Great Britain, France and Italy were represented in authoritative British quarters tonight as satisfied with the elevation of Prince Ernst von Starhemberg to the head of the Austrian government. The three powers, which have undertaken to guarantee the integrity of Austria, it was stated, will abandon any thought of joint action in the Austro-German situation on the ground that the Nazis have done themselves more damage than could possibly be inflicted from any other quarter. Nazi Threat Believed at End. The danger of Nazi control in Austria is definitely past, in the view of British authorities. It is now regarded as unlikely that Austria will make any protest to the League of Nations, or to the powers against Germany in connection with the putsch and the killing of Chancellor Dollfuss. Beyond making separate declarations—such as those of Premier Mussolini and

LONDON, Eng. —(P)— A well-informed foreign diplomat revealed Friday that the massing of Italian troops on the Austrian border was fully approved in advance by both France and Great Britain. He explained it as the most practical means of preventing Germany and the countries of ‘the Little Entente’ from starting to march.

Associated Press Staff writer. As the candidates for office in Texas approached the end of the voters’ long line today, tomorrow the contest will be definitely settled at the ballot boxes for some. Others who fail to obtain a majority vote will hustle back over the tedious campaign trail for another month's canvassing before the runoff primary Aug. 25. Chief interest was in the outcome of the governor's race with six aspirants. Where They Speak C. C. McDonald, choice of Governor Miriam A. Ferguson and her ex-governor husband, James E. Ferguson, will close at Sulphur Springs, where plans were being made for a big showing, with J. K. Brim, chairman of the state democratic executive committee, participating. Attorney General James V. Allred was booked for an address over a statewide radio hookup from Dallas. Lieutenant Governor Edgar Witt planned to have his last say before a homecoming cro

PARIS, July 27 (UP)—France, England and Italy are in complete accord on the Austrian situation, it was learned today, and have agreed they will take the initiative in diplomatic moves, thus to Premier Benito Mussolini, once feared to be a threat and even now with 40,000 men at Austria’s frontier, is entrusted with the task of safeguarding Europe’s peace. France and England, it is understood, have agreed that they will support Mussolini. The Austrian charge d'affaires visited Foreign Minister Louis Barthou today to acquaint him with developments. He emphasized that Austria was seeking to curb Nazi propaganda, and it appeared that this might prove an important policy soon. It was hinted in government circles that the Austrian government might be wise to take advantage of the present diplomatic situation to ask Adolf Hitler, as a sign of good faith, to dissolve the Austrian Nazi legion, lon

LONDON, July 27.—(?)—An Italian suggestion that a joint three-power protest be sent to Germany for that government's alleged connection with the assassination of Chancellor Dollfuss is expected today from Rome. Reports of the proposal brought a reply from a government official that “you must look to Rome for

Tuettlingen, Wuerttemberg, Germany. —(AP)— Twelve persons including seven German and two Swiss passengers, and the Swiss pilot, co-pilot and stewardess were killed today in the crash of a Swiss trimotored airplane. The plane had left Zurich for Stuttgart and Berlin and crashed forty miles north of Friedrichshafen.

BERLIN, July 27 (4)—Chancellor Hitler named the conservative vice chancellor, Franz Von Papen, to become ambassador to Austria today in what was regarded as an astute move to assure the world Germany’s attitude towards Austria is everything that can be desired. “The propaganda ministry announced that Von Papen, now in Switzerland, had accepted the appointment. He has long been a storm center of the Nazi government because of his sharp criticism. In keeping with custom the ap- (Continued on page 5)

VIENNA, July 27 (UP)—The Austrian government today smashed another bold attack by Nazi plotters, who had planned to seize the chancellery and hold the cabinet prisoners. Simultaneously, heavy fighting with large loss of life was reported from the provinces. Scores of arrests were made by police spies, who reported the plotters were infiltrating into the central section of Vienna, disguised in uniforms, and had planned to start their desperate putsch this afternoon or evening. Discovery of the plot brought heavy military reinforcements to the chancellery, and the muzzles of machine guns were trained on the streets from the chancellery windows. Every person approaching the government buildings was stopped and searched, and the utmost precautions were taken by the guards.

1934-07-25.text: WIMBLEDON, England — Sidney R.B. Wood, Jr., and Shields, both of New York, fought back today to give the United States victory in the interzone final Davis Cup tie with Australia. America has gained the right to meet Great Britain in the final or challenge round. Wood completed the victory he started yesterday, defeating the great Jack Crawford, 6-4, 9-7, 4-6, 4-6, 6-2. Then, with the momentum on every form, Shields bested Vivian McGrath, 6-4, 0-2, 6-4. The American came, regarded as hopeless one after the two opening singles matches were lost on Saturday, was revived when the one doubles match was won on Monday. This was seen as a crucial point as experts virtually conceded the doubles to the United States’ side. When play was continued Friday, the Americans were underdogs. (Continued on Page 5 Col. 1)

- LONDON, July 25,--(UP)— Torrential rains, hail, drought and blistering heat brought death to some, ruin to thousands and discomfort to millions in Europe. While Poland suffered floods, there was a heat wave in Germany and the Balkans. In Italy, a torrid sun ruined crops in one province while hail ruined crops in an adjoining one. There was a general heat wave along the Adriatic and a hail storm in Portugal. A cyclone in the Nyireghaza district of Jugoslavia rained down fish. Hailstones killed chickens. There were forest fires in France, Germany and Greece.

LONDON, July 25—(AP)—The Austrian legation confirmed the death of Chancellor Dollfuss and announced that Dr. Kurt Schuschnigg is forming a new government, “They murdered him,” said an attache of the legation, who was half sobbing as he spoke. “One hundred and thirty-four Nazis entered our dear chancellor’s office and one shot him down, wounding him so that he died later.” ROME, July 25—(AP)—Military circles said tonight

WASHINGTON, July 24.—(/P)—The trade commission today formally began its investigation into charges of monopoly and racketeering in the milk industry. Charles H. March, commissioner in charge of the inquiry, said six investigators would move into New England this week, and that another group would be sent to Chicago a little later. March made public copies of a commission resolution showing that the inquiry would delve into virtually every aspect of the industry, from prices, through investigation of charges of racketeering and even gangsterism. The New England phase of the inquiry will be headed by Professor Paul D. Converse, temporarily attached to the commission from the University of Illinois, and A. H. Tackett of the commission's legal staff. They will leave the latter part of this week. The investigation was ordered in a congressional resolution which said monopolistic efforts had b

Vienna, July 24 ()--A 22-year-old Socialist, who said that “My ideals are more important than my life,” was hanged in the Vienna District Prison courtyard tonight as the Dollfuss Government carried out for the first time in months its threat of death for terrorists. Just before the youth, Josef Gert, went to the gallows, a companion, Rudolf Anzhoeck, who was sentenced along with him in connection with a bombing and the shooting of a policeman, received clemency from President Miklas who reduced his punishment to life imprisonment. While preparations for the hanging were under way, police arrested 300 Nazis and Socialists, bringing the total under arrest in a general round-up to 1,500. The other 1,200 had been taken into custody earlier by political police who claimed to have evidence that Socialists, Communists and Nazis had merged into a common front against the Government. Practically

Vienna, July 24 (®)—Two Socialist bombers, convicted by a court martial of dynamiting the Danube river bank railway, were sentenced to death today. The death sentences were the first imposed since Chancellor Dollfuss started his latest drive against terrorists.

Paris, July 24. (AP)—Premier Gaston Doumergue today averted a governmental crisis and the cabinet of France remains intact. The premier came back from his vacation in the south of France especially to smooth over the rift in the government which developed between former Premiers Edouard Herriot and Andre Tardieu, now serving as ministers without portfolio.

Rome—()—Military circles said tonight that Italy has 75,000 soldiers near the Austrian border for use in case of need, A government spokesman declared that no orders for a further concentration of troops had been issued however.

1934-02-02.text: Paris, Feb. 1.--(4)--France rejected Germany's offer of non-aggression pacts and charged Chancellor Hitler's program "would lead directly to an armaments race" in a note, published tonight, which was sent to the German government on January 1. A cool reception likewise was given to British and Italian arms plans which recognized Germany's claim to equality in armaments and proposed that the heavily armed powers do not increase their forces. The French note to Chancellor Hitler stressed "disarmament," official quarters said, while the German, British and Italian projects all emphasized "rearmament." Leaves Door Open France accepted none of Hitler's recent proposals, but left the door open for future conversations, and made a strong appeal to Germany to "associate herself in the indispensable policy of International collaboration within the framework of the League of Nations." The declarat

(By the Associated Press) The demand for dollars and dollar obligations was again feverish in today’s financial markets. The dollar commanded a large premium over the London gold price and the French gold franc. More than $10,000,000 in the yellow metal had started toward New York. Bankers expected the movement would swell to large proportions, and eventually bring the dollar down to its new parity with the gold currencies. Or it might force the European gold currencies off the free gold standard. The New York bond market again experienced one of its busiest sessions, with prices advancing to new highs for more than two years. This market was stimulated by the cut in the federal reserve rediscount rate. But the stock market encountered profit-taking and sagged in spots. Principal prices were narrowly changed. After a slight decline in the dollar in foreign centers, it started to rise, an

| BY the Associated Press | The anticipated depreciation of the American dollar occurred on foreign exchange markets Thursday as a sequel to President Roosevelt’s devaluation plan, but traders were surprised that the weakening tendency was not greater. In London, extreme uncertainty at the opening of the market gave way to a reassurance that financiers attributed to a continued repatriation of American funds, the existence of a favorable American trade balance, and a growing bull- (Continued on Page 7),

London, Feb. 2, UP)—Dr. Desidcrous Papp, noted German scientist, presented to the world today an unlovely picture of mankind, 500,000,000 years from now. In his book on the future of the race—and there may be no future at all, since the doctor says human beings will lose the battle against bugs—Dr. Papp gave the following description of the average citizen: He will be 10 feet tall and have X-ray eyes. His head will be high and massive, but bald as a porcelain bathtub. He will have no teeth, and his lips will be thin and pale. His brain will be able to receive and transmit electromagnetic waves, and his eyes will see through things they weren't intended to see. But he will have long since lost the fight to giant mosquitoes and such, so what's the use anyway?

London, Feb. 2. (INS).—President Roosevelt's new monetary policies scored a major victory to-day when the international gold price, as determined in London, was marked up to a point within a fraction of the $35 an ounce figure which provided the basis for devaluation of the dollar. Abandoning the French franc in favor of the new 59.06 cent dollar as the gold price base, the British gold arbiters advanced the rate four shillings (about $1.00), to 139 shillings, six pence per ounce. This was equivalent to about $34.85 re American currency at to-day’s opening exchange rate of $4.99 1-2 to the pound.

New York—Scramble for securities follows dollar devaluation; bonds highest since 1931 in heavy trading. Washington—Quick use of stabilization fund predicted as market reactions fall short of expectations; Morgenthau calls policy "new 1934 model gold bullion standard." Chicago—Verne Sankey taken to Sioux Falls, S. D., as Robettscher kidnapper. Jury deliberates Touhy's fate in Factor kidnapping. Washington—Senate appropriations committee, by 12-10, votes veterans’ legislation in order, overruling sub-committee; Robinson seeks St. Lawrence vote by Feb. 10. Austin, Tex.—Doctor and wife of university professor found dead in a hotel room; narcotic suicide pact seen. Washington—House group to probe contracting profits with £570,000,000 naval program in offering. Foreign Tokyo—Gen. Hayashi, new war minister, says Japan is “out for peace;” scouts talk of possible war with U.S. Athens—Insull expul

COLUMBUS, O., Feb. 2—Doctors at the Ohio penitentiary hospital have abandoned hope of saving the eyesight of J. T. Jenkins, 44, a London prison farm inmate attacked yesterday by James Prater, 34, a patient in the tuberculosis ward at the farm. Prater, prison officials said, beat Jenkins with an iron window attachment, as he slept, and then poured a caustic disinfectant into his eyes.

LONDON, Feb. 2 (4) — The United States dollar closed today nearly 5 cents to the pound better than yesterday with a quotation of $4.92 to the pound as compared with the overnight figure of President Roosevelt's devaluation of the dollar and his offer to buy gold from the world market created a scramble for gold and gold shares. The early effect here was a heavy demand for French francs with which to buy gold at the current price of the of France and to resell in the United States, thereby netting a big profit for the operators.

1934-03-01.text: Associated Press Staff Writer LONDON, Feb. 28—(AP)—The grim story of a tragedy that rocked Russia and startled the world—the killing of the sinister monk, Rasputin by Prince Chegodieff Youssoupoff—was related by the prince himself today in the tense atmosphere of a crowded courtroom. Attired in conventional English morning clothes, the prince, tall and slim, crisply gave details of the slaying during a hearing of his wife’s suit for $2,000,000 damages against the Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures, Ltd. in which she alleges the film “Rasputin and the Empress” libeled her. “In doing what I did,” said the prince, “I thought I was acting in the service of my country.” He took the stand after the

SPRINGFIELD, Mass., Feb. 28.—(AP)—A bomb containing two sticks of dynamite was hurled at Sheriff David J. Manning in superior court late today by John Kaminski, 26, of New Britain, Conn., who then shot the sheriff in the leg when the contents of the bomb failed to explode. Overpowered by deputy sheriffs and stripped of his clothing, Kaminski was found to have two other crudely constructed bombs, two pistols and two knives in his possession. He wore a steel vest. Court had just adjourned in the trial of Kaminski’s brother, Alexander, and Paul Wargo, of Wallingford, Conn., for the murder of a jail guard when John Kaminski strode down through the room. Confronting Manning, Kaminski pushed a paper-wrapped package at the sheriff's feet. A percussion cap exploded with a weak report. Manning pushed the youth into a seat but before he could act further, the boy whipped out a pistol and fired. As

LONDON, March 1.—(P)—Another picture of the slaying of the grim, black-bearded monk, Rasputin, in the gloomy cellar of the imperial palace at St. Petersburg was drawn today in a London court. Prince Felix Youssoupoff, testifying in his wife's libel suit against a film company, stoutly maintained under cross-examination that he was responsible for the death of the "mad" monk. The defense counsel described Rasputin as a “brutal libertine.” Admitting he had been hypnotized by Rasputin, Prince Youssoupoff said he was not a "professional" killer. He reiterated details of the monk's death by poison, gun and club as Sir William Jowitt of the defense read passages from the prince's book, Rasputin, in which the slaying is described. Jowitt said he was attempting to show the death as portrayed in the Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer film, Rasputin And The Empress, is not historically correct. He asked Youssoup

WARSAW, Poland, Mar. 1. (UP)—Eleven school children were killed and three injured today when a shell with which they were playing exploded at the village of Mozna, 30 miles from here. Eight of the children were killed instantly and three died en route to the hospital. The children found the shell, an unexploded relic of the war, in a field and tried to take it apart. It went off with a shattering roar, plowing a great hole in the ground and hurling some of the children many feet.

Helsingfors, Finland, Mar. 1—()—All fifty of the passengers aboard the Polish steamer Zieszys, dangerously sinking in violent seas, were taken off the stricken vessel early today by a salvage ship. SOS calls were flashed from the vessel and rockets were fired when she struck the rocks last night. Later, wireless messages said the ship was in critical condition, a hole in her hull, the engine room flooded and the engines stopped.

Warsaw, Poland—(M—A heavy wartime grenade exploded in the arms of a railway assistant today, tore him to pieces and killed four schoolboys. Nine children were badly injured. The railroad man had found the grenade in a pond and it blew up while he was removing it, with the children interested onlookers.

MADRID, Mar, 1.—(UP). —The cabinet resigned today, it was officially announced. A crisis had threatened for several days because of division between right and left wing policies among members. President Niceto Zamora at once began consulting political leaders preparatory to naming someone to form a new cabinet.

1934-11-07.text: GLASGOW, Nov. 7.—(UP)—Prof. James G. Gray, inventor of gyro- scopic aerial and marine appliances, died today. Prof. Gray since 1920 had been Professor of applied physics at Glasgow University. Appliances he invented included Stabilizers, artificial horizons, cloud-leveling apparatus, and steering devices.

New York, Nov 7—(i—Leading the Democratic sweep in the home state of President Roosevelt, Governor Herbert H. Lehman was re-elected. The Tammany incumbent, Dr. Royal S. Copeland, was also re-elected on the basis of incomplete, but decisive returns. Robert Moses, the progressive Republican opponent of Lehman, conceded his defeat less than three hours after the polls closed. At this time Lehman had piled up a victorious lead in New York City and gained a surprising lead upstate. Following the lead of Moses, Melvin C. Eaton, chairman of the Republican state committee, conceded the election of both Lehman and Copeland.

BERLIN, Nov. 6.—Miss Lillian Steele, of Hollywood, Cal., spent her 88th day in grim Moabit prison today, because a Nazi friend betrayed her freely expressed confidences and opinions. The charge against the youthful and attractive music student was described as “extremely serious” involving treason or espionage. It was so serious that “American consulate authorities perhaps cannot help her much,” a reliable source said. She is the fourth American involved recently on suspicion of espionage. Her case was made additionally grave by the government’s recent warning that the death penalty is enforceable for spying. Richard Roederer, 40, a naturalized American citizen who came to Germany from Chicago, has been held for more than four months in a Bavarian prison. It is reported unofficially that treason charges may be filed against him because of material found in his notebooks. Miss Helen Lyste

By The Associated Press Paris, Nov. 7.—President Le-Brun cast about today for a new premier to replace Gaston Doumergue, whose fall is imminent. The aged Doumergue, former president who came from retirement to form a government after fatal street riots last February, is expected to give LeBrun the resignation of the entire cabinet.

Paris, Nov. 6 (AP)—A nine months political truce in France ended today as Premier Gaston Doumergue's national government fell, and tonight Paris, recalling the riots that brought “Papa” Doumergue to power, feared new bloodshed. Edouard Herriot, vice premier, and his five fellow Radical Socialist ministers forced Doumergue out, quitting the cabinet after the party had differed with the premier over his program for constitution revision. To Herriot, as leader of the faction that broke the truce, President Albert LeBrun will assign the task of forming another government. Friends said Herriot would accept. He will keep the Doumergue lineup almost intact, they said, leaving out only Henry Lemery, minister of justice, and putting in his place former Premier Andre Tardieu, minister without portfolio under Doumergue, who will serve as vice premier. So vivid was the fear of disorders that the ret

MADRID, Nov. 7.—The government today extended martial law for 30 days after the execution of two men selected as symbols of its determination to suppress disorders. Syndicalists and anarchists went on a general strike in protest against the executions. Reports from Barcelona, one of the trouble centers, were that the strike had failed because the Socialists, leaders in the revolt of October, had not joined it. There the strike was reported to be general only in the textile and metallurgical industries. The strike was called in protest against the executions of Jose Naredo and Jose Guerra Pardo, chosen as symbols of the government's determination to stamp out internal disorders.
ROME, Nov. 7.— (4) —Former King Alfonso of Spain today announced the engagement of his daughter, the infanta Beatriz to the Italian Prince Alessandro Torlonia.

BERLIN, Nov. 17.—United States automobile manufacturers were declared taboo for Germany today by Dr. Hjalmar, the minister of finance. He ordered, in the future, that only two automobiles of each American company be permitted to enter Germany yearly through clearing arrangements with third countries.

1934-01-13.text: RIO DE JANEIRO, Jan. 12 (4)— Seventy-eight persons were reported today to have drowned in floods which followed heavy rainstorms in Brazil and Argentina. The raging Mendoza river in Argentina carried away bridges and washed out highways. In British Guiana five days of heavy rain caused damage estimated at $1,000,000.

Washington, Jan. 12. (4)—President Roosevelt enjoyed a good laugh last night at the diplomatic dinner as he heard a sequel to the American-British negotiations for an exchange of American pigs in return for Scotch whiskey. It seems that R. Walton Moore, assistant secretary of state and a native of Virginia, presented a Virginia ham to Ambassador Lindsey of Great Britain this week. The British ambassador sent back to the assistant secretary of state a bottle of Scotch.

(Copyright 1934 By United Press) LONDON, Jan. 11.—Fascism and parliamentary government were at death grips in all Europe today, with indications that 1934 might prove the decisive year in the struggle between the new and old political orders. Governments of five nations—Austria, Roumania, Holland, Latvia, and the Irish Free State—have taken sternly repressive measures since the new year against Fascists or Nazis, their counterpart. A premier, Ion G. Duca of Roumania, has fallen victim to a Nazi assassin. Roumanian and Austrian prisons are filling with Nazis. Two Austrian Nazis were shot in a fight yesterday with the armed Schutzkorps, Emergency police auxiliary, and Nazi bombings were general over the country. With Nazi Germany as the center of the new Fascist movement, agitation and violence by those who believe the old form of government is doomed have spread over the continent. Exclud
HOVE, England, Jan. 13 —The quacking of ducks in flight was blamed today for an alarm that sent a lifeboat a large flock of ducks must have been mistaken for “a hu-
LONDON, Jan. 11. (P)--Lloyds reported from Land's End today that the American steamer Tripp, en route from Houston to Liverpool, reported a fire in her cotton cargo between decks at 7 p.m. yesterday.

(By Associated Press) PORTSMOUTH, Eng., Jan. 12. Battleship Nelson, “wonder ship” of the British navy, was safely refloated shortly after 6 o’clock tonight after having been aground at the entrance of the harbor for nearly 12 hours.

TOKYO, Jan. 13,—(4)—Japan must prepare and is preparing to defend herself against what appears to be “America’s policy of hostilely encircling Japan by every possible means,” said a published statement attributed today to Vice Admiral Nobumasa Suetsugu, commander of the navy’s combined fleets. The statement was made in an interview published in the widely-circulated monthly magazine, Gendai. Instances of encirclement, the interview cited, were Col. Charles A. Lindbergh’s leisurely flight along the Kuriles in the summer of 1931 and Harold Bromley’s abortive attempt to fly the Pacific in 1930. “I may be mistaken, but I think it is possible they are spying on those islands,” the admiral was quoted as saying. “Some time ago, an American lieutenant hopped off from Japan on an alleged trans-Pacific flight attempt and turned back after flying we don't know where. I think the failure was purpose

Paris—(fA)—Despite two victories wrung from the chamber of deputies over the Bayonne pawnshop bond scandal, the Chautemps government was still on uncertain footing today, obviously shaken by the washing of so much dirty linen in public. Premier Camille Chautemps scored a personal triumph in two smashing votes of confidence, leaving the investigation of the $40,000,000 financial fiasco entirely in the hands of the cabinet. But parliamentary lobbies were inclined to doubt whether he can succeed again in welding a majority to support him across the formidable hurdles awaiting the government in the near future. The chamber gave one vote of confidence, 360 against 229, supporting Chautemps’ opposition to a parliamentary investigation. The second, 376 to 205, was a resolution of faith in Chautemps’ promises to personally investigate the debacle, “sparing no names.” The cabinet’s insecure footi

1934-08-02.text: United Press Staff Correspondent (Copyright, 1934, by United Press) LONDON, Aug. 2.—(UP)—Adolf Hitler, commander in chief of the German army! That epitomized today the thought in the minds of Europe’s leaders as they paid sincere respects to Paul Von Hindenburg. As president the reichswehr (army) is Hitler's. This was regarded as of highest significance to Germany and Europe. Soldiers are traditionally loyal to the constituted government. It was held that Nazism by Hindenburg's death was immensely strengthened. The reichswehr, as viewed in Europe's capitals, is becoming more and more the really dominant force in the state. In the view of many observers Hitler's accession to the presidency may foreshadow a military dictatorship in event the masses slip from his grip. Even during the World War years, when the so-called “Hindenburg pillboxes” on the Belgian coast menaced England, all Britons held the German military leader in great respect.
