BERLIN, Aug. 1 (UP)--Private sources said tonight that President von Hindenburg’s death agony had started. Doctors refused to predict the time of his death, saying he might die tonight or linger a day or two. The doctor was quoted as saying the length of life depended entirely on the strength of Hindenburg's heart.

Vienna, Aug. 1—(T)—With armed opposition crushed, the Austrian government today began a mopping-up campaign against Nazis inside and outside the country. On the one hand was the issuance of an order forbidding salary payments to any public employees suspected of aiding or encouraging the revolt; with the other hand, Austria officially pointed an accusing finger at Germany for the blood which flowed from the Nazis’ attempt to seize the government one week ago today. Sent from Germany An announcement approved by the cabinet said directions to Austrian Nazis were sent into the country several weeks ago from Germany. The plans, which included the possibility of civil war, said Walter Adam, propaganda chief, in a radio address were seized in the shoes of a man arrested in upper Austria. This man confessed receiving $100 for delivering the documents—now partly decoded, Adam said. Included in t

VIENNA, (7). With the hangman’s rope, a sentence of imprisonment and empty pay envelopes, the government of Chancellor Schuschnigg pressed its fight against the defeated Nazi rebels of Austria. Freiderich Wurnig, a Nazi, was hanged at 8 o'clock Wednesday night at Innsbruck, three hours after he was sentenced to death for killing Police Commandant Franz Hickl in that city last Wednesday. Wurnig, the third Nazi to die on the gallows in two days, collapsed when he was told that clemency was refused and had to be carried to the gallows. His crime occurred about the same time that Chancellor Dollfuss was killed by Nazi putschists, but had no direct connection with that outbreak. An alleged accomplice, Christian Meyer, was sentenced to twenty years imprisonment, receiving clemency, it was reported, because he had revealed Nazi secrets to the government. Trial of another Nazi is scheduled to be

- BERLIN. (AP). The field marshal is dead; a corporal takes his place. “The dead president, Paul von Hindenburg, commanded Germany’s armies of 7 million men in the World War; the new president, Adolf Hitler, as a lance corporal, led a squad of four, including himself.

DOORN, Holland (U.P) — Former Kaiser Wilhelm II, who 20 years ago watched from a palace window German troops marching to death or glory, sent from his place in exile at Doorn house Thursday condolences to President Paul Von Hindenburg's son, He wired to the son, Col. Oskar Von Hindenburg, at Neudeck, signing himself, (Signed) “Wilhelm, La The “J. R.” was for “Imperator” — emperor and king. It seemed that Wilhelm was reminding the nation that his abdication in 1918 was forced and that he still regarded himself king of Prussia and German emperor. The court marshal at Doorn house told the United Press that when the news came of Hindenburg’s death all members of the household were deeply shocked,
BERLIN, Aug. 1. Pi—President Paul Von Hindenburg, after increasing general weakness, early today lapsed into a deep coma, according to a physician's communiqué at 5:45 a.m.

1934-04-19.text: (Copyright, 1934, United Press.) London, April 19 (UP)—European statesmen looked with dismay today on the wreckage of six months’ disarmament negotiations and a complete belligerent deadlock between Germany and France. Germany demanded unequivocally the right to rearm. France, with perhaps the strongest cabinet in the Third Republic’s history, comprising among others five former premiers of all shades of political opinion, accused Germany of violation of pledges and demanded guarantees of her security before consenting to any increase in Germany’s military strength. “White Paper.” Great Britain, despairing of efforts to effect a compromise, resorted last night to the ominous diplomatic instrument of a foreign office “white paper” to make the situation public. Aside from a French note refusing to continue disarmament negotiations on the present basis and demanding that the world disarmame

PARIS (AP) — France threatens in a note to Great Britain to scrap all current disarmament negotiations unless she is given something equivalent to the military alliance in the old entente cordiale, it was revealed today. The threat is expressed in a memorandum drafted by Premier Gaston Doumergue and Foreign Minister Louis Barthou. It supplements a previous note in which France expressed a desire for a new arms "limitation conference," on the thesis that present negotiations have failed. The note frankly says it is "useless" to argue about conditions until the full truth of Chancellor Adolf Hitler’s rearmament program in Germany is determined. Germany’s "own revelations" of re-arming, the note says, make it impossible to continue discussion of an arms convention based on the idea of German moderation in rearmament. These revelations are Hitler’s assertions and new German budget figures wh

PARIS, April 18 .P -- Germany was charged today with scuttling arms limitation hopes by rearming in defiance of the world. A strong French note to Great Britain was interpreted as wrecking any chances of an immediate armament agreement and said negotiations are "impossible" since Germany has officially admitted to be rearming her land, air and sea forces.

The rising danger of a new World war was feared in Europe as disarmament efforts reached a new crisis Wednesday. The French government sent a boldly worded note to the British refusing to lay down a single gun if Germany is permitted to rearm. The British issued a "white paper" outlining the futile disarmament efforts of the current year, to date, and designed to absolve Great Britain from blame for the world armaments race now inevitable. The French note blamed Germany for making impossible further direct arms discussions, declaring the Reich's increased war appropriations undermined the good will basis of the negotiations. In Berlin, Ernst Roehm, head of all Nazi military units, declared every man in the Reich was ready to defend the fatherland against "illegal attack." In Geneva, arms delegates regarded France's move as a desperate appeal for security, with war the alternative. Observ

Washington, April 18 (INS)— Great Britain's failure to make any budgetary provision for payment of the debt installment due the United States in June serves to complicate an already well complicated situation. The action is tantamount to notice that the British government plans either to ignore the debt altogether or make another insignificant "token" payment on the $85,670,765 due on June 15. The impression prevails here that she will again resort to the small token payment in order to avoid the onus of complete default. The situation poses a pretty problem for President Roosevelt. He has indicated at various times that he will communicate with Congress before it adjourns on the whole broad question of the foreign debts, but no hint as to the nature of this communication has been forthcoming. Meanwhile, negotiations for amelioration of the British debt, begun last October, are in a stat

Rome, April 18 (AP)—Delegates to the Rome meeting of the world wheat advisory commission went home today with a lot of work done but with a new unsolved problem awaiting their attention when they meet again in London in June. A suggestion of the United States that further reduction of wheat acreage would be necessary to eliminate surpluses among wheat-exporting nations was favorably received last night by representatives of the major producers with the exception of Australia. Interested governments will be asked to instruct their delegates on any definite action they are prepared to take to eliminate surpluses in the next biennium. The commission gave approval last night to the final text of recommendations to governments calling for world wheat export minimum prices, denaturing wheat to render it unfit for human consumption and reducing the amount of flour to be extracted from wheat.

LEXINGTON, Mass., (UP).— On Lexington’s battle green, where the minute men clashed with British troops 159 years ago, citizens of this historic town today formally protested against ‘unreasonable interference by the federal government” in the affairs of a free people. Robert Trask of the selectmen, read a “Declaration of Protest” by 1,200 townsfolk, against: - Federal interference in business, under the guise of promoting social reform and economic recovery, The increase of bureaus, boards and commissions and the delegation of arbitrary powers to such governmental agencies, Extravagant and wasteful expenditure of public funds on unneeded and unproductive projects, thereby creating a constantly mounting national debt. At Washington, a Lexington delegation was to present a copy of the resolutions to the Massachusetts delegation to congress.

Paris — (7?) — A sensational plot by Leon Trotzky to use the February riots to set up his own dictatorship in France by a red revolution was revealed in his party organ, authorities disclosed today. Urged Revolt. A revolution by “an armed workers’ militia” was urged, they said, in a manifesto issued by the exiled former Russian leader after the fatal rioting in the streets of Paris on Feb. 6. “The two forces have just measured swords,” the manifesto said. “War has begun between them. There is no possible peace, but in a fight to the death. In the street, by force, will be decided the future.” Desired Prompt Action. The manifesto urged “a vast workers’ alliance of all proletarian bodies and the organization of a workers’ militia without delay.” As a result of the new disclosures of the political activity of Trotzky, the government was expected to speed its moves for his expulsion, ordered

1934-08-13.text: REVERE, Mass. Aug. 13.—(P)—Nate Siegel, former New England welterweight boxing champion and for ten years one of the most popular fighters in this section, was slain early today by machine gun bullets that zipped through his living room window. He was sitting in the room with his wife, when a window was quietly lifted and the nose of a machine gun edged above the sill. He slumped to the floor, his chest riddled, with the first rat-tat of the gun. His wife ran to the window in time to see three men climb into an automobile bearing Maine registration plates and speed away. She immediately called police. Siegel was 37 years old and began his boxing career, as an amateur, in 1913. Later he became a professional and won honors quickly.
MONTREAL, Aug. 13.—(#?)—The British naval sloop Dragon struck the small oil-burning vessel “Maple Branch” and sank it in the harbor today. The crew of the “Maple Branch” was rescued.

Londin, Aug. 13—(A P)—Argentina will make an important “peace gesture” at the international wheat conference opening tomorrow by announcing arrangements for at least a 15 percent acreage reduction, a source usually reliable said today. This would mark the first time since international negotiations began that Argentina joined a movement to cut production. Last year she agreed not to increase stocks on hand, but declined to join the United States and Canada in pledging a 15 percent acreage cut. Whether Argentina will formally pledge any reduction is doubted. It is understood D. G. Arias, her delegate, will inform the wheat commission steps have already been taken to remove about 3,000,000 acres. This is reported being done by withholding government seed loans and encouraging farmers to plant linseed and maize. Attempts to bring such countries as France, Germany and Italy into extensive ac

"A liar's punishment is not being believed." AUGUST 13—First taxicabs appear in New York City, 1907. 14—Allies capture Pekin from Boxer rebels, 1900. 15—Panama Canal is opened for sea traffic, 1914. 16—British capture Detroit from U. S. troops, 1812. 17—Davy Crockett, great frontiersman, hears the call of the wild. 18—Virginia Dare, first U. S. white child, born 1587. 19—Five witches are hanged at Salem, Mass.

CORK, Irish Free State, Aug. 13. —(iP)—One man was fatally injured and several others were less seriously hurt today in a riot during a sale of cattle which had been seized by the sheriff. The seizure was from two farmers who were unable to pay their land taxes. Neighboring farmers rushed the barricaded gates of the farm where the sale was taking place, in automobiles. Detectives on duty at the sale tried to block the attack, firing revolvers and rifles point-blank. Disturbances also broke out in other parts of the city and the police swung their batons in an effort to restore order.

A settlement of 150,000 pounds, or $763,500 at the present rate of exchange is reported by the London Daily Herald to have just been made by an American film company in the suits brought by Princess Irina Youssoupoff who charged libel in the film 'Rasputin and the Empress'. The case was based on the allegation that the character Natasha, in the film, represented the princess as an adulteress. The settlement, said to constitute the largest sum ever paid in a libel action, includes the $127,000 verdict awarded in the English courts, and will result in withdrawal of $2,000,000 suits in the United States and other countries, says the Herald.

VIENNA, Aug. 13.—(UP)—Prince Gonzalo, second heir to the now non-existent throne of Spain, died today of injuries he received in a motor car accident—victim of his sister's effort to save the life of a bicyclist. Gonzalo, 20, and his sister, the infanta Beatrice, 25, were motoring near Krumpendorf. Beatrice was driving. She saw a bicyclist on the dark road. Swerving, she ran the car into a wall, The prince, fourth and youngest son of the former King Alfonso, died at 12:45 a.m. today of contusions of the stomach and burst blood vessels, 17 hours after the accident. Gonzalo bled to death, and thus fell under the Hapsburg curse of hemophilia from which his eldest brother suffered.

TOKIO, Aug. 12—Had dinner and long chat with Roosevelt in Honolulu, and he gave me practically the same advice that Calvin Coolidge gave Dwight Morrow on Mexico. The president told me, “Will, don't jump on Japan. Just keep them from jumping on us.” Arrived Saturday. Everything peaceful and fine. They want a bigger navy, and I think I will let ‘em have it, for they are going to build it anyway. Yours, WILL ROGERS

1934-10-14.text: London —(#)— Japan will serve advance notice that it intends to denounce the Washington treaty later this year and will reveal its proposals for a new agreement to replace that treaty, when tri-power naval conversations between American, British, and Japanese representatives open here probably next Thursday. Ambassador Tsuneo Matsudaira and Rear Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto are expected to announce that Japan wishes the Washington pact to end Dec. 31, 1936, and will propose a new scheme for naval regulation drawn on the following bases: Parity in principle among the three main powers. A global tonnage arrangement to replace the 5-5-3 ratio now in force, and abolition of the principle of ratio. Reduction, looking toward eventual abolition, of “offensive” ships, meaning big battleships and aircraft carriers; with Great Britain and the United States making the chief sacrifices. Unlimited author

While central states basked in Indian summer, winter struck two icy blows in New England and the northern Rockies. Sections of Maine were blanketed by a fourteen inch snow, only the third fall reported this early in weather bureau annals, while a wintry storm churned New England sea coasts and sent thermometers to shivering depths. The mercury fell to 32 degrees in Boston, a new record for Oct. 13, and numerous New England football contests were postponed because of bitter weather. Snow also fell in the Rocky mountain passes of western Montana, where a dozen motorists were stranded, and the temperature dropped to 32. More snow was forecast for Wyoming and northern Colorado early Sunday.

BOSTON, Oct. 18 (—) Heavy snowstorms and record-breaking cold gripped northern New England Saturday, Some parts of Maine reported a 14-inch snowfall, while Boston shivered in the coldest weather ever recorded for Oct. 13 in the 59 years of local meteorological history. Heavy snow and bitter weather gripped many parts of northern New England. In Aroostook County, Maine's great potato region, conditions threatened the crop, much of which is as yet unharvested, The heaviest snowfall was in Maine, 14 inches. Temperature readings as low as 16 degrees above zero were recorded in the White Mountains of New Hampshire.

PARIS, Oct. 13—A Balkan terror band called the Ustashi, whose agents included a beautiful Slavic ‘gun girl’ and a mysterious ‘doctor’ now being tracked into the obscure corners of Europe, was revealed by French police today as the sinister power that sent its suicide squad to assassinate King Alexander at Marseille. French Cabinet Shake-Up Two of the band’s agents have confessed, police said, they came to France on a mission which “the doctor” told them at Lausanne was to slay the Yugoslav monarch. That bullets from the deadly weapon supplied by the “gun-girl” also slew Foreign Minister Louis Barthou, tore apart the cabinet of France and sent a boy king flying from his school books to the throne of Yugoslavia, combined to make the hunt for missing links in the plot the most sensational Europe has known in a generation. A drastic cabinet shakeup was in progress in Paris following upon the

Paris, Oct. 13.—(4)—France accorded her foreign minister, Louis Barthou, slain at Marseilles, a martyr's burial today, then witnessed the sudden reorganization of the cabinet, so sadly depleted by his assassination and the attendant storm of controversy. Premier Gaston Doumergue eulogized Barthou in public as a man of peace. Then he retired into a special cabinet meeting to face a ministerial war. He made Pierre Laval, his minister of colonies, successor to Barthou as minister of foreign affairs. He placed Paul Marchandeau, a former minister of finance, in the chair vacated by Albert Sarraut, who resigned as head of the ministry of interior because of the assassinations at Marseilles. He replaced Laval as colonial minister with Louis Rollin, a former minister of marine. At the close of the cabinet meeting, which had been attended by President Lebrun, Henry Cheron, minister of justice, cl

MUNICH, Germany, Oct. 13—(AP)—Adolf Hitler's church leaders, Reichbishop Ludwig Mueller and Dr. August Jaeger, commissioner of Protestant churches in Prussia, were called “tools of Satan” in a fiery manifesto issued today by the Confessional synod, which is the backbone of Protestant opposition to Nazi religious policies. The ten commandments are denied by the Reichbishop, the manifesto asserted. Strong denunciations were expected to reverberate tomorrow from many pulpits, possibly evoking equally strong Nazi counter-measures. The next few days are looked to apprehensively by church folk.

MUNICH, Bavaria, Oct. Bu Open revolt against nazification of the German protestant church spread through Bavaria today, constituting the frankest opposition to the Hitler regime since it came into power. Bavarians, intensely loyal to the religion of Martin Luther, appeared determined to defend it, despite their acquiescence to nazification of their private and civil lives. The parish council of St. Matthew's church, from which Bishop Hans Meiser was removed and placed under arrest, issued a sharp protest, assuring Meiser of their undivided loyalty. They were supported by their brethren in Berlin, where the executive council of the opposition confessional synod issued a manifesto bitterly denouncing the methods of Reich Bishop Ludwig Mueller in removing Meiser. “In a church which calls itself a church of the gospel, the gospel is cast out and despotism and lying have gained control,” the

BEVERLY HILLS, Cal., Oct. 11—Say the republicans have turned the coming election into a real “youths’ movement,” just signed up for the coming society hop are those ex-White House coeds, Mrs. Benjamin Harrison, Mrs. Theodore Roosevelt, Mrs. William Howard Taft, Mrs. Calvin Coolidge and Mrs. Herbert Hoover. And nothing is any more gratifying to America than to welcome back into the fold all those gracious and sturdy American women. Funny thing about that White House, it wears down the most hardy of our menfolks, but the women seem to thrive on it. By the way this is Mrs. Franklin Roosevelt's birthday. I wish I knew where she was today. I would send her a message of good wishes, as I am very fond of her. So here is a kind of blanket good wish to all of 'em, and Mrs. Woodrow Wilson. Sure you should all keep up your political affiliations, and public interests. Don't retire we want you to ke

1934-07-04.text: LONDON. (UP). Acting Prime Minister Baldwin caused a stir in naval conference circles by telling the House of Commons that the 1935 parley must achieve some end in view of distressed economic and political conditions. “World conditions,” he said, “in many ways are more difficult than at the time of the London conference and therefore it is more than ever necessary to survey the entire ground before the conference.” The acting prime minister’s statements created some life on the otherwise extremely dull day in naval negotiations. There was no formal meeting of the Anglo-American delegations and there has been none yet this week. There probably will be little activity until the arrival of Foreign Minister Barthou from Paris Sunday.

WIMBLEDON, England, July 4. (AP) — Fred Perry, British ace, eliminated Sidney B. Wood, 6-8, 3-6, 7-5, 5-7, 6-3, from the semi-finals of the Crawford, — not champion from Australia, in the first of the semi-finals.

A rose bush, imported from England in 1788 and planted by Abigail Adams, wife of John Adams, second president of the United States, bloomed recently for the 146th time, says an Associated Press dispatch. The bush in the rear of the Adams family mansion at Quincy, Mass., bears white flowers with a yellow center. It has bloomed each year since it was planted by Mrs. Adams.

BERLIN, July 4.—(4)—Franz von Papen will remain vice chancellor of Germany, the propaganda ministry announced today. As Von Papen’s health has been undermined by events of the last few days, he will shortly take a leave of absence, it was expected.

SALLANCHES, France, July 4. —Madame Marie Curie, 65, co-discoverer with her husband of radium, died today. She was under treatment many weeks for an anemic condition. She preserved throughout her life the best traditions of science. Fame came to her threshold, but she shut the door of her workshop in its face; wealth was hers for the asking, but she turned all money prizes back into her chemistry or gave them to hospitals for cancer research; luxury might have been her lot without reproach, but she spurned it and lived frugally on her modest salary as a teacher in the University of Paris. She consented to take but a mite of the huge debt owed by the world for the Curie gift to mankind in 1898 of a substance which enriched many persons and brought relief or cure to countless thousands of cancer sufferers. She never even owned a speck of radium of her own until 1921 when the women of Ameri

(Copyright, 1934, by the Associated Press) BERLIN, July 4 (Wednesday) (#)—Out of a momentous night conference between Chancellor Adolf Hitler and President Paul Von Hindenburg at the latter's country estate, Germany looked Wednesday for an answer to the big question mark arising from the “second Nazi revolution”—the political fate of Vice Chancellor Franz Von Papen, staunch friend of Von Hindenburg. The future of Von Papen was acknowledged to be of paramount importance to the nation, and, in turn, the world, for if he remained in the government Hitler would be hindered in his reported scheme for tightening the Nazi reins and if he went out a sweeping cabinet shakeup was foreseen. As the vigorous Hitler and the aged president came together, after an airplane dash from Berlin to Neudeck by the chancellor, speculation arose as to whether Von Papen, also the soldier, had told Hitler Tuesday

Edmonton, Alta., July 4—2?—Justice Ives of the Alberta supreme court today dismissed the findings of a jury which awarded $10,000 damages to Vivian MacMillan who charged Premier John E. Brownlee with seduction. The premier announced yesterday that he intended to retire from office as soon as he could clear up pending executive details. The jury also awarded $5,000 to Vivian's father, a railroad engineer of Edson. Vivian, 22-year-old government stenographer, claimed the premier offered her a government position in Edmonton and that subsequent disclosure of their relations over a period of several years caused a suitor to withdraw an offer of marriage. Justice Ives, who is acting chief justice of the supreme court, also refused to confirm the damages awarded to the father. At the time the verdict was returned last Saturday Justice Ives told the jury he did not agree with its findings.

— TOKYO, July 4—()—Admiral Keisuke Okada, regarded as a friend of the United States and a conservative on the subject of military expansion, began formation today of a new Japanese cabinet. Emperor Hirohito summoned Admiral Okada, 66, twice a minister of the navy and for more than 40 years in naval service, to the palace and commissioned him to select a government. It will succeed that of Premier Makato Saito, which resigned because of a financial scandal. Saito approved Okada’s resignation and is working with him in forming the new cabinet. A number of old ministers probably will be retained. Okada likely will follow Saito’s general policies. Although naval circles and militarists are clamoring for a government which will demand equality in ton-

1934-12-12.text: BOSTON, Dec. 12.—(AP)—Explosions ripped out the interiors of four moving picture theatres early today and sent the bomb squads of three Southern New England police departments into action. The theatres, which police believed were wrecked by planted bombs, were: The Majestic and Tremont, in downtown Boston, the Capitol Theatre, Pawtucket, R. I., wrecked the concrete projection booth and tore great chunks from the walls and ceiling of the auditorium. A half hour later the front of the Tremont Theatre, in the center of Boston’s downtown shopping area, was blown out. Then, the lounge of the Majestic Theatre, almost diagonally across Tremont Street, was wrecked. Fourth Show Bombed, Just before 5 a. m. a dull roar came from the interior of the Capitol Theatre, in Lynn, Mass., and investigating officers found the basement rest rooms torn apart. Deputy Fire Chief William P. Connolley of Pawtucke

BEVERLY HILLS, Cal. Dec. 12--The biggest news in the papers today was furnished by the Japanese ambassador. It was pretty strong medicine. He just said that if England and America made Japan mad enough they would go and take all of North China. In other words, if Max Baer, the world’s champion, does anything to me, I am going to jump onto little Shirley Temple and give her a good spanking. Well, if America is just even half smart diplomatically, they will laugh the whole thing off and stall things along till Russia is ready, and just say “Sic ‘em. Tige, he is your meat.” Yours,

London, Dec. 12.—(UP)—The preliminary naval conversations among the United States, Great Britain and Japan will be adjourned this week, it was indicated authoritatively today. The decision of the British cabinet to propose adjournment of the stalemated conversations was communicated to a meeting of the United States delegates for their approval. It was suggested that adjournment might be made in time to enable the American group to leave for home on the Manhattan, sailing Saturday. The present conversations, which have been in progress for two months, may now be regarded as finished, it was stated. The next step appears to be to determine whether the step should be regarded as complete termination or whether postponement should be made at some future date.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 11 () Reiterating its arguments for other defaults during the last two years, Great Britain today told the United States it would not pay its Dec. 15 war debt installment. On the other hand, Finland formally notified the State Department it would pay her installment on the date due. Finland's payment will be $8,228,598. Ten other European nations are expected to announce shortly their decisions whether to pay obligations due next Saturday.

TOKYO, Dec. 14—Regardless of "changes of time, methods of conversations" in naval parleys, present or future, Japan will stand firmly on its demand for equality, it was indicated today. The Japanese position was outlined anew, it was understood, in instructions sent to its delegates in London regarding the possibility of continuing the naval conversations, now deadlocked, to next spring. The Japanese anticipate a breakdown of the London meeting. The spokesman for the foreign office personally believes that prospects for an agreement are remote unless the situation changes. So looking ahead to a continuance of the conversations, the foreign office already has informed Ambassador Tsuneo Matsudaira and Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto on what conditions Japan will engage in further parleys preceding the 1935 general conference. The instructions to the delegates were said to have been four-fold: 1.

SHANGHAI (#) — A young American missionary couple and their two-month-old baby have been seized by bandits in Southern Anhwei province, the China Inland Mission was advised today. The kidnap victims are the Rev. and Mrs. J. C. Stam, both graduates of Wilson College, Chambersburg, Pa. Mr. Stam’s parents live in Paterson, N. J., and Mrs. Stam’s father and mother, Dr. and Mrs. C. E. Ease, live in Holyoke, Mass. Fears were felt also by the mission for the safety of two other missionaries, the Rev. E. A. Kofield and Mrs. Kofield, formerly of Bend, Ore. They are stationed at Tunki, Anhwei, 60 miles south of Tsingteh, where the Stams lived. Mission headquarters here had sent a wireless message to the Kofields to evacuate the bandit-infested region but no reply was received.

| MOSCOW, Dec. 12. — The list of dead from firing squad bullets following the assassination of a high MSt official December 1 stood at 75 today. Nine alleged enemies of the regime were executed yesterday immediately after their conviction by the military collegium of the supreme court. Some 45 'enemies of the people' remain to be tried.

(United Press Staff Correspondent) (Copyright 1934 by United Press) Paris, Dec. 12.—Mrs. Harrison Williams, society beauty of New York, was re-elected by Paris dressmakers today to succeed herself as the best dressed woman in the world. Two other American women were in a list of the 12 best dressed. They are Louise Van Alen Mdivani of Newport and New York and Baronne Eugene de Rothschild of Paris. This year the dressmakers could not agree on the usual 10 best dressed women but expanded their list to 12. They estimated it cost each of the 12 an average of $50,000 a year to maintain their paramount places. The women selected, in order, are; 1. Mrs. Harrison Williams. 2. Princess Sixte de Bourbon Parma. 3. The Hon. Mrs. Richard Norton. 4. Countess de Saab. 5. Begum Aga Khan. 6. Baronne von Drieger. 7. Marquise Nicoletta Visconti. 8. Louise Van Alen Mdivani. 9. Duchess of Alba. 10. Baronne E

1934-05-25.text: By United Press LONDON, May 25.--The United States government today agreed to conduct naval limitations negotiations with Great Britain, designed to prepare the way for the 1935 naval conference and halt a world arms race. Immediately after announcement of the American negotiations, the foreign office said invitations had been sent to Japan, France and Italy to conduct similar separate negotiations with Britain. No replies had been received from them. Ray Atherton, veteran counsellor of the American embassy, visited the foreign office at noon and orally conveyed the American government's readiness to discuss naval armaments, with a view to smoothing the path of the 1935 naval conference, a British source disclosed. An invitation to discuss naval arms was sent to the American embassy last weekend after more than 10 days of cautious preparation in which Britain sounded out not only the Uni

- HESTON, Airdome, London (4) — Capt. George Pond and Lieut. Cesare Sabelli landed here at 12:30 P.M. today after a short flight from Cardiff, Wales. After the fliers had climbed out from behind their smoking motor, Sabelli said the hop today was “almost as tough as the last part of our trans-Atlantic journey.” The Italian flier said they had “a very bad engine” and added: “We barely made it.” A private plane accompanied the “Leonardo Da Vinci” from Cardiff, keeping an anxious watch as the trans-Atlantic fliers creaked along. Captain Pond indicated he was uncertain when they would be able to get away to wind up their flight to Rome and he taxied the plane to a nearby hangar preparatory to starting work on the engine.

Prestwick, Scotland, May 23.— Lawson Little of San Francisco entered the final of the British amateur golf championship this afternoon by defeating Leslie Garnett, Great Britain. Little won at the nineteenth hole in the semi-final round after he and Garnett were all square at the eighteenth. In tomorrow’s thirty-six hole final Little will meet James Wallace, unemployed Scot carpenter, fighting for golfing honor and also for a job. He is now on the dole but has been promised a job if he wins the championship.

PRESTWICK, Scotland, May 25. —(P)—W. Lawson Little, husky San Francisco youth, today gained the final round of the British amateur golf championship by defeating Leslie Garnett of London, by one up at the 19th hole.

Japan's demands for a larger navy as compared to the United States and Britain today disclosed international negotiations in preparation for the 1935 naval conference. London—Japan believed willing to forego battleship equality if conceded equality in light cruisers. Britain seeks to avoid combination with U. S. against Japan. Washington—U. S. and Great Britain expected to oppose Japanese equality demands. Rep. Fred A. Britten urged U. S. to increase Pacific possession arms if Japan insists on larger navy. Tokio—Japan expected soon to outline naval demands in conversation with U. S. Secretary of State Cordell Hull.

PRESTWICK, Scotland, May 25 —(AP)—George T. Dunlap, Jr., amateur champion of the United States, was eliminated today in the semi-final round of the British amateur golf championship by James Wallace, an unemployed carpenter. Wallace won by two and one. Dunlap became the fifth Walker cup player to fall before the hammering drives and brilliant putting of the Scottish youth, whose financial circumstances are so lean that he lives on a dole. The others were H. Chandler Egan, Cyril Tolley, Eric Fiddian and Jack McLean. Dunlap, who was beaten in the semi-finals of the 1933 championship by the Hon. Michael Scott, was out in 35—even par—to be one up. Wallace squared the match at the 16th and then shot a birdie at the 17th to take the lead for the first time. Wallace closed the match at the 17th with a birdie three after Dunlap’s 12-footer for a birdie missed the cup.

LONDON, May 25.—(UP)—The prospect of a duel between former Crown Prince Wilhelm of Germany and Vontschammer Osten, chief Nazi sports commissioner, was reported today by the Daily Herald. Quoting German sources, The Herald asserted that at a recent Nazi sports meeting Osten remarked that Wilhelm was courting public sympathy by attending. Friends of Wilhelm, the story went, overheard the remark and relayed it. Wilhelm sent his card to Osten as a challenge, the Herald asserted, and though Osten declined the invitation to battle, Wilhelm hoped he would change his mind and accept the challenge.

PARIS, May 25 (AP).—Louis Barthou, French foreign minister, today bluntly proclaimed a French policy of “no immediate disarmament of France—no immediate rearmament of Germany.” Barthou openly declared his opposition to the Briand proposal of “partial” rearmament for Germany and the disarmament of France.

1934-02-26.text: BOSTON—(AP)—This city and southern New England, not yet thoroughly broken out of the ice and snow which had bound it since last week's blizzard, today was swept by another gale-borne snowstorm. More than five inches fell during the night and the local weather bureau held no hope the fall would cease before tonight. Then it was predicted colder weather would succeed. Temperatures ranging between eight and 14 degrees above was the bureau forecast. Today's fall, as recorded here this morning, brought the total to 47 inches thus far this winter. Road conditions which already were dangerous grew increasingly hazardous as snow concealed icy spots. Low visibility caused a slowing up of all sea traffic and the gale which veered from northeast to northwest piled up ice floes in many of the harbors, causing damage to the moored fishing fleet. Vermont and New Hampshire did not feel the storm with t

Vienna, Feb. 25. — (P) — Rumors of heavy fighting on the Austro-German border flitted briefly over the telephone wires of Austria today, but boiled down finally to the fact that one Nazi had been wounded and another captured in a skirmish with a border patrol. Reports said two Austrian Nazis, members of the so-called Austrian legion, were trying to cross the border from Germany near Koesen, in the vicinity of Kufstein, when they were intercepted. Both sides opened fire and a lively exchange of shots continued until one of the Nazis got a bullet in the arm. The defending patrol expressed the suspicion the men may have been entering Austria seeking to kill leaders of the Heimwehr. Fascists Fail to Appear Rumors concerning a march on Vienna by the Fascist Heimwehr forces of Prince Ernst von Starhemberg and Vice Chancellor Emil Fey had not materialized, at least up to this evening. Munich, Germany, Feb. 25.—(/P) Adolf Hitler became the de facto sovereign of Germany today when in a ceremony equal in pomp to an ancient Roman triumph, more than one million Nazis throughout the reich swore obedience to him personally. A blare of trumpets announced the arrival, shortly before 10:30 a. m., of Rudolph Hess, Chancellor Hitler’s personal representative, who presided at the ceremony. In Munich's famous Koenig Square, not far from the beer garden where Hitler started his famous putsch, was a brilliant spectacle. Three hundred Nazi banners waved in the light of a warm spring-like sun, while column on column of “amtswalter” or officers of the various political, economic, professional, social and labor organizations constituting separate Nazi divisions marched by. The Oath Precisely at 10:30, reich leaders of the manifold Nazi organizations stepped forward and joined hands with

BERLIN, Feb. 26.—()—More than four million Germans—one citizen out of every fifteen—stand pledged to-day to “unquestioning obedience” to Chancellor Hitler. On the fourteenth anniversary of the founding of the Nazi Party 4,017,000 Nazi functionaries took an oath yesterday to which more than 1,000,000 storm troopers and steel helmeted veterans already had subscribed. Three thousand crowded into the beer cellar in Munich where Hitler launched the party to raise their hands in salute and swear fidelity. Thousands of others repeated the oath simultaneously in other Munich gatherings, while the remaining functionaries participating repeated before radios: “I swear unshakable fidelity to Adolf Hitler and unquestioning obedience to him and the leader designated for me by him.”

By W.F. RR. ANIVAEREYV REM, international News Service Staff Correspondent. (Copyright, 1934, by International News Service. Reproduction in whole or part forbidden). Rome—In the most famous big room in the world, in the room where Duce sits in the Palazzo Venezia, the only other furniture besides the Duce’s desk is a low bookcase be- hind him, and at his right a stand that holds an atlas. The atlas is open to the map of Europe. Beneath the atlas, resting on the crossed legs of the stand, are half a dozen fencing foils. They are not decorative. They are for use. But they have not been used for some time. Signor Benito Mussolini, capo del governo, minister of foreign af- fairs, the interior, war, navy, avia- tion, corporations, chief of staff of the fascist militia, Il Duce, brains and will of Italy, is too busy these days for sport. Always Busy. He sits in a loose black suit, soft white

(Copyright, 1934, by the Associated Press) VIENNA, Feb. 26.—(4)—Forty thousand Fascist heimwehr troops were reported concentrating today along the Austro-German border. The purpose of the movement was not announced. It was rumored that the troops had reached Ried, Braunau and Wels and were resuming border patrols abandoned during the civil war. Another version was that Vice-Chancellor Emil Fey was shifting the heimwehr units away from Vienna to forestall any movement in the direction of disarming them on the pretext of leaving maintenance of the peace to the army and police—now that the Socialists have been eliminated. Excited conjecture was aroused Saturday when truck loads of heimwehrmen were taken out of Vienna for unannounced destinations. The story went then that Fey and Prince Ernst von Starhemberg, leader of the heimwehr, planned a march on Vienna. Some said the heimwehr would sei

PARIS (#) — A mysterious new pretender to the French throne introduced himself to amused Parisians through the medium of posters today. One Theodebold Ascaris Merovee, claiming descent from Clovis and the good King Dagobert, threw his mythical crown in the ring against the Duc de Guise and Prince Louis Napoleon, over the signature of the “Merovingian party.” Harking back to the middle ages when “kings were kings” he disputes the claims of such “upstarts” as the Bourbons and Napoleons. The posters neglected to announce when and where the new pretender would make a personal debut.

Berlin, Feb. 26 (AP)—Prince August Wilhelm, fourth son of the exiled former kaiser, is a good beggar—but a fellow Nazi is even better. Participating in a two-day Nazi drive for winter relief funds, the prince obtained enough contributions to fill ten tin cans in his first afternoon’s “work” Saturday. Jingling 965 marks (about $376), he proudly believed he had taken off first honors. But he was doomed to disappointment. Storm Troop Leader Richter succeeded in collecting 1665 marks (about $650) in the same length of time. Today, with the second day’s beginning efforts still unannounced, Nazi leaders said 45,000 marks (about $17,500) was raised for the needy Saturday and predicted Sunday’s total also would reach that figure. Instead of merely standing on corners, however, the storm troopers held up automobiles and demanded contributions as “ransom.”

1934-09-07.text: Washington — (U.P) — Testimony that the king of England intervened in negotiations between an American munitions firm and the Polish government in 1932 in behalf of Vickers, Ltd., English armament company, was presented today to the senate munitions committee. Louis L. Driggs, president of the Driggs Ordnance and Engineering company, New York, testified that the king summoned the Polish ambassador to London to a conference about the Driggs firm’s efforts to sell arms to Poland. “The king intervened in behalf of Vickers,” Driggs testified. Senator James P. Pope, democrat, Idaho, read a cablegram from Driggs’ Polish agent, dated Jan, 20, 1932. LONDON, Sept. 7. (AP)—A case of liberal party members of parliament began a movement today to force a government inquiry into international armaments trading similar to that now in progress in Washington.

Edinburgh, Scotland, Sept. 7 (Friday)—Unknown to aviation authorities, Prof. Richard U. Light of Yale University and Robert Wilson of New Rochelle, New York, landed safely last night at Granton Harbor, Edinburgh, after a flight from Kirkwall, Orkney Islands, completing a crossing of the North Atlantic. Unannounced, they came to the city and were staying with friends. When they were not reported at the usual landing places in the vicinity of Edinburgh, it was assumed they had made a landing somewhere along the coast, possibly a forced one.

ABERDEEN, Scotland, Sept. 6—(P)—The belief that the black and white races in America will merge into one was expressed today by Lord Raglan, chairman of the Anthropological society, before the British association for the advancement of science in convention here. “Y I believe,” he told scientists, “that before many centuries have elapsed there will not be a single person in America without a certain portion of negro blood,”

LONDON, Ont., Sept. 7 (INS)-- In open defiance of the mobilized strength of Canadian law enforcement services, John Labatt’s abductors have struck again. Over the signature of “Three Fingered Abe,” who signed the original ransom demands, they have sent a second and third letter to Labatt at London. They charge he has broken his “solemn promise” to pay $25,000 for his release, demand fulfillment of the pledge, and in their threats indicate that he...

Temporary lull in serious violence which has left 10 dead and scores wounded. Pennsylvania, however, reports striker sabotage in large centers, 4. Troops guard mills in 14 North Carolina textile against “flying squadrons” of pickets. All North Carolina guardsmen under arms. Virginia police guard border against “squadron” invasions. 5. Sympathy strikes by allied textile industries loom,

Bari, Italy.—()—Italy and France have reached an accord for common action to prevent the rearmament of Germany, it was stated here today by French delegates to the Levantine Fair. It was also stated that the nations have come to a complete agreement on the question of Austrian Independence, and have pledged themselves to common action against the Nazis. French sources said that another phase of the agreement is that Italy renounces her rearmament policy. It was added that Italy will join France in her fight to keep German armaments at the level prescribed by the Treaty of Versailles. It was pointed out, however, that this was not to be interpreted as a renunciation of an impression that the peace treaty could be revised. The French delegates said the accord had been reached August 31, and that as a result a trip by Louis Barthous, French foreign minister, to Rome, is possible. It was sai

HELSINKI, Sept. 5.—I just saw the finest capitol or house of parliament in the world. Brand new. They vote by electric buttons. I got to get home to tell you about it. Not just because they paid their debt, but these Finns are a knockout. Did you know they are the seventh biggest country in all Europe? And eat? Brother, you haven't had a meal till you have one in Finland, Viva Finland Yours, Will...

1934-08-31.text: LONDON, Aug. ue (P)- Hope that the United States will be the next in line is held in official circles today with Russia's entrance into the League of Nations all but assured. Swift action to give the Soviet a permanent seat at Geneva, on a par with Great Britain, France and Italy, is expected when league sessions begin next Friday. Diplomatic quarters recall that old aspirations of league adherents are only half-way realized by this step. The group has held out hope for several years that when the opportune time came both the United States and Russia would join simultaneously. After early years of the league, when aversion to the Bolshevist regime in some quarters was wearing away, the world’s two largest non-members were invariably linked as possible converts. Japan and Germany are now the only other major powers which are not members and they resigned. Informed circles here said they c

TORONTO, Aug. 31.—Edward Chard today was sentenced to imprisonment of 18 months definite and six months indeterminate after being found guilty of attempting to steal $5,000 in connection with the recent kidnapping of John Labatt, wealthy London brewer. Chard was alleged to have demanded the money in a telephone conversation with Hugh Labatt, brother of the kidnapped man.

BOHINSKO LAKE, Yugoslavia, Aug. 31 (The gracious Princess Marina of Greece must limit the trousseau for her wedding to Prince George of England to modest proportions, informed circles said today, unless the British royal family comes to her aid. Marina's parents are almost as poor as the proverbial church mouse. This was cited as further evidence that the affair is a “love” match. Prince Nikolas, 27-year-old Marina’s father, has been jobless and without an income ever since his brother, the late King Constantine, lost the Greek throne 12 years ago. The princess’ mother has given Marina her old pre-war wedding gown to wear when she goes to the altar with George in Westminster Abbey this winter. This nuptial garment, although considered gorgeous in the days of Czar Nicholas in the brilliant court at Petrograd, will require considerable alteration to make it fit Marina, who is taller and mo

TORVO, AUE. 3 (AP)—The Sixty-ton steamer Taian Maru foundered near Antung, Manchuria, today and fears were expressed that 136 passengers and members of the crew were drowned, it was stated by a Rengo (Japanese) news agency dispatch. Twenty-six persons were reported to have been saved. Two vessels named ‘Taian Maru' are listed in Lloyd's register, one of 5,655 gross tons and the other 5,158 tons. Only the larger ship is recorded in the Marine register. This steamer, formerly Hanna Nielsen, was built at Seattle, Wash. in 1916, and is owned by interests in Hashidate, Japan. It left Nagoya, Japan early in July and on July 14, arrived at Yamuke.

HARBIN, Manchukuo, Aug. 31.— Two American motion picture officials were missing today after bandits wrecked the Harbin-Hsinkiang Night Express, killing five persons including three professors of the Imperial University at Tokyo. Those missing were Robert Lurt Dana, Manchukuo representative of the Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Company, and John Johansen, the company’s far eastern manager, believed to be a Danish subject. J. J. Russell, far eastern manager of the company, escaped.

GENEVA, Aug. 31. (UP)—A secret meeting of the League of Nations is planned, probably for September 8, to adopt a resolution declaring that council members are prepared to support Soviet Russia's entrance into the League unanimously, it was learned today. If the resolution is adopted unanimously, it is expected that the Russian government will express its willingness to join before the opening of the annual league assembly September 10. A resolution would be submitted to the assembly inviting Russia to join.

Tokyo, Aug. 31—(AP)—Representations against a proposed trade agreement were sent to Washington and the Philippines by the Japanese government today, and were interpreted as the start of a “Trans-Pacific trade war.” Such a heading was placed over the story by the Japanese financial newspaper Chugai Shogo. The protests claimed the pending agreement between Manila and the United States, which would allow tariff increases on imports into the islands, would discriminate against Tokyo's trade in the Philippines.

BERLIN, Aug. 30 (4)--Fighting for favorable unemployment figures, the government tonight ordered Germany’s younger working women back to the homes and the kitchens. A decree designed to make places for older workers transferred male and female workers less than 25 years old to the so-called “voluntary” labor service, an auxiliary of the labor service. Young women ousted from their jobs were advised they might find new occupations in homes or kitchens. While officials could not give figures as to the number of workers affected by the new decree, it was believed to be large.

1934-10-08.text: By The Associated Press Hongkong, Oct. 8—A sea rescue of 80 men aboard the freighter City of Cambridge hard ashore since Friday in a typhoon was attempted today by H. M. S. Suffolk, a British cruiser. The typhoon has been pounding the City of Cambridge since Saturday. Sixty of the Cambridge’s crew were reported taken off under the utmost difficulties in extremely heavy weather. The Suffolk was dispatched to Pratas Reef at full speed on Saturday from Hongkong. All day Sunday the crew of the Suffolk attempted to enter the lagoon where the Cambridge was beached but their efforts were without avail. The small boats used were in constant danger of swamping in mountainous swells.

MADRID. (UP), The government, crushing the socialist revolt in every part of the country, poured troops into Asturias, the chief remaining center of resistance. Resistance in other parts of the country was scattered and confined to guerilla fighting, although a general strike was proclaimed in Corunna province. The Catalonian secession movement was definitely broken. Don Luis Companys and thirty-one other revolt leaders were under arrest on a warship in Barcelona harbor and were to be taken to Minorca for court martial. Death sentences were possible, although it was believed Companys, if convicted, would be given commutation to life imprisonment. The country was under strict martial law and the government appeared to be getting things well in hand. It was unofficially estimated the revolt cost more than 350 lives, with 1,200 wounded in hospitals and thousands under arrest. Municipal guar
BARCELONA, Oct. 26 Gonzalo Massano, of the Spanish general staff, was killed by rebels Monday while he was riding in a staff automobile.

(Copyright 1934, by the Associated Press) Madrid, Oct. 8. (AP)—A communistic republic was declared at Pardo del Rey in southern Spain today as the rightist Madrid government, fighting for its life, repulsed determined rebel assaults on three government ministries. Reports from Barcelona, meanwhile, said scattered fighting continued through the separatist-minded province of Catalonia. Captain Gonzalo Massano, of the army general staff, was dead of rebel bullets. Extremists still held over Oviedo, northern munitions center. The ministries of war and of communications and the ministry of the interior were attacked almost simultaneously. The attack on the ministry of communications, the third in two days, placed the offices of the Associated Press directly in the line of fire. The building was struck several times by bullets, but the Associated Press office was not touched. Confusion prevail

| Istanbul, Turkey—(#)— Turkey protested to France Monday, charging violation of her territorial waters by two French destroyers which were shot at Saturday by Turkish coastal batteries. The French returned the fire. The skirmish occurred in the gulf of Smyrna. The Turkish protest followed representatives by the French embassy, but it was expected the matter would be settled amicably, since there were no fatalities.

CADIZ, Spain, Oct. 8 (AP)—A communist republic was declared today at the nearby town of Padro Del Rey, as rebels set fire to the city hall and all churches, destroyed municipal archives and killed the mayor and several other dissenting citizens. BARCELONA, Oct. 8 (AP)—Captain Gonzalo Massano, of the Spanish General staff, was shot and killed by rebels today while he was riding in a staff automobile. Reports from Barcelona said three towns on the outskirts of the city, Matorell, Sabadell, and Badalona were in the hands of anarchists. Troops were dispatched to the trouble centers. Reports reaching Madrid also said troops were bombarding Ugo and Gijon, in Asturlas province, where the rebels were reported solidly entrenched. Warships were bombarding Gijon, laying down a barrage for advancing troops. The reports said the rebels were equipped with machine guns and light artillery and were well

Shanghai, Oct. 8.—(/P)—Chinese authorities who discovered the theft of national art treasures valued at more than $20,000,000 from a Peiping museum today launched a search for the persons responsible. The stolen objects were part of the famous collection at the Peiping Palace museum. They included many irreplaceable relics of former Chinese imperial households—priceless objects of gold and jade.

Madrid, Spain, Oct. 8.—Socialist rebels in the north of Spain fought savagely today against the government which concentrated troops and warships against Asturias and the Basque country to put down the revolt. Elsewhere in the country general strikes were in progress, in Seville, Granada and Corunna provinces. Heavy guerrilla fighting was going on in Barcelona, which was occupied by government troops after the collapse of the "Catalan free state." The situation in the northern portion appeared grave. Nearly all communications were cut and the news was difficult to get. Columns of troops were converging on Bilbao and Oviedo to drive out the rebels from those important cities. The cruiser, Libertad, opened bombardment on Fort Murcell near the seaport of Gijon on the Biscay coast after rebels had seized the fort. Rebels opened heavy fire on police headquarters in Madrid at 5:30 p.m. Simulta

1934-09-24.text: NEWPORT, Sept. 24—(P)—Fighting off a closing rush by the British challenger Endeavour, the America's Cup defender Rainbow today scored her third straight victory over the invader in the fifth race of the international yachting series and needs only one more victory to retain the cup. Endeavour was approximately a mile astern as the white-hulled defender swept majestically across the finish line.

Wrexham, Wales. Sept. 24 ()—- The death list in the Gresford colliery disaster was officially placed today at 261, classifying it as one of the worst mine accidents in the history of Wales. Only 15 bodies have been recovered. Rescue efforts, carried on since the original explosion Saturday, were abandoned yesterday when a series of new explosions, fire and deadly fumes endangered the workers. Officials, “with great reluctance,” decided no one was still alive in the workings and ordered the shaft sealed to shut off a flow of carbon monoxide gas.

Aboard U.S.C.G.C. Argo, off Newport, R.I., Sept —(UP)— The United States crashed into the lead for the first time in the America’s Cup series today when Harold Vanderbilt sent his gleaming white Defender, Rainbow, heeling over the line ahead of Tom Sopwith's blue-hulled British challenger, Endeavour, for Rainbow's third straight triumph. The series now stands three victories to two with four wins needed to decide. Rainbow outsailed the challenger from the start. She stepped away into a lead when the Briton’s crew bogged down handling Endeavour's big spinnaker as they glided over the starting line. Vanderbilt outlucked Sopwith on an accident to Rainbow's headrig when her big spinnaker blew out and forced the defender's crew to change sails. Endeavour was caught out of position when the accident happened, and was unable to take advantage of it. It was a grueling, stern chase, after the tur

(By the Associated Press) Wrexham, Wales, Sept. 23.—It was officially stated tonight that 260 miners had lost their lives in an explosion and a fire in the Gresford collieries. Frantic rescue efforts were halted today by a succession of new explosions in the workings. Rescue workers were called from the mine and it was decided to seal the shaft at the top. Up to noon volunteers continued in relays to venture into the murky gas-filled mines. Fifteen bodies were recovered yesterday, but no more were found. The rescuers had almost reached by midday the branch of the workings known as the “Dennis Main” where their mates or the bodies were believed to lie. Colliery authorities were trying to check the names of men entombed in order to attend a football game.

WREXHAM, Wales (4) — The explosion and fire in the Gresford collieries, taking 273 lives and perhaps more, was admitted today to have been one of the worst mine disasters in the history of Wales. The bodies of the victims — all except the 12 that have been recovered — lie half a mile below the surface, under the ground on which many of their cottages stand. Rescue efforts, carried on since the original explosion Saturday, were abandoned yesterday when a series of new explosions, fire and deadly fumes endangered the workers. Officials, “with great reluctance,” decided no one was still alive in the workings and ordered the shaft sealed to shut off a flow of carbon monoxide gas.

Aboard U. S. CG. G. Cutter Argo, off Newport, Sept. 24 (?)-——The American defender Rainbow, profiting by sail and halyard trouble aboard the British challenger Endeavour and overcoming an accident to her own spinnaker by fast sail-handling, today led the way around the 15-mile mark in the fifth race of the America’s cup series. She rounded the turn at 12:18 PM, some 1400 yards ahead of the British boat. Endeavour rounded the turn at 12:23, five minutes after the defender. Rainbow had covered the 15-mile leeward leg of the 30-mile leeward-windward course in 1 hour, 38 minutes to pile up a long lead over the unlucky challenger.

WREXHAM, Wales, (U.P)—Laborers sealed the Gresford mine today, entombing 261 men, victims of an explosion and fire Saturday. Total deaths were 271. Relatives identified bodies of ten men brought to the surface.

Warsaw—()—With four out of 20 big balloons in the Gordon Bennett cup race landed safely today, advices from Riga, Latvia, said one of the balloons had been shot at by Soviet border guards. It was not known which was the balloon. The Polish air club was informed of the reported incident, but could give no further information until the matter is investigated. There was no confirmation of the report from other sources. Advices from Moscow said the United States navy balloon, piloted by Lieutenants C. H. Kendall and H. T. Orville, had landed safely on the boundary between Estonia and Russia. The two balloonists proceeded to Leningrad. Two German entries and the Czechoslovak balloon “Bratislava” were reported down safely. The German “Stadt Essen” and the “Van Opel” both landed on Estonian soil. The latter came to earth near Kudina, and was slightly damaged in the descent. The Bratislava lande

1934-08-09.text: SOUTHAMPTON. (CP). Andrew W. Mellon, former Secretary of the Treasury and former Ambassador to Great Britain, arrived here en route to Scotland for a vacation.

LONDON, Aug. 9 (7) — Yes, there is a Loch Ness monster—if you accept the findings of Sir Edward Mountain. The reported presence of the mysterious marine animal in the Scottish lake had piqued the public curiosity for many months, along with the curiosity of Sir Edward, a leading businessman. Determined to get to the bottom of the thing, he organized a party of 20 watchers. After peering into the lake for a month they report that beyond doubt Loch Ness harbors some “unidentifiable monster.” Seen 21 Times Sir Edward's watchers agree the creature has a relatively small head, shows “two or three” humps when near the surface, and moves with such remarkable speed through the water, he, she or it creates a big wash. During the month, the patient observers said, they were rewarded 21 times by glimpses of the animal. But they are not yet fully satisfied and will continue the look-out for another

WASAGA BEACH, Ont., Aug. 8 — James Ayling and Leonard Reid, aviators with no experience at long-distance flying, sped eastward tonight determined not to land until they see the minarets of Baghdad, 6300 miles away. They set out from here to break the existing nonstop flight record of 5657.6 miles, a feat requiring them to cross the Atlantic Ocean, all of Europe and Asia Minor. Various Canadian communities reported that their big, black, twin-motored biplane was making steady progress. It crossed over Quebec at 10:12 a.m., eastern standard time. If nothing goes amiss and the fliers’ calculations prove correct they should reach their distant destination in 65 hours, at 10:12 p.m., eastern standard time, Friday. Their plane, “The Trail of the Caribou,” was heavily loaded as it taxied down the beach of Georgian Bay. Plane, fuel, provisions and aviators weighed a total of 7350 pounds. There w

BERLIN, Aug. 9.—(4?)—Germany's Protestant pastors and church officials will be required to take an oath of fealty to Chancellor Hitler, just as Nazi storm troops and members of the regular army did last week. This important step to secure Hitler's uniform support following his assumption of the powers of president was announced by Dr. August Jaeger, Nazi commissioner for Protestant churches. Jaeger at the same time explained new rules to be imposed by the national synod today which will deliver the Protestant church bag and baggage into the hands of Reichsbishop Ludwig Mueller, Hitler follower, and the German Christians (Nazi churchmen.) No Independent Thought They appear designed to stamp out independent thought and action by the clergy, a considerable number of whom have strongly opposed Mueller’s dictatorial steps toward achieving the Nazi program of a unified Protestant church. Muell

BERLIN, Aug. 9—(UP)—The Hitler government today decreed amnesty for minor criminal offenders and political prisoners. The amnesty was declared in accordance with German custom as a mark of generosity to make memorable the accession of a new chief executive. Political offenses made subject to amnesty include the following: 1. Slander against Hitler or the government, 2. Acts against the National prestige, provided they were not deliberate or malicious, 3. Acts resulting from overzealousness in the Nazi cause.

Geneva, Aug. 9, W.P)—Six American college girls, arriving in Geneva today, told how they unwittingly helped the Austrian government crush the recent Nazi uprising in Styria. The girls actually helped to build a bridge that had been demolished by Nazis, thus permitting detachments of Heimwehr troops to cross and surprise a group of Nazi rebels. In the group were: Josephine Burnee, an instructress at Mt. Holyoke; Mary White, of Evanston, Ill., who has just been graduated from Wellesley; Muriel Farnum, of Providence, R. I., and Elizabeth Hallett, of Hackensack, N. J., both of whom were in this year's graduating class at Mt. Holyoke; and Vivienne Espeut, of Passaic, N. J., and Betty Buenting, of Pittsburgh, Pa., both Mt. Holyoke undergraduates. The girls had left Vienna on July 27 by automobile, and were en route.

'HALIFAX, N.S., Aug. 9. (4)—— Flying for Baghdad and a new non-stop distance record, James Ayling and Leonard Reid dared fog and rain over the North Atlantic today. There was no word from their black-winged biplane, “The Trail of the Caribou.” It carried no radio. Fog swallowed up the twin-motored ship shortly after the government steamship Aranmore reported sighting it off Flat Island, in the Strait of Belle Isle, at 2:24 p.m. (Eastern Standard Time) yesterday. At that point the fliers were starting the most dangerous lap of their grueling projected 6,300 mile flight. Weather reports indicated rain but there were fresh west winds to help the plane along. Huge Supply Reid and Ayling left Wasaga Beach, Ontario, 650 miles from the coast, at 5:12 a.m. yesterday, carrying an enormous gasoline supply and food for four days. Should they conquer the Atlantic, they planned to turn at the Souther

(BY Associated Press) BERLIN, Aug. 9—Between 8,000 and 10,000 prisoners in concentration camps throughout Germany will be granted their liberty by a sweeping amnesty decree announced today by Chancellor Hitler. The step was taken in memory of the late President von Hindenburg. (By Associated Press) OSSINING, N. Y., Aug. 9—Tonight, unless Gov. Lehman interferes, Mrs. Anna Antonio, 75, will be executed in the electric chair for the murder of her husband for insurance.

1934-05-18.text: London—(A)—Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, declared today that Great Britain is not pledged to “preserve” the integrity of China and will not participate in direct sanctions against Japan or any other power in other parts of the world unless the United States gives its full cooperation. Reaffirming Great Britain’s determination to “respect” China's political integrity, Sir John asserted: “Great Britain has never signed any treaty to preserve the territorial integrity of China.” Referring to the demands of some of the opposition that Great Britain embark on a policy of economic sanctions in an effort to forestall any war, the foreign secretary declared: “Economic sanctions cannot be applied without the risk of war. (Continued on Page 7. Col. 1)

New York, May 18—(P)—Cass Gilbert, 74, architectural father of the skyscraper, is dead. The noted architect, who pioneered for beauty in commercial buildings and was regarded generally as a leader of his profession in America, died unexpectedly yesterday in a hotel room at Brockenhurst, England, while on a pleasure trip. A heart attack caused death. Mrs. Gilbert and their daughter, Mrs. Charles Morgan Post, were at his bedside. Gilbert designed the Woolworth building in New York—the world’s tallest for many years—and numerous other notable structures. Born in Zanesville, O., he attended public schools at St. Paul and then studied architecture at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

London, May 18 (AP)—Charges that Japan is planning to carve out of China "Manchukuo number two" were made on the floor of the House of Commons today. The charges were aired by Sir Stafford Cripps during a debate on foreign affairs. Asserting that Great Britain, through vacillation and weakness of policy is helping the Japanese hand in China, he suggested cooperation of Great Britain, Russia and the United States in a program aimed at halting Japanese expansion in the Far East.

Associated Press Foreign Staff GENEVA, May 17. (AP) — Led by Great Britain, seven nations today lined up in a movement to end the Chaco war by an embargo on arms and ammunition and called up the rest of the world—particularly the United States and other American republics—to join them. Support of the British project to shut off supplies of war from Bolivia and Paraguay by the United States was regarded here as essential to an effective embargo. Hugh R. Wilson, observer at the League of Nations council, promised to ask for instructions. Capt. Anthony Eden, British lord privy seal, brought the issue before the council, with a proposal that 17 nations be asked to agree. Chicago, Ill., May 18.—(?)— Whoopee trips John Factor, the international speculator, is rumored to have taken from the DeKalb county jail at Sycamore, Ill., took on an international aspect today. Franklin D. Overmyer, counsel for the British Crown, said he would take the matter up with Sir Ronald Lindsay, the British ambassador at Washington. Factor, who is held pending his removal to England on stock fraud charges, was rumored to have made several night trips to Chicago as well as to have gone to a beer party at an Aurora, Ill., hotel while awaiting the issuance of a presidential order to surrender him to the British government. Both Sheriff Isaac George of Sycamore, who was reported to have gone with Factor to Aurora last Tuesday night, and Factor himself made denials of the reports.

By Saited Press DUBLIN, May 18.—Cesare Sabeili and George R. Pond, trans-Atlantic flyers, will fly to Rome tomorrow, they announced today. They said they would return here in two weeks and complete plans to fly back to New York from Portmarnoct strand.

LONDON, May 18 (UP).—The British government is “closely studying the question of sanctions” [penalties] against Japan, Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, told the house of commons today. Sir John was replying to Labor and Liberal critics of the government policy towards Japan. They charged it was one of vacillation in the matter of curbing Japan’s expansionist activities. Although he admitted economic penalties by other nations as a means of curbing Japan had been studied, Sir John nevertheless recalled that neither the Lytton commission’s report nor the League of Nations had urged sanctions. They recommended conciliation with Japan. John, who was “Jake the Barber” before he became a millionaire, is supposed to be in jail twenty-four hours a day at Sycamore, Ill. A United States commissioner ordered him there because he is accused of taking $7,000,000 from British investors in an unlawful manner. It was somewhat more than disconcerting, therefore, when the British crown attorney — here, Franklin R. Overmyer, announced that he had evidence that Factor and his supposed jailer, Sheriff Isaac George, were seen Wednesday night in an Aurora hotel, sociably drinking with two attractive young women. 1934-04-20.text: WASHINGTON, April 19. Pi— President Roosevelt is as ready as ever to renew war debt discussions with Great Britain, but a view today from an official quarter held little hope for such a parley or any immediate successful settlement. Authorities here noted a demand in London for writing down Britain’s debt, made by Sir Herbert Samuel, liberal leader, during a debate in the house of commons on the new budget. For the third successive year it omits any provision for debt payment. Policy Not Altered, It can be stated that Mr. Roosevelt has not altered his policy “that a debtor may at any time approach a creditor with representations concerning the debt and ask for readjustment.” The chief executive now has under consideration a message to congress on the war debt situation. It is generally expected that he will confine himself to a factual report on the existing status. In less than two mont

WASHINGTON, April 20—(4)—The White House made known today that President Roosevelt feels that the answer to the silver remonitization problem lies in formulas presented at the London economic conference whereby all nations would fix definite reserves of silver in the ratio to their gold supply. This could bring for the first time in history, a fixed ratio throughout the world between gold and silver. It was proposed at London that nations establish silver reserves up to twenty-five per cent of their gold supply. As a result, this informal exposition of the president’s attitude, it was believed today he would stand pat against a mandatory silver legislation this session.

LONDON, April 20.—(UP)—Great Britain will stand by treaties affecting China and will resist any attempt to override them when and if they are challenged, official quarters asserted today. Discussing statements by a Japanese foreign office spokesman regarding Japan's far eastern policy, a commentator said that treaties involved were primarily the nine power treaty, and the four power bankers’ consortium concerning China. The Japanese spokesman had emphasized Japan's intention to ensure far eastern peace in its own way. The official view as explained today indicated Great Britain would not openly disclose its reaction until a test case arose. It was said there had been no exchange of views with other governments since the Japanese “hands off” statement. European newspaper comment on statements from Tokyo showed general anxiety. Official quarters, however, said that no communication was planned with Premier Mussolini, originator of the Italian plan, on the subject. (The Italian plan was communicated by Premier Mussolini to Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, Jan. 4, and suggested a partial rearming of Germany, re-formation of the League of Nations, and supervision of the armaments of other powers. The possibility of an accelerated European armament race and the collapse of prospective disarmament parleys was noted. They were spurred by the French contention, stated in a note to London, that Germany's increased defense appropriations have smashed all hope of disarmament through bilateral negotiations, Authoritative sources said Britain is determined to continue efforts to obtain at least a limited arms convention. Reverse Position The definite French position was revealed in a British government "white paper" released after London had received from Paris a demand that a full disarmament conference resume discussions where they were dropped last fall, Delegates to the conference left Geneva, after the withdrawal of Germany from both the parley and League of Nations, hoping to find agreement through diplomatic exchanges. This was made known in an authoritative statement by the foreign office. The British government, sponsor of the two-party arms talks and believer in the policy that oriental peace lay in the province of the United States, was jolted by both documents. British statesmen conferred about the newest disarmament impasse and decided the only remaining hope lay in a return to Geneva conferences, as France demanded. In Berlin the French note was called a “bitter disappointment to all who had an agreement at heart” and was said to “destroy every positive foundation that has been built up since last fall” and to disavow France’s own standpoint giving Germany equal treatment. 1934-02-12.text: BEVERLY HILLS, Cal., Feb. 10. --In England statistics show that over 50 per cent of criminals commit suicide before being caught, knowing what will happen to them when they are captured. Can you imagine ours doing that, look at the publicity they would miss. But, are our courts and judges changing, for didn’t this Sankey commit suicide in jail? Maybe this is liable to start a fad. Monday France wanted communism, Tuesday they wanted a king, Wednesday an old man told them go home and have a good drink of wine, take a nap, and forget it. Just about what will satisfy any mob. Yours.

New York, Feb. 11 (Industry). led by the automobile makers, began to catch up with the boomlet in retail and wholesale distribution during the past week in business. Retail trade was given a further fillip by the extremely cold weather, breaking records for low temperatures in many sections of the country. And many of the wholesale markets, reported Dun and Bradstreet, "now actually are booming," as preparations are rushed for an active Easter trade. But it was in industrial operations that the most striking gains were noted last week.

(Copyright, 1934, by U. P.) LONDON, Feb. 13. (UP)—British trade has begun to feel the full force of United States commercial competition, sharpened by the depreciated dollar, a survey showed. Whatever Wall Street bankers may think of President Roosevelt’s monetary policy, British manufacturers and exporters are convinced the “baloney dollar” is not “baloney,” after all, and that it has been helping the United States to overtake its British commercial rivals. After the pound sterling went off the gold standard in September, 1931, British trade benefitted substantially and foreign buyers were quick to take advantage of the cheaper prices of British-made goods. Since Washington followed suit by abandoning the gold standard in April, 1938, the United States has steadily been recovering lost trade from Britain. LONDON—British opinion, viewing the Far East and central Europe as potential danger points for war, was concerned primarily today in keeping Great Britain out of any war and strengthening naval defenses in event of a threatened armaments race. Despite hostile statements by influential men in Russia and Japan, and a dangerous atmosphere of suspicion, fear here of a Russian-Japanese war this spring was somewhat diminished. Siberia and Manchukuo remained, however, in British authoritative opinion, as the greatest menace to peace. In Europe Germany was watched. The more or less pacific German Nazi penetration in Austria, that has brought Austria to the verge of an appeal to the League of Nations, was regarded here as an inevitable development.
