| VIENNA, Feb. 12—(AP)—All the armed forces of Austria were mobilized today to crush a nation-wide socialist uprising. Socialists rose up against Austria today and at least forty-two persons were killed and fifty seriously wounded in the first skirmishes of the day. The government sent the artillery into action after sixteen were killed in a battle at Socialist headquarters. The battle began when government forces attempted to raid the headquarters, and Socialists tried to beat them off with hand grenades. Police and soldiers replied with machine guns. Linz was a center in the suddenly strife-torn nation. The Socialist party called a nationwide general strike. Chancellor Dollfuss replied with a declaration of martial law in Linz and Vienna.

Vienna, Feb. 12—From 82 to #: persons were reported killed in pitched battles between socialists and authorities today as socialists proclaimed a nation-wide general strike and the government threatened with martial law. Martial law was enforced in Vienna, Graz and Linz. The fighting in the last city accounted for 31 to 41 of the dead, while one was killed in Vienna. A large number were reported wounded and it was reported that 60 of these might die of their injuries. The deaths in Linz came in two pitched battles. In the first, machine guns and bombs were used, killing 16. In the second, the government forces used artillery and 15 to 25 more were reported killed.

| PARIS, Feb. 11—(#)—A nationwide general strike against “Fascist reaction” began at midnight tonight, with 1,000,000 workers ordered to stay idle for 24 hours, stopping virtually all activity in France. The strike was a warning to the government of Premier Gaston Doumergue against the adoption of dictatorial methods. It was anticipated to be the biggest in scope since the strike of 1919. Anti-Fascist Moves. The start of the strike found most of France asleep after a day of national anti-Fascist demonstrations by socialists and communists, but the walkout was expected to make its effects felt soon after daybreak. More than 100,000 workers in the Paris region alone were called out. The tie-up in city transportation threatened to prevent non-striking workers from reaching their offices and factories, which have been ordered picketed by strike leaders. 1934-12-08.text: OSLO, Norway, (4)—Arthur Henderson, president of the League of Nations disarmament conference, is to be awarded the Nobel peace prize Monday, it was learned here today. Henderson, it was understood, would be the official guest of the British legation during his visit here.

Geneva—()—A secret session of the council of the League of Nations formally approved today the dispatch of an international army to patrol the Saar territory prior to its plebiscite Jan. 13. The council voted to issue official invitations to Great Britain, Italy, the Netherlands, and Sweden to contribute contingents to the armed forces. The army, officially designated "the international force," will be placed under the direction of the league’s Saar governing commission, the president of which is the dynamic Englishman, G. G. Knox. The size of the army and of the national negotiations for its support was left to a special committee composed of representatives of Argentina, Italy, Spain, Great Britain, the Netherlands, and Sweden. Great Britain assumed the role of neutrality. The Balkan conflict brought before the League of Nations Council, amid talks of war, resolved itself into a dispute over revision of the post-war treaty, by which Hungary, as well as Austria and Germany, lost territory in formation of the new Danubian state. Hungary has been charged with a terroristic campaign such as the assassination of King Alexander of Jugo-Slavia, designed to revive the treaty. The line-up before the council today: France, through Foreign Minister Pierre Laval, placed herself squarely on the side of Jugo-Slavia, which brought the charges of terroristic responsibility against Hungary. Yugoslavia-Hungarian tension increased, Italy and Ethiopia clashed in Africa, Britain, Japan and the United States found themselves still far from an agreement for naval limitation. Paraguay and Bolivia fought doggedly on. GENEVA:—Eduard Benes, Czechoslovak foreign minister, warned the world the Little Entente—Yugoslavia, Rumania and Czechoslovakia—would fight if its alliance is attacked. Hungarian and Yugoslav delegates hurled bitter charges at each other as the responsibility for King Alexander’s assassination at Marseille Oct. 9 was discussed. HONOLULU, TT. H. (UP)—Picturesque blue Japanese sampans and rusty old tramp steamers were drawn into the search for a lost airplane Star of Australia and its crew of three today by promises of rich rewards. The Australian government, through W. P. W. Turner, British consul, offered $5,000 to the person rescuing Capt. Charles T. P. Ulm, eon Skilling and George Littlejohn. A $1,000 reward also was offered for recovery of authentic wreckage of the plane or of the bodies of the men who had tried to cross the Pacific from California to Honolulu and who came down at sea when near their goal. All authorities have abandoned hopes of finding the men alive. They had a land type plane, which, according to expert opinion, would remain afloat only 48 hours after landing on the ocean surface.

QUEENSTOWN, IRISH FREE STATE — UP The America steamship Cold Harbor arrived today after heaving to for 48 hours in a hurricane during which seaman Roy E. Hall of Seattle, Wash., was swept overboard and lost. Seaman John J. Hodson, of Philadelphia, was saved by chief officer O'Connor, who pulled him back as he was about to be swept away. Hall and Hodson were working on deck when a great wave struck the ship. One lifeboat was torn from its davits and other davits were twisted. The Cold Harbor is en route from New York to Liverpool.

GENEVA, DEC. 8. (AP).—France dramatically resumed discussion of the Central European conflict before the League of Nations council today with a declaration of Foreign Minister Pierre Laval that “in this grave affair France stands beside Yugoslavia.” Amid an impressive silence in the council chamber, Laval said that in striking the cavalier King Alexander “it was peace they sought to strike.” “It was the work of Alexander they sought to destroy,” he continued dramatically. “This work subsists and depends upon us as the council of the League of Nations to see that peace shall not be placed in peril.” Laval, co-operating with the great powers of Europe in efforts to prevent the Yugoslav-Hungarian dispute from becoming a major crisis, demanded that the League of Nations justify the high confidence reposed in it. 1934-01-01.text: Fatalities in English Fog London, Jan. 1—(AP)—Four persons were killed and several injured in accidents as a cold, gray curtain of fog lowered itself over England’s greeting to the New Year. Road, rail, air and water travel were paralyzed. The Manchester races were cancelled.

BERLIN, Dec. 31 (4)--Some 400,000 mental and physical defectives in German asylums and prisons, or still at large, come under the sterilization law with the new year. This sweeping law promulgated by the Nazi government is the most sensational of 26 major measures which go into effect January 1. Under threat of 150 marks (approximately $55.50) fine, medical authorities in prisons and public and private hospitals, nurses, midwives and welfare workers have been racking their brains to hand in as complete lists as possible of all hereditary incurables in their care so that the 1,700 new eugenic courts with power to decree sterilization can begin work at once. WASHINGTON, Jan. 1.--Congressional leaders were agreed today that the pledge of almost a third of the Senate to stand for free coinage of silver has thrust bimetallism forward as the major issue before the session beginning Wednesday. CALLS CONFERENCE President Roosevelt will meet tonight at the White House with eight or more Democratic chieftains from the Senate and House, and from this conference new majority plans for the session may emerge. Observers feel the talk almost certainly will turn at one point to the silver question, and the administration's thus far guarded attitude made clear. A growth of inflation sentiment behind the silver drive, congressional leaders say, has made the money question so predominant a note as to overshadow even such important and perplexing issues as taxes, appropriations, and conflict over President Roosevelt's recovery program. Woodin as secretary of the treasury and appointed Henry Morgenthau Jr., now acting secretary in his place. The resignation of Woodin on account of his physical condition was made effective today. Morgenthau has been serving as acting secretary for more than a month. He was sworn in as secretary at the White House. The new secretary is an intimate friend of the president. He is a resident of Dutchess County, N. Y., the home county of the president. Morgenthau is a graduate of Cornell University and for several years has operated a farm in Dutchess County and has run a farm paper. He came to Washington with the president and served first as governor of the farm credit administration. Woodin. Morgenthau had been acting secretary several weeks while Woodin was on leave attempting to regain his health. In a letter to the president dated around the middle of last month, however, Woodin said he felt it best that he resign. “Happy days are here again.” That was the keynote of the nation’s New Year celebration as it welcomed the year 1934. For the first time since 1920, Americans in more than a score of States were able to greet the New Year with a cup of cheer, no longer outlawed by prohibition law. New York's celebration, reflecting those in many parts of the nation, was the gayest since prohibition became effective. Times Square was a bedlam of noise and cheer as the clock struck 12. The nation’s capital observed a comparatively quiet New Year’s Day celebration. President Roosevelt departed from the usual custom and held no White House reception. Chicago greeted the New Year with revelry as thousands crowded into Loop streets to welcome 1934. SANTA MONICA, Cal., Dec. 31.—A few hours from the time I am penning you these lines, the old year will be going out, and it looks like she is going out without a single mourner. And at that, it hasn’t been a bad old year (as years have been going lately). In fact, in years to come, when all these professors switch from economists to historians, they are liable to label 1933 as the historical year, the year of the big switch, from worse to better. So, so long '33. Panics come every 20 years, so we will be seeing you in '53, Yours, WILL ROGERS.

1934-01-26.text: CHICAGO, Jan. 26. (UP)—John (Jake the Barber) Factor today retold the story of his kidnapping from the witness chair as Roger Touhy and three henchmen, charged with the abduction, watched with smirking smiles. In a low husky voice the colorful promoter, who is charged with bilking English investors of millions of dollars, told how he was seized by a desperate gang early in the morning of last July 1 as he returned from the Dells, a northeast side roadhouse, with a party of friends; He could identify Touhy, Factor, and Gloomy Gus Schaeffer. He did not expect to identify the fourth man, Edward McFadden. Factor was the first of the witnesses produced by the state in the trial in the heavily guarded courtroom to identify the defendants. SHANGHAI, Jan. 25 (#)--Two hundred and sixteen men, women and children were burned to death or drowned the night of January 21 when the Chinese steamer Weitung caught fire in the Yangtse River, belated reports revealed today. The vessel exploded and sank a few minutes after the blaze started. Only 34 persons escaped.

Paris—(#)—The resignation of the entire French cabinet was reported imminent in the lobby of the chamber of deputies today after Eugene Raynaldy, minister of justice, quit the government because of the Bayonne pawnshop scandal. Premier Camille Chautemps was quoted by the socialist delegation in the chamber as saying he would go to the Elysee palace of President LeBrun tonight to resign.

Rome, Jan. 26. (AP)—A strong Japanese protest will be made tomorrow to Premier Mussolini personally against a recent article written by Il Duce on the Far East, it was learned today. Japanese Ambassador Hajime Matsushima, who will deliver the protest verbally, on instructions from Tokyo, also will voice his government’s objection to a speech by Marquis Giacomo Medici Del Vascello in the Chamber of Deputies. It will mark the first Japanese protest for a long time, despite the fact that a campaign has been waged in the Fascist press against Japanese economic aggression. This aggression, it is asserted, has seriously injured the Italian silk and cotton goods market.

Paris, Jan. 26.—The cabinet of Premier Camille Chautemps was believed on the verge of a break-up today under the stress of the Bayonne bank scandal. Friends of five cabinet members said the ministers favored either the immediate resignation of the cabinet or its fall “arranged” on some minor point, rather than a further swelling of charges against the government.

Paris, Jan. 25 (/P)- Two prominent Frenchmen sought “satisfaction by arms” today in a huge football stadium, fired four small and ineffectual bullets at each other, and stalked away, still angered by a dispute over the Bayonne pawnshop scandal. Deputy Andre Hesse and John Beineix, a lawyer and editor, faced each other at 32 yards in the Parc des Princes within the shadow of gaunt goalposts. Both wore black, but eschewed the top hats prescribed by tradition in favor of derbies, which they tipped before the encounter. Thirty seconds, doctors and friends were present at the duel, which occurred before 20,000 empty seats. In Raw Wind Uninvited newspapermen and photographers scaled the walls of the stadium, on the outskirts of Paris, and watched from a distance, shivering, like the others, in a raw morning wind.

NEW YORK, Feb. 21—(UP)—A cold wave descended today on the Eastern Seaboard, still sorely crippled by the most paralyzing snowstorm since the celebrated blizzard of 1888. Temperatures of close to zero complicated efforts to "dig out" in the hardest hit regions as the frigid blasts sheathed snow piles with thick crusts of ice. The cold wave extended as far south as Florida. At least 20 were dead as the result of the storm, 12 in the New York metropolitan area alone. Thousands of others were suffering from injuries and exposure. Transportation and communication facilities, which in many sections were completely demoralized, were slowly returning to normalcy. A lashing gale in New England which caused postponement of the initial flight of the Newark, N. J., to Boston leg of the service Tuesday was slackening. Better weather also was expected at Las Vegas, Nev., where an eastbound plane was stormbound. At the Newark airport planes were leaving on schedule for the west and the south. The first plane flown to Cleveland had made the return trip safely. Though the marriage means not only renunciation of his right of succession to the throne but abandonment of his royal status, Sigvard intimated firmly, and with some heat, that he is a prince only by the accident of birth and that his romance is his own idea and a good one. The worst winter weather in years clamped down over the northeastern seaboard yesterday, crippled ships on the Atlantic, left several hundred thousand New Yorkers without transportation for hours, tied up the railroads throughout New England, delayed the air mail and caused deaths and intense suffering. Sixty mile an hour winds put coastwise shipping in distress. Thick ice locked doors in New York City and made skating rinks of streets. The New York Stock Exchange opened an hour late, and thousands of workers were much later at offices, shops, and factories. Snow Drifted Whistling gales swept snow ranging in depth from six inches to a foot into drifts that blocked trains between Boston and New York, and in many other sections of New England. Ships were battered by high winds, ice floes, and pounding waves. Lives of crews aboard were endangered. Although some delays could not be avoided,

A paralyzing blizzard in northeastern United States and a severe cold wave in other sections last night left more than a score of deaths in its wake. New York City, which saw its transportation system tied up for hours, reported nine deaths attributed to the weather; New England, which was covered by a snowfall as deep as 2 inches in some places, had a like number; Pennsylvania reported six, Colorado one, and 10 women lost their lives in the burning of a home for indigent at Brookville, Pa. Covers Wide Area The northeastern storm swept over a wide area, crippling ships on the Atlantic, tying up rail transportation throughout New England and delaying the air mail. The weather forecast, however, held prospect of relief today in most of the most severely storm-assailed regions. Sixty mile an hour winds put coastwise shipping in distress. * London, Feb. 21.--(4)--A royal envoy failed today to convince Prince Sigvard of Sweden that he shouldn't marry a blonde German movie actress. The actress is Fraulein Erka Patzek. The prince’s father, Crown Prince Gustaf Adolf, objects to the marriage on the grounds that she is a commoner. So Count Folke Bernadotte, himself the husband of an American girl, the former Estelle R. Manville, boarded an airplane and plunged into the family argument. He spent a good deal of time trying to find the headstrong prince and his beautiful fiancée, only to discover today that the royal young Swede has a very headstrong mind of his own. The count left town and headed back to Sweden, figuratively washing his hands as he went. The young couple after dodging parental envoys, diplomats, and interviewers several days, quietly went to lunch in a cozy west end restaurant. Still the prince refused to discuss

‘By The Associated Press. BERLIN, Feb. 21.—Chancellor Adolf Hitler called in person today at the British embassy and it was believed in political circles the German leader had been won over to the British disarmament plan. It was the first time Hitler has set foot within a foreign embassy since he became chancellor of Germany. There was every indication that Captain Anthony Eden, lord privy and British disarmament expert, now can proceed to Rome for conversations with Premier Mussolini with the backing of Chancellor Hitler. Hitler was accompanied by Konstantin Von Neurath, foreign minister; Rudolf Hess, minister without portfolio, and Paul Joseph Goebbels, minister of propaganda and public enlightenment. The call was regarded not only as a friendly gesture but as a sign of mutual determination to achieve an Anglo-German understanding on disarmament. After lunch, Hitler and Von Neurath re

1934-12-03.text: | London, Dec. 3.—(Monday)— A Warsaw dispatch to the London Daily Express today said 10 red army officers had been executed as the result of a plot to assassinate all Soviet leaders at the same time. The dispatch said, in reporting the assassination of Sergei Kirov, that the OGPU had discovered the plot and that the 10 officers were put to death within the hour. Sixty others were rounded up, the dispatch continued.

London, Dec. 3—(4)—Many private appeals were made today for clemency for a 62-year-old mother, condemned to death for the “mercy slaying” of her imbecile son. Mrs. May Brownhill, a frail woman of Leeds, received the sentence because she gave her son Denis 100 sedative tablets and gas. Her plea that she had nursed Denis for 30 years and killed him only when she learned she would have to undergo an operation which might cost her life, thus leaving him without her attention. The jury recommended mercy but the judge carried out the strict British law. A leader in the campaign to save Mrs. Brownhill from death is George Lansbury, labor leader in the House of Commons, who said “I most fervently hope that the Home Secretary (Sir John Gilmour) without any delay will recommend that His Majesty grant a free pardon.” Mrs. Brownhill’s attorney plans to apply to Sir John for a reprieve. Many persons

Leningrad, U. S. S. R., Dec. 2.—(AP)—The assassin who shot to death Sergei Kirov, right hand man of Joseph Stalin, was identified today by the government as a 30-year-old Russian, formerly employed by the Workers and Peasants Inspection Bureau. His name was given as Leonid Nicolieff. He had been employed in the Leningrad branch of the inspection service. The announcement, made by the commissariat of home affairs, contained no statement concerning a motive of Nicolieff's political affiliations. His identification as a former communist worker, however, was considered by many to minimize the possibility of a wide-laid external plot against the Soviet. Mourning Black-bordered red flags fluttered at half staff throughout the Soviet Union today in honor of the slain Kirov, member of the all-powerful political bureau of the communist party, while communist workers were clamoring for vengeance a

(Copyright 1934 by United Press) Leningrad, Dec. 3—(UP)—Joseph Stalin, supreme Soviet ruler, was here under extraordinary guard today to mourn his comrade Sergei Maronovich Kirov and to supervise an investigation into the motive for his assassination. Political police, investigating Kirov's assassination by Leonid Micoliev, 30, former government worker, sought to find the slayer’s motive and to learn whether he had accomplices in a plot that might have serious ramifications. Kirov, secretary of the Leningrad communist party and a member of the all-powerful political bureau of the communist party which, under Stalin, directs the Soviet’s destinies, was shot and killed Saturday afternoon at headquarters of the Leningrad Soviet. Micoliev entered the headquarters with false identification papers. He fired one shot at Kirov from close

LENINGRAD, Russia, Dec. 3 (UP).—Ruthless extermination of enemies of the Soviet regime was proclaimed today because of the assassination of Sergei Maronovich Kiroff, one of the high leaders of Communist Russia. A decree of the tzik (parliament) was made public, ordering prompt execution of persons found implicated in the assassination. The tzik assembled immediately after the assassination on Saturday and passed a resolution evoking the most important weapon of the dictatorship of the proletariat—the summary "red terror" under which many thousands of potential foes of the government faced extinction before firing squads in the early years of the revolution. The resolution precluded the possibility of delaying executions by appeals from persons found guilty of terroristic acts. The foreign office was instructed to carry out the sentences of the "highest measure of social protection" witho

Rome, Italy, Dec. 3.—(U.P.)—An accord was reached by France and Germany today on the Saar mines, making a long step toward settling what has been generally regarded as the greatest existing menace to peace in Europe. The agreement involves the terms under which Germany will reimburse France for the mines after next month's plebiscite decides whether the territory will remain under control of the League of Nations or pass to France or Germany. It was revealed that under the agreement Germany is pledged to pay France 900,000,000 francs (approximately $59,400,000) as soon as possible. Part will be paid in cash and the remainder in coal and supplies.

ROME, Dec. 3—The French and German governments today signed a complete agreement on all questions concerning the Saar basin territory. An official communique on the agreement, which was reached through the two nations’ respective ambassadors to Rome, said the agreement included not only the financial question of the territory but all other points. It is to be presented Wednesday to the League of Nations council, the body charged with the government of the mining area. The pact was signed by Count de Chambrun, ambassador of France, and Ambassador Ulrich von Hassell of Germany. Both French and German circles announced the agreement had been achieved in a most conciliatory manner but details of the settlement were not immediately announced. It was learned on good authority, however, that the principal plank in the settlement is that if Germany wins in the Jan. 13 plebiscite she agrees to pa

Melbourne, Australia, Dec. 3. (UP) — Thirty-one persons were known dead today and thousands were homeless in towns throughout the Melbourne area as the result of the worst storm on record. The dead included the crew of the steamship Coramba, which foundered. Rain fell for 30 hours and there was a 50-mile an hour wind. Food was dropped from airplanes to the destitute in isolated areas.

1934-11-05.text: Melbourne, Australia, Nov. 5.—(P)—K. D. Parmentier and J. J. Moll of the Netherlands were officially declared the winners of the England to Australia handicap race prize money today upon the expiration of the 16-day limit for the contest, While C. W. A. Scott and T. Campbell Black were the actual winners in the handicap as well as the speed race, the rules precluded their taking both prizes.

PARIS, Nov. 4.—(#)—Renewal of civil strife such as that which took 28 lives last February was feared today by authorities as the result of Premier Gaston Doumergue's forthcoming challenge to parliament on Wednesday. The aged premier, guardian of French political truce, has challenged the chamber to a quick finish fight over constitutional reform, the issue which already has produced a dangerous split in his cabinet. Troop Movements, Rumors of troop movements into Paris to prevent an outbreak of rioting like that which brought Doumergue into power were circulated tonight despite a denial from the war ministry. Officials indicated the police would be reinforced with mobile guards from the outskirts of the city, since one of the worst political crises in recent French history is forecast if Doumergue is defeated in parliament. It is to be a one-man battle against political opponents for the

Paris, Nov 5.—(P)—A wave of popular support for Premier Gaston Doumergue in his fight for constitutional reform rolled across France Monday, indicating that stubborn deputies and senators might be swept into line. Socialist quarters, however, predicted that the cabinet crisis would result in greater civil strife than did the “bloodiest days of February.” Those days of rioting cost 28 lives. Doumergue started popular sentiment surging Sunday with a broadcast appeal in which he asked the voters to judge between him and the lawmakers who seek to block the reform. The venerable premier had threatened weeks ago to take his case to the people. Doing it, he made such an impression that some quarters foresaw the breaking of party lines in parliament voting as the result of public pressure. Popular support of the statesman was believed so great that all parties except the socialists and communist

GENEVA, May 5 (U.P.) Charges that Japan is fortifying the South Sea Islands which she holds under mandate of the League of Nations were aired today at a meeting of the permanent mandates commission of the League. Nobubumi Ito, Japanese delegate, was questioned about allegations that the ostensible “public works” and harbor enlarging program of Japan in the Pacific paradise really mask naval bases and military fortifications. The charges have been made before and stoutly denied by Japan. Suspicion was aroused by the fact that in 1926, Japan spent 94,145 yen in harbor improvements in the islands, but in the next year the sum jumped to 3,097,896 yen. The islands comprise a vast area in the Pacific north of Australia, lying strategically between Hawaii and the Philippines. They include the Marshall, Caroline, Pelew and Marian groups with a population of about 70,000. Britain and Australia ho

Geneva, Switzerland, (INS)———For the second time in a little over a year, the charge was voiced today that Japan is utilizing her mandated possession in the Pacific to strengthen her naval forces. Members of the League of Nations mandate commission said that they had received information that Japan has been constructing naval bases in four islands of the Ladrone group, shoring out strategically.

Geneva, Nov. 5.—(U. P.)—The League of Nations permanent mandates commission insisted today that Japan give a satisfactory explanation of the expenditure of large sums of money for harbors and airports on the South Sea Island, which she holds under mandate. Charges that Japan is fortifying the isle were aired and insistence on a satisfactory explanation came after the members of the mandates commission questioned Nobubumi Ito, Japanese delegate at length concerning the island. Ito denied the island was being fortified.

BERLIN, Nov. 5, (#). — From various sides, efforts were under way today to effect some sort of a compromise between the warring Protestant church factions of Germany. These efforts were brought into bold relief by a demonstration at Nurnberg yesterday. Thousands of Protestants defied a prohibition against open air meetings to cheer Bishop Hans Meiser, released from arrest and reinstated as Bishop of Bavaria. Bishop Meiser had been arrested by orders of Dr. August Jaeger, recently deposed adviser to Reichbishop Ludwig Mueller, and the tumultuous ovation given his homecoming was in open disregard of the ban on open air meetings imposed by Julius Streicher, Nazi leader of Nurnberg. One of the most active men in seeking a compromise is Dr. Arthur Kinder, leader of the German Christian church, who was chiefly instrumental in eliminating Jaeger from the church cabinet.

MESSINA, Sicily, Nov. 5 (INS)—Thirteen persons were buried alive when a huge mass of earth broke loose from a mountain and poured down in an avalanche, crushing a house in the village of Ordonaro. All are believed to be dead, and rescue attempts were abandoned as useless.

1934-03-22.text: LOS ANGELES, March 21—(AP)—A book salesman who allegedly wouldn't sell books was divorced here today by Miriam Jordan, blonde, blue-eyed English actress. Miss Jordan told the court she tired of the “laziness” of her husband, Joseph Davis, more than four years ago and had left him to come to Hollywood. The film capital had thought she was single and got a real surprise a few weeks ago when she filed the divorce suit.

(By The Associated Press.) Dublin, Irish Free State — President Eamon de Valera incensed at the Irish Free State senate rejecting a bill to prevent the wearing of political uniforms, suddenly introduced a bill in the Dail, or the lower house, today to abolish the senate.

TOKIO, March 22. — Japanese Authorities, checking the toll of the holocaust of fire which swept the city of Hakodate yesterday, officially announced that 660 persons had been killed and 460 injured. These figures were not regarded as the final casualty list, however, since the checking was still in progress, hampered by a driving blizzard and general chaotic conditions. The Government announced that 27,000 victims of the fire were being cared for in 32 refuge camps, hurriedly established. There are 90,000 homeless, the official announcement said, and nearly 25,000 homes and buildings have been destroyed. The fire was virtually extinguished today, only a few smouldering embers remaining of the raging blaze that practically destroyed the largest city in Japan north of Tokyo and the chief port of the island of Hokkaido. Quick-piling snowdrifts which settled over the ruins of 25,000 homes wh

DMABRVYALH, Japan, (UL) — Deaths from burns and injuries tonight continued to increase the heavy casualty toll already set officially at 1,000 deaths in the destruction by fire of a greater part of this thriving seaport city. Police estimated that 300 additional have died since the fire in which 700 are known to have perished. Two thousand others were injured or missing. HAKODATE, Northern Japan (By Radio via Tokio) — (UP) — A terrific fire which razed this northern port during the night, killing more than 1,000 citizens, had virtually burned itself out today. The major part of the city of 80,000 persons lay in ruins. When the flimsy Japanese houses had burned like tinder and the business section of sturdier buildings had been destroyed, damage was estimated at more than ten million yen. Homeless refugees numbering approximately 120,000 fled to the hills in the utmost terror and confusio

MUNICH, Germany, Mar. 21 — (AP)— The aid of a loan-granting capital has been enlisted today by Chancellor Adolf Hitler to carry out a billion-mark anti-unemployment campaign. Twenty-one words in his address announcing a labor program — including the construction of highways, land reclamation, and the building of ships and houses — made the hearts of marriageable frauleins beat faster as they envisaged wedding bells ringing for them. Said the bachelor leader of Nazi Germany: “In order to enable 200,000 more to enter upon matrimony, some 150,000,000 marks (about $60,000,000) will be set aside as matrimonial loans.” The provision was made, however, that the bride-to-be has been engaged in a gainful occupation at least six months prior to the contemplated marriage and that she promises not to resume gainful employment as long as her future husband's earnings exceed 123 marks (about $50) a mo

PORT SAID, Egypt. Port authorities redoubled their lookouts for Samuel Insull's cruising haven in the belief that unless he has changed his plans the former financier will reach the Suez canal before long. As darkness fell over this picturesque gateway to the mysterious east, officials had no information regarding the whereabouts of the little Greek freighter, the Maiotis, on which the one-time utilities executive is fleeing American writs. The tardiness of the grimy 'Maiotis led to the general opinion that the fugitive has no intention of putting in here.

Paris, March 22, UPI—New sensational revelations of Alexandre Stavisky's political influence were threatened today as 3,500,000 war veterans—already disgusted with alleged official corruption—threatened a Fascist march on Paris. Tomorrow the National Confederation of War Veterans, representing 3,500,000 men, will meet here for a three-day congress. In a speech wirelessed throughout the country from the Eiffel Tower last night, Maurice De Bartal, secretary of the federation, warned that the congress might decide to offer the government its choice between accepting suggestions for reform or facing direct action by the veterans.

It was believed that the woman had “escaped” to the United States, the announcement said. Police described her as suspected with Marjorie and Robert G. Switz, young Americans held here since December. Believed Leader of Gang It was recalled that several days ago British secret service men were quoted as saying that a mysterious woman whose name they never had been able to learn was the real leader of the gang and despite all their efforts had operated in and escaped from England. 1934-08-04.text: PARIS, (UP).—The United States and Great Britain were reported today to have been in communication regarding the possibility of naval cooperation in the Pacific in event the 1935 naval conference failed. Though the reports were not confirmed, they came from informed naval quarters here. It was said that the discussions concerned defense plans from Australia to Alaska, based on the possibility that Japan would insist on maintaining its claim to equality, causing the great powers to engage in a building race. New Defenses Planned. The United States, it was said, if the agreement were concluded would proceed with defense plans in Alaska and the Hawaiian Islands, while Great Britain would proceed with plans to build a second giant naval and air base at Port Darwin, on the Australian continent, and simultaneously complete the great Singapore base. Presumably both bases would be available to t

LONDON Aug. 3—(AP)—Europe’s mighty nations gazed on a little man today and asked: "What now?". Governments, figuratively a bit pale, wondered where Germany was headed under the rule of Adolf Hitler, erstwhile alien, house painter and army corporal. Uncertainty is noted in all of Europe's capitals. First foreign-born ruler in Germany's history—he is a native of Austria—Hitler has shown so far that he can make the grade. He has climbed to the point where he holds the peace of the continent in his hands, Europe believes, now that he has become what one Berlin newspaper called “executive of the divine will.” France In Quandary Dread for the future underlies French comments on the question whether he will seek a goal of friendship or assume a belligerent attitude. Pope Pius XI is disturbed by fears that a sudden change in German rule may add to Europe's myriad difficulties. Mussolini, Italian

ROME ()—Air-minded Italy rejoiced today at Premier Mussolini’s decision to keep pace with England, the United States and other countries in an aircraft construction program. The decision was made known through an appropriation decree published by the official gazette allotting 1,200,000,000 lire (about $100,000,000) for “extraordinary expenses” connected with Italy’s aerial defense. A similar decree providing for the expenditure of 354,000,000 lire (approximately $28,320,000) for the already large naval construction budget also found sympathy in ardent Fascist ranks.

DUNKIRK, France, Aug. 4. — The rigors of the French foreign legion proved too much in advance today for Lord Edward Montagu, 28-year-old Englishman, and he changed his mind at the last moment after flying here to enlist. Instead of going to the hot sands of the Sahara, he returned to London, and presumably, the haven of marriage. “Five years is really too long,” said the young nobleman, who had sought—and found—adventure in North America. Montagu said he thought of enlisting because of “difficulties” of his family. He was to have been married today, he said, and after telephoning his fiancée near London decided to return. Lord Edward, the second son of the Duke of Manchester, was one of several persons held as material witnesses in the investigation of the slaying of Captain Walter Wanderwell, world adventurer aboard a yacht, at Long Beach, Cal., in 1932, just before the start of a South

LONDON, Aug. 4 (UP)— Twenty years ago today Europe really went to war. The horror with which sober minded Europeans had contemplated hostilities gave way to the human thrill at the tramp of soldiers’ feet to the blare of military bands. Statesmen who signed the war defended their action before cheering parliaments and expressed their determination to fight to the last able bodied man, until they alone should be left to hurl defiance from their rostra at the foe. Men, women and children of warring countries became to each other fiends of another world.

' Foochow, China, August 3. (INS) — British and Japanese warships were reported on their way here to-day to protect their nationals in the current outbreak of violence here by Chinese Communists. The Communists are now grouped a distance outside the city, and cut off from all supplies, are reported to be in desperate need.

BERLIN, Aug. 4 (4%.--Adolf Hitler, seeking to consolidate his position as the “New Napoleon,” summoned the all-Nazi Reichstag today to assemble Monday for a memorial service to the late president, Paul von Hindenburg. Chancellor Hitler’s address, a chancellery spokesman intimated, will be of a political nature, with a direct eulogy of von Hindenburg reserved for the funeral services Tuesday at Tannenberg. Because of the unusual circumstances of his coup d'état, whereby he merged the offices of president and chancellor, Hitler was believed to be intending to seize the occasion to justify his assumption of the powers of a monarch. Hitler's last appearance before the Reichstag was July 18 when he defended to Germany and the world his bloody purging of Nazi ranks June 30. Displaying a lively interest in world reaction to the situation, Hitler is understood to be especially desirous of having

(By The Associated Press) BERLIN, Aug. 3. — The events of the last few days, coupled with an historical parallel, caused some observers to wonder tonight whether Germany is headed again toward monarchy—with Adolf Hitler on the ‘throne instead of a Hohenzollern. Hitler's assumption of the chief executive's powers and functions after the death of President Paul Von Hindenburg and then demanding a plebiscite seemed strikingly in line with the practices of Napoleon III. Napoleon Elevated On November 7, 1852, Napoleon was elevated by the senate from the presidency to the throne, and five days later a plebiscite put the stamp of popular approval on the action. The association of ideas with Napoleon put the thoughts of some speculative minds on this question: Is the presidency of Hitler (even though he hasn't the title) but the forerunner of a “volkskaisertum” or rule by the people's kaiser, wh

1934-03-05.text: NEW YORK, Mar. 5 (PE) — Plans to file as quickly as possible thousands of suits estimated to run into many millions of dollars against every United States and British theater that exhibited the picture 'Rasputin and the Princess' were reported today by legal authority close to Princess Youssoupof. The princess today was awarded $126,800 damages in a similar suit tried in London. Almost 300 of the suits have already been prepared. Filing had been delayed pending a decision in the key libel suit against Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer in London. The London suit was on the ground that the honor of the princess had been impugned by one of the incidents of the film. An injunction will be sought against exhibition of the picture in Italy, it was said.

By The Associated Press Galway, Irish Free State, Mar. 5—Free-for-all fighting between ‘Irish Blueshirts and their opponents disrupted a mass meeting yesterday attended by 10,000 persons welcoming Gen. Eoin L’Duffy, United Ireland Party leader. Three hundred civic guards rushed the crowd several times, freely using their clubs, before order was restored. Walls were levelled and trees cut down by Blueshirt opponents to prevent them from reaching the meeting, but after 600 of them arrived by roundabout routes from all parts of the country.

LONDON, Mar. 5. — Princess Trina Youssoupoff was awarded a verdict of 25,000 pounds, about $126,000, in her suit against the Metro-Goldwyn Mayer Film company, whose movie picture “Rasputin, the Mad Monk” she charged had libeled her.

London, Mar. 5 (INS)—Princess Zina Youssoupoff today was awarded a verdict of 25,000 pounds (about $125,000) in her suit against the Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Film company whose movie, “Rasputin, the Mad Monk,” she charged has libelled her. The jury deliberated for less than two hours. The princess had asked damages of approximately $2,000,000, alleging that the character “Princess Natasha” in the film was intended to represent her and led the world to believe that she had actually been seduced by Rasputin, where she did not know him. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer's defense was that Natasha was an entirely fictional character. This was stressed in a closing statement to the jury delivered today by Sir William Jowitt, former attorney general, and chief of defense counsel. The trial brought out a dramatic recital by Prince Youssoupoff, nephew of the murdered Czar Nicholas, of his part in the actual slayin

Los Angeles, Calif, March 5.-(U. P.) William Peet, 87, founder of the soap manufacturing company bearing his name, died last night, after a long illness, at his home in Beverly Hills. A native of England, Peet came to Kansas City, Missouri, in 1862, and in 1872 established his company.

Villach, Austria, Mar. 4 (#).— Police were required to restore order today when a crowd of Austrian Nazis shouted “Heil Hitler!” and hoisted Swastika banners at the conclusion of an address by Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss. Thirty of the Nazis were jailed. The little chancellor, bitter foe of Nazism, had just assured a mass meeting that a new constitution would replace the recently discarded one of the republic within a week. It will be based, Dollfuss said, on the Pope's encyclical “Quadragesimo Anno” and will be maintained inviolate against any efforts of “those who follow false prophets.” Despite recent events, Dollfuss said, his government is not filled with a desire for revenge, but stretched out “a friendly hand” to everyone. “Christian love must unite all sections of the populace,” the leader asserted. “Our youth must be trained in the Christian spirit, but at the same time every

By United Press MUENSTER, Germany, March 5.—Dieudonné Costes, French transatlantic aviator, landed at Loddenhülde airport Saturday on his way from Paris to Copenhagen. Bad weather caused the landing. Costes apparently was unaware of the anxiety felt for him over the weekend.

“ATHENS, March 5.—Police today notified Samuel Insull, Chicago utilities man, that he must leave the country tomorrow. Insull, whom the United States government seeks to extradite in order that he may be tried on charges concerning the collapse of his utilities interests, was isolated at his hotel and said he was gravely ill. The foreign ministry on Saturday notified the ministry of interior, which is the police authority, that Insull must go. The government insisted on Insull’s departure because it feared the American government would be angry if Insull were sheltered here longer. Originally he was to be expelled January 31, but won extensions of time on the plea of illness.

1934-01-23.text: LOS ANGELES, Jan. 23—(UP)— Col. Roscoe Turner, holder of transcontinental speed records, will compete in an air race from London to Australia next October if he can find a backer, he told the United Press today. Turner returned last night from New York City where he conferred with a group of sportsmen who may sponsor his entry, he said.

PARIS, Jan. 24. (AP) — France today appeared to have virtually abandoned hope of a disarmament agreement with Germany and looked to Great Britain for the next step in the tangle. High French quarters said German notes clearly indicate such "profound differences" between them that it was doubted if France would continue efforts to find a solution. England, it was reported, is seeking an arms meeting in Paris of German, French, British and Italian representatives. France, however, apparently is not enthusiastic for such a conference.

PARIS (P)—A new banking scandal, royalist and communist riots, a virtual state of siege throughout the capital, and a momentous meeting of parliament combined Tuesday to give a smashing climax to the crisis arising out of the Stavisky financial collapse. More than 700 agitators, a majority fiery young royalists devoted to the pretender Duke of Guise, were under arrest after all-night scenes that recalled the disturbances of the old commune. For hours, reforming in valiant bands after being dispersed by the police, these young “Camelots Du Roi,” the royalist fighting corps, threw Paris into an uproar, storming the boulevards, building impromptu barricades against traffic, tearing up iron railings, and throwing billboards, benches and sewer lids into obstructive piles in the streets. Police, augmented by the crack garde républicain, maintained heavy forces around the chamber of deputies, t

Tokyo, Jan. 23—(Tuesday)—(AP)— Foreign Minister Koki Hirota told the Japanese diet today that “between Japan and the United States of America there exists no question that is intrinsically difficult of solution.” He asserted that Japan “fervently desires American friendship.” At the same time he said “it is most surprising and regrettable” that Soviet Russia should direct “unwarranted criticisms against Japan.” He told the legislators that the Japanese government believed that “proper adjustment of the tri-partite relationship between Japan, Manchukuo and the Soviet Union was of paramount importance for the tranquility of East Asia.” Withdrawal From League The foreign minister gave the question of Manchukuo, the nation which Japan created in Manchuria, first place in his address. He referred at once to the withdrawal of Japan from the League of Nations last year giving as his reason “tha

PARIS, Jan. 23 — (AP) — The cabinet of Premier Camille Chautemps appeared tottering today in the face of repeated attacks from both inside and outside the chamber of deputies. Police resources were taxed during the night as 4,000 battled 1,500 royalists demonstrating around the chamber and 3,000 disgruntled civil employees crying out against pay cuts in a manifestation near the city hall. "Down with Chautemps!" was the royalists’ cry. Stones, sticks and torpedoes were hurled during their struggle with police. Hundreds were arrested, but released. The possibility of the government’s being overthrown as a result of the increasing opposition born of the Bayonne pawnshop scandal was discussed freely in chamber of deputies lobbies. Royalists charging government leaders were to blame for conditions which led to the pawnshop’s resounding collapse, said they would continue their manifestations.

PARIS, Jan. 4 (4)—Fumarees of determined rioters, throwing torpedoes, stones and other missiles, and shouting “down with Chautemps,” battled police two hours today in the vicinity of the chamber of deputies. Between 700 and 1,000, it was estimated, were arrested, but most of them were released after questioning. A cabinet crisis was predicted in chamber lobbies as a result of continued attacks on the government since the Stavisky scandal, growing from the collapse of the Bayonne pawnshop, revealed December 30. Premier Camille Chautemps, who once apparently had survived a wave of opposition following the scandal, was in the chamber within hearing of the noise, a cross between an artillery barrage and a Fourth of July celebration. He was represented as being “discouraged.”

Madrid, Jan. 22.—(AP)—Ambassador Claude G. Bowers of the United States asked the Spanish government today to pardon four Americans held in jail in Palma, Mallorca, because they 'insulted' a civil guard. The Americans are Mr. and Mrs. Clinton B. R. Lockwood, West Springfield, Mass., Roger F. Mead, New York, and Edmund A. Blodgett, Stamford, Conn.

Tokio, Jan. 23. — No problem exists between the United States and Japan that is not capable of solution, Foreign Minister Jeki Hirota declared in his address to the Japanese Diet. In a speech regarded as extremely pacific in tone, Hirota reviewed the events of the past year in Manchoukuo, the Japanese withdrawal from the League of Nations, and the Japanese-American position in the Far East. “Between Japan and the United States of America,” he said, “there exists no question that is intrinsically difficult of solution. Far from having any thought of picking a quarrel with America, Japan fervently desires American friendship. “It is hardly necessary to reiterate that Japan is actuated by no ulterior motives other than her desire to establish enduring peace in East Asia . . . If America will clearly perceive the actual condition of the Orient and realize Japan's role as a stabilizing force,

1934-08-29.text: London, Aug. 29 (AP).—A Balkan romance, its setting the picturesque Slovenian Alps of Yugoslavia, culminated Tuesday night in the engagement of Prince George of England to wed Princess Marina of Greece. Like any other young lover, King George’s fourth son, asked first for the hand of the Princess and then telegraphed home for his royal parents’ consent. It was given gladly. Palace Announcement Made “It is with the greatest pleasure,” the announcement from the palace said, “that the King and Queen announce the betrothal of their dearly beloved son, Prince George, to Princess Marina, daughter of Prince and Princess Nicolas of Greece, to which union the King has gladly given his consent.” An acquaintance that dated back five years to the young couple's first meeting in London ripened into love, London understood Tuesday night, at the summer home of Prince Paul of Yugoslavia, where Prince Ge

LONDON, Aug. 28 (#)—Confident the "next" war would be fought at high speed, Europe tonight was grooming fast iron soldiers to do the job. While London and Paris army men tended to differ with the opinion Italian military authorities expressed today to the effect that trench warfare was obsolete, Great Britain and France nevertheless went forward with Italy in efforts to speed up the movement of troops. The League of Nations’ armament yearbook published at Geneva today estimated the world spent between $3,471,000,000 and $4,399,000,000 on armaments in 1933. A great part of this, army men agreed, went for tanks, airplanes and other fast fighting machines designed to wage war at maximum. Calculating the results of the recent army maneuvers, Premier Benito Mussolini's military experts asserted the first onslaught of tanks and fast moving troop detachments would break through trench lines, fo

BOY HMANKNI Ll. Fists United Press Staff Correspondent London, Aug. 29.—(UP)—Romantically inclined English men and women read with “ohs” and “ahs” today the news that Europe's handsomest royal couple—Prince George of England and Princess Marina of Greece—are to marry. King George announced the engagement at his castle of Balmoral, Scotland, while George and Marina were holidaying at Salzburg, Austria. These seemed more than the usual formality to the accompanying report that the marriage would be one of love and not politics, because George is nowhere near the throne; Greece has no king; George has shown marked independence and a determination to lead his own life and finally because the Prince of Wales, George's mentor, expressed surprised disbelief at Biarritz, France, when he was informed of the announcement. Grave Ellison, author and friend of the Prince said today that Marina always

HOLLYWOOD, Aug. 29.—(INS)—Heather Angel, young English actress, and Ralph Forbes, also a native English actor, and former husband of Ruth Chatterton, the star, left by automobile early today for Yuma, Ariz., where they announced they would be married. The elopement surprised Hollywood.

Tokyo, Aug. 29—(AP)—Japan is determined that neither the Washington nor the London naval treaties shall bind her beyond December 31, 1936, the date of their expiration, a foreign office spokesman said today. She is prepared to join other powers in a scheme of naval limitation on a drastically changed basis which she intends to propose at preliminary conversations this autumn in London. If the powers show a determination to extend essentials of present compacts, including Japan's position of inferiority to the United States and Great Britain, Tokyo is ready to withdraw from the entire naval limitations scheme, just as she withdrew from the League of Nations 18 months ago, the spokesman said.

HOLLYWOOD, Cal, Aug, 99.-(?}— A romance of six weeks will be culminated today in the marriage at Yuma, Ariz., of Ralph Forbes, screen player and former husband of Ruth Chatterton, film star, and Heather Angel, the English actress. The couple left by automobile last night for Arizona after surprising friends with an announcement of their plans for marriage. More than a year ago they met at a dinner party but their friendship did not ripen into love until six weeks ago, after they had met again while playing tennis at the home of Charles Boyer and Pat Patterson, screen players.

London, Aug. 28,— (WP) — Prince George, son of the king and queen of England is engaged to marry the Princess Marina of Greece, an official announcement said Tuesday night. The prince is 31 years old. His romance was rumored last week, when it was reported by the United Press that George intended to meet the Prince of Wales, his brother, at Cannes this week, after travels in Yugoslavia. The rumors then said the engagement of Prince George to the Princess Marina was expected shortly. She is the daughter of Prince Nicolas and Grand Duchess Helene Viadimirovna of Russia. The princess is a brunette, stylish although not stunningly beautiful. She is 27. Her family resides in Paris. The announcement of the engagement of Prince George, fourth son of the king and queen, was made in Tuesday night’s court circular, issued at Balmoral castle, in Scotland. It said: “It is with the greatest pleasure

Vienna, Aug. 28. P} — Too much work has driven Austria’s hangman crazy, it was reported tonight. The nervous and emotional strain in connection with the execution of 12 nazis and nine socialists since February sent Johan Lang, famed as perhaps Europe's most meticulously dressed executioner, into an asylum, the reports said. and an ordinary policeman put the last nazi to death. Lang invariably wore evening clothes to work. It was his custom, on entering the condemned man's cell, to doff his high silk hat and introduce himself with the words: “My name is Lang. I am the government executioner.” “These are my two assistants,” he would continue. “I am very sorry you must hang. You will have a few minutes in which to make a last request or give a message to your family.” The few minutes over, Lang led the prisoner to the gallows. For each “job” the hangman received $33.50, half of which he had

1934-10-18.text: London, Oct. 18.—(#)—The belief was growing in American quarters today that Japan may accept a naval limitations plan somewhat similar to present ratios if she gets two concessions. They are tonnage quality in "principal" and replacement of the term "ratio" by one less offensive to her indicating relative strength. Enthusiasm over this possibility, however, was overshadowed by the problem of reconciling the vast differences between the basic program of the two countries. Americans held hope a suitable compromise might be effected during the tri-power naval conversation to open next week preliminary to the 1935 conference.

By The Associated Press BOSTON, Oct. 17—A method of detouring living skin from one part of the body to another to improve plastic surgery was described to the American College of Surgeons here tonight by Sir Harold Gillies, London surgeon. A steadily rising tide in cures of cancer was reported by a large group of surgeons in a symposium on malignant diseases. The detouring of skin is one of the latest bits of skill. By its use, skin, without ever losing its living connection with the patient's own blood supply, can be taken from virtually any part of the body, even the back, and transferred anywhere else. By this method skin has been taken from the outside of the body and detoured to interior cavities to save life. The detour trip across or lengthwise of the body takes six to nine weeks. The method is known to surgeons as the tubed pedicle flap. The “flap” looks like the handle of a vali

(Copyright, 1934, by United Press) Paris, Oct. 18 (UP)—Return of Britain to the gold standard was forecast by economists today on the eve of the second ‘defense conference’ of the gold bloc countries in Brussels. The seven gold bloc nations—France, Belgium, Holland, Luxembourg, Italy, Switzerland and Poland—will gather in the Belgian capital tomorrow and probably will consider an invitation to Great Britain to adhere to the agreements reached. The invitation would be designed to show that the gold bloc is not directed against Sterling area—the countries which use the pound as a monetary standard. It was hoped the move would bring Britain into the gold bloc by granting her important trade concessions in continental gold countries and that Britain would agree to return to gold at an early date.

| LONDON, Oct. 18 — Over the trail which won knighthood for Keith and Ross Smith 15 years ago, 20 aircraft will set out Saturday for Melbourne, Australia, in the world’s longest air derby. | The Brothers Smith took 228 days in 1919 over the 12,000 mile route, and won $50,000 in addition to honors from the King. Sir Ross was killed in 1922 when his plane fell in a practice flight at Brooklands, England. Sir Keith, who was to have made the flight, arrived late, and was in the crowd which witnessed the tragedy. He is now living in Sydney, Australia. | The present record between England and Australia is 6 days, 17 hours and 56 minutes, set a year ago by Charles T. P. Ulm and three companions, G. U. Allen, P. G. Taylor and John Edwards. Air Commodore Sir Charles Kingsford-Smith holds the solo record of 7 days, 4 hours, and 47 minutes, set in October last year, just before the Ulm flight. The

Mindenhall Airdrome, England. Oct. 18.—Restrictions on weight forced American and other foreign competitors in the England to Australia plane race to make a wholesale sacrifice of gasoline and other equipment today. Colonel Roscoe Turner and Clyde Pangborn, a favored American team, made drastic reductions, but after making them Turner said his machine was ready for the take-off Saturday. His biggest loss was the sealing of a 90-gallon tank and a number of other changes had to be made including the stripping off of sound proof material and replacement of glass windows with a composition which saved 18 pounds. The American indicated a part of the overweight was caused by the fact that American gasoline is a different specific gravity from English petrol, therefore upsetting his calculations somewhat.

LONDON, Oct. 18.—America’s bridge team defending the Schwab trophy had narrowed the gap between it and the British challengers to 3,070 points when play was resumed today. A spurt by the visitors last night made the score: England, 62,699 points; America, 65,620 points, with 180 hands played.

Purin, Italy, Oct. 18.—(U. P.)—Dr. Ante Pavalic, described as the “master mind” of the Croatian terrorists, and Eugene Kvaternik, his aide, were arrested today on the suspicion of being implicated in the Marseilles assassination. The arrests came just as the murdered King Alexander was being buried in Jugo Slavia. Kvaternik was known as the “delegate” and was supposed to have acted as contact man for Pavalic, making contact with the Marseilles assassin. Police had hunted them throughout Europe. Continental police are still seeking two other members of the band, and when they are caught believe they will have rounded up the entire group of principals.

Paris, Oct. 18 (4?)—The Surete Nationale was informed today that the Italian police had arrested Ante: “master mind” Pavelich, head of the terroristic secret society Ustashi and his alleged chief of the assassination squad, Exon Kvaternik, known as “the delegate.” The police claim that the Pavelich organization was responsible for the assassinations of King Alexander of Yugoslavia and Louis Barthou of France at Marseille October 9. Three more members of the killers’ organization were said by the Surete to be still at large. They were described as the beautiful “gun moll,” Marie Voudroch, a man called Mio Bzik, alias, “The Glassmaker,” and another still unidentified. Police said “The Glassmaker” whom they know as a dangerous terrorist, aided “the delegate” in instructing the gang in Pavelich’s assassination plans. The Surete said Bzik was implicated in the confession made by Mio Kraj who

1934-08-23.text: ANGMAGSALIK, Greenland, Aug. 23—(AP)—John Grierson is ready today to fly Greenland’s ice cap on his way to America, thanks to a half-breed Eskimo minister who found him lost and shivering in a desolate fjord. The British aviator, who has spent a month flying the Atlantic by stages, became lost on the bleak Eastern coast of Greenland Tuesday. Unaware that he was near this little settlement, the flier sent out an S. O. S. and landed. He was found the next morning by the minister, the Rev. Rosing. Later he flew to Angmagsalik. Grierson said he had no idea of his position and had resigned himself to a wait of a week for rescuers. The flier had only pemmican to eat, but had a 10-day supply of that. He spent a chilly night in his plane, getting little sleep.

Washington, Aug. 23 (UP)—Secretary of Treasury Henry Morgenthau, Jr. said today he was “not disturbed” over the sensational foreign monetary developments of the past few days. Paris, Aug. 23 (UP)—French financial circles predicted a new monetary war today when the British pound sterling slumped precipitously, closing at a new low record of 76.03 francs. Washington, Aug. 23. (UP)—The United States for the second time within a few weeks today was ready to pay out gold to foreign banks if necessary for defense of the American dollar on its new gold standard of 15 5-21 grains of gold. A selling flurry in the foreign exchange market sent the American gold dollar to a sharp discount compared with the gold French franc. The franc reached 6.695 cents, compared with parity of 6.630, making it apparently profitable for French banks to buy American dollars and turn the dollars into gold here. Sever

PARIS, Aug. 23.—French financial circles predicted a new monetary war today when the British pound sterling slumped precipitously, closing at a new low record of 76.03 francs. The dollar, fractionally stronger than at the opening of the foreign exchange market, closed at 14.93 (6.695 cents a franc) as against an opening of 14.98 (6.698 cents a franc). After having practically ceased operations yesterday, the huge stabilization fund of £350,000,000 (more than $1,750,000,000) set up by Great Britain, was inactive again today in the Paris bourse. As a result, French economists believed London was preparing for a fresh devaluation of the pound which, if put into effect, would be followed, it was assumed here, by another devaluation of the United States dollar.

London, Ontario, Aug. 23—Predictions of “imminent” arrests in the John S. Labbatt kidnapping mystery have failed to materialize, and suspicion grew today that Canadian police may not be as close on the heels of the men who snatched the wealthy brewer as the public has been led to believe. For the past 48 hours Dominion newspapers have been running first-page stories purporting to contain “inside” information and indicating arrests were only a matter of hours, but the hours have passed, and with them the “deadline” for arrests, and still nobody has been taken into custody.

Moscow, Aug. 23.—(4A.—Soviet Russia presented a demand today to the foreign office of Manchukuo for an explanation of the arrest of eighty-eight Soviet citizens and insisted upon prompt measures for their release. Acting Consul General Rayvid of Russia presented the demand to a representative of the Manchukuoan minister of public affairs in that city, "The arrests were made without documents, accompanied by the searching of the apartments and offices of Soviet employees of the Chinese Eastern railway which have not been explained," Rayvid said. Some of the prisoners were beaten by police, the dispatch asserted and subjected to third degree methods by officers and anti-Soviet white guards. They are charged with plotting against Manchukuo and Japan and with sabotaging Japanese military trains. Tokio, Aug. 23—(7)—The Japanese government fired the latest salvo Wednesday in the conflict of pr

Montreal, Que. Aug. 23 (TP)— Gene Tunney, former heavyweight boxing champion, said today he had been offered a post in the National Recovery Administration in the United States. Tunney would not divulge details but said the offer came from Gen. Hugh Johnson, NRA administration.

Messina, Sicily, Aug. 23.—(U.P)—Mt. Stromboli burst into its most violent explosion since the beginning of the present series of eruptions shortly before 4 p. m. today. After its first terrific explosion, the volcano sent forth a huge and startling pillar of gas and incandescent materials. Then the eruption subsided. Vessels within a radius of ten miles felt strong shocks, and it was believed the sea bottom was disturbed.

BERLIN. (UP). The government admitted that 150 persons had been arrested since the recent elections, but denied the arrests were because the suspects had voted "nein" or Reichsführer Hitler's policies. It was explained the arrested persons were "communists, charged with treasonable activities." The government denied foreign reports of mass arrests of Catholics and Jews who dared to vote against the dictator.

1934-01-20.text: London, Jan. 19,—(AP)—The husky, six-foot Clarence Guy Haddon, pleaded guilty to a charge of menacing King George, whose nephew he claims to be, and then went his way today, promising to put aside the “maggot” of his alleged grievances aside. The 48-year-old unemployed engineer was placed under two sureties of $100 each to keep the peace for three years and upon his honor, by Justice Charles of the famous Old Bailey court, to abandon the belief—“this maggot preying on your mind,” the court called it—that he is the illegitimate son of the Duke of Clarence, the monarch's late elder brother. Haddon was accused of writing letters to the king demanding money and threatening to publish widely, through various means, the details of the alleged kinship.

Madrid.—(#)—Four United States citizens were sentenced to six months and a day imprisonment today for assaulting a civil guard last year at Palma, Mallorca. At the same time the court acquitted Rutherford Fullerton, Columbus, O., one of five Americans concerned in the incident. Those who must go to jail are Mr. and Mrs. Clinton B. Lockwood of West Springfield, Mass.; Roger F. Mead of New York, and Edmund W. Blodgett of Stamford, Conn.

SHANGHAI, Jan. 19. (4)—Mrs. W. S. Grooch of El Paso took two sons, William, 6, and Thomas, 7, one under each arm, and jumped off the roof of an eight-story apartment house here today. All were killed. Mrs. Grooch was the wife of the operations manager of the Pacific American Airways. Their home in the apartment building from which she jumped was in a French concession. When he heard of the tragedy, Grooch lost consciousness and is now in serious condition as a result of shock. Cause of the suicide was not explained. Mrs. Grooch was scheduled to sail tonight for the United States to reach the bedside of her father, who was reported seriously ill. Grooch is a leading aviation official in the Far East.

Little America, (via Mackay Radio) Jan. 19.—Admiral Richard E. Byrd's Antarctic flagship narrowly escaped destruction today when a huge ice cliff toppled into the Bay of Whales. The flagship bearing most of the members of the expedition was moving slowly through the Bay of Whales seeking a permanent mooring place from which supplies could be transferred to the permanent camp. Admiral Byrd himself was on the bridge. The ship was moving at slow speed about 200 yards off the barrier. Suddenly one quarter of a mile of the barrier ice rising 50 to 70 feet above the surface of the bay roared into the water.

Calcutta, Jan. 20. (UP)—Reports reaching Calcutta today from the devastated state of Bengal indicate that the recent earthquake may have caused one of the most stupendous human tragedies of modern times, with perhaps 20,000 persons dead in the ruined cities. Refugees reported an estimated death toll in Monghyr of between 6,000 and 8,000. An unofficial estimate in the province of Behar showed 15,000 dead. Damage, according to officials, will amount to at least $37,500,000. For three successive days and nights, bodies of the dead have been thrown into the river Ganges, to float down to the sea in gruesome hundreds.

ATHENS, Jan. 20. — (P)— The Greek government was represented today as determined to expel Samuel Insull, Sr., former Chicago utilities operator, no matter what decision may be taken on his case by the Council of State. This attitude was stated today by the secretary of the ministry of the interior. The council itself, following a hearing yesterday at which attorneys for Insull spoke, deliberated the case two hours today. The council members argued heatedly but adjourned until next week without reaching a decision.

Paris, Jan. 20—(UP)—French royalists stormed the bourse during the height of this afternoon's stock trading, and fought brokers with their fists, shouting "Down with Chautemps and Bonnett." Gendarmes locked the doors and corralled the demonstrators, arresting four out of 40.

Calcutta—(A—LU unofficial estimates of the death roll of last Monday's earthquake were raised to 15,000 today. Workers are laboring day and night at the task of gathering the bodies of the dead and carrying them into the Ganges river. Bihar province was hardest hit, the damage there being estimated at $40,000,000. Many buildings in Muzaffarpur sank five feet into the ground in the course of the tremors.

1934-01-05.text: Rome (7) - Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, departed at noon today for London to report to the British government that there was “no use crying for the moon” in matters of international disarmament. His report will be based on the result of his conferences here with Premier Mussolini and in Paris with French government leaders. These conferences decided him to favor the shortest road to an arms agreement that can be reached as against devious and perhaps endless talk in an attempt to gain more utopian accords. He carries the assurance of Italy’s support for a short road thesis and also it is understood the support of the French.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 5.—(P)— The RFC price for newly mined domestic gold remained today at $35.06 an ounce. The price was posted as sterling opened in London at $5.15%% to the pound, making bar gold worth on that basis $32.86 an ounce. Today's RFC price represented the thirteenth repetition of its peak quotation on domestic gold.

ROME, Jan. 4—(AP)—A continued effort to find a solution to the Franco-German disarmament impasse occupied Premier Mussolini and Sir John Simon, the British foreign secretary, today. The statesmen talked alone for an hour and a quarter and carried a step farther the conversations on international problems they began yesterday. Sir John planned to leave for home shortly leaving Fulvio Suvich, the Italian under-secretary, and Sir Erie Drummond, the British ambassador to Rome, to continue the discussions, if necessary. The Fascist press, meanwhile, pleaded for unity, harmony, and solidarity to face President Roosevelt’s expressed disinclination to participate in the League of Nations and the so-called “menace to world peace arising in the Far East.” Forming the groundwork of today’s discussions, informed circles said, were the four basic objectives of Italy’s foreign policy—a reform of the L

Placerville, Calif., Jan. 2.—Edmund Cooper, believed to have been one of the oldest white men in the world, died today at the age of 115 years. He was born in Dublin, Ireland, September 18, 1818. In his youth he was employed by Lord Tenryn, an English nobleman, whose ship he deserted to come to California during the gold rush. He had lived in the state eighty years.

PARIS, Jan. 5 (#)—Parliamentary circles predicted today that Premier Camille Chautemps and his cabinet might be overthrown when parliament airs the $40,000,000 scandal of the Bayonne pawnshop. The government sent out a second series of messages to ships at sea and to French representatives in North and America. D. Albert Dalimier, minister of colonies, was summoned to his office at noon and demanded a clear statement of his connection with the Stavisky affair, of which the minister asserts he is entirely innocent despite rumors. In parliamentary circles, which until a few days ago had conceded the present government several months of life, it was said the cabinet’s danger is real. The police said Dalimier had sent out letters urging insurance companies to invest in pawnshop bonds without, however, specifying the Bayonne organization. Oppositionists to the government immediately commented

(By The Associated Press) Athens, Greece, Jan. 8—The public hearing on Samuel Insull’s appeal from an order deporting him from Greece January 31 was set by the state consul today for January 19. The verdict will not be returned on that day but will be made public later.

PARIS, Jan. 5.--Airing of the great credit municipal Bayonne financial scandal in parliament was assured today when Deputy Jean Ybarnegaray, a right wing leader, announced he would raise the question when the chamber of deputies meets Tuesday. Names of cabinet ministers were mentioned freely and Ybarnegaray was expected to attempt to embarrass the government to the utmost, perhaps forcing a vote of confidence. Alexander Sacha Stavisky, mysterious head of the organization which crashed with a possible loss of $30,000,000 or more to investors, continued in hiding. Newspapers hostile to the government alleged he was being protected by members of the Surete Generale—the much respected French Scotland Yard. Surete Generale agents, raiding Stavisky’s luxurious suite in the Hotel Champs Elysees, seized many documents. Premier Camille Chautemps, denying any government favors to Stavisky in his d

Farts, Jan. 5 UP.—A formal plea for liberty by Mr. and Mrs. Robert Gordon Switz of East Orange, NJ, in connection with investigation of an alleged spy ring, was denied today by a magistrate, who asked that they be held in jail pending completion of the inquiry. "The first court hearing was granted the American couple along with scores of other prisoners— including eight others the police charge are spies—in accordance with a law providing that every prisoner appear in court at least once monthly. Questioned as to documents police said they seized in their hotel room, the Americans replied that they were victims of a 'frame-up.'

1934-11-03.text: WESTERHAM, ENG., NOV. 3. (AP)—The original Alice In Wonderland, Mrs. Alice Hargreaves, is gravely ill at her home here. In an old hilltop house in this Kentish village, far from the scenes of 72 years ago in Oxfordshire when Lewis Carroll told her of the Cheshire cat and the mad hatter, Mrs. Hargreaves was being constantly attended by her sister and her son. She was taken ill a few days ago and her condition is causing great anxiety. She is 82 years old.

| WESTERHAM, England, Nov. 3 (UP).—Alice in Wonderland—Mrs. Alice Liddell Hargreaves, original of the Alice in Lewis Carroll’s immortal book—lay dying today at her old white house in this peaceful Kentish village. She was unconscious. Mrs. Hargreaves, 82, was taken ill while she was motoring 10 days ago. Physicians said she could not survive. During periods of semi-consciousness she was unable to speak. At her bedside on a table was a group of little china figures of characters in Alice in Wonderland which she acquired when she visited the United States in 1932. Her son, Captain Caryl Hargreaves, and her sister, Miss Rhoda Liddell, who went with her to the United States, were with her. On a summer afternoon 72 years ago Rev. Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, who wrote under the name Lewis Carroll, took 10-year-old Alice Liddell and her two sisters boating on the upper Thames. It was hot and they

Lympne Airport, England, Nov. 2.-~ (UP)—Smashing air records right and left, Lieut. Cathcart Jones and Ken Waller, British fliers, landed here today after a phenomenal round trip flight to Australia. They broke the round trip record between England and Melbourne, making the 22,600-mile flight—11,300 each way—in 13 days, 6 hours 45 minutes, 30 seconds. They broke the Melbourne-England record, taking 6 days, 15 hours, 39 seconds. Other records included those between Darwin and England; Melbourne and Charleville, Australia; Charleville and Darwin; Melbourne and Darwin; Darwin and Singapore; and Melbourne to Singapore.

London, Nov. 2.
