Washington, Oct. 25,—(?)—The United States has made representations to Japan against the proposed Manchukuo state oil monopoly on the grounds that the monopoly would be detrimental to American oil companies and in violation of the open door policy and the nine power treaty. Great Britain and the Netherlands, whose nationals are likewise affected, were understood to have made similar separate representations, but there has been no joint action by the three nations. The American representations were made because the proposed state oil monopoly would cause a great loss in investment and business to the Standard Oil Company, an American concern.

LONDON, Oct. 25 (UP)— Great Britain, foreseeing a clash between the United States and Japanese delegations on naval armaments, appeared ready today to offer its mediation and take the key position in negotiations. Even the generalities in speeches of the chief Japanese delegates at their first meeting with the Americans yesterday sufficed to unveil the contrast between Japanese and American outlooks. Japan wants formal recognition of its contention that it is entitled to naval equality. The United States takes the view that under the present naval ratios Japan has relative equality, considering its geographical position and entire security.

MELBOURNE, Australia, Oct. 26. (Friday)—(UP)—A fourth airplane crew in the England-Australia air race was here today after breaking the old flying record, and ten more crews, scattered over Asia and Europe, seemed still hopeful of completing the 11,300-mile air-line course. Lieutenant Cathcart Jones of the British Royal Air Force and Ken Waller, Great Britain, finished over Flemington race course at 2:54 p. m. Melbourne time yesterday (11:54 p. m. Wednesday E. S. T.) They are eligible for the handicap prize of $8,000 and $4,000. Next behind them were Squadron Leader Malcolm McGregor and Henry Walker, Great Britain, who left Batavia, Java. Then came flight leader J. D. Hewett and squadron leader C. E. Kay, New Zealand, at Batavia; squadron leader D. E. Stodart and K. G. Stodart, Great Britain, at Alor Star, Malay Peninsula; Lieut. Michael Hansen and Daniel Jenson, Denmark, who left Rangoo

Washington, Oct. 25.—The basis of naval limitation adopted here by the World Powers in 1922 is about to be discarded. Naval discussion begun in London this week between representatives of the United States, Great Britain and Japan in the guise of conversations preliminary to a 1935 conference are developing into a showdown of objectives. The informal London discussions have a better than even chance during the next few weeks of growing into a full-fledged conference of the naval powers in which naval armaments problems will be settled finally so far as this generation and the next are concerned: The 1935 conference then never would take place. Great Britain invited the United States and Japan to participate in preliminary conversations which have just begun in London. It was understood when the invitations were issued that the London talks would be limited to: 1. Fixing the time and plac

MELBOURNE, Oct. 25 (Thursday) — Anxiety over the fate of John H. Wright and John Polando, American derby fliers feared lost, ended today as word came from Basra, Iraq, that they landed near the Turco-Persian border, to be arrested, clapped into prison and held overnight. A roaring welcome to the first three arrivals in the derby had given place to fear for the two Americans, flying the smallest ship in the race, when hour after hour passed without reports from them following their takeoff from Baghdad at 10:10 A.M. (GMT) Tuesday. The difficulties of the American pair, who previously had experienced engine trouble, served to emphasize the troubles of nine other entrants in the derby straggling back along the course as far as Athens. Their arrest and the consequent more than 24 hours delay apparently wiped out their chances of placing in the handicap division of the derby, in which they we

MOSCOW, Oct. 25.—()—Two Soviet officials were put to death by firing squads today for counter-revolutionary activity and sabotage which resulted in the destruction of state property. They were Kokhan Nikolai, chief of the Sosnovsky state grain farm, and Mikhail Strebkov, president of the collective farm in that state. Nikolai was charged with failing to dry grain and place it in the warehouse with the result that 300 tons were ruined. The prosecutor charged Strebkov permitted horses to be neglected with the result that many of them died. He was a former czarist officer,

1934-04-22.text: London.—-(AP)—With the precision of a chess player, Great Britain is carrying out a recovery program designed to enlarge her export trade and, diametrically opposite to the American agricultural objective, to increase the productivity of her farms. This ‘new deal,’ which started when the national government abandoned free trade, entered a new phase this week with the adoption of a plan of federation of the iron and steel industry under an authoritative group not unlike an American code authority. The iron and steel industry is one of the four key groups involved in the program, the others being cotton manufacture, coal mining and agriculture. The government has taken a hand directly, so far, only in agriculture and coal mining, but a “big stick” hangs over iron and steel manufacturers in the form of a threat to let the protective tariff expire next October unless the industry voluntarily

PARIS, April 21. - Police ruled the streets of Paris again today after a night of violence seen by some as setting the stage for serious outbreaks to come. Before police and mobile guards could quell a raging mob of 6,000 Communists and extremists, at least 200 persons were injured by clubs, feet and fists. Out of the howling throng, officers grabbed 940 persons and hustled them off to jails, but all were released. The mob shouted its defiance around the city hall in a demonstration against the government's recent decrees slashing the pay of civil employees. Although pleased with the improved system of handling riots used in putting down the mob, some quarters wondered how long it will be before riots flare again. The disorders were viewed as merely a sort of “rehearsal” for May Day. Under the system worked out after the fatal riots of February, the police attacked groups of manifestants

MOSCOW, (#)—Under the lash of President Michael Kalinin, Soviet leaders pushed forward today a vast program for defense against war, Returning from a countrywide tour, the president struck at the vulnerable spots in Russia's defense armor. He urged particularly in a call published in the newspaper La Pravda the training of women and children “and others not fit for military service” to carry on should their men be called to fight. “Some think,” President Kalinin said, “that since war has not yet been proclaimed against the Soviet Union it will not be done at all. Those so thinking have lost their vigilance.” He condemned rural soviets for their inactivity in training women, children and men not physically capable of going to war “to carry out the work of the collective farms when all able-bodied persons are mobilized.” Lending impetus to the drive to emphasize the need for preparedness,

MADRID, April 22,—(Sunday)— WH—Scattered gunfire broke out on the streets of the city to-day as the political unrest which has kept the nation disturbed for months was climaxed by a declaration of general strikes throughout Spain. "In one of the duels a gunman fleeing from police wounded a guard and was in turn brought down by a bullet. Meanwhile, bombs exploded on different streets, causing considerable damage. Two other bombs detonated near the home of Prime Minister Alejandro Lerroux. One person was killed by a fifth bomb in a neighboring street. The remainder of Spain was described as peaceful. Soldiers will replace bakers when the latter go on strike today, it was announced.

ROME, April 21. (P)—The two thousand six hundred and eighty-seventh birthday of Rome was celebrated today. Premier Benito Mussolini inaugurated many public works and accepted on behalf of the city a monument to Simon Bolivar erected outside the national stadium by Venezuela, Peru, Ecuador, Chile, Colombia and Panama. Para Perez, Venezuelan minister, offered the monument to Rome in the name of the six Bolivarian republics recalling the ties uniting Italy and South America and the oath taken by Bolivar at Monte Sacro to liberate South America from Spanish rule.

Moscow, April 21. (AP)—A sharpening of Japanese-American relations as a result of the recent Japanese statement warning the rest of the world to keep its hands off China was predicted today by the Soviet press which views the Tokyo proclamation as giving a serious impetus to the danger of war in the far east. Terming the Japanese action “an open attempt to proclaim a protectorate over China,” the newspaper for industrialization says its purpose appears to be an attempt to break down negotiations between China and the foreign bankers who have been invited there by the Nanking government. “The arrival of these bankers,” says the newspaper, “who are directly connected with the League of Nations is interpreted by the Japanese as an attempt made by the United States and European powers to organize a united front against the pan-Asiatic plans of Tokyo. “At the same time Tokyo seeks to halt the

TOKYO, Sunday, April 22.—UP— Japan is ready to “make any sacrifice to safeguard justice,” War Minister Senjuro Hayashi told Soviet Ambassador Konstantin Yurenev in receiving Yurenev at the war office, according to a story printed today in the newspaper Asahi. The Asahi said it understood Hayashi, who a few weeks ago succeeded Sadao Araki as minister of war, also told Yurenev that the change in war ministers did not mean “even the slightest change” in Japan's defense program. Hayashi, according to the Asahi, pointed out to Yurenev that Japan could still have a peace-loving spirit and yet consolidate its defense program, and that no contradiction was involved in such an attitude. The new war minister emphasized to Yurenev, the Asahi said, that Japan is “as anxious for security guarantees as the other powers.”

Washington, D. C.--(AP)-- President Roosevelt has been advised directly by a special cabinet committee that the creation of a zone on price fixing is not yet feasible. This conclusion was rested on the White House desk by Secretaries Perkins, Roper and Wallace and Attorney-General Cummings despite demands of price-fixing friends and foes that a policy be enunciated. The report, still withheld from publication, was authoritatively described as recommending that positive steps be taken to get information which would make an objective judgment possible. The report is short. It makes no attempt to decide the merits of questions as to whether prices have risen too far under N. R. A. price control provisions in codes or whether such provisions have been conducive to monopoly. The document was said authoritatively to state that many factors besides prices, or the misuse of price control methods

1934-11-24.text: BEVERLY HILLS, Cal., Nov. 23--It's been hard for nations to start another war, because they didn't have any particular reason or alignment. But now it looks like the next war will be between the nations that were invited to the big English wedding, and those that were not. The funny part about it is, the whole mess of ‘em are all kin folks, and nobody can fall out and get as sore at each other as kin folks. Yours, WILL ROGERS

(Copyright, 1934, by United Press) LONDON, Nov. 24.—(UP)—Germany's rapid rearmament in deliberate violation of the treaty of Versailles, and the danger of its forcing a regrouping of continental powers for the eventuality of the next major war were drawn sharply to the forefront of Europe’s fears today. Attention was focused on a long serious situation by this almost casual statement in the French chamber of deputies yesterday of Leo Archimbaud, reporter of the budget: “Russia has a solid, well equipped army which she offers us in case of conflict between Germany and us.” There has been disagreement whether Archimbaud was disclosing officially a long rumored alliance between France and Russia. Perhaps he intended to fix the world's attention on the fact that Germany is fast rearming and will soon be among Europe's strong military powers despite treaty restrictions to prevent her rearming

LONDON, Nov. 24.—(#)—In the event the present naval limitations treaty is junked, the United States probably will seek an informal accord with Great Britain in a general naval policy in order to prevent a naval building race between the two powers, it was learned authoritatively today. Such an informal accord probably would include undertakings to keep each other fully advised of the other's building program as well as an agreement to make both fleets complementary. It was stated, however, that no discussions on this matter have as yet taken place, and it was expected there would be none until it could be evident there was no further hope of reaching a compromise on a naval treaty. The threat of a limitless naval building race between the three great rulers of the seas hung today over the tri-power conversations as hope was virtually abandoned for a compromise on Japan's demands for nava

Washington, Nov. 24. (4P)—A vanishing island, unseen since it was swallowed by the “serpent's mouth” 20 years ago, has suddenly popped up high and dry on the coast of Trinidad to the consternation of the inhabitants of the British West Indies. Flabbergasted by the phenomenon, the American vice consul at Trinidad forwarded a report to the state department today describing the antics of the strange “jellylike” visitor from the sub-oceanic regions. The geological freak, he reported, had apparently changed into something like a “well ploughed farm” and erupted on Trinidad’s shoreline like a gigantic wart on a dill pickle. “In November, 1911, this strange island rose from the sea in Erin Bay in southern Trinidad,” the vice consul reported, “accompanied by extraordinary commotions in the sea and immense columns of smoke and flame. People thought the end of the world had come.” The island was c

Washington, Nov. 23. The United States served an indirect notice upon Japan today that Nipponese naval building beyond treaty limits would find this country and Great Britain shoulder to shoulder in solving problems that might arise. In a statement considered of the highest significance, in view of the London naval deadlock, Secretary Hull forecast close, active and friendly cooperation between the United States and Great Britain. Simon Given Praise After praising Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, for his House of Commons speech on armaments, Hull pointedly emphasized friendly Anglo-American relations by paying tribute to the fair and cooperative attitude which has been shown by the British delegates. Hull's statement, coupled with observations by him at a press conference, was generally interpreted as a warning that if the Japanese denounce the Washington treaty and begin const

Conversations among representatives of the United States, Great Britain and Japan in an effort to devise new methods of limiting navies to replace the Washington and London treaties have practically broken down, the Americans, Norman D. Davis and Admiral William H. Standley, agreed. Japan Insistent, With Japan insistent that she should be granted the naval equality denied her under present pacts and America and Britain equally insistent the basic principles of those pacts, including the 5-5-3 ratio, shall be maintained, the Americans would not predict the consequences of the breakdown. The United States and Russia were prominent in the international arms picture today in new moves to safeguard the peace of the world. With the naval parley in London apparently at a deadlock due to Japan's insistence on parity with the United States, it was learned the Americans would seek an informal accord with Britain to prevent a building race between the two powers. A French budget official in urging larger national defense appropriation said that an “understanding” with Russia had been reached placing the Russians' huge military machine in support of France in the event of a German attack. The doom of the Washington naval limitation treaty as far as Japan is concerned was regarded as virtually sealed by Hirasi Saito, Japan's ambassador to the United States. CHICAGO, (P)—The climax of a life that led from an English farm to the throne of an industrial empire came to a climax today in the musty, old fashioned courtroom where for nine weeks Samuel Insull has fought his greatest battle. His trial with his son and 15 others on charges of mail fraud was scheduled to go to the jury at noon.

1934-06-28.text: SHANGHAI, June 28 (P).-— Street rioting in which Japanese attacked British troops threatened another ugly international incident today on a far eastern scene, Shanghai's international settlement, virtually a war zone, was the center of the controversy. Japanese objected angrily when British troops attempted to arrest two Japanese sailors in the territory. Missiles—bricks, bottles and clubs—began to fly. Unusual vigilance was exercised in the settlement, with further outbreaks feared. The affair started when British policemen attempted to arrest the two sailors, accusing them of striking a woman.

London, June 27 (4)—Great Britain in a note made public tonight rejected the American suggestion for payment of war debts in kind as impractical and a threat to Anglo-American trade. The British note, answering a communication of Secretary of State Hull in which the suggestion was made, expressed a desire for a final settlement of the debt problem, but stated that the government sees the same effect on economic conditions by payment in goods and services as by payment in cash. Former Vice-President Charles G. Dawes was quoted to back up this argument. “In their effects, deliveries in kind are not readily distinguishable from cash payments,” the British quote from a statement made by Dawes as head of the 1924 reparations committee. Shanghai, June 28 (Thursday) (4) — An angry crowd of 300 Japanese attacked British police of the Shanghai international settlement before dawn today, hurling bricks, bottles and clubs at them. The affair threatened to precipitate an international incident. The British authorities had sought to arrest two Japanese sailors ashore in international territory. The Japanese, styling themselves "patriots," objected to a Britisher undertaking to arrest one of their countrymen and quickly assumed an ugly mood, Missiles began to fly. Japanese naval shore patrols and British police reinforcements quickly ended the affair, which for a time threatened to assume proportions of an armed clash. High Japanese naval authorities and British international settlement police officers managed finally to prevent a pitched battle, although numerous British policemen were struck by bricks and other weapons hurled

LONDON, June 28 (7—London read with alarm today sensational disclosures of alleged German experiments at innoculating the vast subway transport systems of London and Paris with bacilli and gas. The magazine “Nineteenth Century Review” printed alleged secret documents describing the spreading of harmless bacteria through underground ventilating systems by secret agents to determine the percentage of germs which could be introduced among the thousands of underground travelers. “If the facts are not true,” said Wickham Steed, editor of the magazine and widely known British publicist, “they are very well invented.” The magazine claimed the documents came from responsible persons in Germany, and that one of them revealed “very good results” from a dozen tests in Paris. LONDON, June 28.—A move to guarantee Belgium's neutrality in view of the increasing danger of war was reported today in usually reliable diplomatic quarters. Information was that at the suggestion of the British government, Belgium would approach Germany with the suggestion of a ten-year non-aggression treaty between Belgium and Germany. There seemed a chance that if Germany agreed, Great Britain might offer itself as a guarantor of Belgium's neutrality. It was said that talk was proceeding at Brussels and Berlin, upon Britain's inspiration, as a preliminary to the possible treaty, and that France was standing aside as an interested observer. It was Germany's violation of Belgium's neutrality that caused Great Britain to enter the World War. The little country is one of the most important strategically in that Britain or France can be attacked through it. The move was said also to be a B

WASHINGTON, June 28 (#)— War debts were deadlocked tighter than ever today after Great Britain turned down a United States hint to make a payment in goods. A British note made public last night cited “economic objections” to payments in kind. Britain, which was among the long list of countries which failed to make cash payments due June 15, put forward a suggestion that deliveries in kind wouldn't prove entirely satisfactory to America. If Britain failed to get paid for all her exports, the note said, she couldn't assure her usual quota of cotton and other goods from this country. “As regards the suggested payments in kind,” the note said, “His Majesty’s government would recall that the experience of German reparations showed that transfer difficulties are not solved by a system of deliveries in kind. SANDWICH, Eng., June 28.—()— Continuing his record-smashing pace, Henry Cotton, British pro, shot the Royal St. Georges course today in 68—seven under par—for a 36-hole aggregate of 132 and an 11-stroke lead over Denny Shute, the defending champion, in the second round of the British open golf championship. Cotton carded a 67 yesterday. A. H. Padgham, who shared British spring pro tournament honors with Cotton, drew within nine shots of Cotton by virtue of a second round 70, giving him an aggregate of 141 and second place. LONDON, June 28.—Great Britain today enacted into a law a retaliatory measure against the German debt moratorium which becomes effective Sunday. It provides that German funds in England will be sequestered to compensate British creditors for money they will lose as a result of the general moratorium. The bill was sped through its last stages in the House of Lords this morning, sent to the King and received his signature immediately.

1934-05-27.text: LONDON, May 26.—(UP). —Great Britain has decided to accept the challenge of the Johnson law and default its $85,670,000 war debt payment due the United States June 15, a high official source close to the treasury told the United Press today. It was regarded as certain that a British default would be followed by defaults of other nations that have been making token payments. In Brussels the United Press learned in authoritative quarters that Belgium had decided to default again. All the debtor governments, like Great Britain, naturally hoped that there might be some miraculous change in the debt situation. But the United Press informant said President Roosevelt, on May 17, told Ambassador Ronald Lindsay that another token payment would not remove the stigma of default and that afterward it was decided that default—barring unexpected negotiations—was the only course. These claims never have been enunciated by responsible officials. They have been hinted so strongly, however, that most observers had come to anticipate a vigorous demand for parity. Peoria, May 26 (AP) - Ending the first sunrise to sunset non-stop run in American railroad history, the Zephyr of the Burlington Railroad swept into Chicago at 7:09 p.m. tonight (C.S.T.) at 9 miles an hour. The rushing little stainless steel train more than doubled the proud record of Britain's Royal Scot for non-stop runs, bettered its own record for short run speed, and set a new American mark for sustained high speed. It had traveled from Denver to Chicago without stopping, a distance of 1,015.4 miles, in 13 hours, 5 minutes, between sunrise in the Colorado capital and sunset in Chicago. The Royal Scot’s record of 56 miles per hour for 401 miles was replaced by a new mark of 77.5 for the 1,015.1 miles. The Zephyr sped 96.3 miles at a sustained velocity of 90 miles and had reached a peak speed of 112.5 miles per hour which it held for three miles, beating its own previous mark by three

DUBLIN, May 26—(/P)}—An official decree of death for the senate of the Irish free state, effective a year hence, brought Ireland today a step nearer the republic of which President Eamon De Valera dreams. The bill abolishing the upper house was passed finally by the Dail Eireann, 54 to 38. And De Valera, storming at British control, commented that the government would expect Great Britain to stand aside and let the Irish form a republic of the people. "We are as old a nation as Britain," he said. "If we want a republic we are entitled to it." The senate, of course, will throw the Dail’s bill out. That will make no difference. The bill thrice passed the Dail, assuring its effectiveness. The republic had little sympathy for opponents who charged De Valera is attempting as a useless institution and a waste of the people’s money.

CANNES, France —(Pj)— After public honors by four nations, the body of Brand Whitlock, American diplomat and author, was lowered into a grave today while only his widow stood by. A simple, friendly ceremony was held for the 65-year-old man, and he was buried in the English cemetery here. Diplomats representing the United States, Belgium, France, and Great Britain attended the Episcopal service in Holy Trinity church where the flags of all four nations hung at the altar. The oak casket was draped with American and French flags. Flowers, wreaths and palms were everywhere. They had been sent by hundreds of friends including King Leopold of Belgium.

Le Bourget, France.—(AP)— Paul Codos and Maurice Rossi, world’s record long distance fliers, decided today they will start tomorrow on an attempt to fly non-stop to San Diego, Calif. They will take off at 5 a. m. (11 o'clock tonight, E. S. T.). They reached their decision on the combined trans-Atlantic and transcontinental flight at 6:30 tonight after a study of a weather map embracing the whole route. Good weather was reported over the north Atlantic route which the fliers plan to take. They immediately discarded the alternative plan for a flight to Rio de Janeiro. The runway here already has been prepared for them. Their airplane is ready to be wheeled out of the hangar and filled with gasoline and oil shortly before their departure. The Frenchmen said they intended to pass directly over New York City, leading to the belief they will fly the regular transcontinental commercial route ov

LE BOURGET, France. (Sunday.) UP), Heading westward for California on a 6,100 mile non-stop flight, the veteran French fliers Paul Codos and Maurice Rossi soared into a dawn-streaked sky in the plane which holds the present world record. They took off at 4:10 (11:10 p. m. e.s.t.) laden with more than 2,000 gallons of fuel and rose slowly and steadily after bumping dangerously over 5,000 feet of runway. Suddenly deciding Saturday, after weeks of quiet preparation, that the time was ripe, the two fliers who flew 5,635 miles in 1933 from New York to Syria, set out on the most ambitious non-stop westward flight ever undertaken. Weather reports favored them in their dangerous westward Atlantic journey. Last reports said the weather was good over the Atlantic, with tail winds. The fliers took off within 10 minutes of the time they had announced. Their wives and Rossi's weeping mother were not

PARIS, May 29 (1).-Wiley Post, who encircled the world in 7 days, 18 hours, 49 1-2 minutes, today was awarded the gold medal of the International Aeronautic Federation for the best air exploit of 1933. In honoring Post, the federation decided the American flier’s feat was greater even than Gen. Italo Balbo's mass flight of 24 Italian seaplanes from Orbetello to Chicago and return.

1934-09-09.text: SAYLESVILLE, R. I. Sept. 8. — Violence broke out anew in the New England textile strike here today when 700 strikers from nearby towns engaged in a spectacular battle with 35 deputies. No shots were fired, but 20 pickets were injured. The deputies were guarding a dye and bleach works here.

OSLO, Sept. 7—You've heard of Norway's beautiful fjords, high walled canyons of water that run back for miles into the land. I took a small seaplane and flew over them for hours. Landed on their lakes and chased herds of reindeer through the snow in the plane. Minnesota can well be proud of their fatherland. It’s wonderful and substantial. Skol. Yours, WILL ROGERS

(4)—The governors of two of Italy’s African colonies started back to their posts today as Italy made known her fear of an attack on those colonies. A high colonial official disclosed that Italy was sending both soldiers and munitions into the colonies of Somaliland and Eritrea, possessions on the coast of the Red Sea. Governor Maurice Rava of Somaliland and Governor Riccardo Astuto of Eritrea were returning hurriedly after interviews with Premier Mussolini. The governors themselves will take charge of the extensive military reinforcements of the areas they administer. Two reasons caused the sudden colonial flurry. Both of those reasons lay in Abyssinia upon which both Somaliland and Eritrea border. ROME, Sept. 8 (AP).—Japanese penetration into Abyssinia is causing considerable concern to Italy, it was stated in informed quarters today, after it became known that troops and munitions have been sent to Italian colonies in eastern Africa. A sense of uneasiness because of Japanese activity was increased, it was said, because of growing militaristic manifestations in the Ethiopian empire of Abyssinia. Army Sent. Soldiers and supplies, consequently, were dispatched to Eritrea, Italy's colony on the Red Sea, and to Somaliland. An official spokesman asserted that the Italian expedition into Africa is not to be interpreted as an aggressive movement. The protection of colonists, he said, was the only immediate concern of the government at Rome. Geneva—(A)—The council of the league of nations ran into a deadlock today on the question of Russia’s admission into the league, and adjourned until Monday in an effort to solve the problem. The immediate difficulty was Poland which balked at the idea of an eastern European security pact as advocated by France and Russia. Joseph Beck, foreign minister of Poland, stated that the government is conducting direct negotiations with Moscow on the subject. The question of the Saar region also came into the forefront of the conference. Intimidation of the population in the Saar valley in connection with the forthcoming plebiscite must cease, Louis Barthou, foreign minister of France, warned the world in a solemn address before the council today.

VIENNA, Sept. 5.—(UP)—Areciduke Otto hopes soon to be able to return to Vienna to advance his claims to the Austrian throne, he indicated in a letter to officers of the old empire, received here today. After expressing regret at being unable to participate in military ceremonies to be held here tomorrow Otto said: "But I hope that the date is no longer distant when I can tell you, man to man, how much the old officers mean to me." The letter revived speculation here as to whether Chancellor Schuschnigg, an outspoken monarchist, would dare defy the "Little Entente" (Rumania, Yugoslavia and Czechoslovakia) by bringing Otto back. The three nations have long been firm in their opposition to a restoration of the Hapsburgs.

Geneva, Sept. 8.—Intimidation of the population in the Saar Valley in connection with the forthcoming Plebiscite must cease, Louis Barthou, foreign minister of France, warned the world in a solemn address before the League of Nations council today. Barthou said that “regrettable incidents occurred in the Saar yesterday and the day before.” He gave no details, but expressed the hope “such incidents will not be repeated.” Barthou did not mention the name of Germany, or Nazi organizations, but his hearers interpreted his remarks as referring to the Nazi elements in the basin. “The people of the Saar must be left entirely free to decide their own destiny,” Barthou continued. Barthou gave assurance that France will abide by the result of the Plebiscite, in which Saar inhabitants will decide whether their territory is to become a part of Germany or France, or remain under a League of Nations p

The Nazi program for women has but one: This is a child. “While man makes his supreme sacrifice on the field of battle, woman fights her supreme battle for her nation when she gives life to a child. The conception of so-called women's equality is a product of decadent Jewish intellectualism.” Hitler said he opposed woman's participation in parliamentary life on the grounds that it degraded and desecrated her. A fine, human man, with great love and concern for his people. Well, England has great love for their King George, too. And Italy, too. Mussolini runs everything, but their little king stands mighty high with 'em. And Mussolini is smart enough to just handle it right. Say, did you hear that little fellow Dollfuss talking on the radio from away over in Austria? He must be a pretty keen little “hombre.” Yours, Ae _

NEW LONDON, Conn., Feb 17—(UP)— Louie Lubchansky, junk dealer, purchased the decommissioned yacht Hildegard and all its contents several months ago. The Hildegard’s safe he sold to a New London businessman for $15. He was pretty well disgusted when the purchaser returned the safe and demanded his $15 back because the safe was locked and Lubchansky could not provide a combination. The safe was around the junk yard several weeks. Finally, unable to restrain his disgust longer, Lubchansky picked up a sledge hammer and delivered three resounding blows. It crumbled and out dropped $10,000 in old large sized $10 bills and about $5,000 in negotiable securities.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 20. —The Weather Bureau this morning issued the following Eastport. “Disturbance of great intensity central off Southern New England coast moving north-northeastward will cause strong northeast winds and gales. Warnings down to Savannah and Wilmington.”

St. JOHN'S, N. Fld. Feb. 16.—Newfoundland lost the right of self-government today. Henceforth, until the credit of the country has been restored and finances rehabilitated, the British Island dominion will be ruled by a commission. Governor Sir David Murray Anderson, three British members and three native Newfoundlanders were designated by the British government as the ruling commission. Their tenure is indefinite, their only assignment to guide the crisis brought on by near default of her bond interest. Plans for the installation of a commission, suspension of the island's legislature and abrogation of the dominion charter were made on the basis of a report by a commission.
London, England, Feb. 19.—UP— The Prince of Wales will represent King George V at the funeral on Thursday of Albert I, King of the Belgians, it was announced today.

London, Feb. 18. — (AP) — England today mourned Albert, king of the Belgians, as if he were one of their own, so close had been his relations with the people of this country during the World War and since. King George and Queen Mary both wore mourning in public this afternoon, court mourning was announced, and flags were flown at half staff throughout London.

Brussels, Feb. 19 (UP)—Belgium, mourning a beloved king, today prepared to honor him in death and to crown formally as Leopold III, his 32 year old eldest son. Parliament was summoned to meet in special session today to hear officially the news that King Albert I had been killed by a fall from a mountain cliff. The king’s body, clad in the uniform of a general which he wore with gallantry in the World War, will be brought from Laeken Palace, outside Brussels, to the royal palace here, where it will lie in state on a giant catafalque tomorrow and Wednesday. The funeral was set for Thursday. Kings, princes and the president of France, departing from rigid tradition against a French chief executive leaving his own country, will attend. Formal Oath. Leopold will take the formal oath of office Friday. The coronation ceremonies will come later, at a time when the intense grief for the dead kin

Press) Brussels, Feb. 19--King Albert, the beloved hero-king of the Belgians, is dead—a victim of the sport of mountain climbing which he loved so well. His tiny nation has been plunged into the deep sorrow it knew when King Albert was leading its soldiers against overwhelming odds in the world war. The late monarch was 58 years old and his son, Crown Prince Leopold, who will become king in his stead, is 32. A piece of frostbitten rock, crumbling in the strong fingers of the royal hand, cost Belgium her ruler and the world an enlightened monarch in an accident which climaxed what the king had planned as a simple Saturday afternoon of sport. Death came to the king some time in the late hours of Saturday but, by a curious quirk of fate, his subjects had no knowledge of his death until early Sunday morning. 1934-12-24.text: LONDON, Dec. 24.—A “gentleman’s agreement between Scotland Yard and the underworld will enable Scotland Yard to release from duty all but 25 of its staff tomorrow. Crooks traditionally keep an unwritten truce on Christmas in London and nearly all of Scotland Yard's 500 officers will be enabled to enjoy the holiday—though it is true that 309 men can be recalled within ten minutes.

Glasgow, Dec. 23.— (4) — Mrs. Pauline Stephens was arrested late Saturday at her ranch home near Tampico, charged with the murder, nearly three years ago, of her husband, James R. Stephens, pioneer resident and one time sheriff of Valley County. On January 27, 1932, Stephens was found lying in a room at his ranch home, shot twice in the head and once in the abdomen. The discovery was made after Mrs. Stephens had run to the home of neighbors, saying that her husband had shot himself. Charge The arrest of Mrs. Stephens by Sheriff Al Fassett yesterday followed the filing of an information by County Attorney Thomas Dignan, in which the degree of murder was not specified. In a statement issued today, Dignan said the action was prompted as the result of additional evidence uncovered following a lengthy investigation. At the time of Stephens’ death a coroner's jury returned a verdict of ‘death

Restaurants received special permission to remain open an hour later than usual on Christmas and New Year’s eve. Fog closed in over part of the city. PARIS, Dec. 24.—(#)—President Albert Lebrun commuted to life imprisonment today the sentence to the guillotine of Violette Noziere, 19-year-old convicted slayer of her father, as a result of her mother’s appeal for clemency. Mme. Noziere had begged the president for mercy although the daughter tried to kill her as well. Testimony at the trial was to the effect that Violette had poisoned her father and attempted to dispose of her mother in the same fashion in order to secure an inheritance. In the first stages of the trial Mme. Noziere was one of the most bitter witnesses against her daughter, but later she relented and they were reconciled.

Athens..-(UP)— An attempt to assassinate Minister of War George Kondylis was averted today when explosives inserted in a book, said to have been a Christmas present, failed to explode when the package was opened. An unidentified man delivered the package addressed to Kondylis to the war office. The package contained the book, written in English: its interior had been carefully cut out and the explosive inserted. Kondylis is one of Greece's best known soldiers. Born in 1879, he was educated in the Athens School of War and was an officer in the Cretan revolution of 1896. He was promoted to regimental commander in 1917 and division general in 1923. In 1926 he organized the movement for the overthrow of the Pagalos dictatorship.

TOKYO, Dec. 22 (#)—Incited by rumors of an alleged case of international espionage for which Catholic fathers were blamed, several hundred inhabitants of the Island of Amamio-Shima destroyed several churches on the island, the newspaper Kokumin Shimbun said today. The newspaper said a boycott had been started against Catholics, and added that foreign Catholic priests and missionaries were evacuating the island for safety. Confirmation of the reported violence was not obtainable. There are fifteen Catholic churches on the island and also a number of Canadian Catholics. Amamio-Shima is a large Japanese island 200 miles southeast of Kyushu.

Tokyo, Dec. 23.—Although further details were lacking concerning the reported Soviet “invasion” of the Tungning district of Manchoukuo—a remote locality with infrequent communications—officials at Tokyo and Hainking said today they did not believe anything had occurred likely to cause a serious clash. The war office and the foreign office in Tokyo both lacked official information of the alleged incident in which Soviet infantry troops from Siberia were reported encamped and installing military equipment in Manchoukuan territory. No Warlike Preparations. Neither in Tokyo nor in Hainking were there any evidences that the incident was regarded seriously, and certainly no warlike preparations were being made. With negotiations for the transfer of the Chinese Eastern railway to Manchoukuo approaching conclusion, authorities considered the Russo-Japanese and Russo-Manchu relations the most ami

TOKYO (UP) — Conversations between Manchukuo and Soviet consular authorities sought today to settle ownership of a sandy island by both countries and reportedly occupied by Soviet troops. The island was formed by a change in the course of the Wusulun river near Tunguska, on the eastern Manchukuo border northwest of Vladivostok. Although some sources said Soviet and Manchukuo troops had clashed over possession of the island, official circles generally denied the report. In Hsinking, Manchukuo capital, it was insisted that the dispute was being settled through the regular channels. The Japanese foreign office said it had no reports of a battle. The border question has been a source of numerous disputes between the Russians and the Manchukuoans. The latest disagreement, which dates from last October, has increased demands that the two nations determine a permanent boundary.

1934-11-22.text: LONDON, Nov. 22.—(UP)—Pacific politics, once taboo as calculated to complicate the technical naval conference here, have entered it now as a possible means of saving the conference from failure, it was reported authoritatively today. Without an approach to agreement on strictly naval matters, the talks seemed entering their final stage. Two political questions of vital moment to the United States, Great Britain and Japan, the participating nations, were understood to have arisen, though as yet in vague form: 1. A non-aggression treaty in event the Washington and London naval limitation treaties are permitted to lapse; the accord to be either between Britain and Japan or among Britain, Japan and America. 2. A separate British-American naval agreement under which any increase in the Japanese navy would be met by the United States and Britain. The next conference on the program will be betw

LONDON, Nov. 21.—(#)—Princess Marina—chic and lovely in fur coat, beige ensemble and flat ‘little sailor hat—came to London today, her trousseau shopping done, to be kissed by both her parents-in-law-to-be. Capacity crowds braved wet, foggy weather, the thickest England has had this season, to cheer the future Duchess of Kent at the railway station and at Buckingham Palace. A salvo of lusty cheers greeted Marina as she arrived. Uninterrupted applause that followed for half an hour finally led Marina and her fiancé, the Duke of Kent, to appear on the balcony of an upper floor for an ovation lasting three minutes.

LONDON, (UP) Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, proclaiming that a breakdown of naval limitation would be a world catastrophe, argued in the House of Commons today for equality in naval security. Equality of security, he said, would not necessarily mean that all fleets should be of equal size. His remarks were interpreted in the Commons lobbies as an appeal to Japan to modify her demand for absolute parity.

LONDON, Nov. 21. (AP) — Great Britain, facing Japan’s stubborn stand for full naval equality, today asked the United States for another conference to see what can be done to save the principle of naval limitation from the scrapheap. Soft-spoken Tsuneo Matsudaira, Tokio’s ambassador in London and Japanese delegate to tri-power naval conversations here, told Sir John Simon, British foreign minister, again today that Japan declines flatly to modify her original demand for naval arms equal to Britain's and America’s. The diplomat made equally clear Japan’s refusal to discuss political questions affecting the Pacific in connection with the naval conversations—so clear, in fact, that the British decided to drop their proposal made yesterday that Japan agree to guarantee China’s integrity and the peace of the Pacific.

(BY The Associated Press) Southampton, Eng., Nov. 22,—Princess Barbara Hutton Mdivani caught the S. S. Europa today for New York. She barely made it, for she missed the boat train from London and had to make a speedy automobile drive in order to arrive in time. Her husband, Prince Alexis Mdivani, bade her a hurried farewell. He is going to India to play polo.

LONDON, (AP).—A visit to her future Belgrave Square home which she has never seen was a likely part of Princess Marina's program today. After waving a greeting from a window of Buckingham Palace to a great crowd as dusk fell yesterday, the princess retired early. Her arrival in England for her marriage a week from today to the Duke of Kent (Prince George) had made for an exciting and fatiguing day. To Ask Mere Allowance, J. LONDON, (AP).—British circles appeared hopeful today that a conference tomorrow with American delegates might produce an approach for a compromise agreement in the stalled tri-power naval negotiations. - The British seemed slightly more hopeful after a conference with the Japanese yesterday. The subject of the Anglo-American discussion tomorrow was a matter of speculation, but it was assumed London would try to find a new path to an agreement. One compromise proposal advanced by England was rejected by Japan and received coldly by the United States. Japan was represented as feeling the next move must come from the British or Americans. She has refused to go outside the main issue of a naval treaty and reiterated yesterday that she would not modify her original demand for tonnage equality.

Geneva, Nov. 22—Yugoslavia today lodged a formal complaint against Hungary, asking the League of Nations council to investigate the assassinations of King Alexander of Yugoslavia and Foreign Minister Louis Barthou of France as acts calculated to disturb international peace. M. Fotich, the Yugoslav delegate to the league, sent a letter to J. A. G. C. Avenol, secretary-general, requesting that the matter be placed on the council agenda for discussion. The Yugoslav delegate alleged: "The investigation into the Marseille assassinations brought to light the fact that they were prepared on Hungarian soil by a band of international terrorists."

1934-06-11.text: LONDON, June 11.--(4%—From his comfortable seclusion at Doorn, former Kaiser Wilhelm has bestowed his blessing upon the Hitler regime. In an interview in the London Daily Mail he is quoted as hinting at the belief that Hitler's work may be “crowned” by the restoration of the Hohenzollern monarchy. Although the former ruler, now 75, did not disclose whether he was looking for reinstatement himself he was quoted as saying: ‘The German people have turned me out. If they want me back they will have to come and fetch me.’ Wilhelm indicated he has his eye on the eventual restoration of the monarchy through some member of his family.

Washington, June 11.— The movement toward a general default of all governments owing war debts to the United States, initiated by Great Britain last week, spread today with notification of two additional debtors that they will default on June 15.

LYMPNE, England, June 11.— Capt. George Pond and Lieut Cesare Sabelli hopped off from here today for Rome, their destination when they were forced down at Moy, Ireland, May 16, after a transatlantic flight from New.

| London, June 11.—Praise for Chancellor Hitler’s ‘“marvelous work” was expressed by former Kaiser Wilhelm of Germany in an interview by the Daily Mail Sunday. The former emperor made strikingly outspoken comments on affairs of the world. At Doorn, Holland, his majesty received Randolph Churchill, son of the former British chancellor of the exchequer. Randolph is a staff correspondent of the Daily Mail. He described his majesty as lively and engaging, with an alertness suggesting an age 15 years younger than his actual three score and 15.

LONDON, June 11.—Cesare Sabelli and George Pond, trans-Atlantic aviators, took off at 8:32 a.m. today (4:32 a.m., EST), for Rome. The motor of their airplane Leonardo Da Vinci, in which they flew to Ireland from New York, had been thoroughly overhauled and they expected to reach Rome late today.

U.P)—Former Kaiser Wilhelm of Germany, in exile at Doorn, Holland, seemed today to retain the sweeping view of world politics that characterized him when, before the war, he sought “a place in the sun” for Germany. A special correspondent of The Daily Mail quoted the former emperor as reviewing the problems of China, Japan, India, the League of Nations, the wheat and coffee situations in Argentina and Brazil, modern youth and Nazism. Japan seemed to impress him most, “It is useless to think that the growth of Japanese power in China can be prevented,” he was quoted as saying. “Japan is as capable of giving China peace and order as the British were in giving them to India. Moreover, Japan constitutes in the East a bulwark against Bolshevism as strong as Germany is in the West.” But he emphasized that he looked on the world entirely from the standpoint of a private gentl

ROME, June 10 (4)—Italy’s answer to intensified naval construction in many lands will be to lay down the keels of two 35,000 ton battle ships this year, it was announced officially today. The announcement precedes new conversations on naval limitation to start at London soon; Italy has been invited. The vessels, which will be a powerful addition to the Italian navy, will be built at Trieste and Genoa. It was expected they will be ready for duty by 1940. Italy's 70,000 tons of naval construction granted by the Washington naval treaty will be used up by the new ships. Up to now the nation has refrained from utilizing this tonnage so as “not to prejudice” the result of the Naval Disarmament Conference, an official communique stated.

1934-12-14.text: | Liverpool England (7P)—A quick thinking janitor was credited today with having averted a major disaster when a collapsing floor dropped nearly 500 persons into a terrified mass 14 feet to the floor below. The floor collapsed at St. Clements school while school children and their parents were enjoying a concert celebrating the beginning of the Christmas holidays. Approximately 150 were injured and 33 of them, mostly women and children, were taken to a hospital. Only the presence of mind of the school’s janitor named Doughty, said officials, prevented a major disaster. When the screaming assemblage was plunged downward in darkness, Doughty ran to the basement and cut off the gas supply, eliminating danger of fire and explosion. Rescuers told stories of narrow escapes: A youngster of eight lay helpless, one foot jammed beneath a beam suffering great pain, but he only murmured, “Do hurry p

London, Dec. 18.—Both Japan and the United States are courting Great Britain for a possible future bilateral naval accord, diplomatic quarters said today. This development came with the current conversations of the three greatest sea powers on the threshold of adjournment. They may be resumed next year. The Japanese delegation joined the British in expressing optimism that an agreement may be possible in 1935 and that it would make every effort to reach one when talks are resumed. There appeared little possibility, however, that Tokyo would give up its demand for full equality which deadlocked the present conversations.

NEW YORK, Dec. 14.—(UP)—All hands were rescued today from the Sinking S. S. Usworth in mid-Atlantic. Two men from the rescue ships were lost. NEW YORK, Dec. 14—(4)—Battling mountainous mid-Atlantic seas to rescue the crew of the foundering British steamer Usworth, two members of a lifeboat crew from the Belgian steamer Jean Jadot were lost when their boat capsized, a wireless message to Mackay Radio reported shortly after noon today. Two members of the Usworth's crew, the message said, were rescued from the water when the lifeboat was tossed over in the running seas. WASHINGTON, Dec. 13 ()— Belgium, following the lead of Great Britain, officially informed the United States today that it would make no payment on World War debt installments totaling $21,578,350, due Saturday. Prince Eugene De Ligne, charge d'affaires, announced Belgium's fifth default in a note delivered to the state department. It answered “a please remit” reminder from William Phillips, undersecretary of state.

NEW YORK, Dec. 14 (?)—McKay radio reported today it had picked up a message from the steamer Black Gull stating that the British steamer Usworth, in distress in the North Atlantic, had broadcast an appeal "Please do your best to get us off." The message said the "situation looking precarious" and added the ship was "listing more." Both the Belgian liner Jean Jadot and the Cunard liner Aseania had reached the distressed ship, but found it impossible to get a line aboard because of heavy seas.

LIVERPOOL, Eng. (U.P) — Two hundred persons, most of them children, of 400 who escaped death in a 40-foot fall when the floor of a school assembly hall collapsed, were recovering Thursday from injuries. It was announced officially that no one was killed. Thirty-three remained in hospitals—16 children, 13 women, and four men. Children of St. Clement's school with their parents were crowded into the second floor hall Wednesday night for a Christmas entertainment. There was a minstrel show and after it an exhibition of children’s school work. A boy was singing a song when there was a loud crackling noise. The floor sagged and collapsed. Those in the hall plunged down, buried in debris and blinded by dust. Lights went out. An open fire flickered in a grate in the wall above while gas hissed from broken pipes. New York, Dec. 14 (/P)—A lifeboat crew from the Belgian freighter Jane Jabot succeeded in crossing mountainous seas today to the foundering British steamer Upsworth and removing safely five members of the crew, according to a wireless message picked up by Mackay Radio. The Upsworth, which sent out distress calls to shipping in the North Atlantic, still has 21 members of her crew aboard, the wireless said, but the Cunard liner Ascania was standing by to lower a boat to assist in the rescue. Messages relayed to Mackay from the black diamond freighter Black Gull reported the Upsworth as describing her condition “precarious” and appealing to nearby vessels to “please do your best to get us off.” A second message from the Black Gull, received at 11:40 a.m., reported: “A Jane Jabot lifeboat has succeeded in rescuing five of the crew of Upsworth and the steamship Ascania, Cunard White Star, now

WASHINGTON, Dec. 14.--(UP) - Default of all of this country’s major war debtors on their December 15 installments was made complete today with delivery of notes of regret from France, Italy, Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary. Great Britain and Belgium already had sent word they could not pay. Of the remaining six major debtors, all except Finland were expected to join the “defaulters’ parade” to the state department. A total of $154,729,976.23 is due tomorrow. Finland will keep her record spotless by meeting in full her installment of $228,538. The state department expects that will be the only cash clinking into its till.

1934-12-22.text: London, Dec. 22. (/P)--Four deaths were attributed today to “black out” fog which blanketed most of England yesterday. Highway conditions are the worst in years with visibility ranging from zero to 7 yards. Fog lifted rapidly today but conditions were expected to be about the same during the whole holiday season. One boy lost his way and fell into a canal and was drowned. A motorcyclist was killed when he collided with a horse-drawn wagon. Two others were victims of traffic accidents.

London, Dec, 21 (#) — Until President Roosevelt lets it be known whether he intends to knock any more coppers off America’s 59-cent dollar, Great Britain will fight shy of any move toward stabilization. That was the consensus in financial circles tonight after Neville Chamberlain, Chancellor of the Exchequer, told the Commons today that Britain under present circumstances cannot “risk” stabilization of her currency. The lack of balance between the dollar, the franc and the pound sterling, cited in Chamberlain’s speech as “the real difficulty with the situation,” makes the perils of stabilization too great, it was felt.

| LONDON, Dec. 21. (AP) — Great Britain will stage its own arms inquiry, but just how all-embracing it will be only the national government knows. A royal commission will be given the task of investigating the arms industry, Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald told the House of Commons just before it rose for the Christmas holidays,

LONDON, Dec. 22.--Four persons were dead today and many were suffering from injuries as the result of the most widespread fog in recent years—the second in a month. This fog blanketed England and Scotland late yesterday, whereas the first, though serious, was confined to the south and midlands. Christmas shopping became an ordeal because railways were forced to abandon regular schedules.

LONDON, Dec. 22. — London newspapers, in dispatches from Warsaw, continued today to report a grave plot against the Soviet government. The Daily Telegraph, one of the more conservative papers, reported that a second plot had been unearthed at Kharkov (Charkov), in South Central Russia, and that there were extraordinary troop reinforcements and general precautions on the frontier. The Daily Express reported that Josef Stalin himself would be one of the judges of Gregory Zinoviev and Leo Kamenev, said to be under arrest, and that Stalin would ask France to expel Leon Trotsky as the real motivator of the assassination of Sergei Kirov. In its dispatch, the Daily Telegraph reported from its Warsaw correspondent that 21 Communist leaders were arrested at Kharkov, including the leader of the Ukrainian Communist party and a high Soviet official.

There was no mention of the fate of Gregory Zinoviev and Leo Kamenev, former leaders of world importance, whose arrest was reported abroad. The fact that the 13 men held faced trial before the military collegium was sufficient indication of the seriousness with which the government regarded their cases. It was announced officially that in addition to Leonid Micoliev, the actual assassin of Kirov, the following were held: Antonov, Khanik, Kotolinov, Levin, Mandelshtam, Myasnikov, Rumyantsev, Shatsky, Sokolov, Sositky, Tolmazov, Yuskin and Zvesdov. TOKYO, Dec. 22, (Fi — Rengo Japanese) News agency dispatches from Harbin tonight said Soviet authorities were seeking to avert bloodshed after Soviet infantry troops invaded Manchoukuo from Siberia. The troops, asserted to have crossed the border near Timgning 50 miles south of Suifenho, were surrounded by Manchoukuan troops and their communications cut "in an effort to check their further military activities," the Rengo report said. The dispatches said Soviet authorities had asked Manchoukuo to allow the Russian soldiers to retire with their arms, and proposed an amicable settlement of the affair. This the Manchurian government was reported considering. While the foreign office in Tokyo had no official report of the affair and indicated it did not credit the report, it was admitted Soviet farmers recently entered Manchoukuo.

PARIS, Dec. 21.—France tonight was ready to announce that, as far as she is concerned, the Washington naval treaty expires at the end of 1936. An official announcement, however, denied that the government has any intention of joining Japan in formally denouncing the pact. “Intolerable For France” As Francois Pletri, minister of the navy, termed the pact “Intolerable for France,” high French quarters pointed out that the government, under parliamentary ratification of the treaty in 1923, stands pledged to denounce it if necessary to ensure France's freedom of action at its expiration. “A secret joint session of the chamber of deputies foreign affairs and naval committees decided denunciation was unnecessary in view of

1934-10-12.text: New York.—(AP)—Lady Furness came to New York today determined to back her twin sister, Gloria Vanderbilt, to the limit in her court fight for the custody of her 10-year-old daughter, Gloria Laura Morgan Vanderbilt, and her $2,800,000 fortune. "It is ridiculous," said the American-born British peeress with a French accent. "My sister is a better mother than our own mother. She at least does not turn against her own children as our mother has." Mrs. Laura Kilpatrick Morgan, mother of Lady Furness and Mrs. Vanderbilt, has allied herself with Mrs. Harry Payne Whitney, little Gloria’s aunt, in an effort to have Mrs. Vanderbilt adjudged unfit to have the custody of the child. "I am amazed at my mother’s attitude. I have no idea of what she is doing. She must be overawed."

Meanwhile, the national parliament took oath of loyalty to young King Peter II en route to Belgrade from London and Paris. PARIS. (Copyright by AP.) A "vast international terrorist ring" was trailed by French secret police as Minister of Interior Sarraut resigned after sharp criticism of police failure to protect King Alexander at Marseille Tuesday. That the ten shots Petrus Kalemen fired still echoed through Europe was evidenced when Yugoslavs staged anti-Italian riots and French political observers confidently predicted Premier Doumergue's cabinet would resign en masse for re-organization. Sarraut’s resignation was expected to be only the first of official heads that will roll in consequence of the tragedy. While the interior minister's resignation was not officially announced, it was stated authoritatively that he was determined to leave the cabinet and Doumergue was only withholding the announcement until the cabinet meets Monday. PARIS, Oct. 12 (UP).—Police announced today they had obtained complete confessions from the men involved in the plot to assassinate King Alexander of Yugoslavia and they believed some foreign government may have been involved. Inspector Rene Petit, conducting the examination at Annemasse of the two suspects, Wladislas Benes and Nalis Stikomir (or Novak), said they had cracked completely under merciless cross-examination and admitted they had been ordered to kill Alexander in Paris if the Marseilles attempt failed. Police contended that the thoroughness of the plot, the quantity of false passports and the fact that the men were well supplied with money indicated they had been financed by some government. Paris. (4—Police said tonight they believed King Alexander of Yugoslavia was assassinated by order of a European terroristic organization whose goal is the elimination of governmental leaders. The Surete Nationale declared officially that there was no suspicion however, that any foreign government was implicated in the plot against Alexander. A report published in the United States that a foreign government may be involved is “completely false,” said officials, who added: “We still are seeking to determine the real identity of Kalemen ‘the assassin,’ Rajtich and Novak (two suspects in custody) and the others mentioned in the investigation, their political affiliations, and who were their accomplices, for they certainly had accomplices.”

(Copyright, 1994, The United Press) PARIS, Oct. 12.—(U.P)—The plot which resulted in the assassination of King Alexander and Foreign Minister Louis Barthou assumed complicated international proportions today. Informed sources believed the men who plotted the assassinations were trying to embroil France, Italy, Jugoslavia, Rumania and Czechoslovakia in a mad scheme to advance the cause of Croatian independence. Secret police, interrogating two suspects at Annemasse, on the Swiss frontier, sought to find a possible connection between the Alexander-Barthou assassinations and the assassination by Nazis of Austria. Suspects Confess. Police announced today that after hours of ceaseless questioning these suspects confessed as follows: They are members of an international secret society whose name they would not give. 1934-05-12.text: St. Andrew's Scotland, May 12— (AP)—The United States successfully defended the Walker Cup, international golf trophy, by trouncing their British challengers today in the singles competition after capturing three of the four foursomes yesterday. The Americans quickly clinched their eighth successive triumph in the team battle by piling up lopsided margins in the first four singles. They were paced by Johnny Goodman of Omaha, national open titleholder, who rallied to trounce the Hon. Michael Scott, British amateur champion, 7 and 6, and W. Lawson Little of San Francisco, victor over Burly Cyril Tolley, by 6 and 5. The sixth and seventh victories for the Americans, in two days of play, settling the issue, were tallied by Captain Francis Ouimet of Boston and George T. Dunlap, Jr. of New York, the amateur champion. Ouimet disposed of Leonard Crawley, 5 and 4, while Dunlap took the measure of

LONDON, May 11—(AP)—Arguments that Great Britain can pay her American war debt because she has a budget surplus were branded today as “fallacious” by Sir John Simon, the foreign secretary. He cited two reasons: “First, because that which lies at the back of the difficulty in connection with these vast international payments is not the question as to whether a particular country has a budget surplus. “It is an injury to world trade and world recovery if we are to contemplate the transfer of enormous quantities which we indeed receive in the form of goods but which we are asked to pay back in the form of money. “Second, it must be borne in mind that, in relation to the national wealth, British taxation last year was at least twice as heavy as the corresponding taxation in the United States.” His remarks were made in a speech at Manchester while newspapers were describing as unfair indicati

ST. ANDREWS, Scotland—(P)—America retained the Walker cup, world’s premier amateur team golf trophy, this afternoon by a final count of nine matches to two, with one match halved. Leading three to one after yesterday's foursomes, America’s flashy crew won six of the eight 36-hole singles matches, halved one and lost one. Johnny Goodman, Lawson Little, George Dunlap, Francis Ouimet, Johnny Fischer and Gus Moreland all won their matches. Jack Westland halved with Eric McRuvie. Max Marston, portly Philadelphian returning to the Walker cup team after an absence of ten years, went down before T. A. ‘Tony’ Torrance, but he tried fighting.

| St. Andrews, Scotland, May 12 | (INS)—Carrying everything before them in an amazing sweep of sheer power, America once again won the Walker Cup from Great Britain’s golfers today. This time by a margin of so great as to leave not the slightest shred of doubt that this is a vast unequal series. The Americans won by 7 matches to 1, their victory being assured long before the twelve matches of the set were concluded. More than that, the manner of their winning was even more impressive. Johnny Goodman, American open champion, beat the Hon. Michael Scott, British champion, by the tremendous matter of 7 up and 6 to play. In the second match, Lawson Little, playing marvelously this morning in the wind and rain and this afternoon in the sunshine, won from Cyril Tolley, former British champion, by as much as 6 and 5.

LONDON, May 11. —(#)— Argentina’s opposition tonight wrecked an international project for boosting wheat export prices by ten per cent as drought in many countries lifted prices above the level sought by artificial means. One European delegate to the conference said that “God has done what we could not do.” He said severe drought conditions in the United States, Canada, and Europe had increased wheat prices recently “much more than the delegates ever hoped they could under the minimum price scheme.”

Bucharest, May 12.—Reports from Paris that Madame Magda Lupeseu had been twice wounded at her hotel were generally discredited here today. The reports said the shooting of King Carol's friend occurred at 10:30 a.m. today. At noon, however, King Carol delivered a speech at the opening of a Bucharest exhibition. Passersby at the Hotel Splendid where the shooting was said to have occurred reported that nothing unusual was apparent.
Geneva, May 12. (AP)—Hungary appealed to the League of Nations today against Yugoslavia because of "frontier incidents."
Helsingfors, Finland, May 11.—(AP)—Six hundred families lost their homes in a fire which swept through the village of Kannus today. No casualties were reported.

1934-02-06.text: Paris, Feb. 6 (Tuesday). (#)—The New York Herald’s Paris edition said in a dispatch from London today that Lord Ashley, 33-year-old son and heir of the ninth Earl of Shaftesbury, has filed a divorce petition with Gordon, Dadds and company, solicitors, and that sealed copies of the petition will be served today. The newspaper said that Douglas Fairbanks Sr., American actor, was named as correspondent. Lord Ashley was reported to have claimed no damages in the petition. If the suit is not defended it may possibly come to trial April 12, the dispatch from London said, but if contested it may not be heard for some time.

London, Feb. 6, (INS)—Douglas Fairbanks, Sr., was formally served today with papers naming him as correspondent in a divorce action presented by Lord Ashley, heir to the Earl of Shaftesbury, against Lady Ashley, the former Sylvia Hawkes, actress. The papers were served upon Fairbanks at the office of his solicitor, F. P. M. Guedalla. Fairbanks declined to make a statement, other than that he was planning to leave today for a holiday on the continent. Serving of the papers upon Fairbanks followed announcement by solicitors representing Lord Ashley that suit had been filed. These steps constitute the only definite action yet revealed in a suit that is certain to become an “affaire célèbre” throughout the world. Details of the suit are as yet unknown but it is believed here that association of Lady Ashley and the famous American motion picture actor at a West End luxury hotel and aboard a y

Chicago. — (AP) — The British government’s motion to take custody of John Factor was continued today to March 8, permitting the state of Illinois to use him again as its principal witness against his alleged kidnappers, Roger Touhy and two codefendants. Factor is wanted in England on a charge of receiving money known to have been fraudulently obtained. The second trial of the alleged abductors will open February 15.

LONDON, Feb. 6. (U.P)—Hope of an eleventh hour settlement which would prevent a Franco-British trade war vanished today. Walter Runciman, president of the Board of Trade, told the House of Commons: “The government will not enter into trade negotiations on the unequal basis constituted by the discrimination imposed by France.’ This was the day for the expiration of Britain's ultimatum, threatening reprisals unless France restores the reduced British import quotas, as she did in the case of the United States. Hence, British reprisals were believed imminent.

LONDON, (P)—London lowered the world gold price Tuesday while the American dollar remained strong. The gold price was fixed at 139 shillings 8 pence with the dollar at $4.93 3/4, equivalent to $34.38. Monday the rate was 140 shillings. The pound opened at $4.93 1/2, unchanged from Monday night, and strengthened only fractionally to $4.93 1/4 in early trading.

PARIS. (UF). France's political crisis approached a climax that threatened to cause riots, wrecked careers and possibly a dictatorship. Government buildings were guarded in anticipation of bloody riots when the new Edouard Daladier government faces the chamber of deputies Tuesday to undergo questioning on its proposals to appease popular anger over the Stavisky banking scandal which involves high political figures. Daladier was prepared to promise the chamber that if it gave him a vote of confidence he would turn over to a parliamentary inquiry committee thousands of checks and other documents—which he as well as opposition members of parliament believe will bring political ruin to prominent men who befriended the late Alexandre Stavisky. The government was reported to have mobilized tanks and two divisions of troops near Paris, to reinforce soldiers and 15,000 police already here. The g

PARIS. (A challenge to the week old government of Premier Daladier in the form of a demonstration by 1,000 war veterans in front of the president's residence was put down by mounted republican guards. That the government feared other disorders was indicated by the mobilization of troops armed with machine guns in the capital as the stern-faced Daladier plunged grimly into preparations for the fight for his cabinet’s life in the chamber of deputies Tuesday. Several thousand police massed in the neighborhood of the Elysee palace and the nearby ministry of the interior, which the crowd also tried to reach, blocked the manifestants, members of the Croix de Feu veterans’ organization. The former soldiers, whose protest was the first of a series of riotings to occur near President Lebrun’s residence, announced they would stage further demonstrations Tuesday night.
