TOKYO, Feb. 6 (P)—Koki Hirota, foreign minister, told the house of peers today that Japan is endeavoring to learn whether a secret treaty exists between the United States and China which obliges Americans to assist in China's aviation development. The foreign minister said the foreign office and the Japanese army also were seeking to determine whether American financial participation in the new airlines southward from Shanghai constitutes a violation of China’s old promises to Japan not to alienate any portion of the Fukien seacoast. (The Pan-American Airways, the international United States airline, recently went into partnership with the Chinese government to establish an air route in China. Mail and passenger planes, piloted by Americans, are now in regular operation over the routes.) Hirota’s statement was in answer to a question by Atsuhi Akaike, who asserted that the new Chinese ai

1934-09-03.text: (Sv United Press) Hardin, Manchukuo, Sept. 3.—— Fatigued but uninjured, Robert Lury, young American held captive with 79 other persons by Manchurian bandits, told today of the hardships the prisoners underwent before Japanese and Manchukuoan sailors rescued them. Lury and E. F. Johansen, a Dane who represents the Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Film Co. in Manchukuo, were the only Caucasians among the 80 passengers kidnapped from the Hsinking-Harbin Night Express last Thursday night. The outlaws wrecked the train, killing five Orientals and injuring many others. Those who escaped uninjured were forced to leave their clothes and baggage behind and to accompany the bandits on their flight into the marshlands of the Sungari River. "Our arms were tied behind our backs," Lury said. "We marched with a rope around our necks and all night long we were prodded like sheep. "Sometimes we waded in water which r

HARBIN, Manchukuo, Sept. 3. — Safe after a terrifying experience as captives of bandits, nine men, one an American, thanked Japanese troops Monday for their sensational rescue. Robert M. Lury, an American, E. F. Johansen, a Dane, and seven bandits on a wooded sand bar in the Sungari river. The soldiers chased the outlaws and in a spirited exchange of fire killed 25 of them. Fifteen more were wounded.

Harbin, Manchuria, Sept. 2.-- Nine men, one of them an American, dramatically rescued from their Manchurian bandit kidnappers by the Japanese gunboat Konei, came to Harbin today to tell how narrowly they had escaped death. The nine—Robert M. Lury, naturalized American, E. F. Johansen, Dane, and seven Japanese—were released from the bandits’ hideout, a wooded sandbar on the Sungari river, at 11:30 a. m. today after airplanes, aiding in an intensive manhunt, spotted their captors trying to cross the river. The gunboats Konei and Kokei, with infantry landing parties aboard, were rushed to the place, near the town of Niuiietzu, 40 miles southwest of Harbin, where their rescue was effected after a sharp brush with the bandits. Seized at Wreck Scene Lury and Johansen, both employees of the Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer company, together with the seven Japanese, were seized after the bandits had wrecked

HSINGKING, Manchukuo, Sey 3. UP—Fire damaged a section of the imperial palace of Manchukuo today but the flames did not reach the quarters reserved for Emperor Kang Teh and the empress. The fire was discovered in the rooms of the household staff. The flames spread to other rooms, but within 40 minutes the fire was brought under control. The young emperor, Henry Pu-Yi, boy ruler of China, is said to have remained quiet in his room while soldiers and firemen extinguished the fire.

ARBIN, Manchuria, Sept. 2. — (P)— After dramatically rescuing nine men, one of them an American, kidnapped by bandits near Wuchia Thursday night, Japanese troops gave chase to the outlaws and killed 25 of them, the commander of the rescuing Japanese gunboat reported. Fifteen of the kidnappers were wounded in the fighting that followed the rescue, the commander said. He expressed the belief he had accounted for the entire band. Robert M. Lury, naturalized American who with his eight companions, seven Japanese and H.E. P. Johansen, Dane, were liberated by Japanese landing forces from the gunboat Konei early Sunday, graphically described the horrors of their experience. “We owe our lives to the heroism of Kumetaro Murakami (Japanese employee of the Manchukuoan government) in crying out “despite threats that we would be killed if we yelled out,” he said. Murakami’s outcry brought the rescue

By The Associated Press Hollywood, Sept. 3—The voice of Russ Columbo, familiar to millions of radio listeners and motion picture fame is still. A sudden shot from an ancient dueling pistol accidentally discharged in the hand of a friend sent a bullet into Columbo's left eye and he died within a few hours late last night. He had called yesterday at the home of Lansing B. Brown, Jr. They were looking at firearms in Brown's collection. "I was absent-mindedly fooling with one of the guns," Brown told detectives. "I was pulling back the trigger and clicking it time after time. I had a match in my hand and when I clicked it evidently the match caught in between the hammer and firing pin. There was an explosion. Russ slid to the side of his chair." Brown was not held but the county coroner said an inquest will be held. Columbo did not regain consciousness.

ODESSA, Sept. 2.——Say these old Russians can really fly. We had about a 65 to 70 foot ceiling today and they stuck right under it. That's what the Japanese are more afraid of than any other thing is that these guys will outfly ’em. Commercial aviation not hot but military and it looks like they got ’em by the thousands. Who hasn't pictured Odessa on the Black Sea? Russia and Turkey been fighting over this for a thousand years. Do you remember it in the Russian picture Potemkin, that long row of steps from the ocean to the hill? Well they are right in this hotel. Yours, WILL.

1934-08-01.text: LONDON (#) — Parliament adjourned today with British recovery at a crisis. For the first time since 1932, when Britain began her steady climb out of the depression, business activity has slumped. The drop is a slight one, but it is the first, and the dominant economic question is whether it is merely temporary or the initial sign of a serious recession in the near future. Whichever it turns out to be, observers say, the limits to Britain's recovery will be reached at a point well below her pre-depression prosperity unless there is an upward trend in world trade.

(The Associated Press) VIENNA, July 31—Almost six days to the hour after Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss died, two Nazis accused of implication in killing him were hanged in the prison yard today. The official account of their execution declared that the Nazis died with the shout “heil Hitler” on their lips. One, Franz Holzweber, convicted of high treason as the leader of the putsch in which Dollfuss died, also shouted "I die for Germany!” the official account stated. Asks Forgiveness Holzweber was followed on the gallows by Otto Planetta, former army staff sergeant, who said he killed Dollfuss without intending to do so and begged forgiveness in court. Holzweber and Planetta were the first Nazis to be hanged in Austria, despite numerous acts of terrorism charged against them before they broke into civil war after the putsch and the killing of Dollfuss last Wednesday. | VIENNA, Aug. 1.—Fascist Austria charged Nazi Germany today with direct complicity in the bloody revolt that took the life of Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss. - The charge was made on the basis of coded documents found in the shirt and shoes of Franz Heel, a secret courier, arrested at Kollerschiag on his way from Munich, headquarters of the German Nazi party and Austrian Nazis refuged in Germany. Col. Walter Adams, Minister of Propaganda, in a radio speech, said the documents showed the German government was connected with the revolt. The documents implicated Anton Rintelen, Austrian minister to Italy, a trusted aide of Dollfuss. Evidence that he conspired with Nazis caused his arrest. He shot himself. Yesterday he was removed to a prison hospital and was retired along with other prominent officials on two-thirds of the normal civil service pension.

PARIS, Aug. 1 (UP).--General Staffs of half a dozen countries pored anew over war plans today because Field Marshal Paul Von Hindenburg—a few years ago the personification of German militarism—was dying. Fears of an impending crisis in German affairs, belief that Austria's troubles were just beginning, talk of a Hohenzollern restoration in Germany and a Hapsburg restoration in Austria excited continental capitals. (Copyright 1934, by the Associated Press) VIENNA, Aug. 1.—Austria officially pointed an accusing finger at Germany today for the blood which flowed from a Nazi attempt to seize the government one week ago. An announcement approved by the cabinet said directions to Austrian Nazis were sent into the country several weeks ago from Germany. The plans, which included the possibility of civil war, said Walter Adam, propaganda chief in a radio address, were seized in the shoes of a man arrested in upper Austria. This man confessed receiving $100 for delivering the documents—now partially decoded, Adam said. Another government announcement stated Franz Holzweber and Otto Planetta, who were hanged yesterday for their part in the putsch, died with cry 'Heil Hitler;' on their lips. TORONTO, Ont., Aug. 1.—James Stanley McLean, millionaire Canadian packer, was saved from kidnapping by a police coup, provincial police announced today. They held five men, three on a charge of conspiracy to commit an indictable offense namely kidnapping, and two as material witnesses. Police said a gang had planned to kidnap McLean today. He was to be captured at his home, beaten and drugged, taken to the outskirts of Toronto and held in a specially prepared tunnel under a house for $100,000 ransom. Police said they had found the tunnel, which had been stocked with several boxes of supplies. Frank Woods, 33, one of the men held, was accused of being the brains of the plot. He is a former employee of Canada Packers, Ltd., of which McLean is president. The others held as conspirators were Harry Leslie, 40, and James Leslie, 38, brothers and proprietors of a tourist camp. Vienna, Aug. 1—Austrian interest was pointed anew toward Germany Tuesday night, following the hanging of two Nazis held responsible for the assassination of Chancellor Dollfuss, and official publication of a deciphered document purporting to show plans to overthrow the Austrian government were matured in the Reich. Propaganda Chief Walter Adam, in the name of the cabinet, announced over the radio that plans for the Nazi putsch, including the possibility of civil war, were found in the shoes of a man arrested at Kollerschlag, Upper Austria. The fact that the cabinet made the document public was held by some to indicate that no definite peace was envisaged. Others interpreted it as a step to force the German government to demonstrate its lack of complicity by acting against Austrian exiles now in Germany. TOKYO, July 31—(AP)—Keisuke Okada, new premier of Japan, whose viewpoint on naval questions was awaited eagerly by the world, said today he believes navies should be reduced to the smallest proportions possible. But he added that Japan is dissatisfied with the arbitrary 5-5-3 ratio fixed by the Washington treaty of 1922 as Japan’s proportion of capital ships in relation to the United States and Great Britain. Whether the Washington treaty is to be abrogated has not yet been decided, he said. “I cannot favor the present ratio principle in naval limitation, which hurts the self-respect of certain nations,” said the premier who was called to the head of the government from a long career as a naval officer. His observations were made at his first meeting with foreign newspaper correspondents. “I hope some better method than the ratio principle can be devised, but at present I am not in a pos

1934-04-23.text: LONDON, April 23 (UP).—Great Britain has addressed a communication to Japan seeking clarification of the recent Tokyo pronouncement of policy in the Far East, Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, informed the House of Commons today.

LONDON, April 22.—(AP)— Hopes of curbing the European armaments race and relieving the increased tension between France and Germany tonight were pinned desperately to Anglo-Italian conversations to be inaugurated in London tomorrow by Mussolini’s envoy, Fulvio Suvich, foreign under-secretary. The new Japanese declaration of policy, threatening activities of western powers in China, is expected to occupy the talks between Suvich and British ministers to a lesser degree. They will discuss all international problems of vital interest to England and Italy, it was announced. A more aggressive attitude by Italy than Great Britain is expected to be directed toward the Japanese manifesto. Italy’s concern over what its responsible leaders have openly described as a Japanese menace to the western world is attributed here to Japanese-Italian friction in Abyssinia as well as Asia. (Copyright, 1931, by United Press) GENEVA, April 20.—League of Nations circles forecast today a dramatic showdown on disarmament May 23. That is the date when representatives of the nations in the world disarmament conference will re-examine the flying strings of the many-sided problem of arms control. There are even unconfirmed rumors that France may insist upon an investigation of German armament before consenting to negotiate any sort of a disarmament treaty. By the differences of France, Germany and Great Britain form but one section of the problem as a whole. A tendency is seen in Geneva to link what one official called the “disturbed” disarmament situation with developments in the Far East growing out of the newly-stated Japanese policy that western powers must keep hands off China, Some progress was seen by well-informed sources here in the Brit-

(Copyright, 1934, by United Press) Paris, April 20 (UP)—Belgium has decided definitely to extend along the German frontier to the sea the “wall of steel” that France has built on her part of the border from Switzerland to Belgium, it was learned today. It was understood that the Belgian staff submitted the plans to the French general staff, which made suggestions for further strengthening. Invisible Barrier As plans are now, military engineers believe that between Germany on one side and France and Belgium on the other, there will be an invisible wall which no army can pass. French authoritative circles said that the Belgian wall probably would be completed within a year when the two countries would lie behind fortifications of steel and concrete really extending from the North Sea to the Mediterranean Sea—for France’s system of forts on the southwest extends from Switzerland to the sea

ROME, April 21 (4).—Guglielmo Marconi, famous scientist and inventor of modern wireless telegraphy, said today that there is no doubt as to the authenticity of the phenomenon of the electric woman, Signora Anna Monaro. From Signora Monaro’s breast, several times every night while she is asleep, there emanates enough light to illuminate a room. “Signora Monaro was brought to Rome at my initiative as head of the national council of research,” said Marconi, “following the indisputable testimony of a number of doctors and credible persons who saw the light come from Signora Monaro’s breast sufficiently strong to light up a room. “This testimony coming from such sources cannot be questioned.”

MADRID. (Special) — ‘Anti-fascists and extremists laid siege yesterday to Madrid and surrounding towns, leaving two dead and eleven wounded in a series of bitter clashes with their opponents and with the authorities. The disorders, flaring despite heavy government precautions, were simultaneous with a strike in the capital that tied up transportation services and public utilities, threatening to become general. Extremists were aroused to a massive meeting of 40,000 Catholic youths demonstrating their loyalty to the popular Agrarian party in nearby El Escorial, a huge enclosure combining a convent, a church, a palace and a mausoleum, located in wild and barren country on a mountainous slope 31 miles from Madrid. Heavy property destruction accompanied loss of life and personal injuries in Madrid and its suburbs. Seven bombs were exploded in one church on the outskirts of the city, which wa

CANTON, China, April 23—An army of 20,000 Communists was reported today to have delivered a crushing defeat to Nanking Nationalist government forces in a battle at Chiceng on the Kiangsi-Fukien border. Dispatches said the Communists surrounded and disarmed five regiments of 7,000 men. As a result, the Canton government ordered a hurried reinforcing of frontier garrisons.
Stockholm, March 31, (A—The Swedish royal board of telephone, telegraph and radio showed a net surplus in 1933 of 30,079,800 kroner, or some 3,000,000 kroner more than in 1932.

1934-07-29.text: VIENNA, July 28 (UP)--While government forces were busy crushing the Austrian Nazi rebellion, Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss, victim of political hatred and assassination, was accorded a royal funeral today. In a setting as magnificent as that of Austria's last emperor, the strong men of the little chancellor's dominant party gathered to eulogize the lost leader and to demonstrate their control over an inflammable civil crisis. Meanwhile fighting between troops and Nazis continued in the provinces. Flowers Bank City Hall The small city hall, wherein the chancellor's body lay in state, was banked with flowers. Wreaths sent from every nation in Europe and masses of bright colored flowers sent by his friends filled every corner of the old structure. At 2:30 p.m., when the first ceremonial began, every business activity in Vienna ceased and every wheel stopped turning. Resistance to the gover

(Copyright, 1934, by Associated Press) VIENNA, July 28.—The spirit of the assassinated Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss was invoked today by Acting Chancellor Ernst von Starhemberg to plead before the throne of God for Austria's independence, as thousands lined up before the Vienna city hall to pay their last honor to the martyred chancellor. Other hundreds of thousands lined the streets through which his body was carried. Millions of persons in every quarter of the world listened to the broadcast of the funeral exercises. Starhemberg’s Eulogy “I am not saying farewell to you, beloved leader, comrade and friend,” declared the tall Von Starhemberg at the casket of his little predecessor, “for, as a Catholic, I know that only that which is mortal of you will perish. You will continue to live. “Already, you have entered the proud history of our fatherland. I implore you to be our mediator befo

By The Associated Press Vienna, July 28—Sporadic fighting continued in several outlying provinces of Austria today, notably Carinthia and Styria, but the day upon which Engelbert Dollfuss was buried was also the day the Austrian government could consider itself in control of the situation. As the slain chancellor was laid to rest after an impressive funeral service, rifles and machine guns—and in some cases artillery—in the hands of loyal troops were steadily suppressing the last of the Nazi rebels. A state of general nervousness both in government circles and among the populace continued, however, making possible such tragic events as shootings at Graz in which three persons were killed and a woman was wounded. This shooting appeared to have resulted from nervousness on the part of the troops. They started firing after a guard had shot a boy on a bicycle who failed to halt upon command.

MALIPAX, N. S., July 24—A bare report of a sea tragedy which claimed the lives of nine Nova Scotia fishermen was received here today in a wireless message from the Danish steamship Alssund, which advised that a Lunenburg schooner had been wrecked by an explosion. The Alssund’s captain said the majority of the schooner's crew were safe aboard his vessel, but nine were still missing. The message came to the east coast radio here through its Canso station, which was endeavoring to obtain further details from the steamship.

(Copyright 1974, by the Associated Press) Vienna, July 28. (AP)—Thousands of watching Austrians wept freely tonight as the bronze casket containing the body of their assassinated chancellor, Engelbert Dollfuss, was borne at the finish of a long funeral procession in the ancient Cathedral of St. Stephen. Even the foreign diplomats present, inured to funerals of state, gave vent to their emotions, but Frau Dollfuss, who entered the cathedral supported by Acting Chancellor von Starhemberg and Fritz Stockinger, minister of commerce, was dry-eyed. Only the privileged could enter the somber Gothic edifice to hear Theodore Cardinal Innitzer pronounce the funeral oration. He spoke with great emotion of the hopes which had animated the Chancellor May 1 when he attended a service there which he hoped would mark the beginning of a new era in Austrian history. VIENNA, July 28—Police reported today the discovery of documentary evidence linking Nazi plotters of Carinthia to interest in Germany. Letters found at the home of the director of the state school of engineering and mailed from Germany were said to have given instruction for the uprising.

HALIFAX, N. S.—Wireless messages received today described a schooner wrecked on the Grand Banks with the probable loss of nine lives as the Astrid W., a fishing boat. Six survivors are being brought to shore by the Danish steamer Alsund.

BERLIN, July 28 — Delay in the formal acceptance by Austria of Franz Von Papen as special minister was causing an undercurrent of worry here tonight; despite official statements to the effect that the matter could not be looked upon as serious. Wilhelmstrasse declared that the delay in approving the appointment of the conservative Catholic was easily explained by the day's events in Vienna. Nevertheless, callers at the foreign office got a distinct impression that the postponement was causing worry, lest it develop an "incident." Austrian officials were said here to have resented Chancellor Hitler’s announcement of Van Papen’s appointment to succeed the recalled Kurt Rieth without first consulting Vienna, in accordance with diplomatic usage. The cabinet, with Hitler presiding, was understood to have met in Munich today to discuss foreign affairs, particularly the Austrian situation. ROME

1934-12-15.text: NEW YORK, Dec. 14 (4)—Mackay Radio reported receipt of a message from the liner Ascania stating that all survivors of the foundering British steamer Usworth were rescued today in heavy seas in mid-Atlantic. Apparently 12 lives had been lost in the tragedy. All of them went down when a lifeboat from the Belgian steamer Jean Jadot capsized. Two of the dead were definitely known to have been of the lifeboat’s crew. Of 12 of the crew taken off the Usworth in the capsized boat, only two were rescued. The Jean Jadot reported that the two were the only survivors they had aboard. The Ascania radioed that there were 18 survivors from the Usworth aboard her. The Usworth was reported to have had a crew of 30.

New York—(AP)—A graphic account of the foundering of the British steamer Usworth, in which was pictured exhausted seamen of the Usworth tossed into the wild seas and choking on oil released from rescue ships to calm the waters, was received in a wireless message to the Radio Marine Corporation today. The message, sent from the rescue steamer Jean Jabot, placed the number of men lost at 12, two from the Jean Jabot’s lifeboat crew and 10 from the Usworth. Advices to Cunard-White Star Line from the liner Ascania reported 17 lost. “It is a terrible tragedy,” stated the message, which made known for the first time that the Jean Jabot itself was in great danger when a heavy cargo of machinery shifted as it raced through moun-

LONDON, Dec. 14.--A last-minute Japanese effort to escape single responsibility for the break-down of tri-power naval conversations here failed today. Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, one of the Japanese delegates, secretly visited Admiral William H. Standley, of the American delegation, and urged the Americans to abandon their intention formally to terminate the conversations. Americans Stand Pat This the Americans refused to do, standing pat on their original decision that the end of the negotiations here and Japan’s denunciation of the Washington treaty, expected Dec. 20, must be simultaneous. In the eyes of the Americans, that will place the blame for the wreck of the conversations—as well as the future of peace in the Pacific and the fate of all further efforts to maintain established principles of government.

NEW YORK, Dec. 14—Twelve seamen apparently lost their lives today in the north Atlantic as a crew of Belgians tried in a frail lifeboat to row British shipsmen to safety. The rescuers, members of the ship's company of the small Antwerp freighter Jean Jadot, put out in face of the worst storm of the winter when the still smaller British freighter Usworth frantically signalled that all hope had been abandoned. The Englishmen, bound from Montreal to Cobh, Ireland, were so exhausted from weary hours of fighting the sea aboard their foundering ship that they were unable to pull on board the lines shot to them by the Belgians. Risking almost certain death in the mountainous waves, the Belgians launched a boat and made one trip from the Usworth to the British liner Ascania, also standing by, with five of the Englishmen on board. Capsize on Second Trip They turned about and made a second trip ac

LONDON (4)—The American delegation to the London naval conversations stood its ground today, grimly awaiting Japan’s formal denunciation of the Washington naval treaty. Despite efforts of British and Japanese groups to persuade the Americans to start for home before the treaty was denounced, the United States delegates were determined to await Tokyo’s action. This stand was resigned to place squarely upon Japan responsibility for the failure of the preliminary negotiations.

Bremen, Germany, Dec. 14 (P)—Chancellor Adolf Hitler’s life was imperiled tonight when his special train, en route from Bremen to Berlin, roared into an autobus near here, instantly killing 13 persons. A fourteenth died later in the hospital to which the seven other passengers of the bus, all seriously injured, were taken. Those killed and injured were described as theatrical performers. Though rudely shaken by the crash, which occurred while his train was returning at high speed from christening ceremonies held at Bremen for the new 18,000-ton North German Lloyd liner, Hitler alighted from the train and walked the mile back up the track where the demolished bus and the bodies lay. After lifting his hand in the Nazi salute over the torn and broken bodies of the dead, Hitler himself helped to pick up the scattered remains. Aboard the train were such Nazi notables as General Werner von Blo

Helsingfors, Finland, Dec. 14, (4) —Finland "promised to pay" the war debt she owes the United States, and she’s paying—because "it's the only honest thing to do." Thus Risto Ryti, quiet-spoken governor of the Bank of Finland, explained to the Associated Press today his government's action in sending to the United States $280,000 due this mid-month on the national war debt. Finland will make formal payment on the amount tomorrow, the day the installment comes due, although, Ryti said, she is well aware she may be the only nation to do so. "It is only natural that we should," he said. "We signed a contract. We promised to pay. It’s the only honest thing to do." Ryti, whose careful management of the Bank of Finland has steered the nation into financial clear waters, made it plain that he spoke only for Finland. "Of course our debt is small," he said, "and, strictly speaking, it isn't a war

BERLIN (U.P) — Fifteen members of a theatrical troupe, nine of them women, were dead Saturday, victims of a crash in which a special train carrying Adolf Hitler struck a bus that crashed in fog through the barriers guarding a railway crossing near Verden-On-Aller. Those killed were in the bus. News of the crash was made public here when Paul Joseph Goebbels, minister of propaganda and public enlightenment, said at the end of a speech at the sports palace Friday night: “We may all thank God from the depths of our hearts that our fuehrer has just escaped unhurt from a train crash.” There were outcries of consternation from Goebbels’ audience. Hitler had been to Bremen for the launching of the liner Scharnhorst. Members of the troupe, in their bus, were on the way from Stade to give a performance at Verden-On-Aller. The train, its engine slightly damaged, halted, Hitler left his coach, dire

1934-07-21.text: London, July (New charges of misconduct during recent months were made today against Douglas Fairbanks Sr. and Lady Sylvia Ashley on behalf of Lord Ashley, who is suing for a divorce from his former chorus girl wife. The allegation was made that the famous motion picture actor and Lady Ashley, who now are in Monte Carlo, continued misconduct at “various places and various dates,” which are cited, since Fairbanks was first named as correspondent in the case of February 5. Fairbanks and Lady Ashley will be served, Lord Ashley's attorneys said, but “it will probably take several days.” Arrangements for the service are to be made through their attorneys. The supplementary petition, an attorney explained, requires an answer within 14 days if the couple wish to resist it.

WIMBLEDON, England —UPI— America’s chances of reaching the challenge round for the Davis Cup all but evaporated today when Jack Crawford and Vivian McGrath of Australia captured the opening matches. Playing the inter-final between Australia and the United States, Crawford downed Frank Shields, New York, 6-1, 6-2, 12-10, and McGrath downed Sidney B. Wood, Jr., New York, 7-5, 6-4, 1-6, 9-7.

(By the Associated Press) Berlin, July 20--Adolf Hitler’s party and government are putting in considerable hard work during the vacation season, it was apparent today, on the tasks of reorganizing the storm troop organization and the industrial life of the Reich. The object of the storm troop shake-up, which is proceeding thoroughly under the surface, is the removal of men whose politics and personal lives do not measure up to the rules laid down after the suppression of the “Roehm revolt.” The economic ministry and the special kommisar, Count Ruediger Von Der Goltz, are devoting their efforts toward establishing the self-sufficiency of Germany against the day when lack of foreign exchange or other reasons makes that necessary. Although silence is being observed with reference to the sifting of the wheat from the chaff in the storm troop organization it is known that the record of every

WINNIPEG, July 20.—(UP)—Ten big army bombers pointed toward Alaska on the United States Air Corps’ goodwill flight; were poised here tonight for an early start tomorrow on the next stage of an 8,000-mile journey. They will fly from here to Regina, 300 miles west. From there they will head north to Edmonton tomorrow afternoon. The 31 officers and men comprising the crews of the big ships were entertained tonight by a local flying club and Royal Canadian Air Force officials, together with the mayor and other city dignitaries. The planes arrived at noon today, making a two hours and 26-minute flight from Minneapolis on the third leg of their journey.

PARIS, July 21 (AP)—The future of France, endangered by a clash between Andre Tardieu and radical socialist members of the cabinet, was once again today in the hands of 71 year old “Papa” Gaston Doumergue. Failing to heal the breach within their ranks, the ministers called the premier and former president in to act as umpire. Doumergue will not return to Paris from the south of France until next Tuesday or Wednesday, counting on time to let party passions simmer down. He also has a full weekend to find a solution to the delicate problem with facts presented him by Henri Cheron, minister of justice and vice premier. Louis Barthou, foreign minister

LENINGRAD P)—In a vigorous effort to wipe out a wave of brutality and public disorder, the Soviet court today sentenced five men to death and handed down prison sentences to 51 others, on charges of public violence. Only one of 57 prisoners was acquitted. The group was charged with raiding workers’ clubs, beating and stabbing the members. The raids took place apparently without reason except possible class prejudice. According to the Press, the group was composed chiefly of sons of Kulaks and other declasse persons, although it included a few misguided workers.

Paris, July 21.—(#)—Fatherly Gaston Doumergue, who six months ago pulled France from the verge of civil war, was called upon today to make a supreme effort to hold his strife-torn "truce cabinet" together. After a heated session of the cabinet yesterday, Henry Cheron, minister of justice, sped by automobile to the aged premier in Tournefeuille to ask him to pour oil on the political storm stirred up by Andre Tardieu’s charges: that Camille Chautemps forged his name to a Stavisky check stub. Herriot May Resign. Tardieu and Edouard Herriot, both ministers in the truce cabinet and former premiers, stuck to their guns during today’s cabinet session which discussed the former's accusations against Herriot's fellow-member of the radical socialist party. At the conclusion of a half hour's talk, which showed no signs of peaceful termination, the ministers decided to ask Doumergue to mediate. Her

Warsaw, Poland, July 21.—Flood waters, which have ravished southern Poland for days, today swirled about the edges of Warsaw itself. Residents of endangered zones were hastily evacuated. The Vistula River, swollen by heavy rains, is expected to inundate lower sections of the city. The flood took from 30 to 40 lives when a bridge at Sandomir collapsed yesterday, while at least 120 others are known to be dead in southern provinces, with more than that number missing.

1934-01-09.text: WASHINGTON, Jan. 9 UP)—The government maintained its domestic gold price today at $34.06 an ounce. A stronger dollar abroad failed to prompt a boost in the RFC offer which now has been repeated for 16 business days. Sterling opened in London at $5.08½. At this level, bar gold was worth $32.22 an ounce.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 8 (P)-Great Britain and the United States decided today upon an arrangement whereby $1,000,000 worth of American pork products in addition to the regular quota will be admitted to Great Britain and the British will be given an increase in their liquor quota for the United States from 607,000 gallons to twice that amount. Announcement of this arrangement was made after British ambassador, Sir Ronald Lindsey and the British commercial advisor H. O. Chalkley had a lengthy talk with Secretary of State.

Paris, Jan. 9—(7)—Huge forces of mounted and foot police were rushed to Place Bourbon today to surround the Chamber of Deputies and guard it against a demonstration resulting from reports that police had killed Serge Stavisky, alleged swindler, to keep him from talking. Newspapers in opposition to the government attacked the truth of the police report that Stavisky had shot himself in order to avoid arrest. One loyalist newspaper asked the public to stage the demonstration as a protest against the Stavisky scandal. All streets leading to the chamber were blocked off by massed patrol wagons. Stavisky died in a villa at the foot of the French Alps after he had been traced there by the secret service.

Kyoto, Japan, Jan. 8. (/P)—Seventy-six persons were killed and 48 were injured today in a sudden, uncontrollable stampede at the Kyoto railroad station when mob terror swept a crowd saying farewell to recruits for the imperial Japanese Navy. An investigation showed that most of the victims died at the foot of a stairway leading from a viaduct over the tracks to the station platform. Scores fell there, crushed and suffocated by hundreds who were shoved down the steps by an irresistible pressure from above. A crowd estimated at more than 10,000, far exceeding the capacity of the station, had gathered to bid godspeed to 750 naval recruits aboard a train bound for the Kure naval base. As usual on such occasions semi-military reservists and youth organizations turned out en masse for the leavetaking. The event was a colorful one with national flags and banners much in evidence. The crowd was

KYOTO, Japan (4) — Liquor was held largely responsible by railway authorities today for a panic in which 80 persons were injured. - The authorities said unsteady drinkers of sake caused the commotion in the Kyoto railway station yesterday which resulted in an uncontrollable stampede. Liquor, they added, increased the crowd's unruliness. Scores of persons were crushed and suffocated at the foot of a packed stairway when one, falling, cried out, and the crowd broke into a mad, shifting mass.

CHAMONIX, France, Jan. 8 UP)—Serge “Handsome Alex” Stavisky, charged with having duped French widows and orphans of $40,000,000, ended an international man hunt today by shooting himself as police closed in. “They'll never capture me alive,” friends quoted him as saying. But he was alive when he was captured. The secret service agents who arrested him in a lonely villa at the foot of the French Alps saw him shoot himself in the head with a revolver as they crashed through a locked door. They saw their quarry collapse in a pool of blood and they thought he was dead. They summoned a physician, however, who revived the wounded man. Death Said Near Stavisky lifted his handsome head, then collapsed in a coma. The doctor said only a few hours of life remained to him. Meanwhile the French government fought for its life as a result of Stavisky’s manipulations. Police claimed Albert Dalimier, min

|. ANKARA, Turkey, Jan. 9 (®) — An opportunity for Samuel Insull, former American utilities operator, to seek refuge in Turkey if expelled from Greece was left open today as parliament adjourned until March 1 without ratifying an extradition treaty with the United States. Insull has been ordered by the Greek government to leave Athens January 31,

Chamonix, France, Jan. 9.—(Tuesday)—(#)— Serge Stavisky, founder of the Fallen Bayonne Municipal pawnshop who shot himself when police closed in on him after an international search late yesterday, died early today. “They'll never capture me alive,” friends quoted him as saying. But he was alive when he was captured. The secret service agents who arrested him in a lonely villa at the foot of the French Alps saw him shoot himself in the head with a revolver as they crashed through a locked door. They saw their quarry collapse in a pool of blood and they thought he was dead. They summoned a physician, however, who revived the wounded man. 1934-11-17.text: London, Nov. 16. — (#) — Winston Churchill, former chancellor of the exchequer, tonight charged Germany with “rearming at utmost speed” and pleaded with Great Britain to make herself without delay “the strongest air power in the European world.” England, he said in an address.

CASSOCIALCd Press Foreign sta) Westerham, England, Nov. 16 (AP) -- Alice of Wonderland—Mrs. Alice Hargreaves---died today. She had been ill for weeks, this little 82-year-old lady who, when she was ten, inspired lean, pedantic Charles Lutwidge Dodgson to desert his fusty mathematics and write of Jabberwocks, mad hatters, march hares and similar delightful absurdities. Mrs. Hargreaves’ death occurred in the beamed, red-brick home “The Breaches” where she spent her later years in peace and quiet, peace interrupted two years ago when the world, wishing to commemorate the 100th birthday of the author of “Alice in Wonderland,” brought her out of retirement. Despite her age, she came to the United States, to be whirled from one function to another, marveling at elevators and tall buildings, made honorary doctor of letters by Columbia University, spoke over the radio and returned home thanking

LONDON, Nov. 16. (AP) — Instructions from Tokyo received late tonight by the members of the Japanese delegation were authoritatively said to reject British compromise proposals for naval limitation. It was understood the Japanese will inform the British early next week of the instructions and will urge Great Britain to reconsider in some way the original Japanese demands for full equality on the seas. Since the Tokyo reply will not be given to the British until next week, there was hope in the British circles the Japanese would make concessions either immediately or at some later time. British sources previously indicated a belief that both the United States and Japan were slowly coming around to the British compromise plan.

London, Nov. 17—(P)—Rejection by Japan of British compromises on the all-important question of naval equality threatened today to deadlock the tri-power naval conferences tighter than ever. It was authoritatively learned that the Japanese government had instructed its delegates from Tokyo to reject the English suggestions that Japan be granted naval equality in name but not in fact. This would bring the negotiations, undertaken by the United States, Japan, and Great Britain for the purposes of reducing naval armaments, to an impasse again. The Tokyo reply was not expected to be given to the British until next week, however, and hope was expressed in official circles that the Japanese would make some concessions from her demands for outright equality. The British indicated they also hoped that the United States might be willing to recede somewhat from its insistence that the present 5-5-3

LONDON, Nov. 16 A three-horned dilemma confronted American delegates to the Tri-Powell Naval conversations tonight after British sources indicated belief that both Japan and the United States are slowly coming round to Britain’s compromise plan for naval limitation. Steadfastly opposed heretofore to any agreement that alters the basic principles of the London and Washington naval treaties, the Americans faced three alternatives in the event Japan agrees to concessions such as those proposed by Britain. They are: 1—To announce that they will walk out of the negotiations, staying Washington on its own independent ship-building program unless the essential features of existing pacts are continued. 2—To suggest postponement of the conversations until there are better prospects for agreement. 3—To agree to accept any compromise plan satisfactory to the British and the Japanese. Japan’s delega

ROME, Nov. 16. (A.—Premier Benito Mussolini went to the railway station tonight to greet Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg of Vienna. Thousands of troops and police surrounding the station kept back cheering throngs as the two men met for the second time in three months to discuss central European politics and economics.

ROME, (AP).—Italian sentiment became noticeably pro-German today as Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg of Austria came for conversations with Premier Mussolini. (Heavily guarded against assassins, Schuschnigg left Vienna last night, accompanied by his foreign minister, Egon Berger-Waldenegg. They arrive in Rome today). Germany and the policies of Adolf Hitler are expected to be a major topic in the ensuing conversations. > £2 << Anti-German Tales Cease. Bitter anti-German newspapers

COPENHAGEN, Denmark, (AP). The romance of Prince Erik, who renounced his rights to the throne of Denmark to marry a Canadian heiress, is ended. The couple have petitioned King Christian, Erik's cousin, for permission to seek a divorce. The princess is the former Lois Frances Booth of Ottawa, who inherited a lumber fortune. They have 2 children.

1934-07-24.text: SALEM, N. H., July 24. UP— Five valuable race horses perished, 300 others ran wild over the darkened countryside and the lives of stablemen were imperiled when fire caused $100,000 damage at Rockingham Park, New England’s greatest racetrack, late last night. The dead: Old Depot, veteran bay owned by J. L. Roberts. Vote, chestnut gelding owned by Mrs. M. J. White. Arrowswift, owned by Mrs. R. T. Flippen of New York. Little Stokes, also owned by Mrs. Flippen, Waydon, owned by Sheldon Fairbanks of Boston. The first four horses were burned to death, some of them dashing back into their blazing stables after having been led to safety. Waydon was destroyed after breaking its back as it crashed against a pipe in the center of the track. Injured in Rescue It was estimated that 50 of the horses that ran wild suffered minor injuries. Several grooms and jockeys were slightly hurt as they dared deat
BERLIN, July 24. U.P’—The government today banned the Paris edition of The Chicago Tribune, The Matin of Paris and The Daily Express of London from the country for two weeks.

Wimbledon, England, July 24.—(UP)—Rain today halted play in the interzone final Davis cup tie between the United States and Australia after Sidney B. Wood Jr. of New York was leading Jack Crawford, 6-3, 9-7. Only one point of the third set had been played when a fresh downpour halted the match. It was officially announced that play would be resumed tomorrow, weather permitting, at exactly the same point.

Vienna, July 24 (#)—Twelve hundred socialists were arrested today in connection with an alleged plot to overthrow the Dollfuss government. It was the biggest roundup of political prisoners since the bloody February civil war. Political police were picking up threads of evidence which they said indicated Socialists, Communists and Nazis had merged into a common front for a huge campaign of terror against the Fascist government. Police were uncommunicative but a government spokesman explained most of the arrests were merely "preventative" pending a search of suspects’ homes for explosives and incriminating documents.

TOKYO, July 24.—Thirty-one persons are known to be dead, thousands are homeless, and 668 houses are wrecked as the result of floods in Keishohoudo and Keishonando provinces in South-Eastern Korea, according to dispatches to local newspapers.

Moscow, July 24—(4)—The Soviet government has smashed what it calls a pro-Japanese spy ring by meting out death sentences to eight and long prison terms to fifteen. A series of train wrecks and sabotage in a locomotive shop were laid to the alleged conspirators. The military tribunal of the supreme court delivered the sentences. It was testified Kim Zagen, a Korean, led the well organized band which sought information about the movement of troops and supplies to the Far East. Zagen was among those condemned to death. Wrecks at stations at Chernaya Panki and Eudelmaya, and sabotage at Norumsk where much machinery and several locomotives were damaged were attributed to the espionage organization.

‘By the Associated Press? Paris, July 23—The veteran premier of France, Gaston Doumergue, was hastening to Paris tonight determined, his friends said, to save the “truce” government, even at the expense of removing both Andre Tardieu and Edouard Herriot from the cabinet, if necessary. At the same time, some quarters believed that a new coolness was developing in the government, involving the premier himself and the minister of Justice, Henri Cheron, who presided over the cabinet in Doumergue’s absence when the row between Herriot and Tardieu developed last week. The Lawted #2 Supper It was pointed out that when Cheron dashed across the country Saturday to Tournefeuille, where Doumergue was vacationing, to ask the premier to arbitrate the cabinet fight, he was not invited to have supper with his chief. Cheron has been criticized by many for alleged failure to “prosecute the Stavisky case

Warsaw, Poland, July 24 (AP) — Eight more villages on the lower Vistula river, near Torun, were flooded today, although there were encouraging signs that the waters which have been on a rampage here are abating. Five new deaths were reported, bringing the known total dead to near the 250 mark.

1934-06-04.text: LONDON, Eng. — (AP) — The British government cabled a war debt communication to Ambassador Sir Ronald Lindsay at Washington Monday, to be delivered to President Roosevelt Monday night. The note was understood to propose a token payment under conditions which would save Great Britain the stigma of being in default. It was said the text would not be made public until Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, makes his statement in the House of Commons Tuesday.

London, June 4—(UP)—Prayers in Christian churches, prostrations before idols in heathen lands and dances designed to appeal to the rain gods in both Christian and heathen countries, testified today to a drought that spotted great wreck all over the World. In some cases, nature or the gods responded, but with torrential downpours that threatened to complete the ruin the drought started. Asia and India, particularly India, Ruane and the Balkans, were affected. Anxiety spread to Great Britain over the weekend after two days in which a brazen sun withered crops all over the tales. More than 180 hamlets and villages were suffering from a shortage of water that added a fire hazard to drought damage. There were fears that a shortage of water might prove graver than in the great drought of 1941. During the entire year, rain has been but 60 percent of normal. Throughout Cambridgeshire paths were

Washington, June 4.—A formal note from the British government setting forth its views on the debt problem has been received at the British embassy and is expected to be delivered to the State Department sometime today, it was stated authoritatively. The text will be made public immediately, Simultaneously the text of the recent American debit note to Great Britain will be made public.

Washington, June 4. (UP)—The British war debt note, formally setting forth Britain’s views on war debts and its intentions regarding the June 15 installment, was received at the state department shortly before 3 p. m. today. The note, signed by the British ambassador, Sir Ronald Lindsay, was delivered to Under Secretary of State William Phillips by Phillips Mainwaring Broadmead, first secretary of the British embassy here. It contained about 2,000 words, but contents were not revealed pending simultaneous publication here and in London. It was understood the text would be made public Tuesday.

DOUGLAS, Isle of Man, June 4 — Kaye Don, British speedboat and auto racing king, was committed to trial today on a charge of manslaughter in connection with the fatal injury of his mechanic in a midnight practice run a week ago in preparation for the Manx races. The mechanic, F. Taylor, was thrown from the car in the accident and his skull was fractured. He died in a hospital May 29. At the coroner's inquest today it was estimated that Don was traveling 60 to 80 miles an hour when his car struck the rear fender of a private automobile. Don’s machine leaped through a hedge and landed back on the road upside down, 75 yards ahead of where it went off. Don escaped with only minor injuries. He was allowed freedom on bail.

MOSCOW, June 4. (U.P.)—Russia, firmly demanding that Manchukuo-an ships cease “observation” cruises to the Siberian side of the Amur River, today suggested that “in the interest of peace” a commission be appointed to investigate recent incidents. The warning and the “peace” suggestion were delivered to the Japanese diplomatic agent at Harbin, Manchukuo. They constituted an unyielding reply to recent Japanese protests against firing by Russian soldiers on Manchukuoan ships.

MOSCOW, June 4.—(#)—Russia, answering a Japanese protest over the alleged firing upon a steamer on the River Amur, charged today that the Soviet border had been violated by Manchukuoan ships. In a firmly worded note in response to Japanese correspondence, Russia gave assurances that regulations regarding traffic on the river would be enforced but said:

Geneva, June 4.—Norman Davis, American representative at the world arms conference, today sought to block consideration of Soviet minister Maxim Litvinov's proposals for 'mutual pacts of assistance.' In a brief speech after the Russian foreign minister had urged the steering committee to begin immediate discussion of his scheme, Davis announced his opposition to consideration at present.

1934-01-07.text: BEVERLY HILLS, Cal. Jan. 5—Mr. Roosevelt proposed in his speech that the NRA and a lot of these other government regulated business ethics would be made permanent. Well, that was a terrible blow to some business men. They had figured they would be required to be honest by the government until the emergency was over. The papers today tell of a little country in the Pyrenees that has six army officers, and only six plain soldiers. Well, that strikes us as being mighty comical. Yet we got 120 million people and sixty million hold government jobs. Yours,

WASHINGTON, Jan. 6—(P)—Republicans began their promised bombardment of the Roosevelt budget today as the Senate and House took time off and prepared for the contests to come. With both houses in recess until Monday and committees and leaders busying themselves for next week's grappling with liquor taxes, the St. Lawrence waterway treaty and appropriation measures, a Midwest Senate Republican gave the cue to the opposition plans for fighting huge additional outlays. Financial Ruin. In a statement Senator Patterson, Republican, Missouri, said President Roosevelt's estimate of a deficit of more than $7,000,000,000 this year made it obvious that "we are traveling along the road to financial ruin." "Both branches of Congress are overwhelmingly under the control of the administration," he asserted, "that only an aroused public opinion can stop the wild orgy of spending now going on." Democrati

By The Associated Press. CHICAGO, Jan. 6—A milk embargo, marked by violence and threatening the city’s comfort and health, tightened around Chicago tonight as 18,000 angry farmers picketed highways and defied their neighbors' attempts to deliver milk. Chicago and scores of towns surrounding it within a radius of 100 miles were menaced with a milk shortage by Monday. In some of the towns, dairy companies announced they would be able to make no Sunday deliveries. Thousands of gallons of milk were dumped on highways, and countless farmers in Illinois, Wisconsin, and Indiana refrained from marketing their milk, or were restrained by neighbors from doing so. Even the big dairy companies of Chicago admitted their supplies had been cut down seriously. An official of the Pure Milk Association, an organization of farmers which called the strike, declared Chicago received “far less than 20 per cen

Washington, Jan. 6.—(4)—The last senatorial objection to the confirmation of Henry Morgenthau, Jr., as secretary of the treasury was removed today by the resignation of Earle Bailie, whom he brought into the department as a special assistant in charge of fiscal affairs. While the Senate Finance Committee voted favorably on the Morgenthau appointment this week, such forcible objection to Bailie’s continuance was raised by Senator Couzens (R., Mich.) that a Senate vote on confirmation was postponed to keep the controversy from flaring on the floor. In Banking Firm Bailie’s integrity was not questioned in any particular, the objections of Couzens and his colleagues being based upon his previous and continuing association with the New York banking firm of J. and W. Seligman and Company, which Couzens contended had floated several issues of foreign bonds now partly or wholly in default.

| By The Associated Press McAlester, Okla., Jan. 6—Beating gangdom to the draw, federal officers bundled Wilbur Underhill, bullet-scarred outlaw, into an ambulance from his Shawnee hospital bed today and rushed him 70 miles to the familiar walls of state’s prison here. "I’m ready to come back home," the outlaw ironically told Warden Sam Brown as his stretcher was carried into the gates of the prison, from which he escaped in 1931. From Washington, the United States Bureau of Investigation announced the transfer was ordered because of rumors that gangsters were planning to deliver the "tri-state terror." As the ambulance and its two-car escort approached the east gate of the prison, an unidentified cabin plane, flying low, caused apprehension among prison guards. However, it disappeared quickly and did not attempt a landing here. Prison officers said the plane seemed to be "scouting" the

Lawton, Okla, Jan. 6.—(AP)—Robert F. Hayter, middle-aged salesman, was freed late today at the close of his preliminary hearing on charges of murder in connection with the slaying late in October of his wife and two of his children in their locked home. Hayter presented witnesses who said he was in Fort Worth, Tex., the Friday night police said the three were shot and clubbed to death.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 6.—With the declaration that “I am personally reluctant to take such a step,” Mrs. Thomas Massie, wife of the naval lieutenant involved in the Honolulu murder trial, tonight prepared to entrain for Reno to file suit for divorce. Mrs. Massie said that “the divorce is being obtained at the insistence of Lieutenant Massie,” and that, because she was “opposed to divorce” she was reluctant to proceed with the suit. The divorce proceedings, Mrs. Massie said, were “in no way connected with the Honolulu trial” of April, 1932, in which Lieutenant Massie, Mrs. Granville Fortescue and two naval enlisted men were convicted in connection with the death of a native. The native was accused by the four as being implicated in an attack on Mrs. Massie. Mrs. Massie said that after procuring a divorce, she planned to return to Washington to work.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 6 (P)—Harry Hopkins, civil works and relief administrator, today separated Gov. Talmadge of Georgia, whom he has accused of “headline hunting” and “yapping,” from all authority and association with the civil works and relief administration in the southern state. The administrator dissolved the Talmadge appointed civil works and relief board and announced he would direct the work from Washington with Miss Gay Shepperson acting as his representative in Georgia. Relations between the governor and Hopkins became strained when Talmadge criticized civil works policies several weeks ago. Talmadge said wages were too high and that as a result people were being lured from farms, thereby threatening a shortage of farm labor when the planting season arrived.

1934-05-31.text: LONDON, May 31. (U.P.) — Great Britain stepped forward as leader of America’s $11,000,000,000 World War debtors today with a note designed to force a showdown on the issue of full payment or default. It suggested a conference for a definite settlement of the war debt problem and it offered, pending settlement, a token payment of something more on its $85,670,000 June 15 debt installment than the $7,500,000 token payment made last December. Evidence that Britain was offering a lead to other debtor nations was plain. While the British cabinet was meeting here yesterday, supposedly still discussing the note, it was announced in Paris that a copy of the note had been received. Apparently unaware that the note had not been published at Washington, French officials gave a summary of it. The French government is expected to make its formal decision on its $55,000,000 June 15 installment next Mo

Geneva, May 31.—()—Russia's revolutionary proposal to make the World Disarmament Conference a permanent organism to safeguard peace today gripped Geneva but was menaced by a Franco-British duel. Serious consideration is being given the plea of Maxim Litvinoff, the Soviet’s indefatigable commissar for foreign affairs, that the conference be turned into a permanent anti-war body. The great possibility of this plan, observers pointed out, is that it might provide means for the United States, Russia, Japan and even Germany—none a league member—to collaborate regularly with Geneva without joining the league or subscribing to its pledges. Because of the situation created by speeches yesterday, particularly that of Louis Barthou, French foreign minister, in which he ridiculed British proposals and attacked Germany, no session was planned today.

GENEVA. (?). A plea by Great Britain's foreign secretary at Wednesday's session of the disarmament conference that France and Germany bridge the gap separating them drew from a French spokesman the rejoinder that "France is willing to bridge the gap but will take care not to fall thru hidden traps into the water." The fiery address by Louis Barthou, French foreign minister, in which he replied sarcastically to the plea of Sir John Simon and lambasted Germany dissipated whatever optimism was felt as the result of the talks Tuesday by M. Litvinoff, Soviet commissar for foreign affairs, and Norman H. Davis, United States ambassador at large. United Press Staff Correspondent. London, May 31.—(UP)—Great Britain today gave the United States government the choice of accepting a token debt payment or declaring Britain in default. A note was drafted for the United States and submitted to the French government for its information offering the token-or-default alternative and suggesting a refunding conference. Then, after the contents of the note were disclosed in substance both here and in Paris, the cabinet held it up in the apparent hope that President Roosevelt would use his knowledge of it to offer negotiations to the United States’ $11,000,000,000 debtors. It was understood that the note would not be sent before next week. The note seemed to leave the debt issue, and the responsibility of making a definitive statement regarding default, entirely to the president. It was drafted carefully so that a new case would be presented.

WORTHING, England May 36 - (AP)—England’s widespread search for a gunman ended today, 48 hours after it started with the suicide of the fugitive accused of wounding a policeman with a revolver. A woman, Mrs. Michael Sadleir, with two bloodhounds on leash came upon the man, Leonard Hill, as he lay under a tree in the woods. “There he is!” she shouted to policemen, who ran up to close in. Hill, trapped and realizing the stern attitude of British courts toward those who use firearms, shot himself with the same pistol with which he had wounded the policeman, Arthur Jex. Hill died a short time later in a hospital. The search for Hill, accused of wounding Jex when the latter with other officers, stopped him for questioning, had attracted huge posses of police and volunteers. The affair, although Jex was not seriously wounded, took on the proportions in England of a sensation even greater than

By The Associated Press Georgetown, British Guiana, May 21—Police here last night were making a careful check of the identity of a man who claims to be Robert Jones, but who is being held on suspicion that he is Arthur C. Wilson of Cleveland, wanted for the murder of a woman in Texas. The man, employed as steward on the Canadian liner Lady Nelson, was taken from the ship here Tuesday night. He insisted that Jones is his correct name and that he was born in Toronto. He claims Montreal as his present home.

Croydon, England, May 31. (INS).— A French airplane pilot and his mechanic were killed and scores of sleeping residents of this London suburb narrowly escaped death or serious injury to-day in the most amazing accident in the history of Croydon Airdrome, Britain's largest flying field. Several houses were badly wrecked and two automobiles were crushed in the accident, which occurred when a giant French freight plane, carrying mails and newspapers, struck an 80-foot radio mast in taking off for Paris. Eight feet of one of the ship's wings was ripped off, sending the big plane crashing to earth in the residential section surrounding the airport. The wreckage was strewn for more than 300 yards. One motor fell in a roadway, demolishing an automobile. Another fell in the front yard of a home, narrowly missing bedrooms in which residents were sleeping. London, May 30. - With many a chuckle and the comment, “hooey, hooey, hooey,” E. L. Cord, American automobile and airplane manufacturer, today read reports that he had left the United States with his family because of kidnapping threats. “According to these accounts, I must have left with my shirt tail flying,” he remarked. The manufacturer carefully limited his comment to such light-hearted statements, however, and said he wouldn't discuss seriously whether fear of abductions sent the family across the ocean.

1934-04-16.text: LONDON, April 16 (UP).—An unconfirmed dispatch to the Exchange Telegraph from Rhodes said today that five peasants were killed and 25 wounded when Italian airplanes bombed villagers at Salecho. Troops also fired on them, it was said. The firing, the dispatch asserted, was the result of conflict with island authorities during municipal elections. Rhodes is the Italian island off the Turkish coast. Its area is 565 square miles and its population is about 30,500.

Washington, D.C.—(WP)—Three thousand American women, whose forefathers battled for the freedom of the United States from Britain, gathered here Monday for the annual convention of the Daughters of the American Revolution. The meeting of the D. A. R., which in past years has provided numerous stormy sessions over the issues of national defense, preparedness and communism, opened with the address of the president general, Mrs. Russell William Magna, Holyoke, Mass. Convention fights similar to those of other sessions were expected to be provided. It was believed the "red flag" charges of Dr. William A. Wirt, Gary, Ind., educator, would receive some attention from delegates. One resolution certain to provoke debate was understood to relate to communism in the United States. Another suggests affiliation with other patriotic societies. Sponsors of resolutions generally maintained secrecy regar

London, April 16.—Five peasants were killed and 25 injured in the village of Salccho, in the Dodecanese Islands, when Italian troops opened fire following a conflict growing out of municipal elections today, according to an Exchange Telegraph dispatch from Rhodes. Italian airplanes later bombed the village, the inhabitants taking flight to the mountains, according to the dispatch.

STUART, Ia. April 16—(F)~ The First National, Stuart's only bank, was robbed of an estimated $2,000 by two young men, with a woman companion, today. The two men, carrying revolvers, entered the bank about 9:10 a.m. They were extremely nervous, Miss Lucille Lyddon, bank employee, said. They threatened the assistant cashier, H. C. Kronkhitt, when informed the time lock on the vault was set, Miss Lyddon said. He convinced them, however, that the vault could not be opened. The two then scooped up available cash on the counters and fled in a black Pontiac sedan with a silver body stripe. It bore an Iowa license. One robber was described as light, slender and dressed in grey suit and grey hat. The other, short and dark with black moustache, wore dark clothing. The woman companion did not come into the bank and was not seen by employees. She was in the car, however, when it stopped for gas at a

PARIS (UP) -— Police charged Monday that Leon Trotsky, former Russian revolutionary leader, had practically completed plans for a fourth internationale, designed to keep the world in constant revolutionary turmoil. Trotsky planned through the organization, police said, to foment revolutions in as many countries as possible. He himself was to be in supreme command, it was said. The organization, police asserted, was to have its headquarters at Amsterdam. It had no relation to Soviet Russia— which, police quoted Trotsky as believing, had lost its fire and had practically turned capitalist. Police said Trotsky was working on the plan when a villa which he occupied at Barbizon was raided. The raid, it was learned, was conducted without the knowledge of higher officials of the ministry of interior. The ministry had given Trotsky permission to live there, instead of at Corsica, where he was ge

Paris, April 16. (AP)—Government employees, in a “national protest” strike today against pay cuts, paralyzed wire communications between Paris and the provinces, but otherwise the walkout was a flop. Police guarded post offices and other public buildings watching for demonstrations which never developed. Telegraph employees who struck for a few minutes daily for the past week stretched their idleness to two hours today, then returned to their instruments. Long distance telephone operators, however, walked out at 11:30 a.m. and stayed out, failing to return by midafternoon. Waterworks employees reached their jobs an hour late and workers in the government tobacco factories loafed for an hour during the morning.

GRAZ, Austria, April 16.—UP To the titles accorded Austria's diminutive chancellor, Engelbert Dollfuss, was added by popular consent today that of champion egg-dodger. Others at a mass meeting the chancellor addressed yesterday were splattered by over-ripe eggs for which Dollfuss himself was the target. He escaped. As he appeared to speak, a bomb of the harmless smoke and noise variety let go with a deafening roar about 300 feet from the chancellor. He ignored it. Enroute from the airport to the meeting, Dollfuss was whisked over a highway painted red all the way to the city limits by socialists. They added such painted slogans as “down with fascism!” and “down with Dollfuss!” Added to all that, mysterious tamperers interfered with the broadcast. Only portions of his speech were heard by radio listeners. “What we want,” said the imperturbable chancellor in his address, “... is a country

SHANGHAI, April 16 (4)—Three American flyers missing since last Tuesday were given up by searchers today as dead. The lost Americans are James Frink, Miami, Fla.; Robert Gast, Louisville, Ky., and Ivan Carlson, Dionna, Tex. Lost with them was a Japanese businessman passenger. Experts, wearing from the strain of the fruitless search, abandoned their efforts today. They believe the lost plane sank in the sea. A search was started in the region of Hangchow bay when the Americans’ Shanghai-Canton mail line plane failed to complete its scheduled flight April 10.

1934-11-16.text: WESTERHAM, England, Nov. 16 (Py) -- Mrs. Alice Hargreaves, the original of "Alice In Wonderland," who Lewis Carroll's imagination sent adventuring after the white rabbit into a fantastic world of nonsense, died today at the age of 62 years. Mrs. Hargreaves, who had lived in retirement for many years, emerged from her quiet home in 1932, long enough to journey to New York and discover a new wonderland of skyscrapers while she took part in the Carroll centenary celebration at Columbia University. Because of Mrs. Hargreaves, all wise children are familiar with the mad hatter, the March hare, the mock turtle, and the Cheshire cat whose big grin lingered after he was gone. They know all that whimsical pageant, for the little old lady who died today not only inspired the tale, but, through her insistence, caused it to be written down. Alice Pleasance Liddell was born May 4, 1852, in Westminste

WESTERHAM, England. Nov. 16. —(UP)— Alice in Wonderland is dead. The fair-haired little girl of the famous book lives on in immortality, but Mrs. Alice Liddell Hargreaves, who as a child inspired Lewis Carroll to write his beloved fantasy, died at 10:30 p.m. Thursday after an illness of two weeks. She was 82.

LONDON, Nov. 16. (4) —Great Britain, apparently convinced that the United States and Japan are bluffing, went ahead today with her own program to reach an agreement in the deadlock naval negotiations. She did so in the face of American and Japanese opposition, both countries having coldly received England's compromise plan. The British believe that both Washington and Tokyo will eventually make concessions in their firm stand for what both insist should form the basis of a new naval treaty. The British think that neither of the other two powers should take an extreme stand but should be willing to make mutual concessions for a compromise which would prevent a break of the conversations and save the principle of naval limitation from being scrapped in favor of a ship building race. The American delegation has kept See PARLEY, Pg. 12, Col. 7

LONDON, Nov. 16, (UP)—Great Britain, acting as mediator in the naval negotiations, has proposed that the United States recognize theoretical Japanese naval equality, with the understanding that Japan would not actually build to the American level, it was learned today. It was believed that the proposal was in the hands of President Roosevelt and Secretary of State Cordell Hull after having been forwarded to Washington by the American naval delegation. Briefly, it purports to suggest that the United States and Great Britain accede in principle to the Japanese demand for naval equality. Actually it would involve a gentlemen's agreement under which each nation would "voluntarily" specify the limit to which it really would build. It was conceded that to be acceptable to the United States and Great Britain there would have to be a "voluntary" statement by Japan that its limit would be well un

LONDON (UP) — Earnest hope that the present naval negotiations might succeed, and a naval race be averted, was expressed by King George Friday in his speech proroguing parliament. In the speech which was read to a joint meeting of the House of Lords and House of Commons in the Lord’s chamber, the king expressed hope for a new naval treaty “in order that the world may be spared the evil of unrestricted competition in naval armaments, so efficiently averted in recent years by international engagements freely entered into by the parties concerned.” “Undoubtedly,” he said, “the assassination of King Alexander of Jugoslavia and Foreign Minister Louis Barthou of France caused a serious setback in the movements then on foot for European appeasement, and I have therefore noted with satisfaction the untiring efforts my government has made in many directions to counsel moderation and promote more

Lon, Nov, 10 (4)—Japan decided again to request full equality with Great Britain and the United States in naval armaments despite Britain’s decision to recognize only the principle of equality. The Japanese decision was taken as Tokyo's delegates to tri-power naval conversations here, Ambassador Tsuneo Matsudaira and Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, awaiting instructions sent from Japan which, it was learned, will dictate rejection of the compromise proposals suggested by the British. Those proposals involved recognition of Japan's right to equality on the high seas, while refusing to let her build enough ships to attain that equality. The British compromise proposal also provided for continuance of the existing 5-5-3 ratio, stipulated in the Washington treaty, to which Nippon strenuously objected.

London, Nov. 13. (AP)—Prime Minister Ramsey MacDonald told the House of Commons today that despite the failure of the allied nations and the United States to reach a new debt accord after the virtual wiping out of the German war debt, he had no intention of calling a new conference to deal with the matter. The British government head made his statement after William Mabane, liberal leader in parliament, reminded him that as chairman of the Lausanne debt conferences MacDonald had declared his intention to call a new debt conference "if no settlement could be obtained on their own debt (with the United States) by the creditor governments." Later Neville Chamberlain, chancellor of the exchequer, stated that he "was not at present in a position to make a statement" as to whether the government had decided a satisfactory settlement with the United States about the war debts could not be obtai

Washington, Nov. 16.-- President Roosevelt is studying tentative overtures from Great Britain which, in effect, pose this question: What can the two great English-speaking nations do in cooperation of naval affairs if the three-sided discussion by Britain, the United States and Japan end in failure in London? When President Roosevelt’s special train left Washington last night for Kentucky and the South, Secretary of State Hull was aboard with dispatches from Norman H. Davis, the American naval delegate, outlining the British overtures. The reply to the cautious inquiry will depend on the decision reached by the President and Mr. Hull.

Diplomatic circles, which revealed the government's plans, expressed the belief the move stood an excellent chance of success. It would be the biggest step toward guaranteeing peace since the world war, they asserted, involving as it probably would satisfactory solution of the old Franco-German hostility and settlement of the Yugoslav-Hungarian controversy over terrorism. London, Dec. 29.—Lydia Binks, condemned to die January 3 for the murder of her child, was reprieved yesterday by the home secretary. Had she gone to the gallows, Mrs. Binks would have been the second woman so to die in England in eight years. Mrs. Ethel Lillie Major was hanged at Hull December 20 for the poisoning of her husband. Frederick Rushworth, 29-year-old farm hand convicted along with Mrs. Binks of burying alive their child born at York last March, was not reprieved. He is in prison at Leeds awaiting execution January 2.

LONDON. UP. A dispatch to the express from Warsaw said 2,000 Soviet soldiers and Mohammedans were killed or wounded in battle Thursday in the Soviet of Turkestan, near the Afghan border. The dispatches said when the Soviet police were resisted, they were sent to the scene and smashed the Mohammedans after an all-day battle. Many of the latter fled to Afghanistan. Later, the dispatch said, fourteen Mohammedan police were executed as a punishment.

Washington, D. C. — Japan’s denunciation of the Washington treaty focuses attention on the comparative strength of the sea powers’ navies. They now are: United States: 373 warships of 1,092,025 tons, Great Britain: 276 warships of 1,158,659 tons. Japan: 220 warships of 756,561 tons. Building or appropriated for: United States: 68 of 234,000 tons. Great Britain: 62 of 171,410 tons. Japan: 45 of 124,696 tons. Additional tonnage which, under the treaty, can be laid down before December 31, 1936: United States: 78 of 136,975 tons. Great Britain: 44 of 132,963 tons. Japan: 1 of 1,500 tons. Strength in new “underage” vessels expected to be in existence when the treaty ends: United States: 113 ships of 734,580 tons. Great Britain: 125 ships of 636,322 tons. Japan: 150 ships of 597,426 tons.
