On the result of today’s hearing will depend whether she will remain under arrest or be paroled pending a formal trial. (Miss Sittell, it was said at Paris, is a naturalized American. She went to the United States in 1925. She was born in Lorraine while it was German territory. When France got it after the World War, her parents elected to go to Germany, she to remain and be a Frenchwoman). Miss Sittell was arrested last Monday, the day after she left Paris to seek the parents she had not seen for 10 years. She has been held at Waldmohr, it was learned, despite a statement by Waldmohr police that she had been indicted and imprisoned at another place which they refused to name. “The charge against Miss Sittell is

HAMBURG, Germany, Dec. 28 (7) The United States liner Washington was grounded tonight 39 miles off Cuxhaven near the fireship Eibe. A thick fog was blamed by the commander, who hoped to refloat the ship with the high tide. The liner Washington, of 24,260 gross tons, left Hamburg for New York at 7 A.M. today, under Commander Schuyler F. Cummings.

MVMME Eh, FRUMREET, 170. OF ~—~(/P)-—-Monarchist circles heard rumors today that Archdukes Otto and Albrecht, Hapsburg claimants to the thrones of Austria and Hungary, had reached an agreement to avoid a conflict in their ambitions. The reports were that Otto would confine his aspirations to the Austrian throne, leaving the Hungarian field to his royal cousin. Royalist quarters expressed the opinion that the chances of both would be enhanced if an “unseemly squabble” were avoided. The throne of Hungary, adjudged by the national parliament to be vacant, is to be filled at some future time when the issue may be decided free from several pressures. The functions of the sovereign are at present exercised by a regent, Nicholas Horthy.

BERLIN, Dec. 28.—(U.P)—Miss Elsa Sittell, young New York woman, has been arrested at Waldmohr, in the Palatinate, southern Germany, near the Saar border, and spirited away to an undivulged prison, the United Press was informed tonight. German police who arrested Miss Sittell at the Palatinate town near Kaiserlautern were vague about the reasons, declaring to queries: “She was arrested because she made insulting remarks about the Reichführer (Hitler).” They refused to specify what she said or how the “insult” occurred, but declared Miss Sittell already had been indicted and was imprisoned, held for trial. She is no longer at Waldmohr, and the police refused to say where she was being held.

| oceania sional | London, Feb. 18.—(Sunday)—(@P)— The Sunday Dispatch said today that a second bodyguard has been assigned to Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald because of threats which have been made against his life. In an article today, the newspaper says two detectives, instead of the one who previously guarded him, “quietly follow” the prime minister when he takes his daily walks each morning in St. James Park, not from his residence at No. 10 Downing Street. Scotland Yard is entrusted with the protection of all cabinet, and orders for the new bodyguard came from chiefs of the famous detective force.

LONDON. (7. Three British ministers made it plain that the United Kingdom will have to build up her armaments if current arms negotiations fail. Sir John Simon, secretary of foreign affairs, declared “a breakdown of disarmament negotiations will mean that Britain will have to look to the state of her armaments, and the world will relapse into unregulated competition.” Lord Stanhope, undersecretary for foreign affairs, emphasized that if no disarmament convention is signed, and a new arms race results, Great Britain must increase her armaments “not a little, but a very great deal, at vast cost to the people, and consequently might have to postpone reduction of taxation.” “In the present state of Europe,” said Sir Philip Sassoon, undersecretary for air, “we cannot continue with only 400 first-line aircraft when our nearest neighbor, France has 997. Brussels, Belgium, Feb. 18.—(Sunday)—(AP)—Albert, king of the Belgians, was killed Saturday afternoon in a mountaineering accident. He was in his fifty-ninth year. Accompanied by a personal servant he set out to climb Rocher de Marches des Dames, a peak near Namur. He slipped and fell in the ascent. His body was not recovered until 2 a.m. Sunday, after an intensive search. Attendants found a deep wound in his head and said there was no doubt that he had been killed instantly.

VIENNA, Feb. 17. — Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss has moved swiftly today toward the formation of a Fascist state on Italian lines with the general removal of Socialist officials from office, widespread arrest and further hangings. Socialism slowly was being leveled into the dust. Its resistance was broken and except for occasional and scattered sniping, violence had ended. Three smoke bombs, a pitiful echo of desperate Socialist aggression were.

Washington, Feb. 17 (AP)—The civil works administration plans to drop 572,500 persons from the payroll next Friday instead of the 400,000 previously decided upon. This, it was announced today by Harry L. Hopkins, the administrator, will leave approximately 3,104,400 persons on the payroll.

1934-11-11.text: LONDON, Nov. 4 — Soviet Russia’s quest for long term loans from leading capitalist nations in order to carry on ambitious programs for industrial expansion seems doomed to failure, British and American officials with close touch with Russian details say. A high authority stated that the strong stand Great Britain has taken against long-term loans to Russia is not likely to be altered by settlement of the Lena Goldfields controversy, particularly since the settlement is regarded as very unfavorable to British interests.

Armistice is “a day of national humiliation.” “Let the English celebrate the Armistice as a great peace day,” one newspaper said, “Let the French wallow in reminiscences of their orgy of victory—to us it remains a day of blackest national disgrace; a day of national mourning for the coming generation. “A great empire fell in ruins,” the paper continued, “unparalleled sacrifice was overwhelmed by a wave of red terror.” To ask why the day is not observed in Germany is like waiving a red flag in front of a bull. There invariably followed the counter-question: “Why should we?” leading eventually to the “odious Versailles treaty.” Germany's homage to its war dead on “the day of repentance” will be paid November 21. The date is changed from year to year and the “Totensonntag” (Memorial Sunday) will be held November 25.

Nineteen years ago today, at dawn, the air raid guns sounded in London, and we knew that the Armistice had been signed and the war was over. The desired, incredible hour had come, and no one will ever forget that glad, sad, mad, wild day. Whether to shout or to weep men did not know, so they did both, mingling a liturgy of laughter with a litany of prayer. Purged by pity and by dread, with muted joy and triumphing grief, mankind, on its knees, thanked God, Something, not ourselves, had made for righteousness, and we were awed by events that marched to an unseen Drummer. All thought, and a yearning no mortal could measure, turned to those gay gallant men, sleeping in the calm amnesty of death, by whose sacrifice—pouring out the sweet blood of youth—the wonder had been wrought, and whose going had taken the spring out of the year. Washington —(4)— American officials in Persia began a thorough investigation today of the treatment accorded two American flyers forced down there on the recent England-Australia air race. The State Department protested to Persia last night. It said it was "reliably informed" that when John H. Wright and John Polando landed with minor engine trouble, their passports were seized and held for 24 hours and their plane detained. Persia denied any discourtesy or undue delay.

(P?)—Spain’s ill-starred revolution, now all but a lurid memory, was the bloodiest and most destructive in many decades. Although chiefly confined to Asturias and the Autonomous region of Catalonia, it was estimated that the movement cost ten times as many lives as all the rest of the Spanish revolts in the last 50 years. Statistics The government has refrained from issuing any official casualty lists, and censorship has prevented conjecture. But data carefully compiled by The Associated Press would seem to make the following estimates fairly conservative: Dead, 3,500. Wounded and injured, 10,000. PARIS, Nov. 10 (UP)—It will be 16 years at 11 a.m. Sunday since 7 million soldiers of the Allies and 5 million of the Central Powers loosened their grips on each other's throats. Today, 20 years after the start of that greatest war of all wars, Europe is playing the same dangerous game of balancing power which brought the world to the brink of that catastrophe.

TOKYO, Nov. 10 (AP).—Japanese military leaders completed last-minute plans today for the annual three-day war games to begin tomorrow, the day on which much of the world was commemorating Armistice Day. Emperor Hirohito left the capital to take personal command of more than 50,000 soldiers who are to participate in the grand maneuvers on the plains north of Tokyo, in the prefectures of Saitama, Gunma and Tochigi.

Berlin Nov. 10.— (#) —A Catholic offer of common cause with Protestants against Nazi paganism marked Martin Luther’s 451st birthday today as the Protestants fighting Nazi interference in church matters found new cause for concern in published incitation to violence. 1934-01-15.text: MOSCOW. (Special) — A new “spy case,” which may rival in sensations the celebrated British Metropolitan - Vickers affair, has arisen in Russia, it was disclosed yesterday, with the arrest of the general manager and five foreign representatives of the ‘Controll company branch of Societe Generale Des Surveillances, Limited of Geneva. They were charged with economic espionage. The company is an international organization which certifies exports to principal ports of the world. Twenty Russian employees of the firm, which has functioned in Soviet Russia for a dozen years, have also been taken into custody. The foreigners under arrest are

GEORGETOWN, British Guiana, Jan. 15, (?)—Runners arrived from up-country today to report 16 dead and hundreds of homeless following floods which swept through scores of villages and farms. Officials said the effects of devastated sugar plantations would be felt for at least three years.

LONDON, Jan. 15 (P)—The London Daily Mail came out strongly today for adoption of fascism in Great Britain. A three-column editorial by Lord Rothermere lauded the methods of Mussolini and Hitler. “Hurrah for the blackshirts,” glared a three-column headline. The editorial lashed at the “half-hearted, sentimental policy” of the old parties and made an appeal to the youth of England to support Sir Oswald Mosley and his blackshirts. Lord Rothermere’s creed of fascism had hitherto been regarded as more or less of a joke by the general public, despite the support given the movement by devoted blackshirt followers. “The blackshirts proclaim the fact, which the old politicians will never face,” the editorial read, “that the new age requires new methods and new men.” The Daily Mail, which is an avowed opponent of the present government, said it was certain that Sir Oswald could “do more in a conf

LONDON, Jan. 14.—(#)—The hardest storm of winter whipped over southern England and Wales today, leaving a trail of wreckage. Shipping in the English Channel, the North Sea and Bristol Bay encountered difficulties. The gale reached a velocity of 80 miles an hour at Plymouth and 60 miles in London.

London, Jan. 14.—(/P)—Strong advocacy of the adoption of fascism in Great Britain was inaugurated today in the Daily Mail with a prominently displayed front page article by Lord Rothermere and a long editorial. Sir Oswald Mosley and his fascist blackshirts were acclaimed by the Mail as leaders of a movement "to break the stranglehold which senile politicians have so long maintained on public affairs."

TOKYO, (Saturday). "P. Aimaro Sato, Japanese ambassador to Washington from 1916 to 1919, died a victim of arteriosclerosis. He was 77. Sato, during his career one of the most widely respected members of the Japanese department of state, was a former minister to Holland and Denmark, Mexico and Belgium, and a former ambassador to Austria before coming to Washington to represent his country in the United States. He was an alumnus of De Pauw University.

Moscow, Jan. 15-(4)-Nine foreigners and twenty Russians were under arrest today in what Soviet police believed was a new case of espionage which may rival the dramatic Metropolitan-Vickers affair. Diplomatic representatives of Germany, Austria and Denmark who sought information in the matter, were refused permission to see the prisoners, and were given no details of the case except that the men had been arrested under a section in the Soviet criminal code covering economic espionage. Six of the foreigners and all of the Russians were associated with the Controll company branch of Societe des Surveillances, limited of Geneva. The arrests were carried on secretly over a period of four months, beginning in September and ending late in December. The 67-year-old minister, a native of Tennessee and a political force in his adopted state, Montana, was replying to congratulatory speeches when he collapsed. Seemed in Excellent Health. He had seemed to be in excellent health and cheerful spirits. His first sentences were given in his normal voice and he was paying tribute to the achievements of the Irish and Americans. He referred to the Irish of Butte, Mont., in the United States, which the minister said was founded by an ‘Irishman named Marcus Daly. Hollywood, April 9.--(?)—An idyllic romance with 23 year old Lord Revelstoke of Britain, was described today by Angela Joyce, English actress, a few hours after her lawyers started a suit in London charging he broke a promise to marry her. She said he adored her “like a goddess in the clouds” and that she “loved him to distraction.” “Imagine my heartbreak and astonishment on learning he had married another woman,” said Miss Joyce, who was the “Miss England” of 1930, and who came here seeking a movie career. Heir to the $2,000,000 estate of his banker father, young Lord Revelstoke married Flora Fermor-Hesketh, daughter of Sir Thomas and Lady Fermor Hesketh, March 2. Miss Joyce said he was “just a Cambridge undergraduate, and a not very wealthy one” when she met him. She charged he was “poisoned” against her. “I met Lord Revelstoke in a London night club in February, 1933,” said the actres

May 2H Meuse Desk London, April 9--Great Britain asked Germany today—and expects an answer within a week—about her projected increased armaments. This was revealed by Sir John Simon, foreign secretary in the House of Commons on the eve of a meeting at the disarmament bureau in Geneva—a meeting which may be the turning point in a long controversy. Replying to questions as to the nature of the German proposal and estimates and whether they are permitted under the Versailles treaty, Sir John said: "The government is giving very serious consideration to this matter. I have instructed the British embassy in Berlin to make inquiries of the German government on the subject." Cheers rang throughout the House as he finished.

Dublin, April 10 (INS)—Diplomatic Dublin was saddened today by one of the most tragic incidents in its history, the sudden collapse and death of William Wallace McDowell, American minister to the Irish Free State, at a banquet given in his honor by Eamonn De Valera, president of the Free State executive council. McDowell, who assumed his post here only two weeks ago today, was said never to have fully recovered from the shock of his wife's death in Chicago last November following an operation. His death was the second and final blow of a cruel fate which had stalked his diplomatic appointment from the first. After a long and successful career in Montana mining, farming and politics, McDowell accepted his appointment largely in accordance with his wife’s wishes. London.—(AP)—Walter Runciman, president of the British board of trade, told the house of commons today that tariff negotiations between the United States and Great Britain were impractical at present. Runciman said: “I do not think commercial conversations between the two governments could be usefully considered at present.” His statement was in reply to a member’s question whether, in view of the fact that “a free interchange of commodities would secure additional employment in the two countries,” he would initiate talk with the United States designed toward the mutual lowering or, preferably, abolition of tariffs.

Brussels, April 9.— (#)— Week-end political clashes in which a communist was slain and more than a score of persons were injured focused attention for the first time on the rise of the nationalist organization called the blue shirts. The blue shirts are pledged to rid Belgium of all political parties and the “present rotten regime,” and so dangerous did they seem tonight that the government ordered quick parliamentary consideration of a measure banning the wearing of political uniforms by any group. Istanbul, Turkey—U.P)—A sore thumb was added Tuesday to Samuel H. Insull’s troubles, and he submitted cheerfully to an operation for an abscess on it. Though facing apparently certain extradition to the United States, the aged Chicago utilities man remained far from downcast in his room at the detention house. His attorneys still considered an appeal to the high council of state against efforts to halt plans for his return. The council is the supreme judicial authority.

GENEVA (®) — The doctors of disarmament huddled over their patient today to determine whether hope yet remains for international control of instruments of war. The experts were members of the world disarmament conference. Upon this diagnosis will be based a decision as to whether the conference shall again be called into session or disarmament dubbed — for the present at least — a lost cause. There was a soberness about the delegates gathering for the opening meeting today that bespoke the difficulties they foresaw in obtaining any arms limitation convention. Chief among these difficulties was the problem offered by Soviet Russia and Japan glowering at one another in the Far East. The former never has been a member of the League, sponsor of the disarmament conference. The latter has resigned. The lord secluded himself at Swindon, 70 miles from London. There the 33-year-old son and heir of the ninth Earl of Shaftesbury waited the serving of the petition today on Lady Ashley and the American actor. A member of Lord Ashley’s household told the Associated Press that he “has nothing to say at this time.” Lord Ashley, whose family is one of the most impressive in England, was educated at Eton and the Royal Military College at Sandhurst—which is the English West Point—and at Cambridge University. LONDON, Feb. 6.—(P)—Germany’s claim to equality of rights in armaments could not and should not be resisted, Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, told the House of Commons today. "There is little likelihood of peace in the world if you endeavor to put a great country and race under an inferior jurisdiction," he said. If a prompt agreement on armaments is not reached, he continued, Great Britain would have to consider its position—if she had to live in a world of unlimited armaments. The question, Sir John said, must be solved within a new treaty and "no progress is possible by merely blowing off steam." Galleries and the floor were jammed for a ‘full dress’ debate on disarmament. The new British memorandum suggesting to interested governments a plan for a disarmament agreement was the text of the debaters.

London, Feb. 6. (4)—Great Britain is following up her disarmament proposals with an urgent effort to make sure they are completely understood by the governments affected, Sir John Simon, the foreign secretary, told the house of commons today. Initiating a parliamentary debate on disarmament before a crowded house, he disclosed that the government is sending Anthony Eden, lord privy seal, to the continent as soon as possible to hear the views of other administrations. Sir John said also that Germany’s claim to equal arms rights “could not and should not be resisted” and that the bothersome disarmament problem must be solved within a new treaty. (The British arms memorandum published January 31 proposed equality for Germany, security for all, and the reich’s return to Geneva conferences. It advocated reduction in forces of heavily armed nations).

LONDON, Feb. 7. (U™)—London lowered its world gold price sharply today as the American dollar strengthened rapidly. Gold was priced at 136 shillings 6 pence, a reduction of 2 shillings 9 pence. The dollar equivalent was $34.36. This was but a two cent reduction in dollars, as the mounting dollar quotation offset the reduction in terms of sterling.

London, Feb. 6 — Gold is estimated to be worth more than 3,000,000 pounds ($24,825,000 at today's closing rate) was landed in London this afternoon during an unprecedented gold rush by airplane from the continent. The greater part of the yellow metal was believed ultimately destined for the United States. The planes—10 or 320 of them—were closely spaced in arriving in a race with time to arrive while the light was still good. They carried more than 20 tons of the precious cargo. Most of the gold was from France, but the Netherlands contributed a quantity aboard a giant plane which started the day's rush, believed to be the largest on record and to eclipse even those of two years ago after Great Britain went off gold, when tons of the metal were sent abroad. LONDON, Feb. 7.— London society, awaiting avidly further details of the divorce suit of Lord Ashley, heir of the Earl of Shaftesbury, in which Douglas Fairbanks is named as co-respondent, switched its interest today to the question of whether the suit will be contested. Fairbanks and Lady Ashley had eight days to sign the register, acknowledging receipt of the divorce petition, and two weeks after that to signify their intention of defending it. If they enter no defense, the suit probably will be heard in April, with only perfunctory evidence entered to establish grounds for divorce. If it is contested, however, there probably will be considerable delay, and elaborate testimony. In any event, the testimony cannot be made public, under British law. Paris, Feb. 6 ()—Firing began at 7:55 p.m. tonight in the Place de la Concorde. A man and a woman were killed with the first shots. Even as the firing broke loose, reports came of a demonstration starting at the Place de l'Opéra, half a mile away, where a group of French Fascists shouting "Fascists" started a parade to the Concorde. They marched with their arms raised in the Fascist salute singing the Marseillaise, the national anthem of France. In the Place de la Concorde all was mad confusion. Paris, Feb. 6. -( )—Troops were called out to reinforce the police battling with a mob in the Place de la Concorde across from the chamber of deputies. — A mob estimated at 3,000 persons had broken into a mad riot across the bridge over the Seine which divides the Place from the chamber building. 1934-09-16.text: NEWPORT, R. I., Sept. 5—The Vincent Astor yacht Nourmahal with President Roosevelt aboard dropped anchor in Newport harbor early tonight after the chief executive had watched with the keenest interest the great but futile contest between the British and American racing yachts. The Nourmahal, with the stars and stripes and blue presidential flags fluttering in the breeze, joined hundreds of craft of all descriptions in tracking the American defender Rainbow and the British challenger Endeavour throughout the 30-mile windward-leeward opening race. It left for Narragansett Bay only after the official committee boat had declared “no contests” because the time limit had been exceeded. Mr. Roosevelt remained aboard the Nourmahal tonight. Unless present plans are revised, he will witness one or more of next week's races.

Sept. 15 (INS)— Closely paralleling the baffling murder of a noted New England educator this morning, the body of Mrs. Sarah Gant, 66, a widow, was found lying in the bedroom of her home today. She had been shot to death. The fatal charge had been fired through the screen of an open bedroom window on the second floor of the house. Police said Mrs. Gant apparently had raised herself on the bed, which is only six inches from the window in response to a call from the murderer who then opened fire. She struck back on the bed, her left shoulder and breast riddled with shotgun pellets. The body was found by her son, Arthur, who lived alone with his mother. BALBOA, C. Z., Sept. 15 (UP).— Hope of saving the cargo of the British freighter Bradburn, which caught fire in the Pacific, was abandoned today and efforts were concentrated on salvaging the vessel itself. The Bradburn, which made port here with fire spreading through her holds, was grounded on the mud flats in Balboa harbor and the holds flooded. The origin of the blaze had not been determined. Reports of sabotage were not confirmed.

PARIS. (UP), Princess Marina of Greece will go to dour old Balmoral castle in Scotland Sunday to meet her future parents-in-law, King George and Queen Mary for the first time. She and her parents, Prince George and Princess Marie, will meet the fiancé, Prince George of England, in London, and together they will go up to Scotland. For the last week Marina has engaged in a shopping tour of Paris, selecting her trousseau, but when she meets Queen Mary, she will learn just how extensive that trousseau shall be.

(Copyright, 1934, by United Press) Vienna, Sept. 15. (UP)—Reports that another Nazi outbreak impends, which might result in Austria’s third civil war this year, caused the government to take extraordinary armed precautions today. Heavy concentrations of Austrian military forces at the Jugo-Slavian frontier as a precaution against a putsch from more than 2,000 Austrian Nazi refugees interned in the neighboring country, the United Press was informed on good authority. Vienna Uneasy Uneasiness was evident in Vienna. During the two preceding rebellions, more than 2,000 persons were killed and wounded in the suppression first of the socialists in February and then the Nazis in July. The government, with the aid of foreign powers, thought it had the situation in hand but its confidence was not shared everywhere. Many informed persons predicted another Nazi uprising before the end of the year.

BUDAPEST, Sept. 13--I am going to keep flying up and down this Danube river till I find a place where it’s blue. This is the star city of all Europe. Hungary is a kingdom but got no king. They are looking for one. I believe the old kingfish will fit ‘em. I can fix it for you, Huey. Yours, WILL ROGERS

Geneva, Sept. 15. —(#)— The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics today formally accepted an invitation extended by some 30 countries to join the League of Nations, and was expected to become a member early next week. At a special session of the league council, Russia at the same time was allocated a permanent council seat, thus gaining the same importance among the select powers of Europe as countries like England, France and Italy. Allocation of the council seat must be approved by the league assembly, to which the question of Russia's election to the league body also will be referred. The invitation to join was dispatched by telegraph to Moscow, and the acceptance arrived speedily. Russia's new place on the council will be in one of two vacant seats, left empty by the withdrawal of Germany and Japan last year. GENEVA, Sept. 15.—()—Soviet Russia today officially accepted an invitation to join the League of Nations. It had been sent to her by telegraph a few hours earlier. The League Council voted officially to create a permanent seat in the council for Russia. Argentina, Portugal and Panama abstained from voting on the subject. The invitation to join the league was sent following weeks of wrangling among delegates. The invitation followed the circulation among the delegates of an invitation which 33 promptly signed. Even as the invitation went out, a movement was under way to obtain from Russia a pledge that religious liberty would be established in the Soviet Republics.

In South Carolina state troops guarded four danger points. Union leaders announced that “flying squadrons” would envelop mills where the strike call was ignored. (By Associated Press) Washington, D. C., Sept. 4—Testimony that Sir Basil Zaharoff, European man of mystery received commissions from an American "building concern" which had agreed with a British concern for a division of the world’s submarine building was put before a senate committee in a munitions inquiry. Henry R. Carse, president of the Electric Boat Co., of New London, Conn., said his concern had paid Zaharoff commissions amounting to $766,000 on business between 1919 and 1930. The Boat Co. official said Zaharoff received commissions on their "Spanish business." "We don’t pay," Carse said, "but under an old agreement a certain percentage and we transmit to Sir Zaharoff and later we get a commission which we retain."

London, Sept. 3. — Three score years of battle to better the lot of the poor and needy were climaxed today as Commander Evangeline Booth, 68, was elected general and commander-in-chief of the Salvation Army. The delegates from 22 countries voted, as well, for restoration of the Booth dynasty that, beginning in 1867 when General William Booth founded the army, held sway over the organization until five years ago, when the high council ousted General William Bramwell Booth, the founder's son, on the grounds of his ill health. Commander Booth is a daughter of General William Booth. Higgins on Throne Bitter recriminations and threats of legal action that followed upon the removal of General Bramwell Booth came to naught as the aged, infirm leader died soon afterward. General Edward J. Higgins of England, chosen to succeed him, ruled the army quietly during the ensuing five years.

London—(AP)—The Salvation Army will go on with another Booth at the head of its far flung enterprises. Evangeline Booth, 68, daughter of the founder of the organization, was elected the Army’s commander-in-chief yesterday by the 47 delegates from 22 nations who constitute the high council. Her selection meant that the high command of the Army had reverted to the Booths after five years. In the interim General Edward J. Higgins, who resigned recently, ruled the Army. She will return to the United States, but plans to come back to the world headquarters here. Evangeline Booth has been leader of the Salvation Army in the United States.

NEW YORK, Sep. 4.--?-- George A. Sloan, president of the Cotton Textile Institute, today said that on the basis of telegrams it was evident "the majority of New England workers are not in sympathy with the strike movement and intended to remain by their jobs." Sloan said he had heard from mills employing 125,000 of the 150,000 New England textile workers. Of this number, mills employing 100,000 were open and running full time, Sloan said. He added only 25,000 employees of mills heard from are out on strike. These mills are located in New Bedford, Mass., where 18 are shut down and only three operating, Sloan said the messages informed him. "In the first day of a strike which reflects the attitude of the workers," Sloan said, "figures to us indicate that the majority of New England workers are not in sympathy with the strike movement and intended to remain by their jobs." WASHINGTON, Sept. 4, (P)—The sale of munitions to foreign governments as well as the United States by the Electric Boat Company of New London, Conn., was disclosed to the Senate Munitions Committee by the head of the concern. Henry R. Carse, president of the plant, after giving this testimony, related that it maintained banking connections with one bank in London as well as six such institutions in New York. D.), selected to head the special committee after initiating the investigation, said its scope would be broad. It is the first inquiry into the industry undertaken by Congress. BOSTON, Sept. 4 (®).— Scores of thousands of textile workers were absent from their posts in New England mills today as a result of a strike called by the United Textile Workers of America, but other thousands reported for work as usual following the Labor Day week-end. Reports from large textile centers in Massachusetts, New Hampshire and Rhode Island, employing an aggregate of more than 125,000 workers indicated approximately 45,000 were idle. Of these, possibly 10,000 could not be definitely said to be on strike inasmuch as the mills employing them remained closed. The full effect of the strike, however, was not known until later in the afternoon. In addition, many plants had been operating on reduced scale. London, Sept. 3.—(W.P)—Commander Evangeline Booth was elected head of the Salvation Army Monday night, succeeding Gen. Edward John Higgins. Commander Booth is the daughter of the late Gen. William Booth, founder of the organization. The election took place during a special meeting of the high council, in session here for the sole purpose of electing a successor to General Higgins, who announced he intended to retire in November, when he reaches 70. The meeting aroused afresh the serious controversial problem which confronted the council when it removed Gen. Bramwell Booth on the grounds of poor health. The struggle started then between the British and American leaders for dominance in Salvation Army affairs;

1934-02-16.text: (Copyright 1934 by United Press) LONDON, Feb. 16.—(UP)—Great Britain and Russia signed here today an important trade treaty regarded, from the British viewpoint, as a move designed to offset disadvantageous stimulation of United States trade with the Soviet republic. The Board of Trade signed for Great Britain, and Ivan Maisky, Russian Ambassador, and A. V. Ozersky, trade representative, for the Soviet Union. The treaty will become effective upon exchange of ratifications. It is subject to denunciation on six months’ notice. It is not a permanent treaty because Britain would not make one that did not include agreement on payment of prewar Russian debts. A feature of the treaty is that it provides for approximate balancing by specified degrees of British-Russian exchange of goods. Paris, Feb. 16.—Premier Gaston Doumergue, armed with the big stick of popular support from France, showed a firm hand to Germany today. His new ministry, with its eyes fixed closely on Austria's troubles, openly charged Chancellor Adolph Hitler with having re-armed Germany. Hence, said a note to Berlin drafted as one of the cabinet's first acts, further Franco-German talks on arms are useless. Today the 71-year-old premier worked to define a foreign policy which “will give us the necessary authority to play a useful role in the League of Nations and international conferences.” The German rearmament charge hurled in reply to a Hitler memorandum in regard to further discussions on disarmament, was revealed while cheers of the chamber of deputies still resounded in the ears of the cabinet last night.

PARIS, Feb. 15—(P)—Armed with authority from the Chamber of Deputies, Premier Gaston Doumergue and his “political truce” cabinet took firm command of France today. The Chamber gave the government an overwhelming vote of confidence as “Papa Doumergue” shut off all debate until the budget for 1934 is voted. Singing the Marseillaise and cheering the 71-year-old leader in the national emergency, deputies from practically all parts of the Chamber drowned out the cries of the Communists and Socialists and deluged their protests with a flood of favorable votes. Winning the support of all but 193 deputies out of 595, the vigorous old premier told parliament exactly what it must do and how it must do it. He ordered all debate eliminated until the budget is approved, and he changed a law, old as the republic itself, to enable passage of the measure in a few days instead of a period of months.

MOSCOW, Feb. 16, (#)—An Arctic blizzard howled today around a party of 100 shipwrecked persons as they camped on the ice in Bering Straits and waited for 60 dog teams racing to the rescue. In the party is a five-months-old baby, born aboard the vessel Cheliuskin, which sank three days ago on its way back from Wrangell Island with scientists and colonists. The party, headed by Professor Otte Schmidt, have dug themselves in. They have supplies salvaged from their vessel, crushed in the ice, and they reported by radio that they are "healthy and strong." Most of the party had been assigned to Wrangel Island, but were unable to land because of the ice, so they turned back, leaving the inhabitants there for another winter. Eight women and a three-year-old girl are among those stranded. The girl was traveling with her mother, who intended to join her husband, commandant of the island colony.

VIENNA, Feb. 16 (P)—Driven underground into the sewers of Vienna, the scattered forces of the fleeing socialist republican guard are fighting a desperate guerrilla warfare today, still disputing the authority of the Austrian government. The secret passages into the roomy sewers, which honeycomb the ground under Vienna, were ways of escape for defeated garrisons of the municipal apartment blocks shelled by government artillery Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. Now the sewers themselves have become a last stronghold for these fighters.

Paris, Feb. 15. -— (P) — Chancellor Hitler has already rearmed Germany, the French government charges in a firm note made public today which virtually slammed the door to further arms talks between them. The French, officially for the last time, stated the Reich had rearmed beyond treaty provisions, which "can no longer be taken as a basis of disarmament discussions." Breach Widened. The note, replying to Hitler's memorandum of Jan. 19, expressed "astonishment" at Germany's arms attitude, said bilateral negotiations were useless on a basis of "rearmament." France is willing, it said, however, to discuss "disarmament." London, Jan. 11.—A dreaded “black fog” settled on London this afternoon so densely that it penetrated the great Albert Hall, where Mme. Galli-Curci sang to an audience which could see her only through a haze. Her white figure upon the platform seemed to the audience like an ethereal being, and her bell-like voice served to heighten the illusion. The fog was not so bad as that of New Year’s day, but it caused a number of accidents. The fog had lifted in most sections of London tonight.

Athens, January 22, (A°*)—* tee Tsaltaris said today Samuel Insull, Sr., former Chicago utilities operator, must leave Greece, no matter what the Council of State may decide on an appeal for permission to remain here. The Council of State will meet again tomorrow to consider Insull’s plea, and is expected to make known its findings at that time. Meanwhile, rumors circulated that Insull, who must leave Greece within the month, is trying to persuade Italy to permit him to fly to the island of Rhodes for refuge from United States authorities who seek to return him to Chicago for embezzlement.

MADRID, Jan. 12—four Americans under arrest at Palma Mallorca, were ordered to remain in jail today while the United States embassy exerted its utmost efforts to settle their case. Ambassador Claude Bowers conferred with both Spanish government and judicial officials in an effort to effect the release of the prisoners pending negotiations for clemency. It was considered practically certain in government circles that a pardon would be forthcoming within a day or so. The Americans are Mr. and Mrs. Clinton B. Lockwood, West Springfield, Mass.; Roger F. Mead, New York, and Edmund A. Blodgett, Stamford, Conn., who were sentenced to six months in jail as the result of an altercation last year with a civil guard at Palma. Authorities there jailed them yesterday when it was rumored they planned to escape, but today they were released temporarily, then returned to custody. Governor Juan Mament of

TOKYO, Jan. 22—(P) Gen. Bae dao Araki, who in the eyes of the world personified the militant spirit with which the Japanese nation has been imbued in the last two years, relinquished the portfolio of minister of war today and at least temporarily retired from the political stage. Premier Saito, after futilely urging the bed-ridden war-lord to reconsider, accepted his resignation. Afterward, the premier acquiesced to the recommendation of members of an informal conference of high-ranking military leaders that General Senjuro Hayashi succeed Araki. General Jinezaburo Mazaki, member of the supreme war council, was chosen to succeed Hayashi as inspector general of military education. Hayashi’s formal installation was scheduled for tomorrow. He will be inducted into office in time to take his seat on the government bench when parliament is reconvened. It was considered too early confidently t

By The Associated Press. - PARIS, Jan. 22.—Hundreds of demonstrators were arrested today when Royalists charged against police massed to protect the chamber of deputies. They were taken into custody by thousands of mounted guards.

NEW DELHI, India, Jan. 21—UP—From the mysterious Himalayan kingdom of Nepal today came a new explanation of the earthquake which a week ago shook all India, causing deaths unofficially estimated at 15,000. From the tiger-shooting camp of a former maharajah of Nepal, 350 miles west of Katmandu, the capital, came word that followers of the maharajah blamed the recent successful flight of three British aviators over Mt. Everest for the catastrophe. They were reported to declare that the gods of the world’s highest mountain, previously unconquered by man, had by the earthquake visitation wreaked vengeance upon humanity for invading their precincts. They pointed out, it was said, that the axis of the severest shocks closely followed the line of flight taken by the aviators, the Marquis of Clydesdale, Col. L. F. Stewart Blacker and Flight Lieutenant E. F. McIntyre, who crossed Everest's peak,

1934-04-21.text: Washington, April 21 (UP)—A request that the British government be asked to recall Gerald Campbell, British consul general at New York, will face Secretary of State Cordell Hull when he returns to his office Tuesday. The request is from Representative Fred A. Britten, Republican, Illinois, who in a speech in the house, said he would call upon Hull to ask for “his recall from the United States because of his personal opposition to legislation that was pending before the American congress.” Britten said that a British subject, C. J. H. MacKenzie-Kennedy, had attempted to address the naval affairs committee “with a view to influencing our judgment.”

ABOARD THE U.S.S. CALIFORNIA, WITH THE UNITED STATES FLEET, AT SEA, April 21,—(By Radio to the United Press)—The most spectacular air combat of peace times today opened a simulated attack on the Panama Canal to determine whether the Isthmian waterway and its defenses are the “Achilles heel” of the American national defense. The canal zone fortifications were revealed mercilessly by the parachute flares dropped in the early dawn by the force of ‘attacking’ planes from the United States fleet. Beneath scudding clouds of tropical sunrise, the warships clashed theoretically with the full strength of the army and navy forces stationed at the canal zone to guard the vital link between the eastern and western shores. As Admiral David Sellers’ gray “bulldogs” of the sea advanced into the Gulf of Panama, 150 defending planes engaged the superior air forces of the fleet in simulated combat. Anti-a

GENEVA, (UP).—Japan’s startling “hands off” Chinese declarations may be raised in what will amount to a world conference when the League of Nations committee on Manchukuo meets here May 14, it was indicated today. League of Nations officials, already chagrined over the complete defeat of the league’s efforts to curb activities of Japan in Manchukuo, frankly took a most serious view of the latest Tokyo statements. Confronted with a new step forward in Japan’s aim to assert full leadership in eastern Asia, league officials seemed inclined to favor a showdown and to welcome a general discussion of far eastern affairs at the May 14 meeting—the first in nearly a year of the Manchukuo committee. From the standpoint of the league as a body, there was no doubt that a strong stand against Japan would be welcomed. But as Geneva is but the shell of the organization, and its members have their own p

By MELVIN K. WHITELEATHER Paris, April 20. —(AP)— A howling mob of 6,000 communists and extremists, embittered over the government’s economy pay cuts, engaged hundreds of mobile guards and armed police in violent skirmishes this evening that resulted in 940 arrests and injuries to about 200. The bloody scenes of mob frenzy and riots early in February were recalled as lying squads of police charged through the streets near the city hall, swinging their clubs right and left in an attempt to disperse the surly throng. City Hall Staged Guards and carabiners threw a solid wall around the city hall neighborhood. Demonstrators, fleeing before the officers’ onslaught, took refuge in subway kiosks and continued to do battle. One policeman separated from his fellows was badly beaten. By the time nearly 1,000 had been arrested and the rest driven from pillar to post by the wildly swinging police cl

Paris, April 1 (AP)—France sped Foreign Minister Louis Barthou on a hunt for support today in the French fight against the rearming of Germany. The minister, with all disarmament negotiations at a standstill, set out with the aim of strengthening France’s alliances with Poland and the Little Entente. His first destination was Warsaw. After trying to patch up differences with Poland, he plans to continue to Praha. From there he may go to Belgrade. Franco-Polish relations entered a new phase when the Poles took the unexpected step of signing a 10-year friendship treaty with the Nazis. Later, Poland began urging France to follow her example and accept Chancellor Adolf Hitler's proposal of a non-aggression pact. A distant coolness developed between the two old friends as a result. Officially, the French say they are happy over the newly found feeling between Germany and Poland. They say it l

Associated Press Foreign Staff SHANGHAI, April 21,—(P) Japanese frowns on aircraft purchases by China have gone unheeded by foreign airplane dealers. Their spectacular selling campaigns, marked by daring aerial tricks over downtown Shanghai, continued unabated today with American and Italian dealers in the forefront. With the skies as their stage, the airmen stunt while noon-time crowds are packing the streets, hoping to impress the public with the prowess of their respective machines. Lieutenant James H. Doolittle, who demonstrated a high-powered American combat plane, began the practice of using overhead Shanghai as a demonstration ground when in recent months he startled Chinese and foreigners alike with his exploits above the rooftops. This famous American speed flier sold dozens of the planes he showed. The Italian air ace, Major Mario de Bernardi, now in China demonstrating an Ital

H. S. Exilona, in the Mediterranean, — 21 (P)—Seven days out from the good ship Exilona, with seventeen more to go, and the thirteen passengers are like one happy family. The fact that one of the passengers—Samuel Insull—is under detention; that another—Burton Berry—is guarding him, and that five others are here to write about these two has not interfered with the harmonious community life which is typical of long voyages. Life on deck and in the saloon passes tranquilly, as if past and future were forgotten by the dozen and one travelers separated temporarily from their accustomed grooves in society. Only the discreet presence of his custodian wherever Insull happens to be and the latter's reminiscences as he talks with newspaper men remind the company that the man is being taken home to face criminal charges in the city where he built up an industrial empire. Five regular passengers at

Near End; Ordered to Leave, BARBIZON, France--Weary gendarmes doubled their guard around Leon Trotsky’s villa today, hoping their vigil over the exiled Russian is near an end. The police went through Trotsky’s baggage last night and notified him he must leave France as soon as possible. An unemployed Russian added to the confusion around the cottage last night by shouting that he intended to “pull out Trotsky’s whiskers.” He was chased away. Soviet President Urges Training Of Women, Children in War, - MOSCOW, — Under the lash of President Michael Kalinin, Soviet leaders pushed forward today

1934-04-07.text: London, April 6.—(4?)—The United States is willing to join in economic and financial action against any violator of an international arms pact, provided Washington could be the sole judge of whether such steps were justified, the Associated Press learned from an authoritative American source tonight. Such modified cooperation in punitive measures to guarantee the enforcement of provisions of a disarmament agreement means that the United States would not commit itself in advance to any definite step along this line. Instead it would await violations before making a decision. Bared by Davis These facts were revealed following upon a conference of Norman H. Davis, American ambassador-at-large, with Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, today. Davis gave Sir John the views of the Roosevelt administration of arms reductions and guarantees for the carrying out of arms treaties, and afterw

Berlin, (AP)—Chancellor Adolf Hitler, striding into the thick of the Nazi-Catholic Affray, directed a swift investigation today of Nazi violence toward Catholic youths. Intervening personally, he ordered the temporary suspension of three Berlin Nazi youth leaders who led a raid on a Palm Sunday Catholic youth meeting. Indicating he planned to deal firmly with any others involved, he demanded complete details of the incident which brought protests from outraged Catholics. Hitler's Voelkischer Beobachter attempted to quiet the controversy today declaring that freedom of religion is assured the Catholics. Beat Up Catholics, Reliable, although belated, reports of the Palm Sunday affair said hundreds of Hitler youths beat those who offered resistance when they swooped down upon 1,500 Catholics at suburban Henningsdorf. The young Nazis were armed with camp knives—their regular equipment, the r

Associated Press Foreign Staff GENOA, Italy, April 6. (AP)— Mrs. Thalia Fortesque Massie, the center of a sensational attack and murder case in Honolulu more than two years ago, tried to kill herself while en route here because she said, “I wanted to die; I regretted having got a divorce from my husband.” Officers of the S. S. Roma disclosed that she slashed both wrists and threw herself from the top deck four days ago on a voyage from New York. Prof. Darrio Borelli, director of the nervous ailments’ clinic of Genoa, where she was taken after the Roma's arrival yesterday, said the contusions she suffered in the 20-foot fall were not serious, but would require 30 to 40 days for complete recovery. Mrs. Massie and Lieut Thomas Hedges Massie, U. S. N., were divorced in Reno, Feb. 28. She had planned a Mediterranean cruise. Tonight she entered a period of deep sleep and restful quiet, under o

ESTAMBUL, Turkey, April T-- (UP)—Attorneys for Samuel Insull today filed in the supreme appeals court a long brief demanding his release on the ground that he is "Innocent of any crime anywhere." Fighting hard to save the aged utilities man from extradition to the United States, the attorneys cheered Insull considerably. He could be seen today smiling from the barred window of his room in the detention house. In their test appeal, the lawyers did not raise the question of Insull’s nationality, it was understood, nor did they ask for bail.

'ROME, April 5. (®)—With an American in the chair, the world wheat advisory commission met today to seek new ways and means of raising and stabilizing the prices of wheat. John Van A. Mac Murray, American minister to Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, presided at the opening session. Two other American delegates, Dr. Mordecai Ezekiel, economic adviser to the secretary of agriculture, and Frederick E. Murphy, Minneapolis publisher, figured prominently.

PATNA, today, April 7 (ENS)—A step of far-reaching significance in India's tangled political situation was taken today by Mahatma Gandhi when he advised his followers to drop civil disobedience as an instrument of policy. Gandhi's surprise action came through a statement to the Indian National Congress, of which he is the leader. He asked the Congress to suspend the policy of civil disobedience as a method of concerted action and leave such action in the future solely to him. The wise leader of India’s militants made it clear he wanted sole authority to say, during his lifetime, whether the policy of civil disobedience shall be resumed. He specified that resumption during his lifetime must be only at his direction, or “unless one arises claiming to know science better than I do. Civil disobedience, or passive resistance to the acts and policies of the government, has been one of the stro

Copenhagen, April 7 (INS)—A freak “tidal wave,” caused by the crashing of an enormous rock into the sea, took a toll of at least 40 lives in Norwegian fishing towns today in one of the strangest disasters in Norway’s history. The huge rock fell into the water with a thundering roar near Aalesund, Norway, causing three successive “tidal waves” which swept inland for a distance of more than 800 yards. Wrecking fishing craft, waterfront structures, and many homes while inhabitants were asleep, the giant waves inundated the small fishing towns of Tafjord and Fijordas. PHILADELPHIA (AP)—A youth identified by the Public Ledger as Franklin D. Roosevelt Jr., smashed a photographer's camera, but his picture appears in the newspaper anyhow. The plate for the picture, snapped at a wrestling match last night was in the photographer's pocket and was not damaged when he was pursued to the lobby of the hall and tripped to the floor. Donald Corvelli, the camera man, suffered bruises and torn trousers. Quoting Corvelli, the Ledger says the 19-year-old son of the president jumped several times on the camera. “This man was taking a picture of me and I don't like to have my picture taken,” was the explanation which police said they received. Told by H. Vaughan Morgan Jr. that “this man is the president's son,” the officers escorted the youth to Morgan's automobile and the party left. Young Roosevelt is a weekend guest at the Morgan home in Bryn Mawr. “Roosevelt kept

1934-05-14.text: LONDON, May 13.--The British government today faced a showdown on the war debt issue and other foreign policies, including the trade war with Japan and its plans for the 1935 disarmament conference. The seriousness of the situation was emphasized when Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, tentatively cancelled plans to go to Geneva for the opening of the League of Nations council Tuesday, apparently believing he would be needed here to defend the government on the floor of the House of Commons. Washington's warning that a token payment on the debt installment due June 15 will be regarded as a default under the Johnson Act aroused the opposition to a determination.

(By Associated Press) GENEVA, May 14.—Disarmament became somewhat involved in League of Nations circles today with France waiting for bids from Great Britain to guarantee security. Hungary likewise called for a security guarantee and published a protest against Yugoslavia which said that the political tension in Europe is now so great that every conflict which risks “putting Europe on fire” should be eliminated. This situation confronted the members of the League of Nations council as they gathered today for that body's 79th session.

London — (CP—Secretary Wallace’s threat that the United States would dump wheat on the world market unless exporting nations got together on an agreement to limit sales was interpreted today by members of the world wheat commission in session here as aimed squarely at Argentina. The American threat was regarded as endangering all exporting nations and the commission will make another attempt this week to prevent Argentina breaking the export quota pact. The United States, Canada, and Australia are expected to offer her part of their quota rights of export on the condition that the South American nation curb her shipments abroad. Representatives of the United States, Canada, Australia, England, France and Germany met today in an attempt to salvage something of the wreckage of the wheat conference which blew up Friday when the minimum price scheme was defeated. LONDON, May 14.—INS—The British steamer Mabriton, carrying a cargo of nitrate from Antofagasta, Chile, to Alexandria, Egypt, caught afire in mid-Atlantic today, according to wireless messages received here from the vessel. The Mabriton, a 6,695-ton ship, was said not to be in any immediate danger. The Dutch steamer Crijnssen was standing by.

FONTAINBLEAU, France, May 14.—Seven persons were dead today because a driver of an automobile road race tried to avoid killing a dog. Eric Lora, 29, a naval ensign, was the driver. He lost control of his car in dodging a dog and it went into a crowd. He and six others, including two women and two soldiers, were killed. Seven were injured seriously.

AD GENEVA, (UP).—The League of Nations council met today in an atmosphere of unrelieved gloom to consider the world’s troubles and seek solutions for seven major problems affecting Europe, Asia, Africa and South America. A war, an impending war, mass cruelties, complaints of oppression and the ever-present disarmament situation were among items which included: 1—The Gran Chaco war between Bolivia and Paraguay, which it is charged munitions manufacturers are prolonging. 2—The Saar plebiscite to be held next year, and Nazi activities in the territory. 3—China’s relations with Japan. 4—Disarmament. 5—Hungary’s complaints of unfriendly Jugoslavian activities on their frontier. 6—Liberia’s alleged oppression of the Kroos tribes in the African interior. 7—The Leticia dispute between Colombia and Peru, which may lead to war within a few weeks. It was indicated that the council would take no imp

GENEVA, May 14.--Members of the League of Nations council, alarmed at moves to rearm in many lands and stirred by fears of a spread of the war between Paraguay and Bolivia, gathered today for the body's seventy-ninth session. Ringing in their ears was the charge of Alvarez Del Vayo, Spanish president of the league's unsuccessful Chaco peace commission, that foreign capitalists were largely to blame for the South American conflict. "Oil has played a big role," Del Vayo declared in a speech last night. He appealed for a halt in the sales of arms materials. He voiced the fear, expressed by many, that unless the Gran Chaco fighting is ended quickly, complications may develop which will involve other nations in South America. In considering the commission's proposal for an embargo on arms shipments to Paraguay and Bolivia if they refuse to arbitrate, there also was a move on foot for a disarm

Halifax, N. S., May 14—(AP)—Sabelli and Pond, flying from New York to Rome, were unreported along their scheduled course today and observers believed they swerved away from Nova Scotia to avoid fog. Harbor Grace reported the fliers would find fog and stiff east wind along the Newfoundland coast. Weather reports from further out in the Atlantic were good. Brooklyn, N. Y., May 14—(AP)—Cap. George R. Pond and Lieut. Cesare Gabelli soared away from Floyd Bennett field at 6:24 A. M., Eastern Standard Time, today with the announced intention of reaching Rome without a stop. They said their large orange and maroon monoplane could make the 4,500-mile flight in about 40 hours. Pond, a former Navy flier, and Sabelli, one-time Italian War ace, had been planning the flight for months. They had hoped originally to make the attempt last fall but abandoned the idea because of unfavorable weather. Their

1934-05-10.text: WASHINGTON, May 10 (AP).— An expected early reopening of conversations with Great Britain gave promise today of a possible break in the war debts deadlock. Now that President Roosevelt has opened the door for negotiations, state department officials frankly anticipated an early call from Sir Ronald Lindsay, the British ambassador. Signs appeared both here and in London of a willingness to talk debts and there were definite indications that officials of both nations are feeling about for some formula that can be placed on the table. French Envoy Calls, Another sign of leavening in the debt mass was seen in calls yesterday by Andre De Laboulaye, the French ambassador, and Paul May, Belgian ambassador, on William Phillips, undersecretary of state. Foreign Minister Barthou in Paris explained that Laboulaye had sought an explanation of the Johnson act which prohibits nations in

LONDON, May 10.—All over Europe today statesmen sadly were proclaiming the end of disarmament efforts, attempting to shift the blame on each other, fixing up old fashioned warlike alliances and selling munitions to future enemies. Many times disarmament has been pronounced dead, only to stagger weakly up from the grave. This time agreement seemed general that death was a fact and that it could be revived only in a new incarnation. Great Britain was reported to have reconciled itself finally to failure, last of the Great European powers. The cabinet agreed yesterday to propose an aircraft limitation treaty in place of a general disarmament treaty, but decided privately, at the same time, that France would not agree to one because it would involve granting Germany the right to maintain military airplanes. Joachim von Ribbentrop, newly appointed German disarmament delegate, was here today t

LONDON, May 10.—(UP)—Lloyd’s world-wide insurance agency is doing a considerable business issuing policies against anything happening to President Roosevelt, it was learned today. Such importance is placed in Europe on the president’s continuance in office and the completion of his recovery program that business men and traders are gambling on his survival and ultimate victory.

| LONDON, May 9. (AP) — The | British cabinet deferred stating its disarmament policies today after a long committee discussion, and reports persisted that a break in the cabinet on the issue is likely. It was indicated that no statement can be expected until after the League of Nations’ council meeting. Arthur Henderson, chairman of the disarmament conference, will leave for Paris tomorrow to discuss the threatened collapse of the parley with Louis Barthou, French foreign minister. It was believed likely that he would ask the French to propose a new basis of arms regulation. The crux of the reported differences is said to be whether in view of failure to arrange a disarmament convention, the British government shall attempt again some plan to harmonize divergent international views and arrive at an accord—or cut loose entirely and take an independent line of action. Prime Minister Ramsa

Cherbourg, France, May 10, (UPI) Six occupants of the Air France channel liner F-AMPH were declared officially lost today when ships from France and England, after hours of work in heavy fog, found wreckage of the plane in the English Channel 19 miles northwest of Boulogne. The French pilot and mechanics, British steward, and two French and a Swiss passenger were lost. The plane left Paris for London yesterday in a heavy fog. It wirelessed an SOS after it passed the French coast.

Paris, May 15.—— The ‘For Rent’ sign is up at Leon Trotsky’s former hiding place at Barbizon. The forest villa, from which the Russian exile was spirited by the French secret service, was advertised in Paris American newspapers. “Owing to the sudden departure of the tenant,” the advertisement read, “the villa Ker Monique is to let. On borders of Fontainebleau Forest. Five rooms, bathroom, garage, every convenience, shaded park.” M. Trotsky himself presumably still is on an automobile tour of France with detectives, pending final arrangements for him to live in some other country or on a French island.

LOS ANGELES, May 10—(?)— Two masked men brandishing pistols snatched William F. Gettle, 47-year-old wealthy oil man, from his newly-purchased estate in the foothills district of Arcadia, at a midnight party, declaring “this is a kidnapping.” James Wolfe, a Westwood furniture dealer, was left bound and gagged and strapped to a tree on the estate. His wife freed him. Gettle was abducted after a party of 10, entertained at the estate by Mr. and Mrs. Gettle, who are residents of Beverly Hills, had left a swimming pool. Eight members of the party entered the house while Gettle and Wolfe stopped in a small summer house to pull on trousers and shirts over their swimming suits. As they bent over they were startled by a voice, which exclaimed: “Stick ’em up and be quick about it!” Two Pistols Pointed They glanced up into the faces of two men and the muzzles of two (Continued on Page Six)

(By The Associated Press) CANANEA, Sonora, May 9.—Their secret plans disclosed by their self-implicated "contact" man, the kidnappers of June Robles were believed fleeing through Sonora today with the 6-year-old girl still in their possession and Mexican police virtually at their heels. Alarms were sounded throughout the northern Sonora country as authorities sought to close in on the trio which sidestepped two traps laid by United States and Mexican investigators on information from the "contact" man who was held in technical custody in Arizona. Two Men And Woman Documentary evidence received from the man, it was said by officials, described the fugitives as an American man, and a Mexican man and his wife. The description fitted three adults who had with them a girl said to resemble June. They disappeared from Cananea a few hours before searchers descended on the hut in which they had b

1934-02-13.text: Sees: (the Associated Press). Lines were drawn between Great Britain and France today for a trade war of serious proportions. At midnight an extra duty of 20 percent was clamped on most French imports by Britain. The duty was in retaliation for French paring down of quotas in British imports to France. Just before the duties became effective France got in another blow by denouncing Franco-British trade treaties of 1828 and 1882. Uncle Sam was an “interested observer” in the conflict although commercial officials at Washington said they believed American trade would not be greatly affected, favorably or adversely.

LONDON, Feb. 12.—(/?)—Strained commercial relations between Great Britain and France reached a critical stage tonight. As the British moved to put an increased duty on French imports because of what it terms unfair quotas on British goods shipped to France, the government at Paris notified the foreign office here it is denouncing two trade treaties under which British goods have had certain preferences at French ports. At midnight, an increased duty of 20 percent is to be levied on most French imports into England, an order on which opinion in the cabinet was divided. The retaliation against the recently announced quotas on British goods shipped into France caused a distinct disagreement in the government here, with the foreign office and the Board of Trade lined up on opposite sides of the question of retaliation.

Vienna, Feb. 13—(by Telephone to London and Berlin) —(WP)—Neighbor against neighbor, war veteran against war veteran, Austrian Socialists and the combined forces of the state clashed bloodily today in town and country. It was impossible to compute the toll of dead. Conservative estimates of those killed ran into the hundreds. Socialists, in groups numbering as high as 3,890 each, replied with bursts of rifle fire and showers of hand grenades to ultimatums threatening bombardment and to bombardment of the half dozen big...

FOREIGN— Vienna—Civil war develops throughout Austria with 129 dead and hundreds wounded; Dollfuss dissolves socialist party in face of general strike. Paris—One reported dead and many wounded in sporadic riots resulting from one-day general strike which paralyzed nation. London—Paris, Great Britain and France move toward trade war: French denounce trade treaties and British put extra duty on French imports. DOMESTIC— Washington—Court refuses to shield MacCracken from Senate contempt charges. Walla Walla—Machine guns end riot of 40 armed felons with six reported killed and 12 injured in Washington state penitentiary. Washington—Government sets up export-import bank to finance Russian trade. Washington—Army airmen prepared to fly mail over emergency schedule of 11,106 miles. Washington—Administration sends Congress Wallace's proposals for commodity exchange regulations.

PARIS (AP)—Fast, firm action to show the world France is able to take care of herself at home and abroad, was planned by the new cabinet after mounted guards early Tuesday rode down rioters in several provincial cities. After a day of comparative tranquility during the general strike of Monday, in which laborers demonstrated against fascism, disorders were quelled. One was known dead and 150 wounded as a result of the strike. A firm attitude toward Chancellor Hitler of Germany to see that Austria is protected will be taken by the cabinet of Premier Doumergue it was indicated.

VIENNA, AUSTRIA, (UP).— Beleaguered Austria, at the turning point in her post-war destiny, writhed under a devastating civil war today as the government sought to crush a socialist revolt in which hundreds were estimated to have fallen. The total of slain was unofficially placed at between 400 and 500, with hundreds more wounded. The socialists, outnumbered and out-equipped, nevertheless fought desperately in Vienna and a dozen other points in the northern part of Austria. It was estimated that 20,000 men, women and children were in danger of their lives in tenements in the Heiligenstadt and Ottakring districts which were being heavily shelled. Machine guns and artillery mowed them down in Vienna, Ling, Steyr, Bruck, Kapfenberg and other points. The uniformed socialist schutzbund corps fought back with machine guns, rifles, pistols and bombs. A desperate, guerilla civil war was waged ove

PARIS, Feb. 13 ()—Mounted guards rode down rioters in Marseilles, Nantes and Roubaix early today. Time after time the guards charged into the shouting throngs in the three cities. It was nearly dawn before order was restored. Both sides counted many casualties, although no one was killed. The outbreaks followed a day of comparative calm that marked the 24-hour general strike by which a million workmen protested the "Fascism" they believe is gaining strength in the government. The casualty list for the day of strike listed one dead and about 150 injured and wounded in various outbreaks of violence. Forty were arrested at Marseilles after a furious pistol battle between police and hoodlums. Riding through the streets of the city, the hoodlums inaugurated a brief nocturnal reign of terror by firing at lighted windows. One Death in Gun Fight. Police swarmed into the streets. (Copyright, 1934, The Associated Press) Paris, Feb. 12.—Shooting and rioting in French provinces, where one person was killed and scores were wounded, marked a 24-hour general strike today in opposition to “a wave of fascism.” One man was killed in Marseille as bands of hoodlums rode through the streets firing at lighted windows and fighting gun battles with police. Communists attempted to storm a prison at Mulhouse and set fire to a wool factory at Roubaix. Prison guards with drawn pistols drove off the mob at Mulhouse. The Communists sought to release three prisoners by battering doors of the jail with heavy beams. Six rioters were shot and wounded at Marseille. Fourteen police were injured. Bonfires of wrecked stands and benches burned in a miniature reproduction of recent Paris riots before calm was restored shortly before midnight. Vital services throughout the country were paralyze

1934-06-13.text: (United Press Leased Wire) LONDON, June 13.—International co-operation to stave off a collapse of the German mark and prevent a new financial crisis in Europe was regarded as possible today after conferences between Montagu Norman, head of the Bank of England, and leading British bankers.

SUSANVILLE, Calif., June 13-- Threats of mob violence were renewed today after the alleged confession of Pete Alosi, mill hand, that he stabbed to death five persons because two of them had broken up his home. The confessions poured from the Italian's lips in broken English. He claimed that Joseph Fazio, 45, a Susanville grocer, had been intimate with his wife several years ago. Unable to break up the relationship, Alosi sent his family to Boston. The separation preyed on his mind. Sunday he went to the Fazio home and stabbed the grocer. The latter's wife found him with the body so he stabbed her. She also had interfered with his family affairs, the mill hand said. John Fazio, 26-year-old son of the victims, entered the house.
