‘by United Press LONDON, June 13.—David Lloyd George, 71, war-time prime minister, was suffering from a slight chill today.

| Churt, Surrey, England, June 13—‘A-P.1--David Lloyd George, 71-year-old World War premier of Great Britain, was ill with a chill at his home here today and his physicians ordered him confined to his room for a few days.

LONDON, June 12 (#)—A dozen American society women tonight realized long cherished dreams when, in the impressive splendor of the throne room at Buckingham palace, they were presented to King George and Queen Mary. The Americans, from all sections of the United States, were among the 300 women who passed in a rapidly moving line into the presence of the royal couple. As they approached the king and queen the names of the women were announced. Each paused a moment before the thrones—a moment which meant supreme social triumph—bowed her plumed head and passed on. The American women presented tonight were Mrs. Claude K. Boettcher of Denver; Mrs. Philip J. Britt, Mrs. Henry W. Catlin, Miss Flora Louise Louis, and Mrs. Charles Sweency, New York; Mrs. Francis C. Gray, Boston; Miss Pauline Le Breton and Mrs. Ben H. Wyatt of Washington; Miss Jean Kingman Lucas, Atlanta; Miss Barbara Macauley, Bu

NORTH BAY, Ont., June 13 — (UP) — Mrs. Olivia Dionne, young mother who gave birth to quintuplets seventeen days ago was reported in a serious condition today. Mrs. Dionne, it was said, was “not so well. She had a very bad night.” The quintuplets, however, still thrived despite the pessimistic predictions of scientists at their birth that all of them could not live.

Rome, June 12.—(7)—An outline of a plan for bringing Germany back into the League of Nations and for closer German-Italian cooperation has been prepared by Premier Mussolini, who will meet Chancellor Hitler Thursday, sources close to the premier revealed today. Il Duce has worked out plans for his talk with Hitler which he hopes will result in checking France's system of alliances, it was stated. Work at Summer Home. The work is being done at Mussolini’s summer home at Rocca Della Carminate. For his staff of advisors Premier Mussolini will have the chief Italian disarmament experts, including Baron Pomeo Aloisi, vice president of the League of Nations council. This fact emphasized the interest the Italian chief of state is taking in getting Germany back to the disarmament conference at Geneva. Meanwhile, at Venice elaborate plans were made for the visit of the German chancellor, who will

Associated Press Foreign Staff PARIS, June 13.—The “possibility of settling defaulted war debts to the United States by a partial payment “in kind” was received in French official quarters as a hopeful suggestion for solution of the vexing problem. It is expected by government officials that the offer to make some payments in goods, made by Secretary of State Cordell Hull to Great Britain, will be extended to France. Payments in goods rather than gold would meet many French objections to settling the account with America. Officially authorities would merely say they are “greatly interested” by Hull’s note to Britain. But it is hopeful. In 1933 France's adverse balances in trade with the United States was competitive goods could be exported to America to offset a part of the debt.

1934-10-28.text: LONDON. (Copyright by AP). Siam's wisp of a king, Prajadhipok, whose royal prerogatives have been cut and curbed throughout his uneasy years, announced he has told the Bangkok government he intends to abdicate his ancient throne. The “supreme arbiter of the ebb and flow of tides,” the “brother of the moon,” the “possessor of the twenty-four umbrellas” and the holder of other venerable and fantastic oriental titles slept in London awaiting word from Bangkok. The Siamese capital was cut off from communication with the outside world, presumably the work of censors, while rumors of revolution in Siam ran about London. A quarrel with Premier Phya Bahol’s government and the national assembly as to whether the monarch should have the last word over the life and death of his subjects furnished the crux of the Siamese political drama revealed here. Until two years ago little Prajadhipok, whose th

London, Oct. 27.—-(4)—A fortnight of talk about ways to limit their navies tonight apparently left an agreement among Japan, Great Britain and the United States as far away as ever. Japan's demands for equality of defensive armaments "in principle" and for reduction or abolition of capital ships fell on deaf ears, and naval circles this evening were certain endless controversy and complete stalemate in the conversations would result unless Nippon modified her position. Peril A general disagreement among the three delegations would ruin chances for constructive work at the 1935 naval conference, it was asserted, and pull down the entire principle of naval equality established in the Washington treaty.

MELBOURNE, Oct. 2.—(?)—(Sunday)—Cathcart Jones and K. W. Waller, English airmen backtracking the London-to-Melbourne derby trial, hopped off from Darwin for Singapore at dawn today as derby stragglers still plodded along toward the finish line. Jones and Waller, who finished fourth, hoped to beat the record time of the derby winners, C. W. A. Scott and Campbell Black, when they left Melbourne yesterday, but stormy weather over the Timor Sea held them all night at Darwin. It appeared, therefore, the mark set by Scott’s Red Comet—70 hours, 59 minutes and 50 seconds—was safe from them.

Nanes, France, Oct. 27.—-()— Reform of the French constitution was virtually assured today, and likewise the continuation of Premier Gaston Doumergue's ‘political truce' cabinet. Edouard Herriot, head of the powerful radical socialist party, averted a possible cabinet rupture by swinging his party over to support the aged Doumergue, but he did it with a personal pledge that he would resist any government changes likely to lead to a ‘dictatorship.’ The congress voted overwhelmingly to continue support of Doumergue, which it had threatened to withdraw over the issue of giving to the premier power to decide constitutional reform. The opposition to ‘dictatorship’ appeared likely to result in the long run in a series of compromises. Aim The premier is determined to remodel the constitution giving him

Berlin, Oct. 27, (P) — Protestant churches tonight prepared to fly their white flag with its purple cross tomorrow for the first time in two and one-half months as Nazis apparently yielded all along the line on their heretofore iron-handed church program. The resignation yesterday of Dr. August Jaeger, Nazi commissioner for Prussia’s Protestant churches, was followed today by discontinuance of police surveillance he ordered for Bishop Hans Meiser of Bavaria and instructions from Karl Koch, head of the opposition synod, that the church flag be flown. Reichsbishop Ludwig Mueller, whose church dictatorship drew criticism second in bitterness only to that directed at Jaeger, declared the flag unnecessary in August because of the unification he said German people had achieved under Hitler. Koch, however, insisted that the new Paganism movement headed by Dr. Alfred Rosenberg, director of Nazi

VIENNA, Oct. 27--A struggle between political and military groups for seats on the country’s new advisory council preoccupied Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg’s government tonight as strife between heimwehr (fascist home guards) and police aggravated political tension. Reports from Wiener Neustadt in lower Austria said heimwehr forces there attacked police barracks yesterday and imprisoned police officials, only to be dislodged and arrested when regular army detachments were called out. Danger Recognized Recognizing the danger of stirring discontent, the government today was planning to announce membership of the new council which begins functioning Nov. 1, only one or two days beforehand. Prince Ernst Von Starhemberg, the heimwehr chieftain, and other leaders have demanded repeatedly that the members be recruited ex-

Washington, Oct. 27.—(#)— Organized business, noting a growing rapprochement between the administration and industry, nevertheless renewed its request upon President Roosevelt today for a statement of his objectives. The Chamber of Commerce of the United States placed particular emphasis in a fortnightly review of business developments on what it saw as encouraging signs that business men and the White House are finding a common approach to the problems of recovery. There existed a ‘growing realization,’ the chamber said, that this peace ‘must come about through the revival of industry and employment.’ But, it added, ‘further improvement is contingent upon the more explicit setting forth of administration aims in the legislation it will offer and the specific steps it will propose in carrying forward its program when Congress convenes.’ Thus the chamber renewed its old and previously unf

By The Associated Press: - MARIANNA, Fla., Oct. 27.—National guard machine guns mounted on the courthouse square brought enforced calm to this town tonight after 24 hours of mob spirit during which one negro was lynched for attacking and killing a white girl and another was threatened for striking a white man. The machine guns pointed out from each corner of the square. Nearby were rifles of 120 national guardmen ordered here from Tallahassee and Panama City by Governor Dave Sholtz to aid civil authorities in protecting Bud Gammon, a negro, charged with striking Walter Cook, a white man, with a bottle. Before the guardsmen arrived, a mob of about 200 to 300 persons which had stormed the courthouse in an unsuccessful attempt to get Gammon drifted away. Small groups appeared at times in the negro residential section, but no violence was reported. Associate Justice Rivers Buford of the stat

1934-04-03.text: ISTANBUL, Turkey, April 3.—Fighting odds that seemed hopeless, Samuel Insull today appealed to a Turkish court of last resort to save him from extradition to the United States. The 74-year-old Chicago utilities man, resilient and hopeful, directed from the prison wing of the detention house the fight for freedom—a fight which authorities said would fail, and end in his return to the United States to face trial for fraud in the management of his utilities companies. Chief State Prosecutor Kenan Bey expressed this official opinion: "There has been no judicial judgment from which to appeal. The penal court gave merely an opinion formally establishing fact and no judicial opinion was involved." The new Turkish-American extradition treaty was ratified last night by the legislature. Although officials emphasized they did not act under the treaty but under the penal code, it was revealed today.

ISTANBUL, Turkey, April 2—Turkey officially notified the American government tonight that it can have Samuel Insull for trial, and put him in jail—despite his tears—to ensure his being on hand when American agents arrive to start him back to Chicago. Turkish authorities, apparently mindful of the 74-year old fugitive's heart, which doctors say has been ailing for some time, agreed, however, to grant him a few liberties not given the ordinary run of prisoners. Go After Meats Among these privileges, it was learned, will be the right to go to a restaurant for his meals. Making the case doubly sure, the national assembly ratified an extradition convention with the United States as the Turkish government formally communicated to American Ambassador Skinner at Ankara, the capital, the cabinet's decision that Insull will be handed over for a return to American shores, which he left after his ut

PARIS, April 3.—(#)—Definite assertions that an armed revolution in France is being prepared by both Rightists and Leftists were made today. The secret service and judicial police under Judge Saussier, investigating magistrate, are known to be hunting hidden arsenals but Desire Ferry, the editor of the newspaper La Liberte, owned by former Premier Andre Tardieu, says the hunt is “too late.” Thousands of rifles—some persons estimate the number to be 14,000—are reported to have been smuggled into France before Marshal Petain, minister of war, induced the cabinet to order a close watch of the frontier. Large quantities of automatic pistols were said to be arriving in Paris daily, consigned to big arms firms. Ferry charged that the rifles are destined for communists and socialists, while the communist newspaper L'Humanité retorted with alleged details of pistol shipments to Rightist factions

Istanbul, April 2 ()—Sam- vel Insull ended another phase of his flight from American justice in a Turkish prison today and awaited extradition to the United States. He was arrested and ordered held for return to Illinois to answer charges of embezzlement and larceny growing out of the collapse of the vast public utilities empire he once ruled. The fugitive was placed in the house of detention tonight and the government announced that he will be handed over to American authorities as soon as they appear with the necessary papers. Taken Prisoner With tears in his eyes and an acutely dejected expression, Insull was taken prisoner in the Hotel London in a suburb of the capital, where he had gone in the morning with a squad of detectives, who, even at that time, had him practically in custody. Insull thus ended his strange and exciting odyssey of several weeks aboard the little tramp steamer,

ROME, April 3 (P)—A year of world-wide prayer to bring all Christians into one faith and to atone for injuries done to God's majesty by militant atheistic associations was decreed by Pope Pius today in a papal bull extending the holy years to all the world. The holy year, strictly speaking, closed yesterday; but the pontiff made it possible for persons in any nation up to the Sunday after Easter in 1935 to gain the jubilee indulgence by visiting four churches to be designated by the bishops. The papal bull says the faithful making visits must pray "for the return of all dissidents to the unity of the fold of Christ and make solemn, pious and devout reparation for the injury done his Divine Majesty by associations with the militant atheists and the godless who seek to snatch from the hearts of men the supreme comforts of religion and deprive them of the benefits of the true civilization w

ARCASSONNE, France, April 2—A bloodless pistol duel on an old jousting ground where knighthood once flowered entertained French politics of this post-Barter holiday. The youthful Jean Mistler, a deputy and former minister of commerce, exchanged shots at 20 paces with businessman Roger De Tour, ardent Royalist, on a rifle range near medieval Carcassonne. They took aim twice, fired and missed, then stalked off the field of honor. Their parting, like their meeting, was as chilly as the early morning air. Politics brought the two together. Mistler was a member of the Daladier cabinet which Royalists blame for the fatalities in street riots early in February. An argument in a cafe Saturday night during which De Tour called Mistler an “ignoble person,” was climaxed when the businessman smacked the deputy on the cheek. Cards were then exchanged. The dueling code was strictly observed. The adver

Istanbul, April 3—Apparently the last door to freedom was slammed in the face of Samuel Insull today when the Turkish court of cassation denied him the right of appeal from the decision of the tribunal which ruled he must be held for the United States authorities. Turkey’s decision to extradite Insull was based on the ruling of the lower court. Refusal by the court of cassation to entertain an appeal indicates Turkey definitely has decided it has the legal right to detain Insull for the United States officers and is determined to turn him over to officials of the country from which he fled when his vast utilities empire collapsed. Insull’s only course now, unless he or his attorneys are able to produce some surprise move, is to wait in the jail in old Stamboul until a qualified officer of the United States takes him in charge and starts him on the long journey back to Chicago. Tokyo, April 2.—-()—Italy's alleged opposition to Japanese connections in Africa caused the cancellation today of the proposed "picture bride" marriage of Wij Araya, an Ethiopian prince, and Miss Masako Kuroda, daughter of the Japanese viscount Hiroyukuku Kuroda. The announcement that Araya had made a long-distance selection of Miss Kuroda as his bride-to-be was quoted in dispatches from Addis Ababa as stating that a "certain power" had interfered. Vernacular newspapers expressed the opinion that Italy was displeased at the idea of a Japanese wife for a member of a ruling family in Africa because of Premier Mussolini's recent statements of his country’s mission on that continent. Although the newspapers published a story from its Ethiopian correspondent giving apparently full reasons for the cancellation of the marriage, the family of Viscount Kuroda announced that it was ignorant of any

1934-08-18.text: SOUTH FORELAND, Eng., Aug 18.—Mrs. Emma Faber, Austrian, swam the English channel today in 8 hours, 45 minutes. If her feat is officially recognized, it will constitute a record. Mrs. Faber plunged into the water at Cape Grisnez at 6:30 a.m., and climbed to the shore at South Foreland at 3:15 p.m.

LONDON, Aug. 18 (AP).—The world wheat conference failed to agree today on export quotas but, as was expected, the estimated 600,000,000 bushels is the estimated world demand during the crop year beginning this month. The conference also agreed that this figure might be increased in view of the worldwide shortage of animal feed and the possibilities of using a considerable amount of wheat stocks for feed purposes. The representatives of the United States, Argentina, Canada and Australia admitted failure in their attempts to agree on the 1934-35 export quotas. Want Guarantee. Argentina demanded a quota of 150,000,000 bushels, but the other big exporters insisted she must guarantee an acreage reduction commensurate to that made by the United States, Australia and Canada before they could grant such an allotment. DOVER, Eng. Aug. 18. (AP)—Emma Faber, Austrian woman, was given credit for a short time today with breaking all records for swimming the English Channel in eight hours, 45 minutes. Re-check gave her total time of 14 hours and 30 minutes which is still the fastest time by one minute ever made by a woman.

LONDON, Ont., Aug. 18.—(INS)—Canadian police were today engaged in a great man-hunt for the four men who kidnaped John S. Labatt, millionaire London, Ontario, brewer, and held him captive for 63 hours before getting “cold feet” and dumping him out of a car near Toronto. The “snatch” victim himself—now back safely in the home of his brother, Hugh Labatt, in this city, and under the care of a physician—was providing “leads” upon which about 1,000 law enforcement officers were working. Whether or not Labatt paid a ransom was being withheld by Labatt. Continued on Page Two

By Associated Press London, Aug. 18.—The “Big Four” wheat exporting nations admitted a failure today in attempts to reach an agreement on a schedule for 1994-96 export quotas. The collapse was made known when representatives of the countries, the United States, Canada, Australia and Argentina, made a report before the full international wheat commission. Argentina demanded a quota of 150,000,000 bushels, but the other big exporters insisted she must guarantee an average reduction commensurate to that made by the United States, Australia and Canada before they would grant such an allotment. Confirmation of the fact that the Argentine, Russian and a few other delegates lack instructions from their governments made it extremely doubtful that an agreement can be reached at this conference. It was recalled a “lack of instructions” was tantamount to a refusal to concur in demands made by the A

London, Ont., Aug. 18 (#)—Gordon McKenzie, a temporary employee of the Labatt brewery, died in a hospital today of a fractured skull. Town Attorney N. Newton said McKenzie’s death “had nothing to do with the kidnapping” of John S. Labatt, head of the brewery, who escaped yesterday from kidnappers who held him almost three days.

LIVERPOOL N. 8. Aug. 18—(UP)—Thomas Howell of Chicago viewed with pardonable pride today a 956-pound tuna fish, caught yesterday, which brought him the world record for tuna caught with rod and line. His fish was more than 100 pounds heavier than the previous record one, caught in the North Sea off Great Britain. Howell landed the tuna in three hours and 39 minutes. Earlier in the day he hooked one that just missed the record—836 pounds. It towed his launch for hours while he played it. He has landed five tuna in two weeks.

(By The Associated Press) RONTO, Ont., Aug. 17. (Pi — John S. Labatt, first victim of ransom-seeking kidnappers in Canada, was restored safely today from a 65-hour captivity under strange circumstances. They brought an official complaint of “lack of co-operation” with the authorities. Whether any ransom was paid was the subject of conflicting statements. Rumors Varied One source described as authoritative said the London, Ont., brewer was freed without payment of any part of the $150,000 demanded by a note left in his abandoned automobile Tuesday. 1934-04-18.text: LONDON, April 18—Hope of general disarmament vanished today and Europe settled down grimly to prepare against fear of an inevitable future war. The British government in issuing a climactic “white paper” this afternoon. It details the failure of disarmament negotiations to date. It will include the text of yesterday's discouraging French note, declaring that France will not submit to the re-armament of Germany and virtually suspending further rearmament negotiations. The French note apparently leaves any further move up to Great Britain. It was believed the British White Paper would be in the nature of an explanation to the world, showing how far Britain has gone in trying to promote an agreement, and absolving her of responsibility for the failure.

His approximate ten per cent reduction in the income tax, 25 per cent slash in the auto horsepower tax, restoration of the “dole” and re-institution of half the pay cuts of government employees enabled him to produce another safe and sound statement of national accounts for 1934-1935. Surplus Estimated It was a budget without sensations and framed to maintain the upward trend of Great Britain's prosperity. BIRMINGHAM, Ala., April 18.—A Negro was killed and another was wounded as violence flared in Alabama’s coal strike today. Deputy Sheriff N. E. Kirkland and Chief of Police L. H. Mason of Leeds shot and killed E. V. D. England, Negro, when he drew a pistol on them as they were investigating the earlier shooting of a Negro named Clisby, wounded by fire from ambush.

By United Press.) Paris, April 18.—France flung a challenge to the world today, declaring that she would not discard a single weapon unless Germany is kept disarmed. The foreign office made public the text of the strong note to Great Britain, declaring that unless France is given absolute assurance of armed help and security against invasion, further disarmament discussions are useless. In issuing the note, a spokesman for the foreign office said: "France realizes the gravity of her act, but henceforth France will not disarm to the extent of a single gun as long as Germany continues to rearm." The government has consulted the commissions of Parliament and is convinced the entire country stands behind the note, which has been approved by the little entente (France's European allies, Roumania, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia).

| Chicago—John (Jake the Barber) Factor, awaiting extradition to England on swindling charges, today protested that he’s practically a pauper. Factor, from whom kidnappers extorted $70,000 last summer, said his fight against the British swindling charges already has cost him $2,170,000, of which $1,300,000 was taken to settle civil suits. “I'm just about broke,” he said. “I wish my family could have something.” | The one-time Halsted street barber, accused of swindling Britons out of several millions, was in custody of a United States marshal awaiting removal to London.

CHICAGO, April 18. (#)—John Factor, the international speculator, estimated today that his fight to escape extradition to England on a stock fraud charge had cost him something like $2,170,000. “I’m figuring the $70,000 paid to the Touhy kidnap gang because when the papers printed the fact that civil claims against me in England had been settled for $1,200,000, I became the likely target for that gang.” In addition to the $1,300,000, Factor figured in $550,000 as loss on investments and $250,000 in attorney’s fees. Federal Judge Philip L. Sullivan has ordered him detained for the British crown. This action left only a remote possibility of escape from extradition through intervention by the state department at Washington.

Barbizon, France, April 17 (4°)— Leon Trotsky’s “fourth international” headquarters in a mysterious villa near this Paris suburb was getting ready tonight to move, Ordered out of France for violating an agreement stipulating he would conduct no political activity, the exiled Red leader, his wife and his “general staff” of two secretaries and two servants scurried about the house, whose blinds were tightly drawn, preparing to seek another retreat. Two watchdogs outside barked continuously because of the activity within, while inhabitants of the residence kept carefully out of sight. The motorcyclist whose encounter with police led to a raid Sunday and the sudden disclosure that Trotsky lived here arrived this afternoon with a batch of mail from Paris—a load similar to earlier ones that aroused gendarmes’ suspicions. He carefully locked the chain at the gate, refusing to talk. Secret servi

Moscow, April 17. (4) — Soviet business planners were admonished today to forego American purchases in retaliation against a new United States law barring loans to debtor nations. The demand was printed in the heavy industry department's organ "For Industrialization" which declared Russia will not be coerced as a consequence. The article states that business is in the process of concrete negotiations and classifies the Soviet government, which never defaulted a penny of its own engagements, with those flatly refusing to pay their obligations. "It is doubtful whether the authors of this resolution realize the serious menace it represents for Soviet-American trade which has finally entered the path of progress."

1934-01-16.text: United Press Staff Correspondent WASHINGTON, Jan. 16 (UP)— President Roosevelt's money plans appeared today likely to lead the two most powerful world powers into a multi-billion dollar battle over foreign exchange but toward ultimate international currency stabilization. Great Britain and the United States, possessed, or soon to be, of huge equalization funds, would be the antagonists. France, still on the gold standard, is a third party vitally interested in the outcome, whatever it may be. London dispatches reflected the fear of British financiers that the "American equalization fund policy will lead to a race for depreciated currency. The goal would be foreign trade. Great Britain has a $1,500,000,900 equalization fund. Mr. Roosevelt proposes $2,000,000,000 for the United States. "We have as many blue chips as the other fellow," was Secretary of Treasury Morgenthau’s cryptic referenc

Prospects of a foreign exchange and trade struggle between the United States and Great Britain as a result of President Roosevelt's gold policy were freely discussed in London and Washington today. The gold program was expected to be passed speedily into law by Congress. The New York Stock Market opened active and fractionally higher. The dollar was weak at the opening in London but strengthened in later trading. The British increased the price of gold to the highest level in months. Great Britain has a $1,800,000,000 equalization fund. Mr. Roosevelt proposes $2,000,000,000 for the United States. "We have as many blue chips as the other fellow," was Secretary of Treasury Morgenthau's cryptic reference to these vast holdings. - LONDON, Jan. 16. (WP)—London raised the open market gold rate to its highest figure in months today. American interests were reported to be buying heavily. The rate was set at 131 shillings nine pence, equivalent to $33.74 at the prevailing rate of the pound, $5.12 1-4. This was a rise of three shillings three pence, or 83 1-4 cents. The London rate was still below the official Washington rate of $34.45. But the rise was larger than that at Washington yesterday, which was 39 cents. The American dollar, after dipping to $5.15 in relation to the pound at the opening of the exchange market, strengthened to $5.12 1-4. Yesterday the pound opened at $5.10 1-2 and closed at $5.12 1-2 after news of President Roosevelt's currency revaluation program. French francs continued sensationally strong, opening at 803-38 and receding but fractionally to 80 7-16. They opened yesterday at 82 5-16 and clo

Washington, Jan. 15.—(AP)—Opponents opened their attack on the St. Lawrence waterway treaty in the Senate today, leading off with a warning from Senator Lewis (D., Ill.), that it would “provide a military avenue through the United States” for Great Britain. When Lewis concluded after speaking most of the day, the vote on the treaty was still as far in the future as ever. The Senate has given two days to discussion of it, and only two senators have spoken—Lewis and Chairman Pittman of the Foreign Relations Committee. The fluent Illinois senator dropped his flowery manner of speech temporarily to warn bluntly that the St. Lawrence development would permit Great Britain in time of war to send her ships into the interior of the United States. He said he did not contend that England wanted to war on the United States, but that America might be drawn into a war as an ally of Britain’s enemy. H

By the Associated Press President Roosevelt’s monetary message, although received with intense interest in Europe yesterday, aroused no great excitement. London financial circles said they expected the dollar to be revalued eventually at the full 60 per cent of its gold content. Cooperative stabilization at less than this level was not anticipated. The dollar, weakened by speculative selling, closed on the London exchange market at $5.14 1-2 to the pound, compared to Saturday’s close at $5.09 5-8. Paris Serene In Paris, the plan was received quietly. Regret was expressed that stabilization was not provided for. The dollar fell 39 centimes, closing at 15.87 francs (6.36 cents to the franc). Corbigny, France, Jan. 15 ()- Five high French officials and five other persons were burned to death when the giant tri-motored airplane, The Emeraude, the pride of the French commercial fleet, fell in flames and exploded near here tonight on a return flight from French Indo-China. The big four-ton plane caught fire apparently from a leaky gasoline line while battling a violent wind and hail storm over Nievre Department, not far from Nevers where an American woman, Miss Evelyn G. Frost of New York and St. Louis, lost her life in a plane crash a week ago. The Emeraude exploded when the pilot tried to land on an open field a mile north of here and 175 miles southwest of Paris. The ten helpless occupants were imprisoned in the cabin. The victims were: Pierre Pasquier, Governor General of Indo-China; Emmanuel Chaumie, director of civil aviation.

Corbigny, France, Jan. 19.—— Air Minister Pierre Cot spurred an investigation today of the crash of the great mail plane Emerande in which ten persons were killed. Five high French officials were among those burned to death when the giant tri-motored plane, flying from French Indo-China to Paris, crashed and exploded near here last night. One eye witness said the plane crashed through the trees on a steep hill and struck a high tension wire, causing the fire. It was flying low in a storm in an attempt to land. The victims were: Pierre Pasquier, governor general of French Indo-China; Emmanuel Chaumie, director of civil aviation in the air ministry; Mme. Chaumie; M. Balazuc, director of technical service in the air ministry; M. Nogues, traffic manager of Air France company; M. Larrieu, air minister attache; Captain Bussault, military aid of M. Pasquier; Pilot Launay; Wireless Operator Quey

Calcutta, Jan. 15. (P)—A death total of 24 and widespread property damage resulted from an earthquake which shook all India today. The tremors began shortly after 2 p.m. (3 a.m. e.s.t.) and ranged from 20 seconds to five minutes in duration. A railway station at Jamalpur collapsed, killing the wife and three children of G. W. Brown, British manager of the railroad’s workshop. Nine died at Gaya and eight at Patna. Three persons were killed in Benares, two in collapsing houses. The third was crushed to death when panic-stricken workers rushed from a mill. Three hundred houses were flattened at Cawnpore and 7,000 others were cracked. Many persons bathing in the Ganges river rushed to the shore in fright upon feeling the sudden motion of the murky waters.

1934-11-29.text: Associated Press Foreign Staff. LONDON, Nov. 29.—()—Amid scenes of glittering pomp and splendor, George, the youngest son of the king of England, and Marina, lovely member of the former Greek reigning house, were married today at Westminster Abbey, the nation’s shrine. The royal couple said “I will” before three kings and three queens, royalty past and present, titled personages, the diplomatic corps and the elite of the nation's government and social life. These were among the 1,500 guests who witnessed the union of the 31-year-old Duke of Kent and his 27-year-old bride. Hundreds of thousands occupied every vantage point outside and cheered the royal processions to the palace. Old London had not seen such scenes since the war. A short while afterward the union of the Duke and the Princess was sealed a second time with the solemnization of the ancient and symbolical Greek Orthodox servic

(By the Associated Press) LONDON, Nov. 28.--London, bedecked in all the finery for the marriage tomorrow of the Duke of Kent and Princess Marina, cocked apprehensive eyes at the weather man’s forecast that fog might mark the decade's most brilliant social event. Buckingham Palace, however, had no idea of letting the weather interfere with the precise schedule and the gorgeous pageantry of the wedding of King George's fourth son and his pretty Grecian Princess. Spend Quiet Evening Kent and Marina, who were expected to spend the evening quietly at Buckingham Palace and York House respectively, paid a surprise visit to the West End theater tonight, accompanied by Queen Mary and the princess’ mother, Princess Nicholas. A capacity audience cheered the young couple for several minutes, delaying the rise of the curtain. A quiet family dinner at Buckingham Palace was on the program for Kent and

LONDON, Nov. 28—?—Great Britain is watchful, but not panicky over the European situation including the rearmament of Germany, Stanley Baldwin, Lord President of the Council, told the House of Commons today. His statement was in reply to an appeal by Winston Churchill, Conservative Party leader, for the nation to put itself in a position of aviation security. Churchill had asserted that Germany’s speedy development of an air force threatened to overshadow British military aviation, but Baldwin said he considered Great Britain’s plans for dealing with the situation adequate. A glittering throng of 1500 guests, including three kings and other royalty, gathered in somber, dimly lighted Westminster Abbey, and heard the Archbishop of Canterbury pronounce the words that made the royal couple husband and wife. Marina, like all Britain’s royal brides, promised to “love, honor and obey.” Addressing the couple, the Archbishop of Canterbury stressed the spiritual significance of vows. “You, sir,” he said turning to the duke, “have already and fully taken your place in the service of the community.” Addressing the princess, the bishop continued, “You, dear bride, as your husband’s comrade will find new happ

LONDON, Nov. 28.—(AP)—The Duke of Kent had his “bachelor’s farewell” party in Buckingham Palace tonight. Members of the royal family and close friends attended, after which the duke and Princess Marina of Greece, to whom he is to be wed in the morning, went to the Lyric Theater to see “Theater Royal,” a play by George S. Kaufman and Edna Ferber, which was called “The Royal Family” when produced in New York several seasons ago. They were accompanied by Queen Mary, mother of the duke, and Princess Nicholas, mother of the princess. The young couple relaxed in preparation for the tedious formal ceremonies which begin shortly after 10 a.m. tomorrow. NAPLES, Italy, Nov. 28—An electric car coursing down the side of Mount Vesuvius, loaded with tourists, left the rails and crashed into an electric power pole today, killing seven persons and injuring nine. The car was carrying a tourist party back from a trip to the top of the volcano. The dead included a French honeymoon couple and an Italian guide.

Washington, Nov. 27.—Statistical indications of improving business were joined Monday by a new call upon President Roosevelt to issue a statement of new deal objectives in furtherance of the move for effective cooperation between business leaders and the administration. C. L. Bardo, president of the National Association of Manufacturers, issued a statement asserting that business "must have more definite ideas as to the direction in which the government is headed." The government, he said, "must project a course that can actually be followed." From the commerce department meanwhile came a report that American export business for October reached its highest total since April, 1931. The figure was $206,352,000 as compared with imports of $129,629,000, producing a $76,723,000 balance of trade in favor of the United States. 1934-07-12.text: DOUGLAS, Isle of Man, July 12. —(#)—Kaye Don, noted British racing motorist, went on trial here today for manslaughter, the aftermath of a racing accident. He pleaded not guilty. The disciple of speed is charged with manslaughter in the death of his 27-year-old mechanic, Francis Tayler, who was killed while Don was practicing for a race here May 28. Don was badly injured and spent several weeks in a hospital. The prosecution charged that Don recklessly failed to slacken speed when rounding a dangerous bend with fatal results.

Paris, July 12 ()—France, it was revealed today, feels she holds the winning hand in the diplomatic poker game with Chancellor Hitler. Foreign Minister Louis Barthou told the cabinet that Great Britain approved France’s “Locarno of the east” which includes political alliances of France, the Soviet, Poland and probably the Little Entente, making a complete political ring around France’s old enemy.

VIENNA, July 12.—A new crisis in relations between Austria and Germany which may end in an open diplomatic breach was threatened today. Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss, it was said on reliable authority, hastened a cabinet reorganization that he might recall his minister to Germany without formally breaking relations. A source equally well informed said the German minister had been ordered by Berlin to be prepared to leave Austria at any moment. Even government officials were puzzled at the full implication of the little chancellor’s sudden reorganization of his cabinet. It was known he planned a drive against Nazis and it was reported that attention would be paid to socialists and communists also. This move emphasized the importance attached by the government to the explanation Hitler will give of his suppression of the “Roehm revolt” on June 30 and the events of succeeding days. SHANGHAI, July 12—Carl A. Nahmmacher, 55, Far-Pastern representative of the United Aircraft Corp., was killed instantly when his plane nose-dived several thousand feet and crashed to the ground. His mechanic, Richard Welsh, parachuted to safety.
LISBON, Portugal, July 12 (UP) President Antonio Carmona’s automobile overturned near Bussaco today, injuring his wife, two grandchildren and a servant. The President was not in the car.

Berlin, July 12. (INS). — Chancellor Adolf Hitler’s speech before the All-Nazi Reichstag to-morrow; the most important pronouncement since the beginning of the Third Reich, will be a protest against the encirclement of Germany just completed, it became known to-day. In effect, the Nazi Chancellor will protest the use of the Locarno Pact in violation of the “Locarno Spirit.” In London, Paris, Moscow, even in the United States world figures will have their ears to the ground, translating, thinking. For that most important mundane element, the peace of the world, can be assured or much disturbed by what Adolf Hitler will say to-morrow. It was the Locarno Pact, the agreement hailed as presaging an era of goodwill and peaceful spirit in Europe, that Louis Barthou, foreign minister of France, used as the basis of the political walls (double walls in the East) he is building around Germany. TOKYO, July 12.—(INS)—Two hundred persons have been drowned and 500 are missing as a result of disastrous floods that have swept three prefectures in northwestern Japan, according to police estimates today. Thirty-two villages have been wholly or partly destroyed and 19,000 houses have been inundated. Property damage was estimated at 10,000,000 yen, or approximately $3,000,000 at current exchange rates.

1934-09-21.text: DETROIT. (P. Asserting he did not “have the first thing to do with this kidnapping” David Meisner, one of two men sought by Detroit and Canadian authorities in connection with the kidnapping a month ago of John Labatt, London, Ont., brewer, surrendered to local detectives. Meisner said he could produce “all the witnesses in the world—even policemen” to prove he was in Cincinnati at the time of the kidnapping. The other man sought is Albert Pegram.
LONDON, Sept. 21 (?).--Prince George of England and Princess Marina of Greece will be married Nov. 29 in Westminster Abbey, it was announced today.

Newport, R. I. —(#)— T. O. 3. Sopwith’s Endeavour, British challenger for the America’s cup, continued the prime favorite today to lift the ancient yachting trophy although Rainbow, Harold S. Vanderbilt's defender, Thursday led the invader around in a leeward-windward course by nearly three and a half minutes. Rainbow's performance would have been more impressive had not the big blue challenger encountered trouble with her canvas which could in no way be interpreted as indicating anything but an extremely fast hull. There was no race today, because Sopwith asked for a postponement until Saturday, so a new genoa jib could arrive to take the place of a badly fitting headsail which Thursday probably contributed much to Endeavour’s defeat.

KAMENZ, Germany, Sept. 21 ~~(/P)--Local residents said today that Bruno Richard Hauptmann, arrested in New York in connection with the Lindbergh baby kidnapping, was the town’s bad boy. Even before he was ordered to jail in 1923, he had been in frequent conflict with police authorities. In those early days he always was let off, but finally a court sentenced him to prison. The police today declined to divulge just what the charges were against him in 1923, but they did say the sentence was for four years. Hauptmann’s father is dead, but his mother is still living.

Tokyo. Sept. 21 (Friday) (P)— A school building collapsed upon 500 small children in Kyoto during a disastrous typhoon which roared across central and eastern Japan today, causing some 200 casualties, including many deaths, Rengo (Japanese) News Agency reports said today. At least 20 persons were reported killed or injured near Kyoto when two passenger trains were overturned by the wind. A falling school house at Momoyama, near Kyoto, caused 10 known deaths. Inrushing seas inundated 2,000 houses in the village of Fukura, near Kobe, and many were feared to have drowned. The blow struck Gifu at 19:30 a.m. at a velocity of 78 miles an hour. Osaka police reported more than 100 persons were known to have been killed there. The office, which has jurisdiction over the town of Kamenz, where Hauptmann's mother lives, said the statute of limitations applies to the offense with which Hauptmann is charged in Germany so that German authorities have no official interest in him. Authorities at Kamenz said Hauptmann broke jail while under arrest for theft, and was sentenced in absentia to four years for a major theft. Madrid, Sept 20,—(4)—The cabinet today armed Minister of Interior Rafael Salazar Alonso with power to put Spain under martial law should asserted plans for an extremist uprising, believed thwarted, be carried out. Meanwhile, "American gangsterism" and Leon Trotsky’s Fourth Internationale figured in Alonso's comment on the abortive "proletarian" revolt, which authorities said would have been the bloodiest in Spain's history. The strategy of the exiled Russian combined with the methods of American gunmen in the plot, Alonso said. "State of Alarm" The cabinet, meeting with President Alcala Zamora presiding, approved precautionary measures taken, congratulated Alonso, expressed confidence that the situation was in hand and drafted emergency decrees, it was learned, for "a state of alarm" and a "state of war" which Alonso may declare at will.

1934-11-19.text: DUBLIN, Irish Free State, Nov, 19—(AP)—Donal Buckley, governor-general of the Irish Free State, has refused King George's invitation to attend the wedding of the Duke of Kent and Princess Mariana, November 29. His action caused no surprise here today, since Buckley is known as a man of simple tastes and one who dislikes ceremony.

Chicago, Nov. 19—(AP)—The climax of a life which led from a farm home on London's outskirts to the pinnacle of one of the world's greatest financial empires approached rapidly today for Samuel Insull. Before the week is out he probably will stand acquitted or convicted of a swindle of more than 500,000 investors. Court attaches predicted that the trial, nearing the end of its seventh week, will go to the jury Thursday or Friday. Maintains His Calmness The elder Insull, whose colorful life and dominating personality have made him the center of the courtroom scene, was apparently unperturbed by its fast nearing end, with its dramatic possibilities in shaping the lives of himself, his son and 15 of his friends. ROME. (PF) Pietro Cardinal Gasparri, wartime secretary of state for the Vatican and a powerful influence in the cause of universal peace, died of pneumonia shortly after 10:30 o'clock Sunday night at the age of 82. Stricken last week with influenza which crept into his lungs, the aged cardinal sank steadily during the day, and by night his heart gave out. At 5 o'clock in the afternoon Archbishop Ottaviani, undersecretary of state, had imparted the special blessing of Pope Pius. Extreme unction was administered Saturday. Eugenio Cardinal Pacelli, Gasparri’s successor in office, visited the dying prelate during the evening. Cardinal Gasparri had been secretary of state under three popes and was regarded as the most noted prelate in the Catholic Church after Pope Pius himself. Cardinals and high church dignitaries had flocked to the home of the aged cardinal by the score during the last day

Rome, Nov. 19.—(4’)--Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg of Austria, here for conferences with Italian leaders, told the Associated Press today that he had issued an invitation to Germany, Yugoslavia, Czechoslovakia and Rumania to join in the Italo-Austro-Hungarian pact in an effort to bring economic and political peace to central Europe. He said Italy is not interfering in the internal affairs of Austria and “has never interpreted her relations with Austria in the sense of a protectorate.”

GENEVA, Nov. 19—(P)——The League of Nations hinted today that Paraguay and Bolivia could avoid possible penalties by laying down their arms in the Chaco Boreal. A report of the league's Chaco consultative committee told the two countries they had broken the covenant of the league by fighting. Under the covenant the league is empowered to sever economic, diplomatic and financial relations with belligerents. Although the report did not actually say so, it intimated this might be done. A comprehensive plan for ending the war was presented by the committee, Both nations were asked to accept the peace plan as soon as possible, provided the other nation also approved it.

1934-05-28.text: London, May 28 (UP) — Barbara Hutton, American five-and-ten-cent store heiress, intends to elude her Georgian prince, Alexis, when her father arrives here, and leave for the United States to obtain a divorce, it was asserted today on reliable authority. Barbara's father, Franklin L. Hutton, sailed from New York Sunday on the liner Bremen. It was said that Barbara intended to accompany her father home. Rumors have been frequent that the marriage was an unhappy one.

London—The United States today delivered a note to the government, reminding it that the British debt installment of $85,670,000 would be due June 15. The note was delivered through Sir Ronald Lindsay, British ambassador, who received it Friday. It contains a statement of the amounts due on the June and December installments of last year, on which Britain made token payments, as well as the advice that the June 15 payment should be made either to the treasury department at Washington or the federal reserve bank at New York. The United Press learned, immediately after the note was received, that it had not altered the government’s present policy, which is to default the June payment unless the debt situation is altered. At present the government is against making even a token payment.

MADISON, May 28 (#)—Prof. J. F. A. Pyre, 62, of the University of Wisconsin English department and one of the most famous of old-time Wisconsin athletes, died at a Madison hospital this morning. He underwent an appendectomy last Saturday. Prof. Pyre, known affectionately by thousands of students and alumni as “Sunny,” became ill suddenly Friday night and was rushed to the hospital for an emergency operation. Physicians discovered a ruptured appendix. Prof. Pyre played right tackle on the Wisconsin football eleven in 1891, 1894, 1895, and 1896 and was a member of the varsity crew in 1893 and 1894, stroking the eight in the latter year. For 26 years he was the university's faculty representative on athletics in the Western conference, being chairman of the Wisconsin athletic council during his entire tenure excepting the year of his appointment, 1906. 1934-10-06.text: SOUTHAMPTON, Oct. 6.—Lady Furness, sister of Mrs. Gloria Morgan Vanderbilt, sailed for New York on the liner Empress of Britain today to aid Mrs. Vanderbilt in her suit to regain custody of her daughter. She said she would certainly testify in court if asked.

| Amsterdam, Oct. 5.—(4—The German steamer Wildenfels reported by wireless today that the Belgian steamer Charles Jose, with a gross tonnage of 651, sank four miles west of Haaks light ship at 11 p.m. last night during a severe storm. Distress signals were received at the lightship but did not identify the sender. Several rescue ships searched the area in vain. The Wildenfels picked up a lifeboat containing one member of the Charles Jose crew, but the other nine who launched another lifeboat were believed to be lost.

Madrid citizens hurried to their homes as the government declared it could not be responsible for the lives of those on the streets, The strike and revolution were the sixth major uprising the second Spanish republic has faced since it was founded in May, 1951. 1934-11-25.text: A statement that stirred Europe to its depths—the assertion France and Russia had renewed their pre-war “understanding”—still reverberated in Paris Saturday, with officials inclined to pooh-pooh the “exaggeration” of Leon Archimbaud, budget reporter. Archimbaud, however, stood pat on his assertion and informed sources declared the Russian offer of military aid to France had been renewed one week ago. In London, Geneva, Rome, Washington and the bloodstained Chaco Boreal events that make peace and war and history continued their rapid pace. Paris—despite denials of any accord, informed sources, friends of former Premier Edouard Herriot, said the Soviet commissar for foreign affairs, Maxim Litvinov, renewed the offer of Russian aid as German attacks increased as recently as last Saturday. LONDON, Nov. 24. [UP]—George Bernard Shaw, world-famous playwright, was stricken with a heart attack tonight. He was sent to bed and a nurse was in attendance. Shaw is 78, but retains an extraordinary vigor, presumably because of his indulgence in exercise and careful diet. He is a vegetarian. His doctor told the press late tonight that his condition was better. "He has been overdoing it, but a few days rest should put him right," the announcement said. "In any case, the attack is not serious." Only one previous illness has afflicted Shaw. That was an attack of smallpox in 1881, when he was 25. A friend told the press that Shaw has not appeared well recently and seems to have aged considerably since his return from his trip to New Zealand.

SHANGHAI, Nov. 24. (AP)—A red tide of communism, rolling slowly westward with General Chiang Kai-Shek's soldiers pressing its rear, today forced missionaries throughout south central China to evacuate their stations. The unnumbered thousands the Nanking government called “red bandits” were streaming into South Fukien, South Kiangsi, Hunan and Kweichow provinces, and dozens of Americans and other foreign missionaries in the path of their advance moved to safety elsewhere. Missionaries also were evacuating posts in Szechuan province, farther to the west, as Chiang Kai-Shek’s four-year campaign bore fruit, Nanking advices said, in the cracking of the communist fountainhead in Kiangsi province. Paris, Nov. 24.—()—The real facts concerning a Franco-Soviet “understanding” remained in dispute tonight—a dispute rumored to have caused a rift in the French cabinet—but Russia’s “offer” of armed aid against Germany was reliably said to have been actually tendered. This offer of military aid by France's old ally in case of a German attack was said by friends of former Premier Edouard Herriot to have been renewed last Saturday. It was asserted to have been made by Maxim Litvinov, the Russian foreign commissar, last spring to the late Foreign Minister Louis Barthou, and again to his successor, Pierre Laval, during a long talk with the Soviet counselor, Marcel Nosenberg, at the foreign office. “Undeniable” Leon Archimbaud, reporter of the budget, stood by his declaration of yesterday before the chamber of deputies that it was “undeniable that this understanding exists.” The foreign office

By The Associated Press Chicago, Nov. 24.—In two hours and two minutes deliberation today, twelve federal court jurors shattered the government's charges of a $100,000,000 mail fraud against Samuel Insull and his 16 business associates with a verdict of acquittal. Between lunch time and the dinner hour, the voluminous case against the ruler of a one-time two billion dollar utility system was put into the hands of a jury and decided in his favor. Jubilant at the near breath-taking speed of the verdict, Insull exclaimed: “This is the start of my vindication.” The jury’s decision read in a hushed courtroom by Foreman John D. Lent, came with a rapidity startling to defense attorneys and prosecutors alike. WARM SPRINGS, Ga., Nov. 24.—(4)—President Roosevelt and Edsel Ford, automobile manufacturer, got together today for a business talk which brought a “very hopeful and optimistic” report from Ford. It was the first meeting of the two since the row between Henry Ford and the administration over subscribing to the NRA automobile code but there was no sign today of hard feelings. “We are very hopeful and optimistic about business conditions,” said Ford. “It is certainly true in our industry and I hear favorable reports all over the country. In stepping up our production to 1,000,000 cars in 1935 we are confident we have come out of the trough and are headed for sustained recovery.” Ford, whose visit was to personal friends, Mr. and Mrs. Lynn Pearson, of Detroit, met the president at the open air swimming pool where Mr. Roosevelt goes every day for a plunge and some water polo. Courtney to be interested in the case in behalf of Factor. * Would Put Factor in Custody. (—Bonnefoy a-bour, successor to Jean Chiappe, as head of the Paris police, was given a violent induction to office today, personally leading his forces in charges to subdue renewed Paris rioting. Several hundred Royalists, chief element in recent public disorders growing out of the Stavisky scandal, together with a new Fascist group called “Francistes” attempted to parade on the boulevards and offered battle to Sibour’s forces. Stores, Cafes Close Cries of “Long live Chiappe! Long live the police!” mingled with shouts against the Daladier cabinet as the manifestants swarmed about the Paris Opera. Cafe owners, remembering violent clashes of a week ago, hastily cleared their terraces, and stores clapped down their shutters. Paris, Feb. 4 (4Pi)—The famous night life of Paris was dimmed tonight by the taxicab strike which is estimated to be holding more than 95 per cent of all the cars in Paris idle. Paris has become a 12 o'clock town, with bridge parties forced to break up at midnight and revelers leaving the city’s hundreds of cabarets in time to catch the last buses and subway trains. The week-end seasonal fashion shows suffered their share of general confusion caused by lack of transportation. The strike started last week in protest against government taxes which have forced the price of gasoline to 40 cents a gallon. In earlier stages of the strike, cab drivers gathered in huge parades, tying up street traffic.

Paris, Feb. 4—Stern "Silent Edouard" Daladier made a spectacular show of sweeping out France's political house today after deposing Jean Chiappe, debonair "Napoleon" of the Paris police. The sudden ousting of the little Corsican as prefect was the most resounding blow in the shakeup, which jarred the cabinet apart and threatened to rekindle rioting, which Chiappe was accused of tolerating. The premier, however, patched up his cabinet with the replacement of three men and will appear in the chamber Tuesday confident of increased support. Former Premier Joseph Paul-Boncour agreed to take the post of Lieut. Col. Jean Fabry as minister of war; Paul Marchandeau accepted the portfolio of minister of the budget and finance, succeeding decrepit Pietri; and Alexis Jaubert replaced Gustav Doussain as minister of technical instruction. Magdeburg, Germany, Feb. 5—(AP)—Its rusty hinges squeaking mightily, the Bishop's Door of the famous Cathedral of Saint Maur-ice and Saint Catherine was opened for the first time in 410 years today. It swung wide to admit the new Nazi bishop of the Province of Saxony, the Rt. Rev. Friedrich Peter, for his consecration by Reichs-bishop Ludwig Mueller. The massive door was sealed when the powerful bishopric went Protestant. In his sermon, Bishop Peter said: "Millions of Germans have regained their faith through the miracle of national regeneration wrought by Chancellor Hitler. Hundreds of thousands have returned to the church."

ROME, Feb. 5.—(UP)—Raging snowstorms in some places and torrential rains at others brought avalanches, landslides and disastrous floods to the Marches region along the Adriatic Sea today. Twenty persons were known dead and 55 injured in the avalanches. Rescue parties, headed by fascist militiamen, struggled on skis over ice and snow to the rescue of five persons isolated in villages. It was feared a high casualty list might be compiled when the full results of damage in the large area affected became known. Nineteen persons were unofficially estimated to have been killed in the region of Bolognola in Macerata province by a landslide. Among the dead at Bolognola were believed to be members of the family of Count Orsini of Perugia, descendants of the Roman Prince Orsini. Inhabitants of the various hamlets comprising Bolognola were extricated from the debris of their crumbled homes. Four we

Berlin, Feb. 4. (/P)—Good Nazis partaking of their one-course Sunday dinners today dipped their spoons into pea soup with pork or green beans and mutton, or bouillon and potatoes, with a special devotion. Ordained by the government to swell the winter relief fund, this monthly meal took on the flavor of a ritual.

PARIS, Feb. 5.—(CP)—A garbled telephone conversation excited official apprehension after the dismissal yesterday of Police Prefect Jean Chiappe. Those who wondered at precautions taken before Bonnefoy Sibour summarily succeeded Chiappe, found that the ministry of the interior had misunderstood the deposed police head. Accepting his dismissal, Chiappe said: “Very well: tomorrow I will be a simple citizen in the street.” But all the ministry heard was: “... I will be in the street.” That means leading a mob in France.

With their time limit for arbitration expired and serious violence developing in New England, Francis J. Gorman, chairman of the United Textile Workers special strike committee, said: “We are now preparing for at least a month of struggle to win the textile strike.” He telegraphed President Roosevelt urging him to advise governors of textile states to use troops in “a strictly impartial manner.” National Guardsmen are out in five states, WASHINGTON, Sept. 12— Labor dug in along the far-flung textile strike front for a hard, drawn-out struggle. WICHITA, Kas, Sept. 12 —Col Roscoe Turner, aerial speed king, and Clyde Pangborn, flying their new bi-motored airplane to New York for shipment to London, where the fliers will compete in the air race from London to Australia, landed here at 3:30 p.m. (Central standard time) today and took off at 9:50. Turner said, during the re-fueling operations, he planned to keep the powerful plane in the air after the take-off here until they reached New York in order that they might observe the ship’s endurance.

LONDON, Sept. 12.—Liberals joined the British Labor party today in a demand that the government investigate the activities of armament firms. Both parties are aroused by testimony at Washington involving several British concerns. The Labor party will urge that private manufacture of arms be suppressed entirely. Nothing short of absolute prohibition of private profit from munitions and armaments will “end this scandal,” a party statement said.

Littlefield, Tex; Sept. 11—a—Lamb County peace officers tonight hunted two men as the kidnappers of Miss Lillian Hopping, 26, teacher of English in the Littlefield high school, while she rested at a slater's home, from which she said she was abducted at pistol point last night. Miss Hopping, who said she escaped from her captors while they were repairing a flat tire, returned to the home of the slater, Mrs. Pal Boone, about 8 a.m. today. The young teacher, a blue-eyed brunet, was not injured other than suffering nervous shock and bodily exhaustion, Mrs. Boone said. After slipping away from the men, Miss Hopping said she walked 15 or 20 miles, all except the last three miles to Littlefield. The men—one tall and dark, the other stocky, blond and nearly bald—evidently believed, she said, that she was Mrs. Boone, whose husband is manager of the Littlefield estate and has property in Littlefi

PARIS, Sept. 12—(4)—Discontent of lagging business apparently is piling up new troubles for the government of Premier Gaston Doumergue. Open hostility toward the man who for several months has managed to hold discordant factions together has been gathering force as a result of several strikes and disorders. The fishermen of Douarnenez are on strike after over-stocked canneries refused to accept all their catches. An angry crowd yesterday invaded the canneries and prevented packers from working. Authorities prepared for more disturbances in this region. Silk manufacturers of Lyon warned the nation that present governmental policies are threatening to inflict a penalty of death on the export industries.

Geneva, Sept. 11. (4P)—Still divided over the wording of the invitation to be sent to Moscow, leaders of the League of Nations tonight were nevertheless determined to secure Russia's membership in the interests of world peace. In the face of the refusal of some delegates to sign, League leaders agreed to eliminate from the original draft of the bid to Russia the assurances it contained of the League’s certainty that Russia has and will fulfill her international obligations. A sincere, direct invitation should suffice, these delegates maintained and France, Russia's chief advocate at the League bar, agreed the important thing was to get as many signatures as possible as quickly as possible. These signatures, it was estimated tonight, probably will number 36, but Portugal and Switzerland, observers believed, will vote no when the Soviet issue is submitted to the League assembly. GENEVA, Sept. 12. (#)—Despite denials, the Associated Press learned today that the League of Nations has encountered difficulties with Russia in seeking an agreement upon terms of an invitation to be made to the Soviet Union toward membership in the League. Russia was reported disappointed that she is unable to join in a blaze of glory and rebels at the hostility of several nations.

BERLIN, Sept. 12 — Germans began to realize today that not only commodities of luxury but the very staples of life have been put under the total and arbitrary control of Dr. Hjalmar Schacht, head of the Reichsbank and minister of economics. It is a dictatorship of the necessities of existence—almost as absolute as in wartime. The latest development was the establishment of fourteen new “control bureaus” over basic commodities, including food, clothing, coal and wood. On the ground of a shortage of foreign exchange with which to deal feasibly in foreign trade, Schacht at one move has brought virtually every commodity under his financial and economic dictatorship, even penetrating deeply into the territory hitherto under sole control of Walter Darre, minister of agriculture. Schacht becomes the arbiter of the nation’s finance and trade.

1934-03-11.text: Rapid expansion of France's aviation force was forecast tonight as the finance committee of the chamber of deputies approved a government request for 980,000,000 francs (about $63,700,000) for new aviation equipment in 1934 and 1935. General Victor Denain, minister for air, spoke in behalf of the project, and told the committee that France will have 6,000 military and civil planes by the end of the present year. At present there are about 5,300 planes in France. "The special air program followed close on the announcement by the government yesterday that it needs a bond issue of three billion francs (about $600,000,000) to make France invincible in the air, and on the land and water. A bill providing for this issue was introduced in parliament.

Attorney General Cummings made this announcement Saturday night, adding that similar suits also would be brought against Thomas S. Lamont, member of a prominent New York banking firm, and Thomas L. Sidlo, law partner of Newton D. Baker, Woodrow Wilson's secretary of war. The cases, Mr. Cummings said, have been referred to the federal attorneys at New York, Pittsburgh and Cleveland "with authority for presentation to grand juries under the laws against tax evasion and avoidance." BIRMINGHAM, Ala., UP)—Twenty-four persons were injured and a property damage totaling $3,000,000 was caused here Saturday afternoon by fire in the heart of the downtown business district in which every fireman in the city and suburbs fought and brought under control early Saturday night. The injured included 20 firemen, most of whom were overcome by smoke and four spectators struck by fire equipment or ambulances. An emergency station was opened in the basement of a department store across the street from the scene of the fire where more than 30 firemen were given treatment for minor hurts and went back to the blaze. Estimate of the damage was made by B. O. Hargrove, chief of the Birmingham fire department.

Lindbergh told Secretary Dern today what he thought was wrong with army aviation and gave his ideas for achieving greater efficiency in procurement, management and actual flying. During the three-hour conference, Harry H. Woodring, assistant secretary of war in charge of army airplane buying, was called into Dern's office to hear some of the famous flier’s suggestions. Woodring’s presence was especially significant as he has been the principal witness in the current congressional and grand jury investigation of war department aviation purchases. Launch With Dern After the conference the Colonel, Mrs. Lindbergh, Woodring and Mrs. Woodring, and General Douglas MacArthur, chief of staff, went to the home of Secretary Dern for luncheon and a further round-table discussion of aviation problems. SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico, (1. Mrs. Franklin D. Roosevelt walked thru the squalid San Juan slums, talked with their poverty-stricken inmates, and then conferred with welfare workers regarding remedies. Following the first lady thru the narrow streets were the clamoring populace, barking dogs, squealing pigs, and naked children. Once she stepped near a pool of dirty water swarming with flies, and asked a photographer to take a picture of it “to show really what it is like.” She was shocked upon entering the poor home of a mother suffering from tuberculosis and was told the family had not had relief or food for a week, eating only rice and beans shared by a neighbor. This was due, the woman said, to a change in the relief reporting form in Washington.

WASHINGTON, March 10 (CP). President Roosevelt ordered consolidation of federal liquor enforcement and taxing agencies today, and in a special message asked immediate congressional approval of his action. Nearly 900 men would be shifted from the justice department's old prohibition division to the treasury’s internal revenue bureau by the plan thereby creating a force of 1600 to handle the liquor problem. “The need for such consolidation at this time springs primarily from the repeal of the 18th amendment,” Roosevelt told congress. “The tax enforcement agencies of the government should be recognized in harmony with the changes which have occurred in the laws relating to the manufacture, transportation and sale of intoxicating liquors. “The changes made by this order will permit a more efficient administration of the internal revenue laws as well as the laws carrying out the protective fe

Washington, March 10 (A)—The senate today ignored agricultural adjustment administration recommendations, doubled the number of basic commodities entitled to benefit payments and increased from $200,000,000 to $350,000,000 a fund to aid the dairy and cattle industry. By 39 to 37, it passed the Jones-Connally bill and sent the measure to conference with the house after adding peanuts, rye, flax, barley and grain sorghum as well as dairy and cattle products to seven basic commodities now defined in the agricultural adjustment act. The adjustment administration had recommended only dairy and cattle products for inclusion. Senator Connally, Democrat, of Texas, co-author of the legislation, accepted most of the additions so as to get the measure to conference. 1934-12-02.text: LEEDS, England, Dec. 1 -— (AP)—Mrs. May Brownhill—62 years old, grey-haired and frail—today was sentenced to be hanged for the “mercy murder” of her imbecile son. A jury which needed only five minutes to find her guilty recommended that she be shown mercy. The judge, who under English law had no alternative but to sentence her to death, told the jury its recommendation would be referred to the proper authorities, meaning the home office. The woman, after 30 years spent nursing her imbecile son Denis, gave him 160 sedative tablets and turned on the gas when she learned she faced an operation which might cost her life. She feared that Denis, left alone, would suffer what a physician called a ‘“vertible living death.”

WASHINGTON The gas- Regal Politics 72°, 8° have been trilling their tongues overtime since the royal wedding. They cannot quite make it out. They have never doubted that there is a Santa Claus, but apparently draw the line on the recent London news yarns, which appear to have been just about the best fairy tales written since Hans Christian Andersen wiped the rainbow ink from his pen and tucked it away forever. The speculation is not entirely unjustified, in view of the fact that the royal household chose to make such a public affair of the wedding that it assumed a public significance beyond its inherent personal nature. As near as our wariest authorities well connected with London can learn, most of the talk, as usual, is bunk. The story accredited here is that the royal family made it the biggest royal wedding in 550 years solely for patriotic effect. England is facing a hard winter.

Copyright, 1934, by Associated Press Moscow, Dec. 1.—An assassin who the Soviet government asserted was “sent by enemies of the working class” today shot and killed Sergei Mironovich Kirov, revolutionist for 30 of his 46 years, a member of the communist party’s political bureau. The assassin, who slew Kirov in the party committee headquarters at Leningrad, was captured by Soviet police. Despite the questioning to which he was subjected, he still had not been identified late tonight. As one of the nine members of the political bureau which makes the decisions on policy unfailingly followed by the government, Kirov belonged to what is generally regarded as the most powerful in the Soviet republic. ROME, Dec. 1.—()—Japan's threatened expansion into African territories where Italy has extensive colonization, it was revealed tonight, is being carefully considered in connection with Japan's invitation to join her in denouncing the Washington naval treaty. A government spokesman said Italy was not yet ready to reply to the invitation, although information had been received from Paris that France had refused a similar Japanese proposal. With the return of King Victor Emmanuel aboard the royal yacht Savola from the African colony of Somaliland, it became known that Italy’s policy with regard to Nipponese expansion had undergone definite clarification.

DENVER, Colo., Dec. 1. UP — Denver police tonight announced solution of the sensational Denver mint robbery in which $200,000 was stolen. Albert T. Clark, chief of detectives here, announced the solution of the crime which defied solution for many years after its commission December 18, 1922. Those named as having a part in the robbery were: Harvey Bailey, Midwestern bad man accused of a number of crimes including the Urschel kidnapping, for which he now is in federal prison. Jim Clark, now serving a life sentence in the Indiana State prison for his part in a bank robbery at Clinton, Ind. Robert Leon Knapp, now dead with the circumstances of his death unknown, Frank McFarland, alias ‘the Memphis Kid,” also dead, Nicholas Trainer, alias Nick Sloan the bandit whose body was found in an automobile after the robbery. The Idaho Republican demanded what he said could be called a "revolution" unless the conservatives now in control hold a meeting at once to cooperate to that end. WASHINGTON. (UP). Proposals by administration aides for enormous relief expenditures became the center of a congressional dispute that forecast a bitter parliamentary battle should President Roosevelt formally recommend their approval. Harry Hopkins, relief administrator, wants to appropriate as much as 8 or 9 billion dollars for work relief, building new houses for the low wage group and an expansion of the subsistence homestead projects. Secretary Ickes has an outlay of from 5 to 7 billions for public works and housing in mind, backed by a contention that business is unable to provide a quick solution for the depression problem or restoring employment. Both were in Warm Springs for the weekend ready to urge these plans upon the president. The chief executive has given evidence that he intends to reserve final judgment for the time being. DUBLIN, March 11,—(4)—Irishmen honored the memory of St. Patrick, their patron saint, in nation-wide celebrations today. Because of the legal ban on the sale of hard liquors, toasts had to be offered with tea or milk, but it was a merry day nevertheless. The big feature in Dublin was the first appearance of the new volunteer army uniformed in gray-green. The uniform, caps and leggings were modeled on the uniforms worn by the Roger Casement Irish brigade of war prisoners in Germany. In many districts of the city the Blue Shirts held parades in competition with that of the Green volunteers.

SILANGHIAI, March 17 — The government made it clear today that, although it approved the London silver agreement, it does not intend to allow that pact to prevent full protection of Chinese international trade. At the same time, officials and trade experts said President Roosevelt's depreciation of the American dollar probably will cause a large increase in Chinese-American business. If the United States raises the price of the white metal in the future, the government will feel free, despite a significance to the London Plan, to take any measures necessary, an official of the foreign office stated.

PIRAEUS, Greece. (Sunday). (Copyright by AP). Samuel Insull pulled another ace from his sleeve early Sunday and sailed for points unknown aboard a grimy Greek tramp steamer which he had made virtually a kingdom of his own. Ordered back by the Greek government after a seventy-five hour false start, the steamer Maiotis sailed again at 1:25 a.m., without being required to tell the Greek government where it is going. Engine trouble halted the steamer in the outer harbor soon after it sailed, but this was merely a temporary setback at worst, since it was learned Insull had three days in which finally to depart. The engine was fixed after a short time and the vessel plodded onward. As real master of the ship himself (he chartered it and is therefore its temporary owner) Insull, the fugitive from justice, is the lone arbiter of his destiny so long as he is on the high seas.
