By The Associated Press “Rome, March 17—Italy, Austria and Hungary became allies today. Their premiers signed three consultative pacts, drawn in an unrestricted manner and inviting the collaboration of all other European nations in a program for peace and commercial cooperation. One agreement was political. Each of the three signatory countries agrees to consult the others before taking any decisions on matters of interest to any or all of them. The other two were commercial. An official communique said their object was to aid in the development of economic exchanges among the three countries. It also was learned that one of the commercial protocols was written in an effort to assure the economic independence of Austria, but diplomatic circles assumed that all three agreements, in effect, bind Austria to confer with Italy before making any move connected with her political independence,

By The Associated Press Piraeus, Greece, March 18, (Sunday)—Samuel Insull sailed at 12:25 a. m. today aboard the Greek freighter Maiolis, seeking a new haven of refuge from American authorities. The hour of sailing was established definitely after conflicting reports had been investigated. The former utilities king said before sailing that he expected to land at Djibouti, French Somaliland, at the southern extremity of the Red Sea, and that he would go to Abyssinia. Though Insull said that he planned to land at Djibouti, it was stated here that the fact he did not have a French visa probably would prevent him from getting off at that port. New Itinerary Some persons believed he would make out a new itinerary when he got on the high seas, and would try to keep secret his future plans. PIRAEUS, Greece, Sunday, Mar. 18 UP—Samuel Insull headed his chartered tramp steamer toward the Red Sea and freedom early today, victor in his fight to prevent the Greek government from deporting him to the United States. The 74 year old fugitive from Chicago justice apparently was in good health and high spirits as the ancient freighter sailed, carrying him to strange lands where he hopes to spend his declining years. The best information available was that his goal was Abyssinia, the mountainous, ancient kingdom of Ethiopia in Africa, whose ruler, the “Lion of Judah,” claims to be a direct descendant of the Queen of Sheba. Happily Reunited The Insull “family”—the graying public utilities millionaire, his former actress wife and his friend, Mme. Paris, March 17——(/P)—-The “Stavisky curse” fell again today in the attempted suicide of Emile Blanchard, an official in the agriculture ministry. Troops on the firing range at Fontainbleau found him lying in a pool of blood, his throat cut by a knife still clutched in his hand. 1934-12-10.text: London, Dec. 8 (PI)—A writ has been issued in behalf of Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, in respect to the statement that he was interested in armament firms and that his conduct of British foreign affairs was thereby affected, it was announced today. This brief announcement from authoritative quarters in London was all that was available for the moment in what appeared to be a sensational development in the proposed British inquiry into the manufacture of arms. (While the exact nature of the writ issued in behalf of Sir John could not be determined from London advices, it was considered probable the action was preliminary to libel proceedings.)

| OSLO, Norway, Dec. 10.—Arthur Henderson, British president of the world disarmament conference, and Sir Norman Angell, British author and lecturer, were awarded the Nobel peace prizes for 1934 and 1933 respectively, it was announced today. The award today of the 1933 and 1934 Nobel prizes for work toward peace is a double triumph for the British labor movement! Henderson is a leader of the right wing of the labor party, and Angell, like Henderson, has served in the House of Commons as a labor member. Henderson is 71. He began life as a moulder at Newcastle, and became an outstanding labor leader. He was a member of the war cabinet. He was home secretary in the first labor cabinet and was foreign minister in the second one from 1929 to 1931. Then in 1932 he was made president of the world disarmament conference. NEW YORK, Dec. 10—(UP)— The crippled Japanese freighter Victoria Maru is “now proceeding toward the English Channel under the escort of the S. S. Amsterdam,” Radio Marine was advised today. Radio Marine officials interpreted the message as indicating the freighter, first believed sinking in mid-Atlantic after a storm cost the lives of the master and two officers, was proceeding under her own power and that the Amsterdam was acting as convoy in case the Victoria Maru encountered further difficulties.

Douglas, Isle of Man, Dec. 10—(/) --Kaye Don, famous British speed driver, was released today after serving 10 weeks and two days of a four-month sentence for manslaughter growing from the death of his mechanic in a wreck on a trial auto spin. He was met by a group of friends and immediately boarded a ship for Liverpool. His health, it was stated unofficially, was the reason for Don's early release. With time off for good behavior, his term would have ended January 6. Francis Taylor, Don's mechanic, was killed when they took a night practice run for a race in Douglas May 28. He himself was badly injured.

BELGRADE, Yugoslavia, Dec. 10. — Yugoslavia ended the mass deportation of Hungarians abruptly today, apparently averting the possibility of border fighting. Diplomatic quarters said they understood the government had been prevailed upon by European powers, chiefly Great Britain and France, to cease expelling the Hungarians. The order was announced soon after Prince Paul, one of three regents guiding affairs of state for the boy King Peter II, returned from London, where he attended the wedding of Princess Marina and the Duke of Kent. Unofficial reports said Yugoslavia was convinced that if the deportations were continued it would prejudice her case at Geneva. She has charged to the League of Nations that Hungary harbored terrorists and was responsible for King Alexander’s murder. Military and local police officials were instructed by the department of the interior to halt the expulsions.

BIRMINGHAM, Eng., Dec. 9—()—Three airmen were killed today near Castle Bromwich aerodrome when a military bomber containing two auxiliary air force men collided with a private plane. The year's royal air force death roll now has reached 72.

Greystones, Irish Free State (JP)—The whole countryside was gathered here today, working, hoping and praying that Joseph O'Leary, trapped in a well, might be brought to the surface alive. At 1 p. m. he had been buried alive with only the upper part of his body exposed for 41 hours. O'Leary, a plumber, was working in a well on a ladder at 8 p. m. Saturday when the walls collapsed. He was trapped with only his neck out and the rungs of the ladder were broken. Rescuers, working from above managed to free his arms and get food and stimulants down to him, but they could not free his legs from the mass of rocks holding him below the surface. Today he was visibly growing much weaker and his voice was fainter.

GENEVA, Dec. 10 (UP) — The Little Entente buried the threat of war across the council table of the League of Nations today, resisting efforts of the big powers to compromise the dispute between Hungary and Jugoslavia. Nicholas Titulescu of Roumania, speaking for the Little Entente—Roumania, Czechoslovakia and Jugoslavia—declared that Hungary’s insistence on revision of the post-war treaties, which carved out new countries in Europe, constituted a threat of war. “To each demand of Hungary for revision,” he said, “the three interested nations have replied with a categorical and final ‘No.’ To insist would no longer be the work of peace, but of war.” Titulescu’s speech shattered the hopeful atmosphere which had been engendered by a resolution of Foreign Minister Pierre Laval of France designed to curb political terrorism and appease Jugoslavia. 1934-01-03.text: Washington, Jan. 6 (P)—The government held its domestic gold price steady today at $34.06 an ounce. This figure for newly mined metal was maintained despite some strengthening of the dollar on the London market after weakness which attended America’s budgetary developments earlier this week. - Sterling opening at $5.1¢% to the pound and at that level bar gold was worth $32.38 an ounce. Continuance of the dollar's $34.06 figure for the fourteenth successive business day was not unexpected. With the government facing a huge financing problem it was considered any action tending to cause fluctuation in the government bond market would be avoided.

LONDON, Jan. 3 (UP) — The "curse of Tut-ankh-amen" was recalled today after the death of Arthur E. P. B. Weigall, distinguished Egyptologist and one of the principal figures present when the Pharaoh’s gorgeous tomb was opened. Weigall died last night at a London hospital after a long illness. He was 53. His death leaves Howard Carter, actual discoverer of the tomb, the only survivor among the principals. The 5th Earl of Carnarvon, Carter’s backer, died only a few weeks after the sepulchral chamber of Tut-ankh-amen was opened and months before the sarcophagus itself was "violated." There were stories then of the Tut-ankh-amen curse on anyone who invaded his sanctuary. The stories have been revived as others died, some mysteriously. Carnarvon's half-brother, Col. ROME, Jan. 3. — While Premier Mussolini and British foreign secretary Sir John Simon prepared today to converse on the world disarmament stalemate, the Chamber of Deputies considered a navy budget report which declared that only a four power pact can save the world from a naval armaments race of the worst kind. The report, signed by Marquis Giacomo Medici del Vascello, budget committee reporter, and accepted as a statement of Il Duce’s own viewpoint, warned that the principal world powers “are already arming at sea.” If the big European nations were to get together on some step looking toward disarmament, world tension would be relieved and the way opened for a broader agreement on arms — including naval as well as land and air — Vascello said. CHESTER, ENG., Jan. 3—(#)—Hope for the potato farmer in the growing feminine tendency toward curves was seen today by Capt. John Mollett, chairman of the British potato marketing board. “If we can get women turned in that direction we shall grow more potatoes,” he declared in a speech here. “The recent decline in our industry has been caused largely by the slimming craze.”

London, Jan. 3.—(/*)—President Roosevelt's message to Congress was awaited here with interest and curiosity today for in excess of that usually shown in American affairs—especially American politics. For days leading newspapers have emphasized what has been described here as the “collapse” of the Republican opposition. “The one certainty in the situation,” said the London Times editorially, “is that wherever President Roosevelt may decide to lead, Congress and the country will follow.” Today the president's familiar portrait faces readers of several London newspapers, accompanying special articles and editorials. The consensus is that the president will carry Congress completely, or at least with negligible opposition.

Washington, Jan. 2.—(P)— In wide contrast to the pulse-throbbing events that brought its first emergency meeting, the 73rd congress will assemble in regular session tomorrow, probably to receive from President Roosevelt a personal accounting and recommendations for the future. The recovery program and the budgetary complexities arising from it bade fair to bulk large in the message that the members will hear, either in joint session from the president himself, or intoned by reading clerks in senate and house separately. On Capitol hill today, members expressed conviction that the president would appear in person. Physical arrangements were made in the house chamber; secret service men visited the capitol to supervise preparations and all gallery tickets were called in. At the White House, however, it was emphasized that the plans of the president still were indefinite. Precedent Set For

The 73rd congress today resumed its tasks with a personal address by President Roosevelt, asserting the nation is “in the process of recovery” and evincing his determination to cleave to the emergency program. Gripping the desk at which he stood before the thronged house of representatives, the president defied advocates of “a return to old methods,” excoriated wrongdoers of the banking and financial worlds in calling for regulatory legislation and spoke of “permanent readjustment” of many social and economic arrangements. His audience comprised the entire membership of senate and house, members of his cabinet and the front rank of official, diplomatic and social Washington that splashed the galleries with brilliant and formal dress. Washington, D. C.--(AP)—The house ways and means committee today formally approved the final draft of the half-billion-dollar liquor tax bill and its introduction in the house was in order. The measure provides a $2 a gallon tax on distilled spirits, $5 a barrel on beer and graduated rates on wines ranging from 10 to 40 cents a gallon. The committee planned to meet in executive session later in the day after the bill was formally introduced in order to report it out and expedite bringing it up for house consideration this week.

1934-12-18.text: SAARBRUECKEN, Saar Basin Territory, Dec. 17— (AP) — The tense situation growing out of the mobbing of a British police captain and the wounding of a Saarite may wind up in the law courts. The incident, which brought angry outbursts from Germany today and vastly increased local resentment against international control prior to the forthcoming plebiscite, was turned over to judicial authorities by Col. These authorities were requested to determine whether any charges will grow out of the violent attack by a Nazi disciplinary band upon Capt. James Justice and his companion, the Earl of Aylesford. TOKYO, Dec. 18—(P)—Japan's desire for a definite date for the resumption of the present preliminary naval treaty conversations in London will be presented to the British government Wednesday in accordance with instructions from the Japanese government to its London envoy. Foreign Minister Hirota cabled Ambassador Tsuneo Matsudaira tonight to order that the Japanese hope for resumption of the parleys be included in the communique in which the London conference will announce its adjournment. It was officially explained that the Japanese desire to fix a date for resumption of the conference, probably in March, is to permit the Tokyo government to prepare adequately for further talks and possibly give Admiral Yamamoto a chance to return to Tokyo, report, and receive further instruction before he goes back to London again.

The conference in London between the United States, Great Britain, and Japan, looking toward the formulation of a new international naval treaty, neared a close today with Japan moving to checkmate any possible allegation by the United States that Japan is responsible for the breakdown of the London parley. The British delegation announced that the conversations would be adjourned Thursday, following consultations with the Japanese and American representatives. Tokyo instructed its delegation to see to it that the communique which the conferees put out, announcing the adjournment, contains the statement that Japan desires that they be taken up again. Such resumption, it was indicated, would suit the Japanese in about March. LEWES, England, Dec. 18.—(AP)—Sir Oswald Mosley, ardent leader of British fascism, and three followers were acquitted today of charges of riotous assembly without calling a single witness to their defense. The judge agreed with the contention of Sir Patrick Hastings, chief defense attorney, that “no case” had been made and directed the jury to find all four not guilty. A motion to assess costs of the action against police of Worthing, where Mosley was involved in a disorder at a Fascist meeting Oct. 9, was refused.

London. Dec. 14 4Pi—Tony Man- the stammering waiter, was acquitted by a jury today of a charge of murdering Mrs. Violet Kaye, professional dancer whose dismembered body was found in a trunk at Brighton. The jury reached its verdict in little more than two hours.

TOKYO, Dec. 18.—The Japanese government sent instructions to its London parley delegates tonight presenting a basis for continuing the naval conversations, the Nippon Dempo news agency understood. The instructions were said to represent a last minute effort of the Japanese to prevent the breakdown of the exploratory conference. Dispatches from London, however, said that the adjournment had been set for Thursday.

NEW YORK, Dec. 18 UP— Her bridge, rudder and lifeboats carried away in a hurricane, the Norwegian freighter Sisto rolled helplessly in heavy seas in mid-Atlantic today. The British tanker Mobiloil stood by “unable to do anything as A wireless message picked up from the liner President Harding by the Radio Marine corporation said the freighter had been pumping oil on the water all night in an effort to calm the seas preparatory to a rescue attempt, but was running short of oil.

1934-10-20.text: (Copyright, 194, Associated Press) Loudon, Oct. 19—Japan wants Great Britain and the United States to recognize the principle of parity in naval defensive armaments before she shows her hand in further conversations here, the Associated Press learned authoritatively today. If the other two nations agreed to the principle, however, it was expected the Japanese would be willing to accept much less than actual tonnage equality. That would be Japan's way of getting rid of the rankling word 'ratio' the sore point that led Japan to its decision to denounce the Washington and London Naval Treaties. The three delegations stand mutually pledged to exert every effort to arrive at some compromise that would avert an armaments race.

London, Oct. 20 —(P)— The Schwab trophy remains in America, but Great Britain's international bridge hopes soared higher today as a result of the stiff fight the English team made against the Culbertson campaigners. Trailing the greater part of the match, the Americans finished 300 boards of the five-day series with a 3,000-point advantage after a match described by Ely Culbertson, the American captain, as the "toughest" of his career. Colonel G. Walsh, leader of the English team, said victory went to the Americans by reason of their greater experience, since they had developed the bidding system and were abler marathon players.

The 19 aircraft entered in the London to Melbourne air derby got off to a perfect start at dawn today, but some of them later were forced down by engine trouble or bad weather. Apparently in the lead were K. D. Parmentier and J. J. Moll, Netherlands entry, who arrived at 11:30 a.m., approximately five hours after they took off from Mildenhall airdrome, England. Parmentier and Moll passed over Athens at 2:15 p.m., seven and three-quarters after taking off from Mildenhall. Col. Roscoe Turner and Clyde Pangborn landed at Athens at 4:35 p.m., today, after being unreported since their takeoff from Mildenhall airdrome at 6:30 a.m. Miss Jacqueline Cochran and Wesley Smith, American entries, abandoned their flight at Bucharest. 1934-03-25.text: - LONDON, March 24.—()— British statesmen were represented tonight as believing there is only the faintest hope of breaking the European arms deadlock, They expect France to show no signs of relaxing her demands for security when she replies to oral inquiries from Great Britain for an amplification of the French disarmament note last week. This anticipation cast gloom over Whitehall, and British official quarters said they could see no reason for calling a conference outside Geneva of principal powers in an effort to save the disarmament cause, American participation in such a meeting has been suggested but the British view is that continuation of bilateral negotiations holds the only prospect—though very faint—of solving the knotty problem. Exchanges between ambassadors began last week regarding the French communication but, said official circles, they have so far been “inconclusive.” S

SHANGHAI, Sunday, March 25 (P)—C. C. Julian, former Oklahoma oil operator, wanted there on mail fraud charges, died suddenly here today. Physicians said death was caused by poison and they believed he had committed suicide. They said he took poison at 1 a.m. and died from its effects five hours later. A girl associate, whose identity was not established, also attempted to kill herself, they said. She is still alive. The girl was said to be of Spanish nationality and it was understood that she had resided in recent weeks at the same obscure hotel where Julian stayed. She was known as his secretary.

PORT SAID, Egypt, March 24.—(4)—Samuel Insull had the port authorities of this gateway to the Suez canal baffled tonight. Having strained their eyes and ears for days, awaiting the arrival here of the Maiotis, the fugitive American’s floating haven, officials said they couldn't figure out the situation. It was supposed that Insull’s little vessel was cruising outside of the regular shipping lanes, awaiting the advice of his agents on the best possible country to use as a refuge. The report at Athens, relayed here, that the Maiotis might be off the island of Rhodes, about 250 miles from the Greek capital, seemed plausible but officials wondered what developments had intervened to halt his supposed original plans to go through the canal. It was just a week ago today that the wheezy freighter steamed out of Piraeus, Greece, bound for an unknown destination.

SHANGHAI, March 25 (Sunday) (UP)—Courtney Charles Julian, one of the most spectacular figures in the history of oil, was found dead today—a suicide by poison—in the Astor hotel here. Julian's end came after he had fallen from great riches massed in oil promotion to poverty and virtual exile in Shanghai. He committed suicide as part of a pact with a Spanish girl who also drank poison but who is expected to recover, authorities indicated today after an investigation. Friends said the promoter was down to his last cent. “Well, I've spent my last dollar,” they quoted him as saying when they last saw him. Julian’s body was discovered in his room when a hotel attache investigated groans heard by adjoining guests. By The Associated Press Courthouse, Lima, O., March 24—The old Dillinger gang was formally dissolved late today when two of its members were sentenced to die in the electric chair and a third was condemned to life imprisonment. Harry Pierpont, brazen, defiant, and Charles Makley, rotund, slow moving, will pay with their lives in the Ohio state penitentiary on Friday, July 13, for the murder of Sheriff Jess L. Sarber last October, when John Dillinger was “sprung” from the county jail by his confederates. Sleepy-eyed Russell Clark alone was given quarter by Allen county juries. For his part in the jail break here he drew a verdict of guilty with mercy, obligating the court to pronounce sentence of life imprisonment. 1934-07-19.text: Quebec, Que., July 19 (UP)—Ramsay MacDonald, prime minister of Great Britain, arrived today on board the S. S. Duchess of Athol. Accompanied by his daughter, Ishbel, the head of Great Britain’s government will spend three months in Canada recuperating from an eye ailment. MacDonald was expected to stay on board until a few minutes before the Athol was scheduled to sail up the St. Lawrence River towards Montreal. He will take a train for Levis, Que., immediately across the river from the ancient capital, for Digby, N. S., and will spend at least a month of his vacation there.

BERLIN, July 19—(P)—Unprecedented hot weather and the absence of many high officials from the capital on their vacation, combined today to make a quiet political situation in Germany, although their absence did not stem a flood of rumors, all of which were officially denied. Rumors have been many and varied, but the political life of the capital was otherwise quiet. When told of a report from abroad that Chancellor Hitler was a virtual prisoner of the German army, an official said: "If that’s true, Hitler is a strange prisoner." The reference was to the fact that yesterday the chancellor went to the Zoosen drill field where he took the salute of the Knight cavalry regiment in the presence of Werner Von Blomberg, minister of war. CAIRO, Egypt, July 19.— Stretched on a special bed installed on an amphibian airplane, Mrs. Martin Johnson, ill, arrived here today with her husband, after twenty months of film-shooting big game in the interior of Africa. Mr. and Mrs. Johnson intended to remain in Cairo a week, then to fly to London, and embark for the United States where Mrs. Johnson will undergo an operation. She said that the operation was not of an urgent character but that her disability had sometimes rendered her useless on the expedition, particularly during the latter stages of the journey when she had to spend much of her time lying down in the plane.

WASHINGTON, July 19 (UP).— Ten brown and yellow army bombing planes, biggest aerial death-dealing machines in the United States, reared away from Bolling field today for a reconnoitering flight to Alaska. The great ships circled the city, dipped over the capitol dome, and cut a bee-line for Dayton, O., and a brief stop for gasoline. Then they will head north, spend the night at Minneapolis and head across Canada for Fairbanks, Alaska, their final destination. About 2000 citizens waved the ships away. HARTSDALE, N. Y., July 19 (AP) — Little Bobby Connor gained steadily in strength today, but left a question as to his disappearance and recovery—lost, strayed or stolen? Frank Fay, chief of the department of justice agents who investigated the case, left town, agreeing with Chief Philip J. McQuilland of Greenburgh police that the boy had been lost and not kidnapped. Chief McQuilland continued his investigation, however, and District Attorney Frank H. Coyne said: "I can not accept the theory that the child wandered away. On the other hand I have nothing to disprove it. However, I do not consider the case closed." The 21 months old baby, who was found in the woods near his home Tuesday after being missing five days, was transferred from the Grasslands to the White Plains hospital yesterday, his family wishing him to be in a private institution.

ABOARD CRUISER NEW ORLEANS, Accompanying President Roosevelt, July 19 (#)—Free from telephone rings and official callers, President Roosevelt is making real progress in a study of Hawaiian affairs as the cruiser Houston cuts steadily for the far-distant American outpost of Honolulu. A trunk full of documents and data on the islands is getting a good share of the president's attention. Mr. Roosevelt also is attending to current affairs through wireless communication with the capitol, but official business has been held to a minimum. The Houston, traveling in the Great Circle course, is scheduled to arrive off Hawaii early Tuesday. Tactical maneuvers in squally seas engaged the Houston and its convoy, the New Orleans, yesterday.

HARTSDALE, N. Y., July 18. (AP)—Mysterious angles in the disappearance of little Bobby Connor, emaciated and seriously ill after having been missing five days, were studied tonight by officials still trying to determine if he had been kidnapped. The 21-month-old baby, found half-starved in the woods yesterday afternoon, showed steady progress at Grasslands Hospital but physicians emphasized his condition remained serious. Although investigators differed sharply on whether Bobby had wandered away and had lain hidden in a bramble thicket since Thursday night, Captain Philip J. McQuillan of the Greenburgh police pressed an inquiry into every phase of the case. Federal agents were officially reported to have withdrawn. By The Associated Press Geneva, Dec. 8—Revision of post-war treaties emerged today as the broad, danger-fraught question facing Europe's statesmen, and France took her place squarely beside the Little Entente for preservation of the territorial status quo. Italy, meanwhile, aligned herself with her friend and ally, Hungary, in advocating equitable revision of the peace treaty as the best means of conserving the peace of Europe. As four of Europe’s big powers—England, France, Italy and Russia—joined to urge that the Yugoslav-Hungarian friction growing out of the assassination of King Alexander of Yugoslavia at Marseille October 9 be not allowed to disturb peace, the problem of the peace treaties lifted its threatening head behind that Central European crisis. Foreign Minister Pierre Laval, speaking for France, said dramatically "France stands beside Yugoslavia" in this “grave conflict,”

NEW YORK, Dec. 3 (A)—In New York City is a 7-year-old Albert Einstein, who is just about the smartest man in the world, the Educational Clinic announced today. - Einstein's intelligence quotient is 205; the child's is 196. The intelligence quotient of Charles Darwin, creator of the celebrated theory of evolution, was 186. Identity of the child was withheld for his own good. He was taken to the clinic, which is a part of New York University, by his mother. She was worried because he was bored by subjects taught in his grammar school, subjects he had mastered soon after leaving the cradle. Dr. Samuel B. Heckman, director of the clinic, professed himself to be amazed. The lad knew his name, address, and the addresses and telephone numbers of a dozen relatives when he was 2 years old. St. Paul, Dec. 8. —- (4?) —- Representatives from eight Midwest states were told today by Congressman Thomas R. Amlie, of Wisconsin, that the political swing of the nation had gone further to the left than the national administration. "The people in the November election," Congressman Amlie said, "demonstrated they are willing to go even further than are their leaders. The shift has been to the left of President Roosevelt." Amlie was one of the principal speakers at the two-day conference of ultra-liberal leaders to discuss plans for a third party movement, possibly in 1936, should President Roosevelt in their opinion, lean too far to the right. The conference was called, Amlie told the meeting, because the ultra-progressives saw in Minnesota's farmer-labor party, a "third party we believe will become a national party." FREEMAN, IL, Dec. 8.—Three members of the crew of a Burlington south-bound freight train were killed tonight when the train crashed into a string of loaded coal cars on a siding here. The dead were Calvin Lewis, engineer; Homer Goodman, fireman; and E.F. F. Elliston, head brakeman, all of Centralia.

By the Associated Press, Statesmen at Geneva Saturday sought to hush talk of war in Europe as the League of Nations council adjourned to Monday its consideration of Yugoslavia's charge that Hungary sheltered terrorists who assassinated her king, Alexander. The Balkans, however, were not the only concerns of peace proponents. Paraguay pushed to Bolivia's very doors in the Chaco war, Ethiopia replied vigorously to Italy's charge that Ethiopians attacked an Italian outpost, and London reported the fate of naval limitation parleys solely up to Japan. The United States watched the Balkan situation, but the State Department said it will keep hands off. Alignment of the Powers, GENEVA. (Copyright by US-INS). Washington, Dec. 8.—(AP)—A decision to increase the army’s air fleet by only 800 planes during 1935, instead of by 500 or more as recommended by the general staff, was attributed today by officials to higher prices caused in part by the administration’s recovery program. Determined to buy as many as possible, however, the army today awarded a contract to the Consolidated Aircraft Corporation of Buffalo, N. Y., for 60 two-seater pursuit planes at a cost of $1,996,700. Those bids and others for 250 more planes to cost roughly $8,000,000 have furnished the service proof that planes cost more than in the past. For Navy Meanwhile the navy reported it is seeking money to add 273 airplanes to its sky forces in the next fiscal year.

1934-07-08.text: Elizabeth Parley, daughter of the Postmaster-General, will christen the $4,000,000 destroyer “Aylwin” at its launching Tuesday, in Philadelphia. The craft is the first of four to be built at Philadelphia Navy Yard under the London Naval Treaty.

The chancellor set an example of outward calmness for the German people by leaving Berlin and going to his retreat in the Bavarian Alps, at least for the weekend. Sub-leaders, who helped Hitler break up revolt with firing squads a week ago today, also were reported resting. AMSTERDAM, Holland, July 7 — Troops with bristling bayonets and military tanks which crushed and swept aside the street barricades of rioting communists and unemployed persons tonight had restored quiet to Amsterdam after disorders in which at least one more was killed. The victim was an old woman. Because of deafness she did not hear a command to citizens to remain in houses, and two bullets struck her in the back as she tried to cross a street. Authorities, after a confusion of reports coming out of the three days of rioting, tonight said that the total killed is six. About sixty were injured. It was pointed out, however, that some casualties may not have been reported. The rioters in many instances cared for their own injured, and possibly for some dead. NICE, France. July 7—(#)— United States sailors and marines strolled along the Riviera tonight under a pledge to “be good” and not repeat the outbreak of last night in which 28 persons were injured. To make certain the promise was not broken a double shore patrol was on duty from the two American battleships, the Arkansas and Wyoming, which lay in Ville Franche harbor. The shore leave for small groups was a reversal of the first policy following the fight. After the sailors injured and arrested in last night's fight had been turned over to naval authorities, all shore leave was cancelled. This afternoon, however, naval and police authorities met with the American consul here and all decided that it would be unfair to punish the crews for the misdeeds of their comrades. AMSTERDAM, July 7. (P)— Six persons were killed today and scores wounded in day-long battling between police and unemployed while army tanks crushed down barricades and gunfire swept the streets of Amsterdam. One of the victims was an old woman who attempted to cross a street. Deaf, she did not hear the command to citizens to remain behind locked doors. She got two bullets in the back. The rioting began three days ago, growing out of protests over a cut in the municipal dole. Confined at first to the Jordaan workers’ district, the disorders spread today to sixteen other areas of the city. Incensed Dutchmen, entrenched behind barricades, withstood a morning onslaught of police and troops until tanks and armored cars went into action, crushing down obstructions. United Press European News Manager (Copyright 1934 by United Press) BERLIN, July 7.—U.)—Chancellor Adolf Hitler has emerged unscathed and perhaps strengthened from the first grave crisis of his Nazi regime. He showed the mailed fist and subdued the opposition within his party. His millions of supporters, still the dominant element in Germany, have been impressed by his show of strength. The mass of the people will continue to regard him as the country’s savior. Other elements, opposed to Hitler and all his works, have been equally impressed, but for different reasons. The lesson has been brought home to them that Hitler has the power and the will, if needed, to introduce the reign of terror and bloodshed characteristic of dictatorships. Paris, July 7.—The National Confederation of War Veterans, whose meeting here may have a serious effect upon the future of the Doumergue government, tonight condemned the government's action in reducing pensions of veterans. The issue was the first of several effective government policies to come before the two-day convention of the representatives of 3,500,000 veterans, and the anti-government vote was overwhelming. Andre Rivollet, minister of pensions, who is secretary-general of one of the groups in the confederation, defended the government's cause and left the hall after the vote. Possibility that Rivollet will resign from the government has been discussed by politicians looking forward to the veterans’ gathering. There is a strong movement afoot, however, to postpone action on the government's other policies until October. Fears of possible clashes in connection with the veterans’

McALESTER, Okla., July 8 (OP).— Three state penitentiary prisoners, one serving a life term for murder, overpowered and bound a guard today and escaped with his car while he was taking them to the sub-prison at Stringtown. A posse of guards and officers with bloodhounds set out in pursuit. William McElhaney, the guard, reported he was disarmed, overpowered, tied to a tree and abandoned. Officials said the trio had been in the prison several years. Recently they had been at work in the prison hospital and were well disciplined.

They were greeted at the station by Sir John Simon, the British foreign secretary. Sir Robert Vansittart, permanent foreign under secretary, and members of the French embassy staff. More than 3,000,000 bushels will be imported this year, this source disclosed, almost entirely for the purpose of feeding an increased Russian military establishment. Despite lack of official statistics from the Soviet Union, it was learned that imports at Vladivostok, which once was an important Russian terminal for Russian wheat exports, gradually have been increasing during the last six years. It was learned that large amounts of wheat were purchased last month from Argentina and Australia. Big Exporter, Too. London, July 9.—(#)—Louis Barthou, French foreign minister, came to Downing street today to ask assurances that Great Britain will once more team with the French in the event of a war with Germany. By FREDERICK OECHSNER (United Press staff Correspondent.) BERLIN, July 9 (UP) — Germany seemed back on a normal Third Reich footing today after a week of crisis and a Sunday marked by a Nazi appeal for European peace and a pronouncement that the Roman Catholic Church would guard its right to worship against Nazi attacks. Rudolph Hess, Chancellor Adolf Hitler's deputy in the Nazi Party, was selected by his chief to make the world peace plea, which included also a warning, patently intended to rouse German patriotism, that Germany would withstand any attack from abroad. Cardinal Faulhaber, head of the Catholic Church in Germany, made the pronouncement regarding religion to 50,000 persons massed at Bamberg. PARIS, July 9—The international spy ring case involving Mr. and Mrs. Robert G. Switz of New York was revived today when Andre Benon, examining magistrate, issued seven new warrants of arrest, including one for an American, Mrs. Pauline Jacobson Levine, 32. The six other warrants were for French suspects. Mrs. Levine was sought as a suspected intermediary between the naturalized Canadian, Benjamin Berkowitz, alleged ring leader, and lesser spies. Police did not know Mrs. Levine's present whereabouts although they traced her from hotel to hotel.

AMSTERDAM, July 28.—-(*)— Bullets spattered in the streets of Amsterdam again tonight as soldiers and police made a determined effort to suppress a new riot of communists and unemployed persons. Many were injured as officers charged on two street barricades in the Wittenburg district, the poorest section of the city. From the housetops many of the rioters stoned the police and soldiers, and officers replied with several volleys of rifle fire. In the Jordaan section of the city, where two bridges were burned last week, military engineers forestalled an effort of a mob of about 200 to burn a church. No disorders were reported in other sections of Holland, but in several communities soldiers were in readiness for eventualities. PARIS, July 6—The massed forces of thousands of police managed to forestall the expected “bloody Sunday” today as they formed a buffer between 20,000 sweltering nationalistic Croix De Feu veterans and 30,000 noisy Leftists. Under a blazing sun police, street helmeted mobile guards and mounted republican guards encircled both the veterans, parading to the tomb of the unknown soldier, and the “common front” demonstration in Vincennes Wood of Socialists and Communists, who loudly berated what they called the “Fascism” of the Doumergue government. Communists stoned a police car and replaced the tricolor on motor buses with red flags, but police generally were pleased with the comparative peace of the day. 1934-07-05.text: LONDON, July 4.—Great Britain and Germany avoided a trade war for at least six months today by signing an agreement providing for the payment of interest on Dawes and Young loan bonds held by British subjects. The agreement extends six months from July 1, the day the moratorium on all foreign obligations became effective. Other long and medium term obligations held in Great Britain, which are mostly commercial, will not be serviced during the moratorium, under the terms of the agreement. Germany agreed to deposit British currency in the Bank of England for payment of all coupons from Dawes and Young loan bonds. In return, Britain will not apply the new clearing house law, under which the government would have been able to seize a portion of German commercial bonds.

RALEIGH, July 4. (AP)— France's hope of inducing Great Britain to promise quick armed aid in case of foreign attacks was seriously shaken today by purported revelations in The Daily Herald of a full-fledged Anglo-French military alliance being prepared by the British cabinet. French officials said the British attitude against anything remotely approaching a military alliance is so well known that the Herald's article is likely to increase British objections to any promise even of the limited nature which France is seeking.

PARIS, July 5 (UP)--All the world today mourned the passing of Marie Curie, co-discoverer of radium, one of the greatest of modern scientists, and one of the greatest women of all time. While her body was being brought back to Paris from the Savoy Alps where she died yesterday, a movement was under way to bury her and her husband in the Pantheon which is to France what Westminster Abbey is to England. Physicians said that the woman whose discoveries saved untold lives and allayed the sufferings of thousands, died a martyr for science. The direct cause of death was a lung infection, but contributing was physical fatigue. For months she had worked 10 and 12 hours a day in her laboratory. Mme. Curie will be buried first beside the simple grave of her husband, Pierre Curie, in a suburban cemetery. Curie died in 1906. If later both bodies are transferred to the Pantheon it will be the greates

Paris—(—The body of Mme. Curie, co-discoverer of radium, was brought to Paris last night in compliance with her wish for a private funeral of the utmost simplicity, devoid of all display. — Only members of the family, laboratory associates and a few scientific friends will attend the burial. She will be placed in a grave beside her husband. Mme. Curie’s two daughters and a son-in-law arrived in an escorting car following an automobile that left Sallanches at dawn to bring the body to Paris avoiding public demonstrations along the rail route or upon arrival in the capital. The Paris municipal council was considering naming a public square after the famous woman scientist. The street on which she lived already has been named Rue Pierre Curie, in honor of her husband, and her house was made number one.

Hutchison, author and publicist who was an official of a British commission in upper Silesia in 1931 and who has crowded plenty of excitement into his 43 years, stuck by his guns, however, but didn’t visit the embassy. CHURCHILL DOWNS, LOUISVILLE, Ky., May 5—(AP)—Cavalcade, the mighty record-breaking colt bred in old England but foaled in America, broke the heart of two renowned queens of the turf today and raced to sensational victory in the sixtieth Kentucky Derby. Heavily backed to win, at short odds of 3 to 2, Cavalcade justified the confidence in his speed and thrilled a tremendous crowd with a glittering stretch drive that easily beat off his gallant eastern rival, Discovery, and left the two fleet fillies, Mata Hari and Bazaar, struggling in the rear. Owned by Mrs. Isabel Dodge Sloane, New York and Florida sportswoman, who was on hand to see her colors triumph, Cavalcade's victory was worth $28,175 net to the owner and gave eastern turf followers their first smashing thrill since Twenty Grand came home in record time three years ago. Ibn Saud, ruler of Saudi Arabia, was reported in control of Hodetdah, one of Yemen’s better known Red Sea ports, and pushing toward Sana, the capital of his conquered foe, the Imam of Jemen. NEW YORK, May 5 (#).—President Roosevelt sat almost motionless today in the old-fashioned "meeting house" of the Presbyterians at Fifth Avenue and 55th Street as the funeral service was read for his old friend and advisor, William Woodin. With his hands clasped in his lap, the president did not lift his eyes once from the long blanket of yellow jonquils which shrouded the coffin of his former secretary of the treasury. He sat with his shoulders bowed, a look of deep sorrow upon his face, throughout the 17-minute service. After the Apostle’s Creed was recited, he joined in the Lord's Prayer. Mrs. Roosevelt put her hand upon his sleeve as the Rev. Dr. Robert W. 1934-12-13.text: (Associated Press) Boston, Dec. 12.--Police stood guard over every Boston theatre tonight and many others throughout New England while every energy was being directed toward apprehension of terrorists who early in the day exploded bombs in four motion picture places. No one was injured in the explosions, which occurred in two Boston theatres, a Lynn theatre and a theatre in Pawtucket, R. I., causing thousands of dollars damage. Police were satisfied a carefully laid plot was behind the bombings, but they could find no connection between the bombings and a fire in a Somerville theatre. They attributed the fire to faulty wiring. No Reward Is Offered The bombings brought an appeal from Governor Joseph B. Liverpool, England, Dec. 12. —(—The floor of a concert hall where nearly 500 parents and children were gathered at the St. Clements school here collapsed with a roar tonight, injuring some 300 of them, many seriously. Although it was feared some of the injured may die, crushed in a mass of wreckage and humanity in a 14-foot drop to the floor below, the full check of casualties and the extent of injuries had not been determined. Firemen and police rushed to the scene of the tragedy and began hacking through beams and sagging flooring to find persons possibly imprisoned below. The room was packed solidly with people, many parents having come to attend the concert celebrating the end of the school term. SOUTH SHIELDS, Eng., Dec. 13 ()—John George Hunter, aged 10, played with a safety razor blade in school today. He swallowed it. John George told his teacher, who sent him home with a companion. On the way, the boy confided in a policeman, who hurried the lad to the infirmary. An x-ray revealed the blade in John George's tummy. While doctors made careful preparations for a difficult operation, John George became sick at his stomach. Up came the blade. The doctors and nurses said they were amazed.

HORNEPAYNE, Ont., Dec. 13 | (P--The unwelcome possibility of spending Christmas in Hornepayne instead of London faced 13 travelers today. They were in quarantine in a railway passenger car because a man who occupied it for half an hour had smallpox. Twenty-six passengers originally were hastening eastward to board steamers for England to spend the holidays. A man was taken aboard at Kowash, Ont., and 30 minutes later it was discovered he had smallpox. The car was switched to a siding and a quarantine placed on it. Thirteen passengers and a news agent were allowed to leave when they showed they had been vaccinated within the last seven years and expressed willingness to submit to a new vaccination. London, Dec. 12.— (7) —Great Britain today decided it was no use to continue further tri-power naval talks going on here for months. The United States agreed. Adjournment before Saturday was expected. Thereby the big question as to whether there shall be any limits set on navies in the future was put squarely up to Japan. Unless Tokyo surrenders her demand for full naval parity, instead of the short end of the famed 5-5.5% ratio assigned her under the 1922 Washington treaty, American quarters consider it highly doubtful that the conversations can be fruitfully resumed.

Liverpool, Eng., Dec. 13.—The floor of a school concert hall collapsed Wednesday night under the weight of hundreds of children and their parents, resulting in injuries to 150 persons. Thirty-six were taken to hospitals. Several may die. More than 100 were hurt badly enough to require medical treatment before returning to their homes. They had been precipitated in a mass of tumbling furniture and sudden darkness from the second to the first floor of the St. Clement’s school building. The disaster failed to reach larger proportions because of the presence of mind of the school’s caretaker who ran to the basement and turned off the illuminating gas supply, eliminating danger of fire and explosion. SHANGHAI, Dec. 13 — (INS)—The brutal murder of Mr. and Mrs. John C. Stam of Paterson, N. J., members of the China Inland Mission, by Chinese communist bandits was revealed today when their bodies were found by the roadside a few miles from the scene of their kidnapping. The fate of their infant daughter, Helen, seized with them at China Inland Mission headquarters at Tsingteh, southern Anhwei province, was not known. The bodies, apparently flung into a ditch alongside the highway leading out of Tsingteh, were found by members of a searching party who had scoured the region since the missionary family was seized early this week. Tsingteh has long been one of the strongholds of the communist rebel hordes which the Nanking government for years has been attempting to obliterate. Protest Is Filed. 1934-07-15.text: | BERLIN, July 14 (UP)—Germany offered to make arrangements with the United States today to pay interest on German bonds held in the United States, despite the moratorium which has been declared. The arrangement would be similar to that made with Britain and Holland, through a banking agreement under which the central banks of the countries concerned would aid in carrying the necessary exchange transfers. Germany notified the United States, through Ambassador William E. Dodd, that she had no intention of discriminating against this country in the transfer of services on loans. The assurance eased a situation which had caused Dodd to make representations, after Britain had threatened a drastic financial and trade war and had been satisfied with a separate agreement of payment. Germany advised Mr. Dodd that transfer of interests on foreign loans is impossible at present because of the fore

EDINBURGH, Scotland, July 14. (UP)—A beer bottle was thrown at King George and Queen Mary while they were motoring through the mining village of Harthill today, en route back to Holyrood Palace from the races at Hamilton Park. The chauffeur of the car stepped on the accelerator and sped away in fear that further violence might be attempted. A physical attack on the King and Queen is unprecedented in modern Britain and the incident caused the greatest excitement. The bottle missed the royal car. Police guarding the royal route immediately pounced on the man who threw it and arrested him. The entire population of Harthill was packed in the streets to watch their Majesties return from the races to the ancient Holyrood Palace, where they have been in residence for the past week. Cheers were raised as the royal automobile approached. When it drew abreast of a crowd of miners—most of them unem

BERLIN, July 14.—The Nazi press poured forth to the German public today its praise of Adolf Hitler for his Reichstag speech and gave assurances of world approval. His address justifying the violent deaths of 77 persons in the "Roehm revolt" was lauded to the skies. The identity of the dead, however, unrevealed by Hitler, remained unpublished by the press, and a government spokesman said the official list will never see the light of day. It was said that had Hitler chosen to have it published he would have announced the names himself. Special correspondents of German papers in New York, London, Paris, Warsaw, Rome and other world cities notified their newspapers in long dispatches that all the world is at least impressed and in most cases approves of the Chancellor's words. "The fuehrer’s speech was received by all listeners throughout the world as the most honest confession of a man who

Vienna, July 15.—Sunday)—(P)—A powerful blast of dynamite at midnight wrecked an electric plant at Opponitz, in Lower Austria, and for an hour stopped every street car in Vienna. Another dynamite charge snapped a power line between the plant and Vienna, and for a time service of the Austrian radio was interrupted. Authorities attributed the blasts to Nazis, and immediately started an energetic investigation to carry out Chancellor Dollfuss's demand for the repression of bombings. Several sections of Vienna were plunged into darkness by the wrecking of the power plant.

Berlin, July 14.— (4) — Germany opened the way to the United States today to effect a settlement under which interest may be paid on the Dawes and Young loans, despite the reich moratorium. Replying officially to Ambassador William E. Dodd in response to the American note of June 27, the government stated it has not the slightest intention of discriminating against the United States in the matter of debt transfers. The German government said it was “ready to negotiate with the American government as with the governments of other countries relative to ways and means of making possible the servicing of the Dawes and Young loans.” The German reply was accompanied by a reminder that there seems to be no hurry about setting up negotiations similar to those conducted with Great Britain in London recently which resulted in a German agreement to pay English bondholders. It was pointed out that t

By The Associated Press San Francisco, July 14—A paralyzing general strike, affecting intimately the one million residents of San Francisco and Oakland, was ordered by union labor tonight to begin Monday. Representatives of 105,000 workers voted the walkout in a desperate maneuver to help Pacific coast longshoremen and marine workers, locked deeply in battle with employers. Howling down "conservative" elements in a zero hour meeting of a huge general strike committee representing the 65,000 union men of San Francisco, the rank and file voted overwhelmingly for the walkout. Unions which already had voted to strike were instructed to walk out Monday. Those not having balloted on the matter were ordered to take strike votes immediately. Fired To Action Like a flash the vote fired Transbay union elements into action. The Alameda County (Oakland) building trades council voted a simultaneous s

By The Associated Press Hartsdale, N. Y., July 14.—The father of the missing Bobby Connor, weary after a 48-hour fruitless search, expressed the belief tonight that his curly-headed 21-months-old baby had been kidnapped. "I have no money to pay a ransom, but I will do anything to get him back," said Charles A. Connor as he waited at home for word from federal and state officers. "I feel certain my baby is alive and well," he added. Although lacking tangible evidence that the child had been abducted, officers pressed their search for an eccentric peddler who visited the neighborhood shortly before Bobby disappeared Thursday evening. They wanted to learn whether he had seen the child in the vicinity. Some of the authorities were checking the possibility the baby might have been struck by a motorist and then carried away to avoid an inquiry.

(Copyright, 1934, By The Associated Press.) LOS ANGELES, July 14.—(AP)— Wandering in a dazed condition, June DeLong, 24-year-old blonde star witness for the state in the "Hollywood morals" case, so-called, was found on a street here tonight, eight hours after she disappeared from her apartment, leaving a note declaring her intention to commit suicide. She said the reason she escaped from under guard was that "Gloria was in trouble and I felt so sorry for her." Gloria is Gloria Marsh, young movie extra player, who with Dave Allen, former head of the Central Casting bureau, is on trial on charges of participating in an immoral party with Miss DeLong in the latter’s apartment last April. Miss DeLong was seen stumbling along the street by Nellise Child, mystery novelist and playwright, who picked her up and took her to her husband's place of business nearby. There the husband, Frank Gerard,

1934-04-30.text: LONDON, April 30—(1Py Japan has promised to maintain the open door in China and to continue observance of the nine-power treaty, Sir John Simeon, foreign secretary, informed the House of Commons today. The assurance was given by Hiroda Japanese foreign minister, to Sir Francis Lindley, British ambassador at Tokio, Sir John said. The announcement was received with intense interest by the House, which had gathered to hear Sir John’s promised statement on Japan's declarations of policy in the Far East, a source of world agitation. The nine-power treaty, signed at Washington in 1922, bound the signatories to “respect the sovereignty, independence and territorial and administrative integrity of China, and to refrain from taking advantage of conditions in China in order to sell special rights or privileges which would abridge the rights of subjects or citizens of friendly states. It was signed

Leigh, England, April 30, (U.P) Five men were killed today by an explosion at Bickershaw coal pit No. 3, caused by ignition of a gas pocket. Three hundred men were in the mine, but the others all escaped.

LONDON, April 30..(7) — Sir John Simon, foreign secretary, told the House of Commons today that Japan has fully accepted the policy of the “open door” for all nations in China. He told his hearers Japan has informed the British government it has no intention of interfering with “the common rights” of other powers in China and has reaffirmed its policy of the maintenance of the open door. He said Japan had given assurance that she will observe the nine-power treaty. WASHINGTON, April 30—Some doubt existed in state department circles today whether Secretary of State Cordell Hull would follow the lead of Sir John Simon, British foreign secretary, in virtually declaring the Japanese attempt to create a Monroe Doctrine for Asia a closed incident. Hull indicated there would be some clarification today of the American attitude toward the Far Eastern situation, but declined to say whether this would take the form of an official statement, or a “background” conference with newspapermen at which he would outline the American viewpoint.

| VIENNA, April 30—(UP)—Austria’s new constitution, converting the republic into a fascist state on Italian lines, was published today as parliament met to approve it and sign the death warrant of parliamentary government. The constitution means that Austria will adopt the guild system of government with all categories of national life represented in two chambers with sharply restricted powers, under a government enjoying strong powers. Austria becomes officially “a Christian German federal state.” The national colors will be red, white and red in stripes, with the coat of arms of the double-headed eagle of the old monarchy superimposed. The constitution was contained in one of 239 emergency decrees issued by the government since parliament was suspended March 4, 1933. Today's session was held merely so that the parliament could formally approve the decrees.

ISTANBUL, Turkey, April 30 — (AP)—Absolute quiet was ordered today for Zaro Agha, who claims to be the oldest person in the world. The Turk, who says he is 164, is in the National Children's Hospital, to which he was taken Saturday suffering from Bright's disease. Doctors said his condition was grave. All visitors—save for the patient's 70-year old grandson —

PARIS, April 30.—(UP)—Serious rioting signaled today the approach of May Day. The cabinet called Minister of War Philippe Petain into council to plan defense of government buildings. Enraged at the narrow defeat by a political maneuver, of a candidate representing the merged left wing parties including socialists and communists, mobs held control of the town of Mantes for five hours until police reinforcements arrived from Paris, 25 miles away. Seventeen thousand police were ordered to constant duty here in preparation for mass demonstrations by socialists and communists. In the suburbs, unobtrusively crowded into barracks, were mobile guards in thousands, ready to speed to the center of the capital if the May Day demonstrators attempted to move or leave government buildings.

PARIS, April 20 (A%--France’s fighting little premier, Gaston Doumergue, whose famous smile hides a stern will, today boldly took up the challenge of a May Day general strike. The former president ordered one of the biggest police mobilizations, backed by the army, since the World War to crush any movement leading to civil war. Rebellion, he has already warned, holds the danger of “foreign invasion.” Capital Under Guard Final plans to throw the tightest possible guard around Paris, with the mobilization of every available man, were drawn today at a conference held with public order officials by Albert Garraut, minister of the interior. Army garrisons in the capital, at Versailles and elsewhere will be held in readiness to support police if necessary. In Paris alone there are 18,000 police, 10,000 mobile guards -- the men who did much shooting and fighting in the February riots--and 1,000

1934-10-29.text: LYMPHE AIRDROME, ENG. OCT. 29. (AP)—Colonel James C. Fitzmaurice returned here today three hours after he had taken off in an attempt to establish a new speed record to Australia. A piece of the shield on the undercarriage of his plane had fallen off. Fitzmaurice said he was well beyond Brussels when the mishap occurred.

LONDON (UP)— Smiling little King Prajadhipok of Siam may win the day against the government whose efforts to curb his royal authority caused him to offer to abdicate, it was indicated Monday. The king’s private secretary said the government at Bangkok had requested him to reconsider his decision to abdicate. He added that the king’s decision was not final. Discussions were being held unofficially, he said, regarding a possible readjustment of the governmental position. Regarding reports that the army was determined to support King Prajadhipok and had dispatched an emissary from Bangkok to persuade him not to abdicate, the secretary said no request to withdraw his abdication offer had been received “independently” from the army. The entrance of Knowle Park, the estate at Cranleigh, Surrey, at which the king is staying, was heavily guarded by police. They even patrolled the lanes near the

LONDON, Oct. 20.—(AP)—The delegations of the three big naval powers—the United States, Great Britain and Japan—reached a crossroads in their pathway toward naval agreement when the British and Americans today termed the Japanese proposals for a new treaty based on the principle of equality unacceptable and put the next move up to Japan. Authoritative spokesmen said the situation was as follows: One road leads to the continuance of the Washington treaty and the continuance of the principle of naval armaments begun by that treaty; The other road leads to the termination of that treaty and a race for naval armaments. Stand Hinges Upon Japanese In American quarters, a belief was expressed that unless the Japanese receded from their position.
